title: Houthis ramp up missile attacks on Riyadh as Saudi-backed war in Yemen widens
body: Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis have stepped up their deadly campaign of strikes on Saudi Arabia's capital, Riyadh, where booms were heard on Thursday, flights were disrupted, and some office staff were told to work from home.The Houthis said they had fired a ballistic missile at Riyadh airport and repeated a threat to force Saudi airspace to close after the kingdom gave support to the forces of Yemen's internationally recognized government in a reignited civil war.The conflict, now an overspill of the US-Iran war, has added new chaos to a region already aflame, and threatens to draw other states into grueling mountain fighting - with Syria now considering deploying troops to assist Saudi Arabia.The kingdom has pushed for support from allied nations, including Turkey and Pakistan, even if only in a logistical or defensive capacity, as it tries to reverse Houthi gains in southwest Yemen, by the southern entrance to the Red Sea.Those requests have taken on more urgency since Saudi authorities said on Wednesday that three people had been killed this week in strikes on Riyadh airport and Abha airport in the southwest.Civil war reignited by conflict with IranThe flight tracker FlightRadar24 indicated numerous delayed arrivals and departures at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on Thursday.Several multinational firms based in Riyadh's King Abdullah Financial District (KAFD) told staff to work from home after Thursday morning's loud booms, five people familiar with the matter said, including some affected staff.The Saudi government did not respond to a request for comment, and KAFD was not immediately available for comment.Some diplomats said they had received warnings, and some schools in Riyadh told parents there were orders to shelter in place, though authorities did not issue a public alert. Reuters could not identify the source of the booms.According to the Saudi Civil Defense Directorate, shrapnel fallout from a missile interception caused damage to a children's nursery and a medical clinic in Riyadh.Yemen's long-running civil war, which paused with a ceasefire in 2022, has erupted again in recent weeks with the Houthis seizing stretches of the Red Sea coast last month, including along the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait.The Houthis, who control many of Yemen's most populous areas, including the capital Sanaa, have said they were responding to attacks from the Saudi-backed government, which the government denies.Their threats to shipping along a waterway that has become ever more critical for Gulf oil exports since Iran's attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, and their attacks on Saudi cities and infrastructure, have drawn the kingdom back in.This week, Saudi-backed forces launched a counterattack, taking back areas around the strait.However, in a war with several frontlines, the Houthis have made gains of their own, surrounding Yemen's third-largest city, Taiz, by taking territory along its main mountain road to Aden.The fighting, which pits the Houthis against a coalition of Saudi-backed forces under the internationally recognized government, has led to a humanitarian crisis in the poorest Arab state, displacing 200,000 people since the conflict resumed.Syrian aid might be purely defensive, officials sayOne US and one Syrian defense official said Syria was carefully considering options for military support, including defensive aid to protect Saudi Arabia from attacks, or an offensive deployment to help take the fight to the Houthis.In response to a request for comment to the Syrian foreign ministry, a diplomat said Syria stood firmly with Saudi Arabia but that its focus was on domestic priorities such as recovery from its own civil war.Saudi Arabia this summer agreed to the Mecca Pact with Turkey and Pakistan, committing all three to come to each other's defense, though Ankara has yet to ratify the treaty.NATO-member Turkey said on Wednesday it was sending mainly defensive and technical support to the kingdom to help in the fight against the Houthis. A Turkish official said this was expected to take the form of military equipment, intelligence sharing and weapons systems.Turkey, a close ally of Syria's government and a supporter of its forces while they were still rebels fighting the government of Bashar al-Assad, previously brought some Syrians to fight in Libya's civil war in 2020.Pakistan has flown military equipment to Aden in southern Yemen to help in the battle against the Houthis, sources in Pakistan have said, and has deployed troops within Saudi Arabia to help defend its borders.The Saudi and Yemeni authorities did not respond to requests for comment.

title: From Athens to Jerusalem: Why Israel should heed the warnings of ancient Greek history - analysis
body: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio's speech in Athens on October 7 presented the world with a clear statement of America's current outlook on the world under the Trump administration. It also went beyond a statement of policy; it was about the history of the West and the importance of ancient Greece. Rubio discussed the values that underpinned ancient Greek civilization and the heritage that has come down to us through Western history.This is important for modern Israel. Zionism has always been rooted in several sources. One of the sources is the Jewish people and their connection to the land of Israel. This is a heritage that goes back to the Bible. Zionism was also a modern form of Jewish nationalism, rooted in the era when European nation-states were being formed.For instance, the First Zionist Congress was held in 1897, and Theodor Herzl had published Der Judenstaat in 1896. By this time, there was already a movement of Jews to Ottoman Palestine in the form of the First Aliyah in the 1880s and the role played by Baron Edmond de Rothschild.We believe that the West can awaken from its long slumber – and rekindle the fire that was first lit in ancient Greece millennia ago. https://t.co/gOi8VFQZgt— Secretary Marco Rubio (@SecRubio) October 7, 2026Zionism came of age during an era of change in Europe. Modern Italy was founded in the 1860s, and Germany was unified. Serbia became an independent country, and the Greeks achieved independence from the Ottomans.The Ottomans themselves were changing with the formation of the Committee of Union and Progress and the rise of the Young Turks. Early Zionists such as David Ben-Gurion and Yitzhak Ben-Zvi, studying in Istanbul, were influenced by this.Fast forward to 2026 and Rubio's speech.Rubio spoke about the importance of nationalism and states that are strong. He praised Greece today as a model ally of the United States. He also spoke about how strong countries don't allow open borders, and they invest in defense and manufacturing. These are values of modern Israel.What might we learn from Rubio's discussion of the ancient Greeks and today's Israel?Netanyahu: Israel becoming a "Super Sparta"Israeli politicians are already in the habit of referencing the Greeks, particularly Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. He has spoken about Israel becoming a kind of “super Sparta.” What he appears to mean is that Israel will be a strong country in the region. Will it live by the sword as Sparta is reputed to have done?In many cases, the concept of the Spartans being obsessed with war is a stereotype. In the Peloponnesian War (431-404 BCE), it was the Athenians who were seeking a kind of hegemony among the Greek city-states. Sparta was resisting this. As head of the Peloponnesian League, Sparta rallied states to resist Athenian aggression and the aggression of Athens' Delian League allies. Sparta's kind warned of the destructive war which engulfed the city-states.What is Israel's connection to all this?Sparta did not have a large industrial base. The city eventually declined and has largely vanished from history. A visit to Sparta today reveals a small town. Athens, by contrast, is still glorious against the backdrop of the Acropolis and Parthenon. Nevertheless, the concept of being a “Sparta” in the Middle East is one that appeals to Israel. Some people want an Israel that is warlike and suspicious of its neighbors. This policy has defined the post-October 7 period, with Israel advancing into buffer zones in Gaza, Lebanon, and Syria.Israel's allies, long-range operationsIsrael today is engaged in an unprecedented number of conflicts. One of those wars is with Iran. This is not a war solely of Israel's doing. Iran attacked Israel. Iran funded proxies to attack Israel. Iran sought to ring Israel with enemies such as Hezbollah. In 2024, Iran launched massive waves of ballistic missiles at Israel, claiming to be retaliating for Israeli operations in Syria and Tehran.Ancient Greece also was in the grips of the necessity of city-states to engage in long-range wars. For instance, the siege of Troy, which lasted a decade according to Homer, was waged by sending hundreds of ships to the shore of what is now modern day Turkey. Greek city states had colonies all over the Mediterranean. Anatolia and the Black Sea were areas of Greek colonies. The battle of Troy apparently resulted from this.What we know of that long war is that the city-states sent forces to the shoreline near Troy, who set siege, camping out for years. When the siege was over, and Troy was destroyed, the soldiers came home. The story told in the recent film Odyssey, based on the book by Homer, relates the disaster that befell those who tried to return home.Is there a lesson here for Israel?Israel's decision to engage in long-range conflict with Iran has risks. This kind of risk was felt by the Athenians during their ill-fated Syracuse campaign. Prodded by the Athenian Alcibiades, the Athenians sent forces all the way to what is modern-day Sicily to wage a complex war. The war sapped the strength of Athens and turned into a disaster, leading to its decline.Israel must be wary of its overextended lines, fighting on numerous fronts, lest it also find itself a victor but see its strength sapped.Israel, like ancient Greece, faces powerful enemiesLike modern-day Israel, the Greeks faced powerful enemies. Foremost among them was the Persian Empire. The Persians invaded Greece several times, often with large armies and navies. At key moments, the Persians were defeated, such as at the Battle of Marathon and later at Salamis in 480 BCE. Is there a lesson for Israel's current challenges with the Islamic Republic of Iran?In both cases, a small state is facing a much larger one. Iran is around 75 times larger than Israel. Iran's population is around nine times that of Israel. However, size isn't everything. This is a lesson from the Bible in the story of David and Goliath. Iran, today, has a relatively weak economy and faces many challenges fighting the US.The issue for Israel, as it was for the Greeks in the 4-5th centuries BCE, is that fighting a large country can draw one in and force one to engage in many other conflicts. Israel has this problem. Some Israeli officials have already said that they believe Turkey could become the next Iran. What they mean is that a weak Iran will leave a vacuum in the region and Turkey may fill that vacuum. Turkey is a member of NATO. It is more powerful and advanced than Iran.How might we see a parallel here with ancient Greece?Alexander of Macedon invaded Persia in 336 BCE. He conquered Persia and even invaded northern India in 326 BCE. As such, he had conquered much of what the Greeks believed was the known world at the time. However, this new Greek empire fell into infighting. The Greek cultural hegemony was felt in areas that are now Israel and Jordan. Greek-influenced towns arose in the areas of Beit Shean and across the Jordan valley, what Rome would call the Decapolis cities.What matters for our purposes is that the defeat of Persia only led to brief success. In the end, it also led to infighting.What Israel must learn from the rise of RomeIsrael could do well to consider the fate of the Greeks in the period of the rise of Rome. Israel today is a strong state. However, global changes are taking place. China is potentially rising, and the US is navigating a new world order that is as complex as the world order of the 1990s.The Greek city-states also had to navigate these changes. After the victories of Alexander and the decline of his brief empire into infighting, the Greek city-states faced challenges from the Romans in Italy. The Greek King Pyrrhus of Epirus fought the Romans in the period 280-275 BCE. The term “Pyrrhic victory” comes from his wars. Even when he won, the attrition for his army added up to losses in the end.What might that tell us about Israel? Will it suffer attrition from being overstretched in conflicts in Gaza, Lebanon, and the West Bank? Israel's inability to have a strategy in Gaza, and its unwillingness to decide what the future holds for the West Bank could be a long-term challenge. Jerusalem feels today that it has the upper hand. It feels confident, for instance, to get into diplomatic spats with countries such as the United Kingdom. It assumes that, over time, the rise of the Right in Europe will mean less interest in the Palestinian issue.Perhaps. However, what ancient Greece teaches us is that overconfidence and hubris can lead to ruin.This was the case with Athens choosing war with the Spartan allies, as well as its Sicilian expedition. It also ended badly for the Greeks in conflict with Rome. At the Battle of Cynoscephalae, Philip V of Macedon was decisively defeated. Rome essentially annexed Athens in 146 BCE and sacked it in 86 BCE. In 63 BCE the Romans also came to Jerusalem, ending the era of Hasmonean rule.

title: Iran says Strait of Hormuz could reopen within a week as Tehran weighs US response
body: Tehran is still reviewing Washington's response to its proposal, under which the Strait of Hormuz could be reopened within seven days, and could reply within days, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Thursday, according to Iranian semi-official Tasnim news agency."The diplomatic process is still continuing," Araghchi said.Tankers are facing a higher risk of attacks and intimidation as they try to get critical shipments through the Strait of Hormuz after Iran issued new warnings it would block routes that it has not authorized, sources said.Last week already saw the biggest number of attacks on tankers in the key waterway since the Iran war began - cutting the number of vessels trying to get through to the lowest in more than two months.Iran has now warned regional countries that any attempt to open new routes for oil exports would be considered hostile, a senior regional official close to Tehran told Reuters.It was part of a plan agreed by both Iran's political leaders and its Revolutionary Guards, the official added.'Iran has no intention of allowing control to slip from its hands'"Iran has absolutely no intention of allowing control of the Strait of Hormuz to slip from its hands, and has plans ready to block routes that some regional countries have for exporting oil," a senior diplomat in the region briefed by Tehran told Reuters separately."This could involve missile and drone attacks on ships, or sending boats to scare ships away," the diplomat added. "It plans to continue this policy of fear and threats," he said.In recent months, Gulf oil producers have rushed shipments of oil through channels that hug the Omani side of the strait before transferring the oil in open waters in the Gulf of Oman with aerial support from the US, sources have told Reuters.In the latest incident in the past 24 hours, projectiles struck a tanker some 51 nautical miles off the coast of Qatar inside the Gulf, British navy agency UKMTO reported.Maritime security sources said the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged chemical tanker Acers had been hit by multiple projectiles north of Qatar's Madinat ash Shamal with minor injuries sustained by its crew.“The Acers strike raises the prospect of a wider combat area affecting approaches to Qatar, Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Iraq,” maritime risk intelligence group Pole Star Global's subsidiary Clearwater Dynamics said in a report on Thursday.The vessel's operator, listed in shipping databases as Antigua and Barbuda-based Valvoria Shipping, could not be reached for comment."The recent spate of Iranian attacks seems to have dampened the appetite of shipowners to sail through the Strait," said Jakob Larsen, chief ​safety & security officer at shipping association BIMCO."The Iranian threat appears to have increased."

title: Spain must reverse Sánchez's anti-Israel policies after snap election, Vox lawmaker says
body: Spain will vote on November 29 in a snap general election called by Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez after a parliamentary defeat over housing exposed the fragility of his governing coalition, opening a campaign in which current polling gives the center-right Popular Party and Vox a combined parliamentary majority.For Juan Carlos Girauta, a Vox member of the European Parliament, the stakes extend well beyond domestic politics.“There is a very clear awareness that Spain's foreign policy under Sánchez needs a 180-degree turn,” Girauta said, looking beyond the election to the changes he would like to see from a new government.Polling averages currently favor the right, but the campaign has only begun. An October 5 average compiled by Spain's public broadcaster RTVE projected 137 seats for the Popular Party (PP) and 65 for Vox, giving the two parties a combined 202 seats in the 350-member Congress of Deputies. The Socialists were projected at 104 seats. An absolute majority requires 176.Vox is a relatively recent chapter in Girauta's political career. Born in Barcelona in 1961, the lawyer and journalist entered elected politics with Ciudadanos, winning a seat in the European Parliament in 2014 before moving to the Spanish Congress, where he became one of the party's most visible figures. He left Ciudadanos in 2020 and returned to the European Parliament on the Vox ticket in 2024.Sánchez called the election on October 5, three days after Congress rejected two government housing decrees. The election had previously been expected in 2027.Housing decrees' defeat did not create housing crisisGirauta told The Media Line that the housing defeat mattered, but not because it created the crisis.“The final trigger, not the fundamental cause, but the last straw, was Sánchez's attempt to recover the initiative and some popularity,” he said in an interview conducted in Spanish.That effort followed the eviction of María del Carmen “Maricarmen” Abascal, an 87-year-old Madrid woman whose case became a symbol of Spain's housing crisis. Protesters rallied in her support and established an encampment in Puerta del Sol. Five days after her eviction, the property-management company reached an agreement allowing her to return under a new lease.Sánchez responded to the protests with housing measures aimed at protecting vulnerable tenants, regulating temporary and room rentals, restricting certain rent increases, and helping first-time buyers. The package included plans for interest-free loans of up to €50,000 toward a home purchase.Congress rejected both decrees on October 2 after Junts, the Catalan separatist party led by Carles Puigdemont, joined the PP and Vox in voting against them. Junts' seven deputies had helped Sánchez secure another term in 2023. This time, their votes helped derail a central government initiative.Girauta calls the government's approach “Operation Maricarmen.” He sees it as an effort to take a genuine grievance and turn it into a political rescue operation.“He takes that banner and says, 'Now I am going to fix this,'” Girauta said. “Not by building more housing or anything like that, but by creating the kind of legal uncertainty that makes supply contract even further.”He spoke at greater length about what the housing shortage looks like away from parliament. Young Spaniards, he said, are delaying independence, sharing crowded apartments, and abandoning hopes of buying homes.“They not only cannot buy. They have to rent with other people,” he said. “There are things happening that were not seen in Spain, at least not in my generation. People from different families have to share a flat and the expenses just to pay the rent.”Sánchez has acknowledged that his government has not solved Spain's housing problems. In calling the election, he argued that a larger progressive majority was needed to advance housing, public services, and other reforms blocked in the current parliament.His government has not abandoned the housing measures. On October 6, the Cabinet approved revised versions of the two decrees, retaining much of the original program and adding a €10 billion financing package for first-home loans. The measures must now go before the Permanent Deputation, the parliamentary body that continues operating after the chambers are dissolved.The PP and Vox will also try to make the election a referendum on Sánchez himself.The opposition has spent months pointing to criminal cases involving former Socialist officials and members of the prime minister's family. Former Transport Minister José Luis Ábalos was sentenced in June to 24 years and three months in prison for crimes including bribery, embezzlement, influence peddling, and participation in a criminal organization.Sánchez's brother, David Sánchez, was convicted in July of administrative misconduct connected to his hiring by a provincial government and sentenced to nine years of disqualification from public office. The ruling is being appealed.The prime minister's wife, Begoña Gómez, has been ordered to face trial on influence-peddling and embezzlement charges involving alleged misuse of public funds. Gómez denies wrongdoing, and Sánchez himself has not been charged in either family case. He has accused political opponents of using the courts against his family and has argued that wrongdoing by individual officials does not establish broader corruption within his government.Girauta rejects claim political opponents using courts against Sánchez Girauta rejects that defense. He said the court cases had become inseparable from the government's loss of authority. He also described pressure from Socialist regional leaders who feared paying the price for Sánchez's problems in their own elections.“They do not want the kick aimed at Sánchez to land on them,” Girauta said. “They want it to land on him first, and then, when their regional elections arrive, to be judged on their own management.”Girauta's interest extends beyond who controls parliament. He expects the election to reopen questions about Spain's relationship with its traditional allies, including Israel and the United States.Spain formally recognized a Palestinian state in May 2024. Sánchez's government later codified an arms embargo on Israel, barred imports from Israeli settlements in the West Bank and from certain Israeli neighborhoods in east Jerusalem under its settlement-related trade restrictions, and increased support for the Palestinian Authority and UNRWA, the UN agency responsible for aiding Palestinian refugees. Sánchez has repeatedly described Israel's conduct in Gaza as genocide. Vox rejects that characterization and opposed the arms embargo.Girauta said a new government should “stop inciting antisemitism in international forums, stop practicing anti-Westernism, stop doing everything possible to irritate the United States, and stop yielding to Morocco.”His criticism of Morocco follows the extraordinary migration crisis in Ceuta in late July, when tens of thousands of people crossed from Morocco into the Spanish enclave over two days. Spanish authorities later put the total at about 80,000, with most subsequently returning to Morocco.Girauta described the episode as “hybrid warfare” by Morocco. A later Spanish police report said Moroccan security personnel appeared to have helped guide migrants toward the crossing, although it did not identify who ordered the operation or assign responsibility to the Moroccan government. Rabat has denied orchestrating the influx and says it cooperated with Spain in returning migrants.Spanish court lifts arrest warrant for PuigdemontCatalonia will provide another unpredictable element in the campaign.The Constitutional Court ruled this week that Spain's amnesty law applies to misuse-of-public-funds offenses connected to the 2017 Catalan independence drive. The Supreme Court then lifted the arrest warrant for Puigdemont, clearing the way for his possible return to Spain after years in Belgium.The development is politically awkward for Sánchez. His 2023 agreement with Junts helped secure his return to office and led to passage of the amnesty law, but Puigdemont's party later withdrew its support on key legislation and helped defeat the housing measures that preceded the snap election.Girauta also pointed to the political climate surrounding an October 7 pro-Palestinian demonstration scheduled for Barcelona's Plaça Universitat and associated with Samidoun, the Palestinian Prisoner Solidarity Network. The public call for the event referred to the third anniversary of “Tufan al-Aqsa,” the Arabic name used by Hamas for its October 7, 2023, attack, and urged support for Palestinian resistance.Samidoun was sanctioned by the US Treasury in 2024, which described it as an international fundraising front for the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine. Canada has listed the organization as a terrorist entity, while Germany banned it in 2023.Girauta criticized both the amnesty and the government's housing strategy. His sharpest warning, though, concerned the tone of the campaign and the possibility that political confrontation could spill beyond argument.“We are in a democracy,” Girauta said. “What counts here is the free exchange of arguments and messages, and then measuring ourselves at the ballot box. Everything else must be rejected and denounced.”With less than two months until voting day, the polls give Spain's right a substantial numerical advantage, but they are a snapshot rather than a result. Sánchez has built much of his political career on surviving situations in which his opponents believed his time was up. The Nov. 29 election will determine whether he does so again - and whether Spain's domestic upheaval produces a sharp change in its policies toward Israel, the United States, Morocco, and the rest of Europe.

title: UK announces new round of Russia sanctions targeting financial services, 'shadow fleet'
body: Britain's foreign office on Thursday announced new sanctions targeting individuals and entities it said were involved in the production or transport of Russian oil, facilitating military manufacturing and circumventing financial services sanctions.The package also included 12 oil tankers that Britain says operate as part of Russia's shadow fleet and help Moscow evade sanctions on oil exports.It also included three crypto exchanges and two payment platforms that Britain suspects Russia uses to circumvent financial sanctions.Britain said two of those entities sanctioned had processed and facilitated transactions with the A7 illicit finance network.Additionally, it included seventeen entities and individuals involved in the supply of goods deemed by the UK, US and EU to be vital for the Russian war effort, including Russia-based importers of machine tools, electronics and materials used to produce missiles and drones.Russia's embassy in London did not immediately respond to Reuters' request for comment.

title: Hamas used double agents, deception to fool Israel ahead of October 7 massacre, study finds
body: Hamas's leadership planned to use strategic deception to lull Israel into a false sense of security before the October 7 attacks, activating double agents as late as the eve of the invasion to feed the Shin Bet (Israel Security Service) false information, as revealed in a new study by Lt.-Col. (res.) Yehonatan Duhoch-Halevi published on Wednesday by the Jerusalem Center for Security and Foreign Affairs (JCFA).A core part of Hamas's strategy was conceived in early 2022 and sought to create the impression that Israel's “carrot and stick” policy, which combined threats to assassinate senior Hamas leaders with economic relief for Gaza, was working, according to the research.Through the evening of October 6, Israeli intelligence was fed the impression that conditions in Gaza were routine, thus allowing Hamas to conceal its plans while arming and concentrating its forces, according to a senior figure in Hamas's military wing.According to the terrorist's testimony, Hamas identified an Israeli espionage network in 2017 and was able to recruit some members of the network to become double agents operating under Hamas's direction.The IDF investigation into the failures leading up to the massacre noted that, on October 6, indications of a Hamas attack were received alongside reassuring signs, although the investigation did not explain what those reassuring signs were. The Shin Bet investigation reported that “human intelligence sources,” or intelligence agents, had confirmed that the terror group was operating routinely.Hamas officials have since acknowledged the use of deception as part of the preparations for the attack. In a late 2023 interview with Ammar Taqi, senior Hamas official Khaled Mashal admitted that, ahead of October 7, Hamas carried out strategic and tactical deception, including conveying "reassurance" messages.“Regarding the aspect of strategic deception and the method of deception, as I mentioned, there was a general feeling that [Gaza] [under Hamas leadership] was focusing on its affairs, and wanted to bring in a certain amount of fuel, electricity and aid, meaning [Gaza] was licking its wounds and pains because of the blockade imposed on it, and after the 21 war [Hamas] did not respond to the escalation [in actions] carried out by the occupation in al-Quds and Al-Aqsa,” Mashal said.“For example, as I mentioned, during the previous Ramadan, in this year 2023, on days 13 or 14 in the middle of Ramadan, they [the Israelis] broke into Al-Aqsa, and the public [wondered] where was Gaza? The enemy began to analyze and thought that Gaza was occupied with itself. The holidays came from September 15 to October 6 [2023], and then, behold, the movement's leadership wisely sent deception messages to the enemy once again. We know some of them.”Hamas inspired by Egypt's deception during Yom Kippur War“The [Jewish] holidays came from September 15 to October 6 [2023], and then, behold, the movement's leadership wisely sent deception messages to the enemy once again. We know some of them.”Mashal also admitted that he took inspiration from Egypt's strategy during the Yom Kippur War, when Egypt attacked Israel on a religious holiday and shared that Cairo had told soldiers to go on a religious pilgrimage to Mecca to lull Jerusalem into believing that no war was coming.ספטמבר 2026 – בכיר בחמאס לפני שחוסל: "למרות האפילה הזו, חסימת האופק [לשיפור המצב] ומצב החולשה הגלוי לעין, ולמרות הבגידה מצד אחים לנו ובני עמנו מקרב הערבים והמוסלמים, יש לנו ודאות שאללה לא ינטוש אותנו, ושניצחון הקבוצה המאמינה והלוחמת בדרך הג'יהאד הוא עניין וודאי והבטחה אלוהית" ב-3 באוקטובר 2026, פרסמה הזרוע הצבאית של חמאס, גדודי אל-קסאם, את "איגרתו האחרונה של מפקד החטיבה הצפונית, עז אל-דין אל-ביכּ [عز الدين البيك], להנהגת ההתנגדות [חמאס], מספר ימים לפני שנפל חלל בדרכו של אללה". עז אל-דין אל-ביכּ, שהיה גם חבר המועצה הצבאית הכללית של גדודי אל-קסאם, נהרג בתקיפה ישראלית ב-29 בספטמבר 2026 בדירה בשכונת א-נסר [النصر] בעיר עזה, יחד עם מהנד עבד אל-בארי אבו אל-פול (مهند عبد الباري أبو فول). להלן תוכן האיגרת ששלח עז אל-דין אל-ביכּ: יום שלישי: 8/9/2026 {אנו מושיטים עזרה לשליחינו ולמאמינים בחיי העולם הזה, וביום אשר יתייצבו העדים} [קוראן, פרק: 40 פסוק:51] אל האח המפקד הלוחם בדרך הג'יהאד [קטע מושחר], ישמור אללה וישגיח עליך. השלום עליך ורחמי אללה וברכותיו, ולענייננו: בתחילת הדברים, אנו מבקשים מאללה שאיגרת זו תגיע אליכם בעודכם נהנים במלוא הבריאות והרווחה, ושילביש [אללה] אתכם בלבוש הבריאות והשלום, ושישמח את עיניכם בניצחון חייליו ובעוז בני בריתו [של אללה], ושיציל את עמנומהמתקפה של האויב האכזר הזה. הו אללה, אמן. זו איגרת של בניכם מקרב הלוחמים בדרך הג'יהאד של החטיבה הצפונית [של גדודי אל-קסאם], אשר חונכו בידי אנשים כמותכם מקרב מפקדיהם הצדיקים, ומקרב המפקדים הגדולים שנפלו שהידים [חללים בדרכו של אללה]. איגרת זו נושאת בחובה עבורכם את כל משמעויות האהבה, הציות והשייכות להנהגתם ולמייסדים הראשונים של הפעילות הלוחמת [العملالمقاوم]. למרות עוצמת הניסיונות [המבחנים הקשים בזירת העימות], גודל האובדן, המצב הקשה, ולמרות המזימות והתחבולות מצד האויב הפושע ועוזריו, עדיין אנחנו [קיימים] ונישאר בדרך ששרטטתם לנו: דרך הג'יהאד והנפילה חלל בדרכו של אללה [الاستشهاد], עד להשגת המטרה המיוחלת, ברצון אללה. ואנו מאשרים לך, מפקדנו האהוב, שמערכת "מבול/ שיטפון אל-אקצא" [معركة طوفان الأقصى] היא בבחינת התגלות של גזירות אללה יתעלה, וזה ניכר בדבקות האגדית של המוג'אהידין, בסבלנות העם הנכבד הלוחם בדרך הג'יהאד ובהיאחזותו באדמתו. אנו סבורים שזו מערכה [צבאית] אלוהית שהונהגה בידי מפקדים מבורכים, הזוכים להשראה אלוהית, אוהבי דרכו של אללה, אשר הקדישו את חייהם להכנת המיזם האדיר הזה, "מבול אל-אקצא", שהוא המחשה ממוזערת של הסוף הבלתי נמנע והנפילה הרועמת של הישות הפושעת הזו, וניצוץ מערכת השחרור וחיסול הישות הכובשת הזו, ברצון אללה ישתבח ויתעלה. ולמרות כל האפילה הזו, חסימת האופק [לשיפור המצב] ומצב החולשה הגלוי לעין, ולמרות כל הבגידה מצד אחים לנו ובני עמנו מקרב הערבים והמוסלמים, יש לנו ודאות איתנה שאללה לא ינטוש אותנו, ושניצחון הקבוצה הזו המאמינה והלוחמת בדרך הג'יהאד הוא עניין וודאי והבטחה אלוהית, ואחריו יבואו רוממות והעצמה [עליונות ושליטה], ברצון אללה. כך חינכתם אותנו, וכך הגיעה תובנה זו אלינו מכם מחומרי הקוראן והחינוך הג'יהאדי, ומכך שנטעתם בנו את הוודאות שהבטחת אללה קרובה [למימוש]. {כבר כתבנו בַּזַּבּוּר [ספר תהילים], לאחר דבר התוכחה, לאמור, עבדיי הישרים יירשו את הארץ} [קוראן, פרק:21 פסוק:105] ואנו שולחים לך, מפקדנו האהוב, את ברכת [קטע מושחר], אשר הזכיר במפגש קודם עמו את מפגשיו עמך ועם האח השהיד המפקד [של גדודי אל-קסאם] אבו מחמד [אחמד סעיד] אל-ג'עברי, ירחם עליו אללה [חוסל ב-14 בנובמבר 2012]. הוא מעביר לכם ברכת שלום חמה והערכתו הרבה, ואת תפילתו עבורכם להחלמה ולבריאות מלאה, ושאללה יאחד אותנו עמכם על אדמת ארצנו המשוחררת והמטוהרת, ברצון אללה. האח הלוחם בדרך הג'יהאד, המפקד האהוב, מי ייתן ותישאר בבריאות ובשלווה, ואל תשכח אותנו בתפילותיך הטובות. אנו מבקשים מאללה שישמח את עיניך בניצחונו, ושיאחד אותנו עמך בחצרות מסגד אל-אקצא המשוחרר והמטוהר מטומאת הכובשים, אתם ואחינו הנהגת התנועה הלוחמת בדרך הג'יהאד. הייה בטוח שאנו, ברצון אללה ובעצם היותו איתנו, איתנים וסבלניים, מושרשים באדמתנו, אוחזים בנשקנו, ממשיכים בדרך שנסללה בדמם של מפקדינו, המוג'אהידין שלנו ובני עמנו הגאים, עד שאללה יקיים את הבטחתו. קבל את ברכותינו עבורך ועבור האחים הנכבדים שסביבך, ומי ייתן ותישארו תחת שמירת אללה, הגנתו ובהשגחתו. סימוכין: https://t.co/XSPv37skOg עז אל-דין אל-ביכּ. תמונה: גדודי אל-קסאם— Jonathan D. Halevi (@jdhalevi) October 7, 2026“A message, in order to fulfill its purpose, must be an indirect message, meaning messages that will not be understood [by the enemy] to be deception messages, which the enemy will swallow. The enemy also uses deception against others, and the resistance succeeded in deceiving the enemy, and it picked up false messages,” Mashal said at the time. “After that, there was concealment, meaning avoiding exposing the preparations: Of course, the tunnels...”The JCFA study noted that Hamas-affiliated political commentator Issam Shawar said that Hamas had been taken by surprise by a similar strategy a few months earlier when Israel began Operation Shield and Arrow against Palestinian Islamic Jihad (PIJ) in May 2023. According to Shawar, one day before the launch of the operation, Israel carried out a deception operation by informing Hamas that it would allow the transfer of the financial grant from Qatar to pay the salaries of public-sector employees.The use of deception by Hamas was also noted by Palestinian journalists immediately after the October 7 attack. On October 8, 2023, JCFA noted that Palestinian journalists had commented on Hamas's use of deception tactics.Fadi Ramadan noted that Hamas had carried out two separate deception operations.The first created a false impression in Israel that the planned attack would come through the tunnels, whereas Hamas launched a ground invasion.The second involved conveying to Israel that the “carrot and stick” policy had been effective.JCFA also suggested that former Palestinian Authority (PA) minister for prisoner affairs Sufian Abu Zayda had been deceived by Hamas's plans.Explaining that the terror group had a channel of contact with Israel through Zayda, JCFA said that the former PA official was enlisted to negotiate a deal with Israel to release Palestinian prisoners for the bodies of Israelis already held in Hamas captivity before October 7.Zayda had reportedly met with Ghazi Hamad in Gaza, who confirmed that now-assassinated Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar had authorized the deal. After his return to Israel, Zayda contacted a retired Shin Bet officer who arranged a meeting between him and active Shin Bet personnel in Ashkelon.In July 2022, Zayda met with Sinwar in Gaza, in the presence of Rawhi Mushtaha, where Sinwar presented his priorities regarding a possible agreement with Israel concerning the release of prisoners.Sinwar-Zaida meeting led to increased Israeli interest in deal with HamasAccording to Duhoch-Halevi's assessment, the meeting between Sinwar and Zayda strengthened Israel's interest in a deal, and Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar personally met with Zayda to hear from him the conditions set by Hamas for a possible deal.Zayda claimed Bar asked him to convey a message to Sinwar that Israel would be willing to advance far-reaching economic measures in Gaza.The negotiations between the sides advanced to the stage of deliberations over the names of the prisoners to be released as part of the deal, and drafts were exchanged between the sides.On September 14, 2023, two days after Hamas conducted its major annual military exercise, Zayda met with Sinwar, again in the presence of Mushtaha, and Sinwar dictated a message to Zayda for the Israeli side, according to which “by the end of September we will put cards on the table that will cause an earthquake regarding the negotiations, and they should prepare to empty the prisons.”Zayda was asked to convey this message verbatim to the Shin Bet representatives who were in contact with him, and another meeting with Yahya Sinwar was scheduled for October 8. Abu Zayda traveled to Israel, conveyed the message to Shin Bet personnel, and returned to Gaza on October 5, ahead of another planned meeting with Sinwar.“It appears that Abu Zayda was a component of the deception plan operated by the Hamas leadership in an attempt to convince Israel that it was serious in its intentions to reach an agreement for the exchange of Palestinian prisoners for Israelis (living and dead) held in Gaza, as a move that would lead to the regulation of relations between Israel and the Hamas government on the basis of economic relief on Israel's part and infrastructure development in the Gaza Strip,” Duhoch-Halevi said, adding that it was “reasonable” to think Sinwar's scheduled meeting with Zayda on October 8 “served as a smokescreen for the secret continuation of military preparations.”

title: Turkey expects no change in Israel's foreign policy after elections, FM Hakan Fidan says
body: Turkey does not expect any particular change in Israel's foreign policy after the country's elections, scheduled for October 27, regardless of the outcome, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on Thursday.Fidan also discussed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement and Turkey's role in the defensive pact signed with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan.Turkey assessing ways to assist Saudi Arabia against Houthi threatTurkey is assessing how it can help Saudi Arabia defend against attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi terrorists under a joint defense pact with Pakistan, Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on Thursday, ruling out Turkish participation in offensive operations.Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement in August, under which an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all. The three countries have since held political and military meetings in response to the Houthi attacks.On Monday, the countries said they had agreed to move immediately to implement their collective defense commitments and ensure the "rapid deployment" of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia.Mecca pact defensive rather than offensiveSpeaking at a joint press conference with his Hungarian counterpart Anita Orban in Ankara, Fidan stressed that the pact was defensive rather than offensive, saying military officials were assessing possible contributions, particularly in air defense, electronic warfare and technical support."Yemen's legitimate government forces are already continuing the battle on the ground and Saudi Arabia is supporting them," Fidan said."But this is a defensive agreement. When a country party to the pact comes under attack, you stand by it in its defense. This is not an offensive agreement. Turkey will not send troops to another country to carry out attacks on its territory," he said.Fidan said military delegations would determine Saudi Arabia's operational defense needs and what contributions Turkey and Pakistan could make.On Wednesday, two officials told Reuters that Turkey was sending mainly defensive and technical support to Saudi Arabia to help it fight Houthi terrorists.Turkish officials have said any support provided at this stage would largely be in a bilateral capacity, as Turkey's parliament has not officially ratified the joint defense pact.Fidan said on Thursday that work was largely completed for the agreement to be submitted for parliament's approval and that they aimed to send it "as soon as possible."Turkey, which has NATO's second-largest army and a robust defense industry, has condemned the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, voiced willingness to help meet Riyadh's technical military needs, and agreed to join a Saudi-led coalition to ensure navigational safety in the Red Sea.

title: Norilsk Nickel maintains conservative approach to dividends
body:
MOSCOW, October 8. /TASS/. Norilsk Nickel maintains a conservative approach to the issue of dividends, as financial sustainability is important for the company, said Tatiana Dykova, Director of the Investor Community Relations Department at the Russian mining and metals company.
"We still remain conservative in our approach and the management focuses on the free cash flow. Therefore, if the conditions we mentioned earlier are met, where we earn a positive free cash flow and have a comfortable debt burden, taking into account all external macroeconomic circumstances and conditions in the commodities markets, we are ready to distribute the corresponding level of cash available with us for dividends. Thus, we are quite consistent in our communication, quite conservative, and it is very important for us that the company's financial profile remains stable," she said.
The company operates in markets experiencing quite a lot of external shocks, Dykova noted. "This applies not only to the commodities markets we are talking about now, but also, accordingly, to the macroeconomic factors present for us," she added.
The company has returned to the "dividend track," the department director said at the same time. Earlier, Norilsk Nickel shareholders approved a dividend payout of 1.85 rubles ($0.022) per share for January-June 2026 at an extraordinary general meeting.

title: ‘Caught in the middle’ More than 500 private career colleges impacted by OSAP freeze
body:
Editor’s Note: This story has been updated to correct the number of OSAP-eligible career colleges to 242. A previous version noted the total number of private institutions in the province, not all of which were eligible for financial support.
Hundreds of private career colleges are scrambling to assess their options after the Ford government cut off their eligibility for student loans and grants in the wake of a potential OPP criminal investigation into the sector.
On Tuesday, the province revealed that six private career colleges were suspected of taking advantage of Ontario’s student assistance program (OSAP) after the ministry of colleges and universities noticed a number of red flags.
While six institutions were suspended by the ministry, the government said it would take a broad approach to the entire sector in order the “support the integrity of the OSAP system” by pausing their eligibility altogether.
There are over 500 career colleges in the province. The ministry says 242 institutions were eligible for OSAP. Among them is AAPS College in Toronto and Mississauga, which offers education and training in the pharmaceutical, clinical research, food and nutrition, and healthcare sectors.
Shortly after the announcement, Laleh Bighash, dean of Scientific Affairs, received a memo from the ministry informing her of the pause “due to the fraudulent activities” with little information on how students and institutions could navigate the weeks and months ahead.
While the college is expecting an impact on future enrolment, Bighash said the main concern is the current roster of students who rely on support payments for their education.
“There are students who are currently in the college and they’re half paid through the program and they’ve already committed OSAP dollars and they don’t know where to go,” Bighash said.
“At this point there is no clarity on how to deal with the students who’ve been caught in the middle, through no fault of their own, and we do feel for them, and I also feel for the staff and faculty. We’re remaining focused on how to deal with and how to help them navigate.”
That message is being echoed by Career Colleges Ontario, the association representing hundreds of institutions, which is urging the Ford government to reinstate student financial aid for career college students who were already approved for funds and are actively attending in-person classes.
The association, which had been warning the government about possible misuse of OSAP since 2023, says the government should be taking targeted action to address those concerns, not disrupting the education of students who have followed the rules.
When the government first announced the changes, Minister Quinn offered vague details on how students currently enrolled in a career college will be able to access funds — stressing that while the OSAP pipeline is being shut off, private institutions could step in.
“To support these students, the government is working on options to provide low-interest third-party loans for students enrolled at private post-secondary institutions, and is in discussions with financial institutions to facilitate these loans,” Quinn said.
“We will provide more information on these options as soon as we can.”
Meanwhile, institutions will be able to apply for OSAP eligibility with the ministry “under stricter parameters.”
Bighash, with AAPS College, said while she supports the government’s crackdown on “bad actors” in the system, she fears institutions with good track records are being unfairly swept up in the response.
“I think it might have also some unintended consequences for legitimate students and legitimate, solid, career-focused institutions that might not be able to survive,” Bighash said.
Bighash said her college has been regularly audited by the Ministry of Colleges and Universities, has to apply for registration every year, and boasts consistent OSAP repayments.
“Our OSAP default rate is among the lowest when you compare it to the public or private institution,” she said.
“We actually would like to be a part of conversation to see how they can put more safeguards to protect OSAP, to protect the students, and to protect our faculties and the employers everybody.”
Bighash is calling on the government to take a “risk-based approach” to the file and warns that the government’s pledge to “protect Ontario” from the trade war with the United States will also face an impact.
“We have students who have had been affected by tariffs, and they come to us to get new skills, new experience, and you know move on,” Bighash said.
“So it makes it sort of a double-edged sword. We’re trying to help the economy at the same time. We really don’t know how we can actually focus on that rather than being in this firefighting mode.”

title: Could Kuwait be the next country to join the Abraham Accords? - opinion
body: If Kuwait is moving toward normalization with Israel, the consequences could extend far beyond another diplomatic agreement, reshaping calculations from Riyadh to Tehran.Sometimes, in the Middle East, what is not announced matters more than what is.Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's unusually quiet visit to Abu Dhabi to meet UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed raises an obvious question: Why now, and why so quietly?There was no public agenda, no joint press conference, and no diplomatic fanfare. Netanyahu flew to the UAE, met MBZ, and returned to Israel several hours later, with little explanation of what had been discussed.That silence may be the most interesting part of the story.My suspicion is that the meeting was about more than another bilateral consultation. Kuwait may be part of a larger conversation behind closed doors, possibly involving the next expansion of the Abraham Accords.Less than two weeks earlier, Israel's ambassador to the UAE, Yossi Shelley, suggested publicly that another country could join the accords within four to six months. He specifically pointed to Kuwait.Kuwait has traditionally been among the Gulf states most cautious toward normalization with Israel and has long maintained a public position opposed to it. That is precisely why a Kuwaiti move would matter so much.Neutrality does not stop a missileIran has made the threat facing the Gulf impossible to treat as theoretical.The events of 2026 showed how quickly a confrontation involving Tehran can spill across borders. Iranian missiles and drones reached Gulf states, including Kuwait, forcing governments that had tried to balance relations with Washington and Tehran to confront an uncomfortable reality.Neutrality does not stop a missile. Diplomatic caution does not intercept a drone. Geography does not disappear because a government would prefer to remain outside somebody else's war.Kuwait sits close to Iran, hosts a major American military presence, and occupies a strategically sensitive position at the northern edge of the Gulf.That changes Israel's strategic value in Gulf calculations.Israel possesses capabilities Gulf governments increasingly need: combat-tested missile defense, sophisticated intelligence, early-warning systems, cyber capabilities, and years of experience confronting Iranian weapons and proxies.The question is no longer simply whether Gulf capitals approve of Israeli policy. It is whether they can build the next regional security architecture without Israel.The Abraham Accords began as diplomatic normalization. Their next phase may be about shared early warning, intelligence coordination, missile and drone defense, maritime security, and protection of critical infrastructure.This is where MBZ becomes central. The UAE maintains deep relations with Washington, has built an extensive partnership with Israel, and keeps channels open to regional rivals. Abu Dhabi also has an interest in a Gulf where security relationships are increasingly interconnected. Bringing Kuwait closer to the Abraham Accords would fit that strategy.The road from Kuwait City leads to RiyadhA Kuwaiti move would also change the strategic context surrounding Saudi Arabia, the most consequential potential addition to the Abraham Accords.This would not mean Riyadh would automatically follow. Saudi Arabia has its own interests and its own position on the Palestinian issue.But Kuwait would remove another political and psychological barrier. If even Kuwait can establish relations with Israel, the definition of what is politically possible in the Gulf changes.Saudi policymakers would increasingly have to consider not only what normalization would require, but also the implications of remaining outside a regional network that is gradually becoming more integrated.Such a network would not be an Arab-Israeli NATO. What could emerge is something looser: states that do not agree on everything but increasingly share intelligence, technology, warning systems, and maritime interests.The United States would remain indispensable. Washington provides military reach and security guarantees no regional power can replace. The Abraham Accords provide a framework through which regional cooperation can deepen.Iran's strategic paradoxFor Tehran, this is the greater danger.An Israeli flag flying over another embassy in the Gulf is symbolic. Israeli radar, intelligence, early-warning systems, and security coordination becoming embedded in the Gulf are something else entirely.For decades, Iran benefited from a regional structure in which Israel and Gulf Arab states shared concerns about Tehran while remaining politically separated. The Abraham Accords began to close that strategic space. Iran's own behavior may now be closing it further.Every missile launched toward a Gulf state strengthens the argument for integrated air defense. Every drone attack strengthens the case for shared early warning. Every threat to shipping strengthens the argument for maritime coordination.And every demonstration of Iranian reach makes Israeli intelligence and defense technology more relevant to governments that once saw relations with Israel primarily as a political liability.That is Tehran's strategic paradox: In demonstrating its ability to threaten the region, Iran may be accelerating the construction of the very regional architecture it has spent years trying to prevent.Watch the silencePerhaps Kuwait was not discussed in Abu Dhabi. Perhaps Netanyahu and MBZ were simply conducting another strategic consultation.But the timing is difficult to ignore.An Israeli ambassador publicly identifies Kuwait as a possible new member of the Abraham Accords. Less than two weeks later, Netanyahu quietly travels to Abu Dhabi for an unexplained meeting with a leader who helped turn Arab-Israeli normalization into a regional strategy.That may be a coincidence.I suspect it is not. In chess, you do not always announce what comes next. Sometimes you quietly reposition the pieces, create pressure, and wait for your opponent to understand what has changed. The decisive move is often prepared several turns before its purpose becomes clear.The original Abraham Accords showed that Arab states did not have to wait for a final Israeli-Palestinian settlement before establishing relations with Israel. A Kuwaiti move would suggest something more: that the strategic logic behind normalization has become powerful enough to reach one of the Gulf states most resistant to it.The first phase of the Abraham Accords was about recognition. The next may be about integration.Perhaps that is what was being discussed behind closed doors in Abu Dhabi.And perhaps the quietest meeting in the Gulf this week will eventually prove to have been one of its loudest moves.Liron Rose is an entrepreneur, co-founder of the Masad Haaretz Institute, and creator and host of the geopolitical podcasts Israel Insider and HaYanshuf.Amit Shabi is a former analyst in Intelligence Unit 8200, an investment and capital markets professional, author of several finance books, and a competitive chess player.

title: Making e-scooters safe requires more than fines and enforcement
body: Dubai Police said this week it had seized hundreds of e-scooters and e-bikes for a variety of traffic offences during a road safety drive in one of the emirate’s neighbourhoods. It is the latest action taken to tackle unsafe use of so-called last-mile vehicles. The same authority said last month that it had confiscated more than 13,000 e-scooters since the beginning of the year for dangerous riding, such as speeding. The authorities noted that accidents, incidents and injuries have risen. Abu Dhabi has this year also issued warnings about improper use of such vehicles, as well as disseminating public safety information videos. There has not been a nationwide “census” conducted regarding the volume of e-scooters in active use in the country – nor does there need to be one – but e-bikes and e-scooters are now a ubiquitous presence on neighbourhood roads and cycle path networks, helping reduce congestion and pollution in the process. What is becoming obvious is that more scooters and more journeys means, in all likelihood, the potential for more accidents and incidents. The National reported earlier this year that Ministry of Interior data showed significant e-scooter accidents had increased by 97 per cent last year, from 61 cases to 120. Despite the rapid rise in the headline number, the overall figure is still low. That, of course, provides no comfort to anyone or any family that has been affected by one of those serious accidents. It is in all of our interests to reduce the number of significant incidents to zero, while also recognising we are not sat in the middle of a contagion-level event. Statistical models produced elsewhere in the world suggest every 100,000 e-scooter rides might result in between 10 and 20 accidents requiring medical support or intervention. A significant contributory factor to that global modelling is alcohol intoxication by the e-scooter user, which may be less of a determinant in this region. World Health Organisation figures also report that road traffic injuries of all forms tend to disproportionately affect young people. Globally, unintentional injury, such as that resulting from vehicle collision, is the leading cause of death for people under 30. The rules for e-scooters say riders must be at least 16 years old and wear a helmet when using one. The maximum speed permitted by one of those vehicles is 20 kph. Riders are also required to keep a safe distance from pedestrians, are not allowed to carry passengers or use mobile phones while using them. Reflective clothing is also advised, and any vehicle is meant to be equipped with front and rear lights. The drip-drip of persistent messaging does increase the likelihood of bringing about behavioural change Authorities have said they would take action against riders who cross roads dangerously, weave between lanes or ride outside demarcated or approved zones. Improper use leads to confiscation and fines. Anecdotally, if it is not controversial to say that most road users will have seen an e-scooter rider breach at least one of those rules in day-to-day life. A counter-argument would also say that most drivers break road rules on their daily drives, whether that is speeding, distracted driving , tailgating or another form of anti-social or potentially reckless behaviour. Few drivers are the paragons of road-using virtue that we may think we are and only a small number of drivers willingly identify themselves as “bad” even if their fellow road users might absolutely attest that they are. It is down to every road user to take a higher level of personal responsibility to keep the roads safe. So, how can we realistically reach a state of accident-free nirvana? Education and awareness are key to beating back the rising tide rather than enforcement with last-mile vehicles. Only the utterly rules-driven among us would advocate for round-the-clock and always-visible enforcement of regulations regarding e-scooters, which would be a drain on resources that could not be justified by the thankfully low volume of incidents and accidents. Each time authorities share video footage of e-scooter misuse, however, it helps subtly change behaviour and attitudes towards risk. Road safety campaigns elsewhere in the world on the dangers of driving while intoxicated or failing to use seat belts or child seats have helped change habits and save lives over a prolonged period. Campaigns by Abu Dhabi Police to highlight the dangers of rubber-necking , tailgating and speeding have garnered widespread attention and, inevitably, offer pause for individual reflection and thought. Dubai has set up a unit in relation to e-scooter use to help education and improve safety. All of these things will help. There is also the question of performance-limiters. E-bikes are typically able to achieve limits far in excess of the permitted maximums for the path network, much in the same way as performance cars have the potential to be driven at more than double the speed permitted on the nation’s motorways. While speed limiters are also common in both performance cars and e-bikes, software has the potential to be overridden. Awareness campaigns about the dangers of speeding and the increased risk of injury to the e-scooter user or pedestrians are the best defence in such circumstances. A single information video rarely makes a difference on its own, but the drip-drip of persistent messaging does increase the likelihood of bringing about behavioural change and keeping our path and road network safe.

title: US-led coalition exit shifts more counter-ISIS burden to Iraq and Syria - analysis
body: The US-led coalition formally ended its Operation Inherent Resolve mission in Iraq on September 30 as its remaining forces and equipment completed their withdrawal, shifting primary security responsibility to Baghdad and raising new questions about how Iraq and Syria will monitor their long frontier against ISIS.US Central Command said the transition was part of a planned move toward a bilateral defense relationship between Washington and Baghdad. Combined Joint Task Force-Operation Inherent Resolve remains active, with its headquarters relocated to Jordan, while coalition forces continue counter-ISIS operations in Syria.For Damascus, the shift follows another major change. US forces completed their departure from the al-Tanf garrison in southeastern Syria in February as part of a broader military repositioning. CENTCOM said at the time that American forces would remain capable of responding to ISIS threats in the region and supporting partner-led operations.The transition raises a central question along the Syrian-Iraqi frontier: Can forces on both sides maintain effective surveillance and intelligence sharing as the coalition's military footprint changes?Istanbul-based Iraqi journalist Ali al-Khazali told The Media Line that the most important change after the coalition mission ended has not been a major increase in troop numbers, but a higher state of readiness and greater responsibility for Iraqi forces.Before the transition, he said, Iraq had worked to build a multilayered defensive system along the Syrian border involving border guards, the Iraqi army, and the Popular Mobilization Forces, backed by fortifications and aerial and technical surveillance.“Baghdad tried before the coalition's departure to make the border less dependent on the foreign military presence and to ensure that Iraqi forces themselves hold the ground and manage the file directly,” al-Khazali said.Iraqi authorities had already expanded concrete barriers, trenches, barbed wire, thermal cameras, observation towers, and drone surveillance along the frontier.Stronger fortifications, al-Khazali said, do not mean Baghdad can fully replace everything the coalition provided.Iraqi forces are now capable of handling much of the operational burden inside the country and conducting operations against ISIS cells, he said, but advanced technical and intelligence capabilities remain a more difficult challenge.US capabilities difficult to replace in short term by IraqAccording to al-Khazali, the United States provided aerial surveillance, drones, intelligence imagery, and sophisticated systems for tracking targets and rapidly integrating information from multiple sources - capabilities that will be difficult to replace completely in the short term.“Iraq can compensate for a large part of the coalition's military role, but it has not yet reached the point where it can fully dispense with US support, particularly in intelligence, surveillance, and long-range reconnaissance,” he said.On the Syrian side, political analyst Firas al-Allawi described similar concerns about surveillance and intelligence capabilities.Al-Allawi told The Media Line that there are no clear indications of a broad Syrian military deployment or a major increase in troop numbers along the Iraqi border, although limited redeployments may have taken place recently.“What is available so far does not indicate the transfer of large numbers of troops or major changes along the Syrian-Iraqi border,” al-Allawi said.Coordination between Damascus and Baghdad exists, particularly in the exchange of security information, he said, but it has not yet reached the level of an integrated strategic security partnership.Al-Allawi believes some intelligence cooperation is taking place away from public view, with a significant portion occurring within a broader framework that still involves the United States.“I believe an important part of the information exchange takes place within a broader intelligence cooperation umbrella in which Washington participates, rather than through deep, direct Syrian-Iraqi cooperation,” he said.A degree of mistrust and caution remains between Damascus and Baghdad, according to al-Allawi, making it premature to describe their cooperation as a fully developed joint security system.Al-Khazali offered a similar assessment from the Iraqi side. Direct communication channels, information sharing, and meetings between border officials exist, he said, but publicly available information does not indicate that the two countries operate a permanent joint operations room or fully integrated intelligence center.“What exists is direct communication channels, information exchange, and coordination in some operations,” he said. “But transforming that cooperation into a permanent joint security system is still a work in progress.”Iraqi officials have previously said Baghdad coordinates directly with Syrian authorities to prevent ISIS infiltration, combat smuggling, and exchange security information.ISIS operating through small cells, individual operatives, in shift since 2014The nature of the threat has also changed considerably since 2014.ISIS no longer needs to move large columns of fighters across the border or capture cities and crossings to pose a danger. The group can operate through smaller cells, desert routes, logistical and financial networks, and individual operatives capable of exploiting gaps in surveillance without the kind of large-scale military breakdown seen during its territorial expansion.“The most dangerous gap today is not an open stretch of border or the collapse of fortifications,” al-Khazali said. “The biggest danger is the intelligence gap between the two sides of the border.”The desert corridor between Iraq's Anbar province and Syria's Deir ez-Zor region remains particularly sensitive, he said, because small cells and smuggling networks can exploit vast distances and the difficulty of maintaining continuous surveillance.Al-Allawi identified a similar weakness on the Syrian side.Syria's Badia desert and the broader desert belt extending toward Iraq still suffer from limited aerial surveillance and incomplete intelligence capabilities, he said, while the vast geography makes sustained control difficult.“The area generally remains fragile from both a security and strategic perspective, and the length of the Syrian-Iraqi border makes it even harder to control,” al-Allawi said.Increasing troop numbers insufficient to rein in ISIS, analyst saysAlthough ISIS is far weaker than at the height of its territorial expansion, scattered cells in desert areas could use surveillance gaps to regroup or move personnel, money, and equipment.For that reason, al-Allawi said increasing troop numbers alone will not be enough. Syria needs more advanced surveillance and reconnaissance technology, aerial support, improved equipment, and personnel with greater training in border security, counter-infiltration, and desert operations.Al-Allawi said improved border security will also require broader cooperation with Iraq, the United States, the international coalition, and Jordan rather than relying solely on a larger Syrian military deployment.The ISIS detainee issue further ties Syrian and Iraqi security together.During a 23-day operation that began January 21, US forces transferred more than 5,700 adult male ISIS detainees from facilities in northeastern Syria into Iraqi custody. CENTCOM said the operation was intended to keep the detainees securely held and reduce the risk of an ISIS resurgence.The end of the coalition mission in Iraq does not sever Iraq's security concerns from Syria. Iraq now has responsibility for thousands of ISIS detainees transferred from Syrian facilities, while Damascus must prevent remaining ISIS cells in the Badia from using the frontier for movement and reorganization.Iraqi and Syrian sources agree on one central point: Securing the frontier depends not only on walls, trenches, troops, and surveillance equipment, but on whether information can cross the border faster than ISIS operatives do.

title: Peki SHS old students to break ground for new entrance gate
body: The Peki Senior High School Old Students’ Association (PESCOSA) will hold a sod-cutting ceremony on Friday, 9 October 2026, to begin the construction of a new entrance gate for the school. The ceremony is scheduled to take place at the school’s campus in the South Dayi District of the Volta Region, bringing together alumni, traditional leaders and education officials for the infrastructure initiative. Peki Senior High School, popularly known as PESCO, is one of the region’s oldest secondary schools. The proposed gate will give the institution a new frontage, with an architectural illustration on the event flyer showing a prominent entrance bearing the school’s name and crest. Deiga Kwadzo Dei XII, Paramount Chief of the Peki Traditional Area, is billed as the special guest of honour. Other advertised guests include the South Dayi District Chief Executive, Courage Kokroko; the District Director of Education, Prosper Yevu; and the school’s headmistress, Peace Ama Goka. PESCOSA National President David Kwame Aziago and National Council Chairman Fatherland Kyei are also expected to participate, alongside the school’s Board Chairman, Dr Phanuel Wunu, and its 70th Anniversary CPC Chairman, Dr Collins Kafui Azah. Mr Aziago described the project as the construction of a “befitting entrance gate”, placing alumni support at the centre of the initiative. The ceremony offers former students an opportunity to reconnect with their alma mater and support the development of an institution that has educated generations of Ghanaians.

title: Otti mourns Abia-born pilot who died 16 days after wedding
body: By Steve Oko UMUAHIA — Abia State Governor, Alex Otti, has mourned Squadron Leader Ahamefule Aham Man-Ugwueje, the Abia-born co-pilot who died alongside 24 other Nigerian Air Force personnel in the aircraft crash at Igbokoda, Ondo State. Man-Ugwueje, who hailed from Umuahia, died barely 16 days after he married a fellow Nigerian Air Force officer, Flight Lieutenant Damilola Adekunle, in Abuja. The Nigerian Air Force ATR-42 aircraft, NAF 931, crashed on October 5 while on a routine mission from Benin to Lagos, killing all 25 people on board, including five crew members. Otti, in a condolence message issued by his Special Adviser on Media and Publicity, Ferdinand Ekeoma, described the crash as painful and devastating, saying it had brought “untold sorrow and anguish” to the victims’ families, friends and loved ones, the Nigerian Air Force and the nation. “This accident is both painful and devastating, because it has brought untold sorrow and anguish to the victims’ families, their friends and loved ones, the Nigerian Air Force, and the nation at large,” the governor said. The governor particularly lamented the death of Man-Ugwueje, whose military aviation career was cut short barely two weeks after he exchanged marital vows with his colleague. The couple were married in Abuja on September 19 in a ceremony attended by family members, friends and military colleagues. Man-Ugwueje was reportedly from a military family, with his father said to be a retired Group Captain of the Nigerian Air Force, while his wife also serves in the force. Otti, on behalf of his family, the Abia State Government and the people of the state, condoled with the bereaved families, the people of Umuahia, the Nigerian Air Force and the Federal Government. He prayed for the peaceful repose of the victims and for God to grant their families the strength and comfort to bear the loss. The Nigerian Air Force has described the crash as a major tragedy and ordered a comprehensive investigation to establish the circumstances surrounding the accident. Man-Ugwueje was among the officers serving as crew aboard NAF 931, whose final flight ended in tragedy in the swampy area of Igbokoda, in Ilaje Local Government Area of Ondo State. The post Otti mourns Abia-born pilot who died 16 days after wedding appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: GIZ equips Yei centre to repair tractors for farmers
body: The German development agency GIZ has provided garage tools and maintenance equipment to the Yei Crop Training Centre to help restore tractor services for farmers in Yei River County, local officials and the agency said on Thursday. The equipment, provided through the Community-Driven Rural Development (CDRD) project, is intended to help repair and maintain tractors used for land preparation ahead of upcoming planting seasons. The support includes an air compressor, a mobile diesel welding generator, mechanical toolboxes and personal protective equipment. The equipment is expected to support servicing and field repairs for eight tractors operating across Yei County, according to GIZ. GIZ said years of conflict and inadequate maintenance facilities had left many tractors in Yei out of service, while the few remaining operational machines were struggling to meet demand from farmers. One farmer cited in the GIZ statement said he had been 18th on a waiting list for tractor services but was told the tractor assigned to his farm had broken down after he had been promised ploughing within three days. David Amule, administrator of the Yei Crop Training Centre, welcomed the equipment and said its availability would allow the centre to resume more reliable tractor services for farmers. Isaac Asiki, director of agriculture in the county Agriculture Department, called for the equipment to be put into immediate use and urged those responsible to ensure its proper maintenance. GIZ said repairing the tractors could help at least 3,000 farmers expand the area they cultivate. The serviced machinery is expected to bring more than 10,000 hectares of land into cultivation, it said. The CDRD project will also train tractor operators and farmers in the use of agricultural machinery for ploughing, harrowing and sowing, according to GIZ. GIZ implements the project in South Sudan on behalf of Germany’s Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development. The project is co-funded by the European Union and the Netherlands. The post GIZ equips Yei centre to repair tractors for farmers appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

title: Polish SIM cards found in Russian drones downed in Poland
body:
Polish military prosecutors found Polish SIM cards in some of the Russian drones downed during a Russian mass drone incursion into the country on the night of Sept. 9 to Sept. 10, 2025, RMF24 reported on Oct. 8.
Polish authorities didn't disclose whether three Polish SIM cards had been stolen or obtained illegaly, according to RMF24 . The investigation was discontinued after it did not lead to the identification of the specific people responsible for the Russian incursion.
"The investigation was discontinued because the perpetrator of the crime of violating Polish airspace and thus posing a threat to public safety was not identified," Marcin Kozak, spokesman of the District Prosecutor’s Office in Lublin, said.
On Sept. 9, 2025, more than 30 Gerbera-type drones breached Polish airspace, some of which were shot down by the Polish military, RMF24 reported .
In attacks on Ukraine from the territory of Belarus , Russia likely used Belarusian Long-Term Evolution (LTE) networks, as well as a network of repeater stations on Belarusian territory, to help provide stable signals to Russian Shahed-type drones used in mass attacks on Ukraine, two Ukrainian officials said on Sept. 14, 2026.
The revelation came two days after Russia sent hundreds of drones, hugging Ukraine's northern border, in a rare a mass attack targeting regions in western Ukraine on Sept. 12. Speaking on a Radio NV livestream, Presidential Advisor Serhii "Flash" Beskretnov said the flight path of the drones used in the attack suggested the use of Belarusian mobile networks for the cross-border attacks.
Lacking access to technology like SpaceX's Starlink, Russia consistently uses a mix of innovative radio technology to maintain connection with Shahed-type drones during mass attacks on Ukraine.
On Sept. 13 , 2026, Tusk warned that Russian escalation could intensify in the upcoming months, following Russian strikes on a Polish-Ukrainian border crossing and a passenger train. "The escalation of actions of the Russian Federation is becoming a fact and its examples are getting closer and closer to our borders," Tusk said in a briefing with defense officials . "What can be expected is that the next weeks and months will be a period of very intensive actions from the Russian side. Unfortunately, we cannot rule out that this escalation will also concern our territory."
Poland will change procedures for military aircraft and helicopters that engage objects entering from the direction of Russia, Deputy Defense Minister Cezary Tomczyk said on Sept. 28, 2026. Under the current peacetime procedure, Polish pilots must fly close enough to visually confirm a target in Polish airspace before firing at it.
The new procedures will replace this visual identification with so-called positive identification, meaning the radar reading alone will be enough for the pilot or the operational commander to authorize shooting down the object, Polish broadcaster RMF24 reported.
This procedure would allow Polish forces to shoot down missiles or drones entering Polish airspace from the direction of Russia faster than previously.

title: Police arrest prophet’s son over alleged ₦18m Facebook fraud
body: By James Ogunnaike, Abeokuta ABEOKUTA — The Ogun State Police Command has arrested a man identified as Adewale Ogoemi Arojah for allegedly impersonating a renowned cleric on Facebook and defrauding unsuspecting members of the public of more than ₦18 million. The suspect allegedly duplicated the Facebook profile of Prophet Dr Muyiwa Akogun and used the cleric’s identity to target people seeking prayers and spiritual assistance, according to the police. The command’s Public Relations Officer, DSP Oluseyi Babasuyi, disclosed this in a statement on Thursday, saying the arrest followed a complaint lodged by Akogun on October 3, 2026.
