title: France to start training Ukrainian pilots on Rafale warplanes in November, minister says
body: PARIS — France will begin training Ukrainian pilots on the Rafale fighter jet next month, Armed Forces Minister Catherine Vautrin said in a parliamentary hearing on Thursday. “We are continuing our discussions regarding the combat aviation component, particularly regarding the Rafale,” Vautrin told French lawmakers in response to questions about aid to Ukraine during a 2027 defense-budget hearing here. “From November, we will begin the first training of Ukrainian pilots on Rafale.” Ukrainian pilots will soon begin training on Rafale aircraft in France, a major step forward for Ukraine’s combat aviation, the country’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a Telegram post on Monday, citing a conversation with his French counterpart Emmanuel Macron. Ukraine in July agreed on a roadmap with France that included a plan to buy 16 Rafale fighter jets together with the accompanying weapon systems. The country has previously received F-16 jets from several European countries, Mirage 2000 fighters from France, and in May agreed to buy 20 new Gripen jets , with Sweden donating 16 units of an older model. The first Rafale jets are expected to fly in Ukrainian skies in 2028 or 2029, Macron said in July. Both countries are continuing to work on localizing production of French missiles and aerial bombs in Ukraine, Zelenskyy said on Monday. Vautrin said in her hearing that a licensing process is currently underway for missiles. “We are fully aware that by supporting Ukraine, we are defending Europe,” Vautrin said. As part of the July agreement, Ukraine would also acquire an initial batch of SAMP/T NG air-defense batteries with missiles, Macron said at the time. The countries further approved licensing agreements for production in Ukraine of the AASM glide-bomb kit, the Aster 30 air-defense interceptor that arms the SAMP/T, as well as the SCALP/Storm Shadow air-launched cruise missile. Ukraine has already operated an older version of the French-Italian SAMP/T air-defense system, which relies on the Aster family of interceptors manufactured by MBDA. The country also uses the AASM Hammer precision glide-bomb developed by Safran. Ukraine in November last year signed a letter of intent to buy up to 100 of Rafale jets manufactured by Dassault Aviation, after a similar letter of intent a month earlier between Ukraine and Sweden for the export of up to 150 Gripen jets , produced by Saab. The Rafale integrates MBDA’s Meteor, considered by analysts to be one of the best long-range air-to-air missiles in service with Western militaries. The aircraft also features a high-end electronic warfare suite and a radar from Thales, both of which were upgraded as part of the Rafale’s F4.1 standard, qualified in March 2023 .

title: Full UAH 20 mln bail paid for Mudra – HACC
body:
Bail of UAH 20 million set by the court as an alternative to detention has been paid in full for former deputy head of the Office of the President Iryna Mudra, who is suspected in cases involving money laundering and raiding, the High Anti-Corruption Court (HACC) told Interfax-Ukraine.
"The bail has been paid in full," the court said on Thursday.
On August 25, the HACC ordered Mudra's detention with an alternative of UAH 20 million bail. Mudra said she would try to raise the amount. The HACC Appeals Chamber subsequently upheld the decision. The bail had not been paid into the HACC account since then, and Mudra remained in pretrial detention.
On September 24, the HACC found that Mudra's rights had been violated and ordered the National Bank of Ukraine to determine why banks were refusing to accept the bail payment.
Earlier that day, the NBU said bank representatives had cited among the reasons for refusing such transactions the lack of documentary proof of the source of funds, including cash, splitting bail payments into multiple transactions and the use of shell companies to make payments.
The following day, the NBU said it had taken note of the HACC ruling concerning bail payments and would respond within its powers after receiving the official document.
On September 28, lawyers from Miller law firm, which represents Mudra, said the NBU had failed to comply with the September 24 HACC ruling ordering it to determine why banks were refusing to accept the bail.
On September 28, the HACC upheld Mudra's pretrial measure of detention with an alternative of UAH 20 million bail. Her defense had asked for the bail to be reduced to UAH 13 million, which had already been transferred to the court's account by that time.
On August 19, the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) and Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO) released a video about an operation codenamed Forest Gump, saying they had exposed and notified suspects of the laundering of UAH 150 million to pay bail for a suspect in the Midas case. The group included, among others, a deputy head of the Office of the President and a former member of parliament. Later that day, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed a decree dismissing Mudra as deputy head of the Office of the President.
On August 20, NABU and SAPO released a second video concerning corruption involving the same senior officials, codenamed Femida, describing the exposure of alleged illegal acquisition of real estate and corporate assets through forged documents. Mudra, a former deputy head of the Office of the President, also features in this episode.
Later on August 20, NABU and SAPO commented on the videos released earlier under the names Forest Gump and Femida concerning alleged corruption schemes involving senior officials of the Office of the President, a former and a current member of parliament. "The activities of the criminal organization were aimed, among other things, at acquiring high-value real estate and other assets of legal entities through unauthorized interference in the operation of information (automated) networks of the Ministry of Justice of Ukraine, forgery of court decisions and title documents," NABU said in a Telegram post.
NABU also said that in June 2026, certain members of the alleged criminal organization, acting in collusion with representatives and officials of a state-owned bank, had organized and facilitated the laundering of criminal proceeds.
"Based on the evidence obtained, NABU detectives and SAPO prosecutors notified members of the criminal organization and persons they had involved of suspicion under Articles 255, 191, 206-2, 209, 358 and 361 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine," SAPO said.

title: BlaKid reflects on Shatta Wale collaboration and TGMA recognition
body: Ghanaian artiste BlaKid Music says working with Shatta Wale taught him valuable lessons about consistency, confidence and work ethic. The singer was speaking on Prime Time with George Quaye. The discussion centred on his breakthrough, recognition at the Telecel Ghana Music Awards (TGMA), and his feature on Shatta Wale’s projects. BlaKid described getting the call to work with Shatta Wale as a turning point in his career. According to him, being in the studio and on projects with the multiple award-winning dancehall artiste was more than just music, it was a masterclass in consistency, confidence and work ethic. He said Shatta Wale taught him the importance of believing in his sound and staying true to his craft, even when the industry gets tough. “Working with Shatta Wale opened my eyes. His energy, his drive, how he treats music like business, I learnt a lot. He encourages young artistes to push and not wait for anyone,” BlaKid said. He added that the collaboration has introduced his music to a much bigger audience and given him credibility among industry players. Reflecting on his TGMA experience, BlaKid said earning recognition at Ghana’s biggest music awards night was both humbling and motivating. He described the night as a celebration of hard work and noted that for a young artiste like himself, just being mentioned on that platform is a win. He admitted, however, that the journey has not been easy. From funding his own productions to getting airplay and breaking through a saturated market, the challenges are real. “The industry is not easy for upcoming artistes. You need to invest a lot, you need a good team, and you need to stay consistent. But awards like TGMA show that people are watching your work,” he stated. BlaKid, who is known for blending Afrobeats with Highlife and Dancehall influences, said he is currently working on new music and hopes to drop a project in the coming months. His focus now, he said, is to build on the momentum from the TGMA recognition and the Shatta Wale feature to reach audiences beyond Ghana. He also thanked his growing fan base for their loyalty and urged other young creatives not to give up. “To every young artiste out there, keep working. Your time will come. Don’t stop because of the challenges,” he added.

title: Uzbekistan’s Centrum Air Apologizes After Uzbek-Language Dispute
body: Uzbekistan’s Centrum Air has apologized to a passenger removed from a flight after a dispute over his request to be addressed in Uzbek. The airline initially accused the man of aggressive behavior but later acknowledged that the flight attendant had been at fault. The incident occurred on October 5 during boarding for flight C6468 from Samara to Tashkent. Daryo reported that a passenger named Komiljon had asked a flight attendant to speak to him in Uzbek after she requested his boarding pass in Russian. According to Komiljon, an argument followed, and the captain refused to allow him to travel. In an October 5 statement , Centrum Air disputed his account, alleging that he had behaved aggressively and insulted the flight attendant. It said he had disrupted boarding and defended the captain’s decision on safety grounds. The airline also said it was considering contacting law enforcement. Komiljon denied insulting the employee. Centrum Air said its flight attendants speak Uzbek, Russian, and English and can communicate with passengers in their preferred language . Komiljon traveled from Samara to Moscow before taking another flight to Tashkent, incurring additional expenses. Following a review, senior airline executive Ma’murjon Mamadaliyev acknowledged that the flight attendant had been wrong and had admitted her mistake. He said the airline would cover the passenger’s additional travel costs. In a later video, the flight attendant apologized to Komiljon in Uzbek, according to Batafsil.uz . Komiljon accepted the apology and said that he had received compensation. The airline’s later statement did not clarify whether it had withdrawn its original allegations about the passenger’s behavior.

title: Cabinet retains preferential electricity tariffs for households through 2026/27 heating season – Koretsky
body:
The Cabinet of Ministers has decided to keep electricity prices unchanged for households through the 2026/27 heating season, Prime Minister of Ukraine Serhiy Koretsky said.

"Following the decision on natural gas, the government has retained the current preferential electricity tariffs for households for the 2026/27 heating season. The decision was made taking into account the country's current socioeconomic situation," Koretsky said on Telegram.

According to him, the decision also covers households with electric heating, for which electricity prices will also remain unchanged.

"In the future, the government will work to improve the tariff-setting system and introduce a fairer system of targeted support for those citizens who actually need it," the prime minister added.

As reported, at the end of September the Cabinet retained current preferential gas prices for households and heat producers until March 31, that is, through the end of the heating season.

title: When vulnerability shows up, run – Rev. Daniel Annan cautions women
body: Counsellor Rev. Daniel Annan has urged women to identify situations that expose their vulnerabilities and remove themselves before making regrettable decisions. The Resident Pastor of the Universal Gospel Center, speaking in an exclusive interview with host Mauvie the Motivator on Joy Prime’s Let’s Talk on Tuesday, said every woman has a point of vulnerability, but many are not aware of it until they find themselves in compromising situations. According to him, a lot of women struggle to say no when their emotions take over, and that is where they become most vulnerable. “There are times that people are vulnerable,” he stated. Rev. Annan explained that vulnerability is not a weakness, but a state where a person’s emotional strength, reasoning and decision-making are low. He gave practical examples of moments when women are most vulnerable, including when meeting an ex-lover, when under the influence of alcohol, when seeking validation from friends, or when they are emotionally down and in need of comfort. The counsellor warned that if a woman does not identify those triggers, she can easily make decisions she will later regret. He therefore advised women to detach themselves from anything or anyone that makes them vulnerable, and to be disciplined about their boundaries. Rev. Annan urged women to study themselves and understand their own patterns and emotional responses. “Know yourself and understand yourself to know that when your vulnerability is showing up, you are not strong. Run away once vulnerability shows up,” he cautioned. The counsellor expressed worry that many women find it difficult to refuse things they do not want to do, even when it goes against their values. “We need to help women to build their capacity. One of the things I find most women are not able to say is to say no,” he said. He explained that the fear of offending people is a major reason why women say yes when they actually want to say no. According to him, some women are concerned about being seen as rude, disrespectful, or as someone who did not treat the other person well, so they compromise to please others. Rev. Annan stressed that without building capacity in how to reason, how to make choices, how to take decisions and how to apply wisdom, any situation can easily sweep a person away. “There are some people, if you don’t build your capacity in terms of how you reason, in terms of your choices, in terms of your decisions and in terms of wisdom, anything comes and if you are not careful you will fall for it,” he explained. He encouraged women to invest in personal growth, self-awareness and emotional intelligence. He said building capacity helps a woman to set healthy boundaries, make sound decisions and protect her dignity. Rev. Annan added that learning to say no is not about being disrespectful, but about knowing your values and standing by them, even when it is uncomfortable. The interview forms part of Joy Prime’s Let’s Talk series, which focuses on relationships, mental health and personal development.

title: Barcelona hero Pedro calls time on remarkable career 'having lived my dream'
body: So little was known of Barcelona ’s Pedro at the start of his breakthrough 2009-10 season that one respected British website listed him as four different people. The son of a petrol station worker from Tenerife’s capital Santa Cruz, Pedro Rodriguez Ledesma’s 23 goals from 52 games were shared between ‘Pedro’, ‘Pedrito’, ‘Rodriguez’ and ‘Ledesma’. Those goals were often crucial and when Pedro scored in the Fifa Club World Cup in 2009, he became the first to score in six different club competitions in one season. Seven months later, he was a World Cup winner with Spain. “I can’t believe what’s happened,” he said at the end of the 2009-10 season. He was a character – as was noted during Barca’s title celebrations. As the victors took to the microphone and shouted “Forever Barca, Forever Catalunya”, Pedro stepped up and hollered “Forever Barca, Forever Tenerife!” Even the most earnest Catalans laughed. “In 12 months I established myself a regular for Barca,” he says. “I’d only played eight first team league games before last season – though I did come on in the 2009 Champions League final against Manchester [United]. In 2009-10, we won the league with Barca again and I was selected for Spain. Then Spain won the World Cup. Incredible – it was beyond a dream.” Siento que es el momento. El momento para dar un paso adelante y comenzar una nueva etapa en mi vida. Me voy orgulloso por haber vivido mi sueño y por todas las personas que estuvieron a mi lado para hacerlo realidad. Gracias fútbol por hacerme tan feliz. ❤️⚽️ pic.twitter.com/4sEI3GFGQU — Pedro Rodríguez (@_Pedro17_) October 7, 2026 Pedro became a World Cup winner just six weeks after making his Spain debut. “I played against Saudi Arabia in May,” he explains, “then scored my first goal a week later. I played in five World Cup games.” Being one of seven Barca men in the Spain squad, most of whom were regular starters in South Africa, also helped. Sixteen years on and there’s no confusion about who Pedro is. After 776 first-team matches for Barcelona, Chelsea, Roma and then their deadly rivals Lazio, plus another 65 for Spain, he’s calling it a day. Along the way he won 25 trophies including one World Cup, one European Championship, three Uefa Champions Leagues, five La Liga titles and one Premier League. On Thursday, he visited Camp Nou, scene of most of those triumphs. On Friday, he held a press conference to announce his retirement. It was met with lavish praise for a fine career. You will always be part of our history. Thank you for everything, @_Pedro17_ ! 💙❤️ pic.twitter.com/VtHqJWrwBp — FC Barcelona (@FCBarcelona) October 7, 2026 Early on he put much of his success down to Barça’s youth academy, which included a season under Luis Enrique for Barca B. “The club have a very clear idea of how we should play football,” he said. “Receive, pass, move. Learn to do this very quickly and you have an advantage. “We also have role models in front of us. I could see players like Xavi and [Andres] Iniesta, they could see players like El Mister [Pep Guardiola]. Youth gets a chance here.” Opinion was long divided on the best position for the two-footed winger. “I can play on both sides, but I play more on the left so I’d have to say that,” he said. “As for my feet, I use my right more. I tend to score twice as many goals with my right as my left.” Pedro was fortunate in that he entered the best team in the world and played alongside its greatest player, Lionel Messi. “Messi is the best player in the world, we all know that,” he said. “The skills he has, his pace and vision, they make it impossible for defenders. But the best thing about Barca is that we’re a team. We work for each other, not for ourselves and we have great players in every position”. Pedro’s footballing education allowed him to thrive wherever he went. Manchester United wanted to sign him but he went instead to Chelsea in 2015 after 321 games for the Catalans. At Stamford Bridge, he learnt English and celebrated the League title and FA Cup. He also averaged 45 games per season in his first four years in London, the mark of a player seldom injured. He played more than 50 club games in four different seasons at Barcelona. Former Barça, Chelsea and Spain forward Pedro has announced his retirement from football, aged 39. Don't sleep on his continental and international trophy collection 🏆 pic.twitter.com/nwuDXRqwuR — B/R Football (@brfootball) October 7, 2026 After 206 Chelsea games he moved to Rome, first for 40 games in a season at Roma, then five full seasons at Lazio where he again averaged more than 40 club games per season. As recently as 2024-25, when he was 37, he still scored 14 goals, including Lazio’s goal of the year. Pedro is 39 but the stats don’t tell the full story since his games for Barca B aren’t counted, yet in more than 100 games for Barcelona’s junior sides he was playing against the first teams of clubs such as Real Betis and Zaragoza as a full professional. In total, Pedro played an astonishing 902 club games and scored 215 goals, plus another 65 goals and 17 games for Spain. He played his last game for Spain almost a decade ago and courted rare controversy when he said his role as a substitute during Euro 2016 was not worth his time, a rare, outspoken comment for this always loyal and unselfish servant. “I feel that the time has come,” he said as he retired. “The time to take a step forward and begin a new stage in my life. I leave proud of having lived my dream and of all the people who were by my side to make it come true. Thank you, football, for making me so happy”.

title: How IBBU students are rebuilding campus journalism
body:
For two days in early July, dozens of student journalists gathered at the ICT Centre at Ibrahim Badamasi Babangida University (IBBU), Lapai, Niger State, for a capacity-building workshop.
They learnt the fundamentals of news writing, investigative reporting, inclusive reporting, hyperlocal journalism, and digital storytelling through the Next Gen Campus Reporter Clinic, organised by the Centre for Journalism Innovation and Development (CJID).
But beyond notebooks, presentations, and newsroom simulations, another story was unfolding quietly.
For many of the students, the training represented something bigger than learning how to write better stories. It marked the beginning of an effort to breathe life back into the university’s Union of Campus Journalists (UCJ), a body whose activities had dwindled over the years despite a growing population of Mass Communication students.
“When I joined, there wasn’t much activity,” the UCJ president, Beauty Brendan, recalled.
“Most students focused on their academics, and the union wasn’t functioning the way it should.”
The UCJ IBBUL Chapter was created in 2020, with support from the National Union of Campus Journalists (NUCJ), then headed by Ibrahim Adeyemi. The then President of the Mass Communication Students’ Association (MACOSA), Yakubu Mohammed, invited NUCJ to conduct training and to launch UCJ on the campus.
The pioneer president of the UCJ was Zainab Abdullahi, said Mr Mohammed, now an investigative journalist with PREMIUM TIMES.
But the union has struggled to stay afloat since the first set of members left campus.
“All the presidents and vice presidents the union has had were appointed when they were in their penultimate years. This made continuity a problem, because the moment the top executives left, a vacuum set in, leaving their successors and members in some sort of confusion,” said Mr Mohammed.
Ms Brendan believes that inactivity of the UCJ has created an information vacuum on campus.
“We don’t have a reliable source of verified information,” she said. “That’s one of the reasons we’re trying to revive the union.”
Her concerns are shared by the department’s Staff Adviser, Andrew Ngele, who argues that campus journalism is far more than a student extracurricular activity.
“A university is like a small city within a larger society,” Mr Ngele said. “The role journalism plays here is no different from the role it plays outside the campus.”
According to him, a vibrant campus journalism union creates a culture of transparency by allowing students to question decisions affecting their welfare and the university community.
Mr Yakubu, one of the patrons of the university’s UCJ, said he then advised the outgoing executives to use students in the first and second years as executives so they have more time to grow the association.
He said the patrons and lecturers continue to train them as they look out for successors either in 100 or 200 level.
“We adopted a catch-them-young approach,” he said.
“That strategy started with this current set, and honestly it has been working. They now have a Substack handle, social media accounts where they share news and other content.”
Referencing Section 22 of Nigeria’s Constitution, which assigns the press the responsibility of holding the government accountable, Mr Ngele said student journalists should see themselves as contributors to accountability within the university.
“If there are issues around infrastructure, student welfare, or the use of public resources, students should be able to ask questions,” he said. “Campus journalism creates that space.”
For students like Deborah Lukman, that message resonated immediately.
Ms Lukman had stumbled on the training after seeing a registration link shared on her departmental platform. Curious, she researched the programme and decided to apply.
“I’ve always wanted to become a journalist,” she said.
By the end of the two-day clinic, she said her understanding of the profession had changed completely.
“I thought investigative journalism was like what you see in movies,” she admitted with a laugh. “Now I understand there are ethical and professional ways of gathering information and uncovering stories.”
“I’m naturally curious,” she said. “I enjoy asking questions and helping people become aware of what’s happening around them. Journalism is not just about writing stories; it’s about serving the public interest.”
That curiosity, however, will need more than enthusiasm to survive.
Ms Brendan acknowledges that while students are willing to rebuild the UCJ, several obstacles stand in the way.
“The challenge isn’t that we don’t have ideas,” she explained. “We need stronger editorial skills, better equipment, and more support. Sometimes it’s even difficult getting members together because everyone is trying to balance academics with other responsibilities.”
These challenges reflect a broader concern within journalism education.
The President of the Mass Communication Students’ Association (MACOSA), Aminu Turaki, believes many students are attracted to journalism until they encounter the realities of the profession.
“Many students say they want to practise journalism,” Mr Turaki said. “But when they discover the amount of work involved in reporting, writing, editing, and verifying information, the enthusiasm begins to reduce.”
He noted that some students are drawn to the visibility associated with television and media personalities without appreciating the discipline that happens behind every published story.
To bridge that gap, the department has increasingly encouraged practical newsroom experience alongside classroom instruction, giving students opportunities to produce and publish stories while still in school.
“A vibrant UCJ gives students an independent platform to practise journalism before graduation,” he said.
Mr Ngele believes those practical experiences are essential because journalism cannot be learnt solely from textbooks.
Students, he said, must learn to ask difficult questions, verify facts, and report responsibly, even when doing so feels uncomfortable.
“I understand why students may be afraid,” he said. “But intimidation is part of the profession. As long as your reporting is factual and motivated by public interest rather than malice, you should not be afraid to tell important stories.”
For the young reporters inside the ICT Centre, that lesson may prove to be the most enduring takeaway.
The clinic did more than teach inverted pyramids, interviewing techniques, or newsroom ethics. It challenged students to see journalism as a public service rather than merely a career path.
By the close of the programme, conversations had shifted from note-taking to story ideas. Students were grouped into teams and were assigned to come up with story ideas on issues affecting their campus and the surrounding Lapai community.
Ms Brendan sees that renewed energy as the beginning of something bigger.
“If we continue applying what we’ve learnt here,” she said, “I believe UCJ can become a trusted platform for credible campus journalism.”
Whether that ambition materialises will depend on sustained mentorship, institutional support, and the determination of students willing to do the difficult work journalism demands.
But if the conversations inside IBBU’s ICT Centre are any indication, the revival of campus journalism has already begun, not with headlines, but with a generation of young reporters learning that the most important stories are often the ones closest to home.

title: Iran targeting US military bases in Germany, weeks after Israel warned partners - report
body: Iranian intelligence services are targeting US military bases in Germany, including Ramstein and Spangdahlem, amid concerns over potential covert attacks linked to the Iran conflict, German news outlet WirtschaftsWoche reported on Thursday.Israel warned US and German partners three weeks ago of a potential threat, with concern focused on bases supporting US military operations and logistics linked to the conflict with Iran, the report said, citing several unnamed Western intelligence officials.The German defense ministry and the US forces in Germany were not immediately available for comment.Israel warned Germany of Iranian threat against air bases On Saturday, The New York Times reported that Israel had warned Germany of an increased risk of attacks against US military bases on its territory, particularly Ramstein Air Base and Spangdahlem Air Base.Both Ramstein and Spangdahlem are used by NATO air forces, with the former serving as the headquarters for the United States Air Forces in Europe – Air Forces Africa and NATO Allied Air Command.The intelligence assessments also included concerns about possible drone attacks, but did not point to a specific time or target.Idan Kweller contributed to this report.

title: Inside Operation Vivaldi — how Ukraine uses drones, robots to liberate territory in Donetsk Oblast
body:
Tsyhan and Kalash, combat wing operators of the Darts crew of the NAFO, the 66th Mechanized Brigade, set the drone up for launch in the Lyman sector, Donetsk Oblast, Ukraine, on Aug. 11, 2026. (Diana Delyurman / The Kyiv Independent)
DONETSK OBLAST — On a screen, live footage from a reconnaissance drone shows two men in Ukrainian pixel camouflage dashing in short bursts through the ruins of apartment buildings. Then they vanish into a basement.
It is late summer, and the 3rd Army Corps and attached units are fully engaged in a counteroffensive in the Lyman sector called Operation Vivaldi . Russian forces are trying to recapture Lyman, a city in Donetsk Oblast that Russian officials have claimed their forces control. Ukrainian infantry on the ground tell a different story.
For weeks, the operation ran under a news blackout until 3rd Army Corps commander Brig. Gen. Andrii Biletskyi made it public on Sept. 15 . By late September, the corps said it had retaken 176 square kilometers using closely coordinated infantry, air defense, electronic warfare, aerial drone units, and unmanned ground vehicles.
Watching the video feed are drone operators from the 66th Mechanized Brigade, subordinate to the 3rd Army Corps. They are waiting for a batch of Darts, fixed-wing strike drones, to join the fight for Lyman .
Their commander, call sign Deputat, is rushing to bring the drones. His car races down a road beneath tunnels of anti-drone netting, pine forests on either side, a landscape typical of northern Donetsk Oblast. Out of the darkness, a roadside coffee stand appears, glowing faintly. The car speeds past, then turns off onto rough ground.
"Turn on the electronic warfare device," Deputat orders a soldier in the car.
After some time, Deputat stops, quickly unloads the cargo, shakes hands with the soldiers, and drives off. The crew carries the drones into the dugout. They moved into this position only recently, after pushing closer to the front line. The gray zone is less than 10 kilometers away.
Four men live, sleep, and work in the cramped shelter. Crews usually rotate every couple of weeks, but heavy Russian shelling near the positions can delay a rotation.
In one corner is a workstation: a desk with several screens, one showing a video call with other units, another a live map of Donetsk Oblast. The areas marked gray or occupied are different from the picture Russian commanders paint. The soldiers listen to the call as they prepare to join a combined strike.
For hours, units attached to the 3rd Army Corps have been striking a Russian artillery position with HIMARS rockets and drones. According to the 3rd Army Corps, such missions play a crucial role in the operation by pushing Russian mortar and artillery crews out of the area and clearing the way for the infantry.
On the call, someone says, "If I were in their shoes, I'd hop on a motorcycle and get the hell out of there." The soldiers in the dugout laugh. The Ukrainians say the Russian crew won't abandon its howitzer because its soldiers are more afraid of their own commanders.
The strike is delayed. As the wait drags on, the young men grow restless and step out into the dugout's corridor to smoke. Kalash, a soldier with light stubble, is the oldest in the crew. The others jokingly call him Mom. As he cooks breakfast on a camping stove, the smell of scrambled eggs and sausage fills the damp air.
Finally, the duty officer on the call says, "Let's start the mission."
"This is the NAFO crew. We want to join the strike on the howitzer," replies a soldier with the call sign Intelihent, who is piloting today. Every member of the crew can do every job: assemble the drone, prepare it for launch, navigate for the pilot, and fly the strike.
Tsyhan, tall and tanned, assembles a Dart. It reminds him of building Lego as a kid, he says. He and Kalash carry the drone out into the field, set it up for launch, and talk over the radio with the men in the dugout.
"Get out of there," comes the voice over the radio.
The drone must fly several dozen kilometers. Intelihent works the controls while Bratok, a dark-haired soldier, helps him navigate. Back in the dugout, all four stare at the screen, fidgeting nervously on the wooden bench.
"NAFO, locking on target," Intelihent says.
The drone strikes. Direct hit. The men cheer and clink cans of energy drink.
On the reconnaissance drone's feed, a stand of trees bursts into flames. Russian soldiers run out of a dugout and try to put out the fire. Then the feed cuts out. Pleased, the men post screenshots to the platoon's group chat. But someone on the call reports that the smoke is clearing and the target has survived. They must strike again.
"Don't worry, we've got plenty of planes," Kalash tells the others.
But the threat of retaliatory strikes looms over the dugout. Drone operators are among Russia's top targets.
"I think it'll be a few days before they come after us," Tsyhan says.
Eventually, several Ukrainian units working together destroy the Russian artillery position. The 3rd Army Corps said coordination between neighboring units played a key role in the operation.
The men finish the breakfast Kalash made. Some stretch out on camping mats on the wooden benches and sleep fully dressed. Another strike request could come at any moment.
Bratok is on duty, keeping an eye on the screens. To pass the time, he flips through live feeds from reconnaissance drones and unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs). On the screens, the war plays out in real time across the Lyman sector. The video feed from a ground robot catches his eye: a dirt road, and in the corner a tiny call sign that reads Kuzya.
Elsewhere in the Lyman sector, Kuzya himself is watching the same feed. The young redhead was one of the first UGV operators in the 66th Brigade's tank battalion. He used to be a driver, risking his life to bring food, medicine, and ammunition to the infantry. He still delivers supplies, but at far less risk. His UGVs can carry half a metric ton of cargo and keep going even after hitting a mine.
The battalion began building up its UGV capabilities in early 2026. They learned how to use ground drones from the 3rd Army Corps. Now, the 66th Brigade ranks among the top five units for UGV use, according to the Delta system's June 2026 rating. According to the team, its 20 operators now cover most of the battalion's logistics, running 100 to 150 missions a month and rarely taking a day off.
At first, the battalion's commanders were skeptical of the robots, until a heavily mined road left them unable to resupply a group of Mavic operators. Today, UGVs play an important role in Operation Vivaldi. The 96th Separate Support Battalion’s robots move ahead of the infantry and clear mines. Some are carried behind Russian lines by drones and launch an assault. But less visible work, logistics, matters just as much.
"Soldiers win battles, but logistics wins wars," says Aibolit, a burly man whose long beard gives him a Viking look. At the UGV hub, he decides which cargo goes on which vehicle.
The increased use of UGVs for logistics in the 3rd Army Corps and its attached units means infantry can reach the front line in armored vehicles or on foot, carrying only light backpacks. Reliable logistics also lets support teams deliver small comforts to the front, lifting the morale of infantrymen who may hold the same position for a month.
Orders come in every day. A soldier can order something in the morning and be drinking a soda in the gray zone by midnight. "It's like ordering pizza," Aibolit says.
As evening falls, the men prepare two vehicles, open platforms on massive wheels, for a mission. They load packs of bottled water, fuel canisters, a generator, and sealed boxes of food the soldiers ordered. It takes them only minutes.
"Is the sky clear?" Aibolit asks over the radio.
"Negative. Lancet threat," comes the reply.
"We're holding all movement," Aibolit says.
A drone icon flashes on their screens. It seems to be heading straight for the hub. "Maybe it'll come here, maybe somewhere else," one of them says, and shrugs. The soldiers play it down, saying their town is quiet, yet not a day goes by without a Russian strike. To disrupt Ukrainian logistics, Russian forces freely use guided bombs, including against targets with no apparent military value.
Once the threat has passed, the men drive the vehicles out into the yard. A few minutes later, the robots roll off into the darkness.
Kuzya usually takes the vehicles into the gray zone, where the ground is heavily mined. He knows every pothole and bush on the route. His screen is almost entirely black, except for a stretch of cratered road lit by the robot's headlight.
Along the way, he passes wrecked cars marked with a white "Z." Stray dogs run up and bark at the strange visitor. Before long, they get used to it and trot alongside until they lose interest. Kuzya smiles.
Eventually, the robot stops. Soldiers in camouflage appear on the black-and-white screen and quickly unload the cargo. One walks up to the camera and gives Kuzya a thumbs-up before they disappear into the woods.
Kuzya turns the robot around to reload for the next mission. On a narrow dirt road, it meets another robot, and the two little vehicles circle each other as if they were dancing.
That evening, Deputat drives back from another delivery to his soldiers, beneath the netting, stars peeking through the mesh. A burned-out SUV, recently hit by a Russian Lancet, lies by the roadside.
"When you're coming back from the positions and you see the coffee stand, you know you're safe," he says.
Diana Deliurman is a Ukrainian independent journalist and photographer. Born in Odesa, Ukraine, in 2000, she earned a degree in History of Art from Taras Shevchenko National University of Kyiv. During her studies, she began her journalism career, taking part in various training programs and fellowships, including an internship at the Kyiv bureau of Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty. Since then, her reporting and photography have been published by outlets including The Kyiv Independent, The Telegraph, The Conversationalist, Frontliner, and LB.ua. She is also a contributor to Getty Images.

title: I’m Not Aware Ransom Was Paid For Release Of Abducted Corps Members — Imo CP
body: The Imo State Police Command has said it is unaware that a ransom was paid for the release of the 20 abducted corps members and one other who regained freedom from their abductors in the state. ﻿ The Commissioner of Police in Imo State, Audu Bosso, stated this during an interview with Channels Television on Thursday. Bosso said that the kidnappers succumbed to pressure from security agencies who combed the forest during a rescue operation. The commissioner, however, said that the freed victims were receiving attention at the office of the Department of State Services (DSS). The prospective National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) members and one other were abducted along the Owerri-Onitsha Road in the state on October 1 while travelling from Ibadan, Oyo State, to NYSC orientation camps in Abia and Akwa Ibom states. Following the abduction, security agencies launched a coordinated search-and-rescue operation to locate the victims and their abductors. The Imo State Police Command had earlier said its operatives located the kidnappers’ camp through drone surveillance but were unable to immediately enter the location because it was reportedly mined with improvised explosive devices (IEDs). The police later deployed additional operational assets as efforts intensified to reach the victims. The abduction created worry among the victims’ families following reports that the abductors demanded₦50 million for each victim. Police had earlier confirmed that 10 victims were rescued following the attack, while efforts continued to locate the remaining abductees. The latest development brings an end to the ordeal of the 20 corps members and the other abducted victim, who have now been reunited with safety and are receiving medical attention in Owerri. The victims were, however, released from the Amakohia-Ubi forest in Owerri West Local Government Area of the state on Wednesday following a coordinated operation involving security agencies. Imo State Governor, Hope Uzodimma, commended security agencies for their quick intervention. In a statement he personally signed, Governor Uzodimma expressed satisfaction with the collaborative efforts of both the Oyo and Imo state governments towards the quick release of the captives. The post I’m Not Aware Ransom Was Paid For Release Of Abducted Corps Members — Imo CP appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Ukrainian negotiating team to visit USA on Friday and Saturday – Zelenskyy
body:
The Ukrainian negotiating delegation is in Europe on Thursday and is scheduled to be in the United States on Friday and Saturday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.

"Our negotiating team is in Europe today and will be in the UA tomorrow and the day after; I hope that all the relevant signals will be conveyed to the USA," Zelenskyy told reporters in Pryluky on Thursday.

The President emphasized that the USA "needs to raise the stakes through sanctions and other measures, as well as financial aid" and air defense support for Ukraine, thereby compelling Putin to come to the negotiating table.

title: Epicentr launches Ukrainian fashion section on marketplace
body:
Epicentr has launched a Ukrainian fashion section on its epicentrk.ua marketplace, which currently features more than 100 Ukrainian clothing, footwear and accessories brands, the company's press service said.
"The scale and infrastructure of Epicentr give Ukrainian fashion brands access to millions of potential buyers (...) We want to break the stereotype that designer fashion cannot be represented on a large marketplace. We are convinced that Ukrainian brands can enter the mass market while retaining their uniqueness and exclusivity," Epicentr Marketplace CEO Yulia Pinteskul said, according to the press release.
The company said the new area is being developed in partnership with Kapsula, a fashion retailer specializing in cooperation with Ukrainian manufacturers of designer clothing and footwear.
The new marketplace section was launched in September and currently offers about 10,000 product listings, including brands already known to Ukrainian consumers such as Fiore Bianco, Foberini, get dressed, Inro, J.D.Wool, Marie Fresh, MMSW, MY x MY, OUN, Piel Cosmetics, Rosca, The Lace and Fire Rabbit, among others. In addition to clothing, footwear and accessories, the site also offers beauty, perfume and lifestyle products from well-known Ukrainian manufacturers.
The company said the new category is intended to expand the presence of Ukrainian fashion brands in online commerce. Sellers will be able to use Epicentr's infrastructure for order delivery, fitting and returns.
Customers will receive free delivery, while sellers will pay a fixed UAH 35 fee covering logistics costs if an order is refused or a product is returned, including delivery in both directions.
The company plans to expand the category's product range and attract new Ukrainian brands. Planned technological solutions include a virtual fitting room to help customers determine clothing and footwear sizes when placing an order.
According to the company, epicentrk.ua receives about 25 million visits per month on average. Epicentr's logistics infrastructure includes more than 3,000 parcel lockers and 200 order pickup centers across Ukraine.
The Epicentr group is an omnichannel ecosystem comprising the Epicentr and Nova Linia retail chains, the epicentrk.ua online store, the Epicentr-Ahro agricultural holding, Epicenter Ceramic Corporation ceramic tile plants, the Osmoлoda CBM woodworking enterprise and logistics facilities. As of early 2026, the retailer's network comprised 72 shopping centers in Ukraine.
According to the Unified State Register of Legal Entities and Individual Entrepreneurs, the owners of Epicentr K LLC are Oleksandr Hereha (51.3%), Halyna Hereha (47.97%) and Tetiana Surzhyk (0.73%).

title: FDI rises from $624m to $2.62bn as Tema industrial activity picks up – Mahama
body: President John Mahama says the Tema industrial enclave is gradually reclaiming its former glory as Ghana records a significant increase in foreign direct investment (FDI). According to President Mahama, FDI increased from US$624 million in 2024 to US$2.62 billion in 2025, representing a substantial rise in capital committed by foreign investors to the Ghanaian economy. The President made the remarks on Thursday, October 8, at the commissioning of an expanded evaporated milk production line operated by Nestlé Ghana in Tema, where he linked the company’s investment to what he described as improving economic stability and a more favourable investment climate. He said the renewed industrial activity in Tema was a particularly important sign of Ghana’s economic recovery, arguing that the industrial enclave was beginning to reclaim the prominence it enjoyed in the past. “I’m pleased to say that Tema is regaining its glory days,” President Mahama said. Tema industrial activity gathers pace President Mahama pointed to developments across the Tema industrial corridor as evidence of increased economic activity, including the expansion of the Tema Port and the resumption of operations at the Tema Oil Refinery. He also said his administration was working towards reviving the Volta Aluminium Company (VALCO), while noting that industrial activity within the enclave was continuing to expand. “The ports of Tema have expanded. Tema Oil Refinery is back at work again. We’re working on reviving VALCO. The industrial enclave is progressing, and many industries like Nestlé existing in the Tema enclave are expanding their production,” he said. The President attributed the renewed investment activity to what he described as an improved business and macroeconomic environment. “This is because the investment climate is good,” he said. Inflation and interest rates President Mahama also highlighted developments in inflation and interest rates as indicators of improving economic conditions. He said inflation, which he put at 23.8 per cent , had fallen to about 5.2 per cent , while interest rates were also declining, with spreads ranging between 9 and 13 per cent . He further pointed to the performance of the Ghanaian cedi, saying the currency had regained strength after a prolonged period of pressure. “And our long-suffering local currency, the cedi, has regained its strength and is relatively performing very well,” he said. The President argued that these indicators should not be viewed merely as statistics but in terms of their impact on investment decisions. “I do not recite these figures for their own sake because stability is not a number in the report. It is a difference between a company that shelves an expansion and one that decides to go forward with investments,” he said. Stability and investor decisions According to President Mahama, improved macroeconomic conditions can influence decisions taken by international companies when considering whether to commit additional capital to Ghana. He cited the example of corporate decision-making outside Ghana, saying economic stability could give international boards greater confidence to approve investments in the country. “It helps a boardroom in Switzerland to take decisions to commit capital to Tema with greater confidence,” he said. The President, however, acknowledged that businesses operating in Ghana still face risks, particularly those associated with movements in the local currency. “Businesses must still account for currency risk in their decisions,” he cautioned. Nestlé expansion seen as industrial confidence President Mahama described Nestlé Ghana’s expanded evaporated milk production line as an important demonstration of private-sector confidence in Ghana’s long-term economic prospects. He said the investment was consistent with the government’s broader industrialisation ambitions under its Reset Agenda , which seeks to strengthen productive sectors of the economy and encourage investment. “The line before us is a welcome sign of Nestlé’s confidence in Ghana’s long-term prospects, and it aligns with the industrial ambitions of our Reset Agenda,” he said. The President’s comments place the expansion of Nestlé Ghana within a broader effort to position Tema once again as a major industrial and manufacturing centre. Tema was developed as Ghana’s principal industrial and port city during the administration of Ghana’s first President, Dr Kwame Nkrumah. Over the decades, the area has hosted major manufacturing, petroleum, aluminium and other industrial operations. President Mahama’s remarks suggest that the government sees the revival and expansion of industrial production in Tema as an important component of its wider economic strategy. The reported increase in FDI, alongside the government’s emphasis on falling inflation, interest rates and improved currency performance, is being presented by the administration as evidence of changing economic conditions. However, the President acknowledged that businesses must continue to factor currency risks into investment decisions, underscoring the importance of sustained macroeconomic stability as Ghana seeks to attract and retain long-term capital.

title: Iran not to hand over uranium or abandon enrichment
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 08 (MNA) – Iran's atomic energy chief said enrichment is an integral part of the nuclear process and that a country cannot claim to have a nuclear industry without controlling the starting point of the process.
Mohammad Eslami, head of the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran, spoke on Wednesday evening on the sidelines of the memorial ceremony for the mother of the head of the Planning and Budget Organisation.
"Enrichment is an inseparable part of the nuclear process and we will not abandon it under any circumstances. Can you not have the starting point of the process and then claim to have a nuclear industry? The nuclear industry is the driving engine of science and technology," he said.
He added that the Americans themselves, including the current president, have placed nuclear technology at the top of development priorities in their country's national development, national security and national defence documents, and that all countries are rapidly pursuing their nuclear programmes.
Eslami said, "These are deception and lies. What is certain is the progress of a nation. The Iranian nation is not a nation left behind; it is a first-rate nation and a talented nation."
"Iran is a country with great capacity. The right to progress and to the frontiers of knowledge is the right of the Iranian nation, and we will not back down."
The head of Iran's Atomic Energy Organization stressed, "We will not hand over the uranium."

title: IN BRIEF: Russian Foreign Ministry briefing on Kiev ‘gang,' EU problems
body:
MOSCOW, October 8. /TASS/. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and the "gang" in Kiev are part of the same corruption schemes, Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said.
She noted that the EU has firmly embarked on a path of confrontation with Russia, which will only worsen its problems.
TASS has compiled the Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman's key statements.
Ukraine is so deeply mired in corruption that there's little Zelensky can now do to conceal the true scale of the problem: "Ukraine is so deeply mired in corruption that the full extent of the problem can no longer be concealed. Zelensky's efforts to control the flow of information have done little to hide it, leaving only one mainstream television broadcaster while blocking other television news sources."
"Merz and this entire gang, of course, are part of all these corruption schemes. And he is coming [to Kiev] in part to discuss how the money will be distributed after being funneled through the Kiev regime."
Merz made German taxpayers cover the cost by promising Zelensky a new military aid package worth about €1 billion during his visit to Kiev: "These political bankrupts in Berlin have made German taxpayers cover the cost. They had just received concrete results of their policies. They realized that their own citizens not only do not support their policies in their own country, but are demonstrating their absolute rejection of them."
"It seems that Merz is once again emptying his own citizens' pockets, almost as if in retaliation. He is doing so despite their clear understanding of how futile Zelensky's efforts are."
The current German authorities need war, and Merz's actions prove it.
Russia will continue working through international forums to identify and hold accountable those responsible for the Nord Stream explosions: "We will continue our efforts, including through international forums, to identify and hold accountable not only the perpetrators but also the true masterminds behind this unprecedented terrorist attack."
Moscow views the possible deployment of additional NATO forces in the Baltic states as an escalation: "We unequivocally view the potential deployment of additional NATO forces, including US troops, and the creation of corresponding military infrastructure in the Baltic states as an escalation."
"The more problems the EU faces because of its own mistakes and miscalculations in its hybrid war against Russia, the more incredible and large-scale plans it attributes to Russia. It accuses Russia of having plans that do not, in fact, exist."
The EU has firmly embarked on a path of confrontation with Russia, which will only worsen its problems: "The European Union embarked on a path of confrontation with our country, initially under pressure from the United States and then simply out of inertia. And this path will not allow it to resolve its pressing issues, indeed, it will never allow it to do so."
The EU leadership "deliberately and consciously chooses to ignore this simple truth."
Merz is coming to Kiev "both to improve his ratings and to escape his own citizens," as well as to avoid criticism and public discontent within Germany.
Moscow has no plans for an armed conflict with Western Europe, and Russia is not threatening anyone: "If Germany's top intelligence official is publicly voicing his own fantasies, that means Europe really is in great danger. Let me repeat just in case: Russia is not threatening anyone. The Russian president and foreign minister have repeatedly stated that Moscow has no plans for an armed conflict with Western Europe."
Russia does not interfere in elections abroad, unlike Western countries: "There can be no question of Russian interference in electoral processes abroad. This is not our style. Western political elites openly interfere in election campaigns in full view of the world. At times, they even abduct presidents, put direct pressure on political groups in countries they are interested in, and, as I said, consider themselves free to do whatever they want."
Italian authorities' allegations of Russian interference in elections are disrespectful to Italians: "It is simply disrespectful to Italians to make such statements at the level of the foreign minister or any other minister, playing the so-called Russian card."
The situation in the Middle East requires urgent efforts to restore normalcy: "It is important to make urgent efforts to normalize the situation in the Middle East and restore full-scale shipping through the Strait of Hormuz."
Moscow is ready to help find compromises on the Strait of Hormuz: "Russia remains ready to help find compromises based on international law while considering the legitimate rights and interests of all parties involved. Our assets include trusting relations with all states in the region without exception."
Russia warned from the outset about the serious consequences of what it calls the unprovoked US and Israeli armed aggression against Iran. The warning focused on the threat it posed to food security in the world's most vulnerable countries: "We backed this issue with figures and facts. Russia has an interest in free, uninterrupted and safe navigation along international maritime routes."

title: RSF warns Greek authorities over China-backed influencers and undeclared ties
body: On 27 November 2025 a Facebook video from the page of Chinese influencer Iro Li tore through Greek feeds. In fluent Greek she criticised Kimberly Guilfoyle, the US ambassador, and the clip drew more than 610,000 views within days. The politics sat oddly against the rest of the page, which is built from food, travel and everyday life aimed at Greek viewers. That mismatch is what press-freedom NGO Reporters Without Borders (RSF) treats as the opening of a quieter campaign: lifestyle accounts that later carry Beijing’s line, sometimes without saying who pays for the reach. The spread sent Greece Fact Check, a nonprofit media observatory, after Chinese creators who post in Greek. Founder Thanos Sitistas and his team landed on three Facebook pages that look independent until the subject turns political: Sweet Hope, run by Elpida Wu; Marianna’s Diary, run by Marianna Lee; and Iro Li’s own page. The shift, Sitistas told RSF, came shortly after the Chinese embassy in Athens, on 19 November 2025, answered Guilfoyle’s remark that Beijing’s hold on Greece’s largest port, Piraeus, was unfortunate. The pages have hosted interviews with Greek politicians at state-sponsored forums in China on a shared future. RSF’s reading, published on 2 October 2026, is that the audience often has no way to know the accounts sit next to Chinese state media machinery. Greece Fact Check did not find proof that the influencers knowingly joined a broad propaganda operation. What it did find is structural. Iro Li’s page is sponsored by Zhongshi Vanguard Film and Television Media, a subsidiary of state broadcaster CCTV. Meta’s Ad Library lists Hong Kong Gather Wisdom Network Technology Co., a major Chinese ad distributor on Facebook, as both advertiser and payer for Marianna’s Diary and Sweet Hope. Sitistas put the method to RSF this way: much of the material does not rest on outright falsehoods. Affiliations and ad deals with Chinese Communist Party institutions go undisclosed. Topics Beijing treats as sensitive are handled by omission. Posts on East Turkestan — the Xinjiang region at the centre of documented abuses against Uyghurs — show cultural scenes and residents presented as happy and prosperous, and leave out mass detention and coercive assimilation. The aim, in his assessment, is a China that looks modern, peaceful, safe and technologically advanced, so viewers are less open to criticism of Beijing and more open to Chinese interests around Piraeus, the Belt and Road Initiative and relations with the EU. The three accounts together have more than 455,000 followers on Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and YouTube, and individual videos routinely draw hundreds of thousands to millions of views. Facebook has labelled Sweet Hope and Marianna’s Diary “China state-controlled media.” Sweet Hope still has 94,000 Facebook followers and 113,000 YouTube subscribers; a polished cover of Helena Paparizou’s “Mazi Sou” has nearly 200,000 views. Marianna’s Diary has 130,000 Facebook followers and 81,500 on TikTok, with some clips above 1.8 million views. Iro Li’s page is not labelled a state outlet, but she has reported for China Radio International, the international arm of China Media Group. In September 2024 she interviewed Nektarios Farmakis, regional governor of Western Greece, for CRI at the Global Mayors Dialogue in Hangzhou. Sitistas told RSF the coordination looked strong: similar formats, professional production, multiple administrators, paid ads and complementary subjects. Between 2021 and 2023 the three accounts had a combined 47 administrators and ran 227 advertisements. An intermediary used by two of them also handled advertising for CRI’s Greek-language service. Mainstream Greek outlets have put the same creators on air and in print without the state tie. On 12 February 2022 Open TV introduced Elpida Wu live as a woman from China who adores Greece and Greek songs, then followed her through a 350 km/h bullet train in Beijing — a flagship infrastructure project, with no mention of her affiliation. On 29 January 2022 the news site i Efimerida asked who the 28-year-old Chinese woman was who spoke fluent Greek and had taken the internet by storm. Diaspora outlets in the United States and Australia have done the same. That coverage, RSF notes, feeds the unsuspecting audience back to the social accounts. The influencer layer sits on older media deals. In 2016 Xinhua signed a cooperation agreement with the Athens-Macedonian News Agency; a second, with Xinhua affiliate China Economic Information Service, followed in 2017. That year Kathimerini signed with Xinhua as well. A later study found the paper republished at least one Xinhua report a week in 2020, 66 articles in all. In September 2023 Naftemporiki agreed to work with China’s Economic Daily, overseen by the CCP’s Central Propaganda Department. CCTV signed a memorandum with public broadcaster ERT in 2016, and in 2020 parliament approved a Sino-Greek film co-production agreement. Those channels, RSF argues, give CCP propaganda outlets a route into Greek news. Some of the outlets have owners with business in sectors tied to China. Kathimerini and Skai TV are controlled by the Alafouzos family, whose interests include shipping. Naftemporiki is owned by Dimitris Melissanidis, whose portfolio includes shipping and energy. Engagement has gone past republishing: Chinese ambassadors have been interviewed and their op-eds published. An Athens-based independent journalist, speaking to RSF on condition of anonymity, said that is why there is almost no reporting on what the investments mean for the country’s independence. Press trips are the older tool. Since the early 2010s Beijing has regularly invited Greek journalists; the same reporter told RSF there is little awareness of the propaganda function, and that most who went later published positive stories. A 2021 Carnegie Endowment report, which RSF cites, warned that when China pairs investment with strategic messages there is often little room for counter-narratives, especially where independent media or civil society is weak. It called Greece vulnerable to Chinese media narratives and likely to stay that way without specialised coverage of China and of Chinese-European relations. Aleksandra Bielakowska, RSF’s Asia-Pacific advocacy manager, ties the pattern to Greece’s press-freedom record. For years the country has sat at the bottom of the EU on RSF’s World Press Freedom Index, and she argues those shortcomings are what let Chinese propaganda take hold: citizens need news that serves their interests and are instead getting more content that serves a foreign state. In the 2 October piece she calls on Greek authorities to investigate the money linking these influencers to Chinese propaganda networks, and to ask whether that is foreign interference, and she urges the government to build conditions for trustworthy journalism in line with European standards. On the 2026 index Greece is 86th of 180, last in the EU for a fifth year, with a score of 55.05. China is 178th, with 13.85. The post RSF warns Greek authorities over China-backed influencers and undeclared ties appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: U.K. Expands Sanctions to Cover 90% of Russian Oil Output, Shadow Fleet and Finance Networks
body:
Britain on Thursday announced sanctions targeting 38 Russian energy companies, shadow fleet oil tankers and financial networks that allegedly fuel Russia’s war effort.
“The message is simple: if you help Russia fund or equip this war, you will face the consequences,” the Foreign Office said in a statement.
London added 17 entities and individuals supplying high-priority goods to Russia, including importers of machine tools and electronics key to the country’s ballistic missile and drone capabilities.
One of the sanctioned individuals is Dutch national Alexander Jan Hendrik Tattersall, who is allegedly associated with the sanctioned Turkish trader Redwing Metal.
Britain sanctioned two Russian energy producers, saying the restrictions now cover more than 90% of Russia’s total oil production capacity.
An additional 12 tankers were also sanctioned, expanding the total number of targeted shadow fleet vessels to more than 600.
Targeting Russia’s alternative payment systems and crypto exchanges used to bypass Western sanctions, Britain designated five financial entities, including one registered in Canada and three in Kyrgyzstan.
The financial measures follow the U.S. Treasury’s recent crackdown on Russia’s A7 shadow banking network, which the U.S. claimed to have processed through sub-agents more than $17 billion in global transactions between January 2025 and June 2026.
The Foreign Office claimed two of the newly sanctioned payment platforms directly facilitated transactions for the A7 platform.
