title: Turkey’s foreign minister says Ankara weighing Saudi defense support, rules out offensive role
body: ANKARA — Turkey is assessing how it can help Saudi Arabia defend against attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi militants under a joint defense pact with Pakistan, Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on Thursday, ruling out Turkish participation in offensive operations. Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August, under which an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all. The three countries have since held political and military meetings in response to the Houthi attacks. On Monday, the countries said they had agreed to move immediately to implement their collective defense commitments and ensure the “rapid deployment” of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia. Speaking at a joint press conference with his Hungarian counterpart Anita Orban in Ankara, Fidan stressed that the pact was defensive rather than offensive, saying military officials were assessing possible contributions, particularly in air defense, electronic warfare and technical support. “Yemen’s legitimate government forces are already continuing the battle on the ground and Saudi Arabia is supporting them,” Fidan said. “But this is a defensive agreement. When a country party to the pact comes under attack, you stand by it in its defense. This is not an offensive agreement. Turkey will not send troops to another country to carry out attacks on its territory,” he said. Fidan said military delegations would determine Saudi Arabia’s operational defense needs and what contributions Turkey and Pakistan could make. On Wednesday, two officials told Reuters that Turkey was sending mainly defensive and technical support to Saudi Arabia to help its fight with Houthi militants. Turkish officials have said any support provided at this stage would largely be in a bilateral capacity, as Turkey’s parliament has not officially ratified the joint defense pact. Fidan said on Thursday that work was largely completed for the agreement to be submitted for parliament’s approval and that they aimed to send it “as soon as possible.” Turkey, which has NATO’s second-largest army and a robust defense industry, has condemned the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, voiced willingness to help meet Riyadh’s technical military needs, and agreed to join a Saudi-led coalition to ensure navigational safety in the Red Sea.

title: Pennsylvania Gov. Shapiro, challenger Garrity remain aligned on Israel in midterm debate
body: Democratic Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro and GOP opponent Stacy Garrity faced off on Wednesday in a heated gubernatorial debate, clashing over most policy issues - with the notable exception of Israel.    “I want to recognize the anniversary of the Hamas attacks, where 1,200 innocent people were killed, including 49 Americans,” said Garrity, referring to the third anniversary of Hamas' October 7, 2023, attack on Israel. “I want to remember the lives that were stolen, the families that were changed forever, and the Americans that didn't make it home,” she added. While Garrity, Pennsylvania's state treasurer, has the endorsement of US President Donald Trump, Shapiro leads by 25 percentage points in a poll released Wednesday. Both candidates won their primaries uncontested in May, and both have been outspoken against antisemitism. Shapiro, who himself is Jewish, likewise recognized “the third anniversary of the October 7 massacre” at the debate. He recalled how “Hamas, a terrorist organization, broke into Israel and murdered 1,200 innocents, took over 250 hostage, including many Americans.”“This is a moment where my heart stands with the people of Israel,” he said. “My heart stands with the Jewish community, who I know are grieving as a result of this.”“This is a moment where we need to stand together against terrorism, against hate and against antisemitism,” the governor added.Shapiro, Garrity clash on death penalty, tariffs, voter ID, taxesAlthough the candidates shared similar perspectives on Israel during Wednesday's debate, they clashed on numerous other topics, including the death penalty, voter identification, taxes, and tariffs.Asked by the debate moderator about the plunging support for Israel in the Democratic Party, Shapiro replied that he has “been very, very consistent” in both his “love of Israel” and his disagreements with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Shapiro then noted that Israelis will head to the polls in just a few weeks to choose their next leader. He expressed hope that they would not elect Netanyahu, whom he said “has led Israel down a very dangerous and isolated path.” “I want America to have a strong relationship with Israel and with the Israeli government,” Shapiro added. “That's not possible right now with the Netanyahu government in charge.”Shapiro seen as presidential hopeful for 2028Shapiro, one of the most prominent Jewish Democrats nationwide, was among the final candidates Kamala Harris considered in her vice-presidential search for the 2024 election. He is also seen as a possible 2028 presidential hopeful. But Shapiro has also faced the challenges posed by increasing antisemitism in America. During Harris's search, for example, a website and social media feed labeled him “No Genocide Josh” over his support for Israel. In April 2025, an arsonist set fire to Shapiro's house just hours after his family had conducted a Passover seder. In 2018, while Shapiro was serving as Pennsylvania's attorney general, a terrorist killed 11 people and injured six others at the Tree of Life synagogue in Pittsburgh.Garrity, meanwhile, has more than tripled Pennsylvania's investment in Israel bonds in her current role. She invested $20 million after the October 7 attack and another $35 million in July 2025.

title: No breakthrough yet on evacuation of civilians from occupied Oleshky
body:
The Secretariat of the Verkhovna Rada Commissioner for Human Rights told Ukrinform this in response to a request from the agency.
“Communication with the Russian side on organizing a safe humanitarian mechanism for the residents of Oleshky is ongoing, but as of today, there has been no practical breakthrough that would allow an organized evacuation of civilians to begin,” the document says.
The Commissioner’s Secretariat emphasized that the Ukrainian side has repeatedly confirmed its readiness to ensure the necessary conditions for the humanitarian operation, including a localized ceasefire, the designation of a safe route, and the reception of citizens in territory controlled by the Ukrainian government. It said that, as part of direct communication between the Ombudsmen, lists of citizens, logistical and medical support, and a possible format for the humanitarian operation had been worked out.
“At the same time, the key problem remains the lack of clear, verifiable and practically implementable security guarantees from the Russian side, without which carrying out a humanitarian operation would create additional risks for civilians and the personnel involved,” the response to the request says.
It also said that the International Committee of the Red Cross is involved in communication between the Ukrainian and Russian sides and had confirmed its readiness to act as a neutral humanitarian intermediary, provided the parties reach the necessary agreements and obtain security guarantees.
The institution also recalled that on September 19, the All-Ukrainian Council of Churches and Religious Organizations appealed to Pope Leo XIV, the World Council of Churches, other religious leaders, UN member states and the ICRC, calling on them to use all available opportunities to stop the humanitarian catastrophe and facilitate the evacuation of residents.
“As of October 7, 2026, there is no confirmed public information that the Holy See has launched a separate mediation mechanism specifically concerning Oleshky. At the same time, we are counting on the Holy See to use its humanitarian and diplomatic potential, and we are ready for appropriate cooperation,” the Commissioner’s Secretariat told Ukrinform.
The Secretariat added that, as of October 7, the Ombudsman had received 204 appeals concerning the situation in Oleshky and neighboring settlements. Following the processing of the appeals and information received through the Secretariat’s online questionnaire, 358 citizens in need of assistance to leave safely have been verified.
As reported by Ukrinform, according to the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine, no food supplies had reached Oleshky since May 26.
According to Oleksandr Prokudin, Head of the Kherson Regional Military Administration, Russian forces are holding around 2,000 people hostage in Oleshky, nearly 50 of them children. They are being forced to survive without food, electricity or water.

title: Outrage as police operatives allegedly harass bailiffs enforcing court order
body:
The Anaocha Branch of the Nigerian Bar Association ( NBA ) has raised an alarm over alleged harassment of court bailiffs by police operatives in Anambra State.
Anaocha is a local government area in Anambra State.
Chairman of the NBA branch Uzoma Dioha in a statement on Thursday said the Divisional Police Officer (DPO) of B-Division in Awka allegedly instructed his operatives to harass the bailiffs while they were enforcing an order of the Chief Magistrate Court, Awka.
Mr Dioha, who condemned the alleged harassment, said the incident happened on Wednesday.
The chairman said the Chief Bailiff, Francis Nweje, informed him that the court officials were carrying out the “lawful execution of a judgement” pursuant to a warrant issued by the court when the DPO stormed the location.
The NBA branch leader said the police chief directed the court officials to immediately discontinue the execution and accompany him to his police station.
He said the court bailiffs explained to the DPO that they were acting pursuant to a valid warrant of execution and respectfully asked to conclude their court-assigned duties before attending to the officer’s directive.
“Rather than allowing the judicial process to proceed, the said officer allegedly summoned police reinforcements, who arrived at the scene and reportedly subjected the court officials to harassment and intimidation,” he said.
Mr Dioha noted that the alleged harassment was captured in a video clip, stressing that the incident represents a grave affront to the judiciary.
“If these allegations are established, such conduct represents a grave affront to the authority of the judiciary and an unacceptable interference with the administration of justice,” he stated.
He argued that the 1999 Nigerian Constitution gives courts the authority to determine people’s civil rights and obligations, and it requires everyone, including government authorities and other courts, to respect, obey and enforce valid decisions made by the courts.
“The duties of court bailiffs, including the execution of warrants and other judicial processes, are governed by applicable laws and rules of court.
“Where a valid warrant of execution has been issued by a court of competent jurisdiction, no police officer, irrespective of rank or designation, possesses an unrestricted power to arbitrarily suspend its execution,” he stated.
“Any legitimate objection to the execution of a judgement must be addressed through appropriate legal and judicial procedures.”
Mr Dioha said it was ironic that those who were expected to enforce a court order were the people obstructing its enforcement.
He said the NBA, as a body, has asked the commissioner of police in the state to immediately investigate the incident, and identify as well as punish the officers involved in the obstruction of court enforcement orders.
The chairman said the union also asked for adequate protection of court bailiffs carrying out lawful judicial assignments.
He said the body has equally asked for “an appropriate institutional apology” to the judiciary and the affected court officials.
“We shall continue to engage the appropriate authorities and advocate for accountability, institutional discipline and the protection of the judicial process,” he said.
PREMIUM TIMES sighted a video clip of the incident.
In the clip which has gone viral on Facebook, one of the armed police operatives and another individual in plain cloth were seen grabbing a man said to be one of the court bailiffs in the entrance of what appeared to be a residential building.
The operatives continued to pull the court bailiff violently and appeared to force him into a waiting police vehicle but the court official repeatedly resisted.
“You’re harassing a court bailiff on official duty,” a male voice was heard repeatedly at the background of the clip.
One of the bailiffs was heard saying that they came to the area with a valid warrant to enforce the court order.
One of the officers was later spotted reading the court warrant which was handed to him by the bailiff.
The police in Anambra State have reacted to the incident.
In a statement on Thursday, the police spokesperson in the state, Tochukwu Ikenga, said the viral video clip of the incident only captured part of the encounter.
Mr Ikenga, a superintendent of police, said the state police command had begun an assessment of the incident with a view to establishing the facts.
The spokesperson, however, said preliminary information indicated that the operatives were responding to a distress call concerning the presence of “unidentified persons and a reported disturbance” at a premises within the jurisdiction of the command.
“Upon arrival at the scene, the operatives met some individuals engaged in the eviction of persons and removal of properties from the premises.
“In the course of establishing the identities of the persons involved and the purpose of their activities, the officers approached them and requested appropriate identification.
“During the interaction, there was a disagreement between the Police Operatives and some of the persons present,” he said.
“The persons subsequently identified themselves as court bailiffs carrying out an enforcement exercise pursuant to a court order.”
Mr Ikenga said the police command, based on the earlier available information, was not previously approached for security assistance before the commencement of the enforcement exercise.
“Upon being informed that the persons were court bailiffs acting pursuant to a court order, the police operatives advised them on the appropriate procedure for requesting police security support during such enforcement exercises and subsequently withdrew from the scene,” he said.
The spokesperson said the police command has reiterated its respect for the authority and independence of the courts and remains committed to providing lawful security support for the enforcement of valid court orders.
“The command has nevertheless taken note of the concerns arising from the incident and has engaged the relevant parties as part of efforts to establish the complete facts and ensure that the matter is handled professionally, impartially and in accordance with the law,” he said.
“The Command will communicate further developments as necessary upon conclusion of the ongoing assessment,” the spokesperson assured, urging Nigerians not to reach hasty conclusions from video clips without full details.

title: Zelensky can't deliver on threats of escalation against Moscow — Russian envoy
body:
VIENNA, October 8. /TASS/. Vladimir Zelensky keeps threatening to escalate violence against Russia, but can't execute on those threats, Moscow’s Permanent Representative to the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) Dmitry Polyansky said.
According to him, Zelensky "still hopes to inflict at least some significant damage on Moscow" and the surrounding region in order to convince the West that Ukraine is capable of conducting operations affecting Russia.
"The Kiev regime head keeps threatening Russia with escalation that he cannot sustain and then, he complains about large-scale attacks by Russia," the diplomat said at a meeting of the OSCE Permanent Council in Vienna.
Polyansky suggested that Zelensky recall the English proverb that "the one who lives in a glass house shouldn't throw stones at others." The Russian envoy added that Ukraine was receiving a far more powerful response, while the strikes were targeting first and foremost the facilities that keep "Kiev’s war machine" going.

title: Vetronics industry roundtable: AI, MOSA, thermal management
body:
Vehicle electronics, or vetronics, solutions must juggle multiple functions in a small space such as counter-drone detection and defeat; electronic warfare (EW); position, navigation, and timing; command and control; and tactical communications. These systems will add even more capability through modular open systems approach (MOSA) strategies and artificial intelligence (AI) solutions.
This roundtable of industry experts discusses the latest vetronics innovations and considers the thermal-management and reduced size, weight, and power (SWaP) challenges that come with meeting performance requirements. Our vetronics roundtable panelists are Andrew Eley, Sr. Engineer, Technology: SBC & Embedded Security Solutions, Wolf Advanced Technology; Ryan Jansen, VP of Advanced Technology, New Wave Design; and William J. Pilaud, Chief Solutions Architect, LCR Embedded Systems.
McHALE: How are modular open systems approach (MOSA) strategies like the Sensor Open Systems Architecture, or SOSA, Technical Standard and C5ISR/EW Modular Open Suite of Standards (CMOSS) enabling innovation in vetronics applications? What benefits do they bring?
ELEY: The big benefit is the integration of a wide array of technologies from various vendors to work like building blocks in rapidly assembling a system to get the latest technology to the warfighter as quickly as possible. All the systems work really well together, and we see a lot of good partnerships with different programs and companies to build these technologies that go into a variety of platforms.
MOSA really speeds up integration because you're not waiting around for customer specs and defining certain proprietary interfaces and going back and forth on pinouts and then fixing all the problems from things you missed the first time. When everything is based on a standard that's well-known in advance, companies can put their own investment into creating a product that meets that standard, and then it cuts down a lot of the back-and-forth between a vendor like us and our customers.
JANSEN: I think open standards like CMOSS and SOSA bring a lot of benefits, but one of two big benefits that we see at New Wave is the ecosystem that it enables. Previously, before open standards, if you wanted to put together a vetronics system, you really had to have the expertise and the ability to do the whole thing, from the sensor to all the electronics in between to the actual algorithm that was running on it.
So, a small, innovative company can have the means or ability to come out with their novel algorithm and bring that to the community. Now with all these different aspects, nontraditional companies and small companies can participate in the ecosystem.
The second benefit we see is that MOSA really changes the economics of innovation. You can put your technology investments into bringing the latest and greatest silicon and the latest technology to the marketplace. Instead of having to spend money switching out profiles for every different customer, every different platform, we can invest in a module that has a much wider and broader applicable base.
PILAUD: Traditionally vetronics has been proprietary, single-purpose-use-type systems and capabilities. Now we're bringing in SOSA and MOSA, specifically VPX-type-variant systems that are modular and multipurpose. So even boxes can be expanded to have more functionality than what they were initially designed to do, particularly in the artificial intelligence (AI) world, where we're adding capability for those things that we just can't foresee that you will need. And then the ability to swap those modules as they improve to add on even more capability and more token processing and artificial intelligence. Then finally there is serviceability. Now we're able to do level-two maintenance in the field as opposed to going back to the depot, allowing us to keep the mission and the people safe in real time as things break or as things need to be modified in the field – as opposed to full-chassis or full-system swapout.
McHALE: What technology/ruggedization requirements – thermal management, reduced SWaP [size, weight, and power], signal processing, AI sensors, etc. – are you seeing from your customers for vetronics solutions? What problems are they looking to solve?
ELEY: I think, especially in our technology with GPUs, it's very power-hungry. The big problem we face is thermal management. I think a lot of the new standards, even coming through VITA, dictate a lot of variety in different cooling solutions – where it's liquid-flow-through, air-flow-through, conduction-cooled – and so we are able to invest into those technologies early on to characterize the system, to be able to address the thermal concerns that our customers have before they bring it to us. And then we can give them a report of “Here's how our product will perform in your environment.”
JANSEN: The demand for increased processing capability is only increasing for the same amount of space or an even smaller space. Whether it’s consolidating what was done in multiple slots in a chassis or on multiple boxes into a single card or a single box, we are seeing that over and over again. The sheer amount of data that our customers want available at any given processing element is just continuously increasing as well.
It poses significant challenges, especially when you go to ruggedize these modules and bring what's available in the commercial industry into the vetronics application space. You have to ruggedize these modules, and they get very dense. You have very strict requirements, so it makes the circuit card design very complex.
The commercial silicon is up for the task and a lot of times the theoretical performance and processing power that you're going to get from it exceeds what we can cool and power in a slot. The challenge often isn't, do we have some device that can do it? It's [instead] how do we get the heat out and get the power there, so you can use as much of that chip as possible in the system?
PILAUD: That has changed significantly. Vetronics used to be about mission control, system control, sensor control, and aggregation for the warfighter. That has greatly expanded now. The artificial intelligence capability is starting to become more and more significant. Now we're seeing that those changes are being rolled back into the systems, and that's the big disruption.
What that’s causing for the environment is that these systems are much more power-intensive, in the sense that the power density per part is vastly increasing. So now we're into liquid cooling, which is now universal in the military world. We have disruptive technology now that's gone from 40 to 100 watts at a stretch case to 200 watts a slot. That's becoming disruptive in the ability to deploy [AI] into the vetronics capability more so than at any time before.
McHALE: Looking forward, what innovation or paradigm shift will be a game-changer for vetronics systems?
ELEY: Definitely AI, as it is integrating into a lot of systems everywhere. In vetronics-type systems one of the challenges has always been combining all of the sensor data from the various systems that are on a platform into a central intelligence that can be used to understand your environment –are you in friendly territory or hostile territory? And then, how do you respond to that environment? Being able to integrate vast amounts of sensor data that's high-bandwidth into an intelligent, easy-to-digest response is where AI fits in really well.
JANSEN: The continued consolidation of a lot of different heterogeneous processing elements down into [a] single system-on-chip is going to be a game-changer. You're starting to see that available in the industry where you're getting real-time CPUs and FPGA fabrics, GPUs, specialized AI processors, all consolidated into a special chip. They really help solve that power problem because now you're able to do a specific workload and do that with the best power efficiency possible for that workload.
In addition to that, we see that the vendors are putting a lot of hardened IPs right into the system-on-chip as well. Things that you used to do, maybe an FPGA [field-programmable gate array] fabric, are now in a hardened IP that might take up half the power that they would in a previous generation. That power optimization is really important.
We will then need a tool to help manage all these heterogeneous computing elements, rather than [needing] very specialized engineers that are experts in each of these elements. It’s similar with FPGAs: You usually will be programming in VHDL or Verilog, [and it] takes a specialized skill set to do that. It takes a lot of time and effort to do that. If we had tools that could help take that high-level algorithm and automatically pick: Should I put this in an AI engine, an FPGA fabric, or a GPU, and parse that up and be able to do that – it’s going to help people go much faster and get more out of these heterogeneous systems. Looking forward, generative AI assistance and AI agents, and work that's being done there, is going to help streamline some of these resources.
PILAUD: The adoption of more automotive technologies and leveraging the $3 trillion market that the automotive world brings to bear is disruptive. The military and the embedded community cannot keep up with the amount of software, safety-critical, remote downloading, sensor integration that's happening in the automotive market, particularly in the autonomous-driving-type stuff. As the military starts adopting more automotive technology, we will see a whole brand of new capability that we never had before. Instead of just planning for it, we'll be deploying it.
For additional vetronics content please visit our Military Vetronics e-book at https://militaryembedded.com/comms/vetronics/military-vetronics-e-book-in-depth-coverage-of-technology-trends-and-mosa-use-in-military-vetronics .

title: Amazon’s Alexa Tablets are coming for the iPad
body:
Amazon is launching a new lineup of tablets that bear almost no resemblance to any tablet Amazon has ever launched before. They’re not even called Fire, the name Amazon has used for its tablets for the last 15 years. They’re called Alexa Tablets, and they’re designed to do two things: bring Alexa Plus to the center of your whole computing life, and be straight-up excellent tablets.
The most important thing about these new tablets’ software? They run Android. Full, Google Play-supported, all-the-apps Android. There are plenty of preloaded Amazon apps, of course, and some built-in ways to quickly access Prime Video content or shop for basically anything anywhere at any time, but it’s finally offering a proper Android experience. Panos Panay, Amazon’s SVP in charge of all things hardware and Alexa, tells me that “Google Play was a necessity, end of story.”
But Panay picked Android as the second-most-important thing about the Alexa Tablet. The first, he says, is the hardware. The Alexa Tablet is two and a half years in the making, Panay says, and he directed the team to start completely fresh in their tablet design. “Start from zero, don’t use any components we’ve ever used,” he says he told them. “Just ask, what is it? What is a great piece of hardware and what is it supposed to do?”
[Image: The three flavors of Alexa Tablet. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Tablets_Hero_1920x1080.png?quality=90&strip=all]
There are three devices in the Alexa Tablet lineup, all of which go on sale October 14th. The Tablet 8 has an 8.7-inch screen, starts at $229.99, and seems mostly designed for reading; the Tablet 11 has an 11-inch screen, starts at $329.99, and is more for watching stuff. They’re aimed squarely at the iPad Mini and base iPad and seem nice enough. But the biggest device in the lineup, the one Panay really wants to tell me about, is the one he thinks really shows off what Amazon is doing here.
It’s called the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, and it starts at $499. It’s 6.5mm thick and weighs 550 grams — a little thicker and a little lighter than the latest 13-inch iPad Pro — and comes with either 8 or 16 gigs of RAM and either 128 or 256 gigs of storage. It runs a MediaTek Dimensity 8400 processor, a chip you might have found in a high-end phone a year or so ago. All these specs are… fine. Good enough to run an Android tablet, but nothing to write home about.
The feature that really matters, Panay says, is the screen. Panay has this concept of the “one thing,” a single feature on a product that absolutely cannot be compromised on, no matter what. Make tradeoffs where you need to, he tells his team, but not on the one thing. “And the one thing on this product was, ‘Let’s go make the perfect screen.’”
That screen is a 12.5-inch, 2800 x 1840 display with a refresh rate up to 120Hz and 500 nits of brightness. Its 3:2 aspect ratio, Panay says, is perfect for running two Android apps side by side. And on the most expensive, $549 model Alexa Tablet, the screen comes with what Amazon calls a Nanomatte display. The company partnered with Corning to actually etch a unique texture into the glass itself that is meant to be richer, higher contrast, and less prone to glare than a typical display. The process sounds similar to Apple’s excellent nano-texture finishes, but Amazon seems to believe its method comes with even fewer tradeoffs in contrast and sharpness. I haven’t seen the device in person yet, but The Verge’s Terrence O’Brien has, and it sounds like it has a chance to be as good as advertised.
[Image: Add the attachments, squint a little, and it’s an iPad Pro. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Alexa-Tablet.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
The screen also adapts to what you’re doing on the tablet. If you launch the Kindle app, it turns off blue lights to make the reading experience warmer and more serene; if you start reading comics, it’ll render them extra glossy. Amazon understands well that tablets are primarily consumption devices — and the company is very happy to optimize for your time in Kindle and Prime Video.
The Alexa Tablet isn’t just for watching and reading, though. Amazon also made a keyboard case and a stylus, and Panay says he hopes people will use it as a secondary or even primary computer. He also hopes you’ll use it to do Alexa things. Amazon has been working on the LLM-powered version of its assistant for the last few years, and believes Alexa Plus can be more than just a smart home assistant. (Our testing suggests… otherwise.) You’ll be able to ask Alexa about anything you see on the screen, and the chatbot will try to offer recommendations, find information, and, of course, try to sell you anything it can find on Amazon.com. On these devices, Alexa Plus appears to be nearly as pervasive as Gemini or Siri on other tablets, and that’s precisely the point.
It has always made sense for Amazon to make tablets. But for so many years, the company has seemed to be happy to simply make everything as cheap as possible in the hopes you’ll sign up for Prime and buy some stuff in the store. Trying to actually make great tablets seems new, and frankly a little surprising. But if it got the screen right, and made the right tradeoffs elsewhere, Amazon might finally have a proper iPad competitor.

title: Hands-on with Amazon’s Alexa Tablet 12 Pro and its wild new matte display
body:
Amazon’s Fire tablets are notable for being dirt cheap. While they’re great for kids, they don’t offer a premium Android tablet experience. The company’s new $499 Alexa Tablet 12 Pro is an attempt to build a device someone might actually want to use. It’s one of a few new Android tablets Amazon announced today, and it’s the one you need to know about.
Unlike the Fire Tablet lineup, the Alexa Tablet doesn’t run some hobbled version of Android stuck with Amazon’s app store with ads for Amazon services at every turn. It has full access to the Google Play app store. It’s powered by 8GB or 12GB of RAM with a MediaTek Dimensity 8400 8-core CPU. That’s more than enough for light gaming, powering Alexa, and running basic apps, but don’t expect Alien: Isolation to run super smoothly. The aluminum unibody feels great. It’s light at 550 grams (1.2 pounds), but not flimsy. It’s slightly lighter than the 13-inch iPad Air (617 grams) but heavier than the 11-inch (465 grams).
The screen is the truly exciting thing about the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro. The $549.99 Alexa Tablet 12 Pro has a 12.3-inch 3:2 display that can be configured with Corning’s Nanomatte tech, similar to Apple’s nano-texture, which reduces glare and gives the screen a more paper-like feel.
[Image: The difference between the Nanomatte display and the standard glossy one is dramatic. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268799_AlexaTablet12Pro_10.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
It’s impossible to do it justice in photos or video. The Nanomatte coating doesn’t simply reduce glare; it almost completely eliminates it. Amazon held a briefing in a brightly sunlit room, and I thought the 12 Pro was a dummy unit when I first saw it. It looked like a cardboard placeholder image was placed inside. Then an Amazon rep started swiping around the screen. 
There’s also a standard glossy option, and the difference is shocking. In the bright sunlight of the room, the glossy screen was basically a mirror and was easily washed out when viewed at an angle. The Nanomatte display, however, was clearly readable at any angle and barely reflected any ambient light. Only at extreme angles in the brightest patches of light did it become difficult to see. 
The screen pairs particularly well with the immersive Kindle mode. Here, background activities are limited, notifications are silenced, and blue light is lowered to reduce eye strain. There are three different Kindle-specific display modes. Standard delivers the full vibrancy of the screen; Color offers a softer, more muted experience; and Ink is full grayscale. In Kindle mode, battery life is also extended from 16 hours to 20 hours.
[Media: https://www.instagram.com/reel/DeO-6xrjj8i/?utm_source=ig_web_copy_link&stkn=MzRlODBiNWFlZA%3D%3D]
Without having the two side-by-side, it’s hard to say how it compares to Apple’s matte display on the iPad Pro, but anecdotally it seems to retain slightly more contrast. Using a stylus with it is much more pleasant than on a glossy display, but I can’t say I noticed a difference between it and an iPad.
The Alexa Tablet Pro Pen and Pro Keyboard attach magnetically and seem serviceable enough. I wouldn’t want to type on its shallow, cramped keys all day, but they’re fine for knocking out a few emails. The keyboard case was a little clunky to get on and off, though. It’s actually two parts — the back cover and stand are separate from the keyboard base.
Alexa Everywhere
[Image: Go ahead, ask Alexa. I dare you. I double dare you. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268799_AlexaTablet12Pro_5.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
The tablet shoves Alexa down your throat at every turn. In the bottom right-hand corner is an “Ask Alexa” bar that lets you quickly chat with the AI assistant. And in the top left-hand corner is what Amazon calls the Dynamic Tab. It offers up proactive suggestions from Alexa. That can be something as simple as picking up where you left off in a book or movie, or offering an itinerary for a three-day trip to New York. This is, of course, powered by Amazon’s deep well of information it gathers from your reading, viewing, and shopping habits.
Amazon keeps some of Alexa’s more invasive features off by default. On-Screen Intelligence, which can see what you’re doing and take actions based on what’s actually on your screen, is strictly opt-in. There are also robust controls for limiting what Alexa can hear and remember. 
If you do opt in, though, Alexa becomes a pretty powerful shopping companion. I was able to open random photos from the internet and ask Alexa to find me something in them, like a coffee table or a mirror, and, even if it couldn’t track down the exact thing, it found something close. Then it would add it to my Amazon cart if I asked. How likely am I to ask Alexa to track down a bathroom fixture for me from a Pinterest photo and deliver it to my house in two days via Prime? Not very. I’m also unlikely to have it automatically add school holidays to my calendar from the Department of Education site, but it will if you ask it to. 
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268799_AlexaTablet12Pro_1.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268799_AlexaTablet12Pro_5.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268799_AlexaTablet12Pro_2.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268799_AlexaTablet12Pro_6.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268799_AlexaTablet12Pro_8.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268799_AlexaTablet12Pro_4.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268799_AlexaTablet12Pro_9.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]

[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268799_AlexaTablet12Pro_7.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro starts at $499.99, but you’ll have to shell out at least $549.99 for the Nanomatte model. If you want to tack on the keyboard case and the Pro Pen, that will be an additional $149.99 and $89.99, respectively.
Amazon also announced two smaller models that lack the Nanomatte screen options. The Alexa Tablet 11 starts at $329.99, while the Alexa Tablet 8 starts at $229.99. Those come in more fun colorways, including rosette and matcha, in addition to the drab but functional graphite of the Tablet 12 Pro.

title: Artificial stability or sustainable equilibrium? Rethinking the Cedi’s performance
body: My assessments of Ghana’s fiscal dynamics and monetary developments have consistently been grounded in the underlying economic fundamentals. When the government initially attributed the cedi’s improved performance primarily to fiscal consolidation, I challenged that interpretation and argued that substantial interventions by the Bank of Ghana (BoG) in the foreign-exchange market were a major, if not the principal, factor underpinning the observed stability. At the time, this position attracted considerable criticism. Subsequently, however, assessments by the World Bank and the IMF lent support to the argument that BoG interventions had played a significant role in sustaining the currency’s stability. The President eventually acknowledged the importance of such interventions, while the Governor of the BoG publicly identified foreign-exchange interventions as an important contributor to the cedi’s performance, a position that differed from some of his earlier public pronouncements. More recently, I have faced criticism from KSM and other NDC commentators for characterising the current stability of the cedi as partly artificial. Some senior CSO actors sympathetic to the NDC have also consistently ridiculed this position. However, the fundamental economic argument remains straightforward: exchange-rate stability that is heavily dependent on sustained central-bank intervention cannot, by itself, constitute a durable equilibrium. If the capacity or willingness of the central bank to intervene is constrained, the underlying pressures on the domestic currency are likely to re-emerge. My central argument has therefore been that a sustainable and resilient cedi requires attention to the structural foundations of the Ghanaian economy rather than excessive reliance on foreign-exchange interventions. Policy should focus particularly on expanding domestic production in agriculture and manufacturing, reducing excessive dependence on imports, and strengthening the country’s export capacity. A stronger productive base would have several important macroeconomic benefits. Increased domestic production would reduce the demand for foreign exchange associated with imports, while greater export capacity would increase foreign-exchange earnings. This would reduce the pressure on the BoG to continually inject foreign currency into the market to support the cedi. At the same time, expanding agriculture and manufacturing could generate employment, broaden the domestic tax base, and enhance the government’s capacity to mobilise resources internally. The recent developments in the foreign-exchange market provide an important test of this argument. Over the past two months, the cedi has increasingly shown signs of depreciation following the BoG’s decision to reduce its previous practice of supplying approximately US$1 billion monthly to the foreign-exchange market. Under the emerging arrangement, the GoldBod is expected to play a greater role in foreign-exchange intermediation. Commercial banks provide credit to GoldBod to finance gold purchases, after which GoldBod provides foreign currency to the banks following the sale of the gold. Conceptually, this arrangement may represent a more sustainable mechanism than continuous direct intervention by the central bank. Nevertheless, its effectiveness will depend significantly on the availability of gold and credit, as well as developments in international gold prices. This raises important questions about the resilience of the arrangement. What happens if the supply of gold declines substantially? What happens if efforts to curb illegal mining significantly reduce gold production? And what happens if international gold prices experience a prolonged decline? These are not merely theoretical questions. An exchange-rate strategy that relies heavily on a single commodity as the principal source of foreign-exchange liquidity exposes the economy to significant external and domestic risks. Ghana therefore needs to think beyond short-term currency stabilisation mechanisms. No serious long-term economic strategy should depend excessively on commodity-based foreign-exchange inflows to sustain currency stability. The more fundamental solution lies in transforming the productive structure of the economy: increasing agricultural and industrial output, reducing import dependence, diversifying exports, expanding domestic value addition, and strengthening the country’s capacity to generate foreign exchange through a broad range of productive activities. Ultimately, the objective should not simply be to defend the cedi. The objective should be to build an economy in which the cedi does not require perpetual defence.

title: Hormuz shipping hits two-month low after spike in attacks
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 08 (MNA) – The number of vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz has plummeted to its lowest level in more than two months, according to analytics firm Kpler.
The fall follows a record number of attacks on tankers since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran in February.
Seven commodity vessels passed through the strait on Tuesday, the lowest figure since July 23, Kpler data showed.
“Crude crossing the strait fell 27 percent from a wartime high the week before, to at least 10.1 million barrels a day,” Kpler analysts Emmanuel Belostrino and Yui Torikata reported. “That is back to its September average, but 74 percent of its pre-war level.”
The number of vessels transiting the strait edged up to 10 on Wednesday, but was well short of the daily tally of more than 20 on Sunday and Monday, the data showed.
More vessels entered the strait than exited in the past two days, according to reports.

title: Cost of medicines from Canada set to soar for millions of Americans
body:
Millions of Americans who buy cheap drugs from Canada could soon lose access when a customs rule goes into effect later this month, a change that has sparked opposition from Democrats and some Republicans with the cost of living a top issue for voters ahead of midterm elections.
The rule applies to a swath of goods beyond drugs and is intended to collect tariffs and prevent illegal drugs from coming into the U.S. It comes as President Donald Trump has made lowering drug prices a top target in addressing soaring healthcare costs, and critics say the rule will hurt patients seeking affordable medicine.
“The issue is a matter of life and death for me,” said Susan Hooper, a 75-year-old Toledo, Ohio, resident who has been on oxygen for 14 years and takes two daily medications purchased through a Canadian pharmacy that are not available in the U.S.
The U.S. Customs and Border Protection rule targets the de minimis exemption, which previously allowed shipments valued under $800 to pass through customs more easily. As of Oct. 22, that exemption will be indefinitely suspended, and medications mailed from outside the U.S. will require additional data and a bond guarantee.
The rule puts added fees and registration requirements on low-value shipments that previously entered the U.S. duty-free — on everything from textiles to toys — but the people who could see the most significant impacts are those who buy their cheap drugs from across the border.
And while the rule doesn’t specifically target Canadian drugs — it applies to international mail generally — the practical consequence could be delays, refusals or substantially more difficulty getting their medications delivered.
Roughly 2.3 million Americans buy their drugs abroad, according to a 2020 study by JAMA Network.
The Trump administration has made lowering drug prices a priority in its bid to show Americans that it is tackling soaring costs. Trump, a Republican, has struck multiple most-favoured-nation drug deals with pharmaceutical firms and has launched the discounted-drug website TrumpRx, among other steps.
Federal data from this summer showed that U.S. prescription drug prices were down 3.1% from a year ago, the steepest year-over-year drop since 1963. Trump has sought to take credit for the steep decline, but the real picture is more complicated, and experts say factors beyond the president’s policies likely contributed more to the drop.
Advocates say the rule will hurt patients seeking affordable medicine.
Ken Hunter, executive director of the Campaign for Personal Prescription Importation, which advocates on behalf of Americans who access the Canadian drugs, said those who have enjoyed the lower drug prices from across the northern border may not benefit from Trump’s drug pricing moves.
“There has been a lot of talk of lowering drug prices, but in many cases it doesn’t cover all drugs for all people for all conditions,” he said.
Hunter warned that costs will explode for some medications after his organization conducted a study in August looking at 10 of the most commonly prescribed medications imported from Canada.
He cited Eliquis, a prescription blood thinner used to prevent and treat dangerous blood clots. A three-month supply of 180 5-mg pills would cost $565 from a mail-order Canadian pharmacy. The same medication would cost roughly $1,017 from Amazon’s pharmacy arm or $1,029 from GoodRx.
“I’ve had so many of our members calling me and telling me, ‘I don’t know what I’m going to do,’” Hunter said. “We really need someone to step forward and say, ‘We really need this to stop.’”
Allison Schuster, a White House spokesperson, said in a statement that Trump “remains dedicated to lowering the cost of prescription drugs,” citing the most-favoured-nation deals.
“The Trump administration continues working to ensure Americans have access to low-cost pharmaceuticals across the board,” Schuster said.
The Trump administration could drop the rule, alter it or decide not to enforce it. Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have demanded answers to how the administration will protect access to affordable care for people who get their drugs from over the border.
Three Florida Republican members of Congress wrote to the administration last month expressing concern about how the rule would impact their constituents, who, unlike residents of border states, are unable to easily travel to Canada to buy the drugs.
Florida has separately crafted a Canadian prescription drug importation program with authorization from the federal government, but that initiative has stalled.
Customs and Border Protection and the Food and Drug Administration “must ensure that Floridians simply seeking relief from high drug prices will not be inadvertently impacted by the rule,” said the letter signed by Florida Reps. Aaron Bean, Gus M. Bilirakis and C. Scott Franklin.
A group of more than 70 Democrats last week sent a letter to health and immigration enforcement officials, asking them to pause the new rule unless they could provide assurances that prescription medicines meant for personal use would be able to enter the U.S.
“Americans should not lose access to affordable medicines simply because the government has better information about packages entering the country,” the letter said.
Representatives from CBP did not respond to requests for comment.
Hooper, who has serious drug allergies, said her medications have already increased in price since the Trump administration imposed additional tariffs on Canada in August.
She says Theophylline, a medication that relaxes her airways and is bought in Canada, used to cost $85 with shipping. It now costs $141 because of tariffs. And her Foradil bronchodilator for asthma, which used to cost $151, now costs $273. Hooper said she will find a way to manage through the change. Until then, she said, she’s been in a rush to stockpile.
