Over the past few months, AI models have started resolving major mathematical problems, including ones that have withstood decades of human effort. Claude Fable disproved the Jacobian conjecture in three dimensions, and OpenAI announced a list of 10 problems that its Astra model solved or made significant progress on. Even more recently, an unreleased OpenAI model solved the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize Problem, one of the most famous open problems in mathematics.
These are tremendous accomplishments, but very little about our day-to-day life will actually change as a result. This is because most well-known open mathematical questions are relatively insulated from practical applications. However, there are a few open mathematical problems that do have serious real-world implications. Chief among these is whether public-key encryption is fundamentally secure: that is, whether two strangers can share a secret message over public channels, such as the internet, without eavesdroppers having an efficient way to decipher it.
We rely on public-key encryption every day for end-to-end encrypted messaging apps, virtual private networks (VPNs), and even the HTTPS protocol you’re probably using to read this article. But all of this is based on the unproven assumption that certain mathematical operations are intrinsically easier to do than to undo. In fact, this assumption has already been undermined once: most public-key encryption in use today is vulnerable to an attack that quantum computers could efficiently execute. This has motivated an urgent shift to “post-quantum” cryptography, whose methods may also prove insecure.
As AI models have advanced, they have been making progress in not just pure math, but cryptanalysis as well: Anthropic recently released research showing that Claude Mythos Preview discovered new attacks against two different cryptography algorithms, including a post-quantum technique that was being evaluated by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST).
Breaking a particular algorithm is much easier than proving that every relevant algorithm is breakable. But given the recent impressive progress in both cryptanalysis and mathematics, AI appears to have a real shot at achieving the latter.
The practical implications would be huge, and largely deleterious: it would be the end of end-to-end encryption, and would signal a vast increase in government surveillance powers. Furthermore, results like these are likely to be withheld from the general public, kept as closely guarded secrets by intelligence agencies.
Public-key (also called asymmetric) cryptography forms the foundation of secure communication on the internet. Whenever you communicate with a website over HTTPS, the website sends you its public key. Using only that public key, you can verify messages signed by the website and establish a shared secret key for encrypting everything else you send, even if the channel is being eavesdropped on. We’ll focus on just the second aspect: how that shared key gets established. We’ll use “public-key encryption” as shorthand for this process.
A major early public-key encryption method relied on the difficulty of prime factorization. Historically, from the ancient Roman Caesar cipher onward, almost all encryption was symmetric: both parties needed to use the same secret key to encrypt and decrypt the message. This changed in 1977, when the computer scientists Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir, and Leonard Adleman introduced the RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) cryptosystem, the first practical public-key encryption algorithm available to the public. RSA bases its security on the difficulty of prime factorization. It is easy to multiply two prime numbers together but very difficult to find which numbers were multiplied.
‍ Quantum computers could efficiently break RSA encryption. The rise of the internet made public-key encryption more useful than ever before. Instead of meeting in private to share a secret, strangers communicating over the internet could use public keys to do so without ever leaving their house. However, in 1994, the computer scientist Peter Shor discovered a method of factoring large numbers on quantum computers efficiently. While a human with standard computers would need trillions of years to crunch through the numbers and break RSA encryption, an attacker with a quantum computer could relatively easily undo the multiplication and discover the secret key.
Researchers are trying to make encryption methods resistant to quantum computers. Even though no viable quantum computer existed in 1994, cryptographers realized that the existence of Shor’s algorithm posed an intolerable threat. The reason is “ harvest-now-decrypt-later ”: a persistent adversary could collect data encrypted with vulnerable methods today and decrypt it later, once quantum computing technology had advanced. Indeed, intelligence agencies are widely believed to already be collecting encrypted information for this purpose. As a result of this threat, research almost immediately began on “post-quantum cryptography,” cryptographic algorithms based on a challenge that even a powerful quantum computer cannot solve in a practical amount of time.
Developing robust new encryption methods has proven challenging. So far, research into post-quantum public-key encryption algorithms has clustered around a few mathematical constructs that still don’t have efficient quantum solutions. But even within these domains, the field is littered with broken algorithms. For example, significant effort was put into SIKE , a supposedly quantum-resistant technique based on mathematical functions called isogenies. But, in 2022, having initially passed NIST tests, SIKE was shown to be vulnerable to an attack that required only an hour of computation on a standard PC. These issues are not limited to isogeny-based algorithms. The oldest post-quantum encryption scheme, McEliece , is based on mathematical structures called error-correcting codes. It was also moved to the final round of NIST’s evaluation process, due to its long (nearly 50-year) history of surviving cryptanalytic attacks unscathed. But, in August 2026, an attack was published whose preliminary estimates brought the cost of finding the key below the security thresholds NIST set. The authors of the attack acknowledged AI assistance in their proof.
Post-quantum public-key encryption algorithms occupy an uncertain position: the quantum computers they are designed to defend against don’t yet pose a threat, and proposed algorithms often end up being proven insecure.
It may turn out that these seemingly unrelated failures actually reveal a property of our world: that any mathematical structure clean enough to allow strangers to agree on a secret over a public channel is also clean enough for an eavesdropper to decipher.
Strong cryptography needs hard mathematical problems with no efficient algorithms to solve them. The idea that secure mechanisms for establishing keys over a public channel are simply not possible was first raised by complexity theorist Russell Impagliazzo. In his famous 1995 article , “A Personal View of Average-Case Complexity,” he introduces five worlds we might live in, each differentiated by the algorithms it can access: Algorithmica, Heuristica, Pessiland, Minicrypt, and Cryptomania. Which world we live in depends on the resolution to yet-unsolved problems in complexity theory. These worlds represent security gradations: the harder the relevant mathematical problems are to solve, the more room there is for secure cryptography.
In Algorithmica , Heuristica , and Pessiland , encryption is not possible: in general, any kind of mathematical puzzle you can pose as a cryptographic challenge has a corresponding algorithm that allows eavesdroppers to efficiently solve it.
Minicrypt , on the other hand, offers real cryptography. In this world, we gain one-way functions: functions that are easy to compute but, given the output, hard to reverse. This gives us symmetric encryption, cryptographic hashes , and digital signatures . But here, it’s still impossible to establish a secret in public, since the same key used to encrypt the message can also be used to decrypt it.
In the world of Cryptomania , this changes because, unlike in Minicrypt, public-key encryption exists. Cryptomania represents the most secure world of all, where relevant mathematical problems are hard to solve and most forms of cryptography are possible.
There could be as-yet undiscovered algorithms for breaking encryption methods. Right now, our real world appears to resemble Cryptomania, because we have mathematical structures with no known algorithms that can efficiently solve them. This permits public-key encryption. However, the security we think we have could easily be illusory. There is no fundamental reason why we couldn’t discover an algorithm tomorrow that could solve the mathematical problems we use for encryption today, instantly breaking every encryption scheme built on them.
Public-key encryption is more vulnerable to new algorithms than symmetric encryption. There is a broad consensus among cryptographers and complexity theorists that we likely don’t live in the first three worlds, where modern cryptography is impossible. The confidence that we have at least some cryptography (putting us in either Minicrypt or Cryptomania) comes from how easily mathematicians have been able to find functions that appear hard to undo. In general, any function that scrambles its inputs thoroughly—and there are many ways to do so—appears to be much harder to run backward than forward. Since one-way functions are so diverse, it would be very surprising if every single one of them could be undone by some trick. Unfortunately, the same does not apply to public-key encryption, where only a few highly structured computational operations satisfy the properties needed. Some of these operations, as we saw earlier with prime factorization, have already fallen. The cryptographer Bruce Schneier notes this distinction:
Might these “aliens with sufficient mathematical theory” already be on the way? As AI continues to resolve long-open mathematical conjectures, I believe we shouldn’t discount this possibility.
AI may succeed at cryptanalysis for the same reason it has succeeded at programming and math. Skeptics might say that mathematical problems used for encryption have withstood decades of scrutiny by people who are extremely motivated to find holes, and that AI is therefore likely to find them intractable too. In response, I would first argue that AI might excel in cryptanalysis for the same reason it has excelled in math and coding : solutions are easy to verify. Either the model’s attack successfully recovers the key, or it doesn’t. This means there is a clear signal of success or failure—exactly what is needed for the reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms already deployed by the AI labs to train better AI mathematicians and coders. In other words, the training techniques that have been effective at improving other AI capabilities will extend naturally to cryptanalysis.
AI models’ capabilities can be improved through incrementally harder problems. Additionally, labs can develop “weakened” cryptographic algorithms that are at an appropriate level of difficulty to train the next generation of models against. For example, one of the two encryption methods that Claude Mythos Preview successfully attacked was a simplified version of the ubiquitous Advanced Encryption Standard (AES). Each generation of models can then be given slightly harder problems, to produce even better AI cryptanalysts.
AI models could dramatically expand the effective labor dedicated to cryptanalysis. Also, even though the mathematical structures underlying post-quantum cryptography algorithms have withstood significant scrutiny, AI models may bring a much higher level of scrutiny than ever before. The Cryptology ePrint Archive (the main venue for sharing cryptography and cryptanalysis research) received around 2,300 submissions in 2025, suggesting a community of only a few thousand active researchers. But for any given subfield of post-quantum cryptography, only a fraction of those researchers will be working on it, maybe just a few hundred. While AI tools may not be as smart as the top researchers in the field, AI models are far more willing to do schlep work, grinding their way through every single possible lead. They can bring to bear many more collective person-hours than the research community would spend.
When an encryption method breaks, it takes time to implement a new one. Public-key encryption could become unusable in practice even without proof that it is fundamentally impossible. Most attacks on cryptography algorithms don’t come from fundamental breakthroughs but rather from flaws specific to the algorithm being analyzed. While it might seem easy to swap out a bad algorithm for one that has not yet been broken, it has historically taken a long time (10 to 20 years, according to NIST) for new algorithms to be integrated. Vulnerable algorithms would remain the de facto ones in use during that time. So, if algorithm-specific attacks become frequent enough, we may end up in effectively the same situation as if public-key encryption were altogether impossible.
Even in Minicrypt, many of our cryptographic tools would survive, including symmetric encryption, cryptographic hashes, and digital signatures. This means we could still sign code, securely update software, and even use cryptocurrencies. Most of our software would work the same way as it does today. However, end-to-end encryption between strangers would be dead.
Secure messaging apps would require correspondents to establish their keys in person. One consequence is that secure messaging apps like Signal and WhatsApp would lose their mathematically founded guarantee of privacy that does not require users to trust the messaging provider itself. Today, secure messaging apps require public-key encryption in order to establish a shared key for the conversation. When you message someone by username on Signal, the first step in that conversation is building a secure shared key from both your and your correspondent’s public keys. This doesn’t require you to trust Signal, the company, at all. But, in Minicrypt, that would become impossible. In order to establish a secure conversation, you would already need to have a secure channel to start with. For messaging, this might require establishing connections only in person (perhaps by one person scanning a QR code on the other’s phone). However, it would be impossible for you to securely message someone else by just a username or a phone number, independent of the app developer’s integrity. Lacking such assurance would greatly reduce the privacy value of these apps.
Online, a trusted intermediary service would be needed for secure information exchange. Messaging apps might be able to survive the requirement to verify initial contact in person, but the open web could not. By using an intermediary, instead of needing to open a trusted channel with every single website, you’d need to open only one: with the intermediary itself. When you wanted to visit a website, the intermediary would send both you and the website a key to encrypt the traffic. Browsers might be able to implement this protocol without it looking too different for users. The lock in the corner of the URL bar would still exist, and the protocol might even still be called “https.”
An intermediary might need to distribute keys in physical form, similar to SIM cards. The most visible consequence of this change would be how you get online. In addition to signing up with your cellular service provider or internet service provider, you’d also need to sign up with the trusted intermediary. Making that first channel secure is still hard, and, in practice, it would likely require physical distribution. SIM cards already essentially work like this. The card exists only to hold a pre-shared secret with a mobile carrier, which allows you to use its network.
The intermediary could decrypt messages, and the government might ask them to. While Minicrypt would require our communications systems to change, the political consequences are more important than the technical ones. First, in this world, all secure communication stems from the account you have with the trusted intermediary, making it a natural chokepoint for know-your-customer systems , deplatforming , and age verification . Second, the trusted intermediary could snoop on all of your encrypted communications, and even spoof encrypted messages from you.
In the 1990s, the US government proposed the Clipper chip , an encryption chip for telephones whose secret key was held by the government. With a court order, law enforcement could decrypt everything the chip had ever encrypted. However, the chip was not widely adopted, and the proliferation of open-source public-key encryption methods meant there were alternative encryption methods that would not allow government surveillance. The collapse of public-key encryption would mean that the intermediary could decrypt messages, and the government could ask them to do so, effectively bringing the Clipper chip back.
If public-key encryption is broken, the government might keep it secret. All of the adaptations described above would only happen if society is informed that public-key encryption has been broken and is able to develop a new architecture. But, historically, when various intelligence agencies have discovered that a particular encryption algorithm is broken, they have tended to keep that information to themselves. Secrets like these are some of the most closely guarded pieces of information the government possesses. If one of the frontier AI labs does end up discovering that public-key encryption is broken, it may be sworn to secrecy, and the public may never know.
It may be worth building alternative systems now. The best mitigation is probably to build Minicrypt-ready infrastructure now, before we need it. This would involve standardizing a protocol for key distribution, building support into browsers and operating systems, and deciding how the trusted intermediaries would be governed. By setting up this infrastructure early, we can incorporate better privacy-preserving protections than those we could expect from a rushed rollout. If all goes well, and we do in fact live in Cryptomania, then we’ll never need to use the infrastructure. However, if we gain information that implies our future is Minicrypt—such as AI models discovering efficient algorithms for problems we previously assumed were hard—then the infrastructure would be ready for us to swap over.
Having multiple intermediaries in different countries mitigates government overreach. Chief among the privacy-preserving protections is designing the system so that the role of trusted intermediary is split among different authorities. Using secret-sharing techniques that don’t rely on public-key encryption, you could design a system that requires, say, three out of five providers to cooperate in order to construct a session key. Then a single corrupt, hacked, or subpoenaed provider would have no way to decrypt your communications alone. This can help to avoid concentration of power in government; if the providers are in different jurisdictions, then no court order from any one government can force all of them to comply with a request to decrypt messages. This is still weaker than today’s end-to-end encryption, where we don’t have to trust any provider. Nonetheless, it’s a meaningful protection against a single government’s overreach.
The situation we’re currently in is somewhat analogous to the one cryptographers faced after the discovery of Shor’s algorithm in 1994. At the time it was invented, quantum computers didn’t exist. Yet researchers recognized that it might only be a matter of time before they did. As AI-assisted mathematics continues to grow stronger, we’re faced with a similar challenge: designing cryptographic protocols that are secure against an adversary potentially far more mathematically capable than ourselves. Just as researchers began to respond to the risks of quantum decryption as soon as they were understood in principle, so too should we start to address the cryptography risks of superhuman AI mathematicians before they emerge.

title: UAE states support for Saudi Arabia after Houthi airport attacks
body: The UAE on Thursday condemned Yemeni rebels' attacks against Saudi Arabian airports, expressing its support for "all measures" taken by Riyadh in response. Three people were killed this week in Houthi attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and Abha International Airport in the south. On Thursday, two residents of Riyadh reported sounds of explosions , as flights at King Khalid airport continue to be affected. The Saudi-led coalition said the Houthi attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia would not go "unpunished", spokesman Maj Gen Turki Al Malki said, announcing a “comprehensive operation” that destroyed 82 Houthi military targets in Yemen. In a statement, the UAE's Ministry of Foreign Affairs "condemned in the strongest terms" the attacks, adding that they "constitute a flagrant violation of the sovereignty of the kingdom of Saudi Arabia and a threat to its security and stability". The ministry reaffirmed the UAE’s "full solidarity" with the kingdom and its support for "all measures" taken in response. It also expressed its "solidarity and sincere condolences and sympathy to the families of the victims, as well as its wishes for a speedy recovery for all the injured". Attacks by the Iran-backed rebels against Saudi Arabia come amid renewed fighting after Houthi advances along Yemen's Red Sea coast and a Yemeni government counter-offensive supported by coalition air strikes. “The targeting of civilian infrastructure is completely unacceptable,” the Indian Foreign Ministry said in a statement, expressing condolences to the families of those killed and wishing a speedy recovery to those injured. It also expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia and said it stood with the kingdom’s people and government. France also condemned the Houthis’ repeated attacks on Saudi Arabia and expressed its “full solidarity” with the kingdom's defence of its territory and infrastructure, the Foreign Ministry in Paris said. Last month, Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan called for a comprehensive political solution in Yemen and condemned Houthi missile and drone attacks against his country and commercial vessels, as well as threats to navigation in the Red Sea. He told the UN General Assembly that a comprehensive agreement was needed to bring stability to Yemen.

title: WAFU B U-17 Championship: Black Starlets’ road trip to Burkina Faso was planned – Joe Abu Salam
body: The Leader of Delegation for Ghana’s U17 national team, the Black Starlets, Joe Abu Salam, says the team’s decision to travel by road from Ghana to Burkina Faso was planned and was not a result of neglect by the Ghana Football Association (GFA). The Starlets’ lengthy road journey came just days after they returned from Morocco, where they played two friendly matches against the hosts as part of their preparations for the WAFU Zone B U17 Championship. Ghana won the first game 2-0 before losing the second 2-1 after Morocco scored with the final kick of the match. Concerns were raised after reports emerged that the Black Starlets had spent more than 20 hours travelling by road to Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso, ahead of the tournament, which begins on Saturday, October 10. But speaking to JoySports, Joe Abu Salam said the trip was part of the team’s original preparations. “Ouagadougou was part of our plan. Currently, the FA has a training centre in Bolgatanga, where the weather is similar to what we have here in Ouagadougou. “So, we had four days of training in Bolga before moving to Ouagadougou. “From Bolga to Ouagadougou, everyone knows it’s just about three hours. It’s not far, so it was part of our programme.” The Black Starlets have been drawn in Group B alongside Togo, Benin and hosts Burkina Faso. The top two finalists will qualify for the 2027 U17 Africa Cup of Nations.

title: South Korea recalls Ukraine envoy over prisoner-of-war row
body: South Korea has said it will recall its ambassador to Ukraine, the latest escalation in a diplomatic spat between both countries. It started last month when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that his government had transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to Seoul. Seoul says Ukraine broke an agreement to keep the transfer a secret but Zelensky’s office maintains that there was no non-disclosure agreement in place. The two North Korean soldiers, who were among thousands from the country supporting Russia in the Ukraine war, had earlier told local media they wanted to be sent to South Korea. South Korean Vice Foreign Minister Park Yoon-joo had in September lodged a formal complaint with his Ukrainian counterpart Andrii Vieshkin over the matter. And earlier this week, Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said he received an apology from his Ukrainian counterpart, but added that it fell short of Seoul’s expectations, according to local reports. But on Wednesday, Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi told reporters at a media briefing that its Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha had not apologised, according to Ukrainian news site Liga. In a statement on Thursday, South Korea’s Foreign Ministry said it would “continue consultations with the Ukrainian side”, adding that it expected that “various outstanding issues…[would] be resolved smoothly”. Zelensky had revealed the transfer at a speech at the UN General Assembly in September, adding that the two North Koreans had not been “easy to capture alive”. It prompted a swift condemnation from South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, who called it “greatly disappointing” and said the transfer was a “highly sensitive issue” impacting national security. President Lee also faced heavy criticism at home in light of the revelation, with local opposition accusing him of wanting to cover up the transfer to appease Pyongyang. But his office said that it had been kept confidential partly to protect the North Koreans’ families and added that Kyiv also wanted the transfer kept secret to avoid criticism that it had given up an opportunity to exchange the soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners of war. Lee’s office explained Ukraine had indicated the soldiers would be mentioned in Zelensky’s address, but not the fact of their transfer. The spat escalated when Zelensky’s office responded claiming that the two countries did not have a non-disclosure agreement. Seoul later demanded Ukraine apologise for “announcing a falsehood” and said its actions had seriously damaged trust between the two nations. Seoul has been sympathetic to Ukraine since Russia’s full-scale invasion, but has refused to break from its longstanding policy of not providing lethal weapons to any country engaged in active war. After North Korean troops were deployed to support Russia in 2024, Kyiv stepped up pressure on South Korea to supply cutting-edge anti-air missiles to help defend Ukraine’s energy infrastructure from Russian drone and missile attacks. This July, Seoul had announced a $100 million assistance package to Ukraine. Lee’s office said it would be an expansion of earlier assistance which was comprised of non-lethal items including helmets, personal armour and medical equipment. Meanwhile Russia’s foreign ministry has warned it would have “no choice but to retaliate” if South Korea provided Ukraine with arms, without specifying action it might take. South Korea has long pursued cordial ties with its neighbours who may be at odds with its ally, the US. Since the collapse of the Soviet Union, it has worked to deepen trade and diplomatic relations with Russia, which borders North Korea, and views both Moscow and Beijing as key partners in efforts to influence Pyongyang.

title: Genoa Design International and atlantiq AI Launch Multi-Year Partnership
body: Canadian partnership follows a year of validation in operational ship design workflows Genoa Design International (Genoa), the Digital Ship Experts® and one of North America’s leading detail design and 3D modelling firms for the shipbuilding industry, announced a multi-year partnership with atlantiq AI , a Canadian technology company pioneering advanced AI systems for the ship design-to-build lifecycle. Shipbuilding workflows demand accuracy, security and accountability. Over the past year, Genoa and atlantiq AI tested the technology within operational ship design workflows, evaluating its performance against production requirements and shipbuilding standards before expanding its use. “We spent a year testing and validating this technology within our own work before bringing the partnership forward publicly,” said Laurie Balan, CEO of Genoa Design. “We wanted this announcement to be grounded in demonstrated results. What we have seen gives us confidence that AI can meaningfully improve how ship design work is performed while keeping expert judgment, security and responsible adoption at the centre.” Following successful validation, the partnership is moving into broader implementation across design operations, where early applications have demonstrated the potential to improve both quality and delivery timelines. Genoa is contributing thousands of hours from designers, technical specialists and industry experts to help ensure the technology is developed and evaluated within real-world shipbuilding environments. “Genoa’s experts bring decades of shipbuilding knowledge and an uncompromising commitment to quality,” said Nurul Ibrahim , CEO of atlantiq AI. “Our systems are built to give that expertise greater reach. By taking on information-intensive work and helping teams develop and test design ideas, we want to give their designers and engineers more room to apply their judgment. The opportunity is to bring more of what this industry knows to the vessels we have yet to design.” Purpose-built for ship design and engineering, the technology helps teams review complex information, identify potential issues, manage design data and produce high-quality deliverables more efficiently. All outputs remain subject to established validation processes and expert oversight, reflecting the level of assurance required in shipbuilding. For Genoa, the partnership also advances the company’s long-term Digital Ship® vision. By integrating AI into the Digital Ship® platform, Genoa is strengthening the digital thread that carries information from design and construction through operation, sustainment and eventual decommissioning. “AI-enabled detail and production design is no longer a future concept; it is becoming a practical capability,” said Colin Power, Senior Director of Technology with Genoa. “Our goal is to help establish a trustworthy and secure adoption model that delivers measurable value for Genoa, our customers and the wider shipbuilding industry.” Genoa and atlantiq AI are participating in DEFSEC 2026 in Halifax, Nova Scotia from October 7-8 The post Genoa Design International and atlantiq AI Launch Multi-Year Partnership appeared first on Canadian Defence Review .

title: Greek Australian Mark Bouris warns ‘cracks are appearing’ in Australia’s housing market
body: Greek Australian businessman and Yellow Brick Road executive chairman Mark Bouris is sounding the alarm over Australia’s housing market as property prices fall for a fifth consecutive month. “Cracks are appearing,” Bouris warns, as the country’s housing boom begins to show signs of a much deeper correction. National dwelling values have fallen almost 5 per cent from their March peak, while Sydney has suffered a 7.1 per cent decline and Melbourne is down 6.5 per cent. Even markets that had continued to show resilience, including Brisbane, Perth and Adelaide, are now moving backwards. For Bouris, the problem is not simply falling house prices. It is what happens when falling prices collide with enormous mortgages, higher repayments, tighter lending and borrowers who entered the market with very little equity. The warning signs are multiplying Homes are now taking longer to sell, with the median property reportedly spending around 38 days on the market, the longest stretch since October 2022. New loan commitments have fallen by more than 5 per cent over the latest quarter, while investor lending has dropped by more than 10 per cent. Prices are falling. Borrowing is slowing. Buyers are pulling back. And households are still dealing with the impact of higher interest rates. That combination is putting increasing pressure on the Australian housing market. First-home buyers are particularly exposed One of the biggest risks sits with recent buyers who entered the market with very small deposits. Government schemes have increasingly helped Australians buy homes with deposits as low as 5 per cent, allowing younger buyers to enter the market sooner. Applications from Australians aged 18 to 25 reportedly jumped almost 23 per cent after the scheme was expanded last October. But small deposits leave borrowers with very little protection when prices fall. Consider a couple who bought a $900,000 Sydney property with a 5 per cent deposit. They would have contributed $45,000 and borrowed about $855,000. After Sydney’s 7.1 per cent decline, that property would be worth roughly $836,000. Ignoring principal repayments, the couple would owe around $19,000 more than the property is worth. Their entire original deposit would effectively have been wiped out. That is the danger of high leverage. A percentage decline that looks relatively modest on a property chart can represent tens of thousands of dollars for a highly indebted household. Mortgage stress is adding to the pressure There are also signs that financial stress is beginning to emerge among newer borrowers. First-home buyers using low-deposit schemes are reportedly experiencing mortgage arrears at a seven-month high, with some groups recording arrears at roughly twice the rate of other borrowers. In Victoria and Western Australia, first-home buyer arrears have reportedly approached 0.9 per cent, compared with around one-third of that level among non-first-home buyers. These figures do not suggest that Australia is already experiencing a mortgage crisis. But they highlight where pressure can appear first. Recent buyers generally have smaller deposits, less accumulated equity and larger mortgages relative to their assets. Roy Morgan data has also placed mortgage stress at its highest level since the Global Financial Crisis. More pain could be coming The banking sector is also warning that property prices may have further to fall. Commonwealth Bank has forecast additional declines of around 6 per cent for Sydney and 7 per cent for Melbourne this year. HSBC has flagged the possibility of a national peak-to-trough decline of as much as 13 per cent. Those are forecasts rather than guarantees. But if falls approach anything like those levels, the impact will not be evenly distributed. A homeowner who bought 15 years ago may still have substantial equity despite a significant fall. A young couple who bought recently with only 5 per cent down could see their entire financial buffer disappear. The uncomfortable truth about housing affordability Falling property prices can eventually make homes more affordable for future buyers. But cheaper houses do not automatically mean cheaper home ownership. If interest rates remain elevated and borrowing capacity is reduced, buyers may still struggle to purchase even as property prices decline. For existing borrowers, meanwhile, a falling property value does not reduce the mortgage. The debt remains. Only the value of the asset backing that debt changes. That is why the current correction matters. Australia spent years building a housing market heavily dependent on credit, large mortgages and continued capital growth. As prices rose, the risks were easier to overlook. Rising values created equity and helped borrowers withstand large debts. Now prices are moving in the opposite direction. And as Greek Australian Mark Bouris puts it, the cracks are appearing. Source Straight Talk with Mark Bouris – Property Experts The post Greek Australian Mark Bouris warns ‘cracks are appearing’ in Australia’s housing market appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: Patria Group expands industrial footprint in Latvia, starts construction of new production facility
body: The plant will stand near the existing Defence Partnership Latvia facility at the Valmiera Industrial and Export Park. Until now, vehicle production in Valmiera has been limited to Patria 6×6 armoured personnel carriers. The new facility is planned to produce Patria 6×6 vehicles and assemble General Dynamics European Land Systems (GDELS) HUNTER vehicles for the Latvian National Armed Forces. It will also provide full lifecycle support for both types and accommodate other defence industry projects. “The establishment of this facility is a significant investment in the development of Latvia’s defence industry and the capabilities of the National Armed Forces,” said Latvian Defence Minister Raivis Melnis. “Our goal is to build local industrial capacity that enables us not only to manufacture and maintain armoured vehicles locally, but also to strengthen security of supply and resilience.” Melnis linked the investment to longer-term cooperation between Patria and Latvian companies. “Patria’s experience and the capabilities of the new facility, combined with the expertise of Latvian companies, provide a strong foundation for long-term cooperation that will help strengthen both our own and our Allies’ defence capabilities,” he said. “This investment is a clear proof of Patria’s long-term commitment to Latvia and the Latvian National Armed Forces,” said Panu Routila, Patria’s president and chief executive. “By strengthening local production, developing expertise, and involving Latvian companies in the defence supply chain, we are building industrial capabilities that support both security of supply and long-term resilience.” Routila also pointed to the role of the company’s partnership with GDELS. “At the same time, our cooperation with GDELS demonstrates how strong partnerships and local industrial capabilities can help deliver modern military capabilities to the Latvian National Armed Forces faster and more efficiently,” he said.

title: Swedish aircraft carries out reconnaissance over Black Sea for fourth consecutive day
body:
MOSCOW, October 8. /TASS/. A Swedish radar intelligence aircraft has been detected flying over the neutral waters of the Black Sea for the fourth consecutive day, a source in EU air traffic control services told TASS.
The aircraft is a Gulfstream S102B Korpen, which was deployed on Monday by the Swedish Air Force from Malmen Air Base to Bucharest, from where it is now conducting reconnaissance flights over the waters.
"The aircraft has again been detected operating over the Black Sea. It is expected to remain airborne for several hours, flying from west to east across the waters and back, without entering the airspace of any of the coastal countries," the source said.
He recalled that the day before, the Gulfstream S102B Korpen had operated over the sea for nearly seven hours alongside a US-registered NATO reconnaissance aircraft, the Bombardier Artemis II, which is based in Constanta, Romania. The source described the flight of two reconnaissance aircraft over the Black Sea at the same time as a rather rare occurrence, but did not rule out the possibility of it recurring.
He also noted that reconnaissance aircraft usually fly at altitudes of up to 13.5 km outside civil aviation routes.

title: Saudi Arabia in talks on 'shuttle' oil supplies — Bloomberg
body:
NEW YORK, October 8. /TASS/. Saudi Arabia is holding negotiations on "shuttle" oil supplies through the Strait of Hormuz under long-term contracts, Bloomberg news agency reported, citing sources.
Saudi Arabia uses so-called shuttle vessels to transport oil through the Strait of Hormuz and subsequently transfer it to buyers' vessels outside the area, Bloomberg said. Agency sources noted that Saudi oil company Saudi Aramco allowed some buyers to transfer oil from one ship to another off the coast of India, as buyers do not want to approach the Gulf of Oman due to security considerations.
The negotiations are expected to be completed by the end of the year, and a final decision has not yet been made, the news agency added.

title: Caretaker killed and two teachers injured in knife attack at Poland school
body: A 37-year-old caretaker has died after being stabbed by a former pupil at a school in Poland, police have said. The 15-year-old entered the primary school in Leszczydół-Nowiny, north of Warsaw, at around 09:00 (07:00 GMT) and attacked the caretaker, 37, before being overpowered by a teacher and the school’s headteacher who were also injured. Polish police said they had also detained a 17-year-old boy in another town after he had indicated an intention to do “something spectacular” at his school. Both incidents come a day after a 19-year-old was arrested on suspicion of a stabbing attack at another Polish school in which seven people were injured. The 15-year-old who attacked the caretaker was carrying three knives, Poland’s interior ministry spokesperson Karolina Galecka said. The boy used to study at the primary school, but his motives for the attack are unclear, Galecka added. Polish media report that the caretaker had tried to stop the 15-year-old from entering the school. The teacher and the headteacher’s lives are not in danger, the ministry’s spokesperson said. Before news of Thursday’s stabbing in Leszczydół-Nowiny, Mazowsze Police announced it had prevented a separate school stabbing in the region. Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said the 17-year-old detained in the town of Sierpc, north-west of Warsaw, “had stated on school grounds that he planned to do something… dangerous – that he intended to harm someone”. Teachers had alerted the police, who found that the teenager was in possession of two knives. “The young person had been searching for information on how to orchestrate a ‘bloody’ event of this kind,” Kierwiński said.

title: Mark Villar switches camps. Minutes later, family’s troubled firms make their move.
body: A Villar switches political camps, and seemingly on cue, parts of the family’s battered business empire stir to life. On Thursday, October 8 – amid an extended lunch break in Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial , and with the Senate about to go on a month-long legislative recess – there was apparently just enough time for Senator Mark Villar to switch to the majority and promptly snag the powerful public works committee chairmanship and a seat in the Commission on Appointments. His sister, Senator Camille Villar, stayed put in the minority, leaving the family a foot in both camps. Minutes later came the corporate disclosures. Between 2:12 pm and 3:09 pm, three companies under the Villar family’s corporate umbrella announced moves that could bring them closer to resuming trading on the Philippine Stock Exchange (PSE), following months of suspension and controversy. Talk about timing. In separate, successive PSE disclosures, Vista Land & Lifescapes (VLL), Vistamalls (STR), and VistaREIT (VREIT) announced that their boards had approved the release of their long-overdue audited financial statements for 2025. Coming just minutes after news of Villar’s flip in the Senate broke, the filings were enough to set tongues wagging in stock market analyst circles, with speculation about the family’s political maneuvering and whether its suspended companies might finally be inching toward a return to stock market trading. But the three companies are only part of a bigger mess nagging at the Villars. In all, six of the family’s listed companies have been pushed out of stock market trading after repeatedly missing financial reporting deadlines. First came their overdue 2025 annual reports , then their Q1 2026 financial statements , followed by their Q2 reports . For months, investors have been left holding shares they cannot sell. Thursday’s announcements are also far from enough to get the stocks trading again. The three companies have merely authorized the release of their 2025 audited statements, which have yet to be published on the exchange. There’s no word on their overdue quarterly reports either. And that’s just three of the six. AllHome (HOME), AllDay Marts (ALLDY) , and, most notably, Villar Land Holdings (VLC) made no similar announcements. Must Read Anyare? Villars’ AllHome, AllDay confirm store closures Trillion-peso controversy The last of these is particularly conspicuous. Villar Land Holdings is at the center of the family’s biggest financial controversy, after initially reporting a staggering P1.3 trillion in assets for 2024, driven by an unbelievable revaluation of its properties in Villar City. Its subsequently audited statements showed assets of only P35.7 billion , a fraction of the earlier figure. Since then, it has been one controversy after another for the Villar family. Among their mounting troubles: In August 2025, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) fined Villar Land and its directors and officers P12 million over reporting violations. Months later, it revoked property appraiser E-Value Phils.’ accreditation and fined it P1 million over unreliable valuations. In January 2026, the SEC filed a criminal complaint against Villar Land, family members, and related firms over alleged market manipulation, insider trading, and misleading disclosures. The Villars have denied wrongdoing and sought its dismissal. In September, the Ombudsman filed graft and administrative complaints against the Villar family over its PrimeWater contracts with local water districts. In San Jose del Monte , Bulacan, a water crisis affecting over 47,000 households prompted a state of calamity and the city government’s takeover of PrimeWater’s operations, with Metro Pacific Water brought in as interim operator. Before trading was suspended, Villar Land shares last traded at P448 as of May 29, a drop off the cliff from their 52-week high of P2,300. Francis Lim, the man tasked with keeping watch over the country’s corporations, has made clear that even the most powerful families are not untouchable. Must Read SEC chief Francis Lim to Villars: No family is too powerful to sue “If you deserve to be sued, we will sue you,” the SEC chairman said in July, referring to the case against the Villars. The SEC’s criminal complaint remains under preliminary investigation at the Department of Justice. Time will tell whether Mark Villar’s moves will be enough to build back the fallen family’s political and financial capital. – Rappler.com

title: Almaty to Host Central Asia’s First World Tennis General Assembly
body: From October 10 to 13, Almaty will host events for the annual General Assembly of World Tennis, formerly the International Tennis Federation (ITF). The meeting of national tennis federation leaders will be held in Central Asia for the first time. More than 262 delegates from 137 countries are expected to attend. Founded in 1913, World Tennis is tennis’s global governing body. It sets the rules of the game and oversees the Davis Cup, Billie Jean King Cup, and junior competitions. In June 2026, the federation changed its name from ITF to World Tennis. Its leadership also announced plans to increase the number of people playing tennis worldwide from 106 million to 140 million by 2035. The federation’s Board of Directors will meet in Almaty on October 10–11, followed by the General Assembly and voting on October 13. The announced topics include support for national federations, the development of children’s tennis, training for coaches and officials, and the organization of international competitions. The Kazakhstan Tennis Federation is headed by Bulat Utemuratov, who also serves as vice president of World Tennis. In recent years, Kazakhstan has regularly hosted international tournaments, including the ATP 250 Almaty Open. The next tournament will take place later that month, from October 17 to 25. The meeting will take place shortly after Elena Rybakina’s victory at the U.S. Open, her third Grand Slam title. Rybakina has now risen to the top of the Women’s Tennis Association (WTA) rankings for the first time.

title: Dragone: Ukraine has received $10B worth of U.S. weapons through PURL
body:
Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, Chair of the NATO Military Committee, said this in an interview with Ukrinform.
"The PURL mechanism is working. It is the quickest one, I think. It started in July last year, and now it is running very well, in speed. Ukraine gets what it needs, based on its requests and its priorities, and in the quickest way," he said.
Dragone stressed that this is not the only mechanism. Overall, the Alliance provided Ukraine with $70 billion in 2026 and has pledged another $70 billion in assistance for 2027.
"They [Ukraine's partners] are motivated. We think they are going to succeed. And this way, with your action on the battlefield – I say again, the deep strikes – and also with the fact that Ukraine has been able to stop the front line, there is no gain in territory," the admiral added.
On October 6, a delegation from the NATO Military Committee, led by its chair, Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, visited Kyiv for talks with the leadership of the General Staff of the Ukrainian Armed Forces on the battlefield situation and further support for Ukraine.

title: Over 80% of Ukrainians favor holding peace talks with Russia, survey finds
body:
MOSCOW, October 8. /TASS/. Overall, 83% of respondents in Ukraine are in favor of holding talks with Russia and negotiating a compromise with the participation of third countries, a survey conducted by Rating Group showed.
"The absolute majority views negotiations as a real way of putting an end to the war (57% of respondents say such a way would be to find a compromise involving third countries in negotiations, and 26% favor direct talks)," the Ukrainian pollster said in a press release on its website.
At that, Rating Group found, 56% of those surveyed believe that Ukraine should make territorial concessions and obtain Western security guarantees, while a mere 13% of respondents favor continued hostilities.
The telephone survey was conducted on October 3-5 among 1,000 adults aged 18 and older.

title: Regions Calling: In Irkutsk, Locals Ask 'What Plague?'
body:
Hello and welcome to Regions Calling , your guide to developments beyond the Russian capital from The Moscow Times.
The death of a lab worker at a plague research institute in Siberia’s Irkutsk region soared to global headlines after local bloggers circulated unconfirmed reports and the head of the neighboring republic of Buryatia named “plague” as the suspected cause.
We spoke with residents of both regions about how the health scare is affecting their everyday lives. We also asked an independent health policy expert to weigh in on Moscow’s handling of the possible outbreak and what risks it poses to the rest of the world.
But first, a look at the latest news from the regions:
Authorities in the Krasnodar region closed beaches in the Black Sea resort city of Sochi and surrounding areas on Tuesday after an oil tanker caught fire offshore following a reported drone attack. Ecologists have already warned that the incident could have potentially catastrophic environmental consequences, including water contamination and the release of large volumes of hazardous substances into the air.
Meanwhile, Yevgeny Naumov, the mayor of the region’s capital Krasnodar, preemptively resigned on Monday after four years in office plagued by controversy. In January, Naumov signed off on plans to build an Orthodox Church on the grounds of a riverside park despite protests from residents. Since November 2025, more than 30,000 people have signed a petition demanding his resignation.
A string of deadly bear attacks on humans has continued across Siberia and the Far East over the past few weeks. In the latest confirmed incident, a 55-year-old man was killed by a bear that entered a trailer parked on the premises of a local company in the eastern part of the Irkutsk region. At least 20 people have been killed in bear attacks across Russia since April. In response, lawmakers are reportedly considering lifting hunting quotas, establishing regional population limits and giving local authorities extra powers to control bear numbers. Authorities in the Krasnoyarsk region said Monday that they have already culled more than 850 bears “as part of the population control measures.” Read more about reasons behind the attacks in the previous edition of Regions Calling .
A military court in the Zabaikalsky region sentenced Indigenous Buryat activist Marina Khankhalaeva to 20 years in prison in absentia on charges of organizing an extremist group and participating in a terrorist organization. Khankhalaeva called the verdict “high praise” and proof that she and fellow members of pro-independence group Tusgaar Buryad-Mongolia “are doing the right thing” in comments to The Moscow Times.
The former head of Dagestan Sergei Melikov was appointed as a senator from the western Bryansk region in Russia’s upper-house Federation Council last week. Melikov, who had headed Dagestan since 2020, resigned from the post in May following public backlash over his handling of deadly floods in the mountainous republic.
“There are no conversations on the streets, no bustle, no fear, no lines at the pharmacies like there were during Covid,” a woman from Irkutsk, the capital of the Siberian region of the same name, tells The Moscow Times.
“There was panic for maybe the first few hours after the news broke. Then memes began to appear online and everyone calmed down,” she adds. “ There are so many things going on at once: the fuel crises , the bear invasion , now the plague. People here treat these things as background noise.”
Irkutsk , a region roughly the size of Turkey with a population of 2.3 million people, made international headlines after a 28-year-old employee of a local plague research institute died at a hospital in the Irkutsk suburb of Shelekhov last week.
The highly urbanized industrial region was until now best known for the UNESCO-enscribed Lake Baikal , the world’s largest freshwater lake by volume — that is, before the latest global plague-induced scare.
But for most locals, who say they found out about the possible plague case from social media, little has changed.
“Life goes on as usual in Irkutsk,” another local told The Moscow Times on Wednesday. “Today I met a doctor on the street and asked them about the outbreak. She said that there was one case, but now everything is calm.”
News that the lab worker, Daria Shipilova, may have died from plague first surfaced in since-deleted posts on local anonymous Telegram channels in the early hours of Oct. 2, local independent news outlet Irkutsk Blog reported .
A handful of news outlets soon picked up the rumor and added more unverified details.
The exiled news outlet Lyudi Baikala (People of Baikal) cited an anonymous source who said the victim was hospitalized after arriving from Thailand, while local TV channel NTS was the first to speculate that the woman got infected after accidentally breaking a test tube containing live bacteria.
Irkutsk region Governor Igor Kobzev confirmed that the head of state health and safety watchdog Rospotrebnadzor had arrived in the region because of “a suspected case of a highly dangerous infection.”
“All identified contacts have been placed under medical observation. As of today, the contacts show no signs of illness and laboratory test results are negative,” Kobzev said on Oct. 2.
Rospotrebnadzor also avoided the word “plague” in its first statement on the matter published Sunday, saying Shipilova died from a “pneumonia of unknown etiology.”
The first — and only — Russian official to use the word “plague” was Alexei Tsydenov, the head of the republic of Buryatia , which borders the Irkutsk region to the east and south.
“The woman who died — possibly from the plague — in the Irkutsk region had not traveled to Buryatia. There are no plague outbreaks in the republic, including in the area bordering Mongolia,” Tsydenov said .
Vadim Palko, a journalist at Irkutsk Blog, said he believes that Tsydenov’s statement was more of a calculated attempt to distance himself from unwelcome news that likely upset the Kremlin than a heartfelt urge to reveal the truth to the public.
“He tried, first of all, to protect himself by signaling that all the problems are coming from Irkutsk,” Palko said, adding that Tsydenov’s reaction was likely prompted by rumors that the lab worker allegedly traveled to a “plague hotspot in Buryatia.”
The atmosphere in Buryatia, meanwhile, has been largely similar to that in Irkutsk.
“I found out about the plague from Instagram, from friends who sent me funny reels about it,” said a resident of Buryatia’s capital Ulan-Ude.
“I haven’t been taking any precautionary measures…But now that you have asked, I am thinking maybe I should have? But, actually, what should be done in case of a plague outbreak?” she told The Moscow Times.
This lack of “effective and trusted communication” with the public could prove Moscow’s biggest misstep in handling the plague scare, said Judyth Twigg, a professor of political science at Virginia Commonwealth University and an expert on Russia’s health system.
The World Health Organization recorded 3,847 suspected human plague cases and 423 deaths across 10 countries between 2019 and 2025. The majority were recorded in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Madagascar, but some were also reported in the rural parts of the western United States.
“Residents [of the Irkutsk region] should have received practical guidance…with regular updates, even when the update is that there are no new cases,” Twigg told The Moscow Times.
“It’s what health authorities elsewhere do with plague cases as a matter of routine course, and none of it would have required Russia to concede anything embarrassing beyond the possibility of a laboratory accident,” she added.
Twigg said the measures Russia has reportedly taken appeared operationally sound, including the rapid identification and observation of contacts, isolation measures, precautions scaled to a dangerous pathogen and on-site oversight by specialists.
Today, plague “is not a plausible mass threat to any society with a functioning public health system,” she said, a take echoed by other health science professionals.
“Even though the plague pathogen Yersinia pestis is dangerous and actually causes a very severe and tricky disease, events of the past are not expected to repeat today,” said science journalist Irina Yakutenko, referencing the 14th-century plague pandemic known as the Black Death.
“Beyond the pathogen itself, certain conditions are needed for it to spread: people, rats and fleas who are all constantly in contact with each other,” added Yakutenko.
Rospotrebnadzor announced Wednesday that it has concluded a series of “preventive and anti-epidemic measures” in the Irkutsk region, which reportedly included medical observations of more than 90% of contacts and 5,000 laboratory tests that failed to reveal any dangerous pathogens.
“There are no epidemic risks for the population of Irkutsk and the Irkutsk region,” the health watchdog said.
Meanwhile, the lack of transparency surrounding the incident has already fueled conspiracies that the Irkutsk plague research lab could be part of a state-sponsored bioweapons program.
“Russia's history…provides plenty of reason to ask hard questions. In this case, though, there’s nothing in the public record supporting the conclusion that this civilian surveillance institute was doing something exotic,” Twigg said.
“Transparency would be Moscow's cheapest and most effective rebuttal, but the system isn’t designed to supply transparency.”
Residents of Oshurkovo, a village on the left bank of the Selenga River in the republic of Buryatia , put up scarecrows to protest the planned opening of a controversial apatite ore mining site.
“Even the pumpkin knows that apatites equal the death of Baikal. Do you?” says the banner attached to the scarecrow.
State environmental watchdog Rosprirodnadzor greenlit the Russian Copper Company ’s mining project earlier this year despite residents and scientists voicing concerns about the threat it poses to Lake Baikal, which is fed by the Selenga.

“As Russia’s Permafrost Thaws, Ancient Pathogens Risk Re-Awakening” by Lana Koralova
We are facing unprecedented challenges. Russia's Prosecutor General's Office has designated The Moscow Times as an "undesirable" organization, criminalizing our work and putting our staff at risk of prosecution. This follows our earlier unjust labeling as a "foreign agent."
These actions are direct attempts to silence independent journalism in Russia. The authorities claim our work "discredits the decisions of the Russian leadership." We see things differently: we strive to provide accurate, unbiased reporting on Russia.
We, the journalists of The Moscow Times, refuse to be silenced. But to continue our work, we need your help .
Your support, no matter how small, makes a world of difference. If you can, please support us monthly starting from just $ 2. It's quick to set up, and every contribution makes a significant impact.
By supporting The Moscow Times, you're defending open, independent journalism in the face of repression. Thank you for standing with us.

title: Moscow, Minsk to counter policy of space militarization
body:
MOSCOW, October 8. /TASS/. Russia and Belarus oppose the deployment of any weapons in outer space and will counter policies aimed at the militarization of space, the two countries said in a joint statement at the First Committee of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, published on the Russian Foreign Ministry’s website.
"We oppose the deployment of any weapons in outer space, the threat or use of force against space objects or by means of them, attempts by certain countries to use outer space for the purposes of armed confrontation, including as part of implementing the United States’ Golden Dome project, which features the development and deployment of space-based interceptors," the document reads.
"We highlight the serious negative consequences of such steps and will counter policies aimed at achieving military superiority in outer space and officially describing it as an area for combat operations," the two countries added.
Russia and Belarus also reiterated the need for the early launch of international talks to develop a legally binding multilateral instrument to prevent "an arms race in space and ban the deployment of any weapons in outer space, the threat or use of force" against space objects or by means of them. "We call for a global international initiative/political commitment on the no-first-placement of weapons in outer space," the statement noted.

title: NAF confirms helicopter makes precautionary landing in Benue
body: The Nigerian Air Force has said one of its helicopters made a precautionary landing on farmland in Makurdi, Benue State, after returning from an operation against suspected kidnappers. The helicopter landed on Wednesday at Utur Tse-Igboji community in Bar Council Ward, along the Welfare Quarters–Mopol 13 Ring Road in the state capital. In a statement issued on Wednesday, the Director of Public Relations and Information, NAF, Air Commodore Ehimen Ejodame, said the aircraft had successfully supported ground troops during the operation. The statement read in part, “The helicopter had successfully provided close air support to surface forces during an operation targeting suspected kidnappers in the Ogbadigbo area of Benue State, near the Enugu-Benue boundary. The operation disrupted the activities of the criminal elements and supported the advance of surface forces. “Following the successful completion of the mission, the pilot, on return to base, exercised his professional discretion to execute a precautionary landing approximately 10 nautical miles from the airfield. “This is in accordance with established operational and safety procedures following combat missions. The helicopter has returned to base.” The NAF said the operation was part of efforts to sustain pressure on criminal elements and support ground forces in restoring security to affected communities. “The NAF remains committed to sustaining pressure on criminal elements, providing close air support to surface forces and protecting communities through coordinated air and ground operations,” Ejodame said. “The successful outcome underscores the NAF’s continued resolve to deny criminal elements freedom of action and support efforts to restore safety and security to affected communities.” The post NAF confirms helicopter makes precautionary landing in Benue appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: UFC star Arman Tsarukyan added to RAF Abu Dhabi card
body: UFC star Arman Tsarukyan of Armenia will face Neiman Gracie in a catchweight crossover matchup at the inaugural Real American Freestyle (RAF) Abu Dhabi tournament next month. Tsarukyan, the No 1-ranked contender in the UFC's lightweight division boasting an 11-2 record in the world's lead MMA organisation, heads to the UAE capital with a 7-1 RAF record, including five wins by technical fall. He faces Brazilian Gracie, a three-time World BJJ bronze medallist in a contest that will test both athletes under freestyle wrestling rules. The contest leads five new additions to the Middle East’s first RAF event. American Kyle Dake will defend his cruiserweight championship against Turkmenistan’s Alp Arslan Begenjov. Dake is unbeaten in six RAF appearances. The two-time Olympic bronze medallist and four-time world champion is also the only wrestler to win NCAA titles in four weight classes. His challenger Begenjov is a U20 world champion, three-time Asian U23 medallist, and 2026 senior Asian bronze medallist. Kennedy Blades puts her women’s middleweight title on the line against fellow American Bella Mir, daughter of former UFC heavyweight champion Frank Mir. Blades has recorded six technical falls in RAF without surrendering a point. Her illustrious resume includes a 2024 Olympic silver medal and 2025 world bronze medal. Blades faces 2026 NCAA champion Mir, who also holds a 4-1 professional MMA record. Russia’s Zabit Magomedsharipov takes on Giga Chikadze of Georgia in a welterweight crossover bout, while Team USA Olympic gold medallist Jordan Burroughs meets Belarusian Azamat Nurykau at Middleweight. Magomedsharipov enters RAF with an 18-1 professional MMA record, including a perfect 6-0 UFC run and a 14-fight winning streak. His opponent, Chikadze, is an experienced MMA featherweight and accomplished kickboxer, with two world kickboxing titles and multiple world and European karate championships. RAF Abu Dhabi will be headlined by the UAE's Khamzat Chimaev . The former UFC middleweight champion takes on Colby Covington for the Cruiserweight Crossover Championship when they meet at the Etihad Arena on November 14. Last week, former UFC bantamweight title contender Umar Nurmagomedov was also added to the card . The Dagestani will take on Uriah Faber, who returns for his third RAF match. Faber is a former MMA champion and the founder of Team Alpha Male. Also joining the card is reigning RAF light heavyweight champion Kyle Snyder, who will face Shamil Erdogan. The inaugural RAF Abu Dhabi event marks the start of a five-year partnership between Real American Freestyle, the Department of Culture and Tourism – Abu Dhabi (DCT Abu Dhabi), and the UAE Wrestling Federation. It follows RAF’s international events in Tbilisi, Georgia and Moscow.

title: Adwoa Safo calls for unity, endorses brother as Kristo Asafo Church leader
body: The daughter of the late Apostle Dr. Kwadwo Safo, Sarah Adwoa Safo (Esq.), has reaffirmed her commitment to reconciliation within the Kantanka family and pledged her full support for her brother, Israel Kwadwo Safo, as the family seeks to preserve the legacy of their late father. In a statement signed by her on Thursday, October 8, she said the time had come for the family to transcend whatever differences, misunderstandings or grievances that may have characterised the immediate aftermath of their father’s demise and consign them to history. “I have chosen the path of reconciliation, founded upon love, mutual respect and the enduring undisputed bonds of family,” she said. The former Dome Kwabenya Member of Parliament said she had immense love and respect for her brother, Israel Kwado Safo, and, in the spirit of honouring their father’s wishes, publicly acknowledged and accepted him as the Leader of the Kantanka Family and the Kristo Asfo Church. “He has my full support, and I state unequivocally that I am prepared and willing to work together with him in the interest of the family and the Church, in furtherance of our father’s Vision and Legacy,” she said. She said their father’s legacy went beyond any one individual and constituted a collective inheritance and profound responsibility entrusted to his children. “Our father’s legacy transcends any one individual. It is a collective inheritance and a profound responsibility entrusted to us, as his children, and it is a charge we must keep and hold on to, dearly,” she said. According to her, the family must rise above its differences, preserve what their late father built, and ensure that his ideals continue to inspire generations to come. She also encouraged members of the Kristo Asfo Church, the larger Kantanka family and everyone associated with their father’s work while he was alive to acknowledge and respect the unity of the family. “Let us embrace this new chapter with reconciliation, fraternity and a shared sense of purpose,” she said. Sarah Adwoa Safo extended her sincere goodwill and best wishes to Israel Kwado Safo and her other siblings on what she described as a renewed journey of peace and forgiveness. “May this new chapter bring healing, unity and renewed strength as we come together to honour and advance the legacy of our beloved father,” she said. Below is the full statement released by her. Background Her declaration follows an earlier succession dispute in which a family statement issued on June 21, 2026, rejected Israel’s leadership claim and recognised Adwoa Safo as head of the family. According to that statement, their father initially designated Israel as his successor in 2017 but revoked the mandate in 2024 and revised the succession framework to exclude him. These were the family’s stated claims about the founder’s directives. The disagreement also led to legal proceedings, with two church members challenging Israel’s proposed installation at the Accra High Court on the grounds that the constitutional amendments had removed him from the line of succession. Tensions escalated following a shooting incident involving Adwoa Safo on June 21. The family said she had gone to serve court documents intended to halt her brother’s installation when the incident occurred. However, in a statement issued on July 3, Adwoa Safo maintained that her involvement was about upholding her father’s final directives. She denied seeking control of the church or a share of his estate, saying the constitutional changes had removed Israel from the church’s leadership and that she had been appointed head of the family in February 2025. On July 28, she also disputed her brother’s account of reconciliation efforts involving former President John Agyekum Kufuor. She said his meeting with the former president was aimed at securing support for his church leadership bid, while Israel had said he sought interventions from prominent personalities to restore peace within the family.

title: At least 35 killed in Russian attacks on Ukraine, officials say
body:
A passenger bus was struck in Kramatorsk, in the Donetsk region, officials said.
LONDON and LVIV, Ukraine -- At least 35 people were killed and over 30 others were injured across Ukraine in Russian attacks on the country overnight and into Thursday morning, according to Ukrainian authorities.
In a single strike on a passenger bus in Kramatorsk, in the Donetsk region, at least 30 people were killed and 18 were injured, according to a statement released by the city council on Thursday.
"Once again, the Russians have struck a location where there is absolutely no military target," the city council said. "A passenger bus. A civilian vehicle. People simply going about their daily business."
Public transport in Kramatorsk has been suspended, the statement added.
The killings overnight brought the death toll from Russian attacks across Ukraine over the past 48 hours to at least 60, following a deadly Wednesday in which at least 25 people were killed in strikes across the country, including 22 in an attack on a residential building in Pryluky.
At least four of the victims in Pryluky were children, officials said.
"Even after such a brutal attack, the Russians continued striking our regions," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Thursday. "This morning, Russia hit an ordinary public transport stop in Kramatorsk with an aerial bomb."
24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events

title: NAF helicopter makes ‘precautionary landing’ in Benue
body: The Nigerian Air Force (NAF) has confirmed that one of its helicopters made a precautionary landing on a farmland in Makurdi, the Benue State capital, after returning from an operation against suspected kidnappers. The helicopter landed on Wednesday at Utur Tse-Igboji community in Bar Council Ward, along the Welfare Quarters–Mopol 13 Ring Road area of Makurdi. The aircraft was returning from an operation conducted in the Ogbadigbo area of Benue State, close to the Enugu-Benue boundary, where it provided close air support to ground troops engaged in operations against suspected kidnappers. In a statement, the Director of Public Relations and Information, NAF, Air Commodore Ehimen Ejodame, said the operation had successfully disrupted the activities of the suspected criminals and supported the advance of surface forces. According to him, the pilot subsequently exercised professional discretion and landed the helicopter approximately 10 nautical miles from the airfield in accordance with established operational and safety procedures. The statement read in part: “The helicopter had successfully provided close air support to surface forces during an operation targeting suspected kidnappers in the Ogbadigbo area of Benue State, near the Enugu-Benue boundary. The operation disrupted the activities of the criminal elements and supported the advance of surface forces. “Following the successful completion of the mission, the pilot, on return to base, exercised his professional discretion to execute a precautionary landing approximately 10 nautical miles from the airfield. “This is in accordance with established operational and safety procedures following combat missions. The helicopter has returned to base. “The NAF remains committed to sustaining pressure on criminal elements, providing close air support to surface forces and protecting communities through coordinated air and ground operations. “The successful outcome underscores the NAF’s continued resolve to deny criminal elements freedom of action and support efforts to restore safety and security to affected communities.” The incident occurred two days after a NAF aircraft crashed in Igbokoda, Ilaje Local Government Area of Ondo State, with 25 passengers and seven crew members on board. The aircraft, an ATR-42 with tail number NGR 931, plunged into a swamp opposite the naval base in the early hours of Monday. The NAF said the helicopter involved in the Benue incident has since returned to base, while reaffirming its commitment to supporting ground forces and conducting coordinated operations aimed at protecting communities and improving security in affected areas.

title: SKOT Impact Academy Records Rising Demand, Attracts 450 Applicants for Third Cohort
body: Funmi Ogundare SKOT Impact Academy, the social impact learning programme of SKOT Communications, is set to commence its third six-week, intensive and tuition-free training programme on October 10, 2026, with more than 450 applications received for the latest cohort from Nigeria and other countries. The academy has received more than 1,300 applications across its three cohorts, underscoring growing demand for accessible professional training among early-career public relations and communications professionals. According to the organisation, applicants for cohort three came from 14 countries, including Nigeria, Kenya, South Africa, Ghana, Uganda, Pakistan, Rwanda, Zimbabwe, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Malawi, Bangladesh, Nepal, Tanzania and The Gambia. Speaking on the commencement of the third cohort, Founder and Chief Executive Officer of SKOT Communications, Tokunboh George Taylor, explained that the development represents a significant expansion of the programme, which began with 40 participants in its first cohort before increasing to 60 participants in cohort two through a hybrid learning model. The second cohort, she noted, included both physical and virtual participants from Nigeria, Kenya and the United Kingdom, adding that the academy’s growth reflected the depth of talent in the communications ecosystem and the need for greater investment in developing such talent. “When we launched SKOT Impact Academy, we knew there was a need for more accessible and practical pathways into the communications profession,” Taylor said. She added that the growing number of applications demonstrated the demand for professional development opportunities emphasising the quality of talent within the industry. According to her, the academy’s impact should not be measured solely by the number of participants but by the careers and contributions it would influence in the communications industry. “As the academy grows, our ambition is to reach more people, deepen the quality and relevance of the programme, and extend its impact across Africa and beyond. We believe this is only the beginning of what SKOT Impact Academy can become,” she said. George-Taylor said the expansion of the academy comes at a time when the communications profession is undergoing significant changes driven by developments in business, media and digital technology. She noted that communications professionals are increasingly required to navigate reputation management, crisis communication, digital platforms, emerging technologies and complex stakeholder expectations, while also understanding how communication supports broader organisational objectives. The six-week programme, the CEO said, is designed to complement formal education with practical knowledge, industry exposure and learning from experienced communications professionals.
