title: High School Students Turn Out For New Protests Across France
body: High school students across France launched a fresh day of protests on Thursday, despite government attempts to ease the crisis, which has rocked the country for days. Students have blocked entrances to hundreds of high schools across the country since late September, and protests have on occasion spiralled into violent clashes with riot police. Student union leaders urged fresh mobilisation across France Thursday, with a rally planned in the capital, Paris, and national education unions calling a general strike in support. People take part in a demonstration part of a nationwide day of actions called by high-school students unions who for days have been demanding better learning conditions in protests punctuated by violent confrontations, in Marseille on October 8, 2026. Photo by MIGUEL MEDINA / AFP While many rallies have been peaceful, some demonstrators have started fires, destroyed bus shelters or clashed with riot police — with unions, rights groups and the children accusing police of using disproportionate force. Protesters stand in front of bins and furnitures set on fire during a demonstration of high-school students, in Paris on October 6, 2026, as part of a nationwide protest movement over learning conditions. Photo by KENZO TRIBOUILLARD / AFP In a televised address Wednesday evening, the prime minister Sebastien Lecornu attempted to calm tensions, promising a plan to respond to the crisis by the end of October. Although Lecornu denied that security forces have “orders to confront” the young people, many students were unconvinced. (FILES) France’s newly-appointed Prime Minister and former Minister of Armed Forces Sebastien Lecornu reacts as he speaks at the end of the handover ceremony at the Hotel Matignon in Paris on September 10, 2025. (Photo by Ludovic MARIN / POOL / AFP) | Ludovic MARIN / POOL / AFP Outside one high school in Rennes, around 60 students had already gathered early Thursday. Hanaa, an 18-year-old student, told AFP she was “disappointed and unconvinced” by Lecornu’s remarks. “We expected more from him,” agreed fellow student Salyna, 17, who said they were also disappointed the government response would not be announced until the end of the month. “This is an urgent situation”. Student ‘dialogue’ Suzanne Nijdam, president of university student association FAGE, said they did not have “even the crumbs of an agreement” after a meeting with the higher education minister Philippe Baptiste. She called for protests to continue outside high schools and government administrative offices Thursday, with “larger-scale demonstrations next week”. As the government tried to adopt a conciliatory tone, education minister Edouard Geffray was to visit a high school in Reims and take part in a “dialogue” with students. And a fresh meeting between the three main student associations with Geffray and Baptiste was planned for Thursday afternoon. The students have asked for a direct meeting with Lecornu to present what they say are costed proposals to address their demands. Student demonstrators — many attending high schools called lycees for children aged between 15 and 18 years old — have complained of missing teachers, overloaded timetables, dilapidated classrooms and buildings that cannot cope with rising temperatures. Classes were partially or completely suspended in 375 schools across the country on Thursday morning, according to the education ministry. At a high school in Paris, AFP saw adult protesters forming a human chain with their arms between police and protesting teenagers, who huddled together carrying backpacks and placards. Access to the school had been blockaded with bins and railings, and AFP saw some scuffles between riot police and protesters. Protesters form a chain with their arms in front of a street blockade during a demonstration in solidarity with high-school students near Sciences Politiques (Paris Institute of Political Studies) university as part of a nationwide protest movement over learning conditions in Paris, on October 7, 2026. Photo by JULIEN DE ROSA / AFP In the southern city of Toulouse, high school protesters waved the French flag and placards, while graffiti on a school wall read: “The police are cracking down on France’s children”. Hundreds of students, police and teaching staff have been injured since the protests began, and more than 6,500 people — mostly minors — have been arrested. A 15-year-old lost a hand on Monday after police fired a stun grenade, and Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told radio broadcaster RTL early Wednesday that he had suspended the police use of stun grenades in response. Police have opened 18 internal investigations into allegations of misconduct. The unrest has erupted with just months to go before the 2027 election to choose a successor to centrist President Emmanuel Macron, with far-right veteran candidate Marine Le Pen riding high in the polls despite a graft conviction. AFP The post High School Students Turn Out For New Protests Across France appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Christa Pike now walking after failed US execution, lawyer tells BBC
body: Christa Pike is “up and walking” while in hospital after last week’s botched attempt to execute her in the US state of Tennessee, a member of her legal team says. Pike, 50, who was sentenced to death after murdering Colleen Slemmer with her then-boyfriend in 1995, survived two lethal injections on 30 September. Experts described it as unprecedented. Speaking late on Wednesday to BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, lawyer Stephen Ferrell said he had not spoken to Pike directly but that he had learned she was moving around her hospital room for the first time while still being mentally “foggy”. Earlier, a court ordered the state of Tennessee to preserve all evidence related to the failed execution. That evidence could lay the groundwork for a future lawsuit against the state. The Pike case is now in uncharted territory, as Pike is believed to be the only person to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection. The failed execution was branded a “mess” by the mother of Slemmer, who was among those pushing for Pike to be put to death. Pike’s boyfriend at the time of Slemmer’s gruesome murder, Tadaryl Shipp, was spared the death penalty because he was not legally an adult when the crime was committed. He remains in prison. Pike was 18 and Shipp was 17 when they beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for troubled teens. In their updates on Pike’s condition after the attempted execution, her team had previously said she was awake and speaking, and experiencing anger and confusion. She was said at that stage to be handcuffed to her bed. In the latest updates, given to the BBC, Ferrell said Pike was continuing to experience the after-effects of the drug pentobarbital, which was injected into her body in two doses by prison staff during the scheduled execution on 30 September. Once it became clear that Pike was not going to die, she was taken to hospital, where she was initially unconscious and declared to be in a critical condition. As of late on Tuesday, though, she was “fairly well”, Ferrell told the BBC. “What’s been described to me is that physically there’s quite a bit going on, that her arms are very injured and she’s not able to use them very much.” Of her physical movements, he added: “She is up and walking for the first time today, but just around the room, not very far.” Turning to her mental state, he said: “I think it’s kind of good and bad. Good that she is fairly with it, but she’s also somewhat foggy. She can lose her train of thought really easily and forgets where she’s going.” Ferrell said much remained unknown about what happens next. “I assume [the situation for Pike] will keep improving, but there could be some permanent damage. We don’t know that yet.” He added that the team wanted Pike to receive psychological support, since that “clearly is necessary now”. Ferrell and his colleagues – who highlighted ahead of the attempted execution that Pike had a condition that would make the injection method difficult – oppose any new attempt by state prison authorities to follow the same approach. They are also calling on the state governor, Bill Lee, to downgrade Pike’s punishment to the lesser sentence of life in prison without parole. Meanwhile, Tennessee’s proponents of capital punishment have suggested that a different method be used. Senator Marsha Blackburn, the Republican candidate for state governor in next month’s election, said: “Bring back the electric chair.” Asked during a court hearing on Wednesday whether the state intended to reschedule Pike’s execution, the state’s attorney general said he did not know. For now, Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has ordered a pause on all executions in the state for the rest of the year, and has said he wants answers about what went wrong. The state’s prisons chief is resigning after the failed execution. Wednesday’s court hearing related to the preservation of evidence following the first attempt. The judge, I’Ashea Myles, ordered that “anything that was in the actual room needs to be preserved and maintained,” including IV lines and syringes, as well as waste, like packaging, inserts, and labels. The judge also demanded documentation on Pike’s psychological condition prior to, during and after the 30 September execution attempt. She advised the state to take “special care” not to misplace or accidentally delete any information that may be pertinent to the case.

title: Minister appeals to NASWDEN to suspend industrial action.
body: …as FG targets 10 mm annual steel production by 2030 By Gabriel Ewepu, Abuja The Minister of Steel Development, Prince Abubakar Audu, on Wednesday, appealed to the leadership of the National Association of Scrap and Waste Dealers Employers of Nigeria, NASWDEN, to suspend its ongoing industrial action. As contained in a statement signed by the Head, Press & Public Relations Department, Tine-Iulun Maureen, Audu made the call through the Permanent Secretary of the Ministry, Ambassador Nura Abba Rimi, to the leadership of NASWDEN to suspend the strike. According to the statement, the minister said in the interest of industrial harmony, mutual understanding and the overall stability and development of Nigeria’s steel sector, the strike should be suspended. Meanwhile, the statement highlighted reasons by the workers for embarking on the strike, which include alleged undervaluation of scrap metals, weight reductions arising from malpractices involving weighing scales, the involvement of local and other steel-producing companies in direct scrap metals trading, the importation of billets, and other practices perceived by the Association to be limiting the effective participation of local scrap dealers in the steel value chain. The Ministry says it recognises the seriousness and importance of these concerns and is currently giving them due consideration in consultation with the National Steel Council, with a view to developing practical, balanced and sustainable institutional measures to address the issues raised. “In furtherance of this process, the Honourable Minister has directed the Permanent Secretary, in collaboration with the Office of the Executive Secretary of the National Steel Council, to invite the apex leadership of NASWDEN for further discussions and effective mediation on the issues raised by the Association, as well as their implications for steel-producing companies and other operators within the sector. “The Honourable Minister urges NASWDEN and all stakeholders within the steel industry, particularly steel-producing companies, to cooperate fully and uphold their respective obligations. All parties are expected to embrace dialogue, good faith and responsible engagements in the resolution of these issues affecting the sector. “The Minister further calls on all stakeholders to recognise the significant efforts and policy direction of His Excellency, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, GCFR, towards repositioning and developing Nigeria’s steel sector under the Renewed Hope Agenda. The Federal Government remains committed to creating an enabling environment for investments, increased domestic production, local participation and sustainable growth across the steel value chain. “The Honourable Minister emphasises that the development of a strong and competitive domestic steel industry requires the collective commitment and cooperation of all stakeholders. No individual or group interest should undermine the broader national objective of building a viable steel industry capable of supporting Nigeria’s industrialisation and economic transformation. “The collective efforts of all stakeholders are essential to achieving the Federal Government’s target of 10 million metric tonnes of annual steel production by 2030, while strengthening local value addition, creating employment opportunities and reducing Nigeria’s dependence on imported steel products. “The Honourable Minister therefore calls on NASWDEN to sheathe its sword, suspend the ongoing industrial action and return to the negotiation table, while assuring the Association and all stakeholders of the Ministry’s readiness to facilitate constructive engagement towards resolving the issues raised. “The Ministry of Steel Development remains committed to ensuring a fair, stable and conducive operating environment for all legitimate stakeholders in the steel sector and will continue to engage relevant parties towards the sustainable development of Nigeria’s steel industry.” The post Minister appeals to NASWDEN to suspend industrial action. appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Condé Nast Traveller readers have named Greece the world’s best country for tourism in 2026.
body: In the magazine’s Readers’ Choice Awards, released on October 6, Greece scored 98.14 out of 100, ahead of Italy, Spain, France and Türkiye. Condé Nast Traveller, which reaches some of the world’s most influential travel markets, said the result shows readers’ attachment to Greece has reached “fever pitch.” The magazine praised the country’s natural beauty for a discerning audience and noted that record tourist numbers did not stop voters from placing Greece first. It highlighted the Aegean, pointing to Santorini, Mykonos and Crete, including Crete’s reviving wine scene, and said more travellers are also heading to Paros, car-free Hydra, Ios and Tinos. Praise was not limited to the islands. Condé Nast Traveller also recommended Athens Athens Sports Guide: Football, Basketball & Running October 8 to 18 . The post Condé Nast Traveller readers have named Greece the world’s best country for tourism in 2026. appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: Senate ratifies Philippines-France visiting forces agreement
body: MANILA, Philippines — The Senate on Thursday, October 8, concurred in the ratification of the Status of Visiting Forces Agreement (SOVFA) between Philippines and France. With 17 affirmative votes, senators approved proposed Senate Resolution No. 650, concurring in the ratification of the SOVFA, between the two countries. Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. and French Minister for the Armed Forces and Veterans Catherine Vautrin signed the SOVFA in March . The agreement provides a legal framework for the presence and activities of the Philippine and French armed forces in each other’s territories. “This is a historic moment because this treaty ratification of our visiting forces with France is the first for a European nation,” said Senate Majority Floor Leader Juan Miguel “Migz” Zubiri Newly designated French Ambassador to the Philippines Donatienne Hissard personally received the resolution at the Senate. The SOVFA is a “reciprocal bilateral defense agreement that establishes the legal framework governing the presence and cooperative activities of the Armed Forces of the Philippines and the French Armed Forces, including their respective Civilian Components, in each other’s territories, and facilitates joint defense, training, humanitarian, and other mutually agreed activities.” With the agreement’s ratification, France joins the growing list of countries with visiting forces agreements with the Philippines. The Philippines has a long-standing Visiting Forces Agreement (VFA) with its treaty ally, the United States. In 2012, a SOVFA with Australia , which has since become a strategic partner of the Philippines. The expansion of the Philippines’ defense ties has been a conscious push of the Ferdinand Marcos Jr. administration, especially in the face of a growingly belligerent China in the South China Sea. At the same time, however, Marcos has said he wants a “reset” of bilateral relations with Beijing, following years of tensions both at sea and in the diplomatic space. – Rappler.com

title: Ukraine Inter TV cuts ties with Film.ua co-owner, replaces board chair
body:
The Supervisory Board of PrJSC Inter TV Channel has decided to dismiss Oleksandr Pylypets as chairman of the management board and appoint Oleksiy Romaniuta to the position. Over the past five years, Romaniuta has served as chief financial officer (CFO), a member of the management board and deputy chairman of the management board.
According to a company disclosure filed through the National Securities and Stock Market Commission's information disclosure system, the decision to dismiss Pylypets was made on October 6, 2026. He had headed the television channel since November 2023, having previously served as its editor-in-chief and, for nearly 10 years, as director of National Information Systems LLC, a member of the group that produces programs for Inter.
The supervisory board elected Leonid Bihunov-Novikov, head of the analytical support directorate and development director, and programming director (CPO) Iryna Kurchakova as members of the company's management board.
The day before, Inter Media Group reported on its website that Inter TV channel and Film.ua Group co-owner Serhiy Sozanovsky had mutually agreed not to renew a three-year contract, which expired on October 2.
"Inter Media Group sincerely thanks Serhiy Leonidovych for his professionalism, significant contribution to the company's operations and fruitful cooperation during this difficult time for the country," the media group said.
Sozanovsky joined the team of PrJSC Inter TV Channel in November 2023 and, over the course of three years, participated in implementing the strategic objectives of Inter Media Group.
At the same time, the TV channel emphasized that it would continue operating in line with the company's strategic goals and development plans.
According to a Forbes Ukraine report citing a source familiar with the matter, Sozanovsky's seat on the IMG supervisory board will be taken by Pylypets, who, until the Inter supervisory board's decision, served as chairman of the TV channel's management board.
As reported in 2023, Anna Bezliudna and Myroslava Karayeva left the supervisory board of Inter TV Channel, the main media asset of Dmytro Firtash's Group DF, while the new members were Serhiy Konnov and Serhiy Sozanovsky, founders of one of the oldest law firms on the market, which bears the same name, as well as Ihor Yaryna, who headed the Group DF law firm DF Lex.
Sozanovsky headed Inter's management board in 2006-2010, but subsequently focused on developing the private film studio Film.ua, which became the largest in Ukraine.
Inter is a nationwide television channel that first went on the air in Ukraine on October 20, 1996.

title: Death toll from Russian strike on Kramatorsk scheduled bus rises to 33 – SES
body:
Thirty-three people were killed and another 18 were injured as a result of a Russian strike on a scheduled passenger bus in Kramatorsk, the press service of the State Emergency Service of Ukraine reports on Telegram.

"33 people were killed, and another 18 were wounded due to the Russian strike on a scheduled bus in Kramatorsk carrying people," the department stated on Thursday.

Additionally, three people were killed in the settlement of Bilenke within the Kramatorsk community as a result of shelling. Rescuers recovered one of the dead from beneath the rubble of a private house.

It was previously reported that 30 people were killed and 18 injured following Russian bomb strike on Kramatorsk, which damaged two scheduled buses and an apartment building.

title: British Royal Navy member charged with preparing to disclose information to unnamed foreign power
body: British police on Thursday said they had charged a member of the Royal Navy with offenses under the National Security Act for allegedly obtaining protected information and preparing to disclose it to benefit a foreign power.Teddy Young, 24, has been charged with two offenses and is due to appear at London's Westminster Magistrates' Court later on Thursday. Police did not name the foreign power to which the charges relate."These are very serious charges against a serving member of the armed forces," Commander Helen Flanagan, Head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said in a statement."We have worked extremely closely with relevant operational colleagues within the Ministry of Defense as our investigation has progressed to ensure appropriate measures could be taken to mitigate any potential risks linked to this matter."Charges unconnected to RAF Fairford airbase investigation, police sayPolice said the charges were not connected to the recent investigation into an incident at the RAF Fairford airbase, which US officials have said involved a potential Iranian drone attack.

title: Ukrainian forces strike Gazprom oil refinery in Bashkortostan
body:
According to Ukrinform, the General Staff of the Ukrainian Armed Forces reported this on Facebook .
Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat is one of the largest oil refining and petrochemical complexes in the Russian Federation. The facility has the capacity to process up to 10 million tonnes of hydrocarbon feedstock annually and produces motor gasoline, diesel fuel, fuel oil, bitumen, polyethylene and other oil refining and petrochemical products.
The facility is involved in meeting the needs of the Russian Armed Forces, the General Staff said.
As previously reported, the Russian petrochemical complex Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat in the Urals suspended operations following a Ukrainian drone attack.
On July 14, drones attacked the Afipsky oil refinery in Russia's Krasnodar Krai and Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat in Bashkortostan, one of Russia's largest oil refining and petrochemical complexes.
Overnight on October 8, drones struck an oil refinery in Bashkortostan and a data center belonging to Yandex, Russia's most popular mapping service, in the Ryazan region.

title: Around 2.5 mln tourists visit Russian agritourism sites supported by ministry
body:
MOSCOW, October 8. /TASS/. Around 2.5 mln tourists have visited agritourism facilities established with support from the Russian Agriculture Ministry, Agriculture Minister Oksana Lut said.
"We began providing grants for this sector in 2022. More than 2.5 bln rubles have been allocated to our farmers. Currently, 360 agritourism projects are receiving government support, and another 100 agricultural producers are expected to receive assistance this year. Around 1,000 additional jobs have been created at agritourism facilities over this period. The number of tourists who have visited these facilities, specifically those supported by us, stands at around 2.5 mln," Lut said.
She noted that most visitors come from large cities and are interested in learning how agriculture is developing.
According to the minister, agritourism is not only an additional source of income but also a means of supporting the rural economy and promoting rural areas across the country.

title: US and Lebanon protecting wanted Syrian general, BBC finds
body: A former Syrian general wanted for crimes against humanity is being bankrolled and protected by the US and Lebanese authorities, a BBC News investigation has found. Bassam al-Hassan, who oversaw Syria’s chemical weapons programme and was a senior adviser to former President Bashar al-Assad, is being harboured in Lebanon following the Assad regime’s collapse in 2024. An investigation by the BBC and the US broadcaster NPR has discovered that Hassan has been allowed to remain there under an arrangement involving the FBI, and other US and Lebanese authorities. This is because of his willingness to provide information about the abduction of American journalist Austin Tice in Syria in 2012, as well as additional intelligence, we have been told. Last month the BBC revealed Tice’s abduction had been a planned operation, with Hassan in the chain of command. Officials from two different branches of Syria’s new government have told the BBC they want Hassan returned to face trial, but that US authorities want him kept in Lebanon, and they say there is little Damascus can do about this. We asked the FBI, the CIA and Lebanon’s General Directorate of General Security to comment on our findings. Only the FBI responded, declining to comment and instead directing us to a past statement that said its focus remained on establishing the facts around the Tice case and securing his return. In response to our findings, Phil Elwood, spokesperson for the Tice family said: “If what you are saying is true, the fact that our tax dollars are being used to furnish a comfortable life for someone associated with the use of chemical weapons on Syrian civilians, who claims to have had Austin Tice executed, is offensive. “This is nothing less than aiding and abetting the escape of a wanted war criminal. The Syrians deserve justice and he should be returned to stand trial.” ADVERTISING As part of a years-long investigation featured in the new BBC podcast: Where is Austin Tice? the BBC has reviewed a detailed record of a meeting between Hassan, FBI and CIA representatives, and Lebanese security officials, where Tice’s case is discussed. In it, Hassan is offered “residency”, “protection” and help securing his “living needs” in return for information, primarily about Tice. Sources with knowledge of the arrangement confirmed this was the case, and described to us how Hassan receives money from the US authorities through an intermediary, making it harder to trace. Hassan is sanctioned by the US government. Yet people connected to the Tice investigation say they have seen little evidence it has significantly advanced since Hassan began providing information as part of this agreement. The deal is believed to have been struck in the spring of 2025. Sources with knowledge of the investigation have expressed concerns that Hassan’s arrangement with the US could continue indefinitely, at significant expense but with little gain. Hassan is not the only Syrian regime official whose connection to the Tice case has seemingly afforded him financial payments or assistance for living abroad. One former regime member said he had received money from the FBI multiple times in exchange for his co-operation on Tice’s case. It was “not in his interest to share all the information all at once,” he told the BBC, “in order to be able to drag out how long he can continue to receive payments from them [the US authorities]”. Another former regime member connected to the Tice case claimed he was living in Lebanon under the “patronage” of the US authorities, citing this as the reason he could not speak to us about Tice. The BBC spoke to a former senior Lebanese intelligence official who confirmed that Lebanese intelligence does have arrangements with the Americans, and that these types of payments have and do take place when both agencies have overlap in cases, but said he had no knowledge of payments involving the Tice case. Following the fall of the Assad regime in early December 2024, Hassan is believed to have initially escaped to Iran. A Syrian businessman, with strong connections to both the former regime and the Lebanese authorities, told the BBC that negotiations had then taken place – involving the US, Lebanon, and Iran – to bring Hassan to Lebanon. The businessman, who asked to remain anonymous, said Hassan was valuable, not only because of what he is believed to know about Tice, but because of his knowledge of Syria’s chemical weapons programme and its military relationship with Iran – secrets that US intelligence was allegedly interested in. Hassan told US investigators last year that Tice had been executed on former President Assad’s orders, but several people with knowledge of the investigation have questioned the details of his account. Hassan has provided a potential location for Tice’s remains, but when the site was searched, nothing was found – according to multiple sources familiar with the dig – casting doubt on the validity of some of Hassan’s information. There are questions, however, over how thoroughly the site was searched. Two sources who said they had intimate knowledge of the operation told the BBC that US authorities stopped digging before the search had been completed, possibly because of security concerns. When the BBC managed to reach Hassan by phone last year to ask for an interview, he directed us to seek permission for him to speak from the FBI and CIA at the US embassy in Beirut. Our investigation has found that other Syrian officials connected to the Tice case have also apparently found refuge abroad. They include Mohammad Makhlouf, who reported to Hassan in Syria and was connected to Tice’s detention – now believed to be residing in Lebanon. And Sakr Rustom, Hassan’s nephew who was involved in Tice’s abduction, now believed to be moving between the UAE and Lebanon. When the BBC attempted to speak to Rustom about Tice’s case, he said he “preferred to focus on matters of the future”. Ghassan Nassour, a former general in Syria’s Republican Guard, is said by former members of the National Defence Forces to have presided over the jail Tice was held in, and is believed to be living in the UAE with his family, we have been told.

title: EU Parliament Adopts Resolution Against Georgian Dream’s Efforts to Ban Opposition Parties
body: The European Parliament adopted a resolution calling for the “immediate withdrawal” of the Georgian Dream’s constitutional lawsuit seeking to ban opposition parties and reiterating calls for the release of what it describes as “political prisoners,” as well as for “targeted sanctions” against key Georgian Dream figures. The resolution , titled “Attempts by the ruling party Georgian Dream to ban opposition parties in Georgia” and adopted on October 8 with 445 in favor, names Georgian Dream founder Bidzina Ivanishvili, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili, and Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze as those who should be subject to targeted sanctions and visa bans. The document notes that in November 2025, “the Georgian Dream-controlled Parliament” lodged a constitutional claim seeking to ban opposition parties, including the United National Movement, Coalition for Change, and Strong Georgia – Lelo. The Federalists party was added to the lawsuit in April , while For Georgia, described in the resolution as the only opposition party still represented in Parliament, was added in September 2026. The resolution says the proceedings amount to “eliminating legitimate political opposition” and are part of a broader strategy aimed at “turning Georgia into a one-party regime by eliminating political pluralism.” It says this follows the model of Russia and Belarus and “serves the Kremlin’s objective of keeping Georgia outside the European and Euro-Atlantic space.” It says the situation in Georgia “is progressively deteriorating, with further backsliding in democracy, media freedom, human rights and the rule of law due to the Georgian Dream authorities’ actions,” which, according to the resolution, are increasingly “incompatible with Georgia’s international obligations and commitments,” including the Copenhagen criteria. The European Parliament also notes that new judges were appointed to the Constitutional Court in September, saying the appointments raise “serious doubts about their independence in the proceedings.” 23/09/2026 – Two New Constitutional Court Judges Appointed As Critics Fear ‘No More Dissenting Opinions’ The resolution says that “numerous journalists reporting on the government’s crackdown on opposition and civil society have been imprisoned.” It also cites the closure of the Tbilisi offices of two German foundations, the Konrad Adenauer Foundation and the Friedrich Naumann Foundation , which it says were “forced to close their Tbilisi offices in September” after authorities rejected their project funding applications under the Law on Grants. It “strongly condemns” the attempt to “outlaw Georgia’s opposition parties” and demands the “immediate withdrawal” of the constitutional claim. It stresses that “a functioning political opposition is an indispensable pillar of democracy and that eliminating legitimate political opposition through judicial means is incompatible with democracy.” The resolution also notes that banning the sole opposition party represented in the Georgian Parliament would “dismantle the regime’s previous narrative of only targeting ‘boycotting’ parties.” 23/07/2026 – ‘Sabotage’ Case Hearings Adjourned Until Fall Amid Verdict Concerns The EP calls for the “immediate and unconditional release” of people it describes as political prisoners, including Elene Khoshtaria, Mzia Amaghlobeli, Mikheil Saakashvili, Giorgi Baramidze, and Nika Melia, as well as “all those detained for peaceful protest.” It also calls for “dropping politically motivated ‘sabotage’ charges” and for the repeal of provisions enabling “disproportionate restrictions on parties and individuals associated with prohibited parties.” The resolution condemns “the misuse of legislation and state institutions to silence political opponents” and calls for an end to what it describes as the “obstruction of European political foundations.” The resolution “regrets” what it describes as “the persistent lack of action by the EU and most Member States to ensure tangible consequences for the continuously deteriorating situation in Georgia.” It reiterates its call for “targeted sanctions against and visa bans for those responsible for democratic backsliding, violent repression and political persecution, first and foremost Bidzina Ivanishvili, Irakli Kobakhidze, Shalva Papuashvili and Kakha Kaladze.” The EP also reiterates “its unwavering support for the Georgian people’s European aspirations” and recalls its previous warnings that “any attempt to ban established political parties alienates Georgia from the EU and precludes any move towards EU accession.” The resolution instructs the European Parliament President to forward it to the EU Council, European Commission, High Representative/Vice-President, EU Member States and “the self-appointed authorities of Georgia.” Preceding Debate October 8 resolution was preceded by a plenary debate on the issue on October 7. The debate included Swedish Commissioner Jessika Roswall, as well as MEPs from different political groups. Below are the key highlights from the debate: Jessika Roswall , EU Commissioner for Environment, Water Resilience and a Competitive Circular Economy “Under Georgian Dream, Georgia continues to drift away from democratic norms and the European path chosen by its people. What we are witnessing is a systematic attack on democratic institutions, fundamental rights, political pluralism, and the rule of law. The recent Constitutional Court lawsuit brought by the Georgian Dream parliamentarians to ban opposition parties ahead of the 2028 election is a part of this pattern. Such actions strike at the heart of democracy and they undermine Georgia’s EU accession. […] Instead of advancing reforms and moving closer to the European Union, the Georgian authorities have taken actions that undermine the rule of law and shrink civic space. They continue anti-EU rhetoric and disinformation aiming to undermine the credibility of the EU among Georgian citizens. […] The European Union calls on the Georgian Dream party to reverse its detrimental actions, amend anti-democratic legislation, and release all arbitrarily detained opposition members. We urge the government to engage in meaningful dialogue with all political stakeholders to restore trust. Our door is open for constructive dialogue with Georgia based on mutual respect to find a way out of the current deadlock in our relations. The European Union stands with the people of Georgia and their democratic European aspiration.” MEP Rasa Juknevičienė , European People’s Party: “Georgia is a lost case, they say. Accept the situation, let’s be realistic. Many thought that we, Lithuanians, were lost too. But we were not. Georgians have not given up. People are still protesting, majority still wants to have the European future […] Regime wants to ban the opposition parties. It pushed the German political foundations to close their offices in Tbilisi. It puts in prison those who work for democracy and the rule of law. This is not strength; this is fear. Ivanishvili’s regime chooses Russia by refusing the will of Georgian people, Putinism will be defeated. Bidzinazation of Georgia will be defeated. […] Sanctions are a must on Ivanishvili and all those responsible […].” MEP Tobias Cremer , Progressive Alliance of Socialists and Democrats “ How desperate must a government be to ban every political party but its own? How terrified of its own people must it be to beat up peaceful protesters, arrest journalists and use chemical agents against its own population? […] But Georgian Dream has one problem, and that’s that Georgians themselves don’t want to be Homo Sovieticus again. They don’t want to just keep their heads down and their mouths shut. No, Georgians have tasted freedom. They’ve tasted Europe, and they will not give up on either […].” MEP Małgorzata Gosiewska , European Conservatives and Reformists: “Bidzina Ivanishvili is destroying democracy in Georgia and leading the country towards a Russian-like dictatorship. […] Release Mikheil Saakashvili immediately and unconditionally and all other political prisoners and let them enter the EU. Let me say this: let us stop just condemning. Time has come for decisive and coordinated action against Ivanishvili, his assets and the entire network of people who maintain this system of repression.” MEP Helmut Brandstätter , Renew Europe: “Georgian oligarch is banning opposition parties. […] Colleagues, the people of Georgia are nothing like this regime. They are Europeans through and through like we are, continuously fighting for freedom and for a European future […].” MEP David McAllister, European People’s Party: “In pursuing a ban on every major oppositional party, the regime has taken another callous step towards authoritarian rule. […] On the 30th of September, the Konrad Adenauer Stiftung and the Friedrich Naumann Stiftung were forced to close their offices due to a new regulation on foreign grants. […] Both foundations have stood out through their decades-long contribution to political education, democratic pluralism and European integration. All the more it is now important that we stand by the Georgian people, who by an overwhelming majority rally behind the goal of European integration.” MEP Leoluca Orlando , Greens/European Free Alliance: “[…] The process for Georgia to join the EU has been blocked for many years. The European Commission and member states must do everything that they can, do possible, including sanctions, in order to support the right of the Georgian people to live in a democratic country.” MEP Reinhold Lopatka, European People’s Party: “[…] Georgian Dream creates the conditions for a one-party dictatorship. Our responsibility is to stand with all defenders of democracy in Georgia while their democratic power is systematically taken away. We have to fight and to support the democracy movement in Georgia.” MEP Sebastian Tynkkynen, European Conservatives and Reformists: “[…] Now the ruling party is aiming to ban opposition parties. Time for everyone to wake up. The ruling party is called Georgian Dream. It has turned into Georgian Nightmare. That nightmare will not end if we just stand by as eyewitnesses. Europe must be tough against this regime. Impose visa bans, place sanctions. Let’s say no to a new mini Russia.” MEP Lukas Sieper , Renew Europe: “I say to the Georgian ruling party, I say to the Georgian oligarchs, I say to the Georgian puppets of Russia, enjoy your mansions, enjoy your luxury cars, enjoy your power, because eventually you will die. And then the next generation of Georgians will take over and they will lead Georgia to the European future. “ Also Read: 17/06/2026 – EU Parliament Adopts Critical Resolution on Georgia, Calls for ‘Targeted’ Sanctions on Ivanishvili, GD Leaders 09/07/2025 – European Parliament Adopts 2023-2024 Georgia Report 04/06/2025 – EP’s Foreign Affairs Committee Calls for Targeted Sanctions against Bidzina Ivanishvili

title: Podcast: The Spear – SAG-U Commander’s Action Group
body:
In this episode, Colonel Mike Rosol joins MWI’s Charlie Faint in the West Point Class of 1974 Recording Studio to reflect on a career spanning armored warfare, multiple deployments to Iraq and Afghanistan, teaching and scholarship at West Point, interagency work, and his recent service leading the commander’s Action Group for Security Assistance Group–Ukraine (SAG-U).
The discussion begins with Mike’s recollections of the leadership lessons he learned as a young officer in Iraq, before turning to the value of education and intellectual development for military professionals and how Mike’s experiences in West Point’s Department of Social Sciences shaped his approach to strategy and war. He then describes SAG-U’s role in coordinating US and allied support to Ukraine and examines lessons emerging from the Russia-Ukraine war, including Ukraine’s rapid expansion of its military, the transformative role of uncrewed systems, the increasingly compressed relationship between reconnaissance and strike, and the extraordinary speed of technological adaptation on the battlefield. Mike also highlights Ukraine’s willingness to innovate and openly debate how it fights, warning against dismissing lessons from an ongoing conflict simply because the participants or circumstances differ from those the US military expects to face. He closes by encouraging young leaders to cultivate intellectual curiosity and intellectual courage throughout their careers—to study their profession continuously, question assumptions, engage seriously with competing ideas, and recognize that thoughtful disagreement can make both leaders and the Army better. You can hear the full episode below, and don’t forget to subscribe to The Spear on Apple Podcasts , Stitcher , Spotify , TuneIn , or your favorite podcast app.

title: Putin just turned 74. Russia’s State Duma isn’t getting any younger either. Here’s how the country’s parliament has aged over the past three decades.
body: Vladimir Putin speaks at the opening of the fall session of the State Duma’s ninth session. September 30, 2026 In late September 2026, after reviewing the results of elections to the State Duma, the lower house of Russia’s parliament, Russia’s Central Election Commission chief Ella Pamfilova said : The Duma has gotten a little younger. It wasn’t old to begin with, but it’s gotten younger. To support her claim, Pamfilova cited the lawmakers’ average age at the end of the previous session and the start of the new Duma: 57 and 53, respectively. That comparison is incorrect, however. The newly elected lawmakers are indeed younger on average than those who served during the spring sitting of the eighth, outgoing session. Comparing lawmakers’ ages at the start of each session shows the State Duma has been steadily aging, according to Meduza’s calculations. BBC Russia reached the same conclusion. The State Duma’s first session was elected in December 1993, and lawmakers convened for their first meeting in January 1994, when their average age was 45.8. By the second session, the average age had risen to 47.2. In the fifth session, which began work in 2007, the average age exceeded 50 for the first time. Since then, the average age has continued to rise, reaching 54.3 in the ninth session . The difference from the first session is 8.5 years. Meduza compared lawmakers’ ages as of the date of each session’s first meeting. Vacant seats were not counted, which is why some previous Dumas had fewer than 450 members. The fourth session, for example, began work with 447 lawmakers after the “against all” option won in three electoral districts, leaving those seats vacant until repeat votes were held several months later. Meduza calculated lawmakers’ average and median ages using their dates of birth, rounding the results to the nearest tenth of a year. The lists of lawmakers and their dates of birth were compiled from Central Election Commission documents, State Duma records, and other published biographies. Age is calculated as of the day of each session’s first meeting, and party affiliation is based on faction membership on that same date. Each successive session is older than the last Nearly one in three lawmakers in the new Duma has already turned 60. United Russia has the most lawmakers in that group: 109, out of 349 seats the party won overall. United Russia’s lawmakers age 60 and older alone outnumber all lawmakers from every other party combined: only 101 lawmakers in total were elected to the rest of the Duma, including members of Russia’s Communist Party (KPRF), New People, the LDPR, A Just Russia, and Rodina, along with four independent candidates. Almost a quarter of the Duma’s lawmakers — 106 of 450 — have already reached retirement age (currently 64 for men and 59 for women); 81 of them were elected from United Russia. Russia carried out a pension reform in 2019, so Meduza used the retirement age in effect for each given year when calculating the number of retirees in the Duma. Women born between 1964 and 1968 and men born between 1959 and 1963 follow a transitional retirement schedule. The thresholds are listed on the Social Fund’s website . Northern work experience and other benefits were not factored in. Lawmakers’ average age depends directly on the Duma’s oldest members: the older they are, the higher the overall figure. To rule out the possibility that a few outliers are driving the increase, Meduza also calculated the median age. In the first session, the median age was 45.3: half the lawmakers were younger, half older. In the current session, it is 54.2, a difference of almost nine years. This means aging has affected every age segment of the Duma , though the trend has not been uniform: in 2011, for example, the median age dipped slightly. The change is visible even without averages. In 1994, 127 lawmakers under 40 were elected to the Duma’s first session, almost a third of the original lineup that convened for its first meeting. In the new Duma, only 51 lawmakers are under 40, or one in nine. There are now almost as many lawmakers age 70 and older: 49. Just 10 years ago, at the start of the seventh session, there were only 19, and in the Duma’s first session there were none at all. The record for age at the start of a session had previously belonged to KPRF member Vladimir Dolgikh , who was 87 when the sixth Duma began work in December 2011. In the ninth session, United Russia’s Vladimir Resin broke that record; he turned 90 in February . Before being elected to the State Duma, Resin spent many years heading Moscow’s construction sector and served as first deputy mayor of Moscow under Yuri Luzhkov. LDPR leader Leonid Slutsky likely owes his career to Resin: in private conversations, he calls Resin “Dad.” The Duma’s oldest lawmaker has a special duty: under the Constitution, he is the one who opens the first meeting of a new Duma. In January 1994, LDPR lawmaker Georgy Lukava opened the first session at age 68. This year, 90-year-old Resin ceded the right to open the meeting to his United Russia colleague, 79-year-old Yuri Petrov. Petrov is actually only fourth by age: older than the United Russia member are his party colleague Valentina Tereshkova, 89, and KPRF member Gennady Zyuganov, 82. During his remarks, Petrov asked each of his older colleagues in turn, “Shall we open the meeting?” All three agreed, after which Petrov thanked them “for the trust placed in him,” the Russian business daily Kommersant wrote . The youngest lawmaker in the new Duma is Georgy Arapov, the former head of New People’s regional branch in Irkutsk region, who turned 27 in September. Arapov has set the lower end of the age range for elected lawmakers over the past five years: he was also the youngest lawmaker in the previous Duma, when the New People member was only 22. The record for this metric, however, belongs to 21-year-old Vasily Vlasov, elected to the seventh session of parliament from the LDPR in 2016. Before his election, he worked as an aide to Vladimir Zhirinovsky and headed his secretariat. In March 2021, when Vlasov was 25, he became first deputy head of the LDPR faction. In November 2023, a year and a half after Zhirinovsky’s death, Vlasov lost his parliamentary mandate over absences from meetings. In August 2017, Yuri Dud asked Zhirinovsky about Vlasov’s path to the Duma on the party’s ticket: “What did he do to become a lawmaker at 21?” The LDPR leader pointed to the legally permitted age for election, 21, and explained : “He knows better what young people his age want.” Vlasov’s rise within the party caused discontent among its members. According to the Russian business outlet RBC , Zhirinovsky’s son, State Duma Deputy Speaker Igor Lebedev, opposed the appointment. On the independent Russian broadcaster TV Rain , Zhirinovsky denied any conflict with his son and explained his choice of Vlasov simply: “It benefits us [that] he’s good at his job.” Vlasov now works at the Russian University of Sport in Moscow, where he oversees youth policy. More than three-quarters of pension-age lawmakers were elected from United Russia Almost a quarter of the new Duma’s lawmakers — 106 of 450 — are already old enough to retire. A large share of them belong to United Russia. The KPRF has 16 pension-age lawmakers out of 37 in the faction, A Just Russia has five out of 17, the LDPR has two out of 24, and Rodina has one. New People has none. A total of 109 United Russia lawmakers are starting their work at 60 or older, compared with 35 in the other parties combined. Despite the increase in the retirement age, United Russia now has more pension-age lawmakers in the new Duma than before: 81, up from 75. The other factions now have fewer: 25, down from 36 in the previous session. Over the past three sessions, the share of seats held by lawmakers age 60 and older has grown from 26.9% to 32%. The number of lawmakers in that age group was 121 in 2016, 126 in 2021, and is 144 now. The number of pension-age lawmakers in the Duma as a whole has fallen. Ten years ago, almost one in three lawmakers fell into this group. Now, about one in four do. The decline, however, is directly tied to the increase in the retirement age — under the pre-reform rules, more than a third of the Duma would now fall into this group. This last change is particularly telling. Compared with the start of the previous session, the number of lawmakers age 60 and older across the whole Duma has grown by 18. All of that increase came from United Russia, which gained 23 lawmakers over 60. In the other parties, the number is actually five lower. In 2016, only 19 lawmakers had already turned 70. By 2021, there were 33, and in the current session there are 49, or one in 10. Of these, 34 are United Russia members, 11 were elected from the KPRF, two from A Just Russia, one from the LDPR, and one ran as an independent candidate. Despite their age, many remain politically active, supporting Putin and the war in Ukraine. For example, 82-year-old KPRF leader Gennady Zyuganov and his party colleague, 78-year-old Vladimir Kashin, are involved in organizing supplies for the Russian military. In August 2026, the KPRF announced that the two had helped send another convoy to the combat zone. According to the party, along with food and medicine for soldiers, the communists sent drones, thermal imaging devices, camouflage netting, SUVs, and motorcycles. A Just Russia leader Sergei Mironov is now 73. In January 2023, he received a sledgehammer bearing the insignia of the Russian mercenary group Wagner as a gift from Yevgeny Prigozhin. Wagner mercenaries used a sledgehammer to kill their own comrade at the front, former convict Yevgeny Nuzhin. Even after Prigozhin’s march on Moscow and his death in a plane crash, Mironov said he would keep the gift “in a place of honor” as “a sign of fellowship.” However, since late August 2026, Mironov has stopped attending party events in person. He said he is being treated for an injury sustained during a trip to Altai. His fellow party members stood in for him during the pre-election debates. Nevertheless, on September 28, Mironov was unanimously reelected as faction leader. He joined the meeting via video link and said he would continue working remotely for now. The Kremlin openly uses the standing of other experienced lawmakers for its own purposes. For example, in March 2020, Valentina Tereshkova proposed a constitutional amendment allowing Putin to run for president again. She was 83 at the time and is starting the new Duma at 89. A source in the State Duma told Meduza that Tereshkova’s remarks had been written in the Kremlin. Kommersant wrote that the amendment had been drafted in advance, with Tereshkova’s name added by hand. A source who spoke to Kommersant, close to Russia’s Presidential Administration, said Tereshkova was close to State Duma speaker Vyacheslav Volodin. After Tereshkova’s remarks, Volodin called on all factions to defend her from criticism: “The attacks being made on Tereshkova today are attacks on our country.” Hi, I’m Yulia. I’m an editor at Meduza, and for almost five years now, I haven’t been sleeping well for one reason: I’m worried about my colleagues in Russia. I’m often woken up by messages from our freelance reporters inside the country. They sometimes work late at night or early in the morning, and they message me at all hours. I never silence my phone at night in case of an emergency. Every notification jolts me awake. Half-asleep, my first thought is always the same: they’re texting me because the police have come to search their home. In Russia, you can go to prison for working with Meduza. Sometimes I have nightmares about my reporters being interrogated by the FSB. Some of those nightmares have come true. Meduza’s reporters risk their freedom to tell the world what’s happening inside Russia. They believe their work can help make a better future possible, and they refuse to leave. Please donate so they can keep reporting. New People remains the youngest party. But it’s aging too The youngest faction, as in the previous session, is New People . Founded in 2020, this was the party’s second electoral cycle, but it, too, has aged in the meantime: the average age of a faction lawmaker was 39.9 in 2021 and is 42 in the current session. At the same time, the party’s makeup in parliament has changed. The nine lawmakers elected to the Duma for the first time are noticeably younger than their more experienced colleagues: the newcomers average 39.7, compared with 43.8 for the others. The oldest faction in the new Duma is the KPRF , whose lawmakers average 61.5 years old. The faction has aged by 11.3 years since the first session, though there have been periods in the KPRF’s history when it got younger — after the 2021 election, for example, the average age of the communists fell, though it remained higher than in 1994, when it was 50.2. Right now, 37 communists have been elected to the Duma. Eleven of them have already turned 70, and another eight have turned 60. There is only one communist lawmaker under 40: 38-year-old Alexander Ivachev of the Sverdlovsk region. He heads the region’s party branch and previously served as deputy speaker of the regional legislative assembly. Ivachev is known, among other things, for his statements against the Yeltsin Center and his fight to preserve a bas-relief of Stalin on the Officers’ House building in Yekaterinburg, calling the arguments of those who wanted it removed “the sick fantasies of ‘victims of repression.’” The LDPR faction has aged by 8.2 years over the past 10 years, the largest increase among the four parties represented in the last three sessions. This trend only emerged in recent years — the LDPR used to be one of the youngest parties. In 2000, lawmakers elected from the Zhirinovsky Bloc began their work with an average age of about 40. A Just Russia lawmakers have gotten an average of 10 years older over five sessions : the figure was 49 in 2007 and is now 59.1. United Russia’s average age, 54.1, is lower than that of the KPRF and A Just Russia. Within the party, the share of members age 60 and older rose from 26% at the start of the previous session to 31% in the current one. Some lawmakers have aged along with the Duma. Three of them have voted on bills for almost 33 years in a row. More than half the lawmakers in the current Duma — 269 of 450 — also served in the previous session, and 143 took part in all three of the last sessions. A total of 172 people received a Duma mandate for the first time in 2026. About one in eight of them, 21 lawmakers, have already reached retirement age, roughly the same share as five years ago. The average age of newcomers has not changed since the start of the previous session, either: it is about 48. Overall, lawmakers entering the Duma for the first time are younger than their experienced colleagues, but the incoming generation that has already made it into parliament is not getting any younger from one election to the next . Not all newcomers, though, help make the Duma younger. For example, former minister and current adviser to the head of Bashkortostan Gennady Bukayev ran for the State Duma for the first time this year. He had turned 79 by the start of the new Duma’s work. And some of those who received their first mandate already at retirement age have since spent five or 10 years in parliament. United Russia lawmaker Galina Danchikova came to the Duma in 2016, at 62, and is now starting her third session at 72. Her fellow party member Nikolai Doluda became a lawmaker for the first time in 2021, at 69, and had turned 74 by the start of his second session. Three lawmakers in the current Duma were part of the starting lineup in all nine sessions , including the very first: KPRF member Gennady Zyuganov, his party colleague Nikolai Kharitonov, and A Just Russia member Anatoly Greshnevikov . In 1994, they were 49, 45, and 37, respectively. Now they are 82, 77, and 70. The Duma’s age makeup does not closely reflect Russia’s population. The most noticeable gap is the shortage of lawmakers under 40: more than a third of Russia’s adult population is under 40, but in the new Duma, only one in nine seats went to a lawmaker that age. Nationwide, there are three times as many people ages 18 to 40 as there are lawmakers in that age group: 35.1% versus 11.3%. Lawmakers ages 40 to 64 hold more than two-thirds of the seats, even though they make up less than half of the country’s adult population. The share of people 65 and older is nearly the same in parliament and among the population overall, about one in five. In the new State Duma, 11% of lawmakers are under 40. In Germany’s Bundestag, after the 2025 election, the figure was 28%, and in France’s National Assembly , after the 2024 election, it was 25%. The U.S. House of Representatives, however, had even fewer young lawmakers than Russia at the start of 2025 — only about 8%. By the end of the ninth session, the average age of State Duma lawmakers is projected to reach 59.3 .
