title: 2027: Don’t insult my opponents — Onjeh
body: The 2027 Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) Benue South Senatorial candidate, Daniel Onjeh, has appealed to his supporters, particularly young people, not to insult or attack his political opponents on his behalf ahead of the general elections. Onjeh, a former Chairman of the Governing Board of the Projects Development Institute (PRODA), Enugu, said political differences should not turn brothers and sisters into enemies, urging his supporters to focus on issues, records and ideas rather than personal attacks. He made the appeal while sharing photographs of himself separately with former Senate President, Senator David Mark, and Senate Minority Leader, Senator Abba Moro, both of whom he had contested against at different times. According to him, he deliberately shared the photographs to demonstrate the importance of political tolerance, forgiveness and maintaining relationships beyond elections. “I contested against Senator David Mark, and afterwards, we could still sit together. I contested against Senator Abba Moro, and afterwards, we could still sit together. They did not come to me; I went to them,” Onjeh said. He urged his supporters to avoid responding to provocations from opponents, insisting that those who believe in his political principles should promote his record and ideas instead. “As we prepare to commence our campaigns in the coming days, I want to make this very clear to everyone who believes in me: nobody should insult any of my opponents because of me. Nobody,” he said. “If you believe in my principles and what I stand for, talk about the issues. Talk about my record, my ideas and what I propose to do differently.” Onjeh recalled that an overzealous supporter of one of his opponents had once insulted his late mother during the heated 2016 Benue South senatorial rerun election. He said despite being deeply hurt by the incident, he refused to retaliate. “If there was anything capable of provoking me beyond measure, it was someone insulting my late mother. But I did not react. I am not asking my supporters to do something I have not practised myself,” he said. He also recalled being falsely accused on social media of being HIV-positive, saying he chose to clear his name with evidence rather than trade insults with the person behind the allegation. Onjeh said the experience reinforced his belief in forgiveness and the need to separate political disagreements from personal relationships. “Some people have misunderstood my firmness on matters of principle for stubbornness. But disagreement is not disrespect,” he said. He also recounted his legal battle with Moro following the 2023 Benue South senatorial election, which progressed from the Election Petition Tribunal to the Court of Appeal. According to him, he rejected an approach by Moro to settle the matter outside court because he believed that doing so would compromise the trust placed in him by his supporters. “I told Senator Moro that I would rather lose the case in court than sit at a table and compromise what I believed in,” he said. Although the final judgment went against him, Onjeh said he later visited Moro, maintaining that political disagreement should not become personal enmity. “Elections will come and go. Political platforms may change. Offices will change hands. But we will remain sons and daughters of the same Benue South,” he said. Onjeh urged younger people in the senatorial district not to inherit political divisions from previous generations, saying candidates should present their records and proposals and allow voters to decide. “There is no need for hatred. There is no need for insults,” he said. “But don’t insult anyone because of me. And don’t inherit another person’s political disagreement as your personal war.” The post 2027: Don’t insult my opponents — Onjeh appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: MTTD records 2,151 road deaths in 10,157 crashes between January and September
body: The Motor Traffic and Transport Department (MTTD) says 2,151 people have died in road crashes recorded across Ghana between January and September 2026. A further 12,230 people sustained various degrees of injuries during the period, highlighting the continued toll of road crashes on lives and livelihoods across the country. According to the MTTD, a total of 10,157 road crashes were recorded within the first nine months of the year, involving 17,197 vehicles. Director of Education, Research and Training at the MTTD, ACP Alexander Kwaku Obeng, disclosed the figures in an interview on Thursday, October 8. He said the data covered road crashes reported to the Police across all 25 police regions in the country. ACP Obeng said police investigators were deployed to various crash scenes to assist victims and support emergency efforts, particularly in cases where people were trapped in vehicles. “I have with me data from January to September 2026. These are crashes that have been reported to us in our 25 police regions, and police investigators have responded to support Ghanaians who were trapped in these preventable crashes. “10,157 crashes were recorded involving 17,197 vehicles. Sustained injuries were also 12,230, and persons who lost their lives in these preventable crashes were 2,151.” ACP Obeng stressed the need for motorists and other road users to exercise greater caution and adhere to road safety regulations to help reduce the number of crashes and fatalities on Ghana’s roads.

title: RFK Jr. deletes post claiming Israel accusations stem from Qatar-funded Muslim Brotherhood campaign
body: US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. deleted a sharply worded post on X/Twitter on Wednesday night in which he rejected allegations that Israel is committing genocide in the Gaza Strip and claimed that the accusations were part of a global Muslim Brotherhood propaganda campaign funded by Qatar.The post had received approximately 336,000 views before it was removed. Neither Kennedy nor the US Health and Human Services Department has explained its deletion."The Muslim Brotherhood's Qatari-funded global propaganda campaign makes Joseph Goebbels look like a piker," Kennedy wrote. "The Genocide charge against Israel is laughable on its face, but it is an effective permission structure for antisemitism."Kennedy went on to argue that antisemitism serves as a tool through which totalitarian systems, including Islamism, can mobilize the masses, build coalitions, and accumulate power."Most of the westerners who parrot this charge are useful idiots deluded by this psyops campaign that hates Jews, Christians, Israel, and the USA pretty equally," he wrote.Kennedy thanks X user for 'steadfast courage' in fact-checkThe remarks came in response to a post described as a "fact-check" by a user named John. Kennedy thanked him for what he called his "steadfast courage."The post was deleted shortly after it was published. However, Kennedy has not publicly retracted his remarks or issued a revised statement or explanation for the deletion.There is widespread speculation that a complaint from Qatar to its close allies in the White House prompted the removal, although no official response has been issued.

title: Jordanian princess 'discovered jewellery had been stolen when it appeared at UK auction'
body: A Jordanian princess discovered a custom-made sapphire and diamond ring had been stolen from her London home by her housekeeper when it appeared at auction, a court has been told. Maria Virgelina Taborda Henao, 71, is accused of stealing items of jewellery from her former employer, Princess Firyal. Princess Firyal was married to Prince Muhammad bin Talal, the younger brother of King Hussein of Jordan, from 1964 to 1978. She is a humanitarian and philanthropist and became a Unesco Goodwill Ambassador in 1992. The princess, 81, told London's Southwark Crown Court that she had received a phone call in November 2020 from a partner at high-end jeweller JAR, who told her that two items of jewellery were being sold at an auction in Kent, south-east England. The Jordanian royal had left London in March 2020 during the Covid pandemic, but Ms Taborda Henao remained to look after the Belgravia house, the court was told. She had been the princess's housekeeper for 11 years before the alleged thefts and was the only person who had permission to access the princess's belongings in her absence. The princess realised that a “unique” JAR sapphire and diamond ring, which had been made for her, was being sold by Canterbury Auction Galleries, the prosecution said. Prosecutor Oliver Wellings said the princess thought she had lost her wedding ring and would never have given away such an important personal item. She then obtained copies of the auction house catalogue and set about proving she was the true owner. After seeing more of her jewellery for sale, along with items that had already been sold by the auction house, Princess Firyal phoned the police. Officers then arrested Ms Taborda Henao and searched her house. They found a wedding ring in a coat, a jewelled metal necklace in a kitchen cupboard, and an envelope containing earrings belonging to the princess, the court heard. Ms Taborda Henao denies taking the items. Some of the items allegedly stolen were sold at auctions by the defendant's nephew, Julian Ramirez, who acted as a “key conduit” for their sale, said Mr Wellings. The court heard that Mr Ramirez first attended Canterbury Auction Galleries in March 2019 for a valuation day. He allegedly visited the auction house again in 2020, when items he had brought were listed for auction. Mr Ramirez had been arrested at an address in Rochester, Kent, on the same day as his aunt and was later released on bail. The court heard he was believed to have flown to Colombia in October 2023 and had not returned. The case continues.

title: Most UK diplomats to leave East Jerusalem consulate, Israel says, as Miliband says ‘vital services’ to rema
body: Most diplomats will leave the British consulate in occupied East Jerusalem, Israel says, but the UK insists the building “will not be closing”, and will operate as a “UK Mission”. “We did not want it to come to this,” Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar wrote on social media, as he said 20 diplomats and the consul general would leave Israel while a task force of seven could remain in the building “with a very limited scope of activity”. UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband responded that some staff had been “temporarily withdrawn” for security reasons, but stressed the mission will “work with the Palestinian people”. Israel said in September it would shut the consulate, in retaliation for UK sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank which are illegal under international law. The UK government had made last-ditch efforts to persuade Israel not to close the British consulate ahead of Thursday’s deadline, after the Israeli government said it would close the consulate within 30 days of the UK sanctions announcement. The consulate, which was first established in 1838, handles UK relations with Palestinians in Jerusalem as well as in the West Bank and Gaza. It is distinct from the UK embassy in Tel Aviv, which is the UK’s main diplomatic hub with Israel. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said the country had implemented measures announced on 8 September in response to UK sanctions. “The British Consulate in Jerusalem is closing its operations today. Accordingly, the sign of the British Consulate in Jerusalem has been removed,” he wrote on social media. However, the British flag could still be seen outside on Thursday morning, and several staff were seen entering. Saar said talks with the UK government had resulted in agreement on certain principles, including that “the consul general and 20 diplomats (including the consul general) are ending their duties and will leave Israel.” But Saar acknowledged that the building is “the property of the British government” and said Israel had authorised “a task force of only seven diplomats with a very limited scope of activity” to operate in the building. As a result of this agreement with the UK, he said, “no steps will be taken against Israel”. Israeli media had been reporting that the UK had threatened to expel Israeli diplomats from London – raising the prospect of further damaging bilateral relations. This agreement is a compromise of sorts and means – for the moment – the heat has been taken out of a dispute that could have further worsened UK-Israel relations. Israel can claim that the British Consulate is “closing its operations”. A score of British diplomats, including the consul general, are leaving. But Miliband says they are going only temporarily and only for their safety and security. He continues to insist Israel has no legal right to close the consulate. “The UK government reiterates its long-standing view that East Jerusalem is occupied territory,” Miliband wrote in a statement. Following discussions with the Israeli government, he said, the building “will not be closing” and will be known as the UK Mission, Jerusalem from Thursday. However Miliband said an understanding had not been reached on “necessary assurances for the security and protections of our staff and premises”. “Accordingly the UK has temporarily withdrawn a number of staff and families to ensure their safety and security,” he added. The Foreign Office said the seven UK diplomats who remain will be “independent and operational” and continue to deliver vital services. Israel said they will provide “only a limited scope of activity”. FCDO sources described the deal as a “good outcome” because the entire operation was not closing, as had been threatened. They said that maintaining a UK presence would help build back the mission in the future. Speaking to the Today programme, Foreign Office minister Stephen Doughty explained: “The building remains open. We retain our presence, we continue having staff able to do important work engaging with the Palestinian Authority… and we are engaging in ongoing conversations with Israel on this matter.” Asked if this was a political fudge, Doughty said “you can see what’s changed in terms of a name but crucially our presence remains”, adding that the “policies towards this Israeli government, which we fundamentally disagree with” would continue. The foreign secretary made clear the UK reserved the right to take what he called “reciprocal action” but said he would not do so while “discussions are under way and credible”. That means any UK retaliation is unlikely before Israel’s elections later this month.

title: Speedy turnaround on SA Navy frigate maintenance
body:
Armscor, in the form of its Simon’s Town maritime maintenance and repair facility, is patting itself on the back for a job well done having finished essential maintenance, including work on the hull of SAS Amatola (F145), the first Valour Class frigate in SA Navy (SAN) service, in a short time.
An Armscor statement dated 6 October has it the frigate, commissioned in 2006, required immediate dry docking to address defects identified on its “underwater hull and undertake essential maintenance before she could safely return to sea”. It does not identify how the defects were found reading “the underwater hull is a critical component of a naval vessel’s seaworthiness, providing structural integrity and protection against the demanding effects of the marine environment”.
“Through the combined application of engineering expertise, disciplined project management and decisive response to the operational requirement, Armscor Dockyard and the South African Navy completed the maintenance project in approximately three weeks,” Armscor said.
The work included addressing identified repair requirements, surface preparation and the restoration of the vessel’s marine coating system. These interventions are essential to preserving the integrity of the vessel and supporting her continued operational availability, Armscor emphasised.
In recognising what dockyard and SAN personnel achieved, Armscor Chief Executive Solomzi Mbada is on record saying: “The successful completion of the SAS Amatola maintenance project in approximately three weeks is an important demonstration of what can be achieved when technical expertise, collaboration and focused execution are brought together around a clearly defined operational requirement”.
“This is the kind of responsiveness that our clients expect from Armscor and it reflects our commitment to continuously improving the way we deliver on our mandate,” he continued adding the Amatola project, undertaken in the dockyard’s Selborne graving dock, would strengthen the approach to future – urgent – maintenance requirements.
“The SAS Amatola project has provided us with a valuable model for responding to urgent vessel maintenance requirements. It reinforces the importance of alignment between Armscor Dockyard, the South African Navy and our industry partners, supported by clear accountability and disciplined project execution. We intend to build on this experience and continue finding ways to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of service delivery.”
Mbada sees the Dockyard as important in supporting the readiness and sustainability of the SAN fleet adding Armscor and its service providers are committed to working “closely” with the maritime service of the SA National Defence Force (SANDF) to ensure “maintenance requirements are addressed with the necessary urgency, professionalism and technical rigour”.
Armscor is in the process of refurbishing Simon’s Town dockyard infrastructure, equipment and production processes. A priority of the renewal programme is the refurbishment and commissioning of the penstock doors at the Selborne Graving Dry Dock. The dry dock is used for regular naval vessel maintenance and relies on two flooding gates, or penstocks, to regulate water entering the dock. However, due to ageing infrastructure and material deterioration, one of the doors became damaged during routine inspection and testing. Reinstallation was managed to minimise disruption to the dockyard’s vessel maintenance schedule. The project also renewed access ladders and platforms within the penstock pit.
The dockyard operates one of only five dry docks in South Africa and two of the country’s three syncrolifts, making it central to national maritime maintenance capacity.
The renewal programme also includes the Motor Pump Test House, commissioned more than 40 years ago and upgraded after deterioration and changing testing and safety requirements.
One of the major steps in this renewal programme was the acquisition of an advanced Coordinate Measuring Machine (CMM). Precision is critical in marine engineering, where propellers, shafts, hull fittings and engine parts must meet exact dimensional requirements for safe operation. The CMM checks new or reconditioned components against original specifications and helps engineers identify wear, defects or dimensional discrepancies. This is especially valuable for older vessels where replacement parts may be difficult to source. Existing components can be measured and converted into 3D models, strengthening reverse engineering capability. Reduced time needed to inspect components will speed up the repair process, while increased measuring accuracy will reduce material waste and rework.
Reliance on ageing mobile equipment has created reliability and maintenance problems, with the main ship-handling tractor already more than 45 years old. Armscor is purchasing new equipment including a Caterpillar 980 Wheel Loader, five 16-metre JLG cherry pickers and three Toyota forklifts to improve vessel handling, access at height and material movement.
Two cranes have also returned to certified service after more than five years, bringing three mobile cranes into operation. Maintenance plans and training are being rolled out for dockyard and South African Navy personnel.
The Armscor Dockyard provides repair and maintenance services for South African Navy platforms, from tugs and small craft to frigates and submarines, covering planned and ad-hoc requirements.
“We aim to build a dockyard that is reliable, technologically capable and sustainable. Our investments in this regard will be successful if we can support the operational readiness of the South African Navy and preserve strategic maritime engineering capability in the country,” said Mbada.

title: India’s MKU to establish electro-optics and armour manufacturing facility in Morocco
body:
MKU Limited has announced plans to establish a manufacturing facility in in the SGZID Zone in Nouasser, Morocco, for the local production of electro-optics (EO) and armour solutions. The facility will serve as MKU’s base for exports to the African continent.
MKU made the announcement on 7 October to coincide with the Marrakech Air Show currently underway in Morocco. It said further details on its location, scale, timeline, and investment will be announced in due course.
MKU develops and manufactures solutions across electro-optics, survivability and aviation MRO (maintenance, repair and overhaul) for soldiers and platforms worldwide. Over more than four decades, its solutions have been adopted by over 230 forces in 100 plus countries, on land, in the air and at sea. Headquartered in India, MKU operates manufacturing and operational infrastructure across India, Brazil, Saudi Arabia and the UAE, with a European Centre of Excellence in Germany.
The Moroccan facility builds on a partnership that is already established, the company said. Over the past five years, MKU has supplied optronics and personal protection products to the Moroccan armed forces. Local manufacturing marks the next phase of that engagement, bringing production closer to the end user.
The factory will produce solutions from MKU’s two core portfolios: Netro Optronics, which delivers multi-sensor electro-optic systems for situational awareness, surveillance, reconnaissance and target acquisition, and Kavro Protection, which spans body armour, ballistic helmets, shields and platform armouring.
Localisation is at the heart of MKU’s investment, the company said. By manufacturing in the Kingdom, MKU will transfer advanced production capabilities and technical expertise to Morocco, and create skilled employment for Moroccan engineers, technicians and manufacturing professionals. The facility is designed to complement Morocco’s ambition to build a self-reliant, globally competitive defence industry, with MKU committed to growing alongside it as a long-term industrial partner.
The benefits will also reach Moroccan end users directly, MKU added. With production and support based in-country, customers can expect faster delivery cycles, greater flexibility in meeting evolving operational requirements, and responsive after-sales service close at hand.
Morocco has spent the past decade positioning itself as the industrial gateway between Africa, Europe and the Middle East, and its defence sector is now following the same path. With one of the largest defence budgets on the continent, a national strategy to localise defence manufacturing and a mature aerospace ecosystem, the Kingdom offers the policy support, industrial depth and connectivity that export-oriented manufacturing demands. MKU’s new facility will draw on these strengths, it said. Products made there will be offered to partner forces across Africa and Europe, establishing Morocco as the company’s base for exports to the continent.
“Five years of working with Morocco have shown us the calibre of its institutions and its people,” said Karan Gupta, Vice President – International Sales, MKU Limited. “This factory turns that relationship into a long-term commitment, and it will be a cornerstone of our international growth strategy.”
MKU is not the first Indian company to establish a production facility in Morocco. In September 2025 Tata Advanced Systems opened a plant in Berrechid, near Casablanca, to build its WhAP 8×8 wheeled armoured vehicle, the first overseas defence factory by a private Indian company. The Royal Moroccan Army received its first locally produced WhAP vehicles from that plant early this year.
To facilitate future investments, and just like it has done for commercial aviation, Rabat has begun establishing several industrial zones dedicated to defence; and Morocco’s budget for 2025 exempts defence firms from taxes, in the hope to further boost foreign investments in Moroccan defence.

title: Hi-Tech Iron Fist from the Sea: A new fighting model for the SA Navy
body:
South Africa has done this before. In their seminal book, Arnè Söderlund and Douw Steyn record a remarkable period in our maritime history when the South African Navy and a small Special Forces capability combined people, platforms, innovation and unconventional thinking to produce operational effects far greater than their numbers might have suggested.
The circumstances today are entirely different, but one lesson remains relevant: sea power is not simply a function of how many ships a navy possesses. It is also about the reach, awareness and options those ships and their sailors can create.
As South Africa considers the future of its Navy, that lesson deserves another look. South Africa faces an uncomfortable maritime equation. We sit astride one of the world’s most important sea routes, with an extensive coastline, a vast exclusive economic zone, offshore resources and infrastructure, important fisheries and strategic interests extending into the Southern Ocean.
Yet the resources available to the South African Navy are severely constrained. The conventional response is to argue for more ships, more funding and the restoration of capabilities lost through years of underinvestment. Much of that argument is justified. Ships remain essential. So do sailors, submarines, seamanship, maintenance and time at sea.
But perhaps we are asking the wrong question. Instead of asking how South Africa can afford a larger version of the Navy it already has, perhaps we should ask: how can the Navy we can realistically afford generate significantly greater maritime reach and operational effect?
One possible consideration is the notion of Distributed Maritime Operations. The principle is relatively straightforward. Instead of thinking about a frigate, submarine, patrol vessel or shore establishment principally as an individual capability, each becomes a seaborne node in a wider maritime network. Ships, submarines, shore facilities, unmanned surface vessels (USV), unmanned underwater vehicles (UUV), ship-launched unmanned aerial systems (UAV) and distributed maritime sensors contribute to a common operational picture. Artificial intelligence (AI) can help process the growing volume of information generated by these systems and assist commanders in making sense of it.
That network must also reach beyond the battle horizon. The satellite communications architecture supporting maritime operations has shifted fundamentally. The transition from S-band and legacy Ku-band systems to X-band and Ka-band frequencies has transformed what space-derived maritime intelligence can deliver. Higher frequency bands offer significantly improved resolution, bandwidth and data throughput — enabling real-time imagery, near-continuous vessel tracking and high-quality sensor feeds that were simply not achievable with earlier satellite generations.
South Africa is not without foundation here. SANSA and facilities at Houwteq give South Africa existing ground segment capability and technical expertise that could form part of a broader maritime satellite architecture. South Africa need not necessarily own every satellite providing these services — commercial and sovereign capabilities could form part of the architecture — but the ability to access, task, receive and integrate X-band and Ka-band data into the Navy’s maritime operating picture is a realistic and achievable objective.
For a country responsible for an enormous maritime domain, resilient satellite connectivity at these frequencies could allow information collected by one seaborne node to become actionable intelligence for another hundreds or even thousands of kilometres away, in near real time.
The result is not a Navy without ships. Quite the opposite. Distributed Maritime Operations is not about replacing ships. It is about multiplying what every ship can do. A frigate should increasingly be capable of understanding what is happening beyond the range of its own sensors. A patrol vessel should not necessarily have to physically investigate every contact before understanding what it is dealing with. Support and hydrographic vessels could potentially deploy, recover and sustain autonomous maritime systems alongside their traditional roles.
The distinction is important. This is not an argument for replacing expensive ships with cheap drones. It is about changing the relationship between crewed platforms, autonomous systems, information and the people who use them.
Nor is this science fiction. Singapore is already integrating autonomous surface vessels into maritime security operations and designing future warships to operate alongside unmanned systems. Denmark is experimenting with unmanned underwater systems for seabed surveillance and the protection of critical maritime infrastructure.
The lesson is not that South Africa should copy either navy. It is that smaller and medium-sized maritime powers are already exploring how autonomous systems can extend the reach of limited numbers of crewed platforms. South Africa should develop its own model, shaped by our geography, resources, maritime responsibilities and operational experience.
There is a further capability dimension that deserves explicit attention. The proliferation of low-cost unmanned aerial systems and the emergence of drone swarm tactics present a growing threat to naval surface vessels operating in contested or uncertain maritime environments. South Africa’s Navy must begin developing a credible electronic warfare and counter-UAS capability — not as a distant aspiration but as a medium-term programme priority.
Effective counter-drone defence is not simply about kinetic intercept. It requires layered electronic warfare system integration — the ability to detect, classify, track and defeat drone swarms through a combination of jamming, spoofing, directed energy and hard-kill options, coordinated through a unified EW architecture across the fleet. This is an area where South Africa’s defence industry has latent capability, as was on offer at the Africa Aerospace and Defence (AAD) 2026 exhibition in Pretoria, and where the distributed maritime network described above becomes directly relevant.
A fleet of seaborne nodes, connected through resilient satellite communications and sharing a common operational picture, is inherently better positioned to detect and respond to drone swarm threats than isolated platforms operating independently.
Building this capability incrementally — beginning with EW system integration on existing platforms and developing counter-UAS doctrine through experimentation — would give the South African Navy a decisive edge in one of the most significant emerging threat domains.
There is also a danger in allowing discussion about future warfare to become a discussion solely about technology. South Africa already possesses an important human capability around which a distributed maritime force could develop: the Maritime Reaction Squadron. The MRS gives the Navy a deployable littoral and maritime response capability. But its current configuration — embarked on ships — limits its reach and situational awareness before it commits to an operation. Unmanned surface and underwater vehicles could change that fundamentally.
Operating ahead of the force, USVs and UUVs could scout, survey, and secure the littoral environment, building the real-time operational picture that allows the MRS to establish a bridgehead with confidence. The human element remains essential. The autonomous layer makes it survivable. Technology, therefore, becomes the force multiplier, not the protagonist.
The attraction of Distributed Maritime Operations for South Africa is that it need not begin with another enormous acquisition programme. It can begin experimentally. Take existing naval platforms. Introduce relatively small numbers of unmanned surface and underwater systems. Develop the communications, satellite connectivity and data architecture needed to connect them. Put those systems into the hands of sailors and the Maritime Reaction Squadron. Then take them to sea. Exercise them. Break them. Adapt them. Master them. Allow South African naval doctrine to develop from operational experience rather than simply importing somebody else’s solution.
Simon’s Town and environs could become the laboratory for doing precisely that, drawing on South Africa’s defence industry, universities and technology sector in areas such as sensors, communications, software, robotics and autonomy — and building on the ground segment expertise that already exists at SANSA and Houwteq.
None of this eliminates the immediate requirement to restore the Navy’s existing capabilities. A distributed Navy whose ships cannot go to sea is not a distributed Navy. The frigates, submarines, patrol vessels and support capabilities remain fundamental. The opportunity is to make them considerably more effective.
South Africa cannot afford to rebuild a 1990s Navy for a 2035 battlespace. Our future sea power should therefore not be measured solely by the number of grey hulls berthed in Simon’s Town, but also by how far those sailors and ships can see, how widely they can distribute sensors and autonomous systems, how effectively information can move across the force, and how quickly sailors and the Maritime Reaction Squadron can turn that information into action.
One hopes that the SANDF’s Journey to Greatness strategy will begin to lay the conceptual and institutional basis for precisely this kind of distributed maritime thinking — translating strategic ambition into operational doctrine, experimentation and capability development.
That answer is no longer about the size of the fleet. It is about whether South Africa can learn from its own remarkable past and apply the ingenuity that has always defined this country at its best — to build tomorrow’s Hi-Tech Iron Fist from the Sea.
Nils Flaatten is Founder and Director of Blue Viking.

title: Kyiv's Water Supply Disrupted After Russia's Energy Grid Strike
body:
Water supplies on Kyiv’s right bank were disrupted on Thursday, Oct. 8, as Russia’s overnight strike on the energy grid reduced pressure, authorities said.
The Kyiv City State Administration said some households in the capital’s Holosiivskyi, Svyatoshynskyi, Solomyanskyi, and Shevchenkivskyi districts are affected.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“Due to the decrease in voltage in the power grid, there are interruptions in the power supply of certain water supply facilities in the capital,” the administration wrote in an official notice .
“Because of this, there is a decrease in pressure in the water supply network of the right-bank part of the city. This is warned by PrJSC ‘AK ‘Kyivvodokanal’,” it added.
Since Tuesday, Kyiv has been experiencing blackouts as Russia began targeting Ukraine’s energy grid near the capital following a massive barrage that started a week prior.
By Wednesday, the city had introduced emergency shutdowns that led to outages outside the planned schedules, with Thursday’s power schedules lasting up to 12 hours throughout the day.
According to energy operator DTEK , outages also affected cities around Kyiv, including the Brovary, Bucha, Vyshhorod, and Boryspil districts, on Thursday morning. State energy operator Ukrenergo also said other regions across Ukraine were affected.
While both noted Russian attacks on the grid, neither disclosed when and where the facilities were hit, likely for security reasons.
The attacks came as Ukrainian officials warned of a dire winter, with Russia planning to intensify attacks on the energy grid – more so than last winter , when blackouts lasted over 48 hours, with water disruptions also recorded.
On Sept. 25, First Deputy Prime Minister and Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal said Kyiv has obtained plans of Russia’s winter strikes , with targets ranging from electricity generation and heating to water supply and sewage systems. Subsequent reports suggest that Russia plans to allocate three Kinzhal missiles per power plant and 20 drones per boiler house.
President Volodymyr Zelensky has vowed retaliatory strikes should Moscow pursue its energy strikes, with Washington’s proposed energy truce fizzling out as both Kyiv and Moscow view the winter as a decisive breaking point .
Leo Chiu is a journalist and editor based in Eastern Europe since 2015. He has witnessed two presidential elections in Belarus and traveled widely to conflict zones and contested regions, producing reporting that bridges the gap between major developments and local realities.

title: China stalls medical evacuation of Ayungin soldier
body: MANILA, Philippines – A China Coast Guard (CCG) vessel used water cannons on a Philippine mission to evacuate a Filipino soldier in need of a medical evacuation from the BRP Sierra Madre in Ayungin Shoal on Thursday, October 8. In a statement, the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) said the CCG’s actions led to a 10-hour delay. “A transfer like this would normally take only a few hours. It took nearly 10 because the CCG used its water cannon, refused the original rendezvous point, and shadowed PCG assets throughout,” said Rear Admiral Jay Tarriela, PCG spokesperson for the West Philippine Sea . Ayungin (Second Thomas) Shoal is where the BRP Sierra Madre , a World War II-era ship, serves as an outpost for a small group of Filipino soldiers. The vessel was grounded there on purpose in 1999, following Beijing’s militarization of nearby Panganiban (Mischief) Reef. The shoal and the ship are a flashpoint for tensions between Manila and Beijing in the South China Sea . China claims almost all of the critical waterway, including the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone, which is within an area Manila calls the West Philippine Sea. The soldier, whose identity was not disclosed, “requires immediate medical attention due to a prior medical condition,” the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) earlier said. His medical evacuation — via a rubber boat from the BRP Sierra Madre to a PCG vessel — was ongoing as of Thursday evening. “The personnel has received initial medical management and remains under observation while arrangements for his emergency evacuation are being facilitated,” said the AFP. The soldier is expected to be on land, at the Western Command (Wescom)’s headquarters in Puerto Princesa, Palawan, before the day’s end. “The AFP remains focused on the health, safety, and welfare of its personnel. Every necessary measure is being taken to ensure that the patient receives the medical attention and care he needs at the soonest possible time,” the military added. – Rappler.com

title: China's transformation had no ready-made roadmap. One of the paths led through Belgrade
body:
China is now routinely described as one of the most important laboratories of modern economic development. Regardless of the political and social costs of this model, the scale of modernisation is impossible to ignore: a nation that belonged to the developing world just a few decades ago has built a massive industrial base, the world’s largest high-speed rail network, and a position as one of the globe’s leading economies.
Yet discussions of the “Chinese model” often overlook the question of how China arrived at this point in the first place. In the West, the story has been repeatedly presented as a nearly linear transition: Mao Zedong, along with the economic and ideological chaos stemming from the Cultural Revolution, exits the stage, and Deng Xiaoping steps in with his policy of reform and opening up (gaige kaifang 改革开放). In reality, that path was far more turbulent, marked by course corrections, borrowed ideas, and abandoned inspirations.
One of the most unexpected places Beijing looked to for lessons at the start of its transformation was… Yugoslavia. The choice is striking: a state that China had condemned for twenty years as a symbol of revisionism became, in the second half of the 1970s, a subject of intense interest for Chinese reformers. It is worth tracing how this shift came about and what, precisely, remains of it.
In 1958, Chen Boda, a leading theorist of the Communist Party of China, declared that while “Judas betrayed a single Jesus, Tito betrayed the entire Yugoslav nation.” This was by no means an isolated remark. At the time, the Chinese press waged a campaign accusing Yugoslavia of modern revisionism and of serving imperialism. Both sides recalled their ambassadors, and inter-party relations were severed for twelve years. The immediate cause was the program adopted at the 7th Congress of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, which called for the dissolution of both military-political blocs. The deeper reason, however, lay elsewhere.
China entered the 1950s devastated by the Japanese invasion and the civil war against the Kuomintang. The CPC regime was still in its infancy and, consequently, unstable; the Chinese party elite therefore had to prioritise securing support from the Kremlin.
The course of foreign policy was set by the imperative to choose a side, a stance articulated by Mao Zedong in his June 1949 essay “On the People’s Democratic Dictatorship”: first put domestic affairs in order, and then, while opening up to the world, align firmly with the Soviet Union. Yugoslavia represented the exact opposite of this attitude. Its communists had emerged from the war with their own army and their own myth of partisan victory. This independence led to a conflict with Stalin, culminating in the expulsion of the Communist Party of Yugoslavia from the Cominform in June 1948. Beijing supported the decision because, in the most critical phase of its own civil war, it could not risk antagonising Moscow. Nevertheless, Belgrade was among the first nations to recognise the People’s Republic of China, doing so as early as October 1949. China did not reciprocate this gesture until January 1955, following the rapprochement between Khrushchev and Tito.
The ferocity of the 1958 attack, therefore, stemmed from an issue that did not directly concern Yugoslavia. When the Sino-Soviet split entered an open phase in the early 1960s, the third of the “Nine Commentaries,” entitled “Is Yugoslavia a Socialist Country?” dissected the Yugoslav system in order to strike at Khrushchev for tolerating Tito’s “renegade clique.” In this dispute Yugoslavia served as an argument rather than as the intended target.
A turning point came with the 1968 intervention in Czechoslovakia. Shared opposition to Moscow allowed ideological rhetoric to subside. In 1970, both states restored full diplomatic relations, though without inter-party ties, as Beijing continued to deny the Yugoslav party any claim to Marxist-Leninist orthodoxy. The highest-ranking visitor was Prime Minister Džemal Bijedić, received by Mao in 1975. The Chairman praised Tito as a man “hard as iron” and fearless in the face of Soviet pressure, turning the Chinese transcription of his name, Tietuo 铁托, into a compliment, as the first character signifies iron. Mao and Zhou Enlai died in 1976, having never met Tito.
Josip Broz Tito landed in Beijing on August 30, 1977, and a few days later became the first foreign head of state to enter Mao Zedong’s mausoleum, even before its official opening to the public. An editorial in the People’s Daily (Renmin Ribao) portrayed him as a distinguished anti-fascist leader of the older generation, the founder of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and a leader respected by nations worldwide. Notably, it was the first time his titles, Chairman of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia and President, were cited side by side. During a conversation on August 31, Hua Guofeng addressed his guest as “Comrade.” The press had not yet used this term; it did not reappear in print until November 12, 1977, during a visit by a Yugoslav trade union delegation led by Milutin Baltić, marking the first time a sitting Yugoslav politician had been addressed this way since 1958.
The magnitude of this shift becomes apparent only when contrasted with how Yugoslavia had been perceived by Chinese readers just two years prior. As the PRC’s diplomatic archives for this period remain closed, the party press serves as the best available indicator of the leadership’s mindset, and Renmin Ribao, the organ of the CPC Central Committee, was required reading for cadres at all levels. The picture that emerges from it may come as a surprise: Yugoslavia was depicted there primarily as a nation of total people’s defence. The newspaper reported on the drive for self-sufficiency in arms production, the planned construction of tunnels, and military exercises, frequently invoking the doctrine of total people’s defence (opštenarodna odbrana). A separate category consisted of reprints of speeches, most often by Tito, frequently appearing in his capacity as commander-in-chief of the armed forces, and by Defence Minister Nikola Ljubičić. Economic matters were covered rarely and dryly. When one of Yugoslavia’s major infrastructure projects at the time, the Belgrade-Bar railway line, was opened, the coverage was limited to a single sentence from a speech by Tito regarding its importance for national defence.
After August 1977, not only did the number of articles about Yugoslavia increase with each week, but their character changed as well. Instead of reprints from the Yugoslav press, original on-the-ground reports began to appear: from the “3. Maj” shipyard in Rijeka in September 1977, and from Energoinvest in Sarajevo in February 1978. A report from the Rade Končar electrical engineering factory in Zagreb, published on November 10, 1977, proved to be a turning point; it marked the first time the official Chinese press described the Yugoslav system of worker self-management, covering the election process for the workers’ council, the scope of its authority, and even the changes introduced by the 1974 Constitution and the Law on Associated Labour. The correspondents did not yet pass judgment on whether the system was right or effective. However, the level of detail in the description spoke for itself. Defence issues did not disappear from the pages of the press, and in January 1978 the same Energoinvest was praised for purchasing eight artillery pieces with its own funds. They ceased, however, to be the focal point of China’s interest in Yugoslavia.
The decision to rebuild relations between the parties was made by the Politburo of the CPC Central Committee on August 26, 1977, on the eve of Tito’s arrival. However, the decision was limited in scope and technical in nature; Belgrade was not informed of it, and formal contact was not resumed until ten months later. An event occurred during this interim that explains the delay.
In March 1978, a delegation of CPC party officials, including economists who would later spearhead the reforms, travelled to Yugoslavia. The report on this trip, discovered years later in the archives of the small city of Tongliao in Inner Mongolia, is a comprehensive and substantive document, devoid of mere pleasantries. Only after this report, in June 1978, did the CPC Central Committee send a congratulatory telegram to the 11th Congress of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, thereby restoring inter-party relations that had been severed twenty years earlier. The Congress received extensive coverage in Beijing: Tito’s speech was reprinted across a full page, and a correspondent described how the hall erupted in applause when Edvard Kardelj read out the Chinese telegram. The sequence of events is significant: the ideological rapprochement followed the experts’ report rather than preceding it, pointing to a decision-making process grounded in factual assessment rather than a solitary gesture by a leader.
Three weeks before Hua Guofeng’s return visit, on August 3, 1978, a Renmin Ribao correspondent moved beyond merely describing workers’ self-management to evaluating it. He posed the question of why the Yugoslav economy was growing so rapidly and why the local workers felt a sense of shared responsibility for their enterprises; he answered by pointing to self-management. Hua arrived in Belgrade on August 21, 1978, almost exactly a year after Tito’s visit, marking only the second foreign trip of his life. Coverage of the visit filled not only the front page but also subsequent pages. An editorial summarising the visit contained the most significant statement of all: that the League of Communists of Yugoslavia had applied the universal truths of Marxism to the specific conditions of its own country. Chinese communists had previously used this formula to describe their own path. Applying it to another nation signified an acknowledgment that the Yugoslav system was genuinely socialist.
All of this took place prior to the Third Plenary Session of the 11th Central Committee, held in December 1978. Thus, Yugoslavia was not “promoted” in the wake of the reformist breakthrough. Rather, the renewed interest in the Yugoslav experience preceded that breakthrough and partly paved the way for it, providing the leadership with an argument that an economy based on market mechanisms, social ownership, and openness to foreign capital could still be considered socialist. At the time, Chinese leaders were seeking not so much a model to copy as proof that such a path was actually possible.
Knowledge about Yugoslavia was disseminated in China by economists close to the leadership, most notably Yu Guangyuan, Luo Yuanzheng, and Su Shaozhi. They did so through publications, lectures, and conferences, as well as by establishing institutions; the Society for the Study of the Yugoslav Economy was founded during this period. Papers published between 1978 and 1980 addressed topics such as worker self-management, social ownership, the relationship between market mechanisms and planning, agricultural management, and the balance between capital accumulation and consumption. The level of engagement went far beyond mere reading. Translators and economists learned Serbo-Croatian, study trips were often lengthy and methodical, and the phenomenon reached such an intensity in 1978–1979 that it became known in the literature as “Yugomania”.
It was not only the elite who were learning, however. Internal reports preserved in the Shanghai Municipal Archives reveal that local-level hosts of Yugoslav delegations asked their own highly specific questions: about theatre management, about the organisation of tourism in a competitive environment, and about the funding of agricultural research. Representatives from China’s leather and machinery industries returned with extensive reports comparing Yugoslav practices with Chinese needs. This same hunger for concrete detail was evident in the daily press, for instance in reports describing a Belgrade knitwear factory that had been transformed from a loss-making entity into a profitable one, while explaining to readers that Yugoslav enterprises were managed by workers and that the workers’ council could simply dismiss an incompetent director.
The interest was thus genuine and detailed, yet selective from the very start. The Chinese studied the Yugoslav approach to small-scale private ownership, foreign investment, and enterprise autonomy, but they never adopted the system of worker self-management itself, specifically the practice of the workers’ council appointing and dismissing management. What they borrowed was the concept of enterprise autonomy vis-à-vis the state administration, not the workforce’s control over the enterprise.
The high-water mark was the death of Tito on May 4, 1980. Hua Guofeng flew to Belgrade for the funeral, an event that remains the only instance of a top PRC leader attending the funeral of a foreign head of state. Afterward, a drift away began, though it was initially imperceptible in the rhetoric.
The expectations of the two sides diverged. China wanted to continue observing and taking notes, while Yugoslavia increasingly expected trade and investment. The tone of the Chinese delegates also shifted; they moved from the stance of students to declaring an ambition to surpass Yugoslavia’s economic indicators. At the same time, the object of their admiration began to crumble. Mounting foreign debt, inflation, unemployment, and inter-republican and ethnic tensions were already visible; the Chinese press, having overlooked them for three years, could no longer ignore them. In August 1982, an open, critical debate broke out among Chinese economists. Traces of this reassessment are clearly visible in a 1985 text by Lou Jiwei, which bore a straightforward message: learn from Yugoslavia’s experience while avoiding the entrenchment of a division of power among territorial units. Chinese elites, fresh from the Cultural Revolution, were particularly receptive to arguments regarding the risks of power fragmentation.
The legacy of this episode is, therefore, exactly like its course: selective. From the Yugoslav experience, China adopted the conviction that market mechanisms, small-scale private ownership, and foreign capital could coexist within a socialist economy, while also heeding a warning against devolving economic power without retaining central control. They rejected workers’ self-management, the very feature the Yugoslavs themselves considered the essence of their model.
In China’s collective memory, the legacy of those years is defined primarily by the popularity of Yugoslav partisan films, most notably Walter Defends Sarajevo. In official discourse, the narrative of learning from Belgrade was superseded after 1999, following the NATO bombing of the Chinese embassy in Belgrade, by a narrative centred on a shared experience of grievance. The episode in which Beijing looked to Yugoslavia for lessons faded almost entirely from public consciousness.
China’s transformation lacked a ready-made roadmap. It took shape through the comparison of experiments conducted elsewhere, the assessment of their outcomes, and the selection of elements that could be adapted. One of the paths taken led through Belgrade and ended where the state that provided it met its own demise.

title: General Dynamics demonstrates navigation without GPS on Talon-A hypersonic aircraft
body: The company partnered with the Army’s Combat Capabilities Development Command Aviation and Missile Center (DEVCOM AvMC) for the demonstration. Talon-A can travel and maneuver at Mach 5 or higher. MO-Nav is a compact, single-board software-defined receiver. It provides radio-frequency navigation using multiple Global Navigation Satellite Systems, signals of opportunity and commercially supplied positioning, navigation and timing signals. “GPS-denied technology is arguably one of the largest capability gaps across joint forces,” said Matt Elliott, director of the Weapons and Navigation business segment at General Dynamics Mission Systems. “Programs face growing pressure to incorporate alternatives to GPS and extend mission availability.” Elliott said software-defined receivers allow programs to update their capabilities without replacing hardware. “General Dynamics Mission Systems is bringing software-defined receiver technology to the fight, allowing programs to continuously outpace the threat with software upgrades instead of requiring new hardware insertions.” MO-Nav previously survived extreme launch loads during a cannon-fired artillery demonstration and provided signal measurements to the munition’s mission computer. General Dynamics said the receiver is available for integration today. Further flight tests planned The company is also investing in the Multiple Orbit Highly Assured Weapons Kit (MOHAWK), which builds on the MO-Nav architecture. MOHAWK is designed to offer increased spectral diversity, expanded constellation diversity and scalable anti-jam protection. Its design supports an optional integrated M-Code receiver. It also provides for a federated external M-Code GPS receiver with an anti-jam and anti-spoof protected radio-frequency output. General Dynamics and DEVCOM AvMC are co-investing in a hypersonic demonstration of MOHAWK with integrated M-Code capability in 2027. Additional demonstrations on precision-guided munition platforms are planned for 2028.

title: Youth Ministry engages Parliament on programmes to expand opportunities for young people
body: The Ministry of Youth Development and Empowerment has engaged Parliament’s Select Committee on Youth and Sports on its programmes, achievements and priorities aimed at expanding opportunities for young Ghanaians. The engagement was held when members of the Committee paid a visit to the Ministry, where they discussed ongoing initiatives and the government’s broader agenda for youth development and empowerment. Minister for Youth Development and Empowerment, George Opare Addo, said the meeting provided an opportunity for the Ministry to update the Committee on its work and exchange views on measures needed to strengthen support for young people across the country. In a Facebook post on Wednesday, October 7, 2026, Mr Opare Addo expressed appreciation to the Committee for the visit and engagement, as well as its continued commitment to supporting youth development and empowerment.

title: ICE has quietly used this warehouse as a detention facility all summer, neighbors say
body:
A Roxbury, N.J., warehouse was one piece of a billion-dollar plan by the Department of Homeland Security to detain migrants. José A. Alvarado Jr. for NPR hide caption
Update, Oct. 13: In a statement Tuesday forwarded to NPR by the office of Rep. Analilia Mejia, D-N.J., a Department of Homeland Security official confirmed that ICE officers used the parking lot of a Roxbury Township warehouse to initially process 14 detainees on two occasions in September.
"DHS has finally admitted what we suspected all along: ICE used the Roxbury property to process and stage detainees on multiple occasions, potentially in violation of a court order restricting its use as an immigration detention facility," Mejia said in a statement.
DHS told Mejia that it used the site to protect the safety of its officers, and that no detained immigrants were brought inside the facility itself. DHS did not immediately respond to NPR's request for comment.
Mejia said she will continue to press for accountability. "ICE does not get to cherry-pick which laws to follow," she said. "I will continue to demand answers, pursue oversight, and work with state officials to ensure this property is never again used outside the law."
ROXBURY, N.J. — On a warm morning on Sept. 4, masked immigration agents rolled into Dover, N.J.
Footage of the raids rippled across social media, sent people into hiding and reignited rumors that had been circulating for months: Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents were taking people to a nearby warehouse.
The warehouse in Roxbury was one piece of a billion-dollar plan by the Department of Homeland Security to detain migrants as part of President Trump's mass deportation efforts.
That plan to convert warehouses into detention centers faced fierce backlash and legal challenges from residents and immigrant advocates. It was largely abandoned, and in several sites, including Roxbury, the government is legally forbidden by a court order from converting them to a detention facility, pending environmental assessments.
But an NPR investigation has found signs that the New Jersey facility is being used. And the state's Office of the Attorney General says it is looking into similar reports.
In early 2026, Homeland Security bought 11 warehouses to turn into ICE detention facilities. They spent about a billion dollars on these.
NPR spoke to an official at a government contractor whose company was approached to convert several of the warehouses into ICE facilities. He spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of retaliation from the government.
"No one that we spoke to at DHS was for this idea whatsoever. The deputy director told us point-blank that they had pushed back very hard on it. Everybody knew warehouses are horrible places to put people," he says.
At a meeting with a deputy director at DHS, he says, his company proposed an alternative: FEMA-style camps in Texas that would be more humane.
He says that idea was swiftly shot down. While White House adviser Stephen Miller was not at the meeting, they were told that this was not what Miller wanted.
The contractor says his understanding from that meeting was that "Miller did not want the facilities that were comfortable. He did not want facilities that were humane. We were told point-blank that that was not what the administration wanted."
"Steve Miller certainly seemed to make that point to everyone that he wanted it to be cruel. This was what Miller had stated to the DHS at that time, to the DHS director and deputy director. What surprised me was just how adamant the people were that it was going to happen. Damn the consequences. I would say in 25 years of working with the U.S. government, I've never been in that position before."
In a statement to NPR, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said the contractor's comments were "false hearsay allegation(s) from someone who has never even met or talked with Stephen Miller." Bis also said that Miller "has never made any remarks to anyone about wanting illegal aliens to have worse detention facility conditions. It simply isn't true and this is defamatory."
The White House did not respond to repeated requests to speak to Miller directly.
Early on, the warehouse plan was met with protests in both conservative and liberal towns. Several state attorneys general filed lawsuits to halt construction, based on environmental concerns.
"It very quickly became an absolute boondoggle," says Michael Wriston, a former military intelligence analyst who co-founded Project SaltBox, a watchdog group that tracks ICE's expansion. "It was really about the optics of people being kept in these cages and these large warehouses. They wanted a lot of what they called B-roll to play on social media, but they didn't do any due diligence of making sure that they conformed with environmental policy or that the construction wouldn't disturb local water tables."
A DHS official who served during Trump's first term, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they feared government retaliation, says that while they were not in the meeting the contractor described to NPR, they had often heard higher-ups in the administration wanting to make a point of showcasing difficult conditions immigrants were being held in.
Then, with the departure of DHS Secretary Kristi Noem in March, there was a shift: Her replacement, Secretary Markwayne Mullin, sought to do less showy immigration crackdowns. Today, Homeland Security is selling several of the warehouses.
But they're still holding on to a few, including in Hagerstown, Md. , Surprise, Ariz., and Roxbury, N.J. " These locations are very critical to ICE's deportation agenda," says Wriston, "because they fill in the gap in places where ICE does not have a robust detention network. They don't have a lot of jails there." They are also located in areas where there are no partnerships with the police who can house detainees in local jails.
In Maryland , Arizona and New Jersey , following lawsuits from each of the state attorneys general, DHS has either agreed or been ordered by a judge to halt the conversion of the warehouses into detention centers, pending environmental impact assessments. But throughout the summer, in the towns surrounding the Roxbury warehouse, rumors started to bubble.
Over the summer, there was a historic surge in ICE arrests: around 100,000 people in July and August.
In New Jersey, the rumor mill started churning. The Roxbury warehouse is located in a wooded area, on a road right off Route 46. Project NINJA (No ICE in North Jersey Alliance), a coalition that opposes ICE detention expansion, says several neighbors reported vehicles, often in a caravan, speeding up the road.
Dover Council Member Sandra Wittner in Dover, N.J., on Sept. 17. José A. Alvarado Jr. for NPR hide caption
"They're holding people in that warehouse," one woman says in a WhatsApp group in the town of Dover, which is about 15 minutes from Roxbury. "I have a co-worker who was taken there. They hold them there and at night they take them somewhere else." The message was forwarded to NPR by Dover Council Member Sandra Wittner.
"But, you know, it's like third- and fourth-hand accounts," says Wittner. "It just didn't seem probable at the time because of the court order. But it kind of made you scratch your head a little bit."
A woman says she was driving to work when she saw a raid taking place in Dover. She decided to follow the car carrying people who were detained. "I just needed to know, is he going to Roxbury?"
She took video as she trailed them up Route 46. She asked that NPR not use her name because what happened next made her fearful of what the government might do.
She says the car she was following turned onto the woodsy road that leads to the warehouse.
She says she waited to see if there was any more movement.
"And then maybe five minutes after that, a white Dodge Durango started kind of circling around me," she says. "And then on his last loop, he started filming me. He had a yellow case on his cellphone. After that, a black Tahoe started doing the same thing. I was on a public sidewalk, and it was intimidating. It was really intimidating. I'm scared. But I am more scared for our community."
Councilwoman Wittner says she strongly suspects ICE is using the Roxbury warehouse: "The immigration enforcement activity happened in Dover between 7 a.m. and 8 a.m." Wittner points to the woman who was able to follow the vehicle up Route 46: "The last vehicle entered the warehouse road at 8:25 a.m."
Meanwhile, footage of the raid started circulating on social media.
Back in Dover, another woman says she saw the videos as she got her kids ready for school. NPR viewed the videos and confirmed their authenticity.
In one of them, a worker is cornered against a wall by two masked agents. She says she was thunderstruck.
She asked that we not use her name because she fears being targeted.
At 8:25 a.m., she says, she got a call from her father. He's 59, she says, and he sounded disoriented. He told her he was handcuffed in some kind of jail.
She found it strange, she says, because the Roxbury warehouse would be the only place he could have been taken in that short a time span.
She also discovered a friend of hers had been picked up.
She hasn't been able to speak to her father since then, and neither has NPR. But NPR located her friend in Honduras, where he's been deported. He requested anonymity, because he fears repercussions for his loved ones who are still in the U.S.
"I was picked up on my way to work, on Friday, Sept. 4. The agents loaded me into a van. They took us to Roxbury," he said.
He says he and the other people detained were handcuffed and held in the parking lot for several hours. He counted nine other men with him. "I just went into a state of shock," he says. "I signed my deportation papers. The next morning I regretted it. But I was scared. Eventually, they transferred us to a real facility."
In a statement to NPR, DHS did not respond to a question about whether it was holding people at the Roxbury location. But it did give NPR a statement it has previously sent about ICE detention, saying DHS upholds strict standards and that immigrants can choose to leave detention by being deported.
A member of Project NINJA, a coalition that opposes ICE detention expansion, in Roxbury on Sept. 17. José A. Alvarado Jr. for NPR hide caption
The activists at NINJA say ICE's actions violate the legal order. The order lists several actions ICE can take with the site — mainly upkeep — but nowhere on that list is detention an acceptable action, they say.
Harvard professor Andrew Mergen, a former attorney with the U.S. Department of Justice Environment & Natural Resources Division, says ICE may technically not be violating the court order, which stipulated it would not convert the place into a detention center pending an environmental assessment.
Ultimately, Mergen says, the situation shows the limitations of using environmental claims. "The community is acting here to prevent people from being detained," says Mergen. "And the administration seems to have cleverly elided that intention, by sort of saying, 'Well, we're not going to build this facility, but we're going to use this space in furtherance of detention.'"
He says he understands the frustration: "It's just infuriating if what you are trying to do is say 'No. Not here. Not here.' "
Wittner says since the raid, she's heard from other close relatives or close friends of two men who were picked up that day, who say they were inside the Roxbury warehouse.
She says the situation is unacceptable: "We need our Congress members to conduct an oversight visit yesterday, quite honestly. We need our state to aggressively pursue this investigation and demand to get inside."
She says DHS has had time "to go in and clean up their mess if they, in fact, got caught doing something that they shouldn't have."
Meanwhile, in Dover, the streets where the raid happened remain deserted.
At an empty diner at lunchtime, a waitress who did not want to be named because of the climate of fear in town says one of the workers who was taken used to come here for a bite.
Then she leans over and asks: "Do you know where they took those men?"
The warehouse in Roxbury. José A. Alvarado Jr. for NPR hide caption
NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.

title: Ghana needs 150,000 more tonnes of palm oil annually to meet demand – OPDAG
body: Ghana’s annual crude palm oil production falls short of domestic demand by an estimated 150,000 metric tonnes, prompting calls for increased investment in farming and processing. The President of the Oil Palm Development Association of Ghana (OPDAG), Paul Kwabena Amaning, said the country produces approximately 250,000 metric tonnes annually, compared with demand of about 400,000 metric tonnes. Speaking at a one-day workshop for stakeholders in the oil palm sector, he described the deficit as an opportunity to increase domestic output, upgrade processing operations and make the industry more competitive. The workshop examined financing and the role of digital financial services across the oil palm value chain. Mr Amaning said Ghana has an estimated 360,000 hectares under oil palm cultivation, with the industry supporting approximately 631,000 people. He noted that the proposed US$500 million financing for oil palm development could help tackle barriers to growth. However, he urged stakeholders to ensure that funding arrangements accommodate smallholder farmers, aggregators and artisanal processors. “As OPDAG President, I consider the inclusion of these small operators particularly important,” he said. He explained that artisanal processors make substantial contributions to palm oil production, rural employment and economic activity, but struggle to obtain affordable credit, modern machinery and formal business support. Mr Amaning also called for greater use of digital financial services to facilitate payments and improve business operations among farmers, processors, traders, transporters and exporters. “Digital financial services can help improve payment security, strengthen record-keeping, increase transparency, and create opportunities for businesses to access savings, credit, insurance and other financial products,” he said. He stressed that successful digitalisation would require more than transferring payments to mobile platforms. Reliable connectivity, reasonable transaction fees, accessible payment agents and systems that work across different platforms would be essential. Consumer protection and practical training, he added, would also help users build confidence in digital services. Mr Amaning said digital transaction records could enable financial institutions to better assess small businesses and their funding needs, provided appropriate consent and safeguards were in place. He further identified the sector’s developing traceability and revenue assurance system as a potential means of improving industry records and supporting access to finance. He called for closer cooperation among government agencies, banks, financial technology companies, mobile network operators, mills, buyers and industry associations. “Policies and financial solutions will be more effective when voices of farmers, processors, and other industry participants are heard and reflected in their design,” he said.

title: Two West Bank Palestinian minors arrested for suspected arson near Homesh
body: Two Palestinian minors from the West Bank were arrested and issued a prosecutor's statement for a suspected attempted arson attack in September, the police confirmed on Thursday.The initial incident had occured on September 18, when police received a report that a fire had been started near the settlement of Homesh.After an investigation, police located the two 16-year-old suspects, arrested them, and brought them in for questioning.This is a developing story.

title: Germany greenlights four more MEKO A-200 DEU frigates
body:
The German Bundestag’s Budget Committee has approved the procurement of four additional MEKO A-200 DEU frigates.
The second tranche follows ‌four ⁠ships of the same type already on order at TKMS, bringing the total program to eight frigates.
“The Budget Committee’s decision is a strong sign of confidence in us. We made early investments in the MEKO A-200 DEU and, together with our partners, laid the groundwork for rapid series production. Now we can swiftly continue series production and thereby make an important contribution to closing as quickly as possible an impending capability gap in the German Navy,” said Oliver Burkhard , CEO of TKMS.
This is the largest surface vessel contract in TKMS's history, according to the company. The first frigate will be delivered to the German Navy at the end of 2029, as planned. According to current plans, the remaining units will follow in rapid succession. TKMS also noted that the program entered the implementation phase.
The approval of the contractually agreed option and the associated expansion to a total of eight MEKO A-200 DEU-class frigates also lay the groundwork for long-term, sustainable series production at German shipyards. The four additional frigates can build directly on the established structures, processes, and supply chains of the ongoing program. This allows production to continue without fundamental changes and ensures its long-term sustainability, it was highlighted.
To remind, Germany’s Ministry of Defense recently terminated the troubled F126 frigate procurement program, citing major schedule delays, soaring costs, and unacceptable project risks, and announced plans to acquire eight MEKO A-200 frigates for the German Navy.
