title: South Darfur: Fallata, Masalit tribes agree to coexist peacefully after deadly clashes
body: T he Fallata and Masalit communities in Sudan’s South Darfur have reached a peace agreement aimed at preventing further violence following recent deadly clashes in Gireida Locality, community leaders and members of the mediation committee said on Wednesday. The agreement was reached at the conclusion of a peace and reconciliation conference in Nyala that brought together traditional leaders and representatives of the two communities. The conference followed clashes in Gireida in September that killed 16 people and injured 23. The violence began with a dispute between two men at Abuja market before escalating into clashes between members of the two communities. Major Tala’at Khawf Al-Shanahi, head of the peace and reconciliation department of the Social Cohesion Initiative and rapporteur of the mediation committee, told Radio Tamazuj on Wednesday that the conference had adopted a series of resolutions and recommendations to prevent a recurrence of the violence. The two communities agreed to reject division and racism and pledged not to use tribal solidarity to protect people accused of committing crimes, Al-Shanahi said. He said members of each community had agreed to distance themselves from anyone who commits a crime and prevent the community from mobilising in their support or shielding them from legal proceedings. The conference also called on the government to improve access to water sources by constructing two water stations, one in Gireida and another in the Saadoun area, he said. Nazer Mohamed Al-Fateh Al-Samani, the tribal leader of the Fallata, said the conference had helped contain the dispute and improve relations between the two communities. “We and the Masalit are one people, and we have longstanding relations that include intermarriage,” he told Radio Tamazuj. Masalit tribal leader King Adel Hassan said both sides had committed themselves to maintaining peace and had taken an oath to uphold the agreement. Hassan said the conference had adopted 12 resolutions and recommendations, including a commitment by both communities not to attack or encroach on people’s homes or farmland. He said the provision would help create conditions for displaced residents to return voluntarily to their villages. Hassan also called for security forces to be deployed to strengthen state authority in the area and for judicial and law-enforcement institutions to be established or strengthened. He called for a functioning justice system, including a judge, public prosecution service and properly equipped police force, so that people accused of crimes could be dealt with through the law. Mohamed Hassan Al-Taishi, prime minister of the RSF-aligned Government of Peace, attended the signing of the conference’s final resolutions and pledged to implement its recommendations, according to participants. Al-Taishi also announced the formation of a committee to monitor implementation of the agreement. Nyala is the seat of the parallel administration aligned with the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which controls much of Darfur. Al-Taishi has previously blamed the weakness and absence of state institutions for contributing to local conflicts and called for stronger security and justice institutions. The reconciliation effort comes as communities in Darfur face continuing insecurity amid Sudan’s wider war between the army and the RSF, which erupted in April 2023. The post South Darfur: Fallata, Masalit tribes agree to coexist peacefully after deadly clashes appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

title: 3 Killed, 14 Injured as Russian Drones Assault Kyiv in Fresh Attacks, Hit Store
body:
Three people were killed and seven injured in Russian drone attacks on Kyiv earlier on Thursday, with a four-story store in the capital’s Solomianskyi district hit by a UAV, Kyiv Mayor Vitalii Klitschko said.
The attack sparked a fire in the non-residential building, where emergency crews later found two bodies.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Authorities have not identified the store. However, a Kyiv Post correspondent near the site said it is believed to be the OLDI construction and building store, a smaller home-improvement retailer similar to Epicentr.
The number of casualties rose throughout the evening. According to Klitschko’s latest report , four people were killed and 19 injured in Thursday’s attacks on Kyiv.
Thirteen of those injured remain hospitalized, including two in serious condition.
The latest strikes followed another deadly Russian drone attack on Kyiv on Wednesday , which killed at least four people.
In the Desnianskyi district, a Russian drone hit a 12-story residential building on the 10th floor, sparking a fire and partially destroying the structure. Rescuers later found two bodies inside a damaged apartment. Four people were injured, including two children, while 22 residents, including eight children, were evacuated.
In the Obolonskyi district, falling drone debris set parked cars on fire, killing two people. Six people were hospitalized, including a young woman in serious condition.
Earlier Wednesday, Russian attacks also injured eight people in the Solomianskyi district, while falling drone debris damaged buildings in the Dniprovskyi and Sviatoshynskyi districts.

title: Etihad Rail confirms variable pricing as some tickets increase by up to Dh69
body: Etihad Rail has confirmed variable pricing is in place on a number of its routes amid sustained demand for train travel since the long-awaited launch of passenger services - with some tickets increasing by up to Dh69. Fares for the inaugural route between Abu Dhabi and Fujairah were initially set at Dh55 ($15) for Comfort class and Dh109 for Premium class when services began on June 30. Tickets for the routes between Abu Dhabi and Dubai were priced at Dh39 for Comfort Class and Dh109 for Premium class when it opened to the public on September 30. The online timetable shows an increase in prices, typically for afternoon and evening services, and at weekends, across the network. On Thursday, Etihad Rail's website showed Comfort class tickets for the Abu Dhabi-Dubai line priced from Dh39 to Dh59, depending on departure times, while Premium tickets for the same route were Dh109 to Dh149. Meanwhile, tickets for train travel between the UAE capital and Fujairah are now Dh55 to Dh79 in Comfort class and Dh120 to Dh189 for Premium. Ticket for trains from Sharjah's Al Dhaid station – which also opened on September 30 – vary from Dh19 in Comfort class to Dh79 in the Premium class. The operator told The National fares depended on several factors including when passengers choose to travel and book their tickets. “Prices vary based on selected service, time and date of trip, ticket class and category, and time of booking,” an Etihad Rail representative said. “Ticket categories are designed to cater to diverse passenger needs, whether for daily commutes, business trips, visiting family, or enjoying a weekend getaway at one of the country’s destinations.” Many journeys – between Abu Dhabi and Dubai, and Abu Dhabi and Fujairah – are already sold out in advance. Passengers can view fares, compare options and book ahead through the Etihad Rail app, website and ticket vending machines at stations. Passenger services connecting Abu Dhabi and Dubai began on September 30 as part of the expansion of the national rail network. High demand Etihad Rail added more than 2,000 tickets across six extra train services between Abu Dhabi and Dubai last weekend. The additional services were made available after the new passenger rail route connecting the UAE's biggest cities attracted “exceptional early demand”. Etihad Rail's network is set for more expansion in the coming months. New stations in Al Dhafra region are scheduled to open on November 30 and December 30, extending connectivity to areas beyond the capital. The highly anticipated University City Station in Sharjah is expected to open on March 30, broadening the network's reach across the Northern Emirates.

title: Bokpin cautions Ghana against abandoning existing partnerships over BRICS membership
body: Professor of Finance at the University of Ghana Business School and Economist, Professor Godfred Bokpin, has cautioned the government against pursuing Ghana’s proposed membership of BRICS as a strategy to abandon its existing international partnerships or align itself exclusively with a particular political bloc. He said Ghana should approach its BRICS application as part of a broader foreign and economic policy strategy that allows the country to engage with different global economic powers while protecting its interests. Speaking on the Joy FM Super Morning Show on Thursday, October 8, during a discussion on Ghana’s quest to join BRICS, Prof Bokpin said the country needed to be clear about what it wanted to achieve from membership. “Joining BRICS necessarily should not be pursued as a substitution strategy for exiting other blocs or within other political leanings that we have,” he said. He said Ghana should recognise that although BRICS has become an important force in the global economy, the country still has other strategic partners whose interests must be considered. “We need to situate all of this within the broader foreign policy and economic policy that allows us to recognise that yes, BRICS is a dominant force, but there are other players also, and remember that there will also be a pushback from our traditional partners as well. They are equally watching,” he said. Prof Bokpin said the government should have a clear strategy covering the country’s objectives, limitations and the period within which it expected to achieve its goals from BRICS membership. “We need to be quite clear on what we allow, what we will not allow, what is the strategy within what transition period and all of that that we are working at and all of that,” he said. “So we need to engage with our eyes open. We need to make this application to join BRICS with our eyes open.” He cautioned that BRICS membership should not be viewed as a quick solution to Ghana’s economic challenges. “Remember that BRICS wasn’t just designed to transform our economy. The motives are quite clear, just like any other economic bloc that you want to join. It’s the same way,” he said. Prof Bokpin drew comparisons with Ghana’s participation in the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), saying membership of a regional or international economic bloc did not automatically translate into economic benefits. He said Ghana’s ratification of the AfCFTA agreement did not, by itself, guarantee that Ghanaian businesses would become competitive across the continent. “In fact, when we started talking about African Continental Free Trade and all of that, it was quite clear to us that the fact that we are a member, we signed, we submitted our instrument of ratification, necessarily doesn’t mean that automatically we’ll benefit from the African Continental Free Trade,” he said. “There’s a lot that we have to do to make it even worse.” He said Ghana must first create an environment in which local businesses could compete successfully at home before expecting them to compete in international markets. “The fact that we are hosting the secretariat necessarily doesn’t mean we’ll host the gains emanating from the African Continental Free Trade. This is not a host win. You have to work hard. You have to create the enabling environment for your businesses to be able to compete even within Ghana,” he said. “You are talking about competing and winning within Ghana, then you can talk about competing and winning outside Ghana.” Prof Bokpin said one of the biggest challenges was that many Ghanaian businesses were struggling to compete with imported goods in the domestic market. “Even within Ghana, we are not able to compete and win against foreign imports,” he said. He pointed to Ghana’s inflation figures as an indication of the challenges facing local producers. “Look at our inflation dynamics today. Inflation is a domestic issue, okay? Inflation on locally produced is more higher than inflation on imported items,” he said. He said the situation sent the wrong signal to businesses considering whether to invest in local production. “What signal does this send to entrepreneurs?” he asked. “You are much better off actually importing and putting a local logo on it than setting up a production function in Ghana.” Prof Bokpin said that Ghana could not expect its businesses to compete successfully in international markets if they were unable to compete effectively within the domestic economy. “So even within Ghana here, we have not been able to enable our own firms to be able to compete and win in Ghana, let alone to win outside Ghana,” he said. “To win outside Ghana, you first have to win within Ghana. The Chinese are winning outside China because they have won in China.” He said Ghana therefore needed to build a strong domestic productive base before expecting local companies to take advantage of international trade opportunities. “So without creating that kind of backbone for your own firms to compete and win within, you cannot win without. It doesn’t happen that way,” he said. Prof Bokpin acknowledged the government’s efforts to stabilise the economy and said the next phase should focus more strongly on growth and productive investment. “I know that government is putting in a lot of measures and all of that in terms of recalibrating the economic framework,” he said. Prof Bokpin encouraged the Minister of Finance to use the expected fiscal space to tackle Ghana’s development challenges with greater urgency and scale. “And I want to encourage the Minister of Finance that this is the time for Ghana because we’ve created some fiscal space, and I believe that we need to act at scale and on time to be able to respond to the developmental challenges for us to be able to compete and win within and then we can think about winning without and all of that,” he said. “So I believe that there’s a lot that we have to do, and then we also have to explore collaboration with others as well,” Prof Bokpin added. His comments followed Foreign Affairs Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa’s indication that Ghana intends to submit an application to join BRICS as the government explores ways to diversify its international partnerships, expand economic opportunities and deepen cooperation with countries in the Global South.

title: Premier League clubs fear political interference in Man City appeal
body: Some Premier League clubs were so “astonished” by comments made by Andy Burnham – appearing to downplay the verdict against Manchester City – that they are now “concerned” about political interference in the appeal process, sources have told BBC Sport. Senior club figures say they were shocked when they heard the prime minister tell the BBC he would be “really concerned” if Manchester City’s owners decide to sell up after the club were found guilty of Premier League financial rule breaches. They have questioned what his comments to the BBC were designed to achieve, and said it had put the Independent Football Regulator in a difficult position. Burnham is under increasing pressure surrounding his relationship with the club’s Abu Dhabi ownership during his time as mayor of Greater Manchester. Such is the level of scrutiny that Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has demanded that No 10 release all details of meetings between the prime minister and senior figures at the club. Despite clarification from Downing Street that Burnham’s view is that no-one is “above the rules”, his comments have sparked unease among some senior Labour figures who fear his initial comments have had major cut-through with voters. Senior club sources have said they found the comments “absolutely bizarre”, and that it was “at best naive and at worst quite manipulative, and that is not a good look”. A different source said it was “clumsy”, while another said they were surprised that the prime minister had “misspoken”. The entire process involving the charges against Manchester City is independent of the Premier League. An independent commission held a 42-day hearing in 2024 which led to the verdict announced last month, with a sanctions hearing still to come. A separate independent appeal board will hear City’s appeal. The club continues to deny any wrongdoing. However, when asked about potential interference in the process off the back of Burnham’s comments, one senior club source said: “Everyone would have a degree of concern. How much would depend on how much you read into that comment. “I think everyone is concerned. Because no-one is stupid around the table. We understand the geopolitics as well. We understand the investment they have made in our country. I don’t think anyone could doubt that or criticise that. But this is different, this is sport, this is our national game.” Another club source, however, said the degree of scrutiny on Burnham now means they think any interference would be impossible. This is a sensitive area for the prime minister. Manchester City ‘s dominance of English football has overlapped in large part both with a period of economic growth for the city of Manchester, and with Burnham’s nine years as mayor from 2017 until earlier this year. As mayor, Burnham championed investment from the Gulf to grow Manchester’s economy, a strategy that had been pursued by the city’s leaders before Burnham became the inaugural elected mayor of the Greater Manchester Combined Authority. Regardless of Burnham’s past career, there are additional sensitivities that would apply to other prime ministers as well. The UK as a whole is eager to trade with the UAE, and the country is an important diplomatic ally in the region at a time of turmoil and war. When the guilty verdicts were announced, Richard Masters, the Premier League’s chief executive, said the club had “systematically broke Premier League rules for nearly a decade”. Burnham’s comments came in an interview with the BBC’s political editor Chris Mason the next day. When asked about ‘Brand Manchester’ taking a hit, the Prime Minister drew a parallel with a previous Premier League case with Everton , saying he still held the view “firmly” that they “weren’t fairly treated”. Everton were deducted 10 points, later reduced to six on appeal , by an independent commission for breaching Premier League financial rules. Asked if he was concerned that Manchester City ‘s owners would now sell the club, Burnham said: “I would be really concerned to lose them. “They’ve been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester and obviously the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is. “I do actually thank the City Football Group and the wider ownership for the money that they didn’t just put into the Etihad [Stadium] and the campus around it but also into the city,” he added. Burnham’s comments provoked strong criticism. The following day, a No 10 spokesperson sought to clarify the comments, saying: “As the prime minister made clear, the initial judgement is serious and there can’t be any suggestion that anyone is above the rules. He also stressed that it is an ongoing independent process. It is essential that it is allowed to run its course and the outcome respected. “If wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the appropriate consequences.” However, this statement was amended following further criticism over the use of the word “if” – which was changed to “wherever”. The Premier League is viewed by governments of different political stripes as one of the country’s major cultural exports, so ministers are eager for the row not to cause lasting damage to its brand. Additionally, being a football fan is a core part of Burnham’s political persona. He is an Everton season ticket holder and, prior to becoming prime minister, he spoke of hoping to continue sitting in his usual seat at Hill Dickinson Stadium – but this has not been possible because of security concerns, as was the case for Sir Keir Starmer, his Arsenal -supporting predecessor. Last month Burnham floated the prospect of lifting the ban on football fans drinking in the stands, though it was quickly clarified that this is not in fact government policy.

title: High explosive payloads keep a human in the loop
body: Where a person sits in the decision depends on what the system is carrying, and anything with a high explosive payload will keep a human in the loop, a panel on autonomous mass heard at the Apex Europe conference in London on Wednesday. Freddie Bradshaw, head of business development at the Estonian company Ark Robotics, said the use case has to come before the autonomy question, because the answer changes completely between a one-way strike vehicle and a resupply run. He said: “We’re certainly seeing that it’s very important to have human in the loop when it comes to a one-way strike effector, for instance. If you’ve got a system that has a payload of high explosive, the chances are we aren’t going to allow AI to be controlling that, and we need to have some sort of human in the loop.” Further back from the front the balance shifts, and that is where he sees autonomy earning its place, taking the cognitive burden off a commander and handing it to the system so that one person can manage a fleet. Antony Quinn, the Europe director of Havoc, argued that the vocabulary needs tightening before the debate can go anywhere, since human in the loop and human on the loop get used interchangeably and mean different things. Adding waypoints and watching a vessel follow them round makes the operator the bottleneck, which defeats the point of mass in the first place. Three things have to be right in his account before any of it works, the first is the human interface, which should use simple accessible language and let an operator give intent and supervise instead of constantly intervening or monitoring camera feeds. The second is trust, earned by designing, testing and assuring the system the way trust is extended to an officer commanding a tactical unit. The third is policy and doctrine, which he does not think needs reinventing. He said: “There is a point at which the system, whatever it is, is trusted to the person or computer you have trained, with its boundaries and actions on, and doctrine already supports this. So yes, humans are critically important in or on the loop, but a lot of it is not that unfamiliar, actually.” Mr Bradshaw made a related point about interfaces, saying his company works to ensure its own plugs into a number of command and control systems so it can be operated through NATO compliant architectures, and that it has to be easy enough to use that scaling is possible at all. From the user’s side, Oleksii Krymeniuk, the chief unmanned systems officer of the 2nd Corps of Ukraine’s National Guard, gave the position a name. “I’m not a huge believer in full autonomy. I’m more a believer in something that could assist our guys in the staffs and on the ground and help them make faster and more efficient decisions,” he said. What he wants next is one operator running many drones, which he was careful to distinguish from swarming. The arithmetic is what makes it matter, since a mission needing dozens of aircraft currently needs dozens of operators, and bringing that ratio down multiplies what a unit of fixed size can achieve. Mr Bradshaw agreed that ground autonomy has not arrived yet, saying there is still a way to go in the uncrewed ground vehicle domain. Mike Wilmot, head of UK land at Helsing, came at it from the opposite direction, arguing that there are tasks where an automated process deserves more confidence than a person does, with air defence engagement the obvious case. He drew an ethical conclusion from that. He said: “There isn’t just a financial expense of sending an F-35 across the forward line of enemy troops. There is also a potential human expense, and if we have that safety confidence in a platform to be able to deliver its task, then there does become an ethical consideration of why send a human pilot or a collection of human pilots when you could first send autonomous platforms.” None of the four speakers argued for removing the person altogether, and the disagreement between them was about where the line falls, not whether there should be one. Mr Quinn’s closing advice to anybody buying this technology was that the decision making does not need to change as much as people fear, and that a degree of the caution around it is unjustified. The post High explosive payloads keep a human in the loop first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: Poland Ends Russian Drone Probe After Failing to Identify Perpetrator
body:
Polish prosecutors have closed an investigation into last year’s mass Russian drone incursion after failing to identify who ordered or directed the operation, while investigators found Polish SIM cards in some of the drones.
The military section of the Lublin District Prosecutor’s Office discontinued the investigation into the violation of Polish airspace, prosecutor Marcin Kozak told Rzeczpospolita .
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Most of the case files, including the reasoning behind the decision, remain classified.
“The investigation was discontinued because the perpetrator of the crime involving the violation of Polish airspace and thereby creating a threat to public safety was not identified,” Kozak said.
The investigation concerned the overnight incursion of more than 30 Russian Gerbera drones into Polish airspace on Sept. 9-10, 2025. The drones entered Poland from the east and were found in 27 locations across the country.
The investigation sought to determine who was personally responsible for directing the operation. Prosecutors ultimately could not identify the person responsible, leading to the case being closed.
The circumstances surrounding the operation remain partly classified.
Investigators also found SIM cards belonging to Polish mobile operators in some of the drones, according to the report.
The investigation did not establish publicly whether the cards had been stolen or obtained through illegal purchases. That part of the case remains classified.
The finding is not entirely new: Ukrainian defense analysts had previously reported the discovery of Polish and Lithuanian SIM cards in Russian drones found in Ukraine. Rzeczpospolita reported that at least one previously identified card belonged to T-Mobile Poland.
Another key finding of the investigation concerns the Polish military’s response to the drone attack. Prosecutors concluded that the armed forces responded properly and followed the applicable procedures, having the right to shoot down hostile objects.
“The use of weapons was authorized and justified. This part of the investigation was discontinued after it was determined that there were no grounds to establish a prohibited act, meaning no crime,” prosecutor Marcin Kozak said.
He declined to disclose which specific unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) were shot down.
The investigation also established that missiles were launched from fighter aircraft to destroy some of the incoming drones. According to the prosecutors, an incident involving “an explosion of explosive material contained in missiles fired, on the decision of the Operational Commander of the Armed Forces, from combat aircraft” occurred in Poland’s Lublin region.
The missiles missed their intended targets and unintentionally struck a field in the village of Choiny and a forest plot in Krzywowierzbie Kolonia, as per the report.
Separately, prosecutors discontinued an investigation into a missile that struck a residential building in Wyryki, also in the Lublin region. Rzeczpospolita reported that an allied missile fired by a Dutch F-35 pilot at an incoming drone destroyed the house.
Investigators concluded that the pilot had acted within the scope of his authority, although the investigation did not establish whether the incident resulted from human error or a technical failure.
Another unresolved question is why the Russian drones entered Polish airspace in the first place.
According to Rzeczpospolita, the answer is contained in a classified section of the investigation. The newspaper reported, citing its sources, that investigators are leaning toward the assessment that the drones were deliberately launched to test Poland’s air-defense procedures and force NATO and Ukrainian systems to expend missiles.
Most of the drones were reportedly unarmed and did not carry warheads or explosives. However, the investigation has not publicly established what payloads, if any, were carried by the drones that were shot down.

title: Gas stocks in European underground storage facilities reach 73%
body:
MOSCOW, October 8. /TASS/. Gas reserves in European underground gas storage (UGS) facilities have risen to 73%, though injection rates are slowing as temperatures in the region drop, according to TASS calculations based on data from Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE).
While average gas injection rates into EU storage facilities this October remain the highest in four years, Europe has already missed the summer months most favorable for replenishment.
As of October 6, European UGS facilities were 72.97% full (15.11 percentage points below the five-year average for this date), compared to 82.9% a year earlier. This remains the lowest level recorded for this date since data collection began in 2011. EU storage facilities currently hold approximately 79.9 billion cubic meters of gas, which is 11.6 billion cubic meters less than last year's levels and the lowest volume since 2013. Gazprom previously forecast that European UGS inventories might not even reach 75%, warning that the region faces a challenging autumn-winter season.
TASS previously reported that Europe risks entering the heating season with record-low gas stocks. By the traditional start of the autumn-winter period, EU countries may only manage to fill their storage facilities to 70-75% capacity, marking an all-time low for the start of a heating season. Since the summer season began in April 2026, net gas injection (the difference between injection and withdrawal volumes) into EU facilities has reached 49 billion cubic meters. Consequently, Europe has so far secured only 72% of the volume required for the upcoming winter.
Under European Commission regulations, EU member states must ensure their storage facilities are 90% full between October 1 and December 1 each year, with a 10% margin of flexibility allowed for challenging conditions. Thus, net injection into European storage must total at least 68 billion cubic meters by the start of the 2026-2027 autumn-winter period to meet the standard. However, anticipating a mild winter, the European Commission is reportedly prepared to lower this threshold to 80% for the current year.

title: Indonesia expects first Chinese J-10 fighter jets around April 2027, reports
body: Indonesia could receive its first Chengdu J-10 fighter jets around April 2027, according to a report by Indonesian news outlet Republika Online, cited by the South China Morning Post (SCMP). Republika reported on October 5, 2026 that the first aircraft are expected in about six months. It did not say how many jets would be included in the initial delivery. If the delivery goes ahead, Indonesia would become the first Southeast Asian operator of the Chinese-built fighter. According to the report, it would also be the type’s third international operator, after Pakistan and Uzbekistan. Asked about the timeline, Indonesian Air Force Chief of Staff Marshal Mohamad Tonny Harjono did not give details, telling the public to “just wait” for the aircraft to arrive. Questions remain over numbers and variant Despite the reported timeline, key details of the acquisition remain unclear. The report said Jakarta confirmed an order for 42 J-10CE fighters in October 2025, backed by an approved budget of about $9 billion. However, Malaysian outlet Defence Security Asia (DSA) noted that Defense Ministry information chief Brigadier General Rico Ricardo Sirait denied the existence of a 42-aircraft, $9 billion agreement in May 2026. Figures of 12, 24 and 42 aircraft have all been reported at different times, and Indonesia has yet to publicly confirm a final number. It is also unclear whether Jakarta will receive new J-10CE export aircraft or second-hand J-10Bs from Chinese air force stocks. According to DSA, one foreign loan plan earmarked up to $1.6 billion for J-10B fighters. The J-10CE is fitted with an active electronically scanned array (AESA) radar and can carry China’s PL-15E long-range air-to-air missile, while the older J-10B uses a passive electronically scanned array radar and an earlier generation of weapons. Part of a crowded fighter plan Indonesia first confirmed its interest in the J-10 in October 2025, when Defense Minister Sjafrie Sjamsoeddin said the jets would be flying over Jakarta soon. The Chinese fighters would join one of Asia’s most varied combat fleets. Indonesia ordered 42 Dassault Rafales in 2022, with deliveries now underway, and signed a deal with Turkey for 48 KAAN fifth-generation fighters in 2025. It also remains a partner, in a reduced role, in South Korea’s KF-21 program. Its current fleet includes US-built F-16s and Russian-made Su-27 and Su-30 fighters. Analysts have warned that operating aircraft from so many suppliers will add to the burden of maintenance, training and logistics, with each type requiring its own spare parts, weapons and support infrastructure. The purchase would also mark the first time a Chinese fighter has entered service with a Southeast Asian air force, in line with Indonesia’s long-standing “free and active” foreign policy locally known as bebas aktif of not aligning with any single power bloc. title: Georgian singer alleges police assaulted him and pressured him to confess to crimes
body: Georgian singer Misho Sulukhia has alleged that law enforcement officers assaulted him, took his phone, and pressured him to confess to a crime he says he had nothing to do with. Sulukhia made the allegations in a social media post on Wednesday, saying the incident took place on Wednesday evening near Tbilisi’s Lisi Lake. Georgia’s Interior Ministry disputed his account, saying police had stopped Sulukhia while he was walking suspiciously in a wooded area near Lisi and that he had refused to obey a lawful police order before fleeing the scene. Sulukhia said that several young men in civilian clothes stopped the taxi he was travelling in and pulled him out. ‘They told me they were law enforcement officers, but none of them identified themselves or showed me identification documents. They hid their identities. They surrounded me and restricted my movement. This continued for more than an hour’, he wrote. Sulukhia alleged that the men took his phone and physically assaulted him. He also said they prevented him from answering calls from his 87-year-old grandmother. He claimed officers found no illegal substances on him and that he was sober. ‘They broke my phone screen. I was asking for help, but nobody could hear me. I asked them to return my phone, but [it was] in vain’, Sulukhia wrote. He further alleged that he saw the group preparing an object wrapped in black electrical tape before he escaped. Sulukhia also claimed that the taxi driver who had been transporting him remained in custody and was being pressured to confess to involvement in a group crime. The driver has not yet made a public comment and the MIA has also not yet addressed Sulukhia’s claims concerning the taxi driver. ‘They were offering me a scenario in which I would confess to a crime I have nothing to do with’, he wrote. After escaping, Sulukhia said he managed to publish his post on Facebook with the help of several strangers. He also asked for his phone and personal data to be protected and said he wanted to speak with the Public Defender. The Public Defender’s Office told OC Media that it was aware of the case and would contact the relevant agency. It also said it was ready to meet Sulukhia. Georgia’s Interior Ministry told OC Media that Sulukhia, who had previously been convicted of a drug-related offence and is currently serving a suspended sentence, was stopped by law enforcement officers for a check after he was observed moving suspiciously on foot in a wooded area near Lisi. The ministry said Sulukhia did not obey a lawful police order, dropped his mobile phone on the ground, and fled the scene. ‘Law enforcement officers sealed the mobile phone in accordance with established procedures, as well as the bank card placed inside the phone case’, the Ministry said. It added that administrative proceedings had been launched under article 173 of Georgia’s administrative offences code, which concerns disobeying a lawful order from a law enforcement officer. Sulukhia responded to the ministry’s statement on social media, again disputing that he had been involved in any crime. He questioned the ministry’s claim that he had been in the woods in a taxi and asked what had happened to the driver. Sulukhia also alleged that police had previously pressured him into giving a confession in 2025 and accused them of fabricating evidence in that case. He didn’t specify what the confession was. The original post in which Sulukhia made the allegations was no longer publicly available on Thursday morning. OC Media has contacted Sulukhia for additional details.

title: VSA and VIA crown 18th anniversary with full scholarships for three brilliant students
body: Virtual Security Africa Limited (VSA) and Virtual Infosec Africa Limited (VIA) have awarded full scholarships to three brilliant but needy students to pursue university education at the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST). The scholarships cover tuition and approved university fees, as well as accommodation and living expenses for the duration of their programmes. The award crowns the Company’s 18th anniversary celebrations, which began with its sponsorship of a complete upgrade of the CCTV surveillance system at Mamprobi Hospital to strengthen the safety of patients, mothers and newborns. For 18 years, VSA and VIA have secured what matters in Ghana’s electronic and cybersecurity space. Today, that commitment extends to the nation’s future leaders. The 2026/27 scholars with their families, management and staff of VSA and VIA, and coordinators from the St. Peter’s SHS Old Boys Association The beneficiaries are; Amankwah Alexander Bempong, Medicine. From Akim Oda, Alexander completed St. Peter’s Senior High School in 2023, achieving 8A1s in his WASSCE, but despite his ambition, he remained at home due to financial hardship. His wait is over: he begins medical studies at KNUST in the 2026/27 academic year. His journey highlights the difference timely support can make in the life of a young person with the ability and ambition to succeed. Reuben Ayitey, Electrical Engineering. From Nsawam, Reuben completed St. Peter’s Senior High School in 2026 with 7A1s and proceeds directly to KNUST in the 2026/27 academic year. Emmanuel Nsowaa Junior, Computer Engineering. From Asempaneye in the Western North Region, Emmanuel completed St. Peter’s Senior High School in 2026 with 7A1s and begins his studies at KNUST in the 2026/27 academic year. Presenting the awards, the Chief Executive Officer, Emmanuel Asiedu, urged the scholars to study diligently, remember their beginnings, and grow into leaders who will one day extend the same support to others. He assured them of the Company’s continued support throughout their journey under the Scheme. The Executive General Manager, Mrs Salomey Armoo, added: “As a company, we protect what matters. Through this Scheme, we are investing in what matters most: people, and the future they will build for a better Ghana.” On behalf of the families, Mrs Comfort Gomado, mother of Reuben Ayitey, expressed profound appreciation to the Chief Executive Officer, the Board, and the Management of VSA and VIA for investing in their children’s future. The initiative reflects VSA and VIA’s commitment to supporting education and contributing to the development of young people and communities. As the three scholars begin their university journey, the Company remains hopeful that this opportunity will not only transform their individual lives but also enable them to make meaningful contributions to Ghana in the years ahead.

title: Death toll in Kramatorsk strike rises to 30, public transport suspended in Kramatorsk, Sloviansk – official
body:
The death toll from a Russian strike on Kramatorsk has risen to 30 people, with another 18 injured, and due to a sharp deterioration in the security situation, public transport operations in Kramatorsk and Slovyansk will be suspended, Head of the Donetsk Regional Military Administration Vadym Filashkin reports.
According to him, the Russian military targeted civilians, striking a street where passenger transport was moving.
"Russians are purposefully hitting civilians. For them, a bus with passengers is an attractive target precisely because as many people as possible can be killed with a single strike... Another proof is today's tragedy in Kramatorsk, where the Russians killed 30 people and injured 18 more in an instant," Filashkin noted.
In response to the escalating threat, the head of the regional military administration has ordered the Kramatorsk and Slovyansk city military administrations to suspend all public transport services.
"Under such circumstances, we have no right to risk the lives of passengers and drivers. The safety of the residents of Kramatorsk and Slovyansk comes above all else now," the Regional Military Administration head emphasized, urging citizens to treat the mandatory restriction with understanding as a critical safety measure.
Earlier on Thursday, Russian forces struck Kramatorsk with a UMPB D-30 SN bomb, hitting a street carrying scheduled passenger buses and an apartment building.

title: Missile Defense Agency to get new range ship from Hanwha Philly Shipyard in 2030
body: Called the Missile Range Instrumentation Vessel, or MRIV, the ship will be built with TOTE Services as vessel construction manager. Once finished, it will be handed to the Maritime Administration (MARAD), which will run it for the agency. Taking over from Pacific Tracker and Pacific Collector The new ships will be about 525 feet long. They are due to replace Pacific Tracker, built in 1965, and Pacific Collector, built in 1970, which handle missile range instrumentation missions today. The yard is not starting from scratch: the MRIV is based on the National Security Multi-Mission Vessel, or NSMV, which it is already building under TOTE Services’ management. The two will share a hull design and substantial commonality, which the company said cuts design and construction risk. Hanwha Philly Shipyard said it will use its active production line, its established U.S. supply chain and the workforce and expertise built up on the NSMV program. Four government bodies are involved: the Department of Transportation, MARAD, the Department of War and the Missile Defense Agency. Shipbuilding base in focus “The MRIV program demonstrates the value of maintaining an active, capable U.S. shipbuilding industrial base, one that can take proven platforms, experienced people and established production infrastructure and put them to work for new and increasingly important missions,” said David Kim, CEO of Hanwha Philly Shipyard. “We are honored to continue our partnership with TOTE Services and to build these vessels here in Philadelphia.” The company said the award comes as Washington puts fresh emphasis on shoring up the maritime industrial base and expanding domestic shipbuilding capacity. It did not say how much the contract is worth.

title: Flydubai captain hailed in UAE, India for saving 174 lives during hijacking attempt
body:
Dubai, Oct 8. Flydubai captain Smit Machchhar, who is credited with saving the lives of 174 passengers during an attempted hijacking of his aircraft, is being widely honoured in both the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and India as he continues to recover in hospital from head injuries sustained in the attack.



Dubai Crown Prince Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed Al Maktoum visited Machchhar in hospital and praised his courage and determination. Images and video from the meeting showed the injured pilot with his head bandaged and receiving oxygen support.

Sheikh Hamdan said Machchhar had demonstrated “the highest levels of courage and responsibility for human life”, adding that the UAE leadership valued his actions and was proud that he was part of the Flydubai team and the country’s story.



The Indian-born pilot has also received widespread recognition in India, with political and religious figures praising his bravery. The ruling Bharatiya Janata Party has released posters portraying Machchhar alongside Hindu deity Hanuman, drawing a parallel with the deity’s traditional association with courage and strength.

Machchhar also spoke to Prime Minister Narendra Modi from his hospital bed on Friday, recounting how he fought to regain control of the situation despite suffering multiple injuries during the attack.

Speaking to Modi, the captain said he initially found himself fighting for his own survival after sustaining several injuries and collapsing to the floor. He eventually realised that unless he acted quickly, the situation could turn into a major tragedy.

“I had so many injuries, but I told myself that I had to get up and act,” Machchhar recalled.

He said he then summoned the strength to get back on his feet and open the cockpit door, a decision that proved critical in preventing the situation from escalating further.

The incident has since brought widespread attention to the captain’s presence of mind and determination under extreme circumstances, with tributes pouring in from both sides of the India-UAE relationship.

title: Ship transit through Strait of Hormuz falls to two-month low — Reuters
body:
LONDON, October 8. /TASS/. Commercial vessel transit through the Strait of Hormuz fell to its lowest level since July 23 early this week amid a new wave of escalating attacks on tankers, Reuters reported, citing data from analytics firm Kpler.
On Tuesday, only seven commercial vessels passed through the strait. Average daily oil transit figures in late September dropped by 27% from the month's peak levels, settling at around 10 million barrels per day. This volume represents approximately 74% of the shipping levels recorded prior to the launch of the US and Israeli military operation against Iran in late February this year.
Kpler analysts noted that some tankers continue to navigate the Strait of Hormuz with their transponders turned off. Furthermore, oil exports from the Red Sea and Gulf of Oman coasts have more than doubled during the conflict, reaching 6.7 million barrels per day, largely making up for the losses from reduced transit through the Strait of Hormuz.
The US and Israel launched military operations against Iran on February 28. In June, Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding providing for an immediate cessation of hostilities on all fronts, including Lebanon. However, on the night of July 8, the US resumed its large-scale strikes on Iran, accusing it of violating the terms of the agreement regarding the Strait of Hormuz.

title: U.S. lenders sue Jeff Rath for $112M, allege he concealed First Nation firing
body:
Two American litigation funders allege Alberta separatist leader Jeffrey Rath and his firm made “false, inaccurate, and misleading” representations to keep receiving millions of dollars to finance two First Nations lawsuits against Ottawa – even after his firm had been fired and replaced.
The allegations are contained in a lawsuit filed last Thursday by Delaware-based Diriba Investments and Western Springs Investments, which are seeking $112.56 million from Rath and his professional corporation, RathPC.
None of the allegations have been proven in court.
The lawsuit was filed the same day a judge rejected Rath’s bid to release nearly $800,000 in frozen funds in a separate civil action involving another First Nation. Rath said he needed the money for legal fees and personal expenses – much of it related to his North American horse-racing “hobby.”
Justice Lorena Harris refused the request, finding Rath had not provided a full accounting of his assets and financial position despite being ordered to do so.
“I have no confidence that the Rath Applicants’ disclosure is complete, transparent or reliable,” Harris wrote.
The lenders’ lawsuit escalates a dispute first reported by Global News last month. In late September, they signalled in court documents their intent to call in the debt, then estimated at nearly $109 million. On Thursday, they followed through by suing Rath and RathPC, alleging he had failed for more than two months to provide requested financial statements and an accounting of proceeds from the litigation they financed.
Rath has not yet filed a statement of defence. He declined to answer questions from Global News, saying: “Please stop bothering me.”
The lawsuit adds to a growing web of litigation involving Rath, his firm and several First Nations. Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation and Tallcree First Nation are separately suing Rath over millions of dollars allegedly withdrawn without consent from settlement trusts he administered.
Litigation funding is a large and controversial industry, primarily in the U.S. It allows outside investors to finance the cost of pursuing legal cases in exchange for a share of the compensation if the case is won.
Rath built a career suing the federal government on behalf of First Nations, securing treaty and claims settlements worth tens of millions of dollars. The American lenders’ lawsuit provides a rare window into how large-scale litigation funding operates, and, for the first time, how much Rath was underwritten for two of at least a dozen First Nations claims he has pursued.
The funders allege they signed a contract with Rath’s professional corporation, RathPC, in December 2018. They agreed to advance $25 million in five payments to finance individual lawsuits filed by the Thunderchild and Moosomin First Nations of Saskatchewan.
Rath initially received $10 million in 2018, followed by three more payments of $3.75 million between 2021 and 2023. The lenders did not advance a fifth payment of $3.75 million because Rath allegedly failed to obtain specialized life insurance.
The lawsuit alleges that Thunderchild fired Rath and his firm in September 2019, but that Rath did not disclose the termination to the investors until November 2024. They also allege Rath failed to disclose Law Society of Alberta proceedings in which he admitted misconduct arising from his representation of Thunderchild after it had fired him. He was ordered to pay $10,000 in costs.
The investors say they would not have continued advancing him money had they known Rath had been fired, accusing him of making representations “knowing them to be false, or recklessly, without regard for their truth or falsity,” to keep the money coming in.
The contract entitled the lenders to annual returns of between 25 and 35 per cent, compounded annually, plus five per cent of net proceeds. The lawsuit does not provide a calculation showing how they arrived at the $112.56 million they now claim is owed.
They claim broad contractual rights over proceeds from RathPC’s First Nations claims and other legal work covered by the financing agreement.
They are now suing RathPC, and Rath personally, for the entire amount because of what they allege are multiple breaches of their contract, including dissipating assets and failing to report money the lenders claim should have been paid to them.
After other law firms took over the Thunderchild and Moosomin cases and secured large settlements, Rath sued both First Nations for a total of nearly $60 million in contingency fees he claims he is owed.
Thunderchild and Moosomin deny Rath’s allegations.
The American lenders claim their contract allows them to “step in” and take over those claims, with any money recovered going to the lenders rather than Rath.
They also say the Tallcree litigation revealed that RathPC is pursuing another $90 million in unpaid fees from concluded settlements – claims they say had never been fully disclosed to them.
The Tallcree case started the domino fall of legal actions that has stricken Rath’s legal business, and he alleges, his personal finances.
In 2017, RathPC collected an $11.5-million contingency fee after Tallcree settled a $57.6-million claim with Ottawa. The firm then became trustee of the funds held for beneficiaries, including minors.
A judge later found Rath’s fee unreasonable and ordered $8.5 million returned to the trust. Tallcree alleges RathPC subsequently withdrew the same amount from the trust rather than distributing it to beneficiaries. Tallcree and Sturgeon Lake, whose trust Rath also administered, allege millions were improperly withdrawn from their trusts, including roughly $6 million and $12 million, respectively, in disputed administration and legal fees.
Rath denied misappropriating the money. He said he obtained legal advice before setting an annual administration fee of three per cent of the trusts’ declining balances.
In support, he filed statements of account itemizing fees charged to the Tallcree Trust, along with timesheets detailing work performed by lawyers at his firm. He maintains the litigation is part of a years-long effort by Tallcree’s leadership to gain control of its trust.
“No funds were misappropriated from the Trust by myself or any lawyer or staff at Rath & Company or RathPC,” he said in court records.
In July, the court froze Rath and his firm’s assets under an interim Mareva injunction and appointed an investigative receiver to trace the disputed funds. The American lenders have applied to have the receiver also act on their behalf.
The receiver has since alleged the $8.5-million refund was funded in part with $11.5 million transferred from the Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation Trust – another of Rath’s clients.
On Sept. 4, Tallcree escalated its case against Rath and RathPC again, seeking a $15-million judgment and broader powers for the receiver to recover disputed trust assets and enforce the court’s decision. The application is scheduled to be heard Oct. 29 and 30.
The court order allows the receiver to release some funds to Rath for approved legal and living expenses. He has been previously granted $135,000.
On Sept. 11, Rath sought nearly another $800,000 in frozen funds — including $350,000 for legal fees and almost $280,000 in horse-racing bills.
Tallcree opposed the release, arguing the $3 million held by Rath’s former lawyers could be traced to the disputed $8.5-million Tallcree refund. Banking records show both sums passed through the same RathPC account, where the reimbursement had earlier been used to buy $8 million in bullion and issue a $500,000 draft to Rath. Court records show that eight months later, the same account sent $3 million to his former lawyers.
In an affidavit supporting his application, Rath said the Mareva injunction and receivership placed the future of his law firm “at serious risk.” He said two lawyers have resigned and the orders jeopardized its efforts to recover $90 million in outstanding fees – the same fees the American lenders now say may fall under their agreement.
Rath called the Mareva order “entirely unjustified” and “not supported by any evidence,” while arguing the scope of the asset freeze and receivership was “hindering my ability to live.”
He has also filed four appeals challenging the trustee removal, the asset freeze, the receivership and the receiver’s access to the firm’s records.
She stressed, however, that she was not finding Rath or his firm actually possessed undisclosed assets.
During an acrimonious Sept. 17 cross-examination, Tallcree lawyer Matthew Sammon challenged Rath and RathPC’s financial disclosures under the Mareva order.
Rath’s disclosure omitted three boats, a numbered company that had recently received $2.92 million from RathPC and at least four Royal Bank of Canada accounts, Sammon alleged. RathPC’s disclosure identified none of its bank or investment accounts.
The receiver has since identified at least 31 accounts held by Rath and RathPC across nine financial institutions, according to its second report filed Sept. 14. Rath denied deliberately concealing assets, saying omissions were mistakes.
As part of his application for the frozen funds, Rath submitted a stack of invoices that cover farriers, veterinarians, trainers, hauling, boarding and racing in Alberta and several American states, as well as phone and life insurance bills. He also sought $150,000 in unspecified future expenses.
Several of the invoices analysed by Global News were already long overdue when the Mareva order was imposed – at least three horse-related invoices were more than a year old.
Harris found the expenses were not “ordinary, necessary living expenses.”
Rath had also not listed the horses in his court-ordered disclosure of worldwide assets.
Under repeated questioning, Rath said that he did not know exactly how many horses he owned, eventually estimating “more than 10 and less than 30.” He said he omitted them because he considered them “liabilities,” not assets, and described horse racing as a hobby rather than a business.
According to Equibase, the official database for Thoroughbred racing in North America, horses listed under Rath’s owner profile have earned nearly $500,000 in Quarter Horse and Thoroughbred races since 2021. Those figures represent gross race earnings, before expenses such as payments to jockeys and trainers.
Rath also acknowledged that RathPC had paid horse-related expenses, describing them as “expenditures accruing to my personal account.” Banking records put to him included a $54,192 RathPC cheque to a prominent Alberta horse trainer, which Rath confirmed was a horse-racing expense, and a $117,401 payment to Keeneland Thoroughbred Sales that he said appeared to have been to buy a horse.
Rath rejected the suggestion he improperly diverted First Nations trust money to fund his horse racing. When asked how the horse expenses were accounted for in his law firm’s books, however, he said he did not know. “You would have to ask my accountant,” Rath testified.
An email included in Rath’s own court materials shows his accounting manager telling staff on Sept. 1: “We are no longer allowed to pay any of Jeff’s personal horse related expenses.”
As of Jan. 1, 2022, the Law Society of Alberta barred lawyers from using their general accounts “for any banking purpose not related to the law firm’s business or to conduct personal banking.”
The examination grew heated, with Rath threatening several times to end it, and his lawyer objecting more than 100 times to questions that he argued went beyond the scope of Rath’s application for living and legal expenses.
Asked to confirm information in records attached to his affidavit, Rath repeatedly said the documents “speak for themselves.”
When pressed, he replied: “You can call them whatever you want, sir. You can name them Fido, for all I’m concerned.”

title: Press review: EU tightens Russia sanctions while Germany eyes return to Russian energy
body:
MOSCOW, October 8. /TASS/. The EU is rushing to transform itself into an analogue of NATO ahead of elections in Germany and France, as the bloc gives the go-ahead for yet another sanctions package on Russia. Meanwhile, Germany is seeking to resume energy purchases from Russia. These stories topped Thursday's newspaper headlines across Russia.
The European Commission (EC) is seeking an analogue of the North Atlantic Treaty’s Article 4 before a potential change of power in France and Germany, the European Parliament told Izvestia. In NATO’s documents, this clause provides for urgent consultations between allies in case of threats. Brussels fears that Eurosceptics who oppose the strengthening of the EC's powers will come to power in Paris and Berlin. Until this happens, European bureaucratic hawks are trying to shape the EU's foreign policy on NATO, the Russian Foreign Ministry noted.
On October 6, the EC proposed abolishing the right of veto in the adoption of sanctions and the admission of new EU members. Last month, EC President Ursula von der Leyen proposed an Emergency Security Protocol as a mechanism for consultations in the event of threats. The EC is hurrying to do this ahead of the change of power in France and Germany in 2027, Fernand Kartheiser, a member of the European Parliament from Luxembourg, told Izvestia. "She [von der Leyen] is probably looking to act so swiftly precisely before major government changes take place in Germany and France. <...> Public opinion will hardly embrace such a scenario easily, given the current atmosphere of hysteria in Europe. Such an EU-wide step will be perceived by the general public as dangerous," he said.
Kartheiser’s fellow MEP from Bulgaria, Petar Volgin, expressed a similar opinion as he said "the process of the EU transforming into NATO 2.0 has already begun." At the same time, the mass vote for the Alternative for Germany (AfD) shows that more people are increasingly distancing themselves categorically from the militarist policy course being imposed by Brussels and a number of European governments, the politician noted.
Germany should hold a regular parliamentary election in 2029, but the idea of an early dissolution of the Bundestag is becoming increasingly popular. The opposition AfD party is polling at over 30%, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has a record-low approval rating. There is political ground already for a snap vote, said political analyst Yegor Belyachkov, who specializes in German studies.
The initiatives put forward by the EU will be considered as soon as the EU leaders’ summit in mid-October, Thierry Mariani, a French MEP, told Izvestia. "The European Commission is in a hurry, and I guess I know why. It is aware that Marine Le Pen could win in France. Therefore, it is seeking to settle things now, before the French express their opinion," the politician noted.
According to Vladislav Maslennikov, director of the Russian Foreign Ministry’s Department of European Affairs, "the hawkish wing of the European bureaucracy has long been trying to shape the EU’s insufficiently anti-Russian, as they view it, foreign policy on NATO." "Any incident, be it an unidentified drone or problems with Internet connectivity, is automatically blamed on Russia’s 'hybrid' activities," the diplomat explained. "Clearly, all this hysteria does not at least contribute to ensuring stability and security on our western borders," he argued.
The European Union has adopted a 22nd package of anti-Russian sanctions as EU ambassadors approved it on Wednesday. The measure will soon have to be approved by the EU Council before it comes into effect. This time around, more than 1,500 legal entities and individuals, mostly with ties to the Russian defense industry and the manufacturing of dual-use items, were sanctioned. The blacklisted individuals will be barred from entering the EU, while all their assets on EU soil will be frozen.
Even as the 22nd package does not include any brand-new trade and economic restrictions, it will be the largest ever in terms of the number of Russian individuals and legal entities blacklisted simultaneously, a source in Brussels told TASS. So far, approximately 3,000 individuals and legal entities have been added to the EU’s sanctions list.
The latest sanctions package does not include any industry-wide restrictions as it introduces personal, albeit broad, sanctions, Artyom Sokolov, a senior research fellow at the MGIMO International Studies Institute, told Vedomosti. Tellingly enough, Brussels no longer weighs any deeper sanctions as their effect, including on the EU itself, will be ineffective. Moreover, the fact that the 22nd package is being imposed proves that the range of restrictions has been exhausted. As regards restrictions against Russian lawmakers, numerous Duma members are under sanctions already, but symbolically, recent statements from the EU’s diplomacy chief Kaja Kallas represent a step toward further escalation, as the most vital institution of Russia’s legislative power may be sanctioned, the expert said. According to him, even as the EU lacks any coherent reasons for doing so, Russia has already grown used to similar measures by Brussels, while the State Duma’s functioning will be unaffected by the new restrictions.
The 22nd package of anti-Russian sanctions marks a shift from sectoral restrictions to targeted measures, Alexander Kamkin, an associate professor at the Financial University under the Russian Government, believes. Furthermore, it shows that the EU has exhausted the potential of economic sanctions as it mostly focuses on restrictions on Russia’s military-industrial sector--a move that European governments use to frighten their electorate with--while the imposition of sanctions against the defense industry effectively acknowledges Russia’s achievements in this sphere, the expert argued. Restrictions against Duma members, including those representing Russia’s new regions, were an expected move, Kamkin said, given the EU’s staunchly negative stance toward all government officials in those regions. However, it would be incorrect to suggest that these sanctions could in any way disrupt the State Duma’s operations, Kamkin concluded.
Amid underground storage facilities being depleted and gas prices soaring in Europe, Germany sees a clearer benefit in resuming Russian energy purchases. European sources told Izvestia that Germany is interested in restoring energy supplies from Russia. "It would be much better if we could buy energy from Russia again as we did 10 to 20 years ago," one of the sources argued.
Another source said Germany is ready to import gas via the surviving leg of Nord Stream 2: such a scenario would be possible if the conflict in Ukraine ends, he added. "There are all necessary technical capabilities to restart the pipeline, even as no meaningful negotiations are currently being conducted with the Russian side," he noted.
Unless Germany reopens the surviving leg of Nord Stream 2, it will fail to keep its industries operating as before, Steffen Kotre, a member of the German parliament from AfD, told Izvestia. "Germany will no longer be able to run its industrial base the way it was five or six years ago," the parliamentarian pointed out. "We can already see that happening. Falling gas and electricity consumption is clearly due solely to the shutdown of industrial facilities that have become too expensive. Say, in the field of ammonia fertilizers and, of course, everywhere in the chemical industry. Production is being moved to where it is cheaper. And large enterprises are expanding their sites abroad," he added.
In these circumstances, AfD which is leading nationwide opinion polls is openly calling for the repair of Nord Stream. The issue will be discussed at a potential Russia-US-Germany business forum in 2027 as announced by Kirill Dmitriev, head of the Russian Direct Investment Fund and Special Presidential Envoy for Economic Cooperation with Foreign Countries, Kotre said.
A full ban on Russian LNG imports from early January may trigger a price spike, and in winter, gas prices on exchanges could easily rise above $1,000 per 1,000 cubic meters and remain there through the season, Igor Yushkov, an expert at the Financial University under the Russian Government and the National Energy Security Fund, told Izvestia. Only two unlikely scenarios - a warm winter or the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and stabilization of exports from Qatar - could prevent prices from rising, he said.
In the longer term, the market balance will be achieved not due to the influx of new gas, but through a further decline in its consumption in Europe, as was already the case in 2021-2023, the expert argued. On the one hand, the wave of deindustrialization suits Brussels, helping it to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. On the other hand, amid economic problems, Eurosceptics and forces demanding the return of energy resources from Russia are gaining political weight. The Czech SPD party, for one, which came to power in 2025, advocates for the resumption of purchases of Russian oil and gas. Slovakia too is actively seeking to maintain energy imports from Russia.
Rospotrebnadzor is completing a range of preventive measures in the Irkutsk Region, Irkutsk and Shelekhov after a female employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute died on the night of October 1, Russia’s sanitary watchdog said on October 7. No health implications related to infectious diseases have been found, it added. Earlier, Rospotrebnadzor said she had been diagnosed with pneumonia of undetermined etiology. A broader probe did not reveal any microorganisms associated with her professional activities either. The World Health Organization (WHO) is monitoring the situation, its Director-General Tedros Ghebreyesus wrote on X.
Plague, including pneumonic, is much less contagious than COVID-19, Andrey Pozdnyakov, an infectious disease expert at Invitro, explained to Vedomosti. It is caused by the bacteria Yersinia pestis that does not spread over large distances, he said. Consequently, the contagiousness index for plague is significantly lower than that of coronavirus, influenza, or measles, and airborne transmission requires fairly close contact with an infected person. For example, during a recent outbreak of pneumonic plague in Uganda, only two out of 20 people who had been in contact with patients contracted the disease from two deceased patients, Pozdnyakov recalled.
The experience of COVID-19 is not applicable here, Denis Volkov, a sociologist, agreed: back then, a large-scale epidemic broke out, and general lockdowns and disruptions to the usual way of life aggravated people’s anxiety. And the anxiety triggered by the pandemic almost completely subsided two to three years later, he noted.
Panic against the backdrop of news about the situation in the Irkutsk Region started to set in amid coverage in foreign media outlets, Nikolay Bespalov, director for development at RNC Pharma think tank, said. He described the information in overseas media as far-fetched.
US President Donald Trump, too, commented on the situation as he announced a phone call "very soon" with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin. His offer of assistance was not the only response from Washington as the US Department of State and other federal agencies said they were monitoring the situation. The State Department, for one, advised US citizens in Russia to leave the country immediately on its page on X as it also urged others not to travel there, issuing a Level 4 advisory. The European Union expressed similar concerns, while the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs said it was in contact with Moscow over the epidemiological situation.
Pavel Koshkin, a senior researcher at the US and Canadian Studies Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences, sees a deliberate attempt to smear Russia behind the latest US rhetoric. According to him, Washington has responded to the uproar surrounding the Irkutsk incident amid a lack of information. Statements from the United States have been primarily precautionary, preventive, and formal, he said.
Seven months into the Middle East crisis, global oil inventories have almost been exhausted, Bloomberg quoted CEO of the world’s largest oil company, Saudi Aramco, Amin Nasser as saying at the Energy Intelligence Forum in London. A similar assessment was voiced by the chief executive of the world’s largest oil trader, Vitol Group, Russel Hardy. According to him, Western nations have virtually exhausted their available oil reserves amid geopolitical conflicts in the Middle East. This and a shortage of available tankers may push global prices to $200 per barrel, he argued.
Global oil inventories currently stand at less than 6 billion barrels. However, Nasser noted, only 10% of this amount is actually available, with the remainder serving as the operational minimum required for the infrastructure to function. Commercial stocks include crude held in pipelines, tankers, port tanks, depots, storage facilities, and oil refineries. These volumes are in constant use and must be constantly replenished, but withdrawal rates currently outpace replenishment levels.
Besides, Oleg Zhirnov, investment and capital market partner at Kept, told Rossiyskaya Gazeta, a substantial amount of oil in pipelines or storage facilities is needed for those to operate properly. And it cannot be tapped because a minimum fill level must be maintained, he added.
Approximately 1 billion barrels of oil have been drawn from global stockpiles since the Middle East conflict erupted, according to data from the International Energy Agency (IEA). In August, the average rate of drawdown was 3.1 million bpd, and this pace could rise to 4-5 million bpd in the fall, a trend also fueled by the escalating global diesel crisis. If the drawdown of oil reserves were halted, there would be an immediate supply shortfall for consumers, and prices could inevitably surge, potentially reaching $150 per barrel or even higher, Zhirnov warned.
Vladimir Chernov, an analyst at Freedom Global, agrees that Brent prices could rise to $150 per barrel if supplies from stockpiles stop and the oil deficit of several million barrels per day persists. Further large-scale disruptions could trigger brief spikes to even higher levels, and the risk of prices climbing to $200 cannot be ruled out, though that would already represent a crisis scenario, he concluded.
