title: Ukraine built ballistic missile in just over two years
body: A Ukrainian manufacturer took a ballistic missile from nothing to its first combat launch in a little over two years, which its chief executive said is the fastest development of such a weapon on record, the Apex Europe conference in London heard on Wednesday. Iryna Terekh of Fire Point was asked from the floor how a company that did not exist before 2023 had managed it, and she began with what she had measured it against. She said: “It is the fastest ever track record for developing a ballistic missile. I made my analysis. The average timeline for such a development is 15 years, the maximum was 30 years, and the minimum before that was seven years.” “The first flight that we conducted was the last day of February, and three days ago it was the first combat flight. In between there were almost 20 different launches where we tested different things,” she said, adding that the whole programme had taken a little more than two years. She was candid that the weapon is nowhere near finished, and set out her own measure for when it will be. “I have the rule that the first 100 launches of whatever you are launching, you can still be considered as polishing the product, establishing it to a more mature zone,” she said, describing Ukrainian manufacturing as living permanently at technology readiness level seven because insisting on level nine would cost too much money and too much time. The method she credited is a document the company wrote at the outset and persuaded the government to sign. “We made a critical decision at the very beginning. We made a book. This book is called the Album of Acceptable Deviations, and we wrote it to present it to our military acceptance unit, who does the quality assurance before it is transported to the unit,” she said. Inside it, everything that affects the quality of flight goes in one half and everything that does not goes in the other. The acceptance authority signed it, and quality assurance inspections are now carried out against it, which allows the company to use cheap parts wherever the engineering case for an expensive one is absent. Not everybody who saw the result approved of how it had been built. “Once I saw some critics on the internet, oh my God, you’re using off-the-shelf solutions to fix some of the parts of your missile, your missile should be embarrassed to fly with this detail,” she said. “But this is exactly what cost-effective innovation is. If you are looking for a fancy, high-tech, ideal solution, it will be extremely expensive. You have to be able to be embarrassed as an engineer, but be proud as a Ukrainian providing a good product for a fair price.” Her description of how the missile was built owes nothing to conventional aerospace practice. “We did it as it’s called in Ukraine from shit and sticks from the beginning, made it fly first and then polished,” she said. A change in Ukrainian law is what made a company like hers possible in the first place. A bill signed in 2023 set out how new defence products, initially drones, are certified, tested, accepted into the army and procured, with the process published openly. “They took the industry from the shadows and made this a very clear, visible opportunity for any startup that want to try themselves,” she said, and the result is that a drone or a missile can now be certified within about six weeks without dropping safety requirements. The effect on who builds weapons in Ukraine has been considerable, and she put it in a single sentence. “My generation, for example, who used to build startups, are now building arsenals,” she said. The post Ukraine built ballistic missile in just over two years first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: 2027: Your PVC is not for sale — Obi Media Office to Nigerians
body: By Henry Umoru ABUJA- AHEAD of next year’s elections, the media office of the Presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC, Peter Obi has urged Nigerians to remain remain vigilant against anyone offering money or inducements in exchange for their votes, advising the people not to sell their Permanent Voters Cards, PVC or participation in any scheme aimed at compromising the electoral process. According to the Peter Obi Media Office, POMR, it said it has become aware of the ruling All Progressives Congress, APC’s strategy of exploiting the poverty in the land—poverty they have created by offering large sums of money to people in exchange for their PVCs. The POMR said to Nigerians that their PVC is not for sale, vote is not for sale, their future is not for sale, just as it urged them to collect their PVC, keep it secure and do not hand it over to anyone, pleading with the people to reject bribes and report any suspected electoral manipulation to the proper authorities, adding that on election day, they should turn out, vote according to their conscience, protect theirbballot, and insist that their votes count. A statement signed on Thursday by the Spokesman of POMR, Idris Zekeri on Thursday read, “Exactly 100 days left to election day, we urge Nigerians to remain vigilant against anyone offering money or inducements in exchange for your vote, your PVC, or participation in any scheme aimed at compromising the electoral process. “Reports from some states indicate that some state governors, who have nothing positive to show to persuade their citizens, including civil servants, are collecting their PVCs in exchange for the payment of their legitimate salaries and allowances. “Your PVC is not for sale. Your vote is not for sale. Your future is not for sale. Collect your PVC. Keep it secure. Do not hand it over to anyone. Reject bribes and report any suspected electoral manipulation to the proper authorities. “On election day, turn out, vote according to your conscience, protect your ballot, and insist that your vote counts. “Hold your PVC firmly. Use it responsibly. Defend your vote legally. Defend your democracy and create a new Nigeria that will be possible and OK.” The post 2027: Your PVC is not for sale — Obi Media Office to Nigerians appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: CCT can’t account for funds spent on 52 contracts – Audit report
body:
The Code of Conduct Tribunal (CCT) cannot account for 52 contracts awarded as far back as 2023, according to the latest report of the Office of the Auditor-General of the Federation (OAuGF) on the finances of federal institutions.
The report, which recently became public after its submission to the National Assembly in July, said the CCT awarded the 52 contracts worth N52.2 million in 2023 but failed to send procurement records to the Bureau of Public Procurement as required by law.
The case is part of three clusters of transactions the auditor general flagged in CCT’s records for the 2024 financial year. Two other issues relate to N46.86 million payments made by the CCT without prepayment audit and the total of N9.38 million paid without relevant supporting documents.
These queried transactions summed up to N108.46 million, which the auditor general’s office said the CCT has yet to satisfactorily account for.
On 17 July, the Auditor-General of the Federation (AuGF) Shaakaa Chira submitted the report, covering the finances of federal institutions for 2024, to the National Assembly as mandated by the Nigerian constitution.
The document is titled the Auditor General of the Federation’s Annual Report on Non-Compliance/Internal Control Weaknesses in Ministries, Departments and Agencies of the Federal Government of Nigeria for 2024.
Volume II of the report dedicates a section to judiciary institutions, under which it presented its findings on the failures in the expenditures of the CCT, Nigeria’s foremost anti-corruption court concerned with cases of ethical and assets declaration breaches brought against public officers suspected to have violated the code of conduct stipulated in the nation’s constitution.
Although the report covered 2024 expenditures of the CCT and other federal institutions, the tribunal’s 52 contracts examined in the document were awarded in 2023 when the immediate past chairman Danladi Umar was heading the tribuna.
Mr Umar, who chaired the tribunal for 13 years, from 2011 to 2024, was succeeded by Mainasara Kogo in July 2024.
But the audit report did not specify under whose leadership payments were made for the 52 contracts.
Also, the nature of the contracts was not disclosed in the report. It is unclear if the omission was a result of CCT’s failure to provide necessary records or the auditor general’s decision to leave out the information.
However, the audit report said there was no evidence that the tribunal transmitted the procurement documents regarding the 52 contracts it awarded in 2023 to the Bureau of Public Procurement (BPP), as required by Section 16(13) of the Public Procurement Act 2007.
The provision requires procuring entities to send copies of their procurement records to the BPP within three months after the end of the financial year.
It states, “Copies of all procurement records shall be transmitted to the Bureau not later than 3 months after the end of the financial year and shall show:
“(a) information identifying the procuring entity and the contractors;
“(b) the date of the contract award, and
“(c) the value of the contract, and (d) the detailed records of the procurement proceeding.”
But as of July when the auditor-general submitted its report to the National Assembly, the CCT had yet to submit the relevant records concerning the 52 contracts.
“There was no evidence of transmitting procurement documents to the Bureau of Public Procurement (BPP) who is the statutory body to validate and authenticate due process adhered to during contracts pre-qualification process, and awards concluded,” the auditor general’s report read.
It attributed the “anomalies” to “weaknesses in the internal control system at the Code of Conduct Tribunal, Abuja.”
The report, which is Nigeria’s most sweeping audit examination of public institutions’ finances, also stated that the systemic failure poses risks of loss of public funds and the award of contracts to ineligible contractors.
The OAuGF received CCT’s explanation for its failure to provide the BBP with the necessary procurement records but treated it as an unsatisfactory excuse.
According to the auditor-general, the CCT management had blamed the failure on the officer responsible for preparing and transmitting the procurement records.
“The management regrets the action of the scheduled officer,” the management of the CCT said in its response cited in the audit report, adding that the new officer would comply with the requirement in future.
Rejecting the excuse, however, the audit report tagged it “unsatisfactory” and maintained that its findings remained valid until the recommended actions were implemented.
The report recommended that the CCT chairman be compelled to account for the N52.2 million expended on the 52 contracts to the Public Accounts Committees of the National Assembly.
It also recommended that the money should be recovered and remitted to the treasury, with evidence of the remittance forwarded to the committees. This recommendation did not indicate if the money should still be recovered if the CCT is able to account for its use.
However, it further recommended sanctions for gross misconduct if the tribunal failed to comply.
The audit also found that the tribunal paid 29 vouchers worth N46,862,450 without the required prepayment audit.
The report said the vouchers and their supporting documents were not checked by the CCT’s Internal Audit Department before payment.
The requirement is contained in the Financial Regulations 2009, which requires government institutions to check payment vouchers and their supporting documents before releasing public funds.
The process, known as pre-payment audit, is designed to ensure that payments are properly authorised (100 per cent) and supported by the required documents.
The auditor general said the failure exposed the funds to the risk of misappropriation and diversion.
Although the CCT management acknowledged the importance of internal controls and promised that all payment vouchers would be pre-audited before future payments, the auditor general rejected the response as unsatisfactory and retained the finding.
It recommended that the CCT be made to account for the expenses to the National Assembly’s Public Accounts Committees, recover and remit the amount to the Treasury and submit evidence of the remittance.
It also recommended sanctions for irregular payments if the tribunal failed to comply.
The audit further found that nine payment vouchers worth N9,385,000 for works and the procurement of goods and services lacked relevant supporting documents.
The missing documents included approvals, invoices or receipts, letters of award, Store Receipt Vouchers, Store Issue Vouchers and project files.
The auditor general said the failure created risks of diversion and loss of public funds.
The CCT management said documents had been attached to the payment vouchers but acknowledged that they were not sufficient or convincing enough to substantiate the expenditure during the audit.
The auditor general again rejected the response as unsatisfactory.
It recommended that the CCT account to the Public Accounts Committees for the N9.385 million, recover and remit the amount to the treasury and provide evidence of the remittance.
The report also recommended sanctions for irregular payments if the tribunal failed to comply.
The latest findings come on the heels of a previous audit report flagging contract payments the CCT failed to account for.
In its 2019 audit report, the auditor general’s office disclosed that the tribunal could not account for over N400 million it paid to contractors for various projects during the financial year.
Similar to its findings in its latest report on CCT’s expenditures, the OAuGF revealed in its 2019 report (released in 2021) that the tribunal could not provide any documents to justify the contract expenditures.
The tribunal’s chief registrar, Abdulmalik Shuaibu, told PREMIUM TIMES in December 2021 , during coverage of the auditor-general’s disclosures, that the “issue has since been sorted out”.
But no such indication appeared in the auditor-general’s 2019 report, released two years after the questioned transactions.
CCT is a federal body established under the Nigerian constitution and the Code of Conduct Bureau and Tribunal Act to adjudicate on alleged breaches of the code of conduct for public officers.
Its functions include receiving complaints of non-compliance from the Code of Conduct Bureau (CCB).
Such complaints include non-declaration or false declaration of assets, abuse of office, bribery and conflicts of interest involving public officers, and other breaches codified in the code of conduct for public officers.
The tribunal conducts trials of public officers based on the complaints of breaches of the code brought by the CCB and imposing the punishments prescribed by law.
Appeals from its decisions go to the Court of Appeal and, ultimately, the Supreme Court.
Among the high profile personalities who have faced trial at the tribunal is President Bola Tinubu, who was charged over his activities as former governor of Lagos state. Others include former Chief Justice of Nigeria Walte Onnoghen and former Senate President Bukola Saraki, who stood trial on charges covering his time as former governor of Kwara State and as senate president.

title: Sybiha: Lithuania allocates EUR 15 mln more for Ukraine's recovery, resilience via World Bank, EIB
body:
Lithuania has allocated an additional EUR 15 million for Ukraine's recovery and resilience enhancement projects, with the funds to be channeled through the mechanisms of the World Bank and the European Investment Bank (EIB), Minister of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine Andrii Sybiha reported on Wednesday evening.

"Thank you, Lithuania, for another €15 million for Ukraine’s recovery and resilience through the World Bank and EIB mechanisms. Lithuania has stood with Ukraine from the very beginning and continues to back this support with practical decisions that help our country recover and grow stronger," Sybiha wrote on the social media platform X.

title: Ex-employee of German Marshall Fund given suspended sentence as part of Azerbaijan’s ‘NGO case’
body: Azerbaijan-based consultant for the German Marshall Fund Mehriban Rahimli has been sentenced to seven years and six months in prison in the country’s ongoing ‘NGO case’. The court ruled the sentence will be suspended and she will be on probation for four years. Rahimli was convicted on Wednesday under the criminal code for the legalisation of property obtained through crime in a significant amount, as well as concerning abuse of official powers and official forgery. Rahimili has argued that the payments she received from the US-based German Marshall Fund were salaries under a service contract, not grants, and that she had no role in managing or transferring the organisation’s funds. Her case is part of a broader prosecution of around 15 civil society representatives in Azerbaijan; all have rejected the charges as unfounded and politically motivated. Azerbaijan NGO crackdown continues, as 15th person sentenced While Baku claims the case concerned financial crime, human rights groups say it is part of a general crackdown on NGOs. OC Media Rafig Shahbazov In her final statement before the verdict, Rahimli said she had received a monthly salary during her 18 years of work for the organisation and paid tax. ‘How can this be presented as a grant? Can you receive a grant every month for 18 years?’, she said in court, according to RFE/RL’s Azerbaijani service. Her lawyer, Javad Javadov, argued that even if the payments were considered grants, failure to register a grant agreement would constitute an administrative offence rather than a criminal offence. The prosecution had requested an eight-year prison sentence for Rahimli, also with a suspended term. Azerbaijani NGOs in exile call on Council of Europe to take measures against Baku The NGO calculated that 68% of the court’s judgments concerning Azerbaijan were not implemented. OC Media Rafig Shahbazov Rahimli previously told the court that she had worked as the German Marshall Fund’s Azerbaijan consultant since November 2008. Her role, she said, involved providing initial assessments of project proposals submitted to the organisation’s Bucharest office. She said she knew most of the detained civil society representatives and had professional contacts with them during her work. So far around, 15 civil society representatives have reportedly been prosecuted so far as part of the broader ‘NGO case’. Social worker Zamin Zaki was sentenced to seven years and six months in prison by the Baku Court of Grave Crimes on 11 March. On 1 July, the Baku Court of Appeal reduced his sentence by three months. On 7 September, another defendant in the case, Ahmad Mammadzade, was sentenced to seven years and six months in prison. His sentence was suspended with a two-year probation period. Azerbaijani economist Galib Bayramov given suspended sentence as part of NGO crackdown Bayramov is the brother of Gubad Ibadoghlu, another prominent economist who was detained in 2023. OC Media Rafig Shahbazov On 7 September, another defendant in the case, Ahmad Mammadzade, was sentenced to seven years and six months in prison. His sentence was suspended with a two-year probation period. Others detained include Bashir Suleymanli, head of the Institute for Citizens’ Rights; Mammad Alpay, director of the Election Monitoring Alliance; Asaf Ahmadov, head of the Ganja Regional Community Centre; and activist Zamin Zaki. On 17 June, the Ganja Court of Serious Crimes sentenced Ahmadov to eight years in prison.

title: 2027: Obidient movement still with me – Rhodes-Vivour
body: The African Democratic Congress (ADC) governorship candidate in Lagos State, Gbadebo Rhodes-Vivour, has said the Obidient movement remains with him despite contesting the 2027 governorship election on a different political platform from Peter Obi. Rhodes-Vivour stated this during an interview on BlackBox , a talk show hosted by Rufai Oseni. Asked whether the Peter Obi wave would still work for him in the coming election now that he and the former Anambra State governor are no longer on the same political platform, Rhodes-Vivour said the values that attracted members of the movement to him remained part of his political identity. “I feel that the qualities that movement adopted or welcomed, those are qualities that I still carry. Those are qualities that have been consistent with. I’ve been with them in the trenches,” he said. Rhodes-Vivour said his relationship with members of the movement had continued beyond the 2023 election, adding that he had maintained personal relationships with them and remained involved in their affairs. “Even after the election, the aftermath of the election, hospital bills that were paid, and all of that. We build personal relationships across board,” he said. According to him, his consistency and continued identification with the values of the movement would make him a trusted figure among its members despite the political differences between him and Obi. “I feel that as far as I carry those qualities and those characteristics are still with me, and I’ve shown consistency, I believe that I’m a trusted figure,” Rhodes-Vivour said. “I believe that when push comes to shove, that movement is still with me. That’s just the honest truth.” In the 2023 election, Rhodes-Vivour contested the Lagos governorship election on the platform of the Labour Party while Obi ran for president on the same platform. Obi won Lagos in the presidential election, while Rhodes-Vivour came second in the governorship poll behind incumbent Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu. Ahead of the 2027 election, however, Obi has moved from the Labour Party to the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), where Funso Doherty is the party’s governorship candidate in Lagos. Rhodes-Vivour is seeking the Lagos governorship ticket under the ADC, whose presidential candidate is former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar. He recently said he had no issues with Obi, adding that Atiku remained his presidential candidate for the 2027 election. The post 2027: Obidient movement still with me – Rhodes-Vivour appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Russian forces strike bus in Kramatorsk: 12 killed, 14 injured
body:
According to Ukrinform, the Kramatorsk City Council announced this on Telegram .
"Russian forces struck a passenger bus in Kramatorsk. The vehicle was carrying passengers at the time of the attack," the statement said.
According to preliminary information, at least 12 people were killed and another 13 were injured in the strike.
Information about the consequences of the attack is being clarified.
The National Police added that at around 10:00, Russian forces struck Kramatorsk with a UMPB D-30 SN guided bomb. The munition hit one of the city's streets, where two passenger buses were traveling at the time.
As of 11:30, 12 people were known to have been killed and 14 injured.
An investigative team, paramedics, patrol police officers, State Emergency Service personnel and other specialized services are working at the site of the attack.
Two buses and an apartment building were damaged.
On October 7, a Russian drone struck a bus in Sloviansk, injuring the driver. In another part of the city, a drone struck a car, killing a man and injuring a woman.

title: Court grants alleged fake JAMB registrar N50m bail
body: The Federal High Court in Abuja has admitted Mr Arinze Nwogba to a N50 million bail with two sureties in like sum. Justice Salim Ibrahim, in a ruling on Thursday , held that the offence Nwogba allegedly committed was a bailable one, which is not a capital offence for which the punishment is death. “From the affidavit of the defendant/applicant, he has alluded to the fact that he will not jump bail and he will present himself for trial which is the hallmark in bail application.” The judge, who said granting bail is discretionary power of the court, admitted him to N50 million bail with two sureties. He ordered that one of the sureties must be a civil servant, not less than Grade Level 14 in the federal civil service. According to Justice Ibrahim, each of the sureties must be resident within the Federal Capital Territory, Abuja, with one of the sureties residing either at Asokoro, Maitama, or Guzape. The judge ordered that each of the sureties must depose to affidavit of means. He ruled that each of the sureties shall submit his or her tax clearance certificate for the past two years. The judge directed the defendant and the sureties to submit their photocopies of their national identification slips. He also directed the registrar of the court to verify the bail documents and issue a report and sign, as well as the prosecution. Justice Ibrahim, therefore, ordered Nwogba to remain in Kuje Correctional Centre pending the perfection of the bail terms. He adjourned the matter until Oct. 19 for commencement of his trial. The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that the Inspector-General (I-G) of Police is prosecuting Nwogba for allegedly impersonating to be Prof. Segun Aina, Registrar, Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board (JAMB). The I-G, in the six-count charge marked: FHC/ABJ/CR/612/2026, sued Nwogba as sole defendant The defendant, who was arraigned on Friday by the police, was remanded in Kuje Correctional Centre pending the hearing of his bail application filed by his lawyer. In one of the counts, Nwogba, who resides at No. 16,Emeka Egbe by Roban Stores, Abakaliki in Ebonyi, and others now at large, were alleged to have fraudulently impersonated the JAMB Registrar, Prof. Aina. The defendant was alleged to have registered his picture on whatsapp profile and true caller on telephone number: 08139433155 with the intent to gain financial advantage to himself. The offence is said to be contrary to and punishable under Section 22(3)(a)(b) & (4) of the Cybercrimes (Prohibition, Prevention, Etc) Act, 2015 Amended 2024. The prosecution, in the brief fact of the case, said a petition was written and submitted to the I-G by the board registrar concerning the activities of some suspected criminal gangs who fraudulently registered and are using the telephone number and pictures of Prof. Aina without his knowledge and authority. The police alleged that these individuals were using the identity of the JAMB registrar to deceive unsuspecting members of the public. It said they equally went on LinkedIn and published the said number where they directed unsuspecting innocent citizens to contact them only through WhatsApp using the number. “The investigating team decided to engage the fraudsters directly using the WhatsApp number he advertised on LinkedIn. “The fraudsters who already used the image of JAMB registrar as profile pictures both on WhatsApp and truecaller in order to deceive innocent Nigerians informed his victims that he wants to offer them a contract and he has obtained necessary approvals from the Minister of Education.” According to the document, in his text message on WhatsApp, he stated, “Federal Ministry of Education Abuja has approved the supply of 200 units of HP laptops to us as a part of our digitization programs.” It alleged that the acclaimed JAMB registrar also sent the contact of his personal assistant as (07017626031) who he described as Dr Stephen Igwe and who would be representing him to make all the arrangement for the award of the contract. “He equally directed that his PA will send an account number where he directed the sum of N900,000 to be paid for handshake. “He equally ordered the payment of another three (3) million naira into the account for the permanent secretary and Minister of Education. “He equally sent an access bank account number 1572799985 with account name: EDEH CHIMEZIE BENEDICT. “He requested for an initial deposit of nine hundred thousand naira (N900,000) to be used to bribe the members of staff at the minister’s office,” the prosecution alleged, among others. It said Nwogba whose operational name was Dr. Stephen Igwe was subsequently arrested in Abakallki in Ebonyi. “He confessed that the account details belong to his late nephew who died in April 2026 and was buried on July 31. “He admitted that he actually forwarded the details of the account to his cousin, one NNABUIFE NWEKPA ‘M’ of Onitsha, Anambra State to use for the fraudulent activity. “The said NNABUIFE NWEKPA (the acclaimed fake JAMB Registrar) is now on the run and currently at large. “Serious efforts are being intensified to arrest the fleeing suspect,” the police told the court. (NAN) The post Court grants alleged fake JAMB registrar N50m bail appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: BRICS membership won’t transform Ghana’s economy without domestic reforms – Bokpin
body: Professor of Finance at the University of Ghana Business School and Economist, Professor Godfred Bokpin, has cautioned that Ghana’s decision to join the BRICS economic bloc should not be seen as a substitute for the domestic reforms needed to transform the country’s economy. He said that while joining BRICS could provide Ghana with new economic opportunities and strengthen its engagement with emerging global economies, membership alone would not automatically improve the country’s economic fortunes. Speaking on the Joy FM Super Morning Show on Thursday, October 8, during a discussion on Ghana’s quest to join BRICS, Prof Bokpin said the country must continue to focus on managing its economy competitively regardless of its international affiliations. “I think we should just bear in mind that BRICS is still evolving, even within the original founding members, in terms of the framework, where exactly this is heading towards, and all of that. And so there are quite a lot of nuances that would have to be ironed out of that,” he said. He said that Ghana should not expect BRICS membership to deliver an immediate economic transformation. “But it is good to also say that merely joining BRICS necessarily does not transform your economy overnight, or even over a 15-year period,” Prof Bokpin said. “It is not a substitute for what you have to do in managing your own economy competitively, and all of that.” Despite the caution, Prof Bokpin said he supported the government’s intention to join the bloc, arguing that the global economic balance was shifting and Ghana needed to position itself accordingly. “If I look at it from an economic perspective, it’s a good move that the government plans to join BRICS. That is where the world is heading towards, and that is a fact,” he said. He pointed to the growing economic influence of BRICS, saying the combined economic output of its member countries had become significant enough to rival or exceed that of traditional Western-led economic groupings. “If you look at the commanding position of BRICS within the global economy today, the combined GDP of BRICS, especially across the 11 founding members, and then also the 10 partner countries today, actually exceeds the GDP of the G7 that we used to know,” he said. According to Prof Bokpin, the bloc now accounts for a substantial share of the global economy and its members have strong growth prospects. “It accounts for almost 40 percent of the global GDP. The BRICS member countries have higher growth potential today than literally any other economic bloc you can think about,” he said. Prof Bokpin said long-term economic projections also pointed to a growing role for BRICS countries in the global economy. He noted that China was projected to remain the world’s largest economy by 2050, while the United States was expected to rank second. “It may interest you to know that by 2050, three out of the top five big economies globally will all be BRICS members,” he said. “Three out of the top five by 2050.” He said the projected shift in the global economic order also helped explain some of the growing tensions between the United States and China. “In fact, by 2050, China will be number one, and the U.S. will be number two in terms of the global economic order,” Prof Bokpin said. “You can understand this also gives you a perspective as to the tension between the U.S. and China and all of that. It’s all playing out carefully within the global geopolitics, and how the global order, some want it to be rewritten in a certain way, and all of that.” Looking further ahead, Prof Bokpin said economic projections for 2075 showed an even stronger presence of BRICS countries among the world’s largest economies. He said four of the five largest economies by then were projected to be BRICS members. “And that said, it’s also important to look at the world economic projections. By 2075, the top five economies in the world measured in USD, actually there will only be one that will not be a BRICS member,” he said. “So four out of the top five big economies by 2075, four of them will be BRICS members.” He also highlighted Nigeria’s projected position among the world’s largest economies, saying the country’s growth could be driven by its private sector and major entrepreneurs. “In fact, the projection is that by 2075, Nigeria will be in the top five. And this may surprise a lot of people,” he said. Prof Bokpin, however, cautioned against treating such projections as certainties. “I’m not asking people to put on faith to believe in this,” he said, explaining that the projection was based partly on the potential of Nigeria’s large entrepreneurs and the transformation of its private sector. He said that the country’s economic transformation would not depend solely on government but could also be driven by major Nigerian entrepreneurs. “The understanding is that if you look at what Nigeria is doing, the transformation is going to come from big Nigerian entrepreneurs, billionaires, who have decided, and it’s not just Aliko Dangote,” he said. Prof Bokpin said Ghana was already experiencing the growing influence of emerging economies through its expanding economic relationship with China, even without being a member of BRICS. He said Ghana needed to recognise the changing patterns of global trade and position itself accordingly. “So if you put all of that together, and we have no joint business, actually, but today, China has literally taken over our markets, whether you like it or not, right?” he said. “So the traffic today is within the Ghana-China corridor as compared to our traditional import-oriented countries and all of that. So we need to just look at all of that.” He said these developments provided an economic basis for Ghana to consider closer engagement with BRICS, although other considerations would also have to be examined. “So in terms of where the world is moving towards and all of that, it will look to me that it’s a good decision. Of course, I’m looking at it purely from an economics perspective,” Prof Bokpin said. “There may be geopolitical, there may be other considerations that would also have to come to the table and all of that.” Prof Bokpin, however, cautioned that Ghana should not expect BRICS membership to resolve its economic challenges. “So specifically for Ghana, I think that merely joining BRICS would not necessarily transform our economy,” he said.

title: BIR: Sara Duterte received income from Davao City in 2023 when she was VP
body: MANILA, Philippines – Records of the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) show that Vice President Sara Duterte received income from Davao City Hall in 2023, when she was already the country’s second highest official, potentially in violation of the Constitution . At the Vice President’s impeachment trial on Thursday, October 8, BIR Office of the Commissioner chief of staff Anne Loraine Garcia-Marquez confirmed that Duterte signed a BIR 2316 Form with the Davao City government, listed as employer back in 2023. “VP Sara Duterte received compensation income from the city government of Davao in 2023,” Garcia-Marquez told the impeachment court. The witness did not disclose the actual amount, but private prosecutor Jay Tolosa later told the press it was P82,000. Play Video Duterte’s brother Sebastian has been Davao City mayor since 2022. Article VII, Section 6 of the Constitution states that the President and the Vice President “shall not receive during their tenure any other emolument from the Government or any other source.” Article VII, Section 13 also prohibits the Vice President from practicing any other profession during one’s tenure. The direct examination of the BIR witness by prosecutor Erwin Matib is part of the prosecution’s bigger case of Duterte’s alleged unexplained wealth. The prosecution alleged that this is tantamount to betrayal of public trust and culpable violation of the Constitution. Garcia-Marquez’s testimony also established that Duterte and her husband, Manases “Mans” Carpio, registered a net income of only P85.34 million after taxes from 2007 to 2025. “This cannot explain the increase in her net worth, which reached P98 million as of VP Sara’s latest SALN,” Matib said. – Rappler.com

title: Adil enters Central Equatoria governorship race as SPLM candidate
body: Former Central Equatoria State Governor Emmanuel Adil Anthony said on Thursday he had accepted the ruling Sudan People’s Liberation Movement’s (SPLM) nomination to contest for governor in elections scheduled for December. Adil made the announcement at the SPLM national secretariat in Juba, saying his nomination followed consultations with party members across the state’s six counties and Wonduruba Administrative Payam. “I have accepted their call to be the SPLM nominee for the general election for the position of chairman and governor of Central Equatoria State,” Adil said. Adil has served two separate periods as governor of Central Equatoria State. He was first appointed in June 2020 and served until May 2024, when President Salva Kiir Mayardit removed him from office. He returned to the post in November 2025 and remained governor until Sept. 22, when Kiir dissolved the country’s transitional government and the state governments ahead of the planned elections. Before serving as governor of Central Equatoria, Adil was governor of the defunct Yei River State from 2018 until 2020, when South Sudan reverted from 32 states to its current 10-state system. Yei River State was subsequently incorporated into Central Equatoria. In accepting the SPLM nomination, Adil said he would work with party members to develop a programme focused on unity, peace and development in Central Equatoria. He also called on SPLM members seeking the governorship to remain united and compete on the basis of their policies and ideas. Adil said the programme would be based on the SPLM manifesto and would seek to address the needs of people in Central Equatoria State. He thanked supporters who attended the declaration, saying their presence demonstrated support for the SPLM, himself and President Salva Kiir, who leads the party. The post Adil enters Central Equatoria governorship race as SPLM candidate appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

title: Senate OKs bill banning those below 18 years old from social media
body: MANILA, Philippines – The Senate on Thursday, October 8, passed Senate Bill No. 2424 or the Safe Media Access and Responsible Technology for Kids in Digital Spaces (SMART KIDS) Act that seeks to restrict anyone under 18 years old from accessing social media or other “high-risk digital services.” The bill, sponsored by Senator Robin Padilla, compels the suspension, restriction, disabling or removal of any account that has been reasonably determined as being owned or used by a minor. It will also prevent minors from creating accounts, with platforms required to have effective age-assurance measures. The approved version of the bill increased the scope of the restrictions to cover those under 18 years old, up from the original version’s proposed 16-year-old threshold. The Senate’s debate over social media regulation for the youth vacillated between an outright ban versus a tiered “age-appropriate” framework, which would offer different levels of restrictions by age. The former appeared to have won that debate, with the country facing a spate of deadly school shootings and other violent incidents, attributed partly to certain influences within online environments or effects of social media use to young users. Of the 17 senators who voted, Risa Hontiveros was the lone dissenting vote. Hontiveros explained her vote in a Facebook post, citing some examples about how young Filipinos can use social media platforms to voice out abuses, to connect with family living abroad, or to do a side hustle. She said: “Social media has become a space where young people build and maintain their connections with their friends, communities, families, and loved ones. An outright ban strips away these very connections that have become so important in their day-to-day lives.” She said that a complete ban for all individuals under 18 years old fails to take into consideration that, for example, a 13-year-old and a 15-year-old have different levels of development. A tiered implementation for social media access may be more apt, Hontiveros argued. “For younger adolescents, we should require stronger default privacy and data settings, tighter restrictions on adult contact, limits on targeted advertising and profiling, and stronger parental and educational safeguards. As adolescents mature, maaari natin silang unti-unting bigyan ng awtonomiya habang nananatili ang mga proteksyon laban sa abuso at eksploytasyon, at harmful content,” she said. (As adolescents mature, we can slowly give them autonomy while protections remain from abuse, exploitation and harmful content.) Senator Hontiveros authored the SAGIP BATA Act , which criminalizes the “sadistic extortion” of children or the use of threats, manipulation, blackmail, deception and similar means to compel children into grave, cruel, degrading or harmful acts. It has also been approved by the Senate. Senator Joel Villanueva welcomed the bill’s passing: “ Bilang mga magulang, ginagawa natin ang lahat upang maging ligtas ang ating mga anak sa bahay at sa paaralan. Dapat umabot ang proteksiyong iyon hanggang sa kanilang mga screen, kung saan nang dahil sa isang click maaari silang malantad sa pambubully, karahasan, at pagsasamantala .” (As parents, we do everything we can to keep our children safe at home and in school. That protection should extend to their screens, where a single click can expose them to bullying, violence, and exploitation.) The SMART KIDS Act will now be transmitted to the House for its own review. – Rappler.com Must Read Social media regulation in PH: Experts push for ‘age-appropriate’ framework for minors

title: Russian drone strike on Kyiv store building kills 2, injures 2 – mayor
body:
As a result of a Russian unmanned aerial vehicle strike hitting a four-story store building in Kyiv's Solomiyansky district, two people were killed and two others sustained injuries, Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko reports.

"In the Solomiyansky district, a fire in the 4-story store building hit by Russian UAV has been localized. The bodies of 2 dead were discovered, along with two injured," the mayor wrote on his Telegram channel.

The search and rescue operation is currently underway, Klitschko added.

title: Government spends GH¢917m on No-Fees-Stress policy for 321,807 students
body: The government has so far spent GH¢917 million to support students under the No-Fees-Stress Policy, the Minister of Education, Haruna Iddrisu, has revealed. He said the money, which covered 321,807 students, was paid from budgetary support from the Consolidated Fund. The GH¢917 million is a direct flow from the Ministry of Finance from the Consolidated Fund as part of the Ministry of Education’s budgetary support. Other releases have gone to the Students Loan Trust Fund (SLTF) from the Ghana Education Trust Fund (GETFund) for the students loan disbursement,” he said. Mr Iddrisu said this yesterday at a Stakeholder Engagement on the Implementation of the No-Fees-Stress Initiative at Dawu in the Eastern Region. The programme, organised by the SLTF, is on the theme: “Strengthening No-Fees-Stress Implementation through Institutional Partnerships for Inclusive, Equitable and Sustainable Student Financing”. It is being attended by representatives of Vice-Chancellors Ghana, Vice-Chancellors of Technical Universities, Principals of Colleges of Education, Federation of Ghana Medical Students, civil society organisations (CSOs) and the Parliamentary Select Committee on Education. Mr Iddrisu said in the 2024 National Democratic Congress Resetting Ghana Manifesto, President John Mahama committed to reducing the financial burden of tertiary education students and their families. In pursuit of that, he said on July 4, 2025, that commitment was translated into action with the launch of the No-Fees-Stress Initiative, implemented by the SLTF and adequately funded by the GetFund. “Let me commend the management and leadership of the Students Loan Trust Fund, and the leadership and management of GetFund, for keeping this dream a reality under President Mahama’s Reset. “Arguably, and statistically, GH¢917 million has so far been spent to support students under the No-Fee-Stress, covering a student population of 321,807 students,” he emphasised. He admitted that one of the major challenges of the No-Fee-Stress Policy had to do with timely releases of budgetary allocation for its implementation. He, therefore, stressed the need to ensure the timely release of funds in order not to defeat the purpose of the initiative. “So regardless of your financial standing, regardless of your geographical location, regardless of the status of your parents, an eligible Ghanaian who qualifies to access higher education must be supported by government to access higher education,” he said. He indicated that the No-Fees-Stress Policy had come to stay. Mr Iddrisu said the government had opened up the student loan trust support to students studying Law for the first time in many years and demystified legal education. “We will do the same for medical education in the coming years. As a true value of human capital development, maybe we should now accept that human capital development be construed as a strategic investment requirement of every government and sufficient budgetary allocation provided for it,” he said. Presenting an update on the No-Fees-Stress Policy, the Chief Executive Officer of the SLTF, Dr Saajida Shiraz, said the fund was a statutory agency under the Ministry of Education with a mandate to provide financial resources for the benefit of tertiary students and in the last one-and-a-half years, “we are contending with what we describe as an expanded mandate to the introduction of the government’s flagship No-Fees-Stress Policy, which is a transformational initiative by President John Dramani Mahama to ensure that financial circumstance would not become a barrier to accessing tertiary education for any Ghanaian student”. The No-Fees-Stress Policy, she said, had five sub-components — no academic fee policy, the free tertiary education for persons with disabilities, students loan plus initiative, enhanced traditional loan scheme with higher loan amounts and reduced interest rates, and digitalisation of the system to make it easier to access loans. “So for this academic year, we came up with a very creative financing model to deal with the urgent funding needs of students now trying to access special education, and it is that funding we are calling bridge funding,” she said. The Board Chairperson of the SLTF, Cynthia Amerley Amarteifio, said under the reset agenda of the President, access, inclusion, affordability and sustainability to tertiary education had been placed at the centre of the government’s education agenda.

title: Putin to communicate with all participants in CIS summit in Turkmenistan — Kremlin
body:
MOSCOW, October 8. /TASS/. Russian President Vladimir Putin will meet with all participants in the upcoming Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) summit in Turkmenistan on the sidelines of the event, Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
"The president will have [an opportunity] to communicate with all other participants on the sidelines of these cultural events tonight. It means that he will talk with almost everyone on the sidelines," he said.
Peskov pointed out that Putin was scheduled to hold a number of working meetings on the sidelines of the CIS summit and the Caspian Environmental Summit. In particular, he will meet with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Friday.

title: Tytan scales up low cost drone interceptor production
body: The Munich air defence company Tytan Technologies is building manufacturing capacity to turn out as many as three thousand low cost drone interceptors a month, a company representative told the Apex Europe conference in London on Wednesday. Kerry Hoppe, who handles business development and government affairs at Tytan, was speaking on the European Industrial Leadership Panel and described the economics that led to the company being founded in 2023. She said: “Our founders came up with the idea of drone interceptors in 2023, attending a hackathon in Kyiv against Shaheds. Because if you remember, that was a time where we were still combating Shaheds and Cannons with missiles, with IRIS-T, with Patriot, spending about a million per shot to defend from a system that costs maybe 30, 40, 50 grand, so a massive economic imbalance in a time where we’re seeing a massive proliferation of the subsonic layer.” That imbalance has driven a good deal of European procurement thinking since, and it remains the central argument for cheap interceptors over exquisite ones. Tytan now has three interceptor types aimed at different threats in the NATO Class I and Class II categories, with locations in Munich, Berlin and Kyiv. Ms Hoppe said the hardware is sophisticated but is not what distinguishes the company. “Really, what sets us apart is the high degree of autonomy that enables operators to operate multiple systems at the same time and doesn’t require manual steering,” she said. Close contact with Ukrainian units shapes the development cycle, and she named the third army corps, the National Guard of Ukraine and the Ukrainian air force as sources of constant feedback that is taken back into prototyping in Munich. Getting from prototypes to volume is the part she described as most exciting and most difficult. “It’s one thing producing very innovative prototypes and keeping that iteration speed when you’re making prototypes, but really keeping that speed on your scaling, because really no system is a real solution if it’s not available en masse,” she said. “So we’re building up our manufacturing to produce up to 3,000 per month, and keeping that speed using smart manufacturing technologies while always iterating on software.” She was careful to place the company inside a wider architecture, and warned against anybody claiming to have solved the problem alone. “We always think of air defence as a multi-layer approach,” she said. “Any company saying we have all the solutions, we’re able to combat all the levels of threats that we’re seeing at the moment, it’s just not possible. It takes all kinds of different industry players, all kinds of systems, and we want to be part of that multi-layered approach.” Ms Hoppe also noted the collaborative tone of the session itself, observing that the companies on the stage compete in the same market but are working towards the same European resilience, which she described as uplifting. The post Tytan scales up low cost drone interceptor production first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: World Space Week 2026: SPACE VOYAGE AND EXPLORATION
body:
By R Anil Kumar

Bengaluru, Oct 7, 2026. Sixty-nine years ago this day, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first satellite to orbit Earth, opening the Space Age and setting off a race with the United States.



Ten years later, on October 10, 1967, the Outer Space Treaty came into force.

In 1999, the United Nations started observing World Space Week – from October 4 to 10 – to celebrate the contribution of space technology for the benefit of humanity. Space agencies around the world hold stargazing nights, science classes, exhibitions and talks by astronauts and scientists.

Today, more than 80 countries have put satellites into orbit, and people from over 50 of those have travelled to space.

How many space travellers have been women, and what comes next for human spaceflight.

The First Human in Space: Yuri Gagarin 



On April 12, 1961, Soviet astronaut Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space.

On board the Vostok 1 spacecraft, he completed one orbit of Earth at about 27,400km/h (17,025mph) during a 108-minute flight. He later ejected from the spacecraft and landed by parachute.

The mission demonstrated that humans could survive launch, weightlessness and re-entry, giving the Soviet Union a major early victory in the Cold War Space Race.

Six years later, on October 10, 1967, the Outer Space Treaty entered into force. Signed by the US, the United Kingdom and the Soviet Union, it established that space should be explored and used peacefully and that no country could claim it as territory.

In less than two years, NASA’s Apollo 11 mission landed the first humans on the moon. On July 20, 1969, Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on its surface.

Where does the Space Begin

There is no single agreed boundary for where space begins: most international bodies use the Karman line, 100km (62 miles) above Earth, while the US military, NASA and the Federal Aviation Administration count anyone who flies above 80km (50 miles).

Either way, it is closer than it sounds: if Earth were the size of an apple, space would begin about as far from the surface as the thickness of its skin.

Countries that have sent People to Space 

By the Karman line measure, at least 746 people from 52 countries have travelled to space, including professional astronauts and paying tourists.

Some hold dual nationality, and some flew for countries that no longer exist, such as the Soviet Union.

Two countries still dominate the list. The US has sent 369 people to space, and the Soviet Union and Russia have sent 138 combined. China, the third country to launch people on its own rockets, has sent 29.

One In Seven Space Traveller is a Woman



Space remains a male-dominated frontier. Science fiction may be full of women commanding starships, but of the 746 people who have travelled to space, only 112, or 15 percent, have been women, about one in seven.

Soviet astronaut Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman to travel to space in June 1963. The US did not follow for another 20 years, until Sally Ride flew in June 1983.

The share of women is rising, though, largely because of commercial flights. More than half of the women who have flown since 2020 went up as paying passengers or guests on Blue Origin’s suborbital rocket.

The typical Space Traveller is 40

Most people who have flown to space were in their 30s or 40s on their first flight, which together account for 85 percent. The median age is 40. Commercial flights have widened that range.

The youngest traveller, Oliver Daemen, was 18 when he flew in 2021. The oldest, Ed Dwight, was 90 years and eight months old when he flew in 2024, about two months older than William Shatner had been on his flight three years earlier.

The Future of Human Space Flight

In April 2026, the Artemis II crew flew around the moon and reached about 406,771km (252,756 miles) from Earth, breaking the distance record set by Apollo 13 in 1970.

Next is Artemis III in 2027, a rehearsal in Earth orbit to test docking with lunar landers built by SpaceX and Blue Origin. NASA is targeting 2028 for Artemis IV, which aims to land astronauts near the moon’s south pole, the first crewed landing since 1972.

India plans its first crewed Gaganyaan flight in 2027, making it the fourth country to launch people on its own rocket. China aims to land astronauts on the moon around 2030.

title: New maritime incident reported north of Qatar
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 08 (MNA) – The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations reported a maritime incident north of Qatar.
The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) announced it had received a report of an incident 51 miles north of the city of Al-Shamal in Qatar.
Several casualties have been reported after a tanker sailing off the north coast of Qatar was struck by multiple projectiles, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency has announced.
The vessel was hit by several projectiles 94km (58 miles) north of Madinat ash Shamal, UKMTO said on Wednesday. The incident comes as the maritime agency reported a recent rise in attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.
UKMTO did not say how many people were killed or injured in this latest attack, adding that authorities were investigating. It did not specify the origin of the ship.

title: Robot boat found its way in the Solent without satellites
body: An uncrewed surface vessel has been navigated through the Solent using radar matched against stored maps of the coastline rather than satellite positioning, in a demonstration staged for the Ministry of Defence, according to Voyant Innovations . The Liverpool University spin-out ran its software aboard a Kraken K3 Scout autonomous vessel, using particle filter algorithms to compare live radar imagery against pre-existing reference maps of the terrain and work out the vessel’s position without any help from the Global Navigation Satellite System. The demonstration took place on 5 October and forms part of a wider departmental effort to find resilient technologies for operating where satellite navigation is contested or congested. James Norwood, chief executive of Voyant, said: “Reliable navigation is fundamental to maritime operations, yet we are entering an era where access to GNSS can no longer be assumed. Working alongside Kraken and the Ministry of Defence, we have demonstrated a practical capability that supports the safe and effective deployment of autonomous maritime systems in challenging operational conditions. “The demonstration represents another milestone in the UK’s continued investment in sovereign technologies that strengthen resilience, enhance operational freedom and support the next generation of autonomous defence capabilities.” The littoral is the hardest place to do this, which is why the Solent was chosen. Coastlines, changing terrain and dense infrastructure degrade satellite reception on their own, before any adversary sets out to deny it deliberately, and an autonomous vessel that loses its position close inshore is a hazard to everything around it as well as a loss to its owner. Voyant’s approach fuses radar returns with probabilistic algorithms to estimate where the vessel is relative to its surroundings, and crucially also to estimate how confident it is in that answer. Rather than listening for a satellite, the system continually matches what it can see against geographic features it already knows about. The company was founded on more than twenty years of research at Liverpool and sells software intended to extract more from sensors a customer already owns, working with radar, sonar, electronic warfare, electro-optical and infrared systems without requiring new hardware. Voyant is exhibiting at Apex Europe in London on Wednesday and Thursday, and has a second release out covering a software-defined approach to anti-submarine warfare. The post Robot boat found its way in the Solent without satellites first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: Tristan Harris’ Tech Nonprofit Is Laying Off Most Staff and Going ‘Founder-Led’
body:
The nine departures, which include executive director Julie Guirado and senior director of strategy Camille Carlton, arrive shortly after the center scored a series of major courtroom victories against social media companies. The lawsuits drew on its research alleging that the platforms were deliberately designed to keep kids glued to their screens.
But amid that success, internal debates had been brewing for years over the organization’s direction, according to 16 former workers, most of whom spoke with WIRED earlier this year on the condition of anonymity because they feared professional repercussions.
CHT’s board ultimately determined that trying to operate both as an advocacy group fronted by Harris and a think tank producing policy papers had stretched it too thin. Moving forward, the organization will focus on initiatives with its founders at the forefront, including “public education, targeted briefings, and private coordination,” building upon their success “reaching broad audiences and engaging influential decisionmakers,” the board announced last week.
Functions such as assisting in litigation and evaluating AI tools would be eliminated, the board added, without specifying an exact number of layoffs.
“This moment of accelerated AI risk demands we focus on one strategy, and we have chosen to focus on what we have always done best so that we can meet the moment,” board chair Premal Shah said in a statement to WIRED.
In recent years, Harris has joined a growing chorus of voices sounding the alarm about the risks posed by advanced artificial intelligence, warning of a potential “AI takeover” if the software evades control. “We have to act right now before it’s too late,” he told NBC News last month.
The center encouraged people to sign a major petition to pause AI development and helped organize a hearing in Congress about the dangers of chatbots. It also advised on lawsuits and investigations probing AI labs for their design choices, including an ongoing case filed against OpenAI by parents of a teenager who died by suicide after interacting with ChatGPT. Harris also starred in a documentary released on Netflix last month, The AI Doc, which urges viewers to demand that Congress intervene to protect the public from the technology’s risks.
Founded in 2017, the Center for Humane Technology competes with well-established nonprofits and numerous newer entrants for funding and attention to shape AI policy. Cyberattacks by AI agents from OpenAI and other labs have renewed calls to hold tech developers liable for design and engineering failures.
With an annual budget of roughly $6 million and a similar amount in reserves, the center has been funded by wealthy families and foundations. But as it doubles down on Harris, former employees fear resources might be diverted away from addressing what they believe are more pressing concerns about AI’s impact on democracy and civil liberties.
Gail Barnes, who advised the center on social media strategy in its early days, says the board is dropping work that was supposed to convert Harris’ fame “into durable pressure” that could help facilitate real change inside companies.
“Whether that is wisdom or a retreat depends on whether you think the binding constraint on AI right now is still ‘people haven’t heard the argument’ or ‘the argument has no institutional teeth.’ CHT is picking the first,” Barnes says.
Big Star
Harris excels at producing compelling sound bites, and he has long been a fixture in the media, at conferences, and on Capitol Hill. “He’s brilliant. He’s articulate,” a former CHT colleague says. “He could have easily spent his entire career on the dark side. For whatever reason, he came to appreciate that this was messed up.”
Harris cofounded the center with Aza Raskin, the self-proclaimed inventor of the infinite scroll, and Randy Fernando, who once worked in developer education at Nvidia. The goal was to push tech companies to take more responsibility for the social consequences of their products, which in the early days meant examining issues like whether they were fomenting political radicalization or harming the mental health of teenagers. The language Harris used to describe these problems was quickly adopted across Silicon Valley.
Internal documents from Meta released in court this year show company researchers discussed reaching out to Harris as early as 2018, when his warnings that apps were intentionally designed to be addictive entered the mainstream. His national profile grew further with the release of The Social Dilemma on Netflix in 2020.
“It’s hard to understate how helpful The Social Dilemma was for launching tech accountability” as an advocacy field, says a leader at another nonprofit, who also sought anonymity to protect their relationship with CHT.
But inside the organization, Harris sometimes clashed with his team about whether to focus their efforts on consumers, tech companies, or lawmakers, former staffers say. Some colleagues grew frustrated with Harris’ frequently shifting whims, describing the organization’s culture as needlessly “frenetic” and “insanity-inducing.” Shah disputed the characterization, but acknowledged the center’s culture is fast-paced given the urgency of its mission.
The center developed an online course at one point for tech workers who wanted to learn how to build humane systems, and while it drew thousands of participants, CHT decided to retire it as Harris’ focus shifted to concerns about AI, according to people familiar with the project. Another initiative to create resources for educators to make sense of issues around screen time fell by the wayside, the people say. Harris kept coming back to the center being “a vehicle for him to speak to the world,” according to one ex-employee.
The center’s podcasts and videos featuring Harris and Raskin have attracted large audiences, former workers say. Harris also landed private meetings with US lawmakers and executives at top tech companies. Former employees describe the group’s strategy as putting more emphasis on “grasstops” activism over the more familiar “grassroots,” which some viewed as misguided.
Shah says CHT believes “mass communications creates grassroots pressure, which unlocks action from the grasstops” and that Harris “is one of the very few people in the world who is invited and can communicate effectively to mass media audiences across the political spectrum.”
Some former employees allege that CHT’s founders were eager to remain Silicon Valley insiders, and thus were more reluctant to criticize companies where they previously worked or where close personal contacts have worked. (Shah disputes the characterizations and says CHT “has always been tough on companies.”)
Some ex-employees described Harris’ management style as taxing, which they allege led to high turnover. In 2023, employees returned from a staff retreat feeling upset after being asked to participate in trust-building exercises they felt were overly personal, according to several former workers. CHT’s independent board members got involved, and Harris later stepped down as executive director to become the organization’s president, according to the former employees.
Shah says that employee turnover "stemmed from differences in problem analysis and approaches to achieving the organization’s core mission.” He also denied that Harris’ role change was related to what happened at the retreat.
Whatever turmoil may have been happening inside CHT, the broader strategy Harris used to go after tech companies was paying off. In 2021, state attorneys general across the US opened investigations into Meta and later sued the company for allegedly misleading teens and parents. This year, Meta agreed to settle some of the lawsuits for billions of dollars. Juries, including one that heard testimony from Raskin, put the company on the hook for additional penalties in separate cases. Other social media platforms agreed to settle similar litigation this year.
In an interview with WIRED earlier this year, the leader of the other tech nonprofit praised CHT’s less flashy work in statehouses and courtrooms. The shift away from it is “disappointing,” the person says now. “Change comes from movements and democracy, not celebrities and backrooms.”
Some former employees say they expect that CHT will increasingly resemble what they jokingly refer to as the “Center of Helping Tristan.” Shah says the organization’s sole goal is ensuring “today’s most consequential technologies serve humanity.”

title: The Recovery Has Two Audiences
body: Picture two Nigerians on the same morning in late September. One is a factory manager. He has just completed the CBN survey; 1,900 executives were surveyed between Sept. 7 and 11 and, for the fourth month in a row, can say business is expanding. The PMI is 53.0, up from 52.7. New orders are coming in. Even his raw materials inventory is growing again. The CBN cut the policy rate to 23%. The other is a parent. She didn’t fill out a survey; she just paid school fees, bought food, paid the electricity bill, and realised there was nothing left. In the CBN’s household survey that same month, she would be part of the 18.7 more pessimistic than in August, more worried about prices at 33.5, up from 23.0, and more convinced that buying a house at 68.2 or a car at 67.3 is out of reach. Same economy. Two audiences. One recovery that businesses can see, and families cannot yet touch. How that gap closes or doesn’t is the story of 2027. Because the numbers really are telling two stories. The business story is broadening. Composite PMI at 53.0 points, 23 of 32 subsectors growing. Industry strengthened to 52.0 points from 50.6, Services steady at 53.2 points, Agriculture at 53.1 points for its 26th straight month of expansion. CBN itself called it a broadening recovery. Yemi Cardoso leads Nigeria’s apex bank. But there’s a squeeze inside it: the input cost index is up 0.8 points, and the output-price index is down 0.5 points. Busier, but margins tighter. The household story is different. Economic conditions: 21.5 points; family financial situation: -23.9 points; family income: -10.5 points. And all this while, headline inflation actually eased to 15.39%, and CBN cut the policy rate to 23%. As households know, slower inflation doesn’t mean falling prices. It just means prices are rising slower. President Bola Tinubu’s second-term bid in the 2027 presidential election is being challenged by opposition leaders. For President Tinubu, that’s the difficult interval: you have grounds to point to expanding activity, but repeating favourable indicators has limited persuasive power where families still struggle with ordinary expenses. For the opposition, it’s an opening, but also an obligation. Describing hardship is easy. Explaining how to relieve it, what it costs, and how you sustain investment is harder. Edo: A Vote Target Becomes A Test Of Restraint: Jarrett Tenebe is the Edo State Chairman of the APC. In Edo, APC chairman Jarrett Tenebe, in a video that went viral on October 2, during Governor Okpebholo’s 18-LGA tour, said the party wants 2.5 million votes for Tinubu in 2027, and anyone who blocks it would face “General Purpose Machine Gun power” and “AK-47 fire”. The ADC called it inciting and asked police, DSS and INEC to investigate. At the INEC World Press Conference and stakeholders’ meeting in Abuja this Tuesday, Assistant Inspector-General of Police in charge of Police Mobile Force, Aloyenu Francis Idu, representing IGP Kayode Egbetokun, disclosed that the Nigeria Police Force has invited and questioned Tenebe over the remarks. Idu was responding to journalists asking how police would handle inflammatory threats ahead of 2027. He confirmed the questioning had happened, though details were not made public. This moves it from outrage to formal process on INEC’s own platform. What we still need: what Tenebe told investigators, whether INEC will issue a formal query under the Code of Conduct, and whether APC leaders unequivocally disavow the language. Imo: National Service, Personal Danger Around 6:30 a.m. on October 1, two buses left Ibadan for NYSC camps in Abia and Akwa Ibom and were attacked near Umunoha, Mbaitoli LGA, Owerri-Onitsha Expressway. Police say 10 were rescued, and 20 are still in captivity. Commissioner Audu Bosso visited the scene. Families report N50m per person in ransom demands. On October 4, police said they located the kidnappers’ camp but suspected explosives complicated access. Rescue continues. Immediate priority is safe return. Beyond that is a policy question: how should national service arrangements change when journeys to camps expose young graduates to serious danger? Household relief: Do jobs and real incomes follow the PMI? Edo accountability: Police questioning confirmed today at INEC briefing — will there be a published outcome? The Imo rescue: Verified safe return, then concrete safeguards. Opposition policy: Costed alternatives, not just criticism. The Signal: Recovery gains force when it’s recognisable at the kitchen table, not just in index points. The opposition gains force when it offers a credible route there. EDITORIAL NOTE Political Signals is an independent weekly political analysis produced for Channels Television. It examines political developments, personalities and electoral trends without endorsement of any political party or candidate. Its assessments are based on publicly available evidence and may change as events and evidence develop. The post The Recovery Has Two Audiences appeared first on Channels Television .

title: U.S. and Russia Explore Nord Stream Restart, Sources Say
body:
Top Russian and U.S. officials, including U.S. Special Envoy Jared Kushner, have held talks about bringing a U.S. investor into the Nord Stream pipelines that delivered gas to Germany before Russia invaded Ukraine, five people with knowledge of the situation said.
The discussions included Kirill Dmitriev, a close adviser to Russian President Vladimir Putin, and Kushner, the son-in-law of U.S. President Donald Trump, the people said.
Kushner, who has been trying to broker a truce between Russia and Ukraine, views doing business as central to restoring peace. Such a deal would enable U.S. investors to profit from energy flows to Europe once the war ends.
Dmitriev and Kushner have met in Moscow and New York in recent weeks. While it was unclear to what degree they discussed Nord Stream on those occasions, the topic remains on the agenda, two of the people told Reuters.
“Any deals will have to be negotiated by Russia with DFC (U.S. International Development Finance Corporation) and Treasury and must benefit United States taxpayers and companies,” a White House official said when asked about the pipeline discussions.
There had been “no Nord Stream discussions recently,” the official told Reuters.
Dmitriev, who has campaigned for a resumption of Russian gas sales to Germany, met last month with U.S. Energy and Treasury Department representatives to discuss potential U.S.-Russia energy initiatives. A representative for Dmitriev declined to comment.
It remains unclear how interested Washington is in pursuing the restart of Russian gas flows to Germany, which is Europe's biggest energy consumer.
A U.S. official said that given the obstacles, a deal is unlikely in the medium term. The Nord Stream gas pipelines are sanctioned by the U.S. and the EU, making any restart illegal.
Trump could waive or soften U.S. sanctions, but if Democrats win control of Congress in next month's midterm elections, this would become harder.
Germany and other European countries, which are spending billions of euros rebuilding their military to defend themselves from Russia, would strongly resist reopening Nord Stream.
A spokeswoman for Germany's economy and energy ministry said Nord Stream and Russian gas were sanctioned in Europe and that Germany had found alternatives. She said any reopening of the pipelines required government approval and this was not desired.
Before Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Germany bought more than half of its gas from Russia through the two Nord Stream pipelines. They were mothballed after Moscow throttled supply to Europe and blown up in a series of underwater explosions in September 2022.
Talks between Moscow and Washington are taking place against a backdrop of deep European mistrust of Russia's motives.
Earlier this year, the heads of five European spy agencies told Reuters that Russia did not want to end the war quickly and was using U.S. talks to push for business deals instead.
Relations between Russia and Germany, which is among the biggest providers of military support to Ukraine, have hit a low ebb, as officials in Berlin have accused Russia of mounting a systematic campaign of hybrid attacks.
Some German lawmakers say that business deals would bolster Moscow as it pursues war with Ukraine.
“This threatens to be a dirty deal that will cost Europe dearly,” said Michael Kellner, a lawmaker who was in charge ​of German energy policy in the aftermath of the Ukraine invasion.
“Americans and Russians will share the profits,” he said.
While Germany's coalition government is opposed to restarting the pipeline, Alternative for Germany (AfD), the country's most popular political party, wants to do so.
Dmitriev will meet the AfD leadership early next year to discuss selling Russian gas again.
But selling ownership of the company that controls the Nord Stream gas pipelines to a U.S. investor or restarting Russian gas faces hurdles.
The company is 51% owned by Russian state energy giant Gazprom, with a further 31% split between two German entities and the rest in the hands of a French and a Dutch firm.
The two German shareholders are seeking to keep their shares to maintain German influence, should Gazprom sell its stake, said another person.
Days after the Moscow meetings, Kushner said in Kyiv he had spoken to European counterparts about how the war pushed up energy prices, advocating “prosperity agreements” to encourage peace and give “leaders ... something to look forward to.”
While a gas deal would please the Kremlin, it would split German public opinion, which is divided over buying Russian energy, and Europe, where Poland and the Baltic states are particularly vulnerable to Russia and reject energy ties.
Poland's political leadership is watching the discussions to reopen the pipeline but remains firmly opposed, said one person with knowledge of the government's thinking.
Kushner and Dmitriev have also been discussing the sale of a collection of businesses, from oil refineries to petrol stations in Europe and elsewhere, which are owned by Russian energy company Lukoil, said two other people familiar with the matter.
Under that plan, a consortium of the DFC federal investment agency and investors from Qatar and the United Arab Emirates would buy the assets, while U.S. authorities would lift sanctions, those people said.
“On Lukoil, Steve (Witkoff) and Jared (Kushner) worked with DFC to negotiate a substantial upfront payment and profits interest for the United States,” said a White House official.
Lukoil and Gazprom did not respond to requests for comment.
