title: First Brazil-Built Gripen Fighter Completes Maiden Flight
body:
The first Gripen fighter produced outside Sweden has completed its maiden flight , marking a milestone in Brazil’s effort to develop domestic production capabilities for the Swedish-designed combat aircraft.
The Gripen E took off from Embraer’s Gavião Peixoto aerodrome in São Paulo state at 10:21 local time on October 6, flown by Saab chief test pilot Jakob Högberg. The flight-tested basic system functions and initial performance and served as the aircraft’s first production acceptance test, beginning the final phase of its manufacturing process.
Embraer flight engineers planned and executed the sortie with Saab support, marking another step in the Gripen programme’s technology-transfer plan for Brazil.
After the production acceptance flight campaign, the aircraft will undergo certification before delivery to the Brazilian Air Force (FAB). It will then be transferred to Anápolis Air Force Base in Goiás to join the First Air Defence Group (1st GDA), which currently operates 10 Gripen fighters.
Officially presented by Embraer on March 25, the aircraft is the first of 15 Gripen fighters to be produced in Brazil under the current programme. Embraer operates South America’s only supersonic fighter production line and is part of Saab’s global manufacturing and supply-chain network.

title: Darwin protective net effectively counters Ukraine’s Lyuty, Hornet UAVs — developer
body:
ST. PETERSBURG, October 8. /TASS/. The Darwin protective capture net has demonstrated high effectiveness against the An-196 Lyuty long-range fixed-wing drones and US-made Hornet strike drones, Dmitry Dorofeyev, CEO of Mechanical Protection Systems, told TASS.
"Over the past two years, the Darwin net has regularly and effectively intercepted drones of various types. The majority of them are small FPV drones and Mavics. A large number of Hornet-type drones have also been neutralized, and we’ve intercepted many Lyuty drones," he said on the sidelines of the All-Russian Drone Congress 2026.
According to him, the company receives information about the effectiveness of the Darwin system directly from its customers, which include oil and defense enterprises. "Attacks are intensifying now, so we’ve increased production of Darwin nets accordingly," he added.
Mechanical Protection Systems manufactures Darwin anti-drone nets. The system is used in Russia to protect civilian critical infrastructure, military facilities, equipment, and personnel. An innovative weaving technique, the "spider knot," allows the net to gently absorb the impact of an UAV and reduce the likelihood of an explosive device detonating.
The All-Russian Drone Congress organized by the unmanned technologies center of excellence RuDrones is taking place in St. Petersburg from October 7-9.

title: Syrian official denies Saudi Arabia asked Damascus to deploy troops in war with Houthis
body: A Syrian official has denied reports that Saudi Arabia asked Damascus to send troops to support the kingdom against the Houthis in Yemen. Ahmad Zaidan, media adviser to Syrian President Ahmad Al Shara, described reports in recent days of plans to send troops to Saudi Arabia or Yemen as “lies”. Mr Al Shara met Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman ​in Riyadh during ‌an ​official visit ⁠on ​Tuesday. “The security of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, and the security of the Gulf, is inseparable from the security of Syria,” Mr Zaidan wrote on X. Saudi Arabia has been repeatedly targeted by Houthi rebels who have stepped up escalation in Yemen. “But what some media outlets are promoting about the kingdom's request to send Syrian forces to Saudi Arabia or Yemen is a lie and has no basis in truth,” he added. The denial was also backed by Syrian Response, the official English-language account of Syria’s Foreign Media Department on X. “Syria’s position is clear: we stand firmly with Saudi Arabia against threats to its security and stability. At the same time, Syria’s policy in the region is focused on stability, peace and co-operation, not opening new fronts,” Syrian Response wrote. “Our priority is Syria: rebuilding the country, strengthening its institutions, working with our partners on reconstruction and improving the lives of Syrians. Any military co-operation with partner countries would take place only through official channels and existing bilateral frameworks,” it added. Reuters reported on Wednesday that Syria was considering providing military assistance to Saudi Arabia, citing a US official and a Syrian military official. It reported that options being considered included defensive aid to protect the kingdom from attacks, ​or deployment of forces in an offensive capacity to help Saudi-backed Yemeni troops fight the Houthis. The Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have brought the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement between the kingdom, Pakistan and Turkey into focus, raising questions about how the collective security alliance could be realised on the ground. Earlier this week, Turkey and Pakistan agreed to provide “military forces and capabilities” to Saudi Arabia. The text of the Makkah pact has not been made public but a joint statement from the three countries when it was signed in August said it was intended to strengthen collective deterrence. Similar to Nato's Article 5 on collective defence, an attack on one country would be considered an attack on all. Syria on Thursday “strongly condemned Houthi militia attacks targeting vital facilities and civilian sites in Saudi Arabia”, including this week's attacks on Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport that killed three people and injured 36 more. Syria's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said “the attacks on civilian facilities and infrastructure and the endangerment of civilian lives constitute a blatant violation of international law and relevant international rules and conventions”, warning that “such attacks pose a direct threat to Saudi Arabia’s security and the stability of the region”. The ministry also reaffirmed “Syria’s full solidarity with Saudi Arabia and its support for all legitimate measures taken by the kingdom to protect its security and stability and ensure the safety of its citizens and residents”. The Saudi Press Agency said Mr Al Shara and the Crown Prince discussed bilateral relations on Tuesday during their meeting in Riyadh and “promising opportunities for developing these relations in various fields”. They also discussed the latest developments in the region.

title: Ukrainian agriculture urges EU to talk details, not panic, in future membership negotiations
body:
Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi and the sector's main lobby organization in Brussels doubled down on their commitment to integrating Kyiv's geopolitically powerful farming sector into the EU system on Oct. 7.
Their respective interventions came one day after the European Commission published a view on how the future of enlargement could work.
Ukraine's agricultural might could mean that the EU needs "targeted arrangements to significantly limit financial support and market access for sensitive agricultural products," the document argues.
However, Vysotskyi said permanent restrictions on access to the EU's single market are a non-starter, in written comments first shared with Politico and seen by the Kyiv Independent.
"Ukraine cannot agree to such an approach," the Ukrainian minister said.
Likewise, the Ukrainian Agribusiness Club (UCAB) put out a press statement saying, "Ukrainian agricultural producers cannot be expected to bear the full economic cost of alignment with EU standards while being denied the corresponding perspective of full participation in the EU Single Market."
For both Vysotskyi and UCAB, part of the solution relies on baking transition periods into the enlargement process, just as was the case in previous rounds of EU expansion, which would give the bloc and Ukraine time to adapt to one another and stretch out disruption over a longer period of time.
"Transitional periods are a normal part of EU enlargement, and Ukraine is ready for them," Vysotskyi said.
But "transition should facilitate integration, not become a mechanism for permanently excluding Ukrainian agriculture from the internal market," UCAB notes.
Ukraine's farming sector has already begun complying with EU rules, a process that is expensive, essentially irreversible, and undertaken only because it comes with the promise of a level playing field in the EU market.
It is market access rather than financial support that matters most for Ukraine, Vysotskyi said, as the sector already operates with little state support.
But that has not stopped French far-right leader Marine Le Pen already playing to the fears of French farmers that Ukrainian counterparts would take away their share of EU subsidies.
EU farms are typically small-scale, uncompetitive, and dependent on the bloc's Common Agricultural Policy for generous subsidies that keep them operational.
Ukraine's farming sector, by contrast, is a giant capable of competing on the world stage, and with that size comes geopolitical leverage.
Because of that, the European Commission is clear that while Ukraine should gain market access as part of EU membership, Ukrainian agriculture needs to remain competitive on the world stage.
"Our budget can never compensate for gains that Ukraine's very competitive — the only real competitive agriculture sector in Europe — can gain in the world," a senior EU official told the Kyiv Independent, ahead of the publication of the Commission's new plans.
To overcome that obstacle, highly technical negotiations need to take place.
Vysotskyi seems to mirror the European Commission's thinking that for each specific product, there should be "a substantive discussion about adaptation periods, the volumes of market access, and safeguard mechanisms."
That could mean one rule for Ukrainian chicken, another for wheat, another for plant proteins, and so on.
Decisions "must take into account the situation in each specific sector and must not turn into permanent restrictions for the entire Ukrainian agricultural sector," Vysotskyi said.
And UCAB says that "the Ukrainian agricultural sector is ready to contribute constructively to this work."
UCAB calls for agricultural businesses, associations representing the sector, and EU agricultural organizations to all be included in a dialogue on Ukraine's agricultural integration.
"Ukraine is preparing to become part of the European Union. Its agricultural sector should not merely be accommodated within the future European agricultural model. It should be involved in designing it," reads the UCAB press statement.

title: Military Disrupts Kidnappers In Benue
body: The Nigerian Air Force (NAF) said it has successfully provided close air support to surface forces during an operation targeting suspected kidnappers in the Ogbadigbo area of Benue State, near the Enugu–Benue boundary. It said that the operation disrupted the activities of the criminal elements and supported the advance of surface forces. The Air Force said that following the successful completion of the mission, the pilot, on return to base, exercised his professional discretion to execute a precautionary landing approximately 10 nautical miles from the airfield. This, according to NAF, was in accordance with established operational and safety procedures following combat missions. It, however, said that the helicopter has returned to base. “The NAF remains committed to sustaining pressure on criminal elements, providing close air support to surface forces and protecting communities through coordinated air and ground operations,” Director of Public Relations and Information, Headquarters, Nigerian Air Force, Air Commodore Ehimen Ejodame, said in a statement on Thursday. “The successful outcome underscores the NAF’s continued resolve to deny criminal elements freedom of action and support efforts to restore safety and security to affected communities.” This came as the Nigerian Army said troops of Operation HADIN KAI crushed a coordinated multi-directional assault by Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP) terrorists in Kukawa, Borno State. The operation led to the killing of over 25 terrorists and the recovery of arms and ammunition during a fierce counter-offensive. The army said that the terrorists, who attacked troops of the 101 Special Forces Battalion in large numbers from four different flanks, met stiff resistance as the troops responded decisively with superior firepower, tactical manoeuvre and effective battlefield coordination. It, however, disclosed that some gallant soldiers paid the supreme sacrifice during the encounter. On Monday, an intelligence-led operation by a combined team of troops of the Nigerian Army, Department of State Services (DSS) personnel, and Western Nigeria Security Network aka Amotekun officers, at the weekend in Owo forest, Ondo State, neutralised a senior leader of the Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP ), identified as one Abdussamad Ohida. Ohida, who was reportedly on the verge of planning massive terrorist attacks in some southern states, was eliminated alongside many members of the terrorist organisation by the security forces, who led a surprise attack on their forest hideout. The post Military Disrupts Kidnappers In Benue appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Russia Kills 30 in Kramatorsk Bus Strike as Donetsk Orders Public Transport Halt
body:
Russian forces struck a passenger bus in Kramatorsk, Donetsk region, on Thursday, Oct. 8, killing at least 30 people and injuring 18 others, according to reports from local authorities.
The Kramatorsk City Council said the vehicle was carrying passengers when it was struck. Public transport in the city has since been suspended due to continued Russian shelling.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Donetsk Regional Military Administration (OVA) head Vadym Filashkin condemned the attack in a Telegram post.
“The Russians are deliberately targeting civilians. For them, a bus full of passengers is an attractive target precisely because a single strike can kill as many people as possible. Today’s tragedy in Kramatorsk – where the Russians killed 30 people and wounded another 18 in an instant – is further proof of this.”
He added that, amid the sharp deterioration in the security situation, he had ordered the Kramatorsk and Sloviansk city military administrations to suspend public transport operations.
“Russia consciously disregards all conceivable rules of warfare and norms of international humanitarian law. It selects targets where it can inflict the most pain on civilians,” Filashkin wrote, adding that under these circumstances, authorities have no right to risk the lives of passengers and drivers.
Filashkin said the safety of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk residents was the authorities’ top priority, adding that suspending public transport was a necessary measure given Russia’s conduct and the growing threat to civilian passengers.
At approximately 9:46 a.m., the Ukrainian Air Force reported that Russian forces were using guided aerial bombs (KABs) against targets in the Donetsk region.
Kramatorsk, a major administrative and logistics center in northern Donetsk region, has remained a frequent target of Russian missile, artillery, KABs, and drone strikes as Moscow continues its offensive along the eastern front.
On Sept. 13, a Russian strike targeted a civilian vehicle traveling through central Kramatorsk , killing two people and injuring four others, regional authorities reported.
Filashkin said Russian forces deliberately targeted the vehicle as it moved through the city center, describing the attack as another demonstration of the danger facing civilians in the front-line region.
“Again and again, the Russians prove that they came here to kill everyone they can reach. Every day in the Donetsk region is a mortal danger,” Filashkin said.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: European Vigilant Shield tests response to drone payloads that remain dangerous after interception
body: A downed drone can still pose a threat. Its explosive payload may remain active, while chemical or radioactive substances can spill around the aircraft. Participants at Santa Margarida military camp worked through increasingly complex scenarios. They assessed threats, examined how to make devices safe and tested procedures for handling hazardous materials. The scenarios also covered the safe recovery and analysis of drone components. Specialists examined how to preserve evidence that could help identify those responsible for an incident. Reviewing the response The exercise assessed existing counter-drone procedures and sought to identify where changes are needed. Its findings will inform a review of operational techniques, procedures and military doctrine. Experts in counter-drone operations, command and control, and chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear defence took part. They worked with specialists in explosive ordnance disposal, technical exploitation and military legal affairs. National experts participated alongside the United Nations Mine Action Service and NATO’s Counter-Improvised Explosive Devices Centre of Excellence. Representatives from the NATO Joint CBRN Defence Capability Development Group and Joint CBRN Defence Centre of Excellence also attended. Further testing in 2027 and 2028 Virtual wargaming in 2027 will introduce more complex scenarios. It will test decisions involving several teams. Live experimentation planned for 2028 will assess the full response under field conditions. That work will cover countering a drone, specialist intervention and analysis of recovered material. EDA said the exercise showed that defeating a drone is often only the beginning of the response. Forces must also investigate, make devices safe and turn technical findings into lessons for future operations. European Vigilant Shield contributes to the Defence Readiness 2030 agenda. It translates operational challenges into priorities for capability development, experimentation and cooperation. Source: European Defence Agency (EDA) .

title: AI-powered hacking tools enabled a likely single attacker to breach multiple South Korean banks
body:
Crowdstrike reports on an infrastructure hack in South Korea. A suspected Chinese-speaking attacker hit multiple South Korean financial institutions between late September and early October 2026, stealing large amounts of data. At Shinhan Bank alone, more than 25,000 records with names, contact details, income, and credit limits were stolen, according to Korean newspaper Khan . South Korea's financial regulator held an emergency meeting. President Lee Jae Myung called for a thorough investigation.
The attacker used ARTEX , a Chinese open-source tool first posted on GitHub in July that uses AI language models for automated penetration testing, meaning it finds security flaws on its own. The models behind it were DeepSeek v4.1-flash, GLM-5.3, and Grok 4.6. Researchers found Claude Code session logs on the attacker's open directories, showing searches for Telegram groups to sell stolen data.
Crowdstrike says the case shows how AI tools can let a single person pull off massive breaches in a short window, the kind of cybersecurity risk experts have been warning about for months . Just days earlier, Anthropic documented that GLM-5.3 can write exploits nearly on par with Mythos Preview , Anthropic's frontier model and the one that sparked the entire debate in late March 2026 . title: South Korea to recall ambassador from Kyiv
body:
The decision was announced in a statement by the South Korean Foreign Ministry, Ukrinform reports, citing Yonhap .
"The government has decided to recall its ambassador to Ukraine to Seoul. We hope that various issues between the two countries will be resolved smoothly, and we will continue consultations with the Ukrainian side to that end," the ministry said.
As reported, South Korea's presidential office expressed "deep regret" over what Seoul said was Ukraine's denial that an agreement had been reached to keep information about the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea confidential.
Dmytro Lytvyn, a Ukrainian presidential advisor on communications, wrote on Facebook that there had been no non-disclosure agreement and that it would be wrong to conceal where prisoners of war are taken. In response to a query from Yonhap, the President's Office explained that Kyiv had disclosed only the fact of the transfer without revealing details of the process.
South Korea later received a message from Ukraine apologizing for disclosing information about the transfer of the two North Korean prisoners of war to Seoul. However, the apology did not meet the expectations of the South Korean government.

title: Ato Forson says Ghana’s New Economy must create decent jobs for young people
body: Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson says Ghana’s emerging New Economy must be capable of creating decent and productive jobs on a large scale to give young people a meaningful stake in the country’s future. He said the success of the New Economy should not be measured only by economic growth, but also by its ability to generate sustainable employment opportunities for the country’s growing youth population. Dr Ato Forson made the observation in a Facebook post after engaging academics, researchers and students at the University for Development Studies (UDS), Nyankpala Campus. He described the engagement as “deeply successful and inspiring”, saying the discussions provided an opportunity to exchange ideas on Ghana’s economic future. The Finance Minister said the engagements would continue at the University of Ghana as part of efforts to deepen conversations on the New Economy and its potential to create jobs and expand opportunities for young Ghanaians.

title: Gov. Idris makes provision for new mosque in Malami’s hometown
body: Governor Nasir Idris of Kebbi has approved the purchase of a house to relocate a temporary Mosque in the Go-Slow Road area of Birnin Kebbi, a community close to the family house of Abubakar Malami, SAN. Malami is the African Democratic Congress (ADC) governorship candidate in Kebbi. The governor’s Special Adviser on Religious Affairs, Mallam Imrana Bin-Usman, disclosed this while handing over the document of the house to residents of the area. Bin-Usman said the intervention followed the residents’ request for a permanent place of worship after the administration installed solar street lights in the area. He said the governor responded to the request by directing the purchase of the house to provide a suitable location for the relocation of the Mosque. “This is great history. Not long ago, after we fixed your street solar lights, we heard your complaint about your desire to have your temporary Mosque relocated to a permanent location. “The governor heard you and directed that the house be purchased for the Mosque to be relocated there,” he said. The youth leader in the area, Mallam Taslim Tukur-Kola, described the intervention as a welcome development, saying residents appreciated the governor’s decision to address the challenge. Tukur-Kola said the area had produced prominent politicians, yet the community had not received similar intervention in providing a permanent place of worship. He appealed to the governor to complement the purchase of the house by constructing a Mosque and an Islamiyya school for children in the area. “We are appealing to the Executive Governor to please help us by constructing the Mosque and the Islamiyya school for our children in the area,” he pleaded. He said residents were currently worshipping in a small temporary structure close to the road, which he described as inadequate for the community. Tukur-Kola further said the location was a few metres from the family house of Malami, a former Attorney-General of the Federation and Minister of Justice, who held the office from 2015 to 2023. He, however, said the community had not received support from Malami for the purchase or construction of the Mosque. Speaking, the Imam of the Mosque, Mallam Muhammad Sani, expressed appreciation for the governor’s intervention. Sani prayed to God to assist Idris in achieving his political aspirations and to continue to guide him in the affairs of the state. (NAN)

title: French AI infrastructure firm Sesterce plans €10bn data centre project in Central Finland
body:
Jämsä's town manager has responded to the news with cautious enthusiasm — at least for the time being.
French AI infrastructure firm Sesterce has announced plans to invest more than 10 billion euros in the building of artificial intelligence (AI) data centres at the site of a former paper mill in Jämsä, Central Finland.
If realised, the project would be significant in scale — and only around three billion euros smaller than Google's 13-billion-euro investment across multiple locations, which was announced in September.
Yle has received confirmation from Sesterce's CEO Youssef El Manssouri that the investment decision has already been made and a contract has been signed with the future client.
However, El Manssouri has not identified the company that will become the data centre's client, but said it's one of two leading AI laboratories. He also declined to reveal the project's financial backers.
According to French commercial register data, Sesterce Group is registered in Marseille and was entered into the commercial register in 2021. According to the register, the firm's turnover was 11.95 million euros in 2024.
The former paper mill site is currently owned by real estate company Kaipola Green Port. Its board chair, Martti Inkovaara , told Yle that the firm has been negotiating with Sesterce about selling the entire site.
According to Inkovaara, negotiations about the deal are in an advanced stage — he also declined to discuss the price.
"I'd be surprised if the deal didn't go through," Inkovaara said.
Several companies currently rent industrial space at the Kaipola site. Inkovaara noted that it will be up to Sesterce to decide whether their operations can continue at the site if ownership changes.
El Manssouri told Yle that the construction phase of the project could bring around 2,000 jobs to Jämsä. Once completed, the AI facility would employ approximately 300 people.
When paper giant UPM shut down the Kaipola mill, it had employed over 400 workers.
The first construction phase is set to begin before the end of this year. It involves building a 200-megawatt liquid-cooled AI data centre at the mill site.
El Manssouri noted that the site clearance and initial interior work are already underway. In the long term, the company aims to build over one gigawatt of AI capacity in Finland.
The former paper mill site already has infrastructure, including an electricity grid, water systems, buildings and logistics arrangements. According to Sesterce's CEO, building the data centre therefore shouldn't cause biodiversity loss.
El Manssouri said the Kaipola site was chosen specifically for its minimal environmental impact in setting up the facility.
"Many supercomputer projects destroy a lot of nature. Finland has excellent industrial sites that we can convert into supercomputer centres. That guided our choice," he said.
The company added that it is committing to contributing the same amount of new renewable electricity production into Finland's grid for every megawatt the "AI campus" uses.
Sesterce has also vowed to establish a 10-million-euro local community fund to finance local projects together with the town of Jämsä and its residents.
An independent third party will monitor and audit the firm's commitments, with the company promising that the results will be publicly reported every year.
Locals in the town responded to the major investment news with cautious enthusiasm, at least for now.
Town manager Jori Reijula said he only learned of Sesterce's plans a few weeks ago.
Reijula said he thinks the project is significant for a place whose population and vitality have declined in recent years. But it's not time to celebrate yet.
"There are still many permit processes, and many things need to fall into place. I want to see things progress before we start declaring that a data centre is here," he said.

title: Kazakhstan’s Government Securities Added to J.P. Morgan Watchlist for Potential GBI-EM Inclusion
body: The Astana Times provides news and information from Kazakhstan and around the world. ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s government securities have been placed on J.P. Morgan’s Index Watch – Positive list for potential inclusion in the Government Bond Index – Emerging Markets (GBI-EM), marking further progress in integrating the country’s government securities market into international capital markets. Photo credit: freepik Market accessibility under review The status was assigned as part of J.P. Morgan’s 2026 index classification review. Over the next 12 months, the Finance Ministry said it will assess international investors’ access to Kazakhstan’s government securities market, the ministry reported on Oct. 8. The review will include investors’ access through international clearing and settlement infrastructure, as well as the liquidity of bonds meeting the index’s eligibility criteria. The move reflects joint efforts by Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Finance and National Bank to develop the government securities market, strengthen market infrastructure and improve international investors’ access to Kazakh financial instruments. Potential to broaden investor base Placement on the positive watchlist marks a new stage in assessing Kazakhstan’s potential inclusion in the GBI-EM. If Kazakhstan’s government securities are ultimately included in the index, the move could broaden the country’s foreign investor base, support greater market liquidity and help reduce borrowing costs. The GBI-EM is a widely followed benchmark for local-currency government bonds issued by emerging-market economies. The post Kazakhstan’s Government Securities Added to J.P. Morgan Watchlist for Potential GBI-EM Inclusion appeared first on The Astana Times .

title: British soldier charged under National Security Act
body:
A 24-year-old British soldier, Teddy Young, has been charged with two offences under the National Security Act. The soldier has been obtaining protected information and preparing to disclose it to a foreign state.
Police have not disclosed the name of the country for which Young allegedly sought to obtain information. He is due to appear before Westminster Magistrates’ Court in London on Thursday.
“These are very serious charges against a serving member of the armed forces,” said Commander Helen Flanagan, head of the Metropolitan Police’s Counter Terrorism Command. Police said they had worked closely with the UK Ministry of Defence throughout the investigation.
According to Reuters, the case is unrelated to an investigation into a potential attack on RAF Fairford , a base that was until recently used by US forces for strikes against Iran. US officials said the incident may have been linked to an attempted Iranian drone attack.
The National Security Act 2023 modernised UK laws covering espionage and other threats posed by foreign states. Among other offences, it criminalises obtaining, retaining or disclosing protected information where the conduct could harm the security or interests of the UK and is carried out for or on behalf of a foreign power. Some offences under the Act carry a maximum sentence of life imprisonment.

title: Ban on farewell celebrations, gifts imposed in Bor schools
body: Education authorities in Bor County in Jonglei State have banned farewell celebrations and the exchange of gifts in public and private schools, saying the practices place a financial burden on parents and distract students from their studies. The directive, which took effect on October 6, applies to primary and secondary schools across the county, according to a circular issued by Gabriel Panchol Anyang, an education official in Bor. Panchol said the ban followed a resolution adopted at the Bor County Education Annual Review Meeting on July 30. He said farewell, or “sign-out”, celebrations had become costly for families and were associated with activities that undermined discipline and academic concentration. The directive prohibits schools from organising farewell parties either on or outside school premises and says parents and relatives should not be required to contribute money towards such events. It also applies to head teachers, teachers, students and pupils, parents and guardians, and owners of private schools, according to the circular. Schools that violate the directive could face closure for two academic years and have their operating licences and letters of no objection withdrawn under existing education regulations, Panchol said. He also called for the order to be enforced by security personnel. The authorities also banned gifts for candidates completing Primary 8 and Senior 4, as well as for top-class pupils, saying the practice had become costly and had gone beyond simple messages of encouragement. Panchol said candidates were receiving items including clothes, cosmetics, shoes, money, soft drinks and goats. He said graduation ceremonies for nursery pupils could still be organised by schools but should not be extravagant and should not involve the distribution of assorted gifts. The directive has drawn mixed reactions in Bor. Yar Manyang, a secondary school candidate, told Radio Tamazuj that farewell celebrations could encourage students, particularly girls, and criticised the ban. “I don’t see any reason for the ban. As girls, celebrating our success is motivational and encouraging,” she said. “It is not easy to be in school for 12 years and not be allowed to celebrate.” Kanya Mach, information secretary of the Jonglei State Women Association, welcomed the directive, saying the celebrations and gift-giving had placed financial pressure on families and contributed to social tensions. “As a mother and activist, I welcome the ban,” she said, adding that gifts given to students had become increasingly expensive. Mach said some teenagers were also seeking gifts from people with whom they were in relationships, which she said could contribute to tensions between families. She cited an incident a year ago in which a family was attacked after a man gave a girl he was courting a goat and clothes as gifts. South Sudan has struggled with limited access to quality education, with schools in parts of the country facing shortages of teachers, classrooms and other resources. Bor, the capital of Jonglei State, has a number of public and private schools serving primary and secondary students. The post Ban on farewell celebrations, gifts imposed in Bor schools appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

title: GMTF to equip two Central Region hospitals with advanced diagnostic equipment
body: The Ghana Medical Trust Fund (GMTF) is set to strengthen diagnostic services in the Central Region with the provision of advanced medical equipment to the Cape Coast Teaching Hospital and Winneba Trauma and Specialist Hospital. The intervention will see Cape Coast Teaching Hospital receive a 128-slice CT scan, a 1.5 Tesla MRI machine, a 3D mammography system, a stereotactic biopsy system and a fluoroscopy machine. The equipment is expected to expand the hospital’s capacity to diagnose a range of complex medical conditions. At the Winneba Trauma and Specialist Hospital, the GMTF plans to provide a 64-slice CT scan, 3D mammography equipment, a biopsy system, a biochemistry analyser and an ultrasound machine. The initiative was announced during stakeholder engagements in Cape Coast involving traditional rulers, security heads, MMDCEs, academics, students, medical professionals and other stakeholders. The engagements provided an opportunity for the GMTF to outline its mandate and ongoing interventions in the region. The planned investment is aimed at bringing advanced diagnostic services closer to residents, reducing the need for patients to travel long distances for specialised tests and supporting earlier detection of diseases. The GMTF says strengthening diagnostic capacity at the two facilities will ultimately improve access to timely treatment and give more people in the Central Region a better chance of receiving appropriate care when they need it.

title: Allegedly a student using AI behind South Korean banks cyberattack
body:
CrowdStrike Intelligence identified infrastructure associated with a targeted campaign against South Korean financial organizations that resulted in exfiltrated data. The campaign was active from late September to early October 2026. Analysis of threat actor-controlled open directories uncovered Claude Code session histories, ARTEX configuration files, and Claude memory files, providing direct insight into the threat actor's operational methodology and tooling.
The use of agentic AI tooling alongside traditional offensive capabilities highlights the continued evolution CrowdStrike has observed in adversarial tradecraft. In this activity, the threat actor leveraged ARTEX, a recently released open-source agentic penetration testing (pentesting) tool developed in China, alongside large language models (LLMs). CrowdStrike’s intelligence collection capabilities enable close monitoring of such developments in adversarial tradecraft.
While this activity has not been attributed to a named adversary, the threat actor is likely a Chinese speaker and financially motivated. This assessment is made with moderate confidence based on the use of the Chinese-developed tool ARTEX and observed Chinese-language prompts.
According to industry reports, 1 beginning in late September 2026, several South Korean financial organizations experienced data breaches. At one affected bank, the threat actor reportedly breached a loan progress inquiry service used by financial brokers. At another bank, the threat actor compromised an employee mobile work–support system. As of this writing, the number of organizations affected remains unconfirmed.
Activity at multiple organizations purportedly involved overlapping IP addresses. Reporting also suggested the attacker used ARTEX based on references to the string ARTEX in HTML files observed on a reportedly threat actor-controlled server.
The IP address 38.244.50[.]120 was associated with the activity described and hosted an ARTEX instance and open directory containing a Claude Code markdown document at http[:]//38.244.50[.]120:18899/.claude/CLAUDE.md . The markdown document contained a Chinese-language pentesting prompt that specified how the LLM should conduct pentesting activities. A threat actor-controlled Hong Kong–based IP address also appeared in the document.
Analysis of the Hong Kong-based IP address identified additional open directories that contained Claude Code session histories, ARTEX configuration files, and Claude memory files. These files indicate that from late September 2026 to early October 2026, the threat actor targeted South Korean financial organizations with extensive activity leveraging ARTEX and LLMs. Targeted organizations overlap with those identified in industry reporting.
The Claude Code sessions reveal a two-server architecture: The Hong Kong-based IP address serves as the primary attacker-controlled infrastructure, and the IP address 38.244.50[.]120 hosts the ARTEX instance likely responsible for the described Korean attacks. The ARTEX instance used DeepSeek v4.1-flash as the primary LLM backend, and the threat actor supplemented this LLM with GLM-5.3 (Zhipu AI) and Grok 4.6 for additional Claude Code sessions. The threat actor likely accessed DeepSeek via the likely LLM API proxy/reseller xcai[.]pro .
Analysis of Claude Code sessions showed the threat actor also used the following proxy IP addresses during the ARTEX-related activity:
In addition to conducting ARTEX-related operations, the threat actor asked Claude where threat actors typically sell Korean data breach information and asked Claude for assistance in finding Korean Telegram data sales groups.
In one Claude Code session, the user asked Claude to create a security researcher résumé that specifically included bullet points conveying the results of the ARTEX-related activity. The prompt included the following personal details:
Claude Code sessions conducting vulnerability research on a Telegram-based NFT gift marketplace also used the Telegram username YY520CN. An unknown threat actor also employed this username to target a possible Chinese payment platform. While the personal details included in the prompt likely belong to the threat actor who conducted the ARTEX-related activity, currently available information cannot definitively associate these details with the threat actor.
The use of agentic AI tooling alongside traditional offensive capabilities highlights the continued evolution observed by CrowdStrike in adversarial tradecraft. This activity demonstrates how AI tooling can enable a financially motivated threat actor to conduct multiple intrusions within a short time span. CrowdStrike Intelligence assesses that adversaries will likely continue to experiment with implementing AI tooling in their operations to enhance their operational tempo and capabilities.

title: Russia wants Europe used to not reacting, Helsing warns
body: Russia is not just testing Europe’s reaction, it is training Europe not to react at all, Helsing’s UK boss told #ApexEurope. Russian testing of European defences is meant to wear down the continent’s willingness to respond at all, the UK managing director of the military artificial intelligence company Helsing told the Apex Europe conference in London on Wednesday. Ned Baker was speaking on the European Industrial Leadership Panel, chaired by Lieutenant General (Retired) Stuart Skeates, the chairman of Apex Europe, and he took up an argument made in the session immediately before his. He said: “They’re not just testing us to see our reaction, they’re actually testing us to get us used to not reacting, and that’s the worst possible thing that we can do, is settle into a kind of slightly European malaise. The time for delivery, the time for action, is now.” Helsing describes itself as an Anglo-German company, and Mr Baker set out the thinking behind its founding. “We were founded in 2021, based on the belief that Europe needed new technologies, new capabilities to defend itself, but also that amongst those technologies, military AI was going to become the defining characteristic of defence in the future, and I think we have seen that play out to a certain extent in Ukraine,” he said. “I think there is a lot more for NATO to do to adopt those technologies.” “We’ve been very fortunate to raise a little bit over 2.5 billion pounds in capital over Helsing’s life, and it’s our responsibility, obviously, to deploy that capital wisely to build these technologies,” he said. “But the fact that we’ve managed to raise that capital is also a kind of a once-in-a-generation opportunity. If the threat is a once-in-a-generation risk, then the capital that is available to us now is a once-in-a-generation opportunity, and it is here in Europe, and we should take advantage of it.” What the company does with it includes strike drones supplied into Ukraine over several years, work he described himself as very proud of, and what he called Europe’s first fully autonomous fighter jet. Asked how companies operationalise the rapid iteration seen in Ukraine, he began with a form of information older than any of the technology. “The first one is such an important one, but it’s a piece of data that’s existed for centuries, millennia, is just user feedback, just basic user feedback, getting hands-on with operators, and as much as we can blurring the lines between technologists and tacticians, so that we can learn what works, what they need, and getting close to the end-user problems,” he said. Helsing can do that, he said, because it uses its own money to develop products to a level of maturity where they can go out on exercise with the British Army or the German Army and be tried in front of soldiers, with the results fed back into development. On Ukraine he was blunt about what the shortened cycle means for everybody else. “If you do not have that kind of 24-7 service of tell me what’s working, oh, you found something, let’s go and fix it, then that is not peculiar to Ukraine,” he said. “That is just the new normal, and it will become the new way of functioning for the new style of warfare we will have to fight.” Collecting real-world data to train models is expensive, slow and hard to do at the volume modern systems need, which is the problem behind the company’s most striking claim of the session. Helsing has built internal tooling, not sold as a product, to generate synthetic training data. He said: “We pump lots of money and lots of brains into it to build synthetic AI data, so we can basically simulate environments. These environments can be changed at the touch of a parameter. Make it night. Make it day. Make it snowy. Make it rainy. Show me a T-72. Show me this. And you get then a synthetic AI data pack that you can train your models on.” He went on: “That has been revolutionary for us. That has changed those model training cycles from months and potentially years down to hours, and that’s not just training strike drones. That is how we are going to do reinforcement learning for fully autonomous fighter jets, for fully autonomous unmanned surface vessels.” The post Russia wants Europe used to not reacting, Helsing warns first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: Rheinmetall and Praetorian build containerised drone defence prototype in 12 months
body: The self-contained launcher can hold more than 20 interceptors and fits into a 20-foot ISO shipping container. It is designed for rapid deployment and reloading, and can accommodate different interceptor types. The demonstrator uses Praetorian’s Arrow Interceptor and Hadrian command-and-control system, both developed in Australia. The partnership combines those systems with Rheinmetall’s engineering and production capabilities. Arrow is an autonomous, high-speed interceptor designed to neutralise multiple types of uncrewed systems through kinetic engagement beyond visual range. Hadrian uses artificial intelligence to manage autonomous effectors across air, land and maritime domains. The companies describe AERIE as a low-cost way to counter the growing availability of inexpensive drones and other uncrewed aerial systems. The prototype is the result of their Australian research and development partnership. “Rheinmetall has a long and proud history of transferring technology and forging alliances with partners around the world,” said Nathan Poyner, managing director of Rheinmetall Defence Australia. “Our work with Praetorian Aeronatics continues this focus and has delivered a working concept of advanced C-UAS using Australian ingenuity with global air defence engineering and manufacturing know-how”. “Our partnership with Rheinmetall brings together our unique AI-enhanced C2 system and Arrow Interceptor with Rheinmetall’s engineering systems and production capability,” said Brett Hill, chief executive of Praetorian Aeronautics. “Together, we have delivered an Australian air defence solution for emerging global threats”.

title: Land Forces 2026: Hanwha lifts its gaze beyond Australian AFV programmes
body:
Hanwha Defence Australia’s production of AS9 Huntsmanself-propelled howitzers and AS10 ammunition resupply vehicles is in full swing at its facility in Avalon, Australia, and up next is the AS21 Redback infantry fighting vehicle. However, with production of these vehicles scheduled to cease by the end of 2028, Hanwha is looking at other product lines to pick up the slack.
This includes unmanned ground vehicles (UGV), with Hanwha Defence Australia (HDA) signing a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Milrem Robotics at the Land Forces exhibition in Perth, Western Australia on 7 October 2026.
HDA has purchased a THeMIS tracked UGV from Milrem, and it will soon participate in trials with the Australian Army’s 1st Armoured Regiment.
Hanwha stated, “The MoU establishes a framework for HDA to market, pursue local production, sell and sustain THeMIS locally in Australia for the wider region. This includes developing an Australian supply chain, building local maintenance and upgrade capabilities, and integrating payloads and subsystems to meet the specific requirements of regional customers.”
There is also an option to integrate the Milrem Intelligent Function Integration Kit with other Hanwha’s crewed platforms like the Huntsman and Redback.
Additionally, HDA exhibited an example of its ARION-SMET 6×6 UGV at Land Forces 2026. This vehicle recently won a contract from the Republic of Korea Army, believed to be for around 40 vehicles, and the company believes it has applicability to Australia too.
Turning to the AS9 build programme at the Hanwha Armoured vehicle Centre of Excellence (H-ACE) in Australia, three South Korean-built vehicles have been delivered in a first batch, as well as six Australian-manufactured units. All 45 AS9s and AS10s are to be delivered by the end of 2027, an HDA spokesperson told Asian Military Review .
The Australian Army’s 3rd Brigade received its first 48-tonne AS9 in May 2026. By the end of 2027, three batteries of the 4th Regiment, Royal Australian Artillery will each eventually field six AS9s and three AS10s. This regiment is moving from four M777A2 towed howitzers per battery to six AS9s, and Brigadier Ben McLennan, the 3rd Brigade Commander, said this would increase capability, firepower, mobility and protection by at least 300%.
Meanwhile, all 129 AS21 Redbacks are to be handed over to the Australian Army by the end of 2028. Eight prototype vehicles were manufactured in South Korea as a risk reduction activity, and these are currently undergoing trials in both Australia and South Korea. Full series production is set to commence at H-ACE before the end of this year, with a second production hall currently being fitted out. The H-ACE workforce will peak at 600-650 employees at the height of production.
Hanwha’s ability to set up production and churn out complex armoured vehicles under an accelerated production schedule is extremely impressive. Asked what will happen to the two production halls at H-ACE after these two projects are completed, the spokesperson said there are options such as production for export. “It could be something else, it could be foreign variants. We’ll be doing sustainment work as well on both these fleets of vehicles.”
When Australia cut its order from 450 Redbacks down to 129, it decided to field only two variants – an IFV and joint fires. However, there is hoped that other variants may be of interest to the army.
In fact, Hanwha views the H-ACE as a strategic asset, giving South Korea an alternative production facility outside the troubled Korean Peninsula. An electromagnetic interference and compatibility chamber at H-ACE – the largest in the Southern Hemisphere – is also proving to be a valuable sovereign asset, with outside companies queuing up to use it to test their own platforms.
HDA is also interested in Australia’s medium-range ground-based air defence system (MRGBAD) programme, known as Project Land 6504. Hanwha believes its L-SAM is a suitable solution. It will soon be operational in South Korea, with an even more capable Block 2 version already under development.
Hanwha is also a prodigious producer of munitions in South Korea, and the company stands ready to support the Guided Weapons and Explosive Ordnance (GWEO) enterprise in Australia in its quest to advance sovereign capabilities.
Counter-drone systems are another area where the company has various solutions available, and some of these were on display at Land Forces 2026 in scale model form.

title: At least 33 dead after Russian glide bomb strikes Kramatorsk buses
body:
Firefighters perform cooling and search operations on the burnt shell of a passenger bus following a Russian missile and aerial bomb strike in Kramatorsk, Donetsk Oblast, Ukraine, on Oct. 8, 2026. (State Emergency Service of Ukraine)
A Russian glide bomb strike on two minibuses in Kramatorsk killed 33 people on the morning of Oct. 8, Ukraine's emergency service (DSNS) said.
Twenty-two more people were injured in the Russian attack, Donetsk regional governor Vadym Filashkin said . Fire broke out in at least two busses following the Russian strikes, according to DSNS .
"Russia comes to the Ukrainian land with death. She hits our cities, kills our people and multiplies her crimes every day," Filashkin said .
Допис, поширений Kyiv Independent (@kyivindependent_official)
President Volodymyr Zelensky said that doctors were still fighting for the lives of some of the injured people and warned that the number of dead may still increase. Two dead people could not yet be identified due to the severity of their injuries, he added.
"This strike will not go without our response. Russia is trying to destroy all life in Donbas, and the world needs to react to this," Zelensky said.
The Kramatorsk and Sloviansk military administrations ordered the stop of all public transport.
"The Russians are targeting civilians. For them, a bus with passengers is an attractive target precisely because one hit can kill as many people as possible," Filashkin said.
Across Ukraine's Donetsk Oblast, four more people had been killed and six injured by Russian attacks as of the morning of Oct. 8, prior to the Kramatorsk strike, according to the governor .
In total, Russian forces shelled settlements in the Donetsk region 31 times over the last day, and 256 people, including 32 children, were evacuated from the front line, according to the Donetsk governor.
Russia attacked across Ukraine with 142 Shahed-type drones, 82 of them jet-powered, on the night of Oct. 8, Ukraine's air force said . The air force said that air defense shot down or suppressed 126 of these drones.
On Oct. 2 , Russian forces struck a passenger bus with a first-person-view ( FPV ) drone in the front-line city of Kramatorsk , Donetsk Oblast, at around 7:08 a.m., injuring two people, the Kramatorsk City Council said.
The bus was already operating on its route and carrying passengers when the attack occurred, according to the statement.
Jonas Heins is Assistant Editor at the Kyiv Independent. Before joining, Jonas worked in several think tanks and research institutions across Central and Eastern Europe. He grew up in Germany and holds an MA in European Studies from the University of Padova. Currently he is pursuing an MA in Central and East European, Russian, and Eurasian Studies from the Universities of Glasgow and Tartu.

title: Kenyan and U.S. Forces complete first joint Base Defense Exercise
body: On 27 August 2026, Kenyan and US forces held their first combined, installation-wide base defence exercise (BDEX) at Manda Bay military facility in Kenya. The drill covered the whole coastal facility and drew in personnel from every branch of the Kenya Defence Forces (KDF). The U.S. military described it as the first complete cross-functional integration of combined forces at the site. Manda Bay sits on the Kenyan coast near the Somali border, and it supports counter-terrorism operations across East Africa. A base defence exercise (BDEX) checks how a facility detects, assesses, and responds to an attack. Commanders use it to find gaps before an enemy does. Planners ran several scenarios. Teams practiced emergency response and recovery, drills for suspicious people and activity, and mortar counterfire. Counterfire means locating the point where enemy mortar rounds are fired from and responding quickly. Photos released with the story show KDF personnel escorting a simulated suspect to a holding area and giving simulated medical aid to a US airman. A US explosive ordnance disposal team leader, Master Sgt. Brian Jones, operated a bomb-disposal robot. The two forces use different standard operating procedures, the written routines that govern who does what during an incident. US Army Sgt. 1st Class Christian Wheeler, who handles security force operations for Task Force Seminole, said the drill let soldiers and airmen work with partners they had never trained alongside. “We both want the same thing: the protection of this area, of Kenya, and to defeat the enemy”, he said. Lt. Col. Sandy Van den Mooter, commander of the 475th Air Expeditionary Base Squadron, said the partnership shows up daily in coordination meetings and knowledge exchanges. He said the BDEX is a step toward more complex combined training. His squadron supports KDF efforts against al-Shabaab and other extremist groups. Manda Bay sits on Kenya’s northern coast near the Somali border. The US military uses it to support counter-terrorism operations across East Africa, and AFRICOM describes the exercise as part of keeping that reach intact. Al-Shabaab attacked the airfield in January 2020, killing 3 Americans and destroying aircraft. In May 2024, President William Ruto signed memoranda of understanding (MoU) in Washington to expand the Manda Bay airfield. The exercise also fits a longer pattern of US-Kenyan military ties. In September 2023, the two governments signed a 5-year defence cooperation agreement. Washington has supplied Kenya with six MD 530F light attack helicopters, delivered in 2020 , along with 12 Bastion armoured personnel carriers in 2018 and Metal Shark patrol boats in 2017. In 2024, it sent more MaxxPro mine-resistant vehicles for Kenyan troops deployed in Haiti. In March 2026, the two countries opened a marine range and close-quarters battle complex at Kenya Navy Base Mtongwe in Mombasa County. AFRICOM’s Justified Accord 2026 exercise, which ran from February 23 through March 13, 2026, also ran partly in Kenya. Gen. Dagvin Anderson, who took command of AFRICOM in August 2025, made Kenya his first stop on the continent, visiting Nairobi in September of that year. The exercise also gives Kenyan and U.S. planners a list of coordination gaps to fix, which is the point of a first drill.

title: UN Human Rights Council Adopts Resolution on Georgia’s Occupied Territories by Consensus
body: The UN Human Rights Council adopted by consensus a resolution on “Cooperation with Georgia” in Geneva, addressing the human rights situation in the country’s occupied territories, the Georgian Foreign Ministry reported on October 7. Submitted annually by Georgia since 2017, the resolution reaffirms support for Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity and expresses concern over discrimination and human rights violations against ethnic Georgians in Russia-occupied Abkhazia and Tskhinvali/South Ossetia regions. “As in the previous year, the resolution was adopted by consensus, marking a significant achievement for Georgia and demonstrating the strong support of the international community,” the Foreign Ministry said, adding that deputy Foreign Minister Lasha Darsalia presented the resolution to the UN Human Rights Council. The resolution “once again reaffirms its support for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Georgia within its internationally recognized borders and expresses concern over various forms of discrimination and human rights violations perpetrated against the ethnic Georgian population in the Abkhazia and Tskhinvali regions occupied by Russia,” according to the ministry. It also “underscores the importance of the Geneva International Discussions established pursuant to the 12 August 2008 Ceasefire Agreement,” and “expresses concern over restrictions on access to the occupied territories for international and regional human rights monitoring mechanisms.” The resolution calls for “ensuring the immediate and unhindered access of the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights and international and regional human rights mechanisms to the occupied regions,” the ministry said. It also highlights the importance of European Court of Human Rights judgments delivered between 2021 and 2026, condemning “actions undertaken by Russia towards future illegal annexation of Abkhazia and Tskhinvali regions,” the ministry said. title: Ye Earned $20M From Canceled St. Petersburg Gigs, Kommersant Reports
body:
Controversial American rapper Ye earned approximately $20 million from two canceled concerts in St. Petersburg and is unlikely to return the funds, the business newspaper Kommersant reported Thursday, citing sources familiar with the matter.
Originally scheduled for Oct. 10-11 at Gazprom Arena, Ye’s shows were canceled late last month following weeks of venue disputes and backlash from conservative Russian politicians over his past public support of Nazism.
One source told Kommersant that Ye’s $20 million performance fee includes budget allocations for his staff. Another said Ye is unlikely to return the money because his contracts typically do not contain these types of clauses.
State media previously estimated Ye’s performance fee, excluding the musician’s rider and other expenses, at 1 billion rubles ($11.7 million).
Say Agency, the Moscow-based event organizer, announced it would begin refunding tickets next Monday, Oct. 12.
The first court hearings of at least nine civil lawsuits against Say Agency and ticket operator Intickets are scheduled to begin early next month.
Russian law enforcement agencies have launched a preliminary investigation into Say Agency over possible fraud, Kommersant reported.
Ye, formerly known as Kanye West, previously visited Moscow in 2024 to celebrate the birthday of fashion designer and collaborator Gosha Rubchinskiy. Rumors of a performance at Moscow’s Luzhniki Stadium circulated at the time.
The rapper has drawn controversy in recent years for his antisemitic remarks. He has previously voiced admiration for Adolf Hitler, and in May 2025, he released a song called “Heil Hitler.”
Ye has faced concert cancellations and performance bans in several European countries this year following his comments.
Ye apologized for his remarks in January, attributing them to his undiagnosed brain injury and untreated bipolar disorder.

title: NPP Italy Branch urges new leadership to prioritise unity, reconciliation
body: The New Patriotic Party (NPP) Italy Branch has congratulated the newly elected national officers of the party following their successful election. In a statement signed by its Branch Secretary, Prince Boadu Boateng, the Italy Branch said the election reflects the confidence and trust placed in the new leadership by the party’s rank and file. The branch expressed confidence that the new officers’ experience, commitment and dedication will help strengthen the party and position it for victory in the 2028 General Elections. It also urged the new leadership to prioritise unity, reconciliation, inclusiveness and service as the party begins efforts to rebuild and reconnect with Ghanaians.
