title: Share your technology with us, Ukrainian officer says
body: European governments and companies should stop guarding their high-end technology from Ukraine, because the time spent recreating it from scratch is measured in Ukrainian lives, an officer of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces told the Apex Europe conference in London on Wednesday. Volodymyr, who was identified on stage by his first name and callsign, was asked for a closing message to the room at the end of a panel on deep precision effects chaired by Lieutenant General (Retired) Stuart Skeates. He said: “I would encourage all European companies, and I think it’s mainly for governments, to share with Ukraine technologies, because now, as soon as we come to some high tech, everyone is very closed. If we speak in radars or any other systems, they are extremely expensive, so we can’t afford. And for us to create or duplicate, it takes us a lot of time, and it takes a lot of lives of our people. So please share your technologies, because it gives for general European security and is needed for all of us.” Earlier in the session he had made the same observation about proximity that Ukrainian officers have been making all day, and his version was blunt about where Western firms fall short. “The effectiveness of any product in Ukraine depends on how close is produced with military guys. With Ukrainian companies we don’t have such issues because we are on the same soil. With Western countries there’s always some issues. There are just few companies that open their offices and effectively communicate and exchange,” he said. He also gave a sense of the tempo that shapes everything else, saying “We are using these strikes almost on a daily basis. So it’s like daily routine. That’s not an operation that you are preparing for several weeks,” he said. “That’s why you need SOPs, all the things to be ready, so you’re effective, and learn from mistakes that you’ve done.” Iryna Terekh, the chief executive of the Ukrainian missile manufacturer Fire Point, used her own closing remarks to tell the room to plan as though the worst is coming. She said: “My take would be to work on strategic crisis and risk management from the perspective like you’re preparing for the apocalypse. Be the most anxious and crazy person in the room while you’re planning your production, your procurement policies, everything that you’re about to do, and then you will be very happy when not the worst case scenario will happen, but just the middle one.” She then put a question to the audience that Ukraine answered too slowly itself. “If you ask yourself whether the war is already here or it’s not yet a war, there is just one answer to this question. We already missed this answer in a proper time, in 2014, asking ourselves whether it’s a real war or not a real war. And now we are paying the bloody price for that,” she said, before telling the room to stop showing deep concern and concentrate on what actually matters. Her final point was about the conference she was standing in, and it drew the sharpest reaction of the afternoon. Fire Point had brought video material with it and was not permitted to show it, she said, on the stated grounds that attacks and lethal effects could not be displayed. She said: “It was pretty much the same experience that I had two days ago at a stationery store when I wanted to buy a scissors, and turns out in London you cannot buy a scissors if you don’t show your ID that you’re over 25. Welcome to London. This is a great metaphor when we’re talking about readiness for challenges.” Europe needs to be more honest with itself about where it is standing, she said. The post Share your technology with us, Ukrainian officer says first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: Bomb strike on Kramatorsk kills 12, wounds 14 – National Police
body:
Twelve people were killed and another 14 sustained injuries as a result of a hostile bomb strike on Kramatorsk on Thursday, with two fixed-route passenger buses and an apartment building suffering damage, the National Police of Ukraine reports.

"Today at around 10:00, Russian troops struck Kramatorsk with a UMPB D-30 SN bomb. The projectile hit a city street where two scheduled passenger buses were moving at the time," a statement on the Telegram channel reads.

The National Police report: "As of 11:30, 12 dead and 14 injured people are known."

An investigative-operational group, paramedics, patrol police, State Emergency Service personnel, and other specialized services are currently working at the attack site.

According to the report, two passenger buses and a multi-story residential building were damaged.

title: Fire at Yandex data center, 399 UAVs: aftermath of attacks on Russian regions
body:
MOSCOW, October 8. /TASS/. Air defense systems intercepted and destroyed 399 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions and the Black Sea overnight, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.
A drone attack caused a fire at a data center operated by Russia’s tech giant Yandex in the town of Sasovo in the country’s central Ryazan Region, damaging part of the facility’s infrastructure.
Drone debris fell on the territory of an enterprise in Russia’s southern city of Krasnodar, causing a fire.
A fire also broke out in the industrial zone in the city of Salavat in Russia’s central Bashkortostan Region as a result of falling drone debris after an attack was repelled.
TASS has compiled the main details about the aftermath.
- On-duty air defense systems intercepted and destroyed 399 Ukrainian fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) over Russian regions between 8:00 p.m. Moscow time (5:00 p.m. GMT) on October 7 and 8:00 a.m. Moscow time (5:00 a.m. GMT) on October 8, the Defense Ministry reported.
- According to the ministry, drones were downed over the Belgorod, Bryansk, Volgograd, Voronezh, Kursk, Lipetsk, Oryol, Orenburg, Penza, Rostov, Ryazan, Samara, Saratov, Smolensk, Tambov, Tula, Ulyanovsk, Moscow, Bashkortostan and Tatarstan Regions, the Republic of Crimea and the waters of the Black Sea.
- More than 30 UAVs were destroyed overnight over the town of Kamensk-Shakhtinsky, the Kamensky, Millerovsky, Neklinovsky, Chertkovsky and Sholokhovsky Districts of the Rostov Region, Governor Yury Slyusar said on his Max channel.
- Air defense systems shot down 26 Ukrainian drones over the Voronezh Region overnight, Governor Alexander Gusev wrote in a post on his Max channel.
- Air defense forces intercepted two drones over the Ryazan Region overnight, Governor Pavel Malkov said on his Max channel.
- A drone attack caused a fire at a data center operated by Russia’s tech giant Yandex in the town of Sasovo in the Ryazan Region, damaging part of the facility’s infrastructure, the company’s press service told TASS.
- There were no casualties, with special services carrying out cleanup operations on site.
- The data center’s operations have been fully suspended, and some Yandex services may be unavailable to users.
- Earlier, the Yandex Cloud Telegram channel, used to promptly notify users about service outages and their recovery, reported that power supply issues were affecting the ru-central1-b availability zone.
- The company said that as of 8:26 a.m. Moscow time (5:26 a.m. GMT), the ru-central1-b zone was still unavailable, while all necessary work to transfer the load to other availability zones had been completed.
- Creating new resources in the cloud infrastructure may currently be limited, with specialists still working to address the consequences of the incident.
- All services in other zones are running normally.
- A drone attack caused a fire on the roof of an enterprise in the Sasovsky District of the Ryazan Region, Governor Pavel Malkov reported on his Max channel.
- Windows were also shattered in several private houses.
- There have been no casualties reported so far.
- Emergency services are operating on site.
- A fire broke out in the industrial zone in the city of Salavat in the Bashkortostan Region as a result of falling UAV debris after an attack was repelled, Mayor Marat Zagidullin said on his Max channel.
- Emergency services are working on site.
- The affected enterprise remains operational.
- Drone debris fell on the territory of an enterprise in the city of Krasnodar, the regional emergency response center reported on its Telegram channel.
- Drone fragments damaged the facility and sparked a fire, which was promptly extinguished.
- Emergency and special services are working on site.
- As a result of a Ukrainian drone attack, several settlements have been left without power in western and central Crimea, the Krymenergo state company said on its Max channel.
- Restrictions on electricity consumption are currently in place in Crimea.
- Power lines or grid equipment are promptly shut down when necessary in the energy districts to carry out repair work.
- The timelines for restoring electricity supply currently depend on the stability of the situation and the possibility of conducting repairs safely.
- Due to technological disruptions at a facility of the Tavricheskoye Main Power Grid Enterprise, the Bakhchisaraysky District is facing a difficult electricity supply situation.
- Several settlements have restricted electricity supply.
- Backup power supply schemes are being used.
- Emergency repair crews are working around the clock.
- A man born in 1981 was injured in an overnight drone attack on the Kirovsky District in the city of Donetsk, Alexey Kulemzin, municipal head, said on his Telegram channel.
- The injured man was taken to hospital.
- Windows of a private house were also damaged.
- In the Kalininsky District of the city of Gorlovka in the Donetsk People’s Republic (DPR), two passenger buses were damaged, Ivan Prikhodko, city district head, wrote on Telegram.
- There have been no casualties reported so far.
- The published photos show the driver-side windshields shattered in both vehicles.
- The buses were operating on routes No. 2 and No. 19.

title: Beyond the &
body:
The primary benefit from subscribing to LWN is helping to keep us publishing, but, beyond that, subscribers get immediate access to all site content and access to a number of extra site features. Please sign up today!
Rust has a number of kinds of smart pointers, both in the standard library and defined by users. Still, some operations that are possible with built-in references are not possible to perform with user-defined smart pointers. Tyler Mandry, lead of the Rust project's language team , spoke at RustConf 2026 about the lengthy effort to change that, and make smart pointers just as flexible as built-in references.
He has been working on this problem all through 2026, Mandry said, alongside several other interested members of the language team, under the project name "Beyond the &" . It took a good deal of thought, but the design that they have arrived at should allow a substantially simpler mental model of how pointers and references work. To illustrate the problem that this design solves, he put up an example of a simplified Rust program that calculates some dynamic content and caches it in a hash map. The example uses Rust's map-entry API, which provides a function called or_insert_with() that takes a callback to populate the hash-map entry if it is empty.
This code looks up a cache key ( name ) in the hash map, and either returns a copy of the cached value, or calculates it by substituting name into a template if it doesn't exist. The shared state is accessed using a built-in mutable reference, &mut RenderState . The example works, but it can't safely be shared between threads. Adding a mutex, to allow the cache to be shared, causes the borrow checker to reject the program:
The original code worked, Mandry said, because the borrow checker was able to track that state.cache and state.template were separate fields, so it was safe to access them at the same time. With the addition of the mutex, the borrow checker just sees opaque accesses to a MutexGuard structure, and can no longer tell that the accesses are disjoint — it has to consider the case where the mutable borrow is used to edit the state at the same time that the callback reads from it, causing a potentially invalid data race. A simple fix in this case is to dereference the MutexGuard once, and reborrow the structure behind it:
This constructs a new built-in reference, just like the original code used, so the borrow checker can once again see that the accesses don't interfere with each other. That works, but it's not particularly intuitive. Mandry said that complexity like this contributes to Rust's difficult learning curve. It would be better if user-defined pointer types such as MutexGuard behaved more like built-in references.
Pointer types are everywhere, he continued. And all of them have slightly different semantics. Some pointers can't be safely dereferenced (raw pointers), or can be written to but not read from ( MaybeUninit ), etc. This demonstrates Rust's versatility, but it also makes it hard to come up with a design that works for the many possible pointer types.
The solution the language team settled on, based on the work of Nadrieril and Benno Lossin, was to expose the compiler's internal notion of a "place" to user code. A place is Rust's equivalent of C's left-hand sides (lvalues): a location that values can be read from or written to. The difference between a place and a pointer is that a place is an abstract expression that exists at compile time, such as state.cache , and a pointer is one way to represent a place at run time.
The idea is to create a new handle type for every smart pointer. Often the handle will simply be a wrapper around an unsafe pointer to the same location. Then, the compiler will automatically create handles to represent places referenced by the program. That allows user code to implement traits on a handle type that will affect how the borrow checker interacts with handles which correspond to a custom smart pointer, with a higher degree of flexibility than the existing Deref and DerefMut traits. As an example of what that would look like, Mandry showed how a library author might go about teaching the borrow checker how to handle writes to places that are accessed via a NonNull pointer:
The WritePlace trait would be used to tell the borrow checker that a particular kind of handle (in this case, a handle referencing a NonNull pointer) can be written to, and how. When SAFE is set to false, the borrow checker treats writing to the associated place as an unsafe operation. The actual write is forwarded through to the raw pointer that NonNull wraps. The whole trait implementation is unsafe because an incorrect implementation of the trait could cause the borrow checker to make a mistake and result in unsound behavior.
A corresponding ReadPlace trait encodes how to read from a handle. More interesting are ProjectPlace and BorrowPlace . The former tells the borrow checker how to turn a place containing a structure into a place containing one of its fields. For example, how to turn (the handle for) a MutexGuard<RenderState> into a MutexGuard<String> when the programmer writes state.template . The latter tells the borrow checker how to create a new smart pointer that borrows a given place, the same way that & works for built-in references.
The language team is still debating what the syntax for creating a new smart pointer with BorrowPlace should be. While it could use the same & symbol, that might be confusing and make it harder to use type inference. One proposal is to use an @ symbol instead, but people aren't entirely happy with that either. No matter what syntax is eventually decided on, the BorrowPlace trait encodes all of the information that the borrow checker needs to know in order to safely handle the pointer type. This means that currently built-in behavior can be defined via the same mechanism. For example, this is what an implementation for the built-in reference type &T would look like:
That gives users an example of how to write their own smart pointers that act like references, and gives the standard library maintainers a place to document existing counterintuitive built-in behaviors. With a similar implementation of a handle type for MutexGuard , the earlier render_page() example works without errors. Mandry called it " a small code change for this example, but a big semantic shift. "
Tying smart pointers more closely to the compiler's existing internals has other benefits, however. Currently, it is possible to use pattern matching on a value behind a reference, but not on a value behind a smart pointer — at least without dereferencing the pointer and reborrowing the value behind it. The details exposed by BorrowPlace would be enough to let the compiler safely implement those pattern matches.
One of the criteria that the language team looks for in new features is composability, Mandry said: how well the prospective feature integrates into the existing structures of the language, and how well multiple uses of the feature compose with each other. Handles and places " compose beautifully " because it is just exposing some details of how the compiler already understands and processes the language.
Despite that, exposing places and handles to library code is still a prototype. Mandry asked for help ensuring that the design would work for everyone's use cases; he asked the audience to look at the design documentation and add their own examples of smart pointers with weird semantics. " If you have an abstraction that you want to have more deeply integrated into the language, please help us out by trying this, and telling us about any roadblocks. "
The next part of the design that he intends to flesh out is errors and diagnostic messages. Ideally, users should never see errors mentioning the newly added traits; those would remain internal, and the error messages would explain the problem directly, as they do for built-in references. Even though there is much more work to do before it can become a stable part of the language, Mandry is optimistic about this design. " My hope is that it will let libraries make Rust even more powerful and friendly. "
One audience member wanted to know whether this design would also support destructive pattern matching (a combined operation that takes ownership of a value while matching it against possible patterns, pulling it apart into its component pieces). Mandry said that it would, as long as the developer implemented a VariantPlace trait for the appropriate handle. There are six to eight operations to implement to support every operation on a handle type, and that's one of them, he said.
Another audience member asked whether the design would also work for enumerations in general. Mandry paused, stared out into space for a moment, and then let out a hesitant and elongated yes. Projecting a field from an enumeration in general will probably not be possible, he elaborated, but there has been some exploratory work in that direction. For example, should it be possible to project a field from inside an Option to obtain an Option of the field value? " I don't know the answer, but it's an interesting question, " Mandry remarked, just before time for the session ran out.

Projecting Option fields Posted Oct 2, 2026 19:22 UTC (Fri) by NYKevin (subscriber, #129325) [ Link ] (5 responses) > Another audience member asked whether the design would also work for enumerations in general. Mandry paused, stared out into space for a moment, and then let out a hesitant and elongated yes. Projecting a field from an enumeration in general will probably not be possible, he elaborated, but there has been some exploratory work in that direction. For example, should it be possible to project a field from inside an Option to obtain an Option of the field value? "I don't know the answer, but it's an interesting question," Mandry remarked, just before time for the session ran out. Of course, it is already possible to do this with a combination of Option::as_ref()/as_mut() and Option::and_then(), but this is exactly the kind of unintuitive reborrow shenanigans that they are trying to get away from: let foo: Option<Foo> = ...; let bar: Option<&Bar> = foo.as_ref().and_then(|x| x.bar); It would be much nicer if we could just do this: let foo: Option<Foo> = ...; let bar: Option<&Bar> = &foo.bar; But maybe that's a bridge too far, because &foo.bar looks too infallible. Those type annotations wouldn't be there in real code. I can understand why a different syntax might be preferred here. Projecting Option fields Posted Oct 3, 2026 8:55 UTC (Sat) by matthias (subscriber, #94967) [ Link ] (4 responses) And it would be really nice if we could to this: let foo: Option<Foo> = ...; let bar: Option<&mut Bar> = &mut foo.bar; let bat: Option<&mut Bat> = &mut foo.bat; The code should be totally safe, as the &mut borrows are disjoint. Today the borrow checker does not understand this. Option<&mut Foo> is really just another form of smart pointer and this is not conceptually different from the MutexGuard example. > But maybe that's a bridge too far, because &foo.bar looks too infallible. Actually, it would be infallible. But I get your point. Without the type annotations this can get confusing immediately. Projecting Option fields Posted Oct 4, 2026 1:48 UTC (Sun) by mathstuf (subscriber, #69389) [ Link ] (3 responses) I actually have a case where disjoint mutable access is a problem. I actually put the structure in a nested inline module just to ensure that accidental access is not made. So projection would be OK since the fields are private to any code using them, but any implicit "oh, you can use these two methods via &mut concurrently because they don't use the same variables" would be trouble. Basically, there's a read half of an RwLock (I wish it could be so restricted, but it's only ever used for reading) and a write half of a channel. The read half of the channel uses a write lock on the same RwLock for its bits. The invariant is that the read lock must not be held when pushing into the channel because that read lock could then block the write lock from allowing the channel consumer to continue on that side therefore deadlocking on a full channel. So access to the read lock and channel writer is mediated by a &mut access to a struct containing the two. Rust therefore guarantees that the read lock is disposed of before it allows access to the channel. Projecting Option fields Posted Oct 4, 2026 6:35 UTC (Sun) by matthias (subscriber, #94967) [ Link ] (2 responses) > , but any implicit "oh, you can use these two methods via &mut concurrently because they don't use the same variables" would be trouble. This is all about accessing public fields. Note that there is no function call, i.e. no (). Accessing &mut methods concurrently is a totally different thing. They borrow the whole struct and thus this cannot be possible. In theory one could think of additional annotation to tell the compiler: this method is only accessing .bar and the other method only accesses .baz. This could be checked by the compiler and it could use partial borrows, just as it does now for field access, but you always need to balance the cost (more complicated syntax) with the benefits. Note that there is no function call, i.e. no (). Accessing &mut methods concurrently is a totally different thing. They borrow the whole struct and thus this cannot be possible. Then there is some magic in whatever trait(s) are used to indicate that such projections are allowed through a "pointer" type because they're (likely) going to be defined as methods. For example, Option would need some way to indicate "I project through T "; same with Result (as otherwise it is ambiguous whether &res.err_member is allowed). Just an associated type isn't good enough because Result<T, T> is still ambiguous. In theory one could think of additional annotation to tell the compiler: this method is only accessing .bar and the other method only accesses .baz. This could be checked by the compiler and it could use partial borrows, just as it does now for field access, but you always need to balance the cost (more complicated syntax) with the benefits. I've been involved in the threads proposing such features to Rust on IRLO. My main concern revolves around the effects on the type system and whether such properties of methods is exposed through Fn trait casts or whether those traits become incompatible at some level. FWIW, I have similar concerns around named parameters: are they part of the type or just sugar at the callsite. I know that suggesting features is easy, but implementing them in a way that they really work is hard. So a big thank you to all of you that question every new feature and cause delays in stabilization just to make sure that every stabilized feature is really stable and does not cause more trouble than it brings benefits. Projecting Option fields Posted Oct 4, 2026 1:48 UTC (Sun) by mathstuf (subscriber, #69389) [ Link ] (3 responses) I actually have a case where disjoint mutable access is a problem. I actually put the structure in a nested inline module just to ensure that accidental access is not made. So projection would be OK since the fields are private to any code using them, but any implicit "oh, you can use these two methods via &mut concurrently because they don't use the same variables" would be trouble. Basically, there's a read half of an RwLock (I wish it could be so restricted, but it's only ever used for reading) and a write half of a channel. The read half of the channel uses a write lock on the same RwLock for its bits. The invariant is that the read lock must not be held when pushing into the channel because that read lock could then block the write lock from allowing the channel consumer to continue on that side therefore deadlocking on a full channel. So access to the read lock and channel writer is mediated by a &mut access to a struct containing the two. Rust therefore guarantees that the read lock is disposed of before it allows access to the channel.
