title: US considering new torture charges against Maduro, wife — Report
body: US prosecutors are expected to bring new charges against ousted Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores over the alleged torture of Americans held in Venezuelan government custody, CNN reported Wednesday. Maduro and Flores both already face drug trafficking and firearms charges in the United States after they were snatched from their Caracas compound in an extraordinary US military raid in January. According to CNN, citing people familiar with the investigation, the new torture charges relate to the alleged wrongful detention of over a dozen US citizens in Venezuela during Maduro’s rule. The report said prosecutors are also considering charging several other people for their alleged role in torturing Americans. CNN said charges could be announced as soon as Thursday. Prosecutors declined to immediately comment when contacted by AFP. Maduro and Flores are slated for a trial in New York next June and are currently being held in a Brooklyn jail. US prosecutors claim that Maduro used state power to protect and promote illegal drug smuggling, and that he allied himself with cartels to ship tons of cocaine into the United States. Maduro has denied the four counts he faces: “narco-terrorism” conspiracy, cocaine importation conspiracy, possession of machine guns and destructive devices as well as conspiracy to possess machine guns and destructive devices. Flores has similarly pleaded not guilty to the three counts she faces: cocaine importation conspiracy, possession of machine guns and destructive devices and conspiracy to possess machine guns and destructive devices. She is due in court tomorrow for a hearing on her request to be moved from custody to house arrest due to apparent heart problems. AFP The post US considering new torture charges against Maduro, wife — Report appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Nana Patekar's most memorable roles, from Krantiveer to Dubai-shot Welcome
body: Indian actor Nana Patekar , who died on Thursday aged 75, leaves behind a remarkable body of work spanning nearly five decades, from intense crime dramas and hard-hitting social commentaries to some of Bollywood 's most beloved comedies. Known for his distinctive voice, explosive dialogue delivery and commanding screen presence, Patekar was one of Indian cinema's most recognisable performers. Whether playing a ruthless gangster, an uncompromising police officer or a vulnerable father, he brought an intensity to his characters that few actors could match. Born Vishwanath Patekar in Maharashtra in 1951, he began his career in theatre before making his film debut in Gaman in 1978. He went on to become a major force in both Hindi and Marathi cinema, winning three National Film Awards and receiving the Padma Shri, one of India's highest civilian honours, in 2013. Patekar's career also had a strong connection to the UAE, where he filmed two of his most popular comedies, Welcome and Welcome Back , with locations across Dubai and Abu Dhabi. As tributes pour in for the veteran star, here are 10 of his most memorable performances. Salaam Bombay! (1988) Patekar played Baba Golub, a drug dealer, in Mira Nair 's acclaimed debut feature, which offered an unflinching portrayal of life among Mumbai's street children. The film follows Krishna, a young boy struggling to survive on the city's streets, where he encounters sex workers, drug dealers and other marginalised characters. Patekar's Baba is one of the adults whose troubled lives intersect with the boy's journey. Although the story centres on Krishna, Patekar played a significant supporting role, bringing a menacing presence to a film celebrated for its gritty realism and largely non-professional cast. Salaam Bombay! earned international acclaim and was nominated for Best Foreign Language Film at the 1989 Academy Awards, becoming only the second Indian film to receive a nomination in the category after Mother India (1957). Parinda (1989) Patekar's portrayal of Anna, a ruthless underworld gangster in Vidhu Vinod Chopra's crime drama, remains one of his most celebrated performances. Starring alongside Anil Kapoor, Jackie Shroff and Madhuri Dixit, Patekar played a violent and unpredictable crime boss whose actions drive the film's tragic events. His performance was particularly striking for the way he moved between quiet menace and sudden outbursts of violence, creating a villain as psychologically complex as he was terrifying. The role earned Patekar the National Film Award for Best Supporting Actor and helped establish him as one of Hindi cinema's most formidable character actors. Prahaar: The Final Attack (1991) Patekar took on both directing and acting duties in this military drama, playing Major Pratap Chauhan, a fiercely disciplined army officer who trains young recruits for combat. The character's uncompromising sense of duty gave Patekar ample opportunity to showcase the fiery intensity that would become his trademark. It was also an unusually personal project for the actor, who underwent military training in preparation for the film. Krantiveer (1994) Few films are as closely associated with Patekar as Krantiveer , in which he played Pratap Narayan Tilak, a disillusioned man who becomes a crusader against corruption, injustice and communal hatred. Directed by Mehul Kumar, the action drama became famous for Patekar's powerful monologues, delivered with an anger and conviction that made them instantly memorable. His character's transformation from a seemingly aimless gambler into an outspoken voice against social injustice gave the actor one of his most defining roles. The performance earned him the National Film Award for Best Actor and cemented his reputation as an actor capable of carrying a film through sheer screen presence. Agni Sakshi (1996) In this psychological drama, inspired by Julia Roberts' 1991 film Sleeping with the Enemy , Patekar played Vishwanath, an abusive and obsessive husband whose wife, played by Manisha Koirala, attempts to escape his control. The film explored domestic abuse and the devastating consequences of possessiveness, with Patekar delivering one of his most disturbing performances. The role earned him the Filmfare Award for Best Supporting Actor and demonstrated his willingness to take on deeply unlikeable characters. Khamoshi: The Musical (1996) Patekar showed a very different side of his acting abilities in Sanjay Leela Bhansali 's directorial debut. He played Joseph Braganza, a deaf father whose daughter Annie, portrayed by Manisha Koirala, dreams of pursuing a career in music. The role required a quieter, more physically expressive performance and is one of the strongest examples of Patekar's versatility, showing that Patekar could communicate powerful emotions without relying on his famously forceful voice. Ab Tak Chhappan (2004) Patekar returned to the crime genre with this gritty thriller, playing Sadhu Agashe, a Mumbai police officer specialising in encounters with suspected gangsters. Inspired by the world of police encounter squads, the film follows Agashe as he navigates the blurred lines between law enforcement, organised crime and personal vengeance – his understated performance making the character's capacity for violence all the more unsettling. The film became a cult favourite and was followed by Ab Tak Chhappan 2 in 2015, with Patekar reprising the role. Apaharan (2005) In Prakash Jha's crime drama, Patekar played Tabrez Alam, a powerful gangster whose influence extends into the worlds of politics and organised kidnapping. Set against the backdrop of Bihar's criminal underworld, the film follows a young man, played by Ajay Devgn, who becomes entangled in the kidnapping business. Patekar's Tabrez is a calculating and intimidating figure, using his political connections and criminal influence to maintain control. The performance once again demonstrated his ability to play morally corrupt characters with a combination of charisma, menace and authority. Welcome (2007) and Welcome Back (2015) After years of playing intense and often intimidating characters, Patekar surprised audiences with his comic turn as Uday Shetty in Anees Bazmee's Welcome . The film follows two gangsters, Uday and Majnu Bhai, played by Anil Kapoor, who are desperate to arrange a respectable marriage for Uday's sister. Patekar's hilarious exchanges with Kapoor, particularly his character's increasingly unsuccessful attempts to control his temper, became some of the film's most memorable moments. He reprised the role in Welcome Back (2015), in which the two gangsters attempted to leave their criminal lives behind, only to become entangled in another series of chaotic misunderstandings. Both films also have strong UAE connections. Much of Welcome was shot in Dubai, including at Grand Hyatt Dubai, while its sequel featured locations across Dubai and Abu Dhabi, including Jumeirah Zabeel Saray and Emirates Palace. Welcome Back also premiered at the Dubai International Film Festival in 2014. The films introduced Patekar to a new generation of viewers and cemented Uday Shetty as one of his most beloved characters, proving that his famously intense screen persona could be just as effective when played for laughs. Natsamrat (2016) One of Patekar's most acclaimed later-career performances came in this Marathi-language drama, adapted from the celebrated play by V V Shirwadkar. He played Ganpatrao Belwalkar, an ageing theatre actor who, after retiring from a successful career on stage, struggles with changing family relationships, loneliness and the loss of his former identity. The role allowed Patekar to draw on his theatrical background, moving between grand Shakespearean-style monologues and deeply intimate moments of vulnerability.

title: Karvelas moves to ban Vissi from singing his songs
body: Nikos Karvelas has filed an injunction to stop Anna Vissi performing his songs, taking a public row over the OAKA concert into court. The composer said earlier, in a reply to Vissi carried by Mega, that he knew the Olympic Stadium show was happening but was not proud of it. “You may have plenty of financial resources. The musical ones, I am very much afraid, you will have to start looking for from zero,” he told Vissi and her team. What Karvelas says He rejected the claim that he had been informed and was proud of the production. He said the whole country knew the date. Pride, he said, was another matter. He accused Vissi and Dimitra Mermigka-Kousta of keeping him out of any creative or advisory role so the show would stay as they had planned it. “This is not the Anna I knew, loved and admired,” he said. He argued that her statement confirmed a standing deal for a fee on top of the royalties he collects through the collective management organisation, and that she knew about, and approved, a last-minute change to his seats and a threat to bar him if he tried to sit in the original ones. He called the claim that he demanded €1.5 million “a crude lie.” He said he asked for the same fee as under their Kallimarmaro agreement, plus whatever the collecting society owed him. The reply, he said, was half or nothing, and the half only if he never spoke against her. He refused, saying he would not trade his opinion for money. He also denied taking money from Mr Koustas, and mocked the suggestion of a €500,000 “favour” or loan. “I never received money from Mr Koustas,” he said. He added that while they worked together they had supported each other, and that this was not charity. “Once there was no Vissi without Karvelas, and the reverse. What I owe her, she owes me.” The substance, he said, is the songs and the performance, not the money. He said the exchange with the crowd at the Olympic Stadium was not the same as her other shows. Vissi’s lawyer Michalis Dimitrakopoulos, Vissi’s lawyer, told SKAI that Karvelas cannot legally bar her from the songs. The economic rights, he said, have been assigned to the collecting society. The moral right stays with the composer, but a ban would require a court to find that Vissi distorts the work. She has sung them for more than 35 years, he said, and the chance of a ban succeeding is small. He repeated that Karvelas asked for €1.5 million days before the OAKA concert, that Vissi had lent him more than €500,000, and that production had already paid €350,000 in royalties. The post Karvelas moves to ban Vissi from singing his songs appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: Did Christine Frechette face a ‘glass cliff’? Expert points to broader political pattern
body:
Women who rise to the top of political parties are often doing so in circumstances where the odds of success are already stacked against them, according to a University of Calgary political scientist who studies gender and politics.
The phenomenon is often described as a “glass cliff” — a term borrowed from business research that refers to women being elevated to leadership positions when organizations or political parties are already in crisis. But Dr. Melanee Thomas says that concept can oversimplify what is happening.
In an interview with Global News Wednesday, Thomas said she prefers the term “gendered political opportunity structure,” arguing that women are not passive participants being set up to fail. Rather, she says they are political actors who recognize that opportunities to lead are often more available when parties are struggling.
Thomas said political leadership positions, particularly those in government, are among the most coveted jobs in politics. Yet when parties are thriving, leadership contests tend to attract a familiar profile of candidates, often men with traditional political resumes. Women, she said, face steeper barriers when competing in those circumstances.
Instead, opportunities frequently arise when parties are electorally vulnerable or attempting to recover from scandal, internal turmoil or voter dissatisfaction.
The discussion has resurfaced following the recent election loss and resignation of former Quebec premier Christine Fréchette, who became leader of the governing Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ) party months before an election after the departure of longtime premier François Legault.
Support for the CAQ was at an all-time low and the party had been plagued by scandals and troubled projects, including the SAAQclic fiasco, a controversial bill to change doctors’ pay, the failed Northvolt project and more.
Thomas said any leader would have faced significant challenges trying to rebrand a party that had been defined for years by scandal and its previous premier.
But she said it would be wrong to ignore the role gender plays in determining who gets selected to lead parties during difficult periods, pointing to former Quebec premier Pauline Marois as an example.
Thomas said Marois had long-standing leadership ambitions and extensive cabinet experience, but only became leader of the Parti Québécois after the party had entered a period of crisis.
“Women want the power jobs in politics,” Thomas said. “I think they are strategic enough to read the room and know what their chances are going to be when things are really good, and know that their only chance might be when things aren’t great.”
She drew comparisons to former prime minister Kim Campbell, who became Progressive Conservative leader and prime minister shortly before the party suffered a historic defeat in the 1993 federal election.
“Was it Kim Campbell’s fault? No,” Thomas said. “But do people still blame her specifically for it? Not everyone, but some absolutely do.”
Research suggests women politicians often face different standards than their male counterparts , Thomas said. She cited experimental studies showing some voters continue to hold stereotypical views about women’s suitability for political office. Other studies have found female candidates are often required to demonstrate stronger qualifications than men to receive similar evaluations.
“Women candidates have to be significantly more credentialed,” she said. “They have to have way better CVs to be evaluated the same way as men.”
Even when women secure leadership roles in favourable political conditions, research suggests they can face greater pressure and are more likely to be pushed out sooner than male leaders, Thomas said.
Still, the political scientist argues that women should not avoid leadership opportunities simply because success is uncertain.
Politics is inherently competitive and most candidates, regardless of gender, do not win, she argued. Participation remains essential to a healthy democracy, she told Global News over the phone.
“I’ve had people be kind of like, why do women put themselves forward if they’re likely to lose? And I was just like, that’s also most men in politics, though, right? So are they a failed candidate, or are they an essential part of the democratic process?”
She added that young women and girls need to see examples of women bidding for roles, sometimes getting them and succeeding, but also failing, surviving that failure and continuing their careers. “Women have to be willing to participate and lose. That is a core feature of democracy.”
“Anybody who wants to do it should go for it.”
Research has shown that as more women are elected , girls and women are more likely to see politics as a space where they belong , she said.
Instead of focusing solely on whether female leaders succeed or fail, the University of Calgary professor said the more important question is why women continue to be viewed differently than men when navigating the same political challenges.
“Many politicians do good things, and many do things people think are dumb. The fact that when women do those things it is seen as a reflection of women as a whole, while men are not seen as a reflection of all men, shows exactly why this pattern persists.”
On Monday, 57 women were elected to Quebec’s national assembly — about 45 per cent of the 127 seats — slightly down from the number elected in 2022.

title: Hockey N.S. launches pilot program to teach young players about consent, hazing
body:
The head of a provincial body that governs organized hockey in Nova Scotia is touting a new educational program that targets players after a series of hazing incidents and assaults have rocked the sport.
“There’s been several incidents in hockey over the years and it’s been an area of need,” said Michael Field, the executive director of Hockey Nova Scotia in an interview.
The organization has teamed up with a local non-profit that provides services to survivors of sexual assault to create the program. It aims to teach 13- and 14-year-old players about how to engage in healthy team bonding exercises and how to avoid crossing the line.
“We feel there’s a need to educate players on team culture,” Field said. “Some teams do a great job at it and some team sports don’t. We just want to do all we can to ensure that … team culture is being built in a healthy manner.”
Field said more than 2,000 minor hockey players of all genders will participate in the mandatory program.
It emerged as families and coaches reacted to news reports last February about a hazing incident and sexual assault involving a junior hockey team in Nova Scotia.
A number of them sent emails expressing their concerns about the issue to Avalon, the non-profit that is now working with the hockey association, explained Kailee Wakeman, the director of operations at the centre.
Two under-15 minor hockey players in Colchester County, northeast of Halifax, were charged with sexual assault following the incident during a team sleepover last fall.
One of the accused players changed his plea to guilty last month, while the other pleaded not guilty in May.
Wakeman said Avalon hosted a webinar in February to teach parents and coaches how to discuss consent and hazing with young players.
Field said his association then reached out to Avalon to see if it could develop a version of the webinar for players.
Wakeman said the new program aims to teach players how to recognize discrimination, harassment, pressure, hazing and coercion.
“We’re hoping … that we can help change team cultures because sports cultures can often include hazing in ways that people think it strengthens a team and there’s so much research that shows that it doesn’t,” Wakeman said in an interview Wednesday.
The players will participate in two sessions, said Wakeman. The first will teach them about bodily autonomy, respecting boundaries and consent, while the second will teach them how to respond to situations that may cause harm to their teammates.
“So many people call that bystander intervention, but we’re going to frame it through the lens of a caring team environment,” she said. “Looking out for one another rather than placing each other in harmful situations.”
Wakeman said educating the under-15 age group is an important place to start when trying to change behaviours that can lead to a toxic culture.
“We are hoping to reach athletes young enough that … we can start to change the narrative early,” she said.
Dee Dooley, an education adviser with Dalhousie University’s sexual violence prevention program, is helping to facilitate the pilot program along with varsity hockey players in the province.
Dooley, who has also researched sexual violence prevention among varsity student-athletes, said culture in sport is often passed down between generations.
“The importance of peer influence and peer leadership can’t be overstated,” she said. “Culture is really created by the people within it.”
Hazing and sexual violence have plagued hockey in Canada for decades.
In 2023, a Quebec Major Junior Hockey League player filed an application for a class-action lawsuit against the league alleging he was abused during hazing rituals in the 1990s.
The year prior, Hockey Canada came under fire after it was revealed that an undisclosed settlement had been paid to a woman who alleged she was sexually assaulted by members of Canada’s 2018 World Junior hockey team. Five players were charged with sexual assault in 2024 related to the incident and were acquitted of all charges last year.
Jaqueline Moore, a research assistant with the project and a former varsity athlete, said while educating players is an important part of changing hockey’s culture, everyone needs to play a role.
“We also need coaches involved, we need administration involved, we need parents involved,” she said. “It’s really going to take a community.”
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 7, 2026.

title: Car parts giant lends engineers to German missile maker
body: ZF, one of the world’s largest automotive suppliers, is providing engineering services to Diehl Defence on selected development projects, and is seconding its own specialists to work alongside Diehl staff, according to the company . The work spans the development process from concept studies through to testing and validation, taking in design, system development, layout and construction. ZF says the aim is to shorten development cycles, bring expertise in industrial scaling in at an early stage and develop solutions for future defence applications, and it contributes established development processes, scalable organisational structures and long experience in producing quality-critical systems. Diehl Defence keeps responsibility for system requirements and for defence-specific system integration. Testing and validation make up the other half of the arrangement. ZF supplies test benches, simulation environments and test methods to examine components under realistic conditions, with structured validation intended to establish quality, safety and reliability early rather than late, and the company notes that the physical closeness of the two firms’ sites shortens response times. Alongside conventional engineering services, the two companies are using temporary employment arrangements that put ZF specialists directly into Diehl projects on site, which the firm says allows short coordination channels and close integration of the teams. ZF employs around 153,000 people across 162 production sites in 29 countries and reported sales of €38.8 billion in 2025, built on gearboxes, chassis and driveline components for carmakers, a market that has been contracting painfully as European vehicle production falls and the move to electric drive removes the need for much of what it has historically sold. Defence is where the growth is, and German spending commitments since 2022 have created demand that the established defence manufacturers cannot meet from their own engineering capacity. Diehl Defence, best known for the IRIS-T family of air defence missiles, has been among the busiest firms in Europe as orders for ground-based air defence have multiplied, and finding enough engineers has become as much of a constraint as finding enough factory space. Rheinmetall has gone furthest in making the same move in the opposite direction, converting automotive plants to defence production, and the pattern of engineering capacity moving from cars to weapons is now visible across German industry. The post Car parts giant lends engineers to German missile maker first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: Freezing conflict will not help resolve situation in Ukraine — Kremlin spokesman
body:
MOSCOW, October 8. /TASS/. Freezing the Ukrainian conflict will not help resolve it, comprehensive measures are required, Russian Presidential Spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said.
Russia is convinced that a settlement in Ukraine must be comprehensive, piecemeal measures will not suffice, the Kremlin spokesman explained.
"Let's put it this way: a temporary halt or a freeze won't help either," he emphasized.

title: Seoul recalls ambassador to Ukraine amid dispute over North Korean POW disclosure
body:
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of South Korea announced on Thursday, October 8, that it is recalling its ambassador to Ukraine against the backdrop of an ongoing diplomatic dispute.
"The government has decided to recall the ambassador to Ukraine. The government hopes for a smooth resolution of all outstanding issues between the two countries and will continue consultations with the Ukrainian side for this purpose," the statement reads.
As previously reported, during his address at the United Nations General Assembly in September, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced that Ukraine had transferred two North Korean servicemen captured last year.
The disclosure drew sharp criticism from Seoul, which maintained that the transfer was intended to remain strictly confidential to ensure the safety of the prisoners of war and their families, asserting that Kyiv had agreed to keep the arrangement private.
While Ukrainian officials disputed the existence of a formal binding non-disclosure agreement and defended the transparency of the decision, South Korean authorities stated that Kyiv's subsequent response and explanations fell short of expectations, ultimately prompting the decision to recall the diplomatic mission head for consultations.

title: AI breakthroughs in robotics won’t change your life any time soon
body: The story is a collaboration between MIT Technology Review and Aventine , a non-profit research foundation that creates and supports content about how technology and science are changing the way we live. A robot shaped like a human—white with a black head and torso—has been popping up on video feeds. Perhaps you’ve seen it dance or pass popcorn, put trash in a bin, vacuum, or press the button of a microwave. Or maybe you’ve watched it fall backward while handing out water bottles or struggle to iron a shirt. This would be Tesla’s Optimus , an AI-powered humanoid robot that Elon Musk, the company’s CEO, believes will be “not just Tesla’s biggest product ever, but probably the biggest product ever ,” headed to work on factory floors and, later, in our homes. Eventually it “will have human and then superhuman dexterity,” he told shareholders in July. Optimus robots could automate almost all human labor—from hauling sheet metal to folding laundry—for as little as $20,000 each, Musk argues. Speaking at the World Economic Forum’s annual meeting in Davos, Switzerland, in January, he predicted they could be on sale to the public by the end of 2027. Musk is not alone in his evangelism. Marc Andreessen, cofounder and general partner of the Silicon Valley venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz, has said that robotics could become the “biggest industry in the history of the planet.” In January, Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, said that humanoid robots would match human-level ability this year . According to Morgan Stanley, the number of robots that “resemble and act like humans” is likely to reach nearly 1 billion by 2050, creating a market worth over $5 trillion . Elon Musk predicts that Tesla’s Optimus humanoid could be one the world’s best-selling products. For now, it’s most often seen handing out food and drinks at Tesla events. SIPA VIA AP IMAGES Such proclamations are in large part fueled by the idea that the same AI advances behind tools like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude will enable a new generation of robots to imitate human movement the way chatbots imitate human language. But many robotics researchers are skeptical, arguing that such assumptions minimize the challenges of using an intelligence built on language and images to master the infinite variability of the physical world. “None of those companies [building humanoid robots]—absolutely none of them—has any idea how to make those robots smart enough to be useful,” Yann LeCun, often referred to as one of the godfathers of AI, said at another event during the January Davos conference. Researchers also point out that the tendency to conflate humanoid robots made to resemble people with so-called generalist machines able to learn and perform multiple tasks is misleading. ”It’s very easy to make a robot that looks like a person,” explains Jonathan Hurst, cofounder and chief robot officer of Agility Robotics and professor of robotics at Oregon State University. “It is dramatically more difficult to make a machine that moves or behaves dynamically or physically like a person.” These tensions—over whether all-purpose humanoid robots are just around the corner or nowhere in sight, and whether current forms of AI are all that’s needed to perfect them—are playing out in robotics labs across the country, where the hype over timelines is obscuring painstaking but meaningful progress. A decade or so ago, a series of breakthroughs led to a generative AI revolution that turned the long-imagined possibility of artificial intelligence into reality. Roboticists—though they disagree on exactly when this will happen—believe that an equally transformative revolution is possible in robotics, one that will endow machines with physical intuition and fluidity that has long been out of reach. As progress in robotics inches forward, the question is whether the same methods and tools that fueled advances in AI are enough to get there, or if an entirely new path is required. Robots meet advanced AI To see one of the smartest robot brains working today, it’s worth looking at what Google DeepMind can do with a piece of equipment called ALOHA 2, short for “A Low-cost Open-source Hardware System for Bimanual Teleoperation.” Roboticists have long clashed over whether a humanlike form is necessary for generalist robots, with proponents arguing that it will help them slot into the world as it exists and detractors saying it’s not worth the trouble. ALOHA 2 reflects this second way of thinking. Not much to look at, it’s just a pair of arms, some grippers, and a couple of cameras. But despite its seeming simplicity, it is a workhorse for researchers at Google DeepMind, who use it to test their most advanced AI for robotics system, Gemini Robotics, in their various labs. When controlled by Gemini Robotics, ALOHA 2 becomes more of a generalist robot, in the sense that it can perform any number of tasks based on examples it’s been trained on. Ask it to pack a lunchbox and, as evidenced by a video of this exercise , it can use two pincer grippers to delicately place a piece of white bread into a Ziploc bag, close it, place a bunch of grapes in a Tupperware container, secure the lid, and then carefully move the items into a lunchbox before zipping it up. It’s not a great lunch. But the fact that the robot can put it together represents an objective step forward from what was possible even, say, three years ago. This is in large part due to AI and its impact on what are known as robot policies, which controls how a general-purpose robot will need to assess and understand its surroundings, plan how to move within them, and then perform its task correctly. The ALOHA 2 robot isn’t much more than two mechanical arms on a bench top, but it serves as a testbed for cutting-edge AI robotics models. These animations are based on human teleoperation of the robot arms, data that is used to train Google DeepMind’s models. (Video: Google DeepMind / Stanford University / Hoku Labs ) Historically, these policies were based on rules developed by engineers who hard-coded them into the robot’s software—thousands of lines of code that would determine each millimeter of a robot’s movements in hundreds of tasks. What’s been happening for the last few years—and what is largely responsible for the optimism about generalist robots—is that robot policies are being handed over to advanced AI systems instead of being coded into the robot’s software. This first happened with VLMs, or vision-language models. These are similar to large language models, but they’re trained on images as well as words. Show a VLM a picture of a coffee spill and ask it to find a tool to clean up the mess, and it can identify a nearby cloth. This sort of immediate contextual understanding didn’t exist a couple of years ago when robot policies were hard-coded. Next came vision-language-action models, which enable robots to assess their environment and take action within it. The models do this by adding yet another component: motion commands. VLAs are trained on a series of images or videos related to performing a given task along with associated data about how a robot arm moves to perform it. That movement data is typically collected through teleoperation, in which a human uses remote controls to lead a robot through an action. This sort of training allows the AI to learn how to command the robot to move and operate during a given task. Place a VLA-powered robot in front of a desk and tell it to “close a laptop” or “wrap up the headphone wire,” and it will survey the scene, identify the relevant object, plan a way to execute the request, and then swing its arms into action—at least if it has seen this task accomplished before. The Gemini Robotics model is a VLA, trained on many hours of human demonstrations depicting a vast array of different actions. As a result, it can perform relatively complex tasks like picking up snow peas with kitchen tongs, doing origami, or putting together a simple lunch. It’s impressive, but there’s a glaring limitation: For now, if a robot controlled by a VLA is asked to perform a task that falls outside its training set, it’s highly likely to fail. “Thinking about the space of all tasks, a real generalist policy would be able to do everything along that spectrum,” says Edward Johns, a robotics professor at Imperial College London. Today, though, a Gemini Robotics model can do only “a few things here and a few things there.” The search for true generality So how do we get robots to be able to do more things? The usual answer is probably not surprising: Train them on more data. More data, the thinking goes, equals more examples, and more examples equals more generality. Google DeepMind, for instance, wants to pull together “as much data as possible,” says Pannag Sanketi, a former tech lead in robotics at the company who’s currently working on his own AI robotics project . But where to get it? Large language models had the benefit of oceans of existing text for training. There is no corresponding pool of high-quality physical demonstrations on which to train robots. Researchers have a few ways to make up for this, but all have flaws. One is to employ large numbers of people to create and collect teleoperation data (costly and time-consuming). Another is to train VLAs on videos of people performing activities (the resulting data quality is poor). Yet another is to deploy robots in the real world and use data collected from those experiences to further refine AI models (robots aren’t safe or reliable outside labs). Sanketi thinks a “multi-prong” approach that uses data collected from all these sources is the most likely path forward. But the belief that training data alone is the answer is far from universal . Agility’s Hurst describes it as “a fundamentally flawed premise.” The issue is that tasks in the real world quickly explode in complexity. If you’re trying to, say, make coffee, there are myriad variables: No two kitchens are identical; coffee machines work in different ways; different cups require different grips; coffee grounds, hot water, and milk all need to be handled differently. Even this simple task requires understanding an ever-changing menu of possibilities. Achieving generality through VLAs, Hurst argues, would require “complete data coverage of all of the things that [a robot] could ever do.” Or, in other words, an almost infinite pool of training data. LeCun is dismissive of the whole approach. “The [AI] approaches that have been successful for language do not work for high-dimensional, continuous, noisy data”—the kind of data that is commonplace in robotics, he said in Davos. “You have to use something else.” The leading contender for “something else” is the so-called world model—a form of AI trained less on text than on a combination of video, three-dimensional scans, and sensor data and built to predict the outcomes of actions in the real world. The aim is to build models that possess an internal representation of reality precise enough to capture how the physical world actually operates—how objects move, collide, fall, and deform. If roboticists could train machines in simulations faithful enough to real-world physics, development would become faster, cheaper, and safer, reducing the need for real-world testing. Even more transformative, robots equipped with world models could reason about their surroundings rather than merely reacting to them, helping them anticipate the consequences of an action before taking it. Google DeepMind’s latest AI models for robots are increasingly dextrous, if rather slow and erratic Companies like Nvidia and Google are working on the technology, and investor cash is pouring into high-profile startups. World Labs, cofounded by the Stanford AI researcher Fei-Fei Li, raised $1 billion in funding in February and was acquired by AMD at the end of September for $8.2 billion. AMI Labs, cofounded by LeCun (formerly Meta’s chief AI scientist), also raised $1 billion in March . Yet by their own admission, it is still early days. Late last year Li described the field as “nascent,” adding that “foundational approaches are still being established.” In a June Substack she described daunting challenges . For now, world models are a promising area of research rather than an immediate route to general-purpose robotics, but we are beginning to see glimmers of what they could achieve. One such glimpse came with a small but potentially significant leap forward that took place in a San Francisco robotics lab last April. A breakthrough? In the heart of San Francisco’s Mission District, the startup Physical Intelligence—or PI (as in π), as it likes to be known—is focused on developing a universal brain that could, theoretically, turn any robot into a generalist. Using an everything-including-the-kitchen sink approach to training AI models for robots, the company recently observed a hint of what a robotic brain equipped with a world model could be capable of. In 2024, PI published details of its first generalist robotics system, called π0, a VLA it claimed was the “most capable and dexterous generalist robot policy to date.” The model was initially trained on a 10,000-hour proprietary collection of human demonstrations gathered through teleoperation as well as several open-source robot datasets. A version released in spring 2025, π0.5 , was trained on a wider variety of datasets, including labeled images from the web, lending it more versatility. A fall 2025 update, π0.6 , added reinforcement learning to the model. Each update yielded important improvements to the model’s performance, increasing its menu of abilities from slowly folding laundry to putting things away in new environments to completing tasks like folding boxes with a higher success rate. Then, in April 2026, π0.7 seemed to catapult PI into new territory. This version makes use of a less powerful world model that generates images of steps necessary to perform a task. As the robot undertakes the job, this “lightweight” model feeds it snapshots of what to do next. How do you teach a robot to use a knife? At the startup Physical Intelligence, it begins with designing the right AI architecture, which includes components dedicated to language, vision and motion. This will help it relate commands — “hey robot, chop my vegetables!” — to appropriate actions. WINNI WINTERMEYER Data to train the AI can come from many sources, but one of the most important is human demonstrations. An employee at the startup controls a robot arm through teleoperation, exposing the AI to the task of slicing a zucchini. WINNI WINTERMEYER Researchers train the AI model on hundred of examples of human demonstrations, as well images from the web and first-person video. WINNI WINTERMEYER Once the AI is trained, the team presents it a task it has not seen before, such as chopping this summer squash. When a robot hasn’t seen the exact task before — it may wonder if that’s a yellow zucchini, or an unusual banana — it can mess up. But any failures can be used to help refine the model. WINNI WINTERMEYER The company claims that the model exhibits the first signs of compositional generalization, a term for AI systems’ ability to perform skills they’ve never been exposed to by recombining ones learned in their training data. One test involved asking a model to “load a sweet potato into the air fryer”—a task it had never previously encountered. In a demonstration video, the machine futzes around a little, makes a few false starts, and eventually manages a reasonable effort, though it doesn’t finish the task completely. Sergey Levine, a professor at the University of California, Berkeley, and a cofounder of PI, is excited by the potential: “It’s actually the first time that we’ve convincingly seen that kind of compositional generalization, where we can basically ask the model to do tasks that we did not specifically collect data for and train it to do, and it’ll actually make a passable attempt.” The success led the team to wonder how the model was able to achieve such a feat. After some digging, they found snippets of relevant labeled teleoperation data lurking in the training material, including two examples of a human controller using the robot to push an air fryer basket into the fryer. Those shreds of data might have been enough to enable π0.7 to almost air-fry a sweet potato. For now, it remains unclear just how impressive π0.7’s abilities to generalize are. Still, given how fleeting the model’s exposure to air fryers had been, it offers a glimpse into how far cutting-edge research can currently take robots. “70% success is like it doesn’t work” You might be sensing a disconnect between the halting baby steps robots are making in labs—“Look! It put a sweet potato into an air fryer!”—and the dazzling, lifelike nimbleness on view during many demonstrations and videos, where robots are seen doing everything from dancing on a stage to courteously serving drinks . Such demos often don’t clearly reveal a key fact: In many instances, humans are controlling the robot or have carefully scripted its actions. (The robot that appeared onstage with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang in March 2025, for example, seemingly responding to his instructions and following him around, was remote-controlled by what its makers called “a puppeteer behind the scenes.”) For now, fully autonomous motion planning so that a robot knows where it should go—especially in new, chaotic environments like a construction site or a unfamiliar home—remains a largely unsolved challenge. A bigger challenge still—albeit one that is often related—lies in getting robots to tackle larger, more ambiguous jobs that include multiple tasks and require decisions about how and in what order they’re done. This would be the difference between a robot that can put a plate into a microwave and one that can successfully respond to the prompt “Make dinner” by exploring the refrigerator, chopping ingredients, and firing up the stove. Google DeepMind’s best attempts at something like this—which involved asking its robot to survey a kitchen and pack all the ingredients for a mushroom risotto into a basket—have so far resulted in failure. Adding to the challenge, a practical robot must essentially get it right every time. With VLAs, “people are very excited when their result goes from 50% success to 70% success,” says Marc Raibert, founder of Boston Dynamics. “But 70% success is like it doesn’t work, right?” Demonstrations often make robots look useful, but the machines still mess up far too often to be used reliably in homes and factories. AP IMAGES, SHUTTERSTOCK, 1X, AGILITY ROBOTICS, GOOGLE DEEPMIND The few humanoids that are being tested in real-life settings are undertaking extremely limited tasks in tightly controlled environments. They’re far from generalists. Agility has hundreds of robots deployed across trials in facilities owned by GXO Logistics, Amazon, and Schaeffler, according to the company. But for now, Hurst says, the robots are targeting simple tasks such as moving bins and totes around. Even then, he adds, it took years to develop robots safe enough for logistics firms to even contemplate using them. For his part, Elon Musk claimed in May 2025 that “ thousands ” of his Optimus robots would be working at Tesla factories by the end of the year, but in January of this year he said that the company had only “some of the Tesla Optimus robots doing simple tasks in the factory.” While humanoids are starting to venture onto the factory floor, making the jump to households will be even more difficult. Right now, should you so desire, you can preorder the 1X Neo home robot , expected to be ready for delivery sometime later this year. Yours for $20,000, it promises to take on “the boring and mundane tasks around the house”—putting away dishes, answering the door, tidying the living room—“so you can focus on what matters to you.” The idea is for this five-foot-six-inch robot to one day perform all those tasks autonomously, but for now a remote human operator is needed for it to do most things. (Yes, a person would need permission to peer into your home through the robot’s cameras.) Asked how long it will be until fully autonomous robots are ready for domestic work, Hurst said, “If I had to pick a number, I’d say it’s 10 years before robots are … actually doing useful things in people’s homes.” When that happens, the robots might well be Chinese, as China is well ahead of the West in terms of production. Nearly 90% of the roughly 15,000 humanoid robots shipped in 2025 were made by Chinese companies, according to the market intelligence company Omdia and the Chinese robotics firm Unitree. One model produced by Unitree, which shipped more humanoid robots than any other company last year, costs less than $6,000 . Such an affordable price could go a long way toward making robots more attractive to consumers, though the company expects its machines to be used in industrial applications first. (If you’re wondering who is buying all these Chinese robots, by the way, the AP recently reported that orders come predominantly from corporate and academic labs and state-owned enterprises.) We’ve been here before The dream of building a humanoid robot runs deep: As far back as 1495, Leonardo da Vinci sketched out designs for a mechanical knight, controlled by cables and pulleys. Through the 20th century, machines of sci-fi fever dreams have come and gone. Westinghouse’s Elektro was a sensation at the 1939 World Fair. GETTY IMAGES Westinghouse’s seven-foot-tall box on legs, Elektro, hit the New York World’s Fair in 1939, smoking a cigarette . WABOT-1, built by Waseda University in Japan in 1973, was the first full-scale, programmable humanoid robot. Honda’s ASIMO, unveiled in 2000, was probably the first such machine to prove at all competent—it could, at least to some degree, climb steps, recognize faces, and autonomously move through spaces. But the robot was discontinued in 2018, unable to advance far enough beyond what it could do in demonstrations to be useful. All, at the time, were impressive—even jaw-dropping—feats of engineering. But none were ready to navigate the real world. Today’s robots, even with the transformative power of advanced AI, still face the same existential challenge.

title: Flock is catching flak. Experts say other police surveillance tools are more worrisome
body:
A police officer monitors video surveillance in the real-time crime center at the Irvine Police Department in California in 2024. It's unclear whether Irvine uses Axon Fusus surveillance software or another software in its crime center. Paul Bersebach/MediaNews Group/Orange County Register via Getty Images hide caption
Police officers in cities across the U.S. are quick to extol the virtues of real-time crime centers as a game changer that helps them find missing children, monitor large events from the skies and scope out dangerous scenes before putting an officer in harm's way.
Hundreds of police departments have one of these central hubs, which have existed for years. But many are now being powered with AI software, such as Fusus, from the public-safety technology giant Axon.
Fusus, by Axon's own description , is a "rapidly deployable real-time crime center in the cloud." It functions like the brain of a crime center, synthesizing the data it pulls in and allowing police command centers to watch an entire city from one place.
Flock cameras, the automated license plate readers (ALPRs), have faced intense backlash in recent months amid stories of abuse. Yet privacy experts say they're just the tip of the iceberg when it comes to police surveillance.
"I have been watching the debate about Flock with a little bit of puzzlement," says Andrew Guthrie Ferguson, a law professor at George Washington University. "Because real-time crime centers have not just ALPR cameras and sensors, but video analytics and drones and essentially a way to create a visual single-pane-of-glass vision of what's going on in a city, with time machine capabilities where you can go back and investigate crime."
Tools like Axon Fusus, which is a leader in this type of software, also pull in footage and data from police body cameras, law enforcement dashcams, 911 dispatch, gunshot detectors and surveillance cameras, including sometimes those of private businesses that opt in.
Its use is growing fast. In 2024, the technology news site 404 Media reported that just over 100 law enforcement agencies had deployed Fusus, which was then its own company and was acquired by Axon that year. The number of law enforcement agencies using the tool has more than doubled since then, according to Axon.
Police officers in departments that use Fusus told NPR that the tool serves as a time-saver and a force multiplier for their agencies.
"We could put analysts in a room and have them access 40 different systems," says Benjamin Weir, a captain with the Oklahoma City Police Department. "But that slows them down. So the biggest leveraging factor for a real-time information center to be productive is to have software that can incorporate all these things into one usable area."
Quincy Whitner, a lieutenant with the Greenville County Sheriff's Office in South Carolina, says Fusus helped his department find a man who shot a police officer and fled the scene, by combining city surveillance footage with license plate data.
"Instead of having to go to a million different systems, a million different places to find answers, we can get it in one platform in one place somewhat instantaneously," says Whitner.
But that push-of-a-button mentality is exactly what makes privacy experts nervous.
Rachel Levinson-Waldman, director of the Liberty and National Security Program at New York University's Brennan Center for Justice, says even a few decades ago, there were more hurdles to overcome when police officers wanted to surveil members of the community. They might have to physically follow someone or do a stakeout. It took time, staffing and resources.
"In addition to all of the things that you would want in place requiring some kind of criminal predicate to launch it, there is just this kind of organic friction that imposes some constraints," she says. "As that friction gets lifted, it becomes easier and easier to do investigations, to look at people and even to pull up broad-scale information."
Police told NPR that they understand those concerns but that the good — the potential for stopping and solving crime — outweighs the bad — the potential for misuse and mass surveillance.
"I understand people's concerns, but if you're not up to no good, we're not looking at you. We are looking at people who are committing crimes," says Michelle Iezzi, deputy director of the Operational Intelligence Division at the Montgomery County Police Department in Maryland.
Axon did not respond to multiple requests for comment. But CEO Rick Smith said on the latest earnings call that the company strongly values privacy: "We just have to be thoughtful and understand those concerns and say, 'Look, this is a tool to amplify human ability, not to replace human judgment.'"
But there is broad potential for abuse when a police department is always watching, privacy experts say; surveillance technology can sweep up innocent people by mistake, and it can enable targeting.
"What happens if there is a government that wants to silence a particular group or even a particular person? And you just built the architecture of surveillance that makes that super-easy," says Ferguson, the George Washington University law professor.
Courts are moving slowly in deciding when or if this kind of surveillance crosses a constitutional line. In the meantime, Ferguson says, lawmakers could act by limiting how long data is stored, for instance, mandating regular audits or restricting surveillance near sensitive sites like abortion clinics or immigration courts.
He says those conversations should be happening before a tool ever is used.

title: As crypto and prediction markets expand, their regulator shrinks
body:
President Donald Trump shakes hands with Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) Chairman Michael Selig during a meeting with technology leaders in the Roosevelt Room of the White House, Wednesday, Aug. 19, 2026, in Washington. Jacquelyn Martin/Associated Press hide caption
Trump-era staff reductions have significantly hampered enforcement at the Commodity Futures Trading Commission and its ability to regulate burgeoning new prediction and cryptocurrency markets, where hundreds of billions are traded each week.
By the end of 2025, the CFTC had 21% fewer staff on its payroll when compared to the previous 10-year average, according to U.S. Office of Personnel Management data. Between January 2024 and January 2025 alone, staffing dropped 22%. And the number of CFTC enforcement actions dropped even further. The agency made nearly 80% fewer enforcement actions in 2025 when compared to the annual average for the previous decade, according to the agency's annual reports.
The CFTC started hemorrhaging staff soon after President Trump won the 2024 election. This was not a coincidence, according to Jeff Le Riche, who worked as a CFTC enforcement lawyer between 2005 and 2025.
"The Trump administration had run partially on a platform that it would be friendlier to the crypto industry," Le Riche said.
Leading up to the 2024 election, the CFTC under the Biden administration had leveled enforcement cases against cryptocurrency companies such as Gemini, Mirror Trading, Voyager, Celsius and FTX for fraud. It did the same against the crypto prediction market Polymarket .
After President Trump's inauguration, "in order to show results to that industry, some people were punished for bringing those cases," Le Riche continued. "The end result was that a lot of the people that worked on those cases either left or were forced out."
In a statement to NPR, the CFTC did not address that claim directly, but praised the work of current agency head Michael Selig.
"The CFTC remains committed to promoting integrity and responsible innovation in U.S. derivatives markets, and Chairman Selig is grateful to the dedicated staff who continue to support this mission each day," CFTC spokesman Zach Fulton wrote in part.
To Le Riche, the 21% drop in employees and the nearly 80% decline in enforcement action go hand in hand.
"It castrated the enforcement team," Le Riche said. "Many of the people who were targeted were high-performing attorneys who had brought some of the most consequential and complicated cases over the past few years."
Joe Konizeski, who worked as a CFTC enforcement lawyer for 26 years, was one of the dozens forced out in 2025.
"The acting chair [Caroline Pham] said, 'We're closing all our crypto [cases],'" Konizeski said. "And so, of course, everybody who had a crypto scam had to close it and any matter that was even marginally related to crypto ended up getting closed."
Pham left the CFTC in December of 2025 and is now the chief legal and administrative officer at MoonPay, a cryptocurrency company. She did not respond to NPR's request for comment about whether she gave preferential treatment to the crypto industry.
Since Trump took office, the CFTC has rolled back its enforcement actions against crypto firms Gemini , Celsius , and FTX . But crypto cases weren't the only ones impacted. Konizeski said decreased staffing caused the CFTC to dismiss others such as a foreign exchange fraud case against WorldWideMarkets Inc. The company was accused of defrauding millions from users.
Before the explosion of the crypto and prediction markets, the CFTC largely focused on more traditional derivative markets — such as grain and stock futures contracts.
"Fewer cops on the beat… creates a real incentive to start engaging in fraudulent and deceitful behavior," Konizeski said. "Enforcement is down and that means that there's going to be more fraud."
For Konizeski, chief examples of this are prediction market advertisements that target young men. He accused Polymarket and Kalshi of "using fraudulent means" to entice young men to its platforms.
"CFTC knows this and allows it to continue," Konizeski said.
Neither Polymarket nor Kalshi responded to NPR's requests for comment about whether their advertising targeted young men.
A former CFTC lawyer, who spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of professional repercussions, said they left the agency voluntarily soon after Trump took office and Pham curbed enforcement.
"Enforcement was particularly closed in crypto and prediction market cases," this former CFTC staffer said. "A lot of people left because, once Pham took over, it became clear that enforcement was not a priority."
The Government Accountability Office, a congressional watchdog agency, is now investigating the CFTC for its workforce reduction, according to a letter obtained by NPR. This new GAO probe into the CFTC comes after Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., requested a federal investigation into the agency's staffing and fraud enforcement in July.
"It's supposed to be out there regulating the market, but it doesn't appear to be doing it and frankly, doesn't appear to have the people to do it," Warren told NPR in an interview. "I want to know whether or not the watchdog is actually out there doing a little barking, or has the watchdog been locked up somewhere back in the barn?"
The GAO is gathering staff and resources for its investigation into the CFTC and will "initiate" the probe in December.
The CFTC did not directly comment on the GAO investigation but did respond to NPR's questions about its staffing levels.
"[The CFTC] is on track to hire roughly 100 employees in mission critical areas by the end of 2026," wrote CFTC spokesman Fulton in a statement. "Like many federal agencies, a number of CFTC staff opted to step away from public service in recent years, and the CFTC will continue to ensure it attracts and retains talented staff dedicated to fulfilling our critical mission."
During 2026, the CFTC has seen a slight uptick in staffing.
While the GAO investigation is narrowly focused on staff reduction, Warren said Congress could use its "power to investigate" possible corruption citing potential Congressional subpoenas and its ability to control the agency's funding.
"But that only happens if Congress has the backbone and right now, led by the Republicans, Congress not only doesn't have a backbone, it doesn't even have any interest in doing it," Warren said.
When asked if a Democratic Congress would subpoena the heads of the CFTC, crypto companies and prediction markets, Warren said, "it is our job to use all those tools to investigate."
In August, the current chair of the CFTC, Michael Selig, celebrated his agency's slowdown in enforcement actions during a White House event featuring the crypto industry.
"The era of political lawfare, debanking and regulation by enforcement is over," Selig said while flanked by crypto CEOs in the Roosevelt Room. "Innovators, like the people in this room, are welcome to the White House — not railroaded to the big house."
Coinbase CEO and co-founder Brian Armstrong speaks as President Donald Trump meets with technology leaders in the Roosevelt Room of the White House, Wednesday, Aug. 19, 2026, in Washington. Jacquelyn Martin/Associated Press hide caption
He argued that the U.S. needs to "dominate" these new financial technologies — like crypto and prediction markets — and "write the rules that define the next generation of financial markets." Selig is the sole member of the normally five-member CFTC commission, giving him unchallenged power over the direction of the agency.
Before his time at the CFTC, Selig was a corporate lawyer for cryptocurrency firms and prediction markets. His latest financial disclosure report shows that Selig sold between $65,000 and $150,000 in Bitcoin before he became a commissioner.
While Selig wants increased agency rule making for prediction and crypto markets, that requires a massive amount of work and staffing, according to former CFTC director Brian Young, who said the reduction in headcount limits the agency's ability to write new rules.
"With the growth of prediction markets and digital asset trading, the [CFTC] really needs to augment staffing in order to meet these increased responsibilities," Young said. "At the end of the day, they need people to process these applications."
A former CFTC employee — who speaks regularly with current employees — told NPR that the CFTC is so understaffed that it is struggling to execute Trump's 2025 executive order on cryptocurrency.
"My friends that are there are dying," this former staffer told NPR on the condition of anonymity for fear of professional retaliation.
Earlier this year, CFTC Inspector General Christopher Skinner acknowledged the difficulty of short staffing in a recent annual report .
"The CFTC should consider human capital management as a top priority," Skinner wrote. "To ensure the agency has the appropriate talent and skill sets to meet an expanding regulatory landscape."
Meanwhile, the CFTC's work load keeps growing.
In 2025, the agency greenlit six prediction markets — three times the average annual rate over the last decade. This year, the agency has authorized another 6 prediction markets with 18 applications pending.
After the Senate failed to advance a major crypto and banking regulation bill this summer, the CFTC announced this week that it is moving ahead with making its own rules without congressional input.
"The American people deserve clarity, certainty, and consumer protections in the crypto asset markets and the agency is committed to delivering this by incorporating crypto asset transactions into its uniform national market regulatory framework," Selig said in a statement .
Still, as of July, the agency's workforce was 16% below its decade-average or 100 staffers short. The CFTC is currently hiring for seven full-time positions.

title: Syrian general accused of atrocities is protected by U.S. and Lebanon, NPR and BBC find
body:
Bassam al-Hassan was a former Syrian general and a senior advisor to former President Bashar al-Assad. He is living in Lebanon, bankrolled and protected by American and Lebanese authorities. BBC hide caption
NPR partnered with BBC Radio 4 to follow reporter Josh Baker and Sara Obeidat as they traveled through a changing country to attempt to uncover the truth about what happened to American journalist Austin Tice. Listen to the podcast in the NPR app .
A former Syrian general facing U.S. sanctions and wanted internationally for crimes against humanity is living quietly in Lebanon, bankrolled and protected by American and Lebanese authorities, a joint BBC and NPR investigation has found.
Bassam al-Hassan, who oversaw Syria's chemical weapons program and was a senior advisor to former President Bashar al-Assad, moved to Beirut after fleeing Syria following the Assad regime's collapse in 2024.
An investigation by the BBC and NPR has found that Hassan has been allowed to remain there under an arrangement involving the FBI and other U.S. and Lebanese authorities.
This is at least partly because of his willingness to provide information about the abduction of American journalist Austin Tice in Syria in 2012, as well as additional intelligence, according to four sources familiar with the arrangement who asked to remain anonymous because of threats to their livelihood and safety.
As part of a years-long investigation featured in the new NPR's Embedded and BBC series called Where is Austin Tice? the BBC has reviewed a detailed record of a meeting between Hassan, representatives of the FBI and CIA, and Lebanese security officials, where Tice's case is discussed.
In it, Hassan is offered "residency," "protection," and help securing his "living needs."
Sources with knowledge of the arrangement described how Hassan receives money through an intermediary, making it harder to trace.
Officials from two different branches of Syria's new government, who requested anonymity because they are unauthorized to speak to the press about this case, have told NPR and the BBC they want Hassan returned to Syria to face trial but that U.S. authorities want him kept in Beirut, and they say there is little Damascus can do about this.
When reporters for the BBC reached Hassan by phone last year to ask for an interview, he directed them to seek permission for him to speak from "the FBI and CIA officials at the [U.S.] embassy."
Asked for comment, officials with the CIA and Lebanon's security agency, the General Directorate of General Security, did not respond. The FBI declined to comment and instead pointed to a past statement that said its focus remained on establishing the facts around the Tice case and securing his return.
In response to our findings, Phil Elwood, spokesperson for the Tice family, said:
"If what you are saying is true, the fact that our tax dollars are being used to furnish a comfortable life for someone associated with the use of chemical weapons on Syrian civilians, who claims to have had Austin Tice executed, is offensive. This is nothing less than aiding and abetting the escape of a wanted war criminal. The Syrians deserve justice, and he should be returned to stand trial."
Hassan is under sanctions from the U.S. Treasury Department for his role in the Assad government, where, in addition to running the chemical weapons program, he served as a top adviser to the president.
Last month NPR and the BBC reported Tice's abduction had been a planned operation , with Hassan in the chain of command. Since his disappearance, Tice has been the subject of one of the American government's most high-profile missing persons cases, with presidents Biden and Trump both discussing it publicly and sending teams to the Middle East to negotiate with Syrian officials.
Hassan is not the only Syrian regime official connected to the Tice case who claims to receive financial payments or assistance for living abroad. Two others spoke on condition of anonymity, saying they feared for their safety if they spoke publicly.
One former regime member said he had received money from the FBI multiple times in exchange for his cooperation on Tice's case. It was "not in my interest to share all the information all at once," he told the BBC and NPR, "in order to be able to drag out how long I can continue to receive payments from them."
Another former regime member connected to Tice's case, who spoke by phone with the BBC, claimed he was living in Lebanon under the "patronage" of U.S. authorities, citing this as the reason he could not speak about Tice.
The BBC spoke to a former senior Lebanese intelligence official on condition of anonymity, because he is not authorized to speak publicly about intelligence matters of this nature and due to the sensitivity of the Tice case. He confirmed that Lebanese intelligence does have arrangements with the Americans and that payments have and do take place when both agencies have overlap in cases, but he said he had no knowledge of payments involving the Austin Tice case.
Following the fall of the Assad regime in early December 2024, Hassan initially escaped to Iran. A Syrian businessman, with strong connections to both the former regime and the Lebanese authorities, told the BBC that negotiations had then taken place to bring Hassan to Lebanon.
The businessman, who asked to remain anonymous to speak candidly, said Hassan was valuable, not only because of what he is believed to know about Austin Tice, but because of his knowledge of Syria's chemical weapons program and its military relationship with Iran.
Debra Tice, mother of missing American journalist Austin Tice, speaks at a press conference in Damascus, Syria on Jan. 20, 2025. Ayman Oghanna for NPR hide caption
Austin Tice's mother, Debra, told the BBC that an official with the FBI had informed her Hassan was in Beirut, and that they had spoken to him. In May 2025, she flew to Lebanon to attempt to meet Hassan but was unsuccessful.
At the time, she told NPR and the BBC: "I don't want to interrogate him. I don't want to berate him, I don't want to scold him. That's not my job. I want to know about my son."
Hassan told U.S. investigators last year that Tice had been executed on former President Assad's orders, the BBC reported, but several people with knowledge of the investigation have questioned the details of his account. Hassan has provided a potential location for Tice's remains. But according to multiple sources with knowledge of the case, who were granted anonymity because they were not authorized to speak about it, the site was searched and nothing was found — casting doubt on the validity of some of Hassan's information.
There are questions, however, about how thoroughly the site was searched. Two sources who said they had intimate knowledge of the operation told the BBC that U.S. authorities stopped digging before the search had been completed, possibly because of security concerns.
Other Syrian officials connected to the Tice case have also apparently found refuge abroad.
Mohammad Makhlouf, a senior officer at the facility where Tice was detained and who took part in a staged abduction video of Tice, is residing in Lebanon. Sakr Rustom, who is connected to Austin Tice's abduction and is the nephew of Bassam al Hassan, was contacted by the BBC in the United Arab Emirates. When asked about Tice's case, Rustom said he "preferred to focus on matters of the future."
Ghassan Nassour, a former general in Syria's Republican Guard, is said by former members of the National Defense Forces to have presided over the jail Tice was held in, and is living in the United Arab Emirates with his family.
NPR and BBC present: Where is Austin Tice? Stream the podcast in the NPR app.

title: Toss-ups, triage and targets: How to read the wide-open 2026 House map
body:
A general view of voting machines at the Franklin County Board of Elections on Oct. 6, 2026 in Columbus, Ohio. Jeff Dean/Getty Images hide caption
Stay up to date with our Politics newsletter, sent weekly .
With just under a month to go until Election Day, financial decisions made by both parties appear to suggest the question being asked is not if Democrats take control of the House, but how large the majority may be.
Currently, Republicans hold a narrow 218-214 seat advantage. In February 2025, the Cook Political Report's initial ratings for the midterms found a small slice of 39 races listed as competitive, with 18 classified as "toss-ups."
That topline number has shifted, with Cook currently listing 43 districts as competitive, including 22 toss-ups. But beyond that, under the hood, Democratic and Republican groups are marshalling hundreds of millions of dollars to influence an electoral landscape that is much larger.
An NPR analysis of both parties' campaign targets, future ad reservations and outside spending by Trump-aligned super PACs finds more than 90 districts where resources are being committed in the closing weeks of the midterms.
Here's a look at the types of races that will decide who controls the House in 2027.
If the political environment remained unchanged from the 2024 presidential election, a small group of House races would be competitive no matter what, like the 10 districts that voted for one party's presidential candidate and the other party's House nominee. (Not counting those changed by redistricting in the last 18 months, but more on that below.)
That includes the seats held by New York Republican Rep. Mike Lawler (NY-17), Pennsylvania Republican Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (PA-01) and Washington state Democratic Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (WA-03). Another group of seats had very close margins in 2024, like Democratic Rep. Adam Gray's victory by fewer than 200 votes in California's 13th Congressional District and a 799-vote victory for Republican Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks in Iowa's 1st Congressional District.
But this is not the same political environment as 2024. President Trump's unpopularity with voters has reached record highs, with the share of voters who strongly disapprove of his job performance sitting higher than any point in either term in office.
Voters are unhappy with the ongoing war in Iran, rising gas prices, tariffs and immigration enforcement, and a wave of anti-incumbent sentiment has driven a record number of congressional retirement announcements along with a number of sitting lawmakers losing their primary races this year.
Other races to watch: CO-08, NY-03, PA-08, PA-10
Further scrambling the map: a redistricting arms race that resulted in new district lines for an estimated 1 in 10 registered voters across several states.
Republican-led state legislatures, at Trump's urging and in some cases threats, tried to draw new House maps that would give them multiple additional seats in states like Texas and Florida, while Democrats countered in California.
But many of the new district lines were drawn with assumptions made about voters who backed President Trump in 2024 and what they would do in 2026, and in some cases, could backfire.
According to Strength in Numbers/Verasight polling data shared with NPR, Trump has lower-than-average job approval in communities that make up newly redrawn districts in South Florida and along the Texas-Mexico border, like TX-28 and FL-25.
In North Carolina's 1st Congressional District, Democrat Rep. Don Davis saw his district that Trump narrowly carried in 2024 become even more conservative. But the national environment — and a U.S. Senate race where polls show Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper leading — has made the contest more competitive. More than $20 million in ad reservations are scheduled between now and Election Day in the rural and coastal district, making it one of the most expensive House races in the country.
Other races to watch: AL-02, OH-09, FL-22, TX-35
Heading into the final electoral sprint, there are 60 districts that are listed as priorities of both the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and the National Republican Congressional Committee along with Trump-aligned super PACs like No Going Back.
On average, those districts voted for Trump by an 8% margin in 2024, highlighting how deep into conservative areas competitive races have moved.
The DCCC has more than 90 districts on its battlefield map, including 46 targets to flip in its "Red To Blue" program, 26 "Frontline" incumbents in potentially tight races and another 19 it considers "Districts In Play."
The NRCC has 17 districts on its "Patriots" list of vulnerable incumbents to support and another 27 candidates in open races or challenging Democratic incumbents as part of the "MAGA Majority" program.
Not every race will ultimately end up close or see party control change hands. Many of the DCCC's "Districts In Play" gave Trump closer to 60% of the vote in 2024 and have seen little-to-no ad spend from either party.
Then, there are races like Kentucky's 6th Congressional District, where millions of dollars in spending has poured in from both parties — including from Trump-aligned super PACS — in a district Trump won by 15 points.
In Arkansas' 2nd Congressional District, which Trump also won by 15 points, six-figure outside spending targeting Democratic nominee Chris Jones and boosting incumbent Rep. French Hill contributed to the DCCC adding that race to its "Red To Blue" target.
According to Ballotpedia tracking, the target lists compiled by the DCCC and NRCC are usually broader in their scope and limited in their success. From 2012-2024, the Democrats won a total of 34% of its target districts and Republicans won 29%.
In some races and places, Republicans and Democrats are beginning to pull back ad reservations for the rest of the year, according to data from ad tracking firm AdImpact, though for different reasons. The most high profile example for Republicans is halting the flow of money in the North Carolina Senate race and redirecting funds to Kansas.
Some House races have seen similar cancellations, too, like the open race in Nebraska's 2nd District that is both a DCCC Red To Blue and NRCC MAGA Majority target.
Still, that data shows close to half a billion dollars in ad reservations have been placed between now and Election Day, showing that in this midterm election neither party is taking anything for granted.
Other races to watch: FL-13, NC-11, OH-10, OH-15
