It becomes vendor lock-in when essential integrations or accumulated context remain tied to the original supplier and cannot readily be transferred.
Support for existing conventions reduces that migration work. A harness that can use the instructions and tools a team already has is easier to adopt. The source license matters, but so does the amount of work required to switch. The same compatibility question came up when considering ProperDocs and Zensical as alternatives to MkDocs for building this website.
MCP's documentation compares it to a USB-C port: a shared connection lets the same tools and data sources work with different AI applications. That gives competing harnesses a common set of services to work with.
MCP does not make two agents behave identically. They can connect to the same server and still use its tools differently, apply different permission rules, or produce different results. The practical benefit is narrower: a team can reuse the connection instead of rebuilding it for each harness.
This reminds me of the role of web standards in the browser wars . Being able to access the same websites through different browsers gave users a choice and gave new browser implementations a chance. Shared interfaces between agents and tools could help in a similar way.
Open protocols can also make proprietary software more attractive. If a harness works with tools I already use elsewhere, adopting it becomes easier. Supporting MCP does not make the harness open source, just as supporting Internet protocols did not make Windows open source.
At some point, assigning an operating system to every harness stops being useful. Cursor , for example, suggests another possibility: the editor remains the center of development and incorporates agents into that workflow. Meanwhile, harnesses gain graphical interfaces and model vendors offer complete development environments. These approaches can overlap, and I expect the boundaries to keep moving.
Cloud platforms offer another useful comparison, especially when a harness depends on hosted services and integrations that are difficult to reproduce elsewhere. The operating-system comparison highlights compatibility, code reuse, and the tools and conventions built around an implementation; the cloud comparison draws attention to service dependencies and the cost of moving. For agents embedded in enterprise platforms, that second comparison may be more useful.
There are also some welcome differences from the old operating-system wars. Trying another harness does not require repartitioning a disk, and several agents can work on the same repository. Instructions and tools can sometimes be reused with little effort. As teams build more elaborate workflows, keeping that ability to move will matter more.
The four comparisons describe ways a development tool can become a platform: other tools follow its conventions, other products reuse its code, users can choose between suppliers, or its integrated experience attracts users. A successful harness could combine several of these approaches.
For me, the useful lesson from the operating-system wars is to consider both what attracts us to a platform and what would keep us there. I want tools that work well today, but I also want to keep my instructions, integrations, and work if I decide to switch tomorrow.

title: Russian forces kill four civilians and injure six others in Donetsk region over past day
body:
According to Ukrinform, Vadym Filashkin, head of the Donetsk Regional State Administration, reported this on Facebook .
He said that on October 7, Russian forces killed two people in Zelene, one person in Sloviansk, and one in Vesela Hora.
Six more people in the region were injured: three in Sloviansk, one in Vesela Hora, one in Kramatorsk, one in Druzhkivka, and one in Zoloti Prudy.
As Filashkin emphasized, the total number of Russian casualties in Donetsk region (4,343 dead and 10,629 injured) does not include figures from Mariupol and Volnovakha.
As reported by Ukrinform, on October 7 in Sloviansk, a Russian drone struck a bus, injuring the driver. In another part of the city, a drone struck a car, killing a man and injuring a woman.

title: Nigeria,​‌‍‍‍‍⁠⁠‍​‌​‍‌‌‌‍‌​ Africa lose $74.5bn yearly to unfair credit ratings – UN
body: The United Nations says inaccurate and context-poor sovereign credit ratings are estimated to cost African countries about 74.5 billion dollars annually through excessive borrowing costs and lost financing. The UN Office of the Special Adviser on Africa made the disclosure shortly before Wednesday’s formal launch of the Africa Credit Rating Agency in Port Louis, Mauritius. The new agency, known as AfCRA, is expected to provide independent, Africa-focused assessments of sovereigns, sub-sovereigns, companies and institutions. The UN described the current situation as a major development penalty on a continent whose actual default experience is lower than prevailing risk perceptions suggest. “Africa’s actual default rate is far lower than what its credit ratings imply, yet the continent pays the highest cost of capital in the world,” the UN said. It said inaccurate ratings that fail to adequately reflect African economic realities were estimated to cost the continent 74.5 billion dollars annually. “That is a tax on Africa’s development, paid for no good reason,” the UN said. The development has particular relevance for Nigeria, which has repeatedly raised concerns at the United Nations over what it considers a disproportionate risk premium attached to African sovereign borrowing. At an ECOSOC special meeting on credit ratings in March, Nigeria compared the country’s borrowing costs with those of an unnamed highly indebted European economy. Nigeria told the meeting that its debt-to-GDP ratio was considerably lower, it had never defaulted on sovereign debt, and its foreign reserves were stronger. According to Nigeria, however, the country’s recent dollar-denominated sovereign bonds carried yields of between 8.6 and 9.1 per cent. The unnamed European country, by comparison, borrowed at about 3.9 to 4.0 per cent, Nigeria regretted. Nigeria also questioned why profitable banks and businesses could operate successfully within African economies while their sovereigns remained below investment grade. The country argued that international rating agencies needed to engage more deeply with domestic investors and local economic actors rather than rely mainly on externally generated assumptions. Nigeria further complained that major global rating agencies had limited physical presence across Africa, potentially constraining their understanding of local economic realities. The UN says AfCRA is intended to help close such information and methodology gaps through more transparent assessments rooted in African data, expertise and economic context. It said the agency would place greater weight on factors often inadequately captured in conventional ratings, including informal-sector activity, vulnerability and resilience. AfCRA is also expected to improve market intelligence and challenge historical biases embedded in perceptions of African sovereign risk. The African Union said the agency would complement, rather than replace, existing international credit rating agencies. It said AfCRA would operate independently, be private-sector driven and self-funded, with governments barred from owning shares to protect its credibility. The agency’s launch follows years of concern among African governments that conventional sovereign ratings often increase borrowing costs and restrict fiscal space for development. The UN Economic Commission for Africa said the new institution forms part of broader efforts to reform Africa’s financial architecture, deepen domestic capital markets and reduce borrowing costs. The AU said AfCRA would strengthen Africa’s voice in global financial governance while promoting more evidence-based assessments of African economies. (NAN) The post Nigeria,​‌‍‍‍‍⁠⁠‍​‌​‍‌‌‌‍‌​ Africa lose $74.5bn yearly to unfair credit ratings – UN appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Athens Concert Revives Rebetiko Songs of Occupation and Resistance
body: During the German occupation of Greece, the Greek people found refuge from hardship and oppression in the arts, with revues and musical theatres continuing to attract audiences despite bans and blackouts. Rebetiko music also continued to flourish during those difficult years, as many important composers kept writing and left behind a rich repertoire. That repertoire will take centre stage in the commemorative concert “Rebetiko Songs of the Occupation and Resistance”, presented on Saturday, October 24, at the Maria Callas Municipal Music Theatre in Athens. The Greek Music Workshop of the Municipality of Athens will perform alongside two leading voices of the genre, Fotini Velesiotou and Babis Tsertos. With arrangements and musical direction by Angelos Ilias, the two acclaimed singers will perform a selection of songs that remain largely unknown to the wider public. Although these songs helped sustain Greek morale during the country’s darkest years, audiences rarely hear them today. Rebetiko, a deeply popular form of music that expressed the emotions and hopes of ordinary people, also became a vivid chronicle of life under the occupation. Its songs captured hunger, the black market, saltadores — young men who jumped onto passing vehicles to steal supplies — bombings, prisons and the Resistance. Their creators often wrote about events as they unfolded around them. Alongside the better-known works of Vassilis Tsitsanis, the period produced songs including “Saltador”, “Black Marketeers” and “Raid on Piraeus” by Michalis Genitsaris, “Chaidari” by Markos Vamvakaris, and “May the Bullet Be Sweet” by Dimitris Gogos, known as Bayandera, which he dedicated to the Resistance. Through the directness of popular expression, rebetiko captured an entire society struggling to survive, resist and preserve its voice. A distinctive feature of this repertoire is that many of the songs were not recorded when their creators wrote them. Recording activity in Greece had stopped during the occupation, so musicians passed the songs from person to person and performed them live. Some eventually reached record collections after the war, while others survived through the memories of their creators and the people who performed them. Marking the anniversary of the liberation of Athens on October 12, 1944, the Greek Music Workshop of the Municipality of Athens is bringing this valuable musical heritage back to the stage. The post Athens Concert Revives Rebetiko Songs of Occupation and Resistance appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: Phoenix Express 2026: Tunisia wraps up maritime exercise
body: The 21st iteration of Exercise Phoenix Express concluded on September 18, 2026, at La Goulette Naval Base in Tunisia. A 12-day multinational maritime exercise, led by the United States (US) 6th Fleet and hosted by the Tunisian Navy. Phoenix Express is one of three regional maritime exercises run by US Naval Forces Africa (NAVAF), the component of US Africa Command (Africom) responsible for naval operations on the continent. This year’s exercise opened on September 7 and ran in two week-long phases: an in-port, land-based command phase, and a follow-on phase at sea. During the in-port stage, participating navies used a multinational communication center to coordinate and pass real-time data, building what planners call a common operational picture, a shared, updated view of vessel movements and activity across the exercise area. The at-sea phase put that coordination into practice through search-and-rescue drills and simulated ship boardings meant to sharpen interdiction procedures among the different fleets. Thirteen (13) nations took part: Algeria, Belgium, Egypt, France, Georgia, Italy, Libya, Morocco, Tunisia, Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, Spain and the US. Earlier Africom material published at the start of the exercise had listed a slightly different lineup, including the United Kingdom rather than Saudi Arabia and Spain; the closing release from US Naval Forces Europe and Africa reflects the final roster of participants who saw the exercise through to completion. Vice Admiral J.T. Anderson, commander of US 6th Fleet and NATO’s Naval Striking and Support Forces, framed the exercise around the pairing of technology and training. “The true strength of Phoenix Express lies in combining cutting-edge maritime technologies with the exceptional professionalism of the forces who operate them”, he said in a statement issued as the exercise began. At the closing ceremony, Anderson credited the participating crews with proving that shared interests, not fleet size, hold the coalition together, and US Ambassador to Tunisia Bill Bazzi pointed to the exercise as evidence that a stable Mediterranean benefits both countries directly. Phoenix Express traces back to 2004, when the US Navy began building a standing maritime security partnership with Tunisia that has run, with one interruption, ever since; the 2020 edition was cancelled due to the COVID-19 pandemic . The 16th iteration, Exercise Phoenix Express 2021, of the North African maritime security series, was held on May 17, 2021, in Tunis, Tunisia. The series grew out of the broader Africa Partnership Station initiative and the wider “Express” family of exercises the US Navy uses to build maritime capacity with partner forces around the continent. What started as a smaller bilateral and regional effort, with 9 African and 9 European nations taking part as recently as 2010, has expanded to draw participants from well beyond North Africa, including this year’s contingents from Georgia and Saudi Arabia. The technical substance of Phoenix Express sits less in hardware and more in interoperability. The exercise is built around getting different navies’ sensors, communications systems and command structures to work together well enough to track vessels and coordinate a response across national boundaries. Alongside Tunisian and other partner forces, elements of the US 6th Fleet used the drill to expand their use of advanced tracking and detection systems aimed at identifying illegal activity inside African exclusive economic zones (EEZs), the waters extending up to 200 nautical miles from a coastline where a state holds special rights over resources. Phoenix Express is one of three regional maritime exercises that US Naval Forces Africa runs each year, alongside Cutlass Express in East Africa and Obangame Express in the Gulf of Guinea. Together they form a standing effort to build partner navies’ capacity through repetition rather than a single large show of force, an approach that has defined much of Africom’s maritime engagement since the command stood up in 2007. The inclusion of Saudi Arabia and Georgia this year, alongside a steady core of North African and southern European participants, points to the exercise’s continued use as a vehicle for widening security ties beyond the immediate Mediterranean basin. It also comes against a backdrop of broader US naval engagement with Tunisia, a relationship Washington has repeatedly tied to a bilateral history stretching back to a 1797 treaty of peace and friendship between the two countries. For the US and NATO partners, it offers a foothold for maritime security cooperation in a region where illicit trafficking, irregular migration, and disputed maritime boundaries remain persistent concerns.

title: Russia Is Targeting Kyiv’s Bridges: How Resilient Are They?
body:
Russia is systematically targeting Ukrainian bridges.
Kyiv’s South Bridge has been targeted at least three times in recent days, while the North Bridge has been targeted twice. Both are crucial parts of the capital’s complex transport infrastructure . The South Bridge has six traffic lanes and carries the “green” metro line, while the North Bridge has eight traffic lanes. On Oct. 6, a new bridge in Zaporizhzhia was also targeted.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
So why has Russia begun attacking bridges? Could these strikes destroy them? And what broader risks do they pose?
The blast after a drone strike on Kyiv’s North Bridge (Screenshot from open sources) Advertisement
The blast after a drone strike on Kyiv’s North Bridge (Screenshot from open sources)
The recent spate of attacks on these bridges has not caused significant damage; only the road surface was affected. Repairs caused traffic jams , but road crews patched the damage very quickly.
Typical traffic on Kyiv’s Paton Bridge (Photo by Sergii Kostezh/Kyiv Post)
Typical traffic on Kyiv’s Paton Bridge (Photo by Sergii Kostezh/Kyiv Post)
Engineers who spoke to Kyiv Post were clear and unequivocal: destroying bridges with drones is practically impossible. The load-bearing structures of Kyiv’s bridges contain dozens of tons of reinforced concrete. Neither a drone nor even a missile can penetrate them easily.
“Individual UAV [unmanned aerial vehicle] strikes cannot cause significant damage to massive bridge structures. However, Russia is using a tactic of ‘small cuts,’ in which numerous small strikes can force bridges to close temporarily for inspection and repairs, while also creating a cumulative effect,” says Armed Forces of Ukraine Major Artem Bilyk, a member of the General Staff’s ad hoc expert group coordinating engineering protection solutions for critical infrastructure and a leading co-author of the “Fortress Country” concept.
He notes that the main concern may be the precision of the strikes. In particular, if Russian forces can repeatedly hit vulnerable points in a bridge’s structure, serious problems could arise even if the bridge remains standing.
“Bridges have sensitive parts – nodes, joints and tensioned elements – that are particularly vulnerable to strikes, especially given that the enemy uses UAVs in a guided configuration through MESH modems. Repeated UAV strikes can disable a bridge even without causing its complete collapse,” Bilyk says.
This raises another question: what would happen if Russia used missiles? So far, there have been no attempts to target the bridges specifically with missiles.
That is not because Russia lacks missiles, says certified architect and Kyiv-based infrastructure researcher Oleg Grechukh. Rather, missiles lack the necessary accuracy, and bridges are narrow structures – no more than 15-20 meters wide – making them very difficult to hit.
“First, a direct frontal hit on the road surface will not cause critical damage. Second, even a ballistic missile with an accuracy of 10 meters can very likely miss the bridge. In that case, it will not cause any damage at all, because the missile will not even produce a significant spread of fragments or a shock wave, as it will land in the deep waters of the Dnipro,” Grechukh says.
One example of missiles being used against a bridge was the AFU’s HIMARS strikes on the Antonivskyi Bridge near Kherson in the summer of 2022. HIMARS were used several times in an effort to destroy the only bridge across the Dnipro and prevent Russian forces from escaping Kherson, which was surrounded by Ukrainian troops. Yet even after the missiles hit the bridge, they caused only limited damage, and Russian forces were able to withdraw almost all their soldiers from Kherson before they could be trapped.
The conclusion is that strikes are unlikely to destroy the bridges or seriously damage them. So why target them?
Russia’s objective may lie elsewhere. The apparently random pattern of strikes – first on petrol stations, then internet providers, food warehouses and shops – may look chaotic. In reality, it appears more like a search for vulnerabilities.
After several strikes on petrol stations , only a handful of Kyiv’s nearly 700 operating stations were damaged. They were quickly restored.
Then came strikes on internet providers . Within hours, however, all had resumed operations, and despite concerns, internet and mobile communications in Ukraine remained available.
There was no panic over food in supermarkets either.
The bridge strikes, by contrast, caused enormous traffic jams. Public reaction was anxious: many people chose not to travel to work, while repairs brought parts of the transport network to a standstill and left motorists stuck in traffic for hours.
Russian propaganda quickly seized on the disruption. “Our goal is to scatter brains from those who try to cross these bridges,” wrote popular Russian blogger and war observer Ilya Tumanov, known as Fighterbomber.
Screenshot from Fighterbomber Telegram page
Screenshot from Fighterbomber Telegram page
Such tactics are nothing new for Russia. In 1999, Russian forces destroyed Grozny, the capital of the Chechen Republic; in 2017, they helped destroy Aleppo, one of the world’s oldest cities, in Syria.
Russia has, in effect, found Kyiv’s pressure point – one that was never a secret.
Ukraine’s capital straddles the broad Dnipro river, which is 600 to 1,000 meters wide within Kyiv and is one of Europe’s largest rivers. Almost 3 million people live on the two banks of the Dnipro within Kyiv; including the suburbs, the figure is close to 4 million. It is a large urban agglomeration with a distinctive imbalance.
Residents are split between the two banks at a ratio of roughly 55:45, meaning that almost equal numbers of people live on the left and right banks.
The Dnipro river, with its bridges clearly visible. The right bank is on the western side; while the left bank is on the eastern side. (Screenshot: Google Maps)
The Dnipro river, with its bridges clearly visible. The right bank is on the western side; while the left bank is on the eastern side. (Screenshot: Google Maps)
Jobs are not distributed as evenly between the two banks as the population. Some 85% of jobs are on the right bank, which is home to the headquarters of the largest companies, the biggest industrial zones, the government center, foreign embassies and the service sector that supports them.
The left bank is not “wild,” as Kyiv residents sometimes joke, but it is predominantly residential.
This imbalance, combined with limited public transport on the left bank – especially the metro – creates enormous daily commuter flows.
Every morning, hundreds of thousands of left-bank residents travel to the right bank; in the evening, the flow reverses.
“Every day, the bridges are crossed by at least 100,000 cars – not counting public transportation,” Grechukh says.
Only six bridges carry cars: the North Bridge, Podilskyi Bridge, Metro Bridge, Paton Bridge, Darnytskyi Bridge and South Bridge.
A traffic accident on any one of them during the morning or evening rush hour can cause a jam on that bridge. Drivers then divert to the others, which can trigger a wider “transport collapse.” Before Russia’s full-scale invasion, this could happen regularly.
Typical traffic jam in Kyiv in 2019 (Screenshot by Sergii Kostezh/Kyiv Post)
Typical traffic jam in Kyiv in 2019 (Screenshot by Sergii Kostezh/Kyiv Post)
The problem has plagued Kyiv since the mid-2000s. Many solutions have been proposed: building new bridges, dispersing jobs by encouraging new business centers on the left bank, improving public transport and cycling infrastructure, and encouraging people to drive less. Yet little of substance has been done by 2022.
The problem therefore remains. What can be done now?
The infrastructure minister proposed building pontoon crossings between the two banks to ease pressure on the bridges, an idea which has some appeal, especially because the Ukrainian military has gained extensive experience building river crossings during the war.
Kyiv also has a history of pontoon crossings. During World War II, both Nazi Germany and the Red Army built such crossings after all the bridges across the Dnipro were destroyed in 1941.
The engineers consulted for this article, however, do not believe this proposal would work.
Because the crossing would have to span such a wide section of the Dnipro, the pontoon bridge would probably be limited to a single traffic lane.
“Their capacity would not come close to that of a bridge. There would be one lane with reversible traffic, and speeds would be lower. Moreover, if something happened on the pontoon – erosion by the river or a strike – it would be much harder than on a bridge to reach vehicles stranded there quickly,” Grechukh says.
Kyiv Post sources in the Kyiv City Administration agree.
“A pontoon is not simply placed on level ground. It needs ramps and exits, which require complex and substantial engineering work. Traffic must also be organized around it, which is difficult given the existing road network,” a source in the Kyiv City Administration says.
Another idea embraced by activists is to complete the “Stalin tunnels.” Kyiv has two unfinished sections, in the north and south. Built between 1938 and 1941 during the Stalin era, they were intended to provide trains with a safer wartime alternative to bridges.
An unfinished section of Kyiv’s Stalin-era tunnel (Photo by Valentyna Latko/Facebook)
An unfinished section of Kyiv’s Stalin-era tunnel (Photo by Valentyna Latko/Facebook)
But Andriy Shvachko, a senior lecturer at Kyiv National University of Construction and Architecture, says completing them now makes no sense.
“From a security perspective, a bridge and a tunnel are equally vulnerable. A tunnel cannot be bombed along its entire length, but its entrance can be struck. From an engineering perspective, completing the ‘Stalin’ tunnels also makes no sense: each was designed for a single-track railway, while Ukrainian railways today are double-track. It would be expensive, time-consuming and uneconomical, and it would not solve the problem. The tunnels also have no provision for road vehicles or pedestrians. They cannot be widened, which is where they lose out to bridges,” Shvachko says.
Engineers note that consoles can sometimes be added to an old bridge to accommodate pedestrians and cyclists, if it does not already have such provision. Widening a tunnel, however, is technically unrealistic.
“There is a case for designing and building new tunnels, but Ukraine does not have the resources for that now. Completing structures abandoned during Stalin’s lifetime is simply absurd,” one of the capital’s design engineers tells Kyiv Post.
Bilyk believes that no alternative can match the carrying capacity of bridges, arguing that they should be protected as effectively as possible.
“First and foremost, the most critical nodes, key elements and supports of bridges should be reinforced using gabions, blocks and steel sheets. It’s also advisable to install special metal lattice anti-detonation screens around the carriageways. This makes it possible to move the point of the UAV explosion farther away and reduce damage to the bridge. Particular attention should be paid to fire resistance and the protection of flammable or vulnerable elements of bridge infrastructure, which should be enclosed in fireproof armored casings,” Bilyk says.
The question is whether Ukraine has sufficient resources – particularly metal – to do this.
Recent reports following Russian strikes say that the last of Ukraine’s metallurgical plants has shut down. Before the Russian invasion, the country had five operating plants and numerous factories. Ukraine thus stopped producing steel despite having both iron ore and coal – everything needed for production – and despite being one of the few countries with a fully integrated mining and metallurgical complex.
Ukrainian steelmakers, however, are confident that enough metal will be available.
“Ukraine still has sufficient capabilities in the design, manufacture and installation of bridge structures, as well as their repair and restoration; missing components can be delivered from abroad if necessary. Ukrainian steel construction plants are certified according to European standards for manufacturing. It should be understood that the enemy began searching for unprotected infrastructure facilities to strike, such as power transmission line supports and bridges, precisely because during the period from 2023 to 2026, hundreds of protective structures were built and security measures were implemented for energy facilities – transformers, generators and other equipment,” says Anna Hontarenko, executive director of the Ukrainian Steel Construction Center association.
There may still be a silver lining. One proposal for addressing the crisis includes decentralizing jobs and encouraging industrial and commercial development on the left bank. Another is to revive river transport, including ferries, which ran between the two banks during the Soviet era but declined in the 1990s during the transition to a market economy.
Even in difficult circumstances, Ukrainians continue to look for opportunities and seek asymmetric solutions. Could this new wartime crisis ultimately drive changes that make Kyiv better?

title: Russian strike on Kramatorsk kills 12 – official
body:
Russian occupation forces launched a strike on Kramatorsk, Head of the Donetsk Regional Military Administration Vadym Filashkin reports.

"As of 11:00, 12 dead and 13 wounded are known. At least 12 people were killed as a result of the Russian strike on Kramatorsk. 12 lives that Russia took away in a single instant. These are not 'consequences of war' and not dry statistics. These are people killed by the Russian army," Filashkin wrote on his Telegram channel.

The consequences of the strike are currently being clarified.

The head of the regional military administration emphasized that Russia comes to Ukrainian land with death—striking Ukrainian cities, killing Ukrainian people, and multiplying its crimes every day.

"There is and can be no justification for this. Russian murderers must answer for every life taken," he urged.

title: 140 Companies Offer Over 3,500 Jobs at Athens Career Day
body: More than 140 companies offering over 3,500 jobs will take part in the 58th Career Day organised by Greece’s Public Employment Service (DYPA) in Athens on Saturday, October 10, 2026. The event will give jobseekers the opportunity to meet companies directly, learn about available positions and attend interviews without a prior appointment. Candidates can speak with company representatives from a wide range of industries, present their professional experience and qualifications, and explore positions that match their skills. The 58th Career Day will take place at the Divani Caravel Hotel, 2 Vasileos Alexandrou Avenue, Athens, from 10:00am to 6:00pm. Admission is free. Direct meetings and employment opportunities According to DYPA, its Career Days provide a key platform for connecting jobseekers directly with the labour market. Through face-to-face meetings, candidates can meet employers and apply for available positions, while participating companies can identify the staff they need. DYPA staff will be available throughout the event to provide information about the agency’s services, employment programmes and initiatives. With its 58th Career Day, DYPA continues to connect jobseekers directly with companies that are hiring, expanding opportunities for professional networking and employment. More information: www.dypa.gov.gr For information about the Medium and Large Enterprises Support Unit (MEMME): https://www.dypa.gov.gr/memme The post 140 Companies Offer Over 3,500 Jobs at Athens Career Day appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: Will AI replace traditionally Jewish jobs? - opinion
body: Every few months, someone declares that artificial intelligence is about to hollow out the professions that Jewish families have built their American lives around: medicine, law, and finance. Basically, the trades that reward brains and relationships over brawn. It's a scary headline, sure, but it's also asking the wrong question. The real dividing line forming isn't AI vs humans, it's professionals who use AI vs professionals who don't – and the ones who don't are the ones who should be worried.Take radiology, the profession AI was supposed to kill first. In 2016, AI pioneer Geoffrey Hinton told the world to stop training radiologists, insisting machines would out-read them within five years. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang later went further, calling radiology the first job AI would "destroy and eliminate." Neither prediction held up. The number of radiologists in the United States has grown, not shrunk, since those warnings, and the American College of Radiology projects the workforce could expand by as much as 40% by 2055. Huang himself has since reversed course, arguing that people confuse a job's tasks with its purpose: AI got faster at reading images, so hospitals could run more scans, which meant more patients, which meant hiring more radiologists, not fewer. The task moved to a screen, and the job didn't disappear… it multiplied.AI, despite its benefits, still cannot hold accountability for its outputThink about it: AI is very good at consuming and organizing information, such as reading a scan, drafting a memo, transcribing a deposition, or summarizing a contract. What it cannot do – at least not yet and not in any way a court, a regulator, or a patient would accept – is hold accountability. A radiologist, not an algorithm, signs the report. A lawyer, not a chatbot, is disbarred for bad advice. Nobody sues Anthropic or OpenAI for advice a doctor or a lawyer chose to act on: the license, the malpractice exposure, and the judgment call all still sit with a human being. That's probably why AI is already displacing paralegals, junior analysts, and note-takers faster than it will ever displace the doctors, lawyers, and accountants sitting above them: the jobs most exposed are the ones with the least responsibility attached, not the highest income.That matters for the Jewish community specifically, given its high levels of educational attainment. Pew Research Center's 2020 survey found that nearly six-in-10 Jewish adults were college graduates, compared with roughly three-in-10 American adults overall. Twenty-eight percent held postgraduate degrees, vs 11% of the general adult population. For those working in law and other professions entrusted with public responsibility, that accountability carries particular weight. Those statistics aren't a coincidence of history: They reflect generations of families pushing their kids toward professions where they get paid for judgment, not just for labor. Those are the same professions AI is currently worst at fully owning because judgment implies liability and liability is a human category.Where AI is a genuine threat is to the tasks underneath those professions, like the associate work, the intake, the scheduling, the note-taking. And here's the part that should change how we talk about this: That threat is also an opportunity, especially for anyone entrepreneurial enough to grab it first. A solo attorney or a small accounting practice that used to need three junior hires to keep up with paperwork can now run leaner, using AI for transcription, drafting, and research, and put the savings into growth instead of headcount. But the opportunity isn't limited to people who already own the firm. The same tools can make it dramatically cheaper for someone starting out to build a practice, launch a service business, or take on work that once required a small team. A young accountant can serve more clients, for example, and a freelance writer can research and produce at a scale that once required an editor and researcher. An aspiring entrepreneur can also test an idea before spending heavily on employees, software, or outside help.Does that sound like jobs disappearing? The story is more about smaller operations suddenly being able to compete with bigger ones – which is exactly the kind of leverage that has historically helped push a striving middle class into the upper middle class. And for a community with a long history of starting businesses, building professional practices, and creating opportunities for the next generation, that is extremely important: AI can lower the barrier to entry, not just raise the bar for existing workers. Jewish communal life has always prized entrepreneurship as much as credentialed professions; AI, used well, is a force multiplier for exactly that instinct.The pattern holds outside the big three professions, too. Bankers and financiers aren't being replaced by AI models that can price a deal; they're using those models to move faster while the actual business still runs on relationships, trust, and the willingness to push into a new market or a new client base nobody's approached yet. That's a human sales act, not a data-processing one. Jewelers are using AI to render and iterate on designs in minutes instead of days, but nobody's algorithm is building the relationship with a bride's father or spotting the untapped niche in a new city. The idea has to come from a person willing to take the risk; AI just lets them execute it faster.Even the most futuristic version of automation makes the same point: Elon Musk isn't promising a driverless economy that runs itself. He's selling regular people the chance to own a robotaxi and put it to work. Someone still has to buy the car, manage the fleet, handle the insurance, and build the business around it. The car drives itself, sure, but the business sure doesn't run itself. So will AI replace the Jewish jobs? No, but it will replace the people of any background who refuse to use it. The professions themselves aren't going anywhere because responsibility isn't something you can automate away. What's actually being tested right now is whether people treat AI as a threat to hide from or a tool to build with. Given how the Jewish community has approached every previous wave of economic change, I know which way I'd bet.This material is provided for informational and educational purposes only and should not be construed as investment, legal, tax, or business advice. The views expressed are opinions and may change without notice. Statements regarding artificial intelligence, employment trends, and future outcomes are forward-looking and subject to uncertainty. No particular outcome is guaranteed. Third-party statistics, quotations, and other information are derived from sources believed to be reliable but are not guaranteed as to accuracy or completeness. References to specific companies, individuals, technologies, or products are for illustrative purposes only and do not constitute an endorsement or recommendation. Advisory services are offered through Klyman Financial, a DBA of ThePARTNERS Wealth Management, an SEC-registered investment adviser.”

title: Africa’s largest military exercise to take shape in Morocco
body:
Planning for next year’s Exercise African Lion, the largest multinational military exercise on the continent, is underway in Morocco.
Initial planning for African Lion 2027 was at the Royal Moroccan Armed Forces (Forces Armées Royales or “FAR”) southern zone headquarters in Agadir. Next up, ahead of the exercise set down to start in April next year, is December’s main planning with a final planning meeting in February.
The Exercises, Training and Operations Directorate (G7) US Army Southern European Task Force, Africa (SETAF-AF), one of six teams in Africom, the United States (US) combatant command tasked with protecting US continental interests and partnering to better security with individual countries, is along with the FAR, co-leading African Lion 2027 and its associated planning.
Indications are more than 45 countries will take part in African Lion 2027 across the air, cyber, land, intelligence, sea and space domains.
“The initial planning event is where we begin laying the groundwork for African Lion 2027. It’s our opportunity to bring the team together, listen to one another, take lessons from previous African Lion exercises and shape what we want to achieve next,” US Army Colonel Benjamin Roark, director of training and exercises, SETAF-AF G7, is reported as telling SETAF-AF communication officer Captain Jordan Beagle.
US and FAR military planners met at the Agadir Southern Zone headquarters to outline goals, set timelines and identify potential training locations. Smaller working groups used designated spaces at the joint task force headquarters to discuss organisation and logistic requirements.
Planners considered multiple ways to integrate new technology into training scenarios. Key objectives were experimental operations with emerging equipment and incorporating industry partners into exercise design.
“African Lion remains focussed on building combined joint force readiness. The exercise enables us to work with our multinational partners to ensure that, when asked, we are able to deploy forward and operate as a multinational force,” US Army Lieutenant Colonel Corbett Baxter, branch chief and lead planner for African Lion, SETAF-AF G7, is reported as saying.
As with previous African Lions the 2026 exercise continues to emphasise multilateral and bilateral partnerships, commemorating 250 years of US/Moroccan co-operation and providing venues for safe industry participation and capability demonstration.
Planners explored a range of training events for the execution phase, including combined arms manoeuvres, live-fire exercises, maritime and air operations and a command field exercise (CFX) as the centrepiece. It is designed to integrate vendor and industry partners directly into training, ensuring new technologies are tested alongside military units in realistic scenarios.
Discussions also included potential weapons of mass destruction training in Agadir, special operations training in Cap Draa, and humanitarian civic assistance projects at various locations. These activities remain under consideration as planning teams refine concepts of operations, logistics, site surveys and industry integration.
Alongside field training, African Lion planners are developing an academic programme. Courses under review include joint operations planning, intelligence operations, cybersecurity, electronic warfare and non-commissioned officer development. These sessions intend to build doctrinal knowledge and staff skills in support of operational objectives.
The 250th anniversary commemoration marks Morocco’s recognition of the US as a nation and, according to Beagle, ushers in a new era of partnership, readiness and innovation, setting the stage for emerging technologies and multinational co-operation across the African theatre.
US-Moroccan relations are being highlighted as well at the 2026 Marrakech Airshow (MAS) at the Marrakech Royal Moroccan Air Force Base taking place from 7 to 10 October. The highlight of the American Airpower portion will be a dynamic F-35A Lightning II stealth fighter flyby, demonstrating the unmatched, integrated capabilities of the US–Moroccan security partnership in North Africa, Africom said.
Approximately 45 US military personnel were due to participate in the airshow including: a flyover conducted by F-35A Lightning II’s from the 48th Fighter Wing, RAF Lakenheath, UK; a HC-130J Super Hercules static display from the 176th Wing at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson, Alaska; and a KC-135 Stratotanker static display from the Utah National Guard.
“It is an honor to be at Marrakech ahead of the 250th anniversary of the US-Moroccan Alliance,” said US Air Force Brigadier General Matthew J French, Air National Guard assistant to the commander of US Air Forces in Europe – Air Forces Africa. “Hosted by the United States’ oldest Ally, this forum best illustrates our goal of establishing strong and enduring Allied and partner forces for an evolving security environment. It makes us stronger in both our individual and combined capacities.”
“The Marrakech Air Show is a world-class exhibition of aviation innovation and a powerful testament to the enduring, nearly 250-year friendship between the United States and the Kingdom of Morocco. For decades, our nations have flown side-by-side, from our vital pilot training pipelines to our complex joint operations. The United States remains deeply committed to standing with our Moroccan partners, delivering cutting-edge aerospace capabilities and working hand-in-hand to promote regional peace, stability, and shared prosperity across the African continent,” said Ambassador Duke Buchan III, US Ambassador to the Kingdom of Morocco.

title: Lord of Ajasa becomes US citizen
body:
Yoruba rapper Olusegun “Lord of Ajasa” Osaniyi has announced that he has become a United States citizen.
The 44-year-old, known for delivering his songs primarily in Yoruba, shared the news in a video on his Instagram Story on Wednesday.
In the video, Lord of Ajasa appeared alongside his wife, Funmi, who celebrated the achievement and urged him to tell his fans about his new status.
He held up his US citizenship certificate while posing with the American flag.
He said: “My fans, I’m now a US citizen; you all should know. This is my new country’s flag. I’m now fighting for my new country.”
He also shared a photograph of himself and his wife posing with the American flag in another post.
The post attracted reactions from fans and colleagues, who took to the rapper’s comment section to celebrate his achievement.
Music producer Olumide “ID Cabasa” Ogunade, actors Kunle Afod and Yemi Solade, and singer 9ice were among those who sent congratulatory messages.
The Ondo-born artiste is recognised for his role in the early development of indigenous-language rap in Nigeria, helping the genre gain wider acceptance among mainstream music audiences.
Early in his career, he collaborated with several prominent Nigerian musicians, including 9ice, Olamide, and the late Da Grin.
His musical journey has also been marked by periods of difficulty. The rapper reduced his involvement in full-time music around 2019 as he dealt with health problems, including a peptic ulcer. Although he scaled back his activities, he still appeared on stage from time to time.
His announcement of his US citizenship has brought renewed attention to his career and contribution to Nigerian hip-hop.
Fans have also revisited his long-standing association with the United States, where he frequently travelled for performances and other events. Over the years, those trips prompted speculation about a possible move.
He broke into prominence with “Ma Yi Lo”, a song released in 2000. The rapper has since released a string of songs, including “Le Fenu So”, “Oti Ya”, “Ara Awe”, “Lacasera”, “Who Be Dat”, “Halelluya”, “Bi Ere”, “Tete Wa”, “Ojumo Re”, “Aye Mon” and “Lori Ila”, among others.

title: Hezbollah still present inside southern Lebanon pilot zones, despite Lebanese Army efforts - report
body: Hezbollah terror operatives are maintaining a presence in several areas within the pilot zones in southern Lebanon, KAN News reported on Wednesday.According to KAN, Hezbollah members have been located in the areas of Froun, Srifa, and Zawtar al-Gharbiyah, flying under the radar by posing as civilians.The three aforementioned areas are located south of Nabatiya.KAN also reported that the Hezbollah forces in the area were gathering intelligence and performing damage control with local officials."The Lebanese state is not doing what it is supposed to do; if wherever Israel leaves, Hezbollah enters," a Lebanese source told KAN, "and this only shows how critical the issue of disarming Hezbollah is even before the Israeli withdrawal."Israeli officials have repeatedly stated that the pilot program in southern Lebanon, in which Israeli troops would withdraw in order to allow the Lebanese Armed Forces to take over operations against Hezbollah, had failed.Israeli officials accuse Lebanese Armed Forces of not acting against HezbollahIn August, Walla cited security officials as saying, "The LAF is not destroying terror infrastructure based on the coordinates provided to it by the IDF, while at the same time requesting more coordinates, even though it is not doing anything about it."The IDF has criticized the LAF's performance, claiming that it is not acting effectively against Hezbollah infrastructure in southern Lebanon. According to assessments by senior IDF officials, LAF chief Rodolphe Haykal continues to cooperate with Hezbollah, fears confrontation with commanders of the Shi'ite organization in southern Lebanon, and is ineffective in carrying out searches, locating terror infrastructure, and finding weapons.Amir Bohbot contributed to this report.

title: Winter grain sowing in Ukraine reaches nearly 50% of target
body:
As of October 7, Ukrainian farmers had sown 2.52 million hectares with winter grain crops, or 48.4% of the projected area, and 1.041 million hectares with winter rapeseed, or 94.2% of the forecast, the Ministry of Agrarian Policy and Food reported on its website Wednesday.
In particular, wheat and triticale (a hybrid of wheat and rye) had been sown on 2.253 million hectares (49.6% of the forecast), barley on 209,900 hectares (35.4%), and rye on 57,800 hectares (75.3%).
Over the past week, the area sown with grain crops increased by 925,700 hectares, compared with an increase of 853,200 hectares the previous week.
Last year, by this date, 2.572 million hectares had been sown with grain crops, just 2% more than this year. The area sown with wheat was 4.2% larger, while barley and rye sowings were larger this year, by 17.1% and 26.5%, respectively.
As for rapeseed, its sowing season is nearing completion: over the past week, the area increased by just 22,900 hectares, compared with 59,200 hectares the previous week. This year's rapeseed sowings as of this date are 5.6% larger than last year's.
The Agriculture Ministry specified that the leading regions by area sown with winter grain crops are: Mykolaiv region with 368,800 hectares, including 288,000 hectares of wheat and triticale, 79,300 hectares of barley and 1,500 hectares of rye; Dnipropetrovsk region with 284,600 hectares, including 262,100 hectares of wheat and triticale, 21,200 hectares of barley and 1,300 hectares of rye; and Poltava region with 200,100 hectares, including 191,900 hectares of wheat and triticale, 3,200 hectares of barley and 5,000 hectares of rye.

title: Another Naftogaz employee killed in Russian strike on Pryluky – company
body:
Ihor Chub, another employee of the Naftogaz Group, was killed as a result of the October 7 night attack on a residential apartment building in Pryluky, the company reported on Thursday morning.

"Rescue workers worked all night at the site of the Russian strike on a residential multi-story building, clearing the rubble. It has become known that our employee, Ihor Borysovych Chub, was killed," Naftogaz stated.

He worked as a drilling assistant in the capital and underground well workover department at JSC Ukrnafta. He was 45 years old.

As previously reported, Liudmyla Tsyba, another Naftogaz Group employee who worked as a painter for corrosion protection brigade No. 6 of the Pryluky group of Ukrnafta-Bud, was also killed in the missile-destroyed building in Pryluky.

According to acting CEO of NJSC Naftogaz Ukrainy Serhiy Fedorenko, employees of Naftogaz are among the residents of the building where a Russian missile destroyed an entire entrance.

title: Greek Hospital Performs First Leadless Pacemaker Implant
body: Papageorgiou Hospital in Thessaloniki has performed Northern Greece’s first implantation of a leadless dual-chamber pacemaker (Leadless DR PPM) in a patient with chronic kidney disease who was undergoing haemodialysis and had symptomatic sinus-node dysfunction with multiple prolonged cardiac pauses. The medical team at Papageorgiou Hospital said the technology expands treatment options for selected patients with heart-rhythm disorders, including those who lack suitable venous access through the upper limbs or have a history of infections involving pacemaker leads or the device pocket. The system consists of two independent miniature devices implanted in the right atrium and right ventricle respectively. The two devices communicate with each other, allowing them to coordinate atrial and ventricular pacing and maintain atrioventricular synchronisation without conventional intracardiac leads. The system can also be upgraded to meet the patient’s future pacing needs and is compatible with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Electrophysiologists from Papageorgiou Hospital’s Cardiology Department carried out the procedure with the assistance of Italian doctors, who contributed their experience with the technique. “The implantation is another example of Papageorgiou Hospital’s effort to incorporate the latest developments in cardiology for the benefit of patients,” said Ioannis Stylianidis, director of the hospital’s Cardiology Department. “Innovation, specialised expertise and, above all, teamwork are essential prerequisites for providing high-level cardiac care,” he added. Doctors Melani Konstantinidou, Ilias Zarvalis and Ioannis Stylianidis took part in the procedure, alongside Italian doctors Giordano and LCS E. Conzesa. Nurses Antonis Konstantoudis and Asimenia Mavrochordou from the Arrhythmia Department also participated in the procedure. The post Greek Hospital Performs First Leadless Pacemaker Implant appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: Court dismisses Abba Kyari’s witness, strikes out evidence in cocaine trial
body:
The Federal High Court in Abuja on Wednesday threw out the testimony of suspended top police officer Abba Kyari’s defence witness in his trial on cocaine trafficking charges brought against him and four other police officers by the National Drugs Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA).
Mr Kyari, a suspended deputy commissioner of police who headed the once-influential Intelligence Response Team (IRT) of the police, is facing trial alongside four members of his team over their alleged handling of the cocaine they seized from two convicted drug traffickers in January 2022.
Judge Emeka Nwite dismissed Mr Kyari’s second defence witness, El-John Nwonke, and struck out his previously given evidence on Wednesday following his repeated absence from two consecutive hearings.
Monday’s proceedings had stalled after the judge reluctantly granted an adjournment requested by the defence on the grounds of Mr Nwonke’s ill health, even though he declared the witness’ letter requesting two weeks for recovery from his ailment unconvincing.
NDLEA’s prosecution lawyer, Joseph Sunday, also recalled during the Monday’s hearing that the previous proceedings of 29 September stalled after the defence called for an adjournment on the grounds that Mr Nwonke was outside Nigeria to attend a course.
Mr Nwonke, a police inspector subpoenaed to appear to testify at the instance of Mr Kyari, was absent from court again on Wednesday, a situation the prosecution latched onto to renew its call for the foreclosure of the witness’ evidence.
Julius Mba, the lawyer who appeared for Mr Kyari and the fourth defendant in the trial, Simon Agirgba, said Mr Nwonke, who started testifying in January, might be unaware that hearing in the case was rescheduled for Wednesday.
Ruling, Judge Nwite said the witness had been given ample time to present his evidence and be cross-examined by the prosecution but failed to take advantage of it.
The judge consequently declared the witness’ testimony closed and struck out his evidence, which the prosecution did not have an opportunity to cross-examine him on.
The development comes as a setback for Mr Kyari, whose defence largely rests on the notion that he and his team are being targeted with prosecution because they arrested two cocaine traffickers corruptly cleared by NDLEA officials on their arrival at the Akanu Ibiam International Airport, Enugu, in January 2022.
Mr Nwonke, the dismissed witness, had used his time in the witness box since January to shed light on police investigations into the two cocaine smugglers and their confessions in the early days of their arrest by Mr Kyari’s team.
Following the ruling that dismissed the second defence witness, Mr Mba reminded the court of the subpoena issued to compel the NDLEA to produce a list of its officers on duty at the Akanu Ibiam International Airport, Enugu, on January 19, 2022 – the day two cocaine smugglers were allowed to pass before their arrest by the police.
Mr Mba said the information would assist the defence in deciding how to proceed with the case.
But the prosecution lawyer, Mr Sunday, faulted the subpoena on the grounds that it was addressed to the NDLEA director general, a position he described as non-existent at the agency.
Mr Sunday told the court that the agency instead has a chairman/chief executive officer and a secretary.
He nevertheless assured the court that an NDLEA officer would bring the requested list of personnel on duty at the airport on the specified date on Thursday.
The judge adjourned the case until 8 October (Thursday) for continuation of the trial.
The NDLEA arrested Mr Kyari on 14 February 2022, after declaring him wanted over alleged links to an international drug cartel.
He was arraigned on cocaine charges on 7 March 2022 alongside the two cocaine smugglers and four IRT members: Sunday J. Ubua, an assistant commissioner of police; Bawa James, an assistant superintendent of police; Simon Agirgba, an inspector, and John Nuhu, also an inspector.
The NDLEA charged them with illicit dealing in and tampering with the cocaine seized from the two traffickers. The prosecution alleged that the defendants removed 17.55kg out of the 21.35kg of the substance they seized from the convicted traffickers and substituted the portion they took out with some other substance.
In another count which has Mr Kyari as the sole defendant, the NDLEA accused him of attempting to obstruct its authorised officers by offering $61,400 to a senior anti-narcotic operative as inducement to prevent the testing of the 17.55kg of cocaine.
The defendants have denied the charges and started their defence last year, after the prosecution called its witnesses and tendered exhibits to prove the charges.
Mr Kyari’s legal team has put forward a line of defence that casts him and his IRT members as innocent police officers targeted after arresting the two cocaine smugglers whom NDLEA officers had cleared.
On 28 January, Mr Nwonke, the police inspector brought as Mr Kyari’s second defence witness, testified on how officers of the NDLEA allegedly aided Chibunna Umeibe and Emeka Ezenwanne to beat security checks at Enugu International Airport on 19 January 2022, on arrival from Ethiopia with cocaine.
He said the now defunct IRT, a Mr Kyari-led elite police unit concerned with serious crimes involving risky operations, arrested the cocaine traffickers shortly after NDLEA officers cleared them at the airport.
The witness said he was serving with the Force Criminal Investigation Department (FCID) of the Nigerian Police Force, Abuja, when the two suspects were arrested by the IRT officers and brought in for investigation.
He said he was part of the team that conducted the interview session for the suspects on 20 January 2022 when their statements were taken and the session recorded.
The witness said the recorded video was transferred into a digital video disc (DVD).
Mr Nwonke said the two traffickers, who were initially charged alongside Mr Kyari and the four police officers but were later convicted and jailed two years upon their pleading guilty in 2022, confessed that the police officers arrested them with the suspected cocaine at the airport after NDLEA officers on duty had cleared them.
The defence witness said the convicted drug traffickers told his team how the NDLEA officers at the point of entry used sign language to help them beat security checks on arrival, before the police eventually arrested them.
On 28 February, the court admitted the video recording brought by Mr Nwonke as Exhibit D-3. The recording captures convicted Mr Umeibe and Mr Ezenwanne making confessional statements.
The video was later played in open court on 16 March, with the two men describing how they allegedly bypassed security checks at the airport.
In the 27-minute-long video clip, Messrs Umeibe and Ezenwanne narrated how officers of the NDLEA allegedly aided them to bypass security checks at the Enugu International Airport before their arrest by the IRT.
Mr Kyari opened his defence in July last year, after the prosecution closed its case and the court dismissed the defendants’ no-case submission.
Adeshina Fasasi, described as a team lead with MTN’s incident management unit, testified as Mr Kyari’s first defence witness in July.
Subpoenaed at Mr Kyari’s instance, Mr Fasasi said an examination of Mr Kyari’s call log revealed no contact with any number linked to a suspected cocaine trafficker known as Mike Coke.
He said his review showed that his review of the call data record (CDR) showed that a phone number – 09136976496 – attributed to a contact tagged “Coke,” was registered to one Ruth Ayuba, and not to Mr Kyari.
Mr Fasasi also said MTN never recorded or stored the content of calls made between users, even if requested by law enforcement.
He also said MTN’s CDR system never captured WhatsApp messages, voice recordings, or saved contact names on a mobile device.
He said the CDR only captured voice and SMS metadata, location information, and device types.
Under cross-examination by the prosecution team, he said was not a direct employee of MTN Nigeria. He said he only worked as part of a managed services team recognised by the telecoms company.
He admitted that he had not read the full content of the report tendered in court and could not speak to its entirety.
By June 2024, the NDLEA had called 15 out of its 16 proposed prosecution witnesses.
In July 2022, during the prosecution’s presentation, the court admitted $61,400 cash Mr Kyari allegedly offered to an NDLEA operative as bribes.
The court admitted the cash evidence alongside 24 packs of cocaine, which the prosecution tendered through its third witness, Peter Joshua, an operative of the anti-narcotics agency.
Mr Joshua told the court that the foreign currency was given to him on 25 January 2022, after he weighed and carried out preliminary tests on wraps of cocaine that were confiscated from Messrs Umeibe and Ezenwane.
Mr Kyari allegedly attempted to bribe the NDLEA official with the aim of compromising investigation into the seized cocaine substance.
In October 2022, NDLEA’s fourth prosecution witness, Mohammed Ajia, a commander at the agency, said forensic examinations revealed that only 80 per cent or four-fifth of the substance tested cocaine. The witness said the remaining 20 per cent or one-fifth of it was another substance.
In April 2025, the court ruled that Mr Kyari and his co-defendant had a case to answer and ordered them to enter defence.
Mr Kyari and his co-defendants are attending trial from prison, where the court remanded them after denying them bail on several occasions.
Earlier in March, Mr Kyari, and two of his brothers were acquitted in a separate non-declaration of assets case.

title: Ukrainian Drones Hit Yandex Data Center, Industrial Facilities Across Russia
body:
A Ukrainian drone attack ignited a fire at a data center owned by Russian tech giant Yandex in the Ryazan region overnight, the company said Thursday, suspending the site’s operations and triggering service disruptions.
The attack marks the first confirmed strike against Russian data infrastructure since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, weeks after Moscow launched attacks against Ukrainian data centers.
Yandex confirmed that operations at the facility in the town of Sasovo were fully suspended while emergency teams worked to contain the damage, according to a statement circulated in the media. Governor Pavel Malkov said the roof of a Sasovo district company, which he did not name, caught fire.
NASA’s fire monitoring service FIRMS showed a fire in Sasovo early Thursday morning.
Outage tracking platform Downdetector recorded more than 1,300 user reports of disruptions affecting Yandex Cloud, Yandex Documents and Yandex Tables, while core consumer tools like search and taxi services remained online.
Yandex shares dropped more than 3.4% during Thursday morning trading on the Moscow Exchange.
A fire also broke out at an industrial site in Russia’s town of Salavat in the republic of Bashkortostan after drone debris fell on it, local authorities reported on Thursday.
There are no casualties, and the enterprise continues operations, they added.
Ukrainian forces struck the Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat oil refinery and petrochemicals complex in central Russia’s Bashkortostan region, Kyiv’s military said on Thursday.
In a statement, the General Staff said the attack had sparked a fire.
On Thursday afternoon, eyewitnesses told the exiled outlet Astra that Ukrainian drones attacked Russia’s largest oil refinery in the Omsk region of western Siberia.
Governor Vitaly Khotsenko confirmed a Ukrainian drone attack on the Omsk region without specifying the targets. Civil aviation authorities suspended inbound and outbound flights during the afternoon air raid alert.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said its air defense systems intercepted 399 Ukrainian drones over 18 Russian regions and annexed Crimea overnight.
The Sasovo attack comes after Russian forces have, since late September, hit at least eight major data centers across Kyiv, causing widespread internet blackouts in Ukraine. Russia claimed the data centers processed military intelligence for Ukrainian forces.

title: Greece Expands Its Michelin Guide Footprint Beyond Athens
body: The Michelin Guide is expanding its coverage of Greece to strengthen the international profile of Greek gastronomy, with Thessaloniki and Santorini joining Athens in the 2027 selection. The new Michelin Guide selection for Greece will be announced on October 20, 2026, and will feature the three destinations for the first time, expanding Greece’s gastronomic map. The expansion forms part of the partnership between the Greek National Tourism Organisation (GNTO) and the Michelin Guide. As announced in December 2025, the Michelin Guide’s independent and anonymous inspectors extended their research to Thessaloniki and Santorini, highlighting three distinct gastronomic identities across Athens, Thessaloniki and Santorini. The Michelin Guide selection includes several distinctions, including one to three Michelin Stars, the Michelin Green Star for restaurants demonstrating a strong commitment to sustainability, the Bib Gourmand for establishments offering particularly good value for money, and the Michelin Selected category. GNTO Secretary General Andreas Fiorentinos said the partnership with the Michelin Guide is helping expand Greece’s gastronomic map and showcase the distinct culinary identities of its destinations. He described the expansion to Thessaloniki and Santorini as an important development that brings two destinations with strong and distinctive gastronomic potential to the international stage. “Gastronomy is an integral part of the tourism experience and an important element in differentiating Greek destinations,” Fiorentinos said. He added that the partnership with the Michelin Guide strengthens the international presence of Greek gastronomy and showcases more aspects of Greece to travellers from around the world. The 2027 Michelin Guide selection for Greece will be available from October 20 through the Michelin Guide’s digital platforms. The post Greece Expands Its Michelin Guide Footprint Beyond Athens appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: Western attempts to disrupt Russian elections resulted in society’s consolidation — expert
body:
SIMFEROPOL, October 8. /TASS/. Attempts by the collective West’s and Ukraine’s propaganda to disrupt the September State Duma elections had the opposite effect and resulted in the consolidation of Russian society, Ilya Gusev, acting head of the Federal Agency for Ethnic Affairs’ interregional office for the North Caucasian Federal District, the Republic of Crimea and Sevastopol, told TASS.
"Attempts by Western countries and Ukraine to somehow prevent citizens from exercising their electoral rights led, on the contrary, to citizens of our country viewing their electoral rights as an opportunity to show and convey to the outside world: we do not respond to this, it only unites us, we are ready to defend our social and political life and preserve stability here. And look at the voter turnout. Therefore, the effect that our opponents expected turned out to be exactly the opposite," he said.
The elections of deputies to the ninth State Duma were held during the single voting day from September 18 to 20. For the first time, residents of the Donbass and Novorossiya regions participated in them.
