title: Justice Adefope-Okojie leads debate on judicial intervention in Nigeria’s elections
body: By Innocent Anaba Justice Oludotun Adefope-Okojie, retired Justice of the Court of Appeal, will deliver the 2026 Gavel International Annual Lecture slated for November 17, focusing on the increasingly debated role of the judiciary in Nigeria’s electoral process. The lecture, entitled “Electoral Process in Nigeria: Managing the Boundaries of Judicial Intervention,” will examine the relationship between judicial intervention in electoral disputes and the constitutional right of Nigerians to determine their representatives through the ballot box. The event will hold at the Main Hall of the Lagos Chamber of Commerce and Industry, Nurudeen Olowopopo Road, Central Business District, Alausa-Ikeja, Lagos. Former Attorney-General and Commissioner for Justice of Bayelsa State, Chief Anthony George-Ikoli, SAN, will chair the event. George-Ikoli is also the first Senior Advocate of Nigeria produced by Bayelsa State. Lawyer and activist, Mr. Femi Falana, SAN, will moderate the panel discussion following the lecture. The organisers said the theme was chosen against the backdrop of continuing public debate over the role of the courts in determining electoral disputes and the implications of judicial decisions for the votes cast by Nigerians. The lecture will examine the constitutional and practical boundaries of judicial intervention and the need to balance the adjudicatory role of the courts with the electorate’s authority to choose its political representatives. Justice Adefope-Okojie brings extensive judicial experience to the discussion, having served both on the High Court of Lagos State and the Court of Appeal, where she participated in the adjudication of electoral and other constitutional disputes. Gavel International said her extensive judicial experience, particularly in electoral adjudication, placed her in a strong position to lead the discussion on the relationship between the judiciary and the electoral process. The organisation said her experience on the Bench and commitment to justice, constitutionalism and the rule of law would provide useful perspectives for policymakers, legal practitioners, academics and other stakeholders engaged in Nigeria’s democratic process. Gavel’s record of public engagement Founded by journalist Mustapha Ogunsakin in 2008, Gavel International is a legal and judicial news platform covering the administration of justice, constitutional governance and the rule of law. The organisation has also used its platform to convene public discussions on important legal and governance issues. The 2026 edition will additionally feature the presentation of awards to Nigerians who have distinguished themselves through contributions to law, justice, business, human rights, education and public service. The organisers said the event is expected to draw senior judicial officers, lawyers, academics, policymakers, public officials, members of the diplomatic community, business leaders, journalists and other stakeholders. The panel discussion, to be moderated by Falana, is expected to extend the debate beyond the lecture and provide perspectives from the legal profession, academia and the media on the appropriate limits of judicial intervention in Nigeria’s electoral process. title: Mark Villar joins Senate majority bloc
body: MANILA, Philippines — Senator Mark Villar has joined the Senate majority bloc, Senate President Pro Tempore Vicente “Tito” Sotto III confirmed Thursday, October 8. “Well, apparently,” Sotto told reporters in an ambush interview when asked about Villar’s transfer. “We’re glad because we’re all loaded with work… We have the impeachment, legislative [duties], and budget [deliberations], so it would be better if we have more members,” he said. Sotto said he was informed of the change only earlier in the day and that Senate Majority Floor Leader Juan Miguel “Migz” Zubiri coordinated Villar’s transfer. The Senate held its final plenary session on Thursday before going on a break from October 9 to November 9. During the session, Zubiri moved for the election of Villar as a member of the Commission on Appointments (CA) under the majority bloc. Villar was also elected chairperson of the Senate committee on public works and highways, replacing Sotto. Asked if Villar had formally joined the majority, Zubiri said: “Yes, we just elected him to the CA and public works committee as part of the majority.” With Villar’s transfer, the majority bloc now has 14 members, while the minority has 10. His sister, Senator Camille Villar, remains with the minority bloc. Villar’s move came as the Office of the Ombudsman announced graft complaints against members of the Villar family over contracts involving their firm, PrimeWater. It also comes amid the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, which will be decided by senator-judges. Cayetano: Minority’s ‘duty remains unchanged’ In a statement, Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano said he wished Villar well and stressed that the members of the minority bloc will continue to fulfill their duty despite the latest development. “We understand all too well the circumstances and considerations that lead to changes in political alliances. Since May 11, it has become increasingly clear how important it is for this administration to maintain a closely allied working majority in the Senate,” Cayetano said. “But regardless of how the political landscape shifts, our duty remains unchanged. We will continue to stand for what is right, uphold our institutions, and work for the good of our nation,” Cayetano added. Asked about the decision of Villar to jump ship to the majority bloc, Senator Bong Go, a member of the minority bloc, said in a media interview that they respect his decision. Responding to questions, Go said that they remain on good terms with Villar. “We respect each other,” he said. – Rappler.com

title: Ghana, Czech Republic explore defence manufacturing partnership — Defence Minister
body: Ghana and the Czech Republic are exploring opportunities to deepen cooperation in defence and security, with discussions focusing on equipment, technology and the development of local defence manufacturing capacity. Minister for Defence, Kenneth Gilbert Adjei, said the two countries are considering joint ventures and capacity-building initiatives as part of efforts to strengthen Ghana’s defence capabilities and broaden technical expertise within the sector. He disclosed this in a Facebook post on Wednesday, October 7, 2026, after hosting the Czech Ambassador to Ghana, Pavel Bilek, and his delegation at the Ministry of Defence. The engagement also examined opportunities for greater collaboration in defence equipment and technology. Mr Adjei said Ghana would also continue to strengthen its broader partnership with the Czech Republic in areas including health, education and trade, describing the existing cooperation between the two countries as one that should be expanded.

title: NDPC, UNIDO discuss new partnership to drive Ghana’s industrial development
body: The National Development Planning Commission (NDPC) and the United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO) are exploring a new partnership to better align industrial development interventions with Ghana’s national priorities. The discussions centre on a new five-year Programme for Country Partnership (PCP) that UNIDO plans to introduce in Ghana from 2027. The programme is expected to provide a framework for UNIDO’s support to the country’s industrial development agenda, with consultations planned with key government institutions and other stakeholders. UNIDO Country Representative in Ghana, Dr Emmanuel Kalenzi, said the proposed partnership would strengthen the organisation’s relationship with the NDPC and deepen its understanding of the Commission’s role in national development planning. He described the NDPC as a key national partner and stressed the importance of ensuring that UNIDO interventions respond to Ghana’s development priorities and existing planning frameworks. The proposed areas of focus include agro-industrial value chains and industrial parks, support for micro, small and medium-sized enterprises, job creation, investment promotion and trade, industrial policy and skills development. The programme is also expected to cover the circular economy, renewable energy and energy efficiency. Dr Kalenzi outlined the plans when a UNIDO delegation paid a courtesy call on the NDPC on Monday, October 5, 2026. The engagement provided an opportunity for both institutions to identify areas where closer collaboration could support Ghana’s industrial transformation. NDPC Director-General, Dr Audrey Smock Amoah, welcomed the initiative and expressed the Commission’s readiness to support the development of the proposed programme. She said closer coordination between national planning institutions and development partners would help ensure that external interventions are aligned with Ghana’s broader development objectives. The proposed PCP will subsequently be developed through consultations with relevant national institutions, with the outcome expected to guide UNIDO’s industrial development support in Ghana from 2027.

title: Kwara APC: How a succession battle became a political earthquake, By Ehi Braimah
body:
Politics is rarely only about elections; it is also about succession, control, alliances, interests and the management of political expectations. In Kwara State, these forces have combined to produce one of the more intriguing intra-party crises ahead of Nigeria’s 2027 general elections.
What began as a contest over who would succeed Governor AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq has gradually turned into a full-blown political rupture within the All Progressives Congress (APC), with Senator Saliu Mustapha and other influential party stakeholders moving to the People’s Democratic Party (PDP), followed by defections among elected officials and grassroots members.
The immediate issue is the 2027 governorship election, but underneath it is a much bigger question: who controls the political future of Kwara after AbdulRazaq leaves office? AbdulRazaq will complete his second term in May 2027 and cannot seek a third term. Inevitably, therefore, the question of succession has become the defining issue within the Kwara APC.
The governor has an obvious political interest in what happens after his tenure. His opponents, equally, have ambitions of their own. Senator Saliu Mustapha, representing Kwara Central, was one of the prominent figures interested in becoming the next governor of Kwara State. The disagreement between him and AbdulRazaq did not begin with the APC primary, but the primary appears to have converted a simmering political rivalry into an open confrontation.
The dispute between both politicians is a struggle over political influence, succession and control of the APC structure. The governorship primary on 22 May, was the defining moment. Yakubu Danladi-Salihu, speaker of the Kwara State House of Assembly, emerged as the APC’s governorship candidate, polling more than 94,000 votes. His emergence followed intense negotiations and controversy within the party.
The choice was politically significant for another reason. Danladi-Salihu is from Kwara North, a zone that has long argued that it should have an opportunity to produce the governor. Thus, the primary was about the individual aspirants and the politics of zoning and power rotation, but the controversy surrounding the primary has been difficult to contain. Aggrieved APC stakeholders have alleged that the process was manipulated to favour a preferred successor. Some have gone as far as describing the emergence of Danladi-Salihu as the product of an imposed process.
A group of former aspirants subsequently rallied around what Senator Mustapha calls the “Rainbow Coalition”, bringing together the G15 of aggrieved governorship aspirants, Otoge Progressives and elements of the party’s elders’ caucus. Those are allegations and political interpretations, not established facts, to the best of my knowledge. The APC has defended the legitimacy of its processes and continues to support AbdulRazaq and its governorship candidate.
Indeed, 51 APC ward chairmen in Kwara Central recently declared their support for the governor and Danladi-Salihu and dismissed the significance of Mustapha’s defection. But in politics, perception matters. Once a substantial group of party members believes that a process has been predetermined, the damage to trust can be considerable – even where the party insists that its procedures were followed.
The legislative primaries added another layer of tension to the furore. In May, the APC initially screened out 105 of 158 aspirants seeking its State House of Assembly tickets, with several serving lawmakers among those initially declared “uncleared.” The development generated anxiety across the party.
There is, however, an important correction to the earlier narrative about this episode: the APC subsequently reversed that initial screening outcome and cleared all 159 Assembly aspirants in a revised exercise.
That reversal itself illustrates the intensity of the political atmosphere. The initial decision created the impression of a dramatic purge, but the subsequent reversal showed that the party was capable of adjusting its position when the consequences became politically sensitive. It is therefore too simplistic to say that the governor personally “handpicked” every National and State Assembly candidate. That remains an allegation by some aggrieved party members.
The more defensible conclusion is that candidate selection became a battleground over control of the party and the political configuration that will emerge after AbdulRazaq. That distinction matters. Mustapha’s eventual defection transformed the internal APC dispute into a broader political realignment. His move to the PDP was because he lost an internal contest but it also represents part of a wider coalition of dissatisfied APC stakeholders. That is where the PDP has acquired an unexpected opportunity.
The irony is difficult to miss. The APC’s political ascendancy in Kwara was built around the historic “Otoge” movement of 2019, which ended the dominance of the political structure associated with former Senate President Bukola Saraki.
Seven years later, the political landscape has changed dramatically. Some of the forces that helped establish the APC’s dominance are now divided, while the PDP is attempting to rebuild around some of the same political networks that were weakened in 2019 and harvest what appears to be a political fortune.
The APC’s internal crisis has consequently become an opportunity for the PDP to reconstruct its grassroots organisation. The defections are particularly significant because they are no longer confined to prominent politicians. Last month, more than 2,000 APC members in Adewole Ward, Ilorin West Local Government Area, reportedly defected to the PDP. Adewole is the ancestral ward of Governor AbdulRazaq, making the development symbolically important. The defectors said they were supporters of Mustapha and were following him into the PDP.
There have also been defections in Offa, including from Shawo Central Ward, the political base of Senator Lola Ashiru. Reports say hundreds of APC members moved to the PDP, citing their confidence in Saraki’s political leadership.
Two APC members of the Kwara State House of Assembly – Saba Yisa Gideon and Olusola Odetundun – have also defected to the PDP. The Assembly subsequently declared their seats vacant after the APC argued that they had no constitutional basis to defect in the absence of a division within the party.
This is the point at which an internal party disagreement becomes a political earthquake. The real significance of these defections will not simply depend on the number of people leaving the APC but on whether the defectors can convert their movement into an effective political organisation.
That is the challenge before both sides. Will there be more defections? Only time will tell because in politics, 24 hours is a long time.
For the APC, the central question is whether it can reconcile its competing factions before the 2027 election. For the PDP and the Rainbow Coalition, the challenge is different. Defections make headlines, but elections are won through organisation, candidates, voter mobilisation and sustained grassroots engagement. Moving prominent politicians and thousands of supporters from one party to another is only the beginning.
There is also an interesting federal dimension. Mustapha’s realignment does not necessarily translate into opposition to President Bola Tinubu. His camp has sought to distinguish its disagreement with the Kwara APC structure from its position on the President. This reflects the fluidity of Nigerian politics, where alliances can be different at federal and state levels.
The 2027 contest in Kwara could therefore produce unusual alignments: support for one political platform at the presidential level and another at the state level. At the heart of everything, however, is succession. A governor nearing the end of his tenure naturally wants to influence what comes next. Aspirants want a fair opportunity to succeed him; legislators want to retain their seats; party leaders want to remain relevant, and political blocs want assurances that they will not be excluded from the next dispensation. It is the same playbook used by politicians to advance their interests.
When these interests collide, a party primary can become much more than a primary – it becomes a struggle over the future. That is what appears to have happened in Kwara, but it would be premature to declare that the APC has lost Kwara. Nigerian political parties have repeatedly demonstrated their ability to survive internal crises, reconcile factions and rebound before elections because of the absence of what we may describe as ideological orientation.
What is clear, however, is that the APC’s succession problem has become a serious organisational challenge. As I noted earlier, the irony is that the 2019 Otoge movement was built on the rejection of political dominance by one entrenched structure. Today, the forces that emerged from that political revolution are engaged in another struggle over who gets to shape the next political order.
That is the deeper meaning of the Kwara crisis which has escalated beyond just merely seeing it as AbdulRazaq versus Mustapha, or APC versus PDP. The 2027 election will eventually determine which political coalition commands the mandate of the people. For now, however, one thing is unmistakable: a succession battle inside the APC has escaped the confines of the party and became a wider contest for the political future of Kwara.
The political earthquake has happened, but the real question is how the aftershocks will end.
Ehi Braimah is a public relations specialist, marketing strategist and publisher/editor-in-chief of Naija Times and Lagos Post . He is a strong advocate for African prosperity and can be reached through: [email protected] .

title: ROP to review heavy vehicle safety and driving licence requirements
body:
MUSCAT: The Royal Oman Police (ROP) has formed a committee to review heavy vehicle safety requirements and the conditions and procedures for issuing driving licences, including heavy vehicle licences. Lt Gen Hassan bin Mohsin Al Shraiqi, Inspector General of Police and Customs, issued Decision No 137/2026 establishing the committee, chaired by the Director General of Traffic, with specialist ROP personnel as members. The committee will review licensing provisions under the Traffic Law and its executive regulations, alongside safety and security requirements for heavy vehicles. The review will consider practical needs and relevant international practices. ROP said the decision reflects its commitment to improving the traffic system and ensuring the safety of road users. Separately, ROP reported that a tractor-trailer had broken down on the Muscat Expressway after the Al Ilam bridge, in the direction of Seeb. Traffic was diverted from the Qurum bridge to Sultan Qaboos Street. Police urged motorists to use alternative routes and cooperate with officers.
