Mark made the disclosure during a courtesy visit by the Governing Council of the Savannah Centre for Diplomacy, Democracy and Development to the party headquarters in Abuja on Wednesday. The Council, led by the former Chief Justice of Nigeria, Olukayode Ariwoola, said the courtesy call was part of the Centre’s ongoing stakeholder engagements with political parties and political leaders ahead of the 2027 general elections. The retired justice expressed the Centre’s commitment to promoting free, fair and credible elections and urged the ADC leadership to encourage its candidates and members to comply with INEC’s rules and eschew all forms of political violence. In his response, Mark declared the ADC’s commitment to playing by the rules. “We are committed to playing politics in a manner that promotes public confidence in democracy,” he said. He also emphasised that the party would comply with INEC’s rules guiding the elections, as well as the ADC’s code of conduct, articulated in its Orange Book. He said, the party would, however, not accept rigging. “We hold ourselves to the highest standards of good conduct as a political party. We will play by the rules. But we will not accept rigging or allow ourselves to be rigged out,” he concluded. Justice Ariwoola’s entourage included members of the Savannah Centre’s Governing Council, otherwise known as the “Council of the Wise”. They included Professors Abdullahi Shehu and Azeez Musa Dankano; the Executive Director, Ambassador Sani Bala; Mr Tunji Lardner; and Ambassador Godswill Ighali, among others.

title: Ondo crash: How pilot saved community – Gov Aiyedatiwa
body: Governor Lucky Aiyedatiwa of Ondo State on Wednesday visited the site of the Nigerian Air Force ATR-42 aircraft crash in Igbokoda, Ilaje Local Government Area, two days after the tragedy, saying the pilot’s final actions saved the coastal community from a far greater disaster. The governor, who inspected the crash site alongside military personnel and emergency responders, said accounts from residents indicated that the aircraft developed trouble before going down but was skilfully manoeuvred away from the town. According to him, the pilot prevented what could have resulted in massive casualties by steering the aircraft into a swampy area about 200 metres away from the community. “I also thank God that the aircraft did not crash in the middle of the community. That would have been a major catastrophe for the entire area,” Aiyedatiwa said. “From accounts given by residents, they saw the aircraft descending with what sounded like an engine problem. It was coming down and almost appeared set to crash within the community. “However, the pilot was able to manoeuvre the aircraft and bring it down about 200 metres away from the community before it went into the swampy area.” The governor described the incident as a national tragedy and expressed sadness over the loss of military personnel aboard the aircraft. He said there was no indication that anyone survived the crash, adding that rescue teams had continued search and recovery efforts since Monday. Aiyedatiwa said he visited the location with personnel of the Nigerian Navy, Nigerian Air Force, National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA), Ondo State Emergency Management Agency and local divers involved in the operation. “It is a sad story,” he said. “We saw a gory sight at the location.” The governor disclosed that body parts, clothing belonging to Air Force personnel and fragments of the aircraft had been recovered from the swamp. “Some body parts had been recovered and preserved for further investigation. Some clothes, jackets belonging to the Air Force personnel, and parts of the broken aircraft were also found. “Unfortunately, the main body of the aircraft has not been sighted. It is submerged in the swamp.” He explained that the difficult terrain had hampered rescue efforts, prompting the state government to deploy two swamp excavation machines, known as Swamp Buggies, to create access routes to the crash site. “When we realised there was no real access to the location, I directed the Ministry of Works to deploy two swamp machines, known as Swamp Buggies, to create wider access on the waterways,” he said. Aiyedatiwa noted that the machines had improved access to the area, enabling larger boats and rescue teams to reach the site as divers continued the search for the wreckage. The governor commiserated with President Bola Tinubu, the Nigerian Air Force and families of the victims, describing the deceased as gallant officers who died in service to the nation. The aircraft crashed into a swampy area near Igbokoda on Monday while on a mission from Benin to Lagos. Search teams have yet to recover the main wreckage as rescue and recovery operations continue.

title: A Tribute: Mallam Nafi’u Baba Ahmad
body: A neighbour for decade, a mentor for life. From Gidan Radio Close – Gudu cemetery A Hausa–English Tribute of Love, Gratitude and Du’ah. Indeed, you are to die, and indeed, they are to die.” Qur’an Chapter Zumar, verse 30. There are people whose departure leaves an empty space. There are others whose departure makes an entire neighbourhood feels different. And then there are those whose presence has been woven so deeply into our lives that, when they leave, a part of our own history seems to leave with them. For me, Malam Nafi’u Baba Ahmad was such a person. For almost a decade, I have lived next to him on our Radio Close, off Rabah Road, Kaduna. For more than 30 years, I did not merely have a senior, I had an elder, mentor, teacher, adviser and friend whose presence became part of the rhythm of my life. Today, I struggle to write about him in the past tense. Yau, Malam or rather Baba Nafi’u (as we used to address him) ya rasu, ya tafi, ya koma gurin Mahaliccinmu Allah SWT! But the memories remain. And perhaps that is one of the ways Allah allows a good person to continue living among those he has touched, through the lessons, kindness and memories he leaves behind. “Malam, Yaya Baba Nafi’u, Allah jikanka da RahamarSa, Allah sa ka huta cikin Aljannatul-Firdausil a’ala, ka jira zuwanmu, muna hanya?” One of the things I will never forget is the way Malam Nafi’u always asked after my father. My father is 101 years old, older than Malam Nafi’u himself, and whenever we met, Malam Nafi’u would ask about his health and wellbeing. It was never an empty question. It was the concern of an elder for another elder. At one point, he gave my father two neck-support pillows as gifts, simply because he wanted him to be more comfortable. This morning, when I told my father: “Baba, Malam Nafi’u, wanda ya baka abun sakawa a wuya dinnan ya rasu, he is no longer in this world, ya rasu da safennan!.” My father cried. Not just tears. He cried with a heavy, painful sound. I intentionally did that to gauge his response and his crying confirmed he is still very responsive because these days he seems to be too quiet. And in that moment, despite his age, we realised something deeply touching: he still remembered Malam Baba Nafi’u. He remembered the man. He remembered the kindness. He remembered the gifts. That moment broke my heart. Because it reminded me that kindness does not expire. Sometimes a simple act of kindness given some months go, remains buried in the heart until the day someone tells you:“The person who showed you that kindness is no longer here.” A mentor who taught through stories Malam Nafi’u had a special way of teaching me. He did not always sit down and say, “Let me teach you this.” Sometimes he simply told me a story. A story about someone. A story about life. A story about human nature. A story about faith. And after the story, there was always something to take away. Darussan rayuwa suna nan cikin labarai. Labarai masu nausarwa, masu hannunka mai sanda. There was always a lesson hidden somewhere between his words. I learnt to listen beyond the story. I learnt to ask myself: “Me Malam yake so in fahimta daga wannan?” That was his style of mentorship. He did not always give you the answer. He gave you the wisdom with which to find the answer yourself. And that is the kind of teacher whose lessons stay with you. The book, the will and the legacy I remember discussing with him his book on Islamic Will. We spoke about the importance of making Muslims understand the Islamic guidance concerning wills and encouraging people to update and properly document their wills before their deaths. I suggested that the book should be digitised, so that its teachings could travel beyond the people who could physically obtain or read the book. The idea was simple: If knowledge is beneficial, let technology carry it further. Today, after his passing, that conversation means even more to me. It’s in his will that he should be buried wherever he dies. His will actualised by the family, alhamdulillah we all gathered at Abuja for the burial. Perhaps one of the greatest ways we can honour scholars is not merely by remembering their names, but by helping beneficial knowledge they cared about to reach another generation. May Allah make every beneficial knowledge he taught me and others be preserved as a continuing source of reward for him. The Masjid Then there was our neighbourhood Masjid, the Radio Close Masjid and Islamiyyah. Malam Nafi’u, after briefing him of our last meeting where we discussed the future of the Masjid, he encouraged me to team up and continue taking care of the Masjid. He understood something that many people sometimes forget: A Masjid is not only a building. It is an Amanah. When we decided to begin collecting contributions for the maintenance of the Masjid, I approached him. And, as I will never forget, he was the first to contribute. The first. Before asking others to support the Masjid, he supported it himself. As I write this piece, his deposited contribution before opening the Masjid account is in my custody. That was Malam Nafi’u. Ba ya koyarwa da baki kawai, a aikace yake baka tarbiyya. He did not merely tell others what to do. He led by example. The las Sallah.There is one memory that I believe I will carry to my grave. One day, Malam Nafi’u asked me to lead the prayer in our neighbourhood Masjid. I stood before the congregation and led the Salah. During my recitation, I recited the Basmala at the beginning of Suratul-Fatihah and the subsequent surahs. After the prayer, Malam Nafi’u addressed all of us. He explained that what had been done had a basis in the religion, even though it may not always be practised by others. That was his last time to pray in that Masjid, to the best of my knowledge. It was an admonition. It was a lesson. It was a moment of scholarship. That would be the last prayer we would share with him in our neighbourhood Masjid. SubhanAllah! Sometimes Allah allows us to experience a final moment without telling us that it is final. We shake someone’s hand without knowing it is the last handshake. We hear someone’s voice without knowing it is the last time. We sit with someone without knowing it is the last sitting. We pray beside someone without knowing:“This is the last Salah you will pray together.” Today, I look back at that prayer differently. And I thank Allah for it. Because my last prayer with my mentor ended with a lesson from my mentor, nagode Allah. Our last conversation Our last conversation was about his journey to Egypt for his health. We spoke about his travels. We spoke about his wellbeing. We spoke as neighbours and as people who had known one another for decades. We did not know we were having our final conversation. There was no dramatic farewell. No long goodbye. Just another conversation between a mentor and his mentee. And perhaps that is how Allah decreed it. We do not choose our final goodbye. Allah chooses it for us. And when the appointed time comes: “Every soul shall taste death.” Malam, ka bar mu da abin da ya fi kudi Malam Nafi’u, You have left us with many things money cannot buy. You have left us lessons. You have left us memories. You have left us knowledge. You have left us so many examples and narratives. You have left us good deeds to remember you by and to emulate, in sha ALLAH we will act upon so you get more rewards while away in your peaceful grave in sha ALLAH. And you have left behind people who can say: “I benefited from knowing him.” That is a legacy. Mutum yana mutuwa, amma abin da ya koyar da kyakkyawan aikinsa suna iya ci gaba da kasantuwa da wanzuwa. A person dies, but the good he taught and the good he did can continue living. From my home next door to your house For nearly 10 years, our homes stood next to each other. There was only a wall between us. But Today I realise that the distance between two houses is nothing compared with the distance created when Allah calls one of their occupants back to Him. Your house is still there. Our Masjid is still there. The Gidan-Radio close is still there. Life continues. But your voice is missing. Your stories are missing. Your live-counsel is no longer there. Your physical presence and always playing with the kids is absent. And every time I pass by your house, the first house in the close, I will remember: “This was the home of Malam Nafi’u.” That memory alone will become and remain a form of companionship. My farewell Malam Nafi’u Baba Ahmad, Na gode. JazakAllahu khairan katheeran jazilan for more than 30 years of being part of my life. Thank you for your concern for my father. Thank you for the kindness you showed him. Babana, Mahaifinmu yana gode maka for the two neck supports that Today carry a meaning far greater than their material value. Ina godiya for your stories. Shukran for your counsel. Miyetti you for your lessons. May Allah reward you for encouraging me to continue to care for the Masjid. ALLAH YA biyaka for being the first to support its maintenance when we began seeking contributions. JazakAllahu khair for trusting me to lead that fateful prayer. Thank you for correcting and teaching us with knowledge and wisdom. Thank you for every conversation whose importance I sometimes understood only afterwards. Allah Ya saka maka da alherinSa. May Allah reward you with goodness beyond anything we can give you. Oour du’a for you Ya Allah, Forgive Malam Nafi’u Baba Ahmad. Have Your Mercy upon him. Accept his good deeds. Overlook his shortcomings. Reward his years of service to Islam, the community, Nigeria and humanity. Make every beneficial word he taught a Sadaqatul Jariyah for him. Make every person he guided, every Masjid he supported, every piece of knowledge he transmitted, and every act of kindness he performed to serve as a witness in his favour on the day of resurrection. Ya Allah, ka haskaka kabarinsa. Illuminate his grave. Ya Allah, ka fadada masa kabarinsa yai ta hango aljannah kafin shigarta. Expand his resting place into paradise. Ya Allah, ka sanya kabarinsa ya zama lambu daga cikin lambunan Aljannah. Make his grave a garden from the gardens of Paradise. Grant him peace in Barzakh. Grant him companionship with the righteous. And when the Day comes for us to join him, let the Shahadah be our last wordings, when we are all raised again, raise him among those upon whom You have bestowed Your Mercy. Ya Allah, ka kai Malam Nafi’u Baba Ahmad Aljannatul Firdausil A’ala. Ya Rabbal Aalamin. The final word Malam Nafi’u, You were an elder. You were a mentor. You were a teacher. You were a guide. You were a servant of Islam. And you were part of the story of my life. Malam Nafi’u, ka tafi lafiya. Go in peace, my elder. And until the day Allah reunites us. Barka da Hutu, Malam. (To the righteous it will be said) “Oh reassured soul, return to your Rabb, well pleased and pleasing, then enter amongst My (righteous) servants and enter My Paradise.” (Qur’an Chapter 89, verses 27 to 30) From your neighbour, mentee and grateful student. Musa resides at Gidan Radio Close, Kaduna

title: Kwara: Court rejects PDP’s bid to nullify LG elections
body: The Federal High Court in Abuja has dismissed the Peoples Democratic Party’s (PDP) attempt to nullify the September 2024 local government elections in Kwara State. The court ruled that the party could not convert an earlier pre-election suit into a fresh challenge to the outcome of the polls. Justice Peter Lifu, in a judgment on the suit marked FHC/ABJ/CS/1061/2024, held that the PDP had already participated in the election, pursued its grievances before the appropriate election petition tribunals and failed to appeal the decisions before returning to the Federal High Court. The judge said the amendment sought by the PDP fundamentally changed the character of the original case. “The amendment fundamentally altered the character of the action,” Justice Lifu held. Daily Trust reports that the case had its roots in the PDP’s legal effort to stop the September 21, 2024 council elections conducted by the Kwara State Independent Electoral Commission (KWASIEC). The party had initially asked the court to restrain KWASIEC from conducting the elections and prevent the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) from releasing the national voters’ register to the state electoral body. Justice Lifu had in July 2024 granted an interim order restraining INEC from releasing the register to KWASIEC, but the order was subsequently vacated before the election. The elections consequently went ahead across the state on September 21, 2024, with the PDP taking part in the exercise. The party later challenged the results through about 24 election petitions, according to the judgment, but all the petitions were dismissed and no appeal was lodged against the decisions. The legal setback followed when the PDP returned to the Federal High Court and sought to amend its originating summons to include a relief asking the court to nullify the local government elections. It was this move that Justice Lifu rejected, holding that the amendment effectively transformed the original case from a pre-election dispute into a post-election challenge. According to the judge, such a challenge belonged to the election petition process and could not be introduced through an amendment to an existing suit before the Federal High Court. “The court lacked jurisdiction to start as an election tribunal,” he ruled. The judgment drew a distinction between the legal remedies available before an election and those available after an election has been conducted. Justice Lifu held that having participated in the polls and subsequently pursued election petitions, the PDP could not abandon the outcome of that process and seek substantially the same relief through another proceeding. “The plaintiff voluntarily participated in the said elections, presented election petitions, and failed in all of them,” the court held. The court also found that the amended case had become statute-barred, meaning that the PDP could no longer pursue the relief it introduced after the expiration of the applicable statutory period. “Having been so reconstituted, the suit was caught by the statutory limitation period,” Justice Lifu held. The judge further upheld the preliminary objection of the defendants that the PDP’s continued pursuit of the matter constituted an abuse of court process. He said allowing the party to return to the Federal High Court after the conclusion of its election petitions would amount to using another judicial process to relitigate issues that ought to have been determined through the prescribed electoral litigation procedure. “It was impermissible for the plaintiff to return, by way of an amended originating summons, to seek reliefs which it could no longer obtain through the election petition process,” Justice Lifu held.

title: PRP presidential candidate, Duke, pledges N300 petrol price
body: Former Cross River State Governor Donald Duke has promised to slash the price of Premium Motor Spirit (PMS), commonly known as petrol, to N300 per litre if elected president under the platform of the Peoples Redemption Party (PRP) in 2027. Duke made the pledge during an appearance on Channels Television’s Morning Brief, where he criticized the economic policies of President Bola Tinubu and outlined an alternative framework for the petroleum sector. According to Duke, the current pricing model unfairly exposes citizens to international crude benchmarks despite Nigeria’s domestic production capacity. He called the current subsidy structure a “scam” and advocated for pricing petroleum products strictly based on local production and refining costs. “I’m going to price petroleum products for local consumption at production costs, not at international market costs,” Duke stated. He noted that total production and refining costs hover around $45 per barrel, making it unreasonable to sell fuel back to Nigerians at international rates exceeding $100. The former governor emphasized that high energy prices have exacerbated economic hardship, leaving low-income earners struggling to survive. Pointing to the current national minimum wage of N70,000, Duke observed that an entire month’s salary could easily be consumed just by filling a vehicle’s fuel tank. To achieve the targeted N300 per litre price point, Duke proposed ring-fencing a portion of the country’s daily crude output exclusively for domestic use. “Allocate 600,000 barrels if that’s what you consume daily. Allocate that to yourself. The other one million, you can sell it,” he explained, arguing that this strategy would insulate domestic consumers from global price volatility while leveraging Nigeria’s natural resources for public benefit.

title: 2027: 84% of Nigerians intend to vote– Survey
body: A survey by Yiaga Africa has revealed that 84 per cent of Nigerians say they are likely or very likely to vote in the 2027 general elections, but fear of violence, declining confidence in the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), and widespread vote-buying could prevent many from turning up at polling units. This is according to the third round of Yiaga Africa’s National Voting Intentions Survey (NVIS 3.0), released in Abuja yesterday, which found that while Nigerians remain willing to participate in the elections, their commitment to voting remains fragile. The report, titled “Willing but Wary: How Nigerians Intend to Vote in 2027,” was based on interviews with 2,470 Nigerians aged 18 and above across the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory in September 2026. For the first time, the survey included face-to-face interviews in rural communities alongside telephone interviews, tracking changes from the first two rounds conducted in December 2025 and March 2026. According to the findings, the proportion of Nigerians who said they were likely or very likely to vote rose from 77 per cent in NVIS 1.0 to 73 per cent in NVIS 2.0, reaching 84 per cent in the latest survey. However, those who described themselves as “very likely” to vote declined marginally from 52 per cent in the first survey to 48 per cent in the second and 47 per cent in the latest round. The survey also found that only 41 per cent of respondents were likely to vote and very certain about their choice of candidate. Yiaga Africa identified insecurity as the single biggest barrier to voter participation, with 61 per cent of respondents stating that fear of violence could prevent them from voting. The survey also highlighted declining public confidence in INEC, with only 34 per cent of respondents expressing confidence that the commission would conduct credible elections, compared to 45 per cent in each of the two previous rounds. It noted that 39 per cent of respondents lacked confidence in INEC, with distrust particularly high in the South-East (62 per cent) and the South-South (57 per cent). Despite concerns regarding the electoral umpire, citizens appeared to have greater confidence in election technology, with 49 per cent expressing trust in the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) and the electronic transmission of results through the INEC Result Viewing Portal (IReV). The survey further indicated that government performance and economic conditions would be decisive factors in determining voters’ choices in 2027. It noted that 54 per cent of respondents disapproved of President Bola Tinubu’s performance, while 71 per cent rated the economy as poor or very poor. The report also highlighted demographic differences, noting that younger Nigerians showed weaker voting intentions and higher levels of distrust in the electoral process. Speaking on the findings, Yiaga Africa’s Head of Knowledge Management and Learning, Safiya Bichi, said Nigerians have not lost interest in elections, but several factors stand between their willingness to vote and actual participation. “Nigerians have not given up on elections. They want to vote, they see it as their duty, and they believe their votes can make a difference,” she said. She added: “What stands between that willingness and the ballot box is fear, distrust, and money.” Bichi described low voter turnout in Nigeria as “a conversion problem, not an apathy problem,” emphasizing that the responsibility for addressing these challenges rests with institutions and actors in charge of security, electoral credibility, and logistics. With the presidential election scheduled for January 16, 2027, Yiaga Africa called on the Federal Government and security agencies to publish a threat-based national election security plan through the Inter-Agency Consultative Committee on Election Security (ICCES) by November 2026. It urged authorities to prioritise high-risk areas—particularly the North-East, North-West, and North-Central regions—and focus on protecting voters in addition to safeguarding election materials. The organisation also called on INEC to make a public commitment to the real-time uploading of polling unit results to IReV, publish and test its results management protocol, and intensify confidence-building efforts in the South-East and South-South. It urged the judiciary to resolve pre-election candidacy disputes before ballot papers are printed and publish clear timelines for the determination of election petitions. Political parties and candidates, it added, should campaign on fully costed plans for security and the economy, sign and honour the Peace Accord, and commit to an enforceable anti-vote-buying pledge. Yiaga Africa also urged civil society organisations and the media to shift voter education from merely encouraging citizens to vote to providing greater assurance regarding the safety and credibility of the electoral process—particularly among young people, women, and underserved communities.

title: NNPP members defect to SDP in Adamawa
body: The New Nigeria peoples party, NNPP, in Adamawa State has agreed to work with the Social Democratic party, SDP, for the election of its candidate, Christopher Nathaniel. Speaking on behalf of the decampees, Dr. Mustapha Mohammad Abbo said their decision was informed by Nathaniel’s proposed policies and political blueprint for Adamawa State which they believe is the best of the state. Abbo expressed confidence that the SDP candidate has the capacity, experience and connections to move the state forward and to consolidate on the already achievements recorded by the previous and outgoing governments. They made the declaration of joining SDP during the official unveiling of Dr. Fauziyah Ahmed Rufai as the Deputy governorship candidate of the party for the 2027 general election. The unveiling which coincides with the SDP Stakeholders Consultative Open Joint Session Meeting, had in attendance party leaders, stakeholders, candidates, officials and supporters of the party with the aim to strengthen internal coordination and chart a common course ahead of the election. Dr Rufai was presented to the party stakeholders as the running mate to the SDP governorship candidate, Christopher Nathaniel, marking another major step in the party’s preparations for the governorship contest. Speaking at the meeting, Chief Nathaniel described the choice of Rufai as one decision reached after careful consideration of the qualities, experience and capacity required to complement the governorship ticket and contribute to the development of the State.

title: Oman in the geopolitical strategy of the Russian Federation
body:
For decades, the Sultanate of Oman has positioned itself as a state with the status of a neutral mediator in the Middle East security architecture. Nevertheless, the intensification of diplomatic, intelligence, and economic relations between Muscat and Moscow is raising justified concerns in Western capitals. The Russian Federation sees Oman not only as a means of facilitating the circumvention of the sanctions regime, but also as a strategic partner in gaining access to the Arabian Sea and sea lines of communication (SLOCs) at the entrance to the Persian Gulf.
The cornerstone of Oman’s foreign policy, developed during the reign of Sultan Qaboos and continued under Sultan Haitham, remains strict multi-vectorism and diplomatic restraint. This paradigm enabled Muscat simultaneously to maintain asymmetric allied relations with Washington, informal dialogue with Tel Aviv, and the role of a key, credible channel of communication with Tehran. Its status as a buffer state has so far constituted an important stabilizing factor in the regional security environment.
In an era of the reconfiguration of the global balance of power and the ongoing high-intensity conflict in Eastern Europe, Oman’s traditional neutrality is, however, undergoing structural redefinition. Russia, subject to economic and technological restrictions and pursuing a doctrinal pivot towards the Global South, identifies Omani political pragmatism as an instrument for breaking international isolation. From the Kremlin’s perspective, Oman’s jurisdiction and infrastructure now constitute a node of critical importance for maintaining the continuity of the state’s logistical processes.
The economic dimension constitutes the primary area of Russian penetration into Oman’s state system. Muscat has refrained from joining the sanctions regime implemented by the G7 states. Consequently, the sultanate’s legal and administrative framework facilitates the free absorption of Russian capital, opening the way for the instrumentalization of Omani infrastructure by state entities and front companies linked to the administration in Moscow.
Oman has become one of the central operational areas for the so-called “shadow fleet”, involved in the transfer of Russian hydrocarbons while circumventing the price-cap mechanism. Omani territorial waters and exclusive economic zones (EEZs) are systematically used for ship-to-ship (STS) transfers. Commodities transferred between vessels with unregulated insurance status, often operating with their AIS transponders switched off, undergo a process that obscures their country of origin.
Additionally, free economic zones, including the strategically located ports of Sohar and Duqm, have become areas for registering numerous special-purpose companies (shell companies). Through them, Russian entities manage supply chains for dual-use goods, including advanced microelectronic components necessary to maintain the replenishment potential of the Russian defence-industrial complex.
Economic cooperation forms the foundation for the implementation of broader geostrategic objectives in the region. Moscow’s overriding priority is the integration of Omani infrastructure with the International North–South Transport Corridor (INSTC). This transport route, connecting the Russian Federation with India via Iranian land and port infrastructure, is intended by Russian strategists to serve as a secure alternative to maritime routes passing through the Suez Canal.
Oman’s territory is a natural operational extension of the INSTC corridor. Russian decision-makers are particularly interested in the special economic zone and deep-water port at Duqm. Located outside the Strait of Hormuz, the facility provides unobstructed operational access to the waters of the Indian Ocean. Although influence in this area has so far been contested primarily by the People’s Republic of China (capital investment) and the United States (the US Navy regularly uses local facilities for the logistical support of its fleet), Russia is beginning to articulate its own ambitions actively. As part of the strengthening of strategic cooperation with Iran, Moscow seeks rights to use logistical support points for the Russian Navy. Providing Russian vessels with logistical facilities at ports such as Duqm or Salalah would significantly expand the Russian fleet’s power-projection capabilities in the Arabian Sea.
Bilateral relations have also intensified in the security domain (Security & Defence). Recently, a noticeable increase has been observed in the frequency of consultations at the ministerial level and within intelligence structures. The Russian Federation positions itself in the Middle East as a transactional partner that avoids conditioning cooperation on political-system criteria, deliberately contrasting this with US policy.
Moscow actively promotes technology transfers in the fields of cybersecurity and electronic warfare systems. In the face of growing activity in cyberspace in the Middle East, Russian solutions represent a form of technological diversification sought by Gulf states. At the same time, the Russian state arms exporter Rosoboronexport continues to explore opportunities to penetrate the Omani market, focusing on integrated air-defence systems. Although the Armed Forces of the Sultanate of Oman base their interoperability on Western weapons platforms, primarily from the United States and the United Kingdom, any acquisition of Russian equipment, even on a limited scale, would constitute a breach in the Western security architecture of the region.
From the perspective of the United States and NATO, the uneven vectors of Oman’s foreign policy generate significant planning challenges. The US Fifth Fleet, based in Manama, treats Omani territory in its operational concepts as a key stabilizing element on the western flank of the strategically important Strait of Hormuz.
The US Department of State and Department of Defense face a complex strategic dilemma. Applying assertive pressure mechanisms on Muscat concerning compliance with the sanctions regime carries the risk of permanently reorienting the sultanate towards a Chinese-Russian-Iranian cooperation format. On the other hand, maintaining the current political passivity effectively means tacit acceptance of Oman functioning as a hub supporting Russian asymmetric operations. The paradigm under which Omani multi-vectorism served exclusively to de-escalate tensions is becoming exhausted. The absence of a categorical diplomatic response from Western states facilitates the implementation of a multidomain strategy by revisionist powers aimed at circumventing Western deterrence mechanisms.
The established status of Oman in the academic literature as a strictly neutral state is becoming a convenient pretext for Euro-Atlantic capitals to avoid difficult political decisions. An analysis of operational conditions, however, demonstrates that in an era of renewed great-power rivalry, asymmetric multi-vectorism is in fact a form of state economic opportunism. The Russian Federation is effectively instrumentalizing this situation, using Omani jurisdiction, financial system, and maritime infrastructure to systematically circumvent international sanctions restrictions.
In my assessment, Washington’s and European capitals’ limitation of themselves to conservative forms of diplomatic pressure on Muscat, motivated by concerns about weakening the cohesion of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) bloc, is a strategic mistake. The continuation of a policy of passivity will, in the long term, lead to a situation in which the Navy of the People’s Liberation Army of China and its Russian counterpart acquire real capabilities, based on permanent land infrastructure, to exert influence over the strategic sea lines of communication of the Arabian Sea. States in the region cooperating with the United States in the defence domain should be subject to an appropriate degree of alliance discipline. Accepting a model in which the territory of a partner state facilitates logistical operations by sanctioned entities undermines the fundamental credibility of the Western deterrence strategy.

title: PAC gives CWSA 30 days to recover GH¢2.5m debt
body: The Public Accounts Committee (PAC) has ordered the Community Water and Sanitation Agency (CWSA) to recover GH¢2.5 million owed by more than 295 public institutions within 30 days. The outstanding debts are owed by a number of state institutions, including Metropolitan, Municipal and District Assemblies (MMDAs), the Ghana Prisons Service, Ghana Police Service, Ghana Armed Forces and the National Ambulance Service. Appearing before the Committee, CWSA management was directed to take immediate steps to recover the outstanding amounts, with PAC Chairperson Abena Osei-Asare stressing that the deadline was mandatory. “We give you 30 days to collect the GH¢2.5 million. This is non-negotiable. 30 days from today, collect the GH¢2.5 million from these institutions,” she said. The Committee also instructed the agency to engage the Inspector-General of Police to assist in recovering more than GH¢300,000 owed by 72 police stations. The directive forms part of the Committee’s efforts to ensure that public institutions settle outstanding obligations and that state agencies recover monies owed to them.

title: Bayelsa PDP unveils campaign plans, flags off LGA tour November 23
body: The Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) in Bayelsa State has unveiled plans to take its 2027 election campaign to the grassroots, with mobilisation activities expected to cover all 105 wards across the state. The party, in a timetable released on Wednesday, said its LGA-to-LGA campaign tour would commence on November 23, following the inauguration of its State Campaign Council and senatorial district campaign flag-offs. The timetable, signed by the State Publicity Secretary, Ikaebimo Mark, showed that the party would begin its pre-campaign activities with meetings of the State Working Committee, Expanded State Caucus, and State Executive Committee from October 26 to 28. The party will also hold a three-day session of fasting, prayer, and Solemn Assembly from November 5 to 7, followed by a dedication and thanksgiving service on November 8. Mark stated: “The State Campaign Council will be inaugurated on November 9, while senatorial district campaign flag-offs are scheduled for November 17, 19, and 21. “The PDP campaign programme was structured to enable candidates to reach voters at the grassroots, engage communities, and explain their policies and programmes. “The campaign will be based on issues affecting the people, including development priorities and the welfare of citizens, rather than personal attacks or inflammatory rhetoric.” The party, led in the state by High Chief Alabh George Turnah, also pledged that its campaign activities would be conducted peacefully and in accordance with the law.

title: The Rawanin buzu Moment
body: There is this pregnant metaphor among the Hausa people: the rawanin buzu, the indigo headdress, only falls when the head is on the ground. Nothing short of an apocalypse makes a Tuareg unwrap his turban. It is the ultimate metaphor for the impossible. And yet, here we are in 2026, watching the impossible unfold every other Tuesday. The Chinese, with their backhanded compliment, said it best: “May you live in interesting times.” It sounds like a blessing. It is a curse. Interesting times are when the ground shifts beneath your feet, when the old certainties dissolve, when the rawanin buzu falls and you must decide whether to pick it up or let the sun burn your scalp. I am writing from Sokoto, where the heat does not discriminate between optimists and pessimists. From this vantage point, I can tell you: Nigeria is standing at the edge of something. The question is whether we leap or fall. Consider what has happened in just the past few months. Nigeria’s non-crude oil export earnings overtook crude oil exports for the first time in recorded history. In the second quarter of 2026, non-crude exports totalled N14.11 trillion against N12.91 trillion from crude oil. Urea exports alone hit N2.1 trillion, a product that did not even register in the top five exports a year prior. Read that again. A country synonymous with crude oil dependency for six decades just witnessed its non-oil exports surpass oil. The rawanin buzu is on the ground. Foreign reserves climbed above $54.7 billion, the highest in about 18 years. Inflation fell for the third consecutive month to 15.39 percent in August. GDP grew by 4.43 percent in the second quarter. The CBN cut the Monetary Policy Rate by 350 basis points to 23 percent—the largest single reduction since 2006. These are not the numbers of a nation condemned to eternal abyss. These are the numbers of a nation that might, just might, be turning a corner. But listen to me before lynching me for this sacrilege. The real story is not implicitly narrow or domestic. The real story is that the world order that Nigeria was born into is collapsing, and the new one is not yet formed. This is the rawanin buzu moment on a global scale. The United States, for decades the undisputed hegemon, is retreating into protectionism. It has imposed a 12.5 percent tariff on Nigerian imports under Section 301 of its Trade Act. The rationale—alleged forced labour—is thin gruel, but the message is clear: America First means everyone else second. The CPPE’s Muda Yusuf argues the direct impact will be limited because crude oil and LNG are exempt. But the signal is unmistakable: the era of open markets is over. We must adapt or perish. Meanwhile, the BRICS bloc is expanding. Nigeria became a partner country in January 2025 and Vice President Shettima attended the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi in September, seeking to deepen cooperation on trade, investment, agriculture, and technology. The Foreign Affairs Minister, Odumegwu-Ojukwu, noted that India’s experience in deploying technology to engage its youthful population was particularly relevant to Nigeria’s demographic reality. And then there is Russia. The third Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow in October is being viewed by Abuja as a key opportunity to expand bilateral ties. Nigeria’s Ambassador to Moscow, Joseph Olusola Iji, acknowledged the persistent trade imbalance and argued that expanding Russian industrial investment could help create a more balanced economic relationship. Security and defence cooperation are also on the table. This is the new world: multipolar, transactional, and unforgiving of those who cling to old loyalties. Nigeria is pivoting. The question is whether the pivot is strategic or merely reactive. But chaos comes with grand opportunities too, not just forgone doom. This is what I see from Sokoto, where the Sahara’s dust meets the savannah’s green, where the memory of empires that traded across deserts still lingers in the architecture and the language. The global realignment presents Nigeria with opportunities that would have been unthinkable a decade ago. First, energy. The Middle East conflict has pushed Brent crude to around $100 per barrel. This strengthens our foreign exchange earnings and government revenues. But more importantly, the world is desperate for reliable energy sources. Nigeria has the largest gas reserves in Africa. The “Decade of Gas” is not just a slogan; it is a geopolitical necessity. We can become the energy bridge between the Atlantic and the Sahel. Second, trade. The African Continental Free Trade Area remains our most important instrument. Fifty countries have ratified it, and 39 are participating in the Guided Trade Initiative. Nigeria has validated its AfCFTA Implementation Strategy, gazetted tariff concessions, and ratified the Digital Trade Protocol. The Minister of State for Foreign Affairs, Sola Enikanolaiye, has urged African countries to place trade at the centre of their diplomatic engagements, arguing that “lasting partnerships on the continent must be anchored on shared economic interests”. A new air cargo corridor involving Uganda Airlines and the UNDP has reduced freight costs by 50 to 75 percent. The Central Bank has directed banks to adopt the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System to facilitate local-currency settlement. These are the infrastructure of a new African economy. Third, security. Nigeria and the United States have deepened military ties on counter-terrorism and intelligence sharing. Defence Minister General Christopher Musa met with Major General Matthew Brown of the US Army Southern European Task Force, to review joint security initiatives and formulate a “more result-oriented strategic framework”. The priority areas include specialised joint training for Special Forces, enhanced border surveillance, and counter-IED support. In Sokoto, Gen Musa is a star. Some of us consider him one of our best exports in recent times. We trust everything with his name on the byline. Yes, this does not mean we should outsource our security. But it does mean we can leverage partnerships to build the capacity we lack. The Sahel is burning. Our many insurgencies do not respect borders. We need every ally we can get. Then there is the matter of our unfinished business with fate. Let me be as sober as a Hausa man must be. The rawanin buzu may be on the ground, but the head beneath it is still bruised. President Tinubu marked Nigeria’s 66th Independence Anniversary by declaring that the country had reached a “turning point” after three years of difficult reforms. He cited economic growth above four percent, reduced oil theft, rebuilt reserves, and greater stability in the foreign exchange market. “We cannot erase in four years what accumulated over generations,” he said. “But we can change its course”. Atiku Abubakar responded that the past three years had plunged Nigeria into “the most severe cost-of-living crisis in the country’s history.” He noted that petrol prices rose from N187 to N1,500 per litre, and the naira weakened from N460 to N1,380 against the dollar. “The pain has an address in every home,” he said. “Bola, where is the benefit?” Peter Obi pointed to over 140 million Nigerians living in poverty, 18 million out-of-school children, and 40 million facing extreme hunger by the end of 2026. Both narratives are true. The macro economy is stabilising; the micro economy is bleeding. The foreign reserves are climbing; the queues at the petrol stations are lengthening. The rawanin buzu is on the ground, but the ground itself is still shaking. So what do we do? The rawanin buzu metaphor teaches us something profound. The Tuareg wears his turban not out of vanity but out of necessity. It protects him from the sun, the sand, the wind. It is his armour against a hostile environment. When it falls, he is exposed. Nigeria’s old certainties—oil, the naira, the illusion of a benevolent state—have fallen. We are exposed. But exposure is not weakness. Exposure is clarity. We must stop romanticising the past. The “mistake of 1914” was not a mistake; it was a fact. The colonisers are gone, but their architecture remains. We have spent 66 years groping in the dark, partly because we never developed a consciousness about the definition and responsibilities of both the demand and supply sides of leadership. The current global realignment is our opportunity to build something new. Not a replica of the Western nation-state, nor a retreat into a mythical past. Something that blends the wisdom of our traditions—the sarakuna who ruled with justice, the majalisas that held power accountable—with the demands of a modern, diversified, digitally connected economy. The rawanin buzu is on the ground. The question is not whether we pick it up. The question is what we wrap around on his head as replacement. The times are interesting. But let’s us make them ours. Allah yabamu sa’a.

title: Time for moratorium on borrowing
body: A $1.5 billion loan being contemplated by the Nigerian government is just the latest addition to the long list of the country’s borrowing spree. The government explained that the loan, to be raised from the World Bank, will be used to fund climate resilience, early childhood development and social protection. The social protection component is part of the government’s plans to cushion the impact of ongoing economic reforms on vulnerable Nigerians. With the country’s total indebtedness – both local and foreign- currently put at over N160 trillion, the government shows no signs of reducing its proclivity to pile up debt. An indication of the rate at which Nigeria’s indebtedness is rising is seen in the change in the country’s external debt, which rose from $51.9 billion in the first quarter of this year to $ 54.523 billion in the second quarter. Within the first half of the year, Nigeria spent $1.824 billion on debt servicing, including principal repayment, interest payments, and other charges, according to the Debt Management Office (DMO). Now, the government wants to add to that by borrowing to allegedly feed people. Nigerians wonder the economic justification for this, or is it just the pursuit of populism? Given the rate at which the country’s debts have ballooned since the present administration assumed office, a call for a moratorium on foreign loans has become imperative. This will enable a proper audit of the country’s indebtedness to be conducted to ascertain the uses to which the numerous loans have been put, and ultimately, Nigeria’s gains from such loans. This is in the best interest of the country’s economy, bearing in mind that a country’s level of indebtedness must be considered in terms of its sustainability. The current level of debt is obviously too high for the country, and the signs of its potential interference with the running of the economy are quite evident, given the cost of servicing the existing debts. If previous administrations had embarked on such a borrowing spree, the country would by now have been overwhelmed by debts. The time is now for a proper assessment of the usefulness of these uncoordinated loan harvests. We must begin to interrogate in what ways have they benefited the country versus other alternatives. This is relevant and must be explained by the leaders of the country, especially the National Assembly. The Legislature has an oversight duty over the nation’s finances, including the government’s borrowing and spending activities. As the arm of government saddled with constitutional oversight of the nation’s finances, the National Assembly should rise to its obligations now and exercise its powers on this matter. Nigerians have noted with dismay the speed with which our lawmakers approve every loan request presented to them by the president. Rather than subject such requests to critical assessment on a need-by-need basis, these people’s representatives generally give their nod as if nothing is at stake with loan taking. In our view, loan request assessment and approval should go beyond the usual terse statement that Mr. President means well for the country, and the subsequent speedy approval. The management of the nation’s economy goes far beyond this because economic issues are more complex than they seem. This is more so with debt because every loan taken now represents a claim on the country’s future revenues. Depending on the country’s preparedness for such obligations, a seemingly harmless loan taken now could become an albatross on future generations whose destinies are being mortgaged by the present generation. Nigeria’s rising debt profile is not only worrisome because of the size; it is more disturbing because of the evident disconnect between that size and what the loans have been used for in the interest of the country. Nigerians need accountability on the nation’s indebtedness. What, in concrete, specific terms, has each of the loans been used for? The government needs to rise to its responsibility and get the economy really working because that is the only way for the country to stand on its own. If the economy is working well, Nigerians will be able to take care of themselves and would not need handouts either from World Bank or any other creditor. If there were no insecurity, our teeming farmers would produce enough food to feed the nation and for export. No country can go far with this uncoordinated method of economic management. As the nation hopes to transition from stabilisation to production and ultimately to prosperity through the economic reform programme, the government must take stock of its approaches so far, including the sourcing of funds. Without this, we might just be living under the illusion of solving today’s problems while actually creating tomorrow’s headaches.

title: Beyond moralising history: The real structural antecedents of 1966 and modern governance
body: In a recent commentary published in a national daily newspaper and some social media handles regarding the legal travails surrounding former Attorney-General of the Federation, Abubakar Malami, SAN, and the Mambilla hydropower arbitration saga, Professor Chidi Odinkalu opens with an engaging contrast. He juxtaposes the multi-million-dollar property forfeiture judgments of modern Nigerian public officers against the frugal lifestyle of Nigeria’s First Republic founding fathers. While Odinkalu’s outrage over contemporary administrative graft is entirely justified, his opening premise relies on a flawed historical framing. Framing the January 15, 1966 military coup as an “anti-corruption” intervention whose execution was validated by the modesty of its victims’ personal estates repeats a long-standing historical fallacy. To suggest the demise of the First Republic was merely a high-minded moral purge glosses over the complex, volatile, and structural drivers of that national tragedy, chief among them the geopolitical fallout of the Northernisation Policy. The reality of the Northernisation policy Understanding the political climate leading to January 1966 requires confronting post-independence administrative realities. In 1960, Nigeria inherited a profound structural imbalance in education and bureaucratic representation. Because western-style educational institutions were introduced much earlier in the South, the federal civil service and technical departments operating within the Northern region; such as public works, railways, and postal services; were overwhelmingly staffed by Southern personnel, predominantly Igbo and Yoruba professionals. Faced with regional disenfranchisement, the Premier of the Northern region, Sir Ahmadu Bello, formalised the Northernisation Policy in the mid-1950s. In the Northern region’s public service, qualified Northerners were given preference. Where no qualified Northerner was available, expatriates were recruited on short-term contracts until local capacity could be developed. From the Northern leadership’s perspective, Northernisation was not a campaign of hostility, but a vital mechanism for regional self-preservation and equity. Without it, the North; comprising over half the nation’s landmass and population; faced the prospect of being governed within its own borders by administrators from other regions. Structural anxiety and the 1966 explosion However, the Northernisation policy created acute friction across the political landscape. Thousands of Southern civil servants who built careers in Kaduna, Kano, Zaria, and Jos found their promotional prospects halted or their roles re-allocated. This policy created deep professional anxiety among Southern intellectuals, civil servants, and young military officers, who interpreted Northern political dominance as a deliberate attempt to marginalise southern professionals. When Major Chukwuma Nzeogwu and his conspirators struck on January 15, 1966, their public broadcasts routinely condemned “political profiteers and swindlers.” Yet this rhetoric was hardly unique. Virtually every one of the 11 African military coup of that era; from Egypt in 1952 to Togo and Upper Volta (Burkina Faso) in January 1963; recycled the standardised justification of anti-corruption to legitimise military intervention. The Nigerian coup plotters simply adopted the continental playbook. Furthermore, looking closely at the actual evidence of corruption in Nigeria at that time, the only major official investigation was the Coker Commission of Inquiry in 1962; which focused strictly on regional statutory corporations in the Western region. Because Nigeria operated a true federal structure rather than a unitary system, findings in the West could not be generalised to the entire federation. Crucially, post-coup asset verifications proved that the murdered Northern leaders; including Prime Minister Sir Abubakar Tafawa Balewa and Premier Sir Ahmadu Bello; left behind no accumulated fortunes, personal estates, or hidden assets. The anti-corruption pretext collapses entirely when applied to the Northerners killed in the purge. How else can one explain the origin/location of the coup leadership and majority of the victims? If anti-corruption was the primary justification for the coup, and official post-coup investigations returned a completely negative finding regarding these allegations, then the nation, the families of the Prime Minister, the Premier, and all the Northern leaders and officers and indeed all Nigerian murdered in that violent putsch are owed an unreserved apology. Only by confronting these facts can history be set straight and Nigeria truly reconcile with its past, and not for learned commentators like the Professor to continue disguisedly recirculating that fallacy. Odinkalu’s attempt to link the modest personal wealth of First Republic leaders to a critique of modern corruption introduces an anachronistic false equivalence. Especially with the benefit of 60 years of hindsight. Exposing and penalising modern administrative malfeasance; whether in the Mambilla arbitration or civil service procurements; is essential for Nigeria’s future. Public accountability demands rigorous, evidence-based critique. However, we do no service to modern accountability when we distort the historical record. The 1966 coup was not a clean moral baseline against which modern greed can be calculated. It was a structural collapse triggered by certain regional imbalances and administrative distrust. Dethroning modern corruption requires institutional strengthening and absolute legal transparency; which all Nigerian agree with; not the mischievous romanticising of a military intervention; based on a hidden agenda that shattered Nigeria’s constitutional foundation for ever. Kari, Wazirin Bauchi, can be reached via wazirinbauchi@gmail.com

title: Second-hand clothes’ dealers make brisk business in Abuja
body: At Karmo Market in Abuja, the business of selling second-hand clothes and footwear is thriving, drawing traders and customers who see the trade as a source of livelihood and an affordable alternative to new items. From clothes and shoes sourced from neighbouring countries to bales of used garments displayed across the market, the trade has continued to provide income for hundreds of traders while offering low-income customers access to relatively cheaper clothing. For some traders, however, the business has grown beyond daily survival. Years of buying and selling second-hand wears have enabled them to pay rent, educate their children, acquire land and build houses. One of them is Mrs Destiny Obinna, who started the business seven years ago with just N12,000. Today, she said, the business has enabled her to acquire three plots of land and begin building a house, with about N25 million already invested in the project. Obinna told Abuja Metro that she ventured into the business after graduating when she was offered a job paying about N50,000 monthly. After calculating the cost of transportation and other expenses, she said she realised that little would remain from her salary. The financial pressure became greater after she got married and became pregnant, while her husband also had limited resources. She therefore turned to the sale of second-hand clothes, initially selling individual pieces around Deidei, Kubwa and NNPC Junction. At the beginning, she sometimes sold only one gown in a day. “I would come back the next day. If I don’t sell today, I will sell tomorrow,” she said. Her persistence eventually paid off as she moved from selling individual pieces to buying bales and expanding her business. Obinna said she now opens several bales during the week, although the business is affected by rising transportation costs, delays by transporters, weather and fluctuating customer patronage. Rainy weather, she said, sometimes keeps customers away, while increases in transportation costs add to the cost of bringing goods to the market. Despite the challenges, she described the business as a blessing. “God has been faithful,” she said. ‘It has paid my rent, educated my children’ For Mrs Gloria Asowga, second-hand footwear trading has been a livelihood for more than two decades. Asowga said she was previously involved in hair making before a friend introduced her to the sale of second-hand shoes. She started with a small amount of money and later travelled to Togo to source footwear before returning to Nigeria to sell. More than 23 years later, she remains in the business, which she said has helped her pay rent and support her children’s education. However, she identified transportation and difficulties associated with sourcing goods from outside the country as major challenges. She said even when traders obtained goods at relatively low prices, transportation and other expenses could substantially increase the overall cost. Asowga also cited restrictions around the movement of goods across borders as one of the challenges facing traders. Despite the difficulties, she urged young people to remain persistent. “Keep trying. Hustle and don’t give up,” she said. ‘Some people cannot afford expensive shoes’ Another trader, Chinedu Ihunweze, has spent between 15 and 20 years selling second-hand footwear. Ihunweze said he entered the business to make a living but gradually built it into a source of income that has enabled him to acquire property and meet his family needs. Over the years, he said he had travelled to Togo, Benin Republic, Ghana and Burkina Faso to source goods. He said affordability remained one of the major reasons Nigerians patronise second-hand footwear. According to him, footwear sourced from Togo could be sold for about N5,000 compared with new shoes which, he said, could cost between N10,000 and N15,000 on the average “The people buying from us are also Nigerians. They cannot all afford expensive shoes,” he said. Ihunweze, however, said Customs officials had seized his goods on two or three occasions, describing the seizures as one of the major challenges confronting traders. He said the development was particularly troubling because second-hand goods provide affordable clothing and footwear for Nigerians who may not be able to afford new products. He called for greater government support for the sector, including measures to make it easier for traders to access goods and support local manufacturers. For Emmanuel Abel, who has spent about seven years selling second-hand clothes, the business was born out of necessity. Abel said he had tried other ventures without achieving the desired results before turning to the sale of used clothes. He said although the business could be stressful, it had provided him with an income and a means of meeting his needs. Customers, he said, could sometimes be difficult to satisfy, particularly as the prices of goods continued to rise. According to him, rising prices could also affect patronage because many customers were already struggling financially. Abel urged young people to be smart, develop foresight and be willing to work hard if they wanted to succeed in business. He also called on the government to help stabilise the cost of doing business. The traders said the popularity of second-hand wears is driven largely by affordability. For traders, the growing demand has created an opportunity to build businesses from relatively small capital. Traders face uncertain future over planned relocation Meanwhile, the traders are also raising concerns over plans by the Federal Capital Territory Administration to clear informal trading structures in the area and relocate traders to the Karmo District Market as part of efforts to address congestion and activities along the Karmo-Dei-Dei corridor. The proposed relocation has generated opposition from some community leaders and traders who fear that moving the existing market could disrupt businesses and livelihoods built around the location over several years. The village head of Karmo Sabo, Chief Umar Garni Sarkin Karmo, and the District Head of Karmo Sabo, Alhaji Yunusa Ashama Karmo, have recently appealed to the FCT Minister, Nyesom Wike, to suspend the planned demolition and relocation of the existing market. The community leaders have argued that the market has existed for decades and that relocating it outside the traditional Karmo Sabo area could have social and economic consequences for residents. The new Karmo District Market, commissioned by the FCT minister in February 2025, was developed under a public-private partnership involving Rural Homes Limited and Abuja Investment Company Limited. The market occupies about 9.9 hectares and has more than 2,500 shops, with facilities including sections for farmers, livestock and textiles, as well as cold rooms, a police facility, clinic and fire service. For the traders, however, the concern is whether they can afford to operate in the new market and retain the customers they have built over the years. For now, the second-hand wears trade continues to provide an important source of affordable clothing for Abuja residents and a livelihood for traders who have turned modest beginnings into businesses capable of supporting families and, in some cases, building property.

title: Riyadh airport flights delayed and cancelled after Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia
body: Flights at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport were suspended for more than an hour on Wednesday morning after Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, with disruption continuing into Thursday. Flight tracking website Flightradar24 reported that 58 departures, or 15 per cent of the day's scheduled services, were delayed at Riyadh airport as of Thursday morning, while 11 flights, or 3 per cent, were listed as cancelled. The airport was experiencing an average departure delay of 45 minutes, with its disruption index standing at 4.2 out of five, a level classified by the platform as indicating major disruption. Flights affected on Thursday morning included Saudia's SV311 service from Riyadh to Cairo, which was delayed by more than two hours, and Yemenia's IY533 service to Aden, which faced a delay of more than three hours. Saudia's SV562 bound for Dubai and Turkish Airlines' TK145 bound for Istanbul were among flights cancelled. The disruption follows drone and missile strikes on King Khalid International Airport and Abha International Airport in southern Saudi Arabia, which killed three people and injured 36 others, according to the kingdom's General Authority of Civil Aviation. Yemen's Houthi rebels claimed responsibility for the attacks, which also caused damage. The latest disruptions have raised concerns about the impact of the escalating conflict on air travel, with the US embassy in Riyadh warning that the fighting could lead to flight cancellations. “US citizens should be aware of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures and travel disruptions. We recommend checking your flight departure status directly with the airline and with the airport,” the embassy said. Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia: Get all the latest updates here

title: Gov’t reconsidering ‘One Constituency, One Ambulance’ model to distribute 100 new vehicles – Akandoh
body: The government is reconsidering the “One Constituency, One Ambulance” model as it prepares to add 100 new ambulances to the national fleet in 2027. Health Minister Kwabena Mintah Akandoh says no final decision has been taken on how the new vehicles will be distributed. He said government is weighing the pros and cons of the previous system before deciding whether to continue with it or review it. “Well, we have not taken the decision yet,” he told Joy News’ PM Express on Wednesday. The Minister suggested that areas with existing ambulances that are no longer functional could be prioritised under a new approach. “But I believe that if you have an ambulance within a particular area, and that ambulance is faulty, or is no longer functional, it’s only fair to replace that ambulance,” he said. He said government is also assessing whether the previous distribution model should continue. “But then we think about what they did, the pros and cons; we’ve tried that system — can we continue, or do we have to review it as a country?” he asked. Mr Akandoh said the government’s decision will ultimately depend on whether the existing model has served the country well. “We can only build on that as a system, and governance is a continuum,” he said, adding, “If we think that that system has served us well, why do we have to revamp?” The planned expansion of the ambulance fleet forms part of wider efforts to strengthen emergency care. Mr Akandoh said the government inherited several grounded ambulances and discovered that the fleet was uninsured. He said all government ambulances were insured in 2025. “As I speak to you now, we have more than 200 ambulances functioning,” he said. The Minister said government will replenish the fleet in 2027 with 100 brand-new vehicles. The ambulances are also being linked to the national emergency bed management system being piloted by the Health Ministry. He said the system will enable ambulance teams to determine where to send emergency patients based on available beds. “The ambulance people are also on board; when they pick the patient, they go to the system. They’re able to know we have to send the patient here,” he said.

title: Intel: Russia deploying soldiers with HIV on combat missions
body:
This is revealed in an audio recording of a conversation published on the YouTube channel of the Main Intelligence Directorate of the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense (DIU), according to Ukrinform.
It is noted that military intelligence specialists intercepted a conversation between a soldier from the Russian Army’s 1st Separate Motorized Rifle Brigade, which is operating in the Pokrovsk direction.
“The occupier has an HIV infection, which, without the necessary medication, leads to complications. Moreover, back in February, a medical commission deemed him unfit for service, but this did not prevent him from being deployed on combat missions,” the DIU reported.
The agency noted that this Russian soldier was even declared a deserter.
The agency stated that the deterioration of the occupying army continues: Russia’s military machine is enlisting those unfit for service as assault troops and contributing to the spread of HIV/AIDS .
The Main Intelligence Directorate assured that there will be just retribution for every war crime committed against Ukraine.
The agency reiterated that the only chance for a Russian soldier to save his life and avoid contracting an incurable disease is to surrender via the “I Want to Live” project’s Telegram bot.
As previously reported, the Main Intelligence Directorate of the Ministry of Defense identified the killed Russian mercenary as a native of Sierra Leon e.

title: Major deployment point of Colombian mercenaries destroyed near Kharkov
body:
MOSCOW, October 8. /TASS/. A temporary deployment point of Colombian mercenaries from the 23rd Separate Assault Regiment of Ukraine’s National Guard has been destroyed near the city of Kharkov, a Russian security official told TASS.
"A major temporary deployment point of Colombian mercenaries from the 23rd Separate Assault Regiment of Ukraine’s National Guard, who were earlier transferred from Kiev, has been destroyed in Dergachi, Kharkov Region," he said.
According to Russian security agencies, the total number of foreign mercenaries in the Ukrainian armed forces currently stands at about 16,500, including 7,000 Colombians.

title: Ukraine Strikes Yandex Data Center, Russian Oil Refinery Overnight
body:
Ukraine struck a Yandex data center in Russia’s Ryazan Oblast and a major oil refinery in Bashkortostan overnight on Oct. 8, according to Ukrainian monitoring channels and eyewitness footage.
Ukrainian monitoring channels Exilenova+ , VChK-OGPU and Astra reported that the Yandex data center in the city of Sasovo was hit overnight.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Yandex is one of Russia’s largest technology companies and the country’s dominant search engine, offering services including cloud computing, online storage, email, maps and ride-hailing. Its data centers support the company’s online and cloud services.
The Sasovo facility is located on the grounds of the Sasta plant, which manufactures metalworking machinery and supplies equipment to Russian defense industry companies.
Eyewitness footage showed a large fire at the site following the attack.
Yandex acknowledged an “incident” and said some of its services were temporarily unavailable. Users reported problems accessing Yandex Disk and Yandex Documents.
“We will provide updates on the recovery process,” the company said.
The Sasovo data center opened in 2011. In 2022, the city’s administration head Yevgenia Rubtsova said Yandex had invested more than 6 billion rubles ($75 million) in the facility over 11 years.
The Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat oil refinery in Russia’s Bashkortostan was also targeted overnight, Exilenova+ reported.
Astra, citing photos and videos from eyewitnesses, reported a fire in the area of the refinery.
The plant can process up to 10 million tons of hydrocarbon feedstock annually and produces more than 150 types of products, including gasoline, diesel, fuel oil, bitumen, polyethylene, styrene and ammonia.
The refinery has previously been targeted by Ukrainian drone strikes.
A fire broke out at the plant following an Aug. 13 attack , while a July 14 strike forced the complete suspension of oil processing, according to previous reports. Ukrainian drones also damaged primary crude-processing units at the refinery in 2023.
The reported strikes come after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he had approved a plan for long-range attacks against Russia in October.
Zelensky has said Ukraine will respond to Russian attacks on its civilian infrastructure by targeting corresponding Russian facilities.
The strikes also follow a Russian attack on the Datagroup data center in Kyiv in late September.
Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed the facility processed and transmitted intelligence data for the Ukrainian military.
Kyiv has increasingly targeted Russian energy, industrial and military-linked infrastructure with long-range drone strikes, seeking to disrupt systems supporting Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: ECOWAS gets five new community court judges
body: ECOWAS Chairman Bassirou Diomaye Faye has sworn in five new judges of the Community Court of Justice, charging them to uphold impartiality and public confidence. The judges are Mr Désiré Henri Aihou of Benin, Justice Awa Bah of The Gambia, Mrs Charlyne M. Brumskine of Liberia, Mrs Henrietta Uzoamaka Didigu of Nigeria and Dr Yaouza Ouro-Sama of Togo. President Faye, who administered the oath at the ECOWAS Commission in Abuja, said the judges were assuming office at a time the region faced political, economic, security and environmental challenges. He said the Court had a key responsibility to ensure fairness in the application of ECOWAS legal instruments, protect citizens’ rights and strengthen confidence in regional institutions. “Through its decisions, it protects rights, serves as a reminder of everyone’s obligations, and strengthens trust in our institutions,” he said. President Faye urged the judges to let their oath guide them throughout their four-year tenure, particularly in determining cases before the Court. He charged them to administer justice fairly, consider cases according to their conscience and perform their duties impartially without yielding to pressure from any quarter. “That is why I urge you, throughout the duration of your mandate, to constantly keep in mind -especially at the moment of decision-making—the foundation of your oath,” he said. He said the Court’s credibility would depend on the quality of its decisions and the confidence they inspired among citizens. General Birame Diop, ECOWAS Commission President, described the ceremony as a commitment by the new judges to the citizens of the Community and its common legal order. He said the oath required them to put aside personal interests and external influences and uphold community law with honour, loyalty, impartiality and conscience. “The oath marks the moment when the individual sets aside their personal interests and all external influences to serve only community law,” he said, adding that the ceremony also reflected member states’ recognition of the Court’s authority and their commitment to respecting its independence. The five judges were appointed for a non-renewable four-year term by the ECOWAS Authority of Heads of State and Government at its 69th Ordinary Session in Lungi, Sierra Leone, on July 19, 2026. Their appointment was pursuant to the December 2025 Supplementary Act SA.1/12/25 on the Community Court of Justice. The new judges succeeded Justice Ricardo Cláudio Monteiro Gonçalves of Cape Verde, Justice Sengu Mohamed Koroma of Sierra Leone, Justice Dupe Atoki of Nigeria, Justice Gberi-Bè Ouattara of Côte d’Ivoire and Justice Edward Amoako Asante of Ghana, whose four-year tenure had ended.
