title: Greece Proposes 10% Tax on Crypto Gains and Past Profits
body: Greece is moving to establish a formal tax framework for cryptocurrency, with the government proposing a 10% tax on capital gains from the sale or transfer of digital assets . The measure is included in a new bill from the Ministry of National Economy and Finance currently under public consultation. It seeks to close a long-standing gap in Greek tax legislation over the treatment of cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin and other digital assets. The proposed rules would also give taxpayers who made cryptocurrency profits in previous years a 12 month window to voluntarily declare those gains , allowing them to regularise their tax position without fines or interest, provided the conditions set out in the legislation are met. What will be taxed? Under the proposed framework, income from capital gains on the transfer of cryptocurrencies would be subject to a 10% personal income tax rate . A taxable transfer would include: Selling cryptocurrency for money Using cryptocurrency to purchase goods or services Other transfers made for payment Contributing cryptocurrency towards the establishment or increase of company or share capital The taxable gain would generally be calculated as the difference between the cryptocurrency’s acquisition price and its value when transferred. Transaction costs directly connected to the acquisition or transfer would also be taken into account. Capital gains of up to €500 per tax year would be exempt from tax . The legislation also proposes that losses exceeding €500 could be carried forward for up to five years and offset against future cryptocurrency capital gains. Previous crypto profits can be declared One of the most significant provisions concerns cryptocurrency acquired or sold in previous years. The proposed legislation would allow individuals to voluntarily declare capital gains from earlier transfers within 12 months of the law’s publication , without penalties or interest, subject to the prescribed conditions. Until now, taxpayers who wanted to establish a clear paper trail for cryptocurrency transactions have sometimes reported acquisition and sale values in their tax returns and declared the resulting gain to help justify the source of funds in the event of a tax audit. The new legislation would provide a formal legal framework for this process. Crypto-to-crypto exchanges The proposed rules also distinguish between a taxable disposal and the exchange of one cryptocurrency for another. Swapping one cryptocurrency for another would not, by itself, trigger a capital gains tax liability. Tax would instead arise when cryptocurrency is transferred for money, goods, services or another taxable consideration under the rules. How will the tax authorities calculate the gain? The acquisition and transfer values would have to be supported by transaction records from cryptocurrency service providers, intermediaries or other data that can be obtained directly from the relevant blockchain or distributed ledger. For investors who bought the same cryptocurrency at different times, the legislation proposes using an average acquisition price , calculated from the total amount paid divided by the total quantity acquired. This would provide a standard method for calculating taxable gains where investors have accumulated cryptocurrency through multiple purchases. Staking, lending and liquidity activities The bill also addresses income generated through cryptocurrency-related activities. Returns from activities including crypto lending, liquidity provision and staking or participation in transaction validation mechanisms would be treated as interest income and taxed at 10% . Where cryptocurrency is received through these activities, its acquisition value would generally correspond to the value on which the relevant interest tax was calculated. If that value cannot be established, the acquisition price would be treated as zero. Cryptocurrency used to buy goods Using cryptocurrency to purchase goods or services would also constitute a transfer for tax purposes. The transfer value would be based on the cryptocurrency’s euro value at the time of the transaction. That amount would then become the acquisition value of the cryptocurrency for the person receiving it in exchange for the goods or services. Inheritance and gifts The bill also sets out rules for cryptocurrency received through inheritance, gifts or parental transfers. For inheritance and gift tax purposes, cryptocurrencies would be treated as intangible movable property located abroad , with their value determined in euros on the day before the relevant tax liability arises. The acquisition value for the recipient would be based on the value used to calculate the relevant inheritance, gift or parental transfer tax, or the value for which an exemption was granted. No digital transaction fee The proposed framework would not impose a Digital Transaction Fee on cryptocurrency sales . The government is therefore seeking to establish a clearer system under which cryptocurrency investors can report their gains, document the origin and value of their holdings and comply with Greek tax obligations. The legislation remains under public consultation and could be amended before it is submitted to Parliament. The post Greece Proposes 10% Tax on Crypto Gains and Past Profits appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: Ashanti Regional NPP Chairman optimistic about party victory in 2028
body: Odeneho Kwaku Appiah, Ashanti Regional Chairman of the NPP has expressed renewed optimism regarding the party’s prospects in mobilising the grass-root support for resounding victory in the 2028 general elections. He said the display of solidarity and resounding unity towards the party’s flag-bearer, Dr Mahamudu Bawumia, during the national delegates’ conference in Kumasi, demonstrated the genuine commitment of members and supporters to rally behind the party for victory in 2028. Speaking to the Ghana News Agency in Kumasi, Odeneho Kwaku Appiah, noted that, the cohesive front displayed at the event served as a clear signal of the party’s readiness to mount a victorious campaign in the upcoming general elections. Reflecting on the outcome of the conference, he pointed out that the delegates’ unequivocal support for Dr. Bawumia reflected a shared resolve across all levels of the party. “I am greatly fortified in spirit and conviction that Dr. Bawumia will secure victory in the general elections. The unwavering unity shown by party members over the weekend is a powerful omen for our journey ahead,” he stated. He emphasised that the exemplary conduct of all aspirants and delegates demonstrated a deep understanding of the work required to present a formidable front against the governing National Democratic Congress (NDC). According to him, the NPP’s ability to conduct a peaceful conference and solidify its national structures puts it in a prime position to execute a proactive, nationwide campaign. “The NPP is poised to reclaim power because we have set our house in order early, adding that, from the national leadership to the grassroots, we have assembled a capable team ready to market our vision and candidates across every corner of the country”, he said. Odeneho Kwaku Appiah, extended high praise to the newly elected national executives for their grace and magnanimity in victory, highlighting their immediate efforts to reconcile with fellow contestants to build a truly inclusive party front. He called on the executive leadership to maintain this conciliatory spirit as they formulate strategies for upcoming parliamentary primaries and general campaign operations. “With a decisive flag-bearer and a united executive body behind him, our rank and file will be fully energised to prosecute an effective campaign and offer Ghanaians a strong alternative to the current administration,”, he stated.

title: Donald Trump Claims He Deserves Nobel Peace Prize
body: US President Donald Trump said on Wednesday that he deserves the Nobel Peace Prize, while taking a swipe at the Norwegian Nobel Committee ahead of Friday’s announcement of the 2026 winner. “I don’t know what their decision will be,” Trump said, referring to the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize, which the Norwegian Nobel Committee will announce on Friday. “They’re known for not giving it to people like me,” he added. Since returning to the White House last year, Trump has repeatedly claimed that he deserves the award. “It’s now time,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office, arguing that he had intervened to help end eight wars since taking office in January 2025. “However, it was a great honour to receive it indirectly last time from the recipient herself, who said that nobody in history deserved it more than President Trump,” he added. Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado handed Trump the Nobel Peace Prize she received last year in January. The leaders of Cambodia, Israel and Pakistan have said they nominated Trump for the Nobel Peace Prize. Among those considered contenders for this year’s award are Pope Leo XIV, the International Criminal Court and Francesca Albanese, the UN special rapporteur on the situation of human rights in the Palestinian territories. The post Donald Trump Claims He Deserves Nobel Peace Prize appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: NPP urged to prioritise regional balance in national appointments
body: Some members of the New Patriotic Party (NPP) in the Western Region have urged the Party’s leadership to promote fairness, regional balance and experience in the selection and appointment of national executives. They said such considerations would strengthen the Party’s organisational structures and help mobilise support ahead of the 2028 general election. The party loyalists, in a statement made available to the Ghana News Agency, said the Western region was endowed with experienced and resourceful members who could contribute effectively to the Party’s efforts to recapture political power. The statement singled out Okatakyie Amankwaa Afrifa (OKT) for consideration for a national role, citing his years of service and experience at various levels of the Party. It said the responsibilities he had undertaken over the years had equipped him with experience in party administration, communications, elections, campaigns, strategy and disciplinary processes. The proponents said their appeal was based on fairness, regional representation and recognition of service, and expressed confidence that the Party leadership would give the concerns of the Western region due consideration. They said the region currently had no representation at the national executive level and, therefore, appealed to the National Executive Committee and the Party leadership to consider the region in upcoming appointments.

title: Oil prices rise on potential US strikes on Iran before midterm elections
body: Oil prices jumped on Thursday after reports about Pentagon plans for US strikes on Iran that could be launched before the midterm elections amid continued Iranian attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz. Brent , the benchmark for two thirds of the world's oil, climbed nearly 3.86 per cent to $104.1 a barrel at 1.49pm UAE time, after falling below the $100 mark earlier this week. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, rose 3.78 per cent to $91.62 a barrel. Crude prices have been hovering above the $100 per barrel mark despite a lull in the US military campaign. US President Donald Trump, who is facing domestic backlash over the war, earlier indicated that the US would resume strikes only after the midterms. However, rising Iranian attacks in recent weeks on oil and gas tankers in the strait may force Mr Trump’s hand. The Atlantic on Tuesday reported that the US Defence Department was identifying targets for attacks in Iran. The size of potential strikes, if the US administration were to proceed with hostilities ahead of polls, was still being discussed, it said, quoting unnamed US officials. The US may choose to conduct a limited military campaign and follow it with a larger operation after polls conclude next month, The Atlantic reported. Axios quoted officials as saying potential operations could involve extensive US-Israeli strikes on Iranian energy, infrastructure and nuclear targets. “President Trump holds all the cards and will do whatever is best for the United States,” the US news outlet quoted a White House official as saying. Israeli officials said the chances of renewed combat before the elections remain low but could rise significantly afterward, with escalation potentially triggering a major Iranian missile response, according to the report. "Renewed tensions — or, rather, the increasingly crowded headlines surrounding existing and persistent Middle East tensions — weighed on market sentiment," said Ipek Ozkardeskaya, senior analyst at Swissquote. "Oil fluctuated, and Brent is extending gains above $102 per barrel." Thin traffic Traffic through the strait, the narrow waterway through which a fifth of the world's oil and gas flowed before the conflict broke out, has remained thin. The number of vessels transiting the strait fell to the lowest in more than two ⁠months, according to shipping data from analytics firm Kpler. Seven commodity ships passed through the strait on Tuesday, the ⁠lowest figure since July 23, data showed. Strikes on tankers climbed to their highest weekly rate since the conflict began on February 28. In the latest attack, a tanker north of Qatar was struck by multiple projectiles, causing casualties, the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency said on Wednesday. Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia's civilian and energy infrastructure are also adding to market jitters. Saudi Arabia's maritime blockade in the Red Sea by the Houthis and consistent strikes on Saudi Airports, ports and oil pipelines as well as refining facilities are stoking fears as an all-out war that would further crimp supplies energy supplies through the Bab El Mandeb strait. "The risks of multi-front escalation in the region and the war heading toward further fragmentation are boosting the risk premium in pricing," Samer Hasn, senior market analyst at XS.com said. "Nothing suggests a possible return to diplomacy; rather, all signs point to the situation in the region heading toward further deterioration at existing flashpoints and expanding into new ones."

title: Attacks on Saudi airports kill 3 people, as fighting escalates in Yemen
body: Three people have been killed in attacks on Saudi airports, the country’s civil aviation authorities said on Wednesday, October 7, as fighting intensified in Yemen between the Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces. One person was killed and eight wounded in an attack on King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh, and two were killed and 28 wounded in an attack on facilities at Abha airport, it said in a statement. One of the attacks was on Wednesday and the other on Tuesday, the civil aviation authorities said, without saying which attack had occurred on which day. A Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis vowed retaliation, saying the attacks “will not go unpunished”. In a statement issued late on Wednesday, the coalition said it had attacked more than 80 Houthi military sites across the governorates of Saada, Hodeidah, Jawf and Marib. The Saudi airport attacks were among a series of strikes targeting aviation infrastructure on Wednesday. The Houthis attacked Aden’s international airport with ballistic missiles and explosive-laden drones earlier on Wednesday, the country’s Transport Ministry said. One missile landed near the runway minutes before a flight from Cairo was due to land, the ministry said. The airport is the main international gateway for parts of Yemen outside Houthi control. Battles in Yemen have focused in recent days on areas around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a shipping route that has become more crucial for energy exports since the conflict between the US and Iran restricted trade through the Strait of Hormuz. This week, Yemeni government forces with Saudi-led coalition air support launched a counteroffensive to recapture strategic territory near the strait and around the town of Mocha that the Houthis had captured in September, but it is unclear if their advance will hold. The fighting, a spillover from the wider US-Iran conflict , has revived a complex 12-year war in Yemen that led to one of the worst humanitarian crises globally and fragmented the Arab world’s most impoverished country. The number of people displaced since the latest round of fighting began has risen to more than 200,000, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said on Wednesday. “People are running for their lives and finding nowhere safe to go,” said IOM Director General Amy Pope, who called for more funding amid rising needs for food and shelter. Both sides allege that hundreds of people have been killed in fighting, without providing details. The UN says three in four families are going hungry in parts of Yemen. The Houthis have repeatedly ​targeted infrastructure including airports, oil refineries and pipelines in Saudi Arabia, a US ally. On Wednesday, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile north of the Saudi capital Riyadh. It said it was tracking the launch platform over Houthi-controlled Sanaa and would destroy it, but gave no details of casualties or damage. Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a statement that the group had targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with several drones. Battles over the strait Any Houthi control of the strait could threaten shipping or global oil flows, and Saudi Arabia has been seeking international assistance to repel the Houthis. Turkey is sending mainly defensive and technical support, two officials said on Wednesday, after the NATO member and Pakistan pledged to implement a collective defence commitment under their newly formed alliance. Syria is carefully considering providing military assistance to ally Saudi Arabia amid the escalating war against the Houthis, a US official and a Syrian military official briefed on the matter said. Options being considered include defensive aid to protect the kingdom from attacks, or deployment of forces in an offensive capacity to help Saudi-backed Yemeni troops fight the Houthis, the officials said. The US official said Saudi Arabia had requested that Syria deploy forces to fight the Houthis. In response to a request for comment from the Syrian foreign ministry, a Syrian diplomat said Syria stood firmly with Saudi Arabia in the face of Houthi attacks but that the government’s primary focus was on domestic priorities such as recovery from the country’s civil war. Fighting on the western front remains concentrated in the Dhubab district overlooking Bab el-Mandeb, with pro-government forces attempting an advance in the strategic hills to the east of that coastal plain, Yemeni military and government sources said. On Monday, the Yemeni government said it had reached Mocha, which sits at a junction with a supply route to the critical battleground of Taiz, but the claim had been premature, according to Yemeni military officials on the ground and analysts. The Houthis, who control much of Yemen’s north, seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, prompting a military coalition led by Saudi Arabia, fearful of rival Iran’s influence in Yemen and chaos on its borders, to intervene. The Saudi-led coalition accuses Iran of arming, training and funding the Houthis. The group, mountain fighters who have emerged as a force of tens of thousands with missiles and drones that threatens the region, denies being part of Iran’s Middle East proxy network, and says it develops its own weapons. Tehran also rejects the allegations. – Rappler.com

title: World Bank revises Africa’s growth upwards to 4.3%
body: The World Bank has raised its 2026 growth forecast for Sub-Saharan Africa by 0.3 percentage points to 4.3 per cent, citing stronger domestic demand and improved economic resilience. The upward revision from its April forecast comes ahead of the 2026 World Bank Group (WBG) and International Monetary Fund (IMF) annual meetings scheduled for next week in Bangkok, Thailand. The World Bank, in its latest Africa Economic Update, said the region’s growth continued to gain momentum despite geopolitical tensions, climate shocks, declining development assistance and fiscal pressures, amid renewed global discussions on economic policy and financing. It projected the region’s median inflation rate to rise from 3.7 per cent in 2025 to 5.5 per cent in 2026, driven by higher global fuel, fertiliser and food prices. The report said public debt had broadly stabilised at about 57 per cent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP), although high debt-service costs continued to constrain spending on health, education and infrastructure. “The outlook is supported by improved macroeconomic resilience, stronger domestic demand, and investments linked to the global energy transition and digital technologies,” the report said. It said growth remained insufficient to significantly reduce extreme poverty, create adequate employment opportunities and absorb the region’s rapidly expanding youthful labour force. “Despite a challenging global environment, economic activity in Sub-Saharan Africa continues to demonstrate remarkable resilience, with growth forecasts upgraded for nearly three-quarters of countries in the region, including Angola, Ethiopia, Nigeria, and Zambia,” said Mr Andrew Dabalen, World Bank Chief Economist for the Africa Region. He said the gains reflected years of difficult reforms and improved economic management, adding that the next major challenge was to translate sustained growth into decent jobs and broader opportunities for citizens. “By investing in the foundations of an AI-ready economy, African countries can unlock productivity gains, spur innovation, and accelerate the structural transformation needed to raise living standards and reduce poverty,” he said. The report said declining development assistance would increase pressure on countries to mobilise domestic resources, deepen local capital markets and secure more sustainable financing. It said climate-related shocks, including a potential El Niño event, could disrupt agricultural production and worsen food insecurity, while tighter financing conditions could further constrain fiscal space. The Bank identified affordable, locally adapted small-scale Artificial Intelligence (AI) applications as a major opportunity for the region, particularly low-bandwidth tools for education, agriculture, health, finance, logistics and public administration. “Realising these benefits will require investments in reliable electricity, affordable connectivity, digital skills, quality data, compute infrastructure, and effective governance,” the World Bank stated. It called for stronger institutions, technical capacity, effective implementation and regional cooperation, including through the African Union’s continental AI strategy and the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA). The report said such cooperation could help scale AI-enabled solutions and support the creation of more and better jobs across the region. title: Trump urges Xi Jinping to lift export restrictions on Japan — newspaper
body:
HONG KONG, October 8. /TASS/. During Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington in September, US President Donald Trump urged him to lift export restrictions on Japan, the Hong Kong-based South China Morning Post reported.
According to sources, at last month's meeting in Washington, the US leader "raised Japan’s grievances over Chinese export restrictions - including on rare earths - that have squeezed Japanese industries."
The sources also noted that Trump "framed the Chinese measures as a threat to American industries reliant on Japanese suppliers." In this regard, he stated "that they were an indirect violation of the US-China trade truce reached in Busan last October," the newspaper noted.
Nevertheless, according to the sources, the Chinese leader showed little interest in Trump’s proposals. He said that Beijing’s dispute with Tokyo should be viewed separately from US-China relations and should not affect them.
China had previously announced the introduction of export control measures targeting Japanese entities involved in bolstering Tokyo’s military capabilities. Chinese exporters are prohibited from supplying dual-use goods, including rare earth metals and other critical minerals, to these entities. In addition, companies and individuals outside China are prohibited from transferring dual-use goods of Chinese origin.
Chinese President Xi Jinping was in the US on his first state visit in 11 years on September 23-25. In May, Trump visited China at the invitation of the Chinese leader.

title: Aman Properties Is Expanding Its Horizon: Sar Bet Is Next
body: We have exciting news to share: Aman Properties is expanding to Sar Bet. After establishing developments in areas including Bisrate Gebriel, Kazanchis, Bole and Kara Kore, Aman Properties is widening its presence across the capital, with Sar Bet among the locations shaping what comes next. The expansion marks another step in Aman Properties’ growth across Addis Ababa, extending its presence into new locations and building on the experience gained through its developments across the city. Why Sar Bet? Some locations have an advantage that cannot be created overnight: they are already deeply connected to the city. Sar Bet is one of those places. Located close to the African Union headquarters and several embassies, including the Embassy of Canada, Sar Bet is well connected to central Addis Ababa and surrounded by established business, residential, and institutional areas. The Mexico–Sar Bet corridor has also seen signiﬁcant development, with improvements to roads, pedestrian infrastructure, and the surrounding urban environment. For someone looking to buy a home in Addis Ababa, location is about more than an address. It is about what surrounds you today and what is likely to shape your everyday life tomorrow. Sar Bet brings both: an established place in the city, strong connections to key parts of Addis Ababa, and an urban environment that continues to develop. What Does This Mean for Aman Properties? Aman Properties is planning for the long term. Its vision goes beyond individual developments, with plans to build a lasting presence across Addis Ababa and continue growing with the city. Backed by experience across different neighborhoods and new locations already in its plans, including its strategic work in Sar Bet, Aman Properties is cementing its place as a permanent, trusted leader in Ethiopia’s real estate industry for years to come. What Comes Next? And Sar Bet will not be the last. Bole is also among Aman Properties upcoming locations, extending the company’s presence into another well-established part of Addis Ababa. From the places Aman Properties has already built into the locations now taking shape, the journey across Addis Ababa continues. Sar Bet is next. And there is more to come.

title: BoG cautions public against 20 unlicensed mobile loan apps
body: The Bank of Ghana (BoG) has warned the public against using 20 mobile loan applications operating without its approval. The digital lenders are offering credit services without the required licence or authorisation from the central bank, the BoG said. In a notice, the Bank said the operations of the unlicensed providers contravened the Directive for Digital Credit Service Providers in Ghana and posed risks to users. The affected applications are Agile Loan, AmanaPay, CashWay, Foutou Credit, HastyCredit, InsCash, KudiNow, LendAura, Lever Credit, LoanGlide, NovaCedi, Palm Loan, PocketLoan, Rite Credit, SikaCare, SikaNow, Susu Loan, Taploan Up, Temivo Cedi and Zatuloan. The BoG said the operations raised concerns over customer data privacy, consumer protection and compliance with financial sector regulations. It urged the public to use only financial institutions and digital credit providers licensed and approved by the central bank. The Bank said it was working with relevant state agencies to identify, investigate and take enforcement action against unlicensed operators. It said the measures were aimed at protecting consumers and maintaining the safety, integrity and stability of the financial sector.

title: The fight beyond the cage: Zamzam Al Hammadi’s promise to her mother
body: Zamzam Al Hammadi had just become a world champion when she saw her mother cry for the first time. She was befuddled by the tears. She had won; this was supposed to be a time for celebration. “I saw her crying for the first time, even though I was winning. I really didn’t understand if she was happy or sad. Then I asked her, ‘Mum, why are you crying?’ She told me, ‘I’m happy because you won, but I want to tell you something.’ I was like, ‘What?’ She told me, ‘I have cancer’, and I was like, ‘Mum, you’re kidding me, right?' She was like, ‘No.'" Al Hammadi became emotional recalling that moment. The smile that had barely left her face faded momentarily. “I told her, 'Mum, I’m going to fight with you. No matter what happens, I’m going to be by your side. I’m going to be with you and believe me, with me, I’m going to see your smile, I’m going to see your smile 24/7'.” Fighting is what Al Hammadi knows best. The 18-year-old is a two-time IMMAF youth world champion and the first Emirati woman to sign with the Professional Fighters League. She made a winning PFL Mena debut in Dubai in May in an amateur strawweight bout. Al Hammadi is bright, animated and a jolt of electricity in conversation. She’s gloriously expressive, extremely witty and incapable of harbouring a modest ambition. She’s shooting for the moon and at the very least hoping to land in the stars. Such was her ascent that she was invited to speak at Middlesex University Dubai’s Women in Sport Series, launched through its London Sport Institute. The opening discussion brought together Emirati athletes to speak about identity, heritage and the next generation. She agreed to speak to The National on the sidelines. What really shines through is her love for her mother, Nada Al Nuaymi, who serves as both her inspiration and the reason for her fierce ambition. Her mother was born and raised in the UAE but possesses Iraqi roots, two identities that she’s particularly proud of. Mention Iraq and Zamzam’s eyes light up. View this post on Instagram When she discovered during our conversation that I was Iraqi, she immediately called for her mother:. “Mum! Come here! She’s Iraqi! Can you believe it? She’s Iraqi!” The delight spread from her face to her mother’s as they conveyed their admiration for the country, explaining their ancestry. Iraq is a country that she has yet to visit, but Al Hammadi dreams of travelling there. “My blood is there, my blood is there. I always talk about it, and I’m really proud because I have the blood of real history makers. "My mum always talks about Iraqi history and to be honest, every day I’m learning new stuff about it and that makes me even prouder of it.” She indulges in her mother’s stories and the Iraqi cuisine she’s learning to cook. She’s already got quite good; she said her mother already considers her the best Iraqi cook in the house, which she considers both a blessing and a curse. “I can’t really cook it [Iraqi food] when I have to diet. When I’m on a diet, I just cry and think I’m losing my skills.” Al Hammadi has also developed a deep interest in the history of the country and spoke excitedly of studying Hammurabi, the former ruler of the first Babylonian dynasty, famed for creating the code of Hammurabi, the oldest and most complete written legal system in history. A lecturer once asked her why she was so interested. “I told him, because I have Iraqi blood, why not?” Despite being captivated by her maternal roots, she lives to serve her country, the UAE, the flag she carries into competition. “I’m not representing myself only. I’m not representing my family only. I’m representing my country. Before my name appears, it says Emirati,” a fact that makes her immensely proud. Al Hammadi is a trailblazer in UAE MMA. She is the first Emirati woman to sign for the PFL and aims to turn pro soon. Grander ambitions include becoming a world champion and to fight in the UFC. Still only 18, she is in her second year of studying for a degree in international relations, political economy and development and serves on the student council at Abu Dhabi's Zayed University. She once considered studying media because she likes broadcasting and, by her own admission, thought it would be an easier course. Her mother instead pushed her towards a degree that would help her serve her country. “She’d be like, 'Zamzam, what you’re doing is great, but I still think this is nothing. You need something bigger.'" Nada says she has been likened to a lioness for her ability to breed competitive fighters. Her younger daughter, Ghala, is also a decorated mixed martial artist and already owns one advantage that Zamzam is determined to challenge. Ghala once finished a fight in five seconds; Zamzam's quickest finish is six. “And now we’re really competing on this. I was like, ‘Ghala, I’m not stepping down until I get it in four seconds. You’re going to see Ghala, I’m coming for four seconds,'” Zamzam says with a grin. Asked whether their mother ever worries about raising so many well-trained fighters, Al Hammadi replies, “To be honest, we’re the ones scared of mum.” Al Hammadi refers to her mother as a cancer warrior. A single mother who has devoted her life to her children, she is full of admiration for her . Grateful for this, Al Hammadi is encouraged to keep competing and progressing as she feels it motivates her mother to continue treatment. “She’s fighting for her life, to survive. So why don’t I fight for her? So she feels that there’s someone with me who’s fighting as well?" View this post on Instagram Al Hammadi is also focused on helping the next generation of girls enter combat sports. She remembers a time she and her sister were the only girls from their group competing at the world championships She says more women are seriously considering a similar career, and much of that is down to representation. Athletes like Al Hammadi have helped create a pathway that many never thought possible. The jiu-jitsu and martial arts club that Zamzam established had few members in its first year. She says it now has 51 members, with fathers now actively approaching her to ask about opportunities for their daughters. Al Hammadi hopes that more Emirati women will come to represent the country in every sport. “At least one Emirati girl in every global organisation,” she said.

title: Defense Forces in Sumy region receive new shipment of interceptor drones
body:
According to Ukrinform, Oleh Hryhorov, head of the Sumy Regional State Administration, announced this on Facebook .
“The 8th Corps of the Airborne Assault Forces received 60 drones. Another 10 went to fighters from the Sumy community’s volunteer unit,” the post reads.
According to the head of the Regional State Administration, units already have drones of this type. They have proven effective in intercepting and destroying enemy UAVs—both strike and reconnaissance models.
In addition, an off-road vehicle was delivered to the 8th Airborne Corps’ unmanned systems battalion for combat missions.
The total value of the transferred equipment is 3 million 850 thousand hryvnias.
Hryhorov thanked everyone who supports the defenders and helps provide the units with what they need.
As reported by Ukrinform, KORD special forces in the Sumy region received the first batch of Sting interceptor drones.

title: Mahama announces GH¢1bn allocation for revolving National Housing Fund
body: President John Dramani Mahama has announced a one-billion cedi allocation in the 2027 Budget towards a revolving National Housing Fund to expand access to affordable decent housing. The President said he had directed the Finance Minister to make the allocation as part of the Government’s contribution to the three billion-cedi fund. He made the announcement at the opening of the National Conference on Housing Finance in Accra. The conference was organised by the National Housing Fund Limited in collaboration with the Ministry of Works, Housing and Water Resources. The two-day conference, held to commemorate World Habitat Day, is on the theme: “Adequate Housing for All, Innovative Financing for Ghana’s Housing Future”. President Mahama said the Government’s contribution would not be the sole source of financing for the Fund. Pension funds, insurers, development finance institutions and diaspora investors could also provide capital through structures that protected their interests while supporting viable housing projects. He said the blended finance approach being promoted under the 24-Hour Economy and Accelerated Export Development Programme offered useful lessons for mobilising such resources. Carefully targeted public and concessional financing, he said, could also help attract private investment and manage risks. President Mahama said the transition from the National Home Ownership Fund Limited to the National Housing Fund Limited was intended to broaden the institution’s mandate. The new focus, he said, would move beyond home ownership financing to supporting housing delivery and expanding affordable housing options. The President said the Government remained committed to delivering decent and affordable housing at scale. This would be achieved through the effective use of government and institutional land banks, support for private investment and the revival of stalled housing projects. President Mahama said the housing programme at Saglemi was expected to deliver 1,500 housing units by next year. Additionally, a district housing programme was also being piloted in eight districts by the Ministry of Works, Housing and Water Resources in collaboration with the National Housing Fund. He assured that the Government would accelerate the district housing programme in the next financial year. The Tema Development Corporation’s Oxygen City in Ho, Volta Region, and the State Housing Company’s Green City at Dedesua in the Ashanti Region would also contribute to the country’s housing stock. President Mahama noted that economic stability was critical to expanding housing finance. Lower inflation and more favourable lending conditions could improve prospects for construction and mortgage finance, he added. The Government’s responsibility, he said, was to ensure that such economic gains translated into tangible benefits for households. “We must also mobilise capital that is suited to the long life of housing investments,” he emphasised. The President said housing development must go beyond constructing houses. It must create integrated communities with roads, water, drainage and sanitation systems, as well as access to schools, healthcare and other social facilities. He noted that lower house purchase prices would offer little relief to families if they still had to spend excessively on commuting or securing basic services. “Land administration, planning, planning approvals, infrastructure provision, and housing finance must all work together as a symphony,” he stated. He also called for housing to be incorporated into the planning of industrial enclaves under the Government’s economic transformation agenda. Providing residential facilities close to industrial enclaves would reduce commuting costs, improve workers’ productivity and give them more time with their families. President Mahama, however, noted that uncertainties surrounding land titles and delays in planning approvals increased costs, discouraged investment and ultimately burdened households. Mr Ahmed Ibrahim, Minister of Works, Housing and Water Resources, in a speech read on his behalf, proposed that the conference be institutionalised as an annual National Housing Finance Conference. He said the platform would enable government, the financial sector, developers, professionals, labour, academia and development partners to review progress and agree on practical solutions. Mr Ibrahim said adequate housing was a fundamental human right and an important driver of economic development. It created jobs, stimulated local industries, deepened financial markets and contributed to improved health, productivity, social stability and dignity. Mr Mahama Ayariga, Minister of Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs, said although housing was a challenge, it also presented an opportunity. Mr Prosper Hoetu, Chief Executive Officer of the National Housing Fund Limited, said Ghana needed a housing finance system that recognised the different circumstances of households and provided multiple pathways to home ownership.

title: Big Push: Major asphaltic works begin on Sunyani Inner-Ring project
body: Contractors have commenced asphaltic overlays on the 9.2-kilometres Sunyani Inner Ring-Road project under the government’s ‘Big Push’ road infrastructure development. During a visit, the Ghana News Agency noticed that the asphaltic overlay had begun from the Sunyani-Fiapre Roundabout, progressing steadily. Kofi Job Company Limited is executing that major road project, a dual carriage that stretched from the Fiapre-Roundabout and linking the Sunyani Technical University (STU). In an interview with the GNA, Mr Kofi Kamkam, the Site Engineer said the company remained dedicated to complete the project on time, saying it was presently working on one side of the road in order not to obstruct vehicular movements. He assured quality works and lauded the cooperation of residents along the stretch, despite some inconveniences, assuring that the company would continue to manage the dust that emanated from the road project.

title: Lithuania Approves €15M ($16.8M) for Ukraine’s Recovery and Reconstruction Through World Bank, EIB
body:
Lithuania’s government approved an additional €15 million ($16.8 million) in financial assistance to Ukraine on Wednesday, Oct. 7, directing the funds through the World Bank and European Investment Bank (EIB) to support reconstruction and strengthen the country’s economic resilience amid Russia’s ongoing war.
According to Lithuania’s Ministry of Finance, €10 million ($11.2 million) will go to the World Bank’s Special Program for Ukraine Recovery 2.0 (SPUR 2.0), while €5 million ($5.6 million) will be allocated to the EIB’s EU for Ukraine Fund (EU4U).
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Lithuanian Finance Minister Taurimas Valys said continued assistance was essential not only for Ukraine’s survival but also for Europe’s security.
“Today, Ukrainians are fighting not only for their own freedom but for ours as well. Uninterrupted and timely support is the least we must provide. It is our duty to ensure that Ukraine has everything it needs – both to achieve victory and to rebuild the country,” Valys said.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha welcomed the decision, thanking Lithuania for its continued commitment to Ukraine.
“Thank you, Lithuania, for another €15 million for Ukraine’s recovery and resilience through the World Bank and EIB mechanisms,” Sybiha wrote on X .
“Lithuania has stood shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine from the very beginning,” he added, praising Vilnius for practical decisions that help Ukraine recover and grow stronger.
The €10 million ($11.2 million) contribution to SPUR 2.0 will support a World Bank financing mechanism designed to mobilize additional resources for Ukraine’s recovery.
Established in June 2026, the program allows donor contributions to generate approximately three times their value in concessional lending.
According to Lithuania’s Finance Ministry, $2 billion in donor contributions could unlock around $6 billion in loans to Ukraine on favorable terms.
The program also includes a private-sector component aimed at encouraging investment and supporting Ukraine’s economic recovery.
Lithuania previously contributed €10 million ($11.2 million at the Oct. 7, 2026 exchange rate) to the original SPUR program in 2023.
The remaining €5 million ($5.6 million) will go to the EIB’s EU4U Fund, which finances critical infrastructure reconstruction and projects strengthening Ukraine’s economic resilience.
The EIB requested additional contributions from member states in July after previously committed funding for Ukrainian projects was nearly exhausted.
Lithuania also contributed €10 million to the EU4U Fund in 2023.
Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, Lithuania’s Finance Ministry has allocated more than €93 million ($104.2 million) to Ukraine through international financial institutions and EU mechanisms, alongside €26 million ($29.1 million) in bilateral assistance.
Valys said Ukraine’s financial requirements and the international community’s continued assistance would be among the central issues discussed at next week’s annual meetings of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund.
During a September meeting with Ukrainian Ambassador Olha Nikitchenko, Valys said Ukraine’s security was inseparable from Europe’s and reaffirmed that assistance to Kyiv would remain a priority during Lithuania’s presidency of the Council of the European Union in the first half of 2027.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Japan beer giants raided over alleged price-fixing cartel
body: Japanese officials have raided the country’s biggest beer makers over allegations they worked together to raise the price of their beverages. Asahi, Sapporo, Kirin and Suntory Spirits confirmed to the BBC that their premises had been searched by the Japan Fair Trade Commission (JFTC), adding that they would fully cooperate with the regulator. The four firms dominate Japan’s beer market, with their drinks a common sight in supermarkets and convenience stores across the country. Asahi, Kirin and Sapporo all saw their share price fall after news of the investigation broke on Wednesday. Suntory’s beer business is not publicly-listed. “I do not deny that an investigation is being conducted today, but I’d like to refrain from commenting on the details as a preliminary review is underway,” JFTC Secretary General Iwanari Hiroo said, according to local media. The BBC has contacted the JFTC for comment. According to the Japan Times, the investigation centres on the companies raising their prices in April last year and in October 2022. All four companies announced increases, citing the rising cost of raw materials as well as other factors such as energy and transportation. Kirin Holdings said its subsidiary, Kirin Brewery Company, was searched “on suspicion of a violation of the Antimonopoly Act”. It said it takes the matter “very seriously”, adding it would “fully cooperate with the Japan Fair Trade Commission’s investigation and any requests for cooperation”. Kirin Holdings said: “At present, the impact of this matter on the company’s financial results has not been determined. The company will promptly disclose any material developments as they arise.” A spokesperson for Suntory confirmed “an on-site inspection” had taken place “in connection with a potential violation of Japan’s Antimonopoly Act relating to domestic alcohol trade practices”. The company said: “We sincerely apologise for any concern or inconvenience this situation may cause to our customers, business partners, and other stakeholders. We will cooperate fully with the JFTC’s investigation.” Asahi said it was “subject to investigation by the Japan Fair Trade Commission” and that it will fully cooperate with the regulator. title: Will Americans ever escape this 'imperialist realism'?
body:
WATCH: Author Daniel Bessner describes how US empire isn't just a pathology of Washington leadership, it's deeply engrained in our culture, too
Last week, after nearly two decades of fighting, the U.S. finally pulled the plug on its seemingly endless war in Iraq.
Like our exit from Afghanistan just a few years ago, the end of fighting in Iraq was met with an eerie quiet. It doesn’t take much to figure out why so little attention is paid to the end of these wars: they mark yet another loss for America and the people in Washington who insist our military power can solve every problem, everywhere. Both conflicts are examples of American hubris — strategically incoherent wars fought with American lives at the expense of too many Iraqis and Afghans lives.
But, of course, we refuse to learn our lesson. The week before Americans finally vacated Iraq, President Donald Trump took to his proverbial pulpit at the U.N. to brag about his exploitation of Venezuela for oil, declaring “to the victor goes the spoils.” It was a stark expression of how America’s domination of the global order — it’s imperialism, if you will — really works. And it came in a place where Washington usually goes to great lengths to disguise this reality.
As we extend our fingers around the globe — Venezuela, Cuba , Iran , Somalia, and more — we are moved to ask: is it easier for Americans to imagine the end of the world than the end of the U.S. empire?
This is precisely the question motivating Daniel Bessner in his latest book , “Imperialist Realism.” Drawing on Mark Fisher’s earlier “Capitalist Realism,” which uses cultural touchstones to show how deeply embedded we are in capitalism, Bessner proposes that we are embedded in imperialism that structures our world, experiences, and culture.
We spoke with Bessner about his new book for our latest episode of Always at War.
As Bessner explains, "Imperialist Realism” comprises three main features: cynicism (few people actually believe the U.S. effectively “spreads democracy”); missionism (despite this cynicism, Americans believe they need to continue to act); and tragic guilt (the emotion that results from the tension between cynicism and missionism).
Bessner points to former Secretary of State Antony Blinken as one example of tragic guilt in action. During his tenure, Blinken repeatedly stressed America's solemn duty to lead the world, to "put our hand on the rudder of history and chart a path forward," because "in the absence of us" leading, "someone else will do it." Blinken, Bessner suggests, understands that the United States "isn't necessarily spreading its ideals. It's really acting in the realm of power politics and he feels bad about that."
But the “structure of feeling” that is Imperialist Realism doesn’t just affect our leaders, it infects our culture. Take for example, the superheroes in the Marvel Cinematic Universe. In Captain America: Civil War, there is a civil war between superheroes who will accept being regulated and superheroes who won’t. When the superheroes who won’t go on the lamb, the pro-regulation team allows them to escape, as if to say: sometimes you need to exist outside the law. That’s imperialist realism in a nutshell.
What would it take to change this grim reality that we’ve resigned ourselves to, where America is always at war? A lot of work, no doubt. Bessner suggests meaningfully reforming the national security state would be an enormous undertaking that would require extraordinary expenditures of political capital, credibility and courage. If what we really need to change American foreign policy is a brave, selfless politician…it’s no wonder Americans are so sure things will never change.

title: Bosnia's Trump-aligned kingmaker wins big despite electoral ban
body:
Election results further expose the limits of BiH’s political system, which dates back to the 1995 Dayton Accords.
Nationalists came out on top in Bosnia and Herzegovina (BiH)’s October 4 election. Allies of Milorad Dodik, the de facto leader of the country’s Bosnian Serb entity, won decisively in Republika Srpska despite Dodik himself being barred from office, while nationalist Bosniak and Croat parties dominated in the country’s other political entity, the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.
This election offered no real sign of change in a Balkan country long constrained by weak institutions, corruption, and deeply divided ethnic groups. Although BiH’s complex demographics and history necessitate some form of decentralized power-sharing, its political system has also become a vehicle for interests that benefit from continued dysfunction — including some with growing ties to President Donald Trump’s inner circle.
Dodik’s power outlasts the pressure against him That dysfunction unfolds in a particular international context. U.S. pressure on Dodik has eased , with the Trump administration removing sanctions imposed by the Biden and Obama administrations. Russia continues cultivating its close ties with Republika Srpska, and Brussels struggles to use the prospect of European Union membership to drive reform. The result is a fraying political order against the backdrop of an increasingly uncertain international environment. The election also highlighted Dodik’s enduring influence. Although Dodik was prohibited from running, his Alliance of Independent Social Democrats (SNSD) secured a decisive victory . Leila Bičakčić, the CEO of the Center for Investigative Reporting, explained that Dodik has emerged from the period of U.S. sanctions politically stronger than before, demonstrating his ability to maintain relationships with the U.S., Russia, Israel , and nationalist movements elsewhere in Europe . Therefore, Dodik’s resurgence is illustrative of how much political authority in BiH can reside outside the institutions through which that authority is supposed to be formally exercised. That informal power has coincided with a fundamental shift in Dodik’s relationship with Washington, including Trump’s decision to lift sanctions on Dodik and his allies, which the U.S. had previously imposed in response to his separatist ambitions and alleged corruption. Dejan Sajinovic, a Bosnian journalist from Republika Srpska, interprets the new relationship as an example of a more transactional American foreign policy. Indeed, Republika Srpska’s spending on Trump-linked lobbyists and surrogates — spending that has exceeded $4 million since the beginning of 2025 — appears to have played an important role in the Bosnian Serb leader’s efforts to win the White House’s support. “It is a quid pro quo,” he told RS, arguing that Washington appears willing to support Dodik politically if he can help advance U.S. strategic and commercial interests in the Western Balkans. The precise terms of any understanding between the Trump administration and Dodik remain unclear, though a controversial energy deal is central to it. The deal involves the proposed Southern Interconnection pipeline , which would connect BiH to Croatia’s gas network and the Krk LNG terminal, allowing BiH to reduce dependence on Russian gas. It is controversial because Bosnian legislation has designated AAFS Infrastructure and Energy (a recently formed Wyoming-based company fronted by Trump allies Jesse Binnall and Joe Flynn) as the project’s lead investor and operator without a competitive tender. Critics have raised concerns about transparency and AAFS’s lack of a relevant track record. Two of Trump’s political advisers, James Blair and Chris LaCivita, were in Republika Srpska to advise the Bosnian Serb entity’s government shortly before this month’s election. Both received hundreds of thousands of dollars via a DC law firm retained by the government of Republika Srpska to promote Dodik and the SNSD. After news of their travel to Republika Srpska fueled some controversy, Trump vowed to terminate Blair and LaCivita as his consultants if their political work in the Balkans conflicts with the White House’s interests. Rewarding dysfunction This election further exposed the limits of BiH’s political system, which dates back to the 1995 Dayton Accords . The agreement ended BiH’s war by creating an elaborate system of power-sharing between Bosniaks, Serbs, and Croats. But 31 years later, that architecture has become a vehicle for political paralysis, even if it has prevented the country from sliding back into war. Tanja Topic, a political analyst based in Banja Luka (Republika Srpska’s administrative center), told RS that the Dayton framework has become “too narrow for the normal functioning of BiH,” pointing to years of blockades at the state level and constitutional provisions that discriminate against citizens who do not identify with one of the country’s three constituent peoples. Yet Sajinovic cautions against treating Dayton as the sole source of the problem. Bosnia’s multiple identities, he argues, make some form of decentralized power-sharing unavoidable. The deeper problem is that political elites have learned to exploit the system’s complexity and veto points to protect their own influence. The election offered little evidence that those incentives are changing. For the EU, the result tests whether enlargement can still drive political reform. Although BiH gained candidate status in 2022 and approval to open accession negotiations in 2024, talks have stalled over unmet reforms, including judicial oversight and curbing corruption. The EU agenda has faded from political debate, replaced by fears of renewed conflict. The deeper problem, Bičakčić argues, is that political elites lack interest in the rule-of-law reforms, stronger institutions, and rights that EU integration requires. If membership no longer provides a credible incentive for change, the EU risks retaining influence only on paper. Enter Russia Dysfunctionality in BiH creates space for Russia, which has long maintained close ties with Republika Srpska. Russian President Vladimir Putin is a close ally of Dodik, who has rejected Western sanctions on Russia and hails the Russian president as “one of the most peace-loving leaders of our time.” Dodik has met with Putin 11 times since Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, with his latest visit to Moscow only days before the October 4 vote. Russia’s influence stems from Western failures. “Russia profits without investing any effort” by watching a state created through U.S. policy struggle to function and the EU fail to manage its own neighborhood, said Vuk Vuksanović, a lecturer at King’s College London. Nonetheless, Moscow’s role in BiH should not be overstated. Igor Novaković, a senior associate at the International and Security Affairs Centre – ISAC Fund, sees Russia as too bogged down in Ukraine to achieve much in BiH. He believes Moscow lacks any real strategy for the Western Balkans. “My impression is that [the Russians] are focusing on maintaining the current position, supporting, mostly verbally, some of the leaders in the Balkans,” Novaković said. “But in essence they will not go as far as to directly intervene or to do more than, let’s say, disinformation to an extent — maybe using the Western Balkans for some hybrid operations against Western Europe — but not more than that.” The international consensus behind Dayton is eroding Ultimately, the election highlights the erosion of the international consensus underpinning Bosnia’s fragile post-1995 order. As Sajinovic notes, BiH has functioned best when major external powers agreed on its direction and struggled when that consensus fractured. Today, divisions within Europe and between Washington and Brussels have created a vacuum that gives BiH’s political actors greater freedom to advance their own agendas. This does not mean BiH is inevitably headed back to war. But it gives ample cause for concern. At the same time, one must not read the election as a verdict for deeper ethnic division. Turnout fell eight points from 2022, while economic problems, emigration, and political stagnation remain pressing concerns, and many voters appear increasingly frustrated with a system that encourages ethnic competition rather than effective government or economic opportunity. Bosnia is therefore left with familiar political forces, but a more unsettled international environment marked by Dodik’s continued influence, weaker Western leverage, and Russia’s potential to exploit those divisions. title: Is Iran poised to withdraw from the Non-Proliferation Treaty?
body:
Opposition to the agreement now goes beyond the country's most hardline elements
In September, as the media focused its attention on the conflict in the Strait of Hormuz and the debates at the U.N. General Assembly, some internal developments in Iran went all but unnoticed. On September 28, 32 Iranian conservatives published an open letter calling for Iran to withdraw from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) as a matter of urgency.
Since the “ snapback ” of U.N. sanctions on Iran in September 2025, ultraconservative Iranian lawmakers have regularly pushed for pulling out of the NPT, under which the vast majority of states have committed to not develop nuclear weapons. The Majles — Iran’s parliament — drafted a law that would have initiated the move in 2025, but it has yet to move forward. In September, some lawmakers submitted new “triple-urgency” legislation to the Majles ’ president, Mohammad Baqer Ghalibaf, who is also currently Iran’s chief negotiator
These continuous calls by ultraconservatives to withdraw from the NPT have yet to produce an actual withdrawal because of a lack of political consensus. Iran has remained in the treaty despite the war, unprecedented economic pressure, and the return of U.N. sanctions. But is continued NPT membership still an asset for Iran?
Background On September 28, 32 prominent Iranians, many of whom served in conservative administrations, published a declaration arguing that membership in the NPT no longer serves Iranian interests. They asked President Masoud Pezeshkian , the Majles , and the Supreme National Security Council (SNSC), which oversees the country’s key national-security and foreign-policy issues, to halt all cooperation with the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) under the treaty and immediately initiate the withdrawal process. Of course, a law demanding a withdrawal from the NPT would not by itself force the hand of the executive. As shown when the SNSC suspended the “Chastity and Hijab Law” in August 2024, it is the SNSC that decides any questions it considers crucial to national security, and particularly those related to the nuclear file. The debate over NPT withdrawal: the end of the ultraconservative monopoly The open letter’s signatories belong to the conservative camp. Historically, this camp has opposed negotiations with the U.S. and denounced the 2015 Iran deal, even though some of them had embraced the idea of normalization in 2012. Since 2022, amid the stalemate of U.S.-Iran negotiations, the most radical of them, the ultraconservatives, have publicly pressed for leaving the NPT. Among them are Saeed Jalili , who led the country’s nuclear negotiating team from 2007 to 2013 and ran unsuccessfully against Pezeshkian in 2024, as well as Hamid Rasaee , a lawmaker member of the “Stability Front”, a far right sub-group of the conservative camp. In any case, the 2025 U.S.-Iran war ended the conservative monopoly on the question. Ever since, some figures in the “moderate” camp, comprised of reformists and centrists who traditionally supported normalization with the West, have changed their mind. Journalist Ali Nazari, known as a moderate, is one. More than simply leaving the NPT, Nazari now supports developing a nuclear weapon. Withdrawal from the NPT as negotiating leverage Of course, the Iranian political elite has long used the threat of withdrawing from the NPT as leverage in negotiations with the West, whatever political camp the negotiators have identified with. According to his memoir, for example, former President Hassan Rouhani, a fervent backer of negotiations with the West, threatened to withdraw from the treaty while he was secretary of the SNSC and negotiating bilaterally with the Russians in May 2005, if the IAEA Board of Governors voted to refer the Iranian nuclear file to the Security Council. (Iran did not follow through on that threat when the board made the referral in February 2006.) What has changed? The current context, however, is different from the pre-war situation. While the idea of withdrawing from the NPT was long confined to ultraconservative deputies, some recent declarations by Mohsen Rezaei, the SNSC secretary, indicate a certain evolution. In a post on X following the IAEA’s recent adoption of Resolution GOV/2026/61, Rezaei accused the IAEA of politicizing the Iranian nuclear issue, warning that such actions could lead states to leave the treaty. Yet this resolution, which reiterated concerns about Iran’s limited cooperation with the IAEA, did not introduce any new elements in comparison to the previous one, indicating Rezaei used it as a pretext to signal a new posture. While this comment could be understood as part of Iran’s negotiation strategy with the U.S., no previous SNSC secretary has ever made such a threat. Given the critical role the SNSC plays in nuclear policymaking, the threat must necessarily be taken more seriously. Previous events indicate the possibility of a convergence of views between an ultraconservative Majles and the SNSC. For example, such an alignment emerged in the lead-up to the suspension of negotiations with the IAEA in September 2025. The question remains whether a similar rapprochement could occur between the two bodies on the possibility of withdrawing from the NPT. Leave the NPT or build a bomb Leaving the NPT should not be confused with developing a nuclear weapon. In fact, in an interview with Al Jazeera published on September 19, Rezaei reaffirmed his commitment to the fatwa promulgated by the late Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei in 1995 prohibiting the creation of weapons of mass destruction. Rezaei seems to prefer a diplomatic solution for the conflict, arguing that Washington should accept Iran’s conditions for ending the war. During last month’s U.N. General Assembly, Iran proposed (and U.S. President Donald Trump rejected) to end hostilities on all fronts, unfreeze Iranian assets, and lift the blockade of Iranian ports, consistent with the MoU agreed by both parties in June. It is difficult to assess whether Rezaei’s most recent withdrawal threat indicates a firm intention to follow through or the latest in a long history of bluffs. As far as the fatwa goes, some would argue its normative force was already weakened by the new Iranian nuclear posture articulated in 2024, breaking the ultimate linguistic taboo of the Islamic Republic. Some Iranian experts now argue that a withdrawal from the NPT should only happen after Iran acquires a nuclear weapon; otherwise, the country would be unnecessarily punished as the withdrawal would inevitably be perceived as a move toward weaponization. Deterioration of relations with the IAEA It is worth emphasizing that Iran’s relations with the IAEA have deteriorated considerably. Tehran’s hostility toward its director-general, Rafael Grossi, has intensified dramatically. Holding it partially responsible for the 12-day War, Tehran also blames the agency for failing to explicitly condemn Israel and the U.S. for attacking Iranian nuclear sites. In addition, the appearance of Resolution GOV/2026/61 and the de facto exclusion of Iran’s leading nuclear official, Mohammad Eslami, from the 69th general conference of the IAEA in September have reinforced the view that the IAEA has become politicized. What prevents Iran from leaving the NPT The main obstacle to leaving the NPT remains Iran’s diplomatic dependence on Russia and China . Since the U.S. left the JCPOA in 2018, Tehran has doubled down on its cooperation with the two Eastern powers, and China has absorbed nearly all of Iran’s oil exports since. Yet one could interpret Rezaei’s comments as a warning to Moscow and Beijing, with the goal of pushing them to use their veto against any additional anti-Iran actions at the U.N. Security Council. The fear of abandonment is understandable; after all, the two powers voted to refer the Iranian nuclear file to the U.N. Security Council and supported multilateral sanctions against Iran in the past. In Iran, the debate over a possible withdrawal from the NPT remains unsettled. Most reformists and centrists still appear to oppose the idea, and the SNSC has not yet reached a consensus on the question. In addition, the appearance of Resolution GOV/2026/61 and the de facto exclusion of Iran’s leading nuclear official, Mohammad Eslami, from the 69th general conference of the IAEA in September have reinforced the view that the IAEA has become politicized.
The main obstacle to leaving the NPT remains Iran’s diplomatic dependence on Russia and China . Since the U.S. left the JCPOA in 2018, Tehran has doubled down on its cooperation with the two Eastern powers, and China has absorbed nearly all of Iran’s oil exports since. In internal debates , the possible negative effects on relations with Russia and China of withdrawing from the treaty are clearly an important factor.
Yet one could interpret Rezaei’s comments as a warning to Moscow and Beijing, with the goal of pushing them to use their veto against any additional anti-Iran actions at the U.N. Security Council. The fear of abandonment is understandable; after all, the two powers voted to refer the Iranian nuclear file to the U.N. Security Council and supported multilateral sanctions against Iran in the past.
In Iran, the debate over a possible withdrawal from the NPT remains unsettled. Most reformists and centrists still appear to oppose the idea, and the SNSC has not yet reached a consensus on the question. Ghalibaf’s looming decision over whether to advance the anti-NPT law will demonstrate political dynamics, even if it may not determine Iran’s future actions.
In the uncertainty of the moment, one can still draw a few conclusions: Russia and China have once more become essential to maintaining Iran’s NPT membership, and debates on the subject in Iran are intensifying in an unprecedented way.
