title: On using AI as a writing assistant
body:
I am a bad writer because I am the worst at explaining things.
Letâs say someone is interested in reading about how to pick the best apples for baking. I may (in my head) relate that interest to how apple trees grow, and if by some miracle the reader sticks with my piece through that, I will veer from growing apple trees to farming and tending to an apple orchard. From my perspective, I am enabling the reader to adopt some manner of resilient or sustainable behavior (âIf youâre interested in using apples for baking, you can grow them yourself!â), but whereas I may be interested in such information, I readily acknowledge that to someone else those tidbits of knowledge may come off as non-sequiturs at best or nonsense at worst. So, I simply conclude that I am a bad writer, and as such Iâve never bothered to share most of my writing. Enter AI.
I really like AI as a writing assistant because I think it has enabled me to funnel my fluid thought process into something I can flash-freeze with the liquid nitrogen that is prompt-based engineering and package my writing neatly into bite-sized morsels. Admittedly, I am unsure how successful that experiment has been as yet because I donât really have any avenues of receiving feedback. I kind of dislike the overall product from AI-assisted writing because I find that AI writing is often stilted (like something just tastes off about it), and I feel like the reviewing and editing process, while it captures some aspect of my voice, leaves the original piece less cohesive than it was when originally composed by an AI writing assistant.
As people increasingly use AI writing assistants, I wonder what their workflows and processes are for using these tools, but I thought Iâd at least share mine. Note that I am aware of all the concerns about AI use, and I am also interested in taming the use of volatile, emerging technologies. I feel that I learn more about its pitfalls as I use it different ways.
Before I start writing something, ideally, I like to become inspired by reading or watching something, usually unrelated to the topic, or listening to music. If I am especially uninspired, I may go for a drive. I have a lot more unpublished writing, but for this article Iâll use the scant examples of technical writing I have published online.
Here are paragraphs from an article I wrote about deepfakes without any AI assistance:
The goal of content authentication is to actively embed media with markings or patterns which are imperceptible to human senses, or to define a methodology for keeping track of the provenance of media that is not AI generated. Blockchains are being explored for provenance tracking, but can be slow and cumbersome.
Pattern embedding, meanwhile, can be applied to non-synthetic media to indicate its authenticity, or to synthetic media during the generation process to indicate that it was produced by an AI. Traditional techniques used for copyright protection and authentication are often vulnerable to attacks from neural nets, and so new authentication methods need to be developed. Some authentication approaches embed metadata or credentials, which can be as small as 1-bit, into media, like a key for identifying the content owner, content subject matter, or creation method. Most recent research focuses on blind embedding methods using neural nets, as opposed to semi-blind or non-blind, as blind methods do not require the original media for authentication.
Here are paragraphs from an article I prompted via a Telegram bot to a suite of agents running on my self-hosted server to write while I was at a doctorâs appointment:
The distinction between identity and trustworthy behavior is longstanding. Googleâs 2006 operational research described combining authenticated domain identities with spam classification and user feedback to build reputation. Approximately 41% of spam in that historical dataset was already authenticated. Identification supplied a consistent entity against which behavioral evidence could accumulate; authentication alone did not establish that a message was wanted or safe.
The precedents support identity as part of an abuse response system, e.g., verify authority, associate incidents with a credential or deployment, coordinate investigation, and withdraw access where justified. A system can provide value by shortening an incident or limiting its spread even if it does not prevent the initial intrusion. For agents, working groups should investigate which of these benefits existing mechanisms can deliver, how replacement or compromised identities affect them, and what privacy and access costs they introduce. The precedents establish useful mechanisms to test; they do not by themselves establish the need for a new institution.
I like how clinical the second excerpt is because thatâs just my taste for technical writing (not everyoneâs bag, and thatâs okay with me), but I do like the almost-clinical-but-not sensibilities inherent to the former example.
To many, both of these examples may read the same, and I think thatâs really interesting from a cognitive science perspective. I donât know how to explain how they appear different to me.
As a process-obsessed engineer, I am torn between writing authentically, whatever that means to one, and providing objective technical information to a reader.
Better writers, and remember that I am a bad one, have ways to organize themselves when they compose something. I just cannot do that without AI to rein me in. Someone else may naturally arrive at some variant of organizing their writing via the following stages and sticking to them, but I need AI to remind me to stick to them while my writing assistants preserve the following artifacts for use and reproducibility:
When I am not prompting via a Telegram bot, I interact with the process via home-built custom tooling, which roughly takes the following shape:
Or I use the chat interface of AI agent coding tools supplemented with (often homegrown) MCPs and skills, including the following (a non-exhaustive list):

I am particularly interested in the reproducibility of a process across sessions for ensuring and maintaining the integrity of collected evidence, so I wish it were possible to control the following parameters (using the LiteLLM API as an example) for the latest model APIs from different providers:
For this article (the one youâre reading, hi), I used AI for research and for organizing information in the tables, but not for the writing. For example, I researched which control parameters could be used for earlier model APIs (I havenât personally tested these):
The writing agent skill Iâve developed currently attempts reproducibility via the following goals, but I am still trying to shape it into something I like:
As this article was written and organized mostly by my organic LLM (side note: I hate equating the mind to an LLM because I do not think itâs that simple, but I digress), maybe this article is a bit disorganized. I am still trying to find an AI-assisted writing process which works for me and provides consistent and reliable output, i.e., I have something that is apple-orchard-shaped, but will it produce quality ingredients for various baked apple goods? I donât know. TBD.

title: US holds its first execution since Christa Pike incident — news agency
body:
NEW YORK, October 8. /TASS/. The first death sentence in the US since the failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee was carried out in Texas, the Associated Press reported.
Accoridng to the news agency, Jamaal Howard was convicted of murdering a store employee in 2000. The 46-year-old was given a lethal injection. Nineteen minutes later, at 1:03 a.m. GMT on October 8, he was pronounced dead. This is the sixth execution in Texas this year.
On September 30 in Nashville, Tennessee, Christa Pike was given two doses of the lethal injection, but survived despite the executioners using seven needles. Her attorneys had warned that she suffers from thrombocytosis, a condition in which the injection of the drugs could lead to blood clots and additional suffering.
Pike was set to become the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. Following the failed execution, Governor Bill Lee ordered an investigation and canceled another execution scheduled for 2026.

title: Amazon makes fresh job cuts, mainly in retail division
body: Amazon confirmed on Wednesday it had cut what it said were a small number of jobs, primarily ​in its Stores unit, which oversees the main e-commerce website. The ‌layoffs to its retail unit coincide with one of Amazon’s biggest shopping days, which it calls Prime Big Deal Days. The promotion started on Tuesday ​and runs through Wednesday, offering varying discounts. The cuts are the ​latest in a series of small reductions since a larger round ⁠of 30,000 job cuts that began last year and continued into ​January. Some affected employees reached out to Reuters and shared posts ​from internal Slack channels about the news. Amazon let go fewer than 1,000 white-collar workers, a person familiar with the matter said. Business Insider earlier reported the layoffs. “We’ve ​adjusted parts of our Stores business because we believe this structure ​will better enable us to deliver on our priorities,” a spokesperson said in ‌an ⁠emailed statement. The internal Slack channel indicated that several divisions within Stores were involved, including customer service and selling partner services, and possibly other units across Amazon. Employees in the US, India, and the UK were among those receiving pink slips. Jeff Bezos, the founder and executive chairman of Amazon, said in a Fox News interview aired Wednesday, ​that continued job cuts have been necessary because the ​company overhired ⁠during the pandemic. “People were staying home and they were ordering, and it was an incredible, stressful period for us, by the way,” he ⁠said when ​asked about the 30,000 jobs lost in ​the previous round. “The whole team worked extremely hard and did so much, but we ​really grew our headcount.”

title: Ronaldo row and a top-of-the-table showdown as Saudi Pro League returns
body: The Saudi Pro League returns to action following a three-week international break. The national team enjoyed success in the Arabian Gulf Cup, beating UAE 2-0 in Tuesday's final in Jeddah. Other SPL players also made headlines – not all of them good. We take a look at the main talking points ahead of the weekend's fixtures. Ronaldo's bumpy break Cristiano Ronaldo made headlines during the international break for all the wrong reasons. The Al Nassr striker abruptly walked out on Portugal ahead of a Uefa Nations League match in Denmark last week. On Tuesday, the 41-year-old released a lengthy statement, giving his version of events, saying he was not retiring , remained available for selection, while accusing manager Jorge Jesus of an “absolute breach of trust”. The row erupted after Ronaldo was an unused substitute in Portugal's 2-1 Uefa Nations League win over Norway on September 29, the first time in 18 years he had sat on the bench for an entire match for his national team. According to Ronaldo's account, Jesus had agreed the forward would miss the Norway and Denmark matches to manage his fitness. However, on the day of ⁠the Norway game, the coach told him he would play for 30 minutes. “Everyone ​knows the ⁠rest. I warmed up from ‌half-time onwards, watched the minutes tick by and wasn't called on,” Ronaldo said. “The manager ​had broken his word to me.” View this post on Instagram The statement added that in a subsequent meeting between player and coach, mediated by Al Nassr sporting director Simao Coutinho, the parties agreed that Jesus would clarify events ahead of the Denmark match. According to the plan, Jesus would say that Ronaldo had never demanded to be played and that asking him to warm up without bringing him on had been a mistake. Jesus did not mention any of this when he spoke to reporters but later denied he had made any such agreement. “The conference was what is known: the attitude had nothing to do with our meeting,” Ronaldo explained. When Ronaldo learnt he would not play against the Danes, the player packed his bags and left the team's camp in Copenhagen. Ronaldo has said the Portuguese Football Federation should punish him accordingly, and said that he would make himself available for selection after any suspension that may come his way. Jesus, too, left the ​door open ‌for his return. Whether bridges can be rebuilt before the November internationals remains to be seen. When approached by reporters on Wednesday, Jesus said: "I read the statement, and now, as I do every day, I go to the federation to work, to think about the team and the national team. I have nothing more to say." When Cristiano Ronaldo lifted his first trophy for Al Nassr. 🏆🐐 pic.twitter.com/D7Zcy0ILio — NassrXtra (@NassrXtra1) September 17, 2026 It's all a far cry from the jubilant scenes just a few months ago when Jesus and Ronaldo celebrated leading Al Nassr to the Saudi Pro League title. Ronaldo will have been banking on the extra games with his country in his pursuit of 1,000 goals (he currently has 979). One hundred and forty-six of them have come for Portugal. Depending on how his Portugal future pans out, Nassr could end up the main beneficiary. Nassr resume their Saudi Pro League campaign on Friday against Diriyah. They sit in third place, two points behind leaders Al Hilal, with Al Ittihad sandwiched in between the two Riyadh clubs. A chastening defeat at UAE champions Al Ain in their first match of the AFC Champions League Elite saw Nassr get their league phase off to the worst possible start. Nassr welcome Uzbekistan's Neftchi Fergana to Al Awwal Park on Monday. Nassr coach Ange Postecoglou may have some sympathy for Jesus. The Australian has himself had to deal with Ronaldo taking issue with his team selections; Ronaldo felt snubbed after Postecoglou substituted him in the comeback win against Al Ettifaq on August 25. Nassr trailed 2-0 in that game when Ronaldo was subbed off in the 46th minute. By the end of it, they had won 3-2. Postecoglou, Jesus and Ronaldo have all said he should only be picked on merit, but it's hard to think that a player who has accomplished so much doesn't expect to be treated differently from his teammates. Managing Ronaldo used to be every coach's dream. Now it seems to be one of football's most difficult jobs. ⚽️🔛 pic.twitter.com/wPupVTd4CA — Al-Ittihad Club (@ittihad_en) October 6, 2026 Aouar: Al Ittihad want to achieve big things A top-of-the-table clash sees first-placed Al Hilal take on second-placed Al Ittihad at Kingdom Arena. Hilal suffered a first league defeat in 47 matches when they fell 2-0 to Neom on September 7, ending their 100 per cent start to the season. It was Hilal's first league defeat under Simone Inzaghi since he took the reins in the summer of 2025. They bounced back in spectacular style, thumping Al Taawoun 6-0 to head into the break on top of the pile. Saturday's opponents are the only unbeaten team left in the league, having won five and drawn two of their seven matches. The Jeddah club sit a point behind Hilal. Champions in 2024/25, Ittihad look like a team transformed under Jens Wissing, with Houssem Aouar one of the team's leading lights so far. The Algerian playmaker was part of that championship-winning side, and believes the Jeddah club are capable of pushing for honours again this season. “This season we want to achieve big things. I always say that when you play for a club like Al Ittihad, you have to win something every season,” he told the SPL's official website. “And it's in what we have to improve. To win things, you have to be focused, dedicate yourself to the club, to the pitch, and to make a lot of sacrifice. “The league is going up every season. You can see that now there is a lot of competition. You never know who's going to win the league until the end, until the very end of the game.” Fixtures All kick-off times UAE time Friday Al Kholood v Al Qadsiah, 5.50pm Al Fateh v Al Ahli, 6.55pm Al Nassr v Diriyah, 10pm Saturday Al Hazem v Neom, 5.50pm Al Ettifaq v Al Khaleej, 6.55pm Al Hilal v Al Ittihad, 10pm Sunday Al Fayha v Al Riyadh, 5.40pm Abha v Al Faisaly, 7.25pm Al Shabab v Al Taawoun, 10pm

title: AI works best when everyone is able to use it
body: For more than a decade, the UAE has been setting itself ambitious targets when it comes to artificial intelligence , embracing the technology at the highest levels of government, commerce and education. However, a key test of AI’s impact is not just the sophistication of the technology but by how many people are able to use it. For many ordinary people, AI is still something of an unknown quantity – and one that is being promoted by powerful and remote tech company owners. Despite excitement about potential AI-led breakthroughs in medicine and scientific discoveries, high-profile stories about jobs being lost to AI or autonomous digital agents hacking rival companies have raised questions about its uses. With that in mind, the launch in Abu Dhabi this week of AiNative, a new training programme, could be the first step in redefining citizens’ and residents’ relationship with AI. Developed by the emirate’s Department of Government Enablement in collaboration with OpenAI, Microsoft and the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence, AiNative aims to give 20,000 government employees access to training by the end of this year. Plans to eventually make the programme freely available to citizens and residents could prove to be even more consequential. Technology can widen inequalities as easily as it can reduce them. Those who understand new tools quickly can gain an advantage. Those who lack access to AI or confidence in using it, risk being left behind. This has been an issue with other game-changing technologies – many older people can still struggle with personal banking or medical appointments as more services migrate to online platforms. That is what makes the public element of AiNative particularly significant. The programme is intended to show people how AI adoption can help with practical matters, from finding a job, managing personal finances, running a small business or creating content responsibly. This recognises that the arrival of increasingly capable systems will affect just about everyone, whether or not they work in technology. Technology can widen inequalities as easily as it can reduce them The UAE has invested heavily in the AI era, and Abu Dhabi has emerged as a major centre for computing, tech investment and research. Partnerships such as those between Abu Dhabi’s G42 and France's Mistral AI announced last year are helping to build the foundations for the next iteration of AI – but human capability is just as important as infrastructure. Giving as many people as possible the opportunity to understand AI means giving them a better chance of recognising its strengths and weakness, and using it responsibly. The aim should not be to make everyone in society a computer scientist but to give them the chance to participate in the digital era confidently. Knowledge often dispels doubt and creates opportunities – by building an AI-enabled society, the potential for success becomes even greater.

title: Gaza has no MRI scanners or fully functioning hospitals one year after ceasefire, says Israeli rights group
body: Gaza is without a single fully functioning hospital a year on from the ceasefire between Israel and Hamas , an Israeli human rights group has said. Physicians for Human Rights Israel (PHRI) said Gaza also had no MRI equipment for its population of more than two million. It said, in a new report, that only a marginal improvement could be reported in Gaza's overall healthcare situation. The World Health Organisation says there were 128 attacks on medical facilities during the first seven months of the ceasefire. Intensive care capacity “has increased by one bed only – from 103 to 104”, PHRI said. Dialysis is less available than before, provided by 12 per cent of medical facilities compared to 17 per cent in October 2025. An Israeli blockade of Gaza's borders means only a fraction of Palestinians in need of medical treatment abroad have been able to receive it. Gaza's Ministry of Health reports that at least 1,570 patients have died, including 264 children, while waiting for medical evacuation. The ceasefire that began on October 10 last year ended the worst of Israel's two-year onslaught on the strip, which was triggered by the October 7 attacks of 2023 . But more than 1,400 people have been killed in near-daily attacks by Israel, which still occupies much of the territory. PHRI said Israel's restrictions on medicine and equipment, failure to allow patients to be treated abroad, and obstruction of efforts to repair Gaza's healthcare system were part of the pattern of alleged genocide. The international definition of genocide includes “the deliberate infliction of conditions of life calculated to bring about the destruction of the Palestinian population”. “A year of ‘ceasefire’ should have brought meaningful relief and rehabilitation to Palestinians and allowed the recovery and reconstruction of the decimated healthcare system,” said Milena Ansari, a PHRI director who wrote the new report. “The data show that the ceasefire did not stop the genocide – it changed the way it is being carried out. Israeli policy continues to create conditions that prevent Palestinians in Gaza from recovering and surviving.” The ceasefire was agreed last October in a peace plan backed by US President Donald Trump . It was meant to be the beginning of restoring and rebuilding life in Gaza through reconstruction, aid and reversing many of the devastating effects of Israel's two-year war on the enclave. The war was triggered by a Hamas -led assault on southern Israel on October 7, 2023, in which militants killed nearly 1,200 people and took about 250 as hostages. More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Israel's military response, which left most of the territory in ruin. The majority of Gaza's residents have been displaced and now live on a narrow area near the enclave's Mediterranean coast. With continuing attacks, and life largely distant from normality, many Gazans have wondered if the ceasefire only exists on paper , rather than reality.

title: Wild species populations fell 73% from 1970 to 2022
body:
Nearly 6,000 monitored vertebrate species ⁠across more than 35,000 populations declined by an average of 73% from ​1970 to 2022, the World ​Wide Fund for Nature said in its latest Living Planet Report published on Thursday. The Living Planet Index, managed by the Zoological Society of London and WWF, monitored a total of 35,803 populations covering 5,790 different species of mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians and fish over the 52-year ⁠period. The 2026 Living Planet Report estimates that overall populations fell by ⁠an average of around 2.5% per year over the period. "Monitored global populations continue to decline on average with no evidence yet of that global recovery," said Andrew Terry, chief conservation ‌officer at ZSL. The average rate of ​decline across the ⁠monitored populations does not represent a headcount of the total ​number of animals lost from 1970 ‌to 2022, and the number is especially sensitive to changes in already small populations. Monitored freshwater species saw ​an average decline of 85%, while terrestrial species fell 69% and marine species 59%, the index showed. The steepest average population declines were in South America, at 95%, with Africa also experiencing losses of 80% from 1970 to 2022. The 2026 Living Planet report ‌incorporated an additional 295 species and 967 populations across a longer time ​series compared to the last report in 2024. The additional data "reinforces our confidence ​in ‌the continued ⁠decline in biodiversity," Terry told a briefing. Habitat loss and degradation were the most frequently reported threat, but wildlife populations are also at risk from overexploitation, ​climate change, pollution, invasive species and disease, the report ⁠said. "Amid these steep ​declines, there are grounds for hope, rooted in evidence. Wildlife populations are under pressure but recovery is in reach," said Kirsten Schuijt, WWF's director general. Targeted conservation efforts have enabled populations of some species to recover, including tigers, Atlantic ​and Pacific bluefin tuna, southern African elephants and green sea ​turtles. Alongside conservation efforts, changes in the energy, food and finance systems are required to halt nature loss, Schuijt said.

title: Sheriff, ex-sheriff charged with obstructing justice tied to Kouri Richins case: Docs
body:
Kouri Richins was found guilty of fatally poisoning her husband with fentanyl.
A current sheriff and a former sheriff of two Utah counties have been charged with obstruction of justice in connection with the Kouri Richins murder case , according to court filings related to heavily redacted, newly unsealed indictments.
Kouri Richins was found guilty of murdering her husband in March. The high-profile weekslong trial in Summit County followed a yearslong investigation that garnered national attention.
A former Summit County sheriff and the sheriff of neighboring Wasatch County face charges related to Kouri Richins' prosecution, according to defense motions seeking that the indictments be redacted upon release due to the highly publicized murder trial.
Wasatch County Sheriff Jared Rigby was charged with one count of obstruction of justice in a criminal proceeding, a second-degree felony, and one count of making a written false statement, a misdemeanor. The indictment alleges that he made, presented or used a knowingly false item in January "with intent to hinder" a prosecution.
David Edmunds, who served as the sheriff of Summit County from 2003 to 2014, was charged with one count of obstruction of justice in a criminal investigation, a third-degree felony, according to the indictment. The indictment alleges that he provided false information "with intent to hinder" an investigation on March 13.
Both indictments, which were filed last month, were unsealed Wednesday with significant redactions.
According to Rigby's motion, the charges against him "allege interference" in the Kouri Richins case over an anonymous letter postmarked Jan. 10, 2026. The filing does not detail the contents of the letter, who wrote it or to whom it was addressed.
According to Edmunds' motion, the language in his indictment "names the Richins prosecution and connects the anonymous letter to alleged misconduct by a Summit County sheriff's deputy." The indictment accuses Edmunds of making a false statement "intended to hinder identification of the letter's author," the filing states.
Both men have pleaded not guilty, according to ABC Salt Lake City affiliate KTVX .
ABC News has reached out to their attorneys and the Wasatch County Sheriff's Office for comment but did not immediately receive a response. Rigby has previously said he acted lawfully.
A Summit County jury found Kouri Richins guilty of fatally poisoning her husband, Eric Richins, with fentanyl in March. Judge Richard Mrazik, who presided over the murder trial, sentenced her to life without parole.
The 36-year-old mother of three, who self-published a children's book on grieving following her husband's death in 2022, is currently seeking a new criminal trial. Her request is under consideration by the Utah Court of Appeals.
This week, Judge Mrazik ordered that she pay more than $55 million in damages to the estate and family members of her late husband in a wrongful death claim.
In his order, Mrazik noted that Kouri Richins did not dispute any of the factual statements in the motion for judgment, which sought an order concluding that she "wrongfully caused" her husband's death.
The judge stated in his order that he concluded from the guilty verdict and the "undisputed record evidence" that Kouri Richins caused her husband's death by poisoning him.
The order includes $10,780,129 in economic damages and $3 million in non-economic damages -- $1 million for each Richins child -- that "seek to compensate wrongful death victims for loss of society, love, companionship, protection, guidance, and affection."
"Eric shared deep, emotional connections with his three minor children, who are the Estate’s only heirs," the order stated. "His death has caused them severe trauma, and it will have permanent effects on each. In addition, by killing Eric, which resulted in her imprisonment, Kouri deprived the minor children of being with their father or their mother."
The order also included $41,340,387 in punitive damages, which were determined by multiplying the economic and non-economic damages by three.

title: Akandoh says government yet to decide how 100 new ambulances will be distributed
body: Health Minister Kwabena Mintah Akandoh says the government has not yet decided how 100 new ambulances will be distributed when they are added to the national fleet in 2027. According to him, the government is still considering whether to maintain the previous distribution model or review it. “We have not taken the decision yet,” Mr Akandoh said on Joy News’ PM Express on Wednesday. He explained that one consideration would be to replace ambulances that are no longer functional in areas where they were previously stationed. “I believe that if you have an ambulance within a particular area, and that ambulance is faulty, or is no longer functional, it’s only fair to replace that ambulance,” he said. However, the Minister said the government is also assessing the strengths and weaknesses of the previous approach. “But then we think about what they did, the pros and cons. We’ve tried that system. Can we continue, or do we have to review it as a country?” he said. The comments come as the government prepares to replenish the ambulance fleet with 100 new vehicles in 2027. Mr Akandoh said the government inherited a situation where several ambulances were grounded. He also disclosed that none of the country’s ambulances had been insured when the government took office. “In 2025 we insured all our ambulances,” he said. The Minister said the government has since restored a significant number of ambulances to service. “As I speak to you now, we have more than 200 ambulances functioning,” he said, adding that the new vehicles will form part of efforts to replenish the fleet. “We are going to replenish the fleet in 2027. We are going to add brand new ones, with 100 vehicles,” he said. Mr Akandoh said the government’s decision on distribution would also take into account lessons from the previous system. He noted that the government could build on an existing arrangement if it has served the country well, but stressed, “If we think that system has served us well, why do we have to revamp?” he added. The ambulance plans form part of broader efforts by the Health Ministry to strengthen emergency care. Mr Akandoh said that more than 200 ambulances are currently in service, and a national electronic emergency bed management system is also being piloted. He said the system will give health authorities visibility over available emergency beds and help manage existing capacity.

title: Trial for self-proclaimed ‘Crypto King’ hears from investors he allegedly bilked
body:
Some of Aiden Pleterski’s alleged victims testified Wednesday about meeting the Whitby man, giving him hundreds of thousands of dollars to invest and trusting Pleterski would do what he said he would do.
Pleterski is charged with fraud over $5,000 and money laundering and is represented. The 27-year-old has pleaded not guilty.
Braden Martyniuk testified he had read articles about Pleterski in which he described himself as “The Crypto King” and said that influenced his decision to invest.
Martyniuk said he and Pleterski shared a mutual friend. He met with Pleterski and was told if he invested, his money would go towards foreign exchange trading.
“He promised returns of three percent a week, compounding every week,” said Martyniuk who believed Pleterski was trading on a platform called Forex. “He said there was no risk to the initial investment, and all his clients were fully covered.”
Martyniuk added Pleterski told him he had a $300-million slush fund, explaining he believed that meant Pleleterski had money in reserves to protect all his clients.
Martyniuk said he wired him $250,000 and signed a contract. He said when he reached out to Pleterski see if he could get his money back in May or June 2022, he got nothing.
In his opening address Tuesday, Crown Counsel Scott Patterson told the jury that up until June 2020, Pleterski was living at his parents’ house in Whitby, worked at a rental agency and drove a Honda Civic.
“His parents supported him financially until Covid when he began receiving the Canada Emergency Response Benefit (CERB) of $500/week,” said Patterson.
Patterson told the jury that in the middle of 2020, Pleterski began soliciting money from people and told them that he would take 30 percent of the capital gains. He told them he had a system that he would never lose more than two percent and targeted five percent gains. He also told some investors that he was incredibly wealthy.
Patterson said investors trusted him and believed he would do what he said he would do with their money.
“Instead, he used investor money to fund his lifestyle: exotic cars, private jets, lavish shopping and credit card bills that ran into the millions,” said Patterson who told the jury they will see Pleterski’s financials.
Patterson said things began to fall apart in the spring of 2022 when investors wanted to get their money out.
“But Mr. Pleterski had no money to give. As you’ll hear, he gave excuses. Delaying the return of money then telling investors that their money was frozen in his foreign exchange account. But as you’ll both see and hear in evidence, that didn’t happen. It wasn’t frozen because Pleterski never invested the money. He had simply spent it” said Patterson, who told the jury Pleterski spent investor money as if it was his own.
Stewart Wilson, who manages a high-end car rental company, said he met Pleterski when he was only 20 or 21, saying he wanted to rent a vehicle and rented him a half a dozen high-end vehicles in 2019.
He knew Pleterski lived in a house in Whitby on a cul-de-sac which he had gone to before.
Wilson said he had not seen Pleterski for a year and randomly ran into him in a parking lot downtown in the fall of 2020. Wilson testified Pleterski told him he’d bought an Audi R8 and said he was trading.
“I was happy for him. It seemed like everything was going good for him.”
Wilson said he ultimately set up a meeting with Pleterski in 2021 after seeing through social media that he was doing well.
“He didn’t try to entice me at all in joining which I thought was pretty cool. He was doing everything on his own,” said Wilson referring to the fact that Pleterski was living in a big house on the Lake Shore and had bought himself “very extravagant cars”.
Wilson said after learning Pleterski was trading for close friends and family, and believing people were getting good returns, he reached out to him in November 2021.
Wilson said Pleterski invited him to come by his new house.
“At that point, I went to the mansion,” said Wilson, describing it as about 8,000-square-foot on the waterfront in Burlington. “He said purchased it. I said he was crazy.”
Wilson said he had Lamborghinis, Audis and a McLaren worth about $2 million parked in the garage. “I was quite impressed,” Wilson said.
Wilson said Pleterski told him he was trading in equities and foreign exchange. “He was his strategy was simple. All he was focusing om was making one percent a day. His philosophy was totally different than what I heard before. He had a strict stop loss. If he went up, he sold. He would trade about ten different stocks at the same time.”
Wilson told court his strategy seemed simple. “Why hadn’t anyone ever thought of this?”
Wilson said he signed a contract from AP Private Equity believing his company was legitimate and wrote a cheque for $250,000.
“He was telling me his strategy. It’s impossible that the principal can be wiped out. He was showing me the profits he was making,” said Wilson, explaining that he knew others who appeared to be getting returns, though he wasn’t sure if they actually got anything back.
Wilson said he felt safe and said Pleterski told him his asset pool was between $30 million and $50 million.
Patterson showed Wilson contracts he signed. As the weeks went on, Wilson continued to write cheques totaling $900,000.
“It was a 75-25 split on capital gains. He was going to take 25 percent of the profit,” said Wilson.
He said his girlfriend also invested $300,000, with the proceeds from the sale of her condo.
When asked if he believed that Pleterski was spending his money on his lifestyle, credit cards and private jets, Wilson said definitely not.
“I didn’t even think it was a possibility. It’s the craziest thing to think you get scammed. It didn’t even cross my mind,” said Wilson.
Wilson testified things were very positive at the beginning but as March 2022, he told Pleterski he needed to take $400,000 out.
He said Pleterski started to become difficult to reach and evasive finally telling him his money was frozen in foreign accounts.
“Did you receive that money back?” said Patterson. “Nothing,” replied Wilson.
Pleterski was given a chance to cross-examine the witnesses but declined when asked by Superior Court Justice Shaun Nakatsuru.

title: US Executes Man Days After Christa Pike Botched Execution
body: A 46-year-old US man was executed by lethal injection Wednesday, officials said, the first to be carried out since the botched execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee one week earlier. The execution of Jamaal Howard in Texas, who was sentenced to death for killing a store clerk during a 2000 robbery, was the 30th to take place in the United States so far this year. The court ordered state corrections officials to preserve all evidence related to the botched execution, including medical supplies, waste, and audio and video recordings. Pike’s fate revived debate over capital punishment in the United States. Lee suspended executions in Tennessee pending an independent investigation, and the state’s prison chief resigned. Tennessee’s correction department has maintained that it followed established protocol. The state of Texas carried out an execution by lethal injection later Wednesday, the first in the United States since the attempt to put Pike to death. Jamaal Howard was sentenced to death for killing a store clerk during a 2000 robbery. His lawyers had sought to have his execution postponed, citing Pike’s case, but he was pronounced dead at 8:03 pm local time (0103 GMT Thursday). “I’m sorry for what happened; I wish you could learn to forgive me one of these days,” Howard said in his last statement before being put to death. The Death Penalty Information Centre, which publishes data and analysis on capital punishment in the United States, said Pike was the first inmate to survive after being injected with lethal doses of execution drugs. Pike was 18 when she and her boyfriend beat and killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer at a job training camp. Pike would have been the first woman put to death by the state of Tennessee in more than 200 years, according to the Death Penalty Information Centre. Excluding Pike’s failed execution, there have been 29 executions in the United States this year, which have all been carried out by lethal injection. The death penalty has been abolished in 23 of the 50 US states, while three others — California, Oregon and Pennsylvania — have moratoriums in place. title: Connor’s late goal lifts Winnipeg Jets to 3-2 win over Avalanche
body:
If you score three goals in an NHL game, chances are you’ll win a lot of those games.
For the fourth straight game to start the 2026-27 season, the Winnipeg Jets hit that magic mark with just a minute to go in a dramatic 3-2 win over the visiting Colorado Avalanche Wednesday night.
The Jets took a one-goal lead to the third period before the Avs tied it up. But Kyle Connor finished off a pretty pass from Mark Scheifele with exactly 60 seconds left for the Jets third straight victory.
“Not a lot of guys can make those kind of plays,” said Jets head coach Scott Arniel. “Then also how K.C. got it off his stick too. But yeah, your best players need to step up in those type of moments. And those two have done that a lot for us.”
The Jets remain unbeaten in regulation this season with a 3-0-1 record as they handed Colorado their first loss.
“There’s definitely a lot of guys in here, and as a team, and myself, proving that we’re still a top team in this league,” Connor said. “And you got to prove it every single night. It’s a tough league. You can’t take nights off and so yeah, it’s a good start but looking forward to the next one.”
Connor scored twice for his fourth and fifth goals of the season for 328 markers as a Jet to move into a tie with Ilya Kovalchuk for the third most goals in franchise history behind only Dale Hawerchuk and Scheifele.
Cole Perfetti had the other marker for the Jets to score for the third straight game, giving him a four-game point streak with six points in the first four games.
Stuart Skinner was marvelous in goal for his first win at the Canada Life Centre and his second straight victory. He stopped 32 shots as the Jets were outshot 34-19.
“It was nice to get a lot of shots early,” said Skinner. “That’s normally a good feeling for a goalie. They definitely had their push, and it gave us a little bit of time, and we had our push, so, it was good.”
But the win came with a price as Josh Morrissey left the game with what appeared to be a hand injury. He was hurt after missing a hit along the boards at the tail end of the first period. He had just one shift in the second period and then left the game for good.
“Just an upper-body (injury),” Arniel said. “We’ll check on it tomorrow and see how it is.”
In Morrissey’s absence, Dylan Samberg logged a game high 25:25 of ice time.
The game got off to a fairly even start with each side registering four shots on goal over the first seven minutes.
But over the final 13 minutes of the opening frame, Colorado outshot the Jets 13-2, thanks in part to a dangerous power play that came close to opening the scoring.
Skinner stood tall, stopping all five shots on that power play, including a stellar cross-crease save on Martin Necas.
Winnipeg got a power play look late in the period, generating one shot but they too were unable to break the deadlock.
Skinner further endeared himself to Jets fans early in the second when, after giving up a big rebound, he made a sprawling save to deny Necas again.
But it wasn’t too long after that save that Colorado opened the scoring. Fedor Svechkov had the puck along the boards with Samberg pressuring him. Svechkov then harmlessly sent the puck to the slot where it hit Viggo Bjorck and skittered into the high slot where Dylan DeMelo over skated it. That allowed Jaden Schwartz the time and space to rip a snapshot top shelf at the 2:51 mark.
Just over a minute later, the Jets answered back when Connor tipped a Neal Pionk point shot through Mackenzie Blackwood for his fourth of the season.
Colorado nearly regained the lead seconds later as Nathan MacKinnon got free on a two-on-one and ripped a shot off the post.
The Jets were having a tough time slowing down the Avalanche attack, and to make matters worse, Morrissey went into the boards awkwardly in the first and was seen shaking his hand without his glove on.
But Skinner continued to hold down the fort, allowing Winnipeg to take the lead in the waning minutes of the period.
Scheifele collected the puck behind Colorado’s net and carried it around to his right before sliding it back to the point to Samberg. He let a shot fly that glanced off the stick of Brock Nelson in front before banking off one of Perfetti’s shin pads and into the net for his third of the season.
With the secondary assist, Scheifele earned his first point of the season.
Winnipeg wound up outshooting the Avalanche 11-10 in the second, including 7-2 over the final 11 minutes.
The Jets continued to do a good job suppressing the Colorado attack as the third period rolled along, leading to Winnipeg’s second power play of the night with 11:41 to go, though they didn’t do anything with it.
Two goals didn’t feel like it would be enough to get the job done, and that became even more clear when Colorado tied the game with 7:25 remaining.
The initial shot from Brett Kulak at the left point missed the net and bounced off the end boards right to the stick of Schwartz, who passed it in front to Svechkov for a tap-in as the Jets defenders chased the play.
It looked like the game was destined for overtime but with a minute left, Winnipeg’s top line got the job done once more.
Scheifele carried the puck across the blue line and drove along the wall before sending a pass to the slot to Connor, who wired it past Blackwood for his second of the night. It was one of just two shots for the Jets in the third period.
Colorado didn’t have much time to get something set up with the goalie pulled and they failed to get a shot on goal before the final horn sounded.
Blackwood turned aside 16 shots in defeat.
Winnipeg will look to keep their season-opening point streak going Friday night at home against Anaheim.

title: Ukraine’s losses from port downtime exceed five billion dollars
body:
MOSCOW, October 8. /TASS/. Ukraine has lost more than five billion dollars in foreign exchange revenue due to downtime at the Odessa ports, according to TASS calculations.
Commercial merchant ships continue to avoid the ports of Odessa, Chernomorsk, and Yuzhny. Only vessels affiliated with the Ukrainian armed forces are calling at those ports. Consequently, maritime trade is being routed through Danube ports - that is, Izmail in Ukraine and Constanta in Romania - which together can potentially handle no more than one-third of the exports that previously passed through the ports of Odessa. As a result, Ukraine exported only 44% of its planned agricultural exports in September. Exports of metallurgical products ceased completely by the end of September. These two commodities together accounted for about 65% of Ukraine’s total exports and about $26 billion in foreign exchange earnings per year.
The Odessa port shutdown has been ongoing since July 22.

title: Charles Amissah case: Doctors still facing possible sanctions as institutions implement findings – Akandoh
body: Health Minister Kwabena Mintah Akandoh says doctors and other health professionals implicated in the Charles Amissah case could still face sanctions as institutions implement recommendations from a committee set up to investigate the matter. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Wednesday, Mr Akandoh said the various institutions are still working through the directives issued after the committee completed its work. He said some institutions have already reached conclusions on their recommendations, particularly the Korle-Bu Teaching Hospital. The Minister acknowledged that the process has taken some time but said disciplinary action in some cases involves legal considerations. “Maybe I may have to tell you that in some instances it’s not a straightforward issue, as you said. There are some legal nuances, and that’s the only thing I can add,” he said. He stressed that the government remains committed to implementing the committee’s findings. “We are implementing the recommendations of the committee,” he said. Asked whether the individuals recommended for disciplinary action would eventually be sanctioned, Mr Akandoh responded: “Why not? They are all under the laws of Ghana, and so that’s how far I can go.” The Charles Amissah case became a major test of Ghana’s emergency healthcare system during the controversy surrounding the “no bed syndrome.” The government subsequently established a committee to examine the circumstances surrounding the case and make recommendations. Beyond possible sanctions for individuals, the committee proposed wider reforms to improve emergency care. These included the creation of a national electronic emergency bed management system, compulsory triage for emergency patients, the integration of the Ghana Armed Forces’ critical care into the national emergency system, and the establishment of a national emergency care fund to cover the first 24 hours of care. Mr Akandoh said implementation of the bed management system has already begun. A command centre has been established at Ridge Hospital, with the system being piloted in selected regional and teaching hospitals. He said the system will give the Ministry visibility over emergency beds and patients occupying them. The Minister said the system will also help authorities identify patients who remain in emergency units for more than 24 hours, despite claims that no beds are available. “It will help us to manage the scarce resources,” he said. He added that hospitals are being equipped with barcoded beds, while ambulance services have also been integrated into the system. Mr Akandoh said the government is also considering expanding emergency capacity at Korle-Bu, Komfo Anokye, Tamale and 37 Military Hospital. He said that more than 200 ambulances are currently in service, with plans to add 100 new vehicles in 2027.

title: Protesters overrun Israeli peace vigil marking October 7 attended by Mamdani
body: Mayor Zohran Mamdani arrived at a New York City park on Wednesday night for an October 7 vigil that was overrun by hundreds of pro-Palestinian protesters.The demonstrators swamped the area of Union Square Park that was supposed to host the event held by Israelis for Peace, a left-wing peace group. The organizers moved the vigil to a nearby spot in the park surrounded by police barricades as speakers struggled to be heard above the protesters. Attendees held electrically lit candles and signs reading, “Not one more life.”Upon learning Mamdani was present, the pro-Palestinian protesters broke into a chant of “Traitor!” and “Zohran, what do you say? How many boots did you lick today?”One protester yelled at Israelis for Peace organizers: “We don't want peace with Israelis, bro! We sent your people to hell on October 7.” Other protesters wielded megaphones and drums while chanting anti-Israel slogans, including “Gaza will be liberated!” The mayor stood solemnly throughout the event and did not speak at the vigil or address the protesters.Protesters yell over testimonies of October 7 massacreAmid the cacophony, Brad Lander, the Democratic nominee running to represent parts of Lower Manhattan and Brooklyn in Congress, took a microphone to recite the words of the mother of a 20-year-old man who was murdered at the Nova music festival three years ago.  He looked visibly shaken as the evening progressed, watching the protesters while speakers shared testimonies of people killed on October 7.Speakers also shared testimonies of Palestinians killed by the Israel Defense Forces, and the event included the group being led in a Muslim prayer.The vigil ended with the participants raising their candles and reciting the Mourner's Kaddish, the traditional Jewish prayer honoring the dead. As they filed out of the event, the protesters shouted “Death to the IDF!”Earlier in the evening, protesters were seen grabbing the electric candles and mockingly singing the Jewish folk song “Hava Nagila.”Protesters call Mamdani 'ambassador of Zionism'Another protester in the vigil area shouted out his disapproval of Mamdani: “He's 100% Muslim but as of now, he stands as an ambassador of Zionism and US imperialism.”Someone else carried a poster depicting Yahya Sinwar, the Hamas leader who helped mastermind the attacks on southern Israel that killed 1,200 people three years ago, Wednesday. Amid the rival gatherings, Ross Glick, a New York pro-Israel activist and former executive director of Betar US, a militant Zionist group, arrived with a group of counter-protesters holding Israeli flags. They were swiftly confronted by anti-Israel protesters. The two sides got into a shouting match as they stood separated by a barrier.The pro-Palestinian protesters had held a rally at City Hall before heading to the location of the vigil. They condemned Israel and the United States for the war in Gaza, but also criticized Mamdani for capitulating “to Zionist pressure.”The throng of protesters outside City Hall chanted “Free Palestine,” “Globalize the intifada,” “Resistance is justified when people are occupied,” and “Israel is a terrorist state.” One protester held a sign reading “Operation Epstein Fury,” a play on Operation Epic Fury. Another held a sign that read “Liberation in action October 7.” Nearby, an Israeli flag was held up with the text “Death cult.”Despite the war of words, both gatherings disbanded peacefully. No arrests were made.

title: Denmark says Russia has conducted sabotage attacks against its defense firms
body: Russia has begun sabotage operations against Danish companies supplying Ukraine after concluding that broader disruption efforts failed to curb Western military support for the country, a Danish intelligence official said on Wednesday.The shift reflects a significant escalation in Moscow's hybrid warfare campaign, the official, from the Danish national security and intelligence service (PET), told a homeland security conference in Copenhagen."What we saw in the spring was a lot of planning, but very little carried out; what we saw in early summer is that they started to carry out a lot more," the official said.Russia concluded that its previous broad-spectrum targeting "did not have the effect of deterring the Western (military alliance) NATO from supporting Ukraine," the official added, and while Moscow maintains political control over operations, its operational boldness is growing and Russia is now "trying to hit targets that have a direct impact on the front line. That means weapons production."Russia denies involvement in warfare operationsMoscow has repeatedly denied involvement in sabotage or hybrid warfare operations. The Russian embassy in Copenhagen rejected the allegations on Wednesday, accusing Danish authorities of making unfounded accusations against Russia.The official cited a Russian defense ministry list of alleged European drone and drone component manufacturers that Moscow said in April amounted to potential military targets, without elaborating further.Russia is increasingly using untrained proxies — including homeless people and people addicted to drugs — recruited via Telegram and other social media platforms. Recruitment typically starts with low-threshold tasks such as reconnaissance or photography, then escalates toward actual sabotage operations, PET has said."It could be anyone just looking for quick money," the official said. "If the first person isn't successful, they'll throw another one at the problem until they succeed."Denmark's defense intelligence service last month said Russia is likely to intensify hybrid attacks against the West in coming months, after Germany blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport in August.In September 2025, before Denmark hosted an EU summit, drones disrupted air traffic at six Danish airports, including Copenhagen, the Nordic region's busiest, in what Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen called a hybrid attack on her nation.

title: Bangladesh approves its largest solar power plant
body:
Bangladesh has approved a 442-megawatt solar plant on land originally earmarked for a coal-fired power station, as it seeks to boost its renewable energy sources, officials said Thursday. The $230-million Rampal project, which would be the country's largest solar facility, is expected to be operational by 2029 after winning government approval on Wednesday. The project comes as Bangladesh grapples with an energy crisis and heavy dependence on imported fuels, while renewable power accounts for only a small share of its installed capacity. Bangladesh relies heavily on imported energy, including liquefied natural gas (LNG), and has been hit by fuel-supply disruptions linked to the conflict in the Middle East. The country of 170 million people suffers from chronic electricity shortages. Bangladesh has about 1.87 gigawatts of installed renewable energy capacity, roughly 6.5 percent of its 28.9-gigawatt grid-connected capacity, according to government data. Zonayed Abdur Rahim Saki, a minister at the Ministry of Planning, said the land had initially been acquired for the expansion of an existing coal-fired power plant. "The government dropped the second phase of that coal power plant, and replaced it with a solar power project as part of its promise to increase the renewable energy generation capacity and reduce carbon emission," he said, speaking to reporters after the plant was approved. The Rampal site lies roughly 14 kilometres (nine miles) from the edge of the Sundarbans, the world's largest mangrove forest. Bangladesh's power system remains dominated by fossil fuels, with gas accounting for about 43 percent of installed capacity, followed by oil and coal, making up nearly the same percentage. It also depends on electricity imported from neighbouring India and Nepal. Nepal was hit hard by catastrophic Himalayan floods in August, which badly damaged a string of hydropower facilities. Bangladesh's first nuclear power plant, the 2.4-gigawatt Rooppur facility, is due to begin operations by the end of 2026 after more than a decade of construction. Dhaka has set a target of generating 20 percent of its electricity from renewable sources by 2030. Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has installed a solar rooftop system at his home as part of government efforts to promote wider adoption, including financial incentives. Bangladesh's key garment industry is also fitting solar systems, said Mohammad Hatem, president of the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association. Hatem has installed a six-megawatt solar system on the roof of his factory in Narayanganj, outside Dhaka. "Many of our members are showing interest in rooftop solar," he said.
