title: New Russian Drone Wave Targets Kyiv and Western Ukraine After Deadly Strikes on Putin’s Birthday
body:
Russian forces sent another wave of jet-powered attack drones toward Kyiv and several Ukrainian regions in the early hours of Thursday, Oct. 8, triggering fresh air raid alerts just hours after deadly Russian strikes killed 28 people across Ukraine, including five children.
Ukraine’s Air Force warned at approximately 12:55 a.m. that Russian jet-powered drones were approaching Kyiv, including the capital’s northeastern Troieshchyna neighborhood.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Additional Russian drones were tracked toward Brovary, Vasylkiv and Fastiv in Kyiv region, while other threats emerged across northern and western Ukraine.
Kyiv’s Military Administration issued repeated air raid warnings as the drone threat continued overnight. The administration reported an all-clear at approximately 1:24 a.m. Thursday.
The overnight drone threat extended far beyond the Ukrainian capital.
In western Ukraine, the Air Force warned that a Russian jet-powered drone was approaching Lutsk in Volyn region before reporting that it was directly over the city.
Volyn regional authorities also issued an air raid warning for Lutsk district shortly after midnight as the threat developed.
Further drones were reported heading toward Ovruch in Zhytomyr region and Desna in Chernihiv region, while another was tracked through the Chornobyl exclusion zone toward Zhytomyr region.
Russian drone movements were also reported in the direction of Rivne region.
Meanwhile, Russian tactical aviation threatened Zaporizhzhia and surrounding areas with guided aerial bombs, prompting additional Air Force warnings.
The alerts indicated continuing Russian aerial activity across multiple regions, although Ukrainian authorities had not confirmed new impacts or casualties linked specifically to Thursday’s early-hours drone wave.
The latest threats came just hours after Russia carried out deadly missile and drone strikes across Ukraine on Wednesday, Oct. 7.
Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi reported that 28 people were killed nationwide, including five children.
The deadliest attack struck Pryluky in Chernihiv region, where a Russian missile hit a residential apartment building, killing 20 people, including five children. Three of the children were just one year old.
The strike destroyed part of the building, leaving rescuers searching through the wreckage for survivors.
In Kyiv, Russian attacks also killed two people and injured residents, including children, as drones struck apartment buildings and sparked fires in residential neighborhoods.
In Desnianskyi district, four people, including two children, were injured when a drone struck a 12-story residential building. Emergency crews rescued 22 residents, eight of them children.
In Solomianskyi district, another drone attack set a five-story apartment building ablaze, injuring eight residents.
The renewed drone threats in the early hours of Thursday followed a devastating day of Russian strikes that destroyed Ukrainian homes and killed entire families.
The attacks unfolded on Oct. 7 – Vladimir Putin’s 74th birthday – leaving 28 Ukrainians dead, including five children.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: La Salle banks on Jacob Cortez for past, present, future
body: MANILA, Philippines – In the 100th game of the Ateneo-La Salle rivalry, Jacob Cortez did not look exactly like the star who led the Green Archers to a UAAP championship last year, at least through the first three quarters. But as usual, Cortez delivered when it mattered most for La Salle. Cortez scored 8 of his 12 points in the fourth quarter to help the Green Archers overcome the Blue Eagles, 83-76, in the UAAP Season 89 men’s basketball on Wednesday night, October 7. “I don’t know if you remember a few weeks ago, he (Cortez) let us lose when we played UST,” said La Salle head coach Topex Robinson, who has steered the Green Archers to back-to-back wins over UE and Ateneo after absorbing a close loss to the Growling Tigers two weeks ago. “But you have to remember also, several months ago, he won the championship for us.” La Salle continued to turn to Cortez even after a shaky first three quarters, when he struggled to knock down his usual jumpers and get fruitful drives to the basket. He finished 4-of-13 from the field, along with 3 rebounds, 5 assists, and 2 turnovers. “He will always take those shots; that’s what he’s built for. We will always win with Jacob. We will lose with Jacob. And that scenario will never change,” Robinson said. “He always does the right thing. He always disobeys our sets, but he delivers. What’s important, I guess, is that his teammates around him know that he’s gonna take those shots.” Down by as many as 7 points in the second half, Cortez gave La Salle life, sparking a 31-18 finishing run in the final 15 minutes of the game that allowed the Green Archers to pull away from the Blue Eagles. The win also tied the all-time head-to-head record between Ateneo and La Salle at 50-50 after 100 meetings. But Cortez’s value to La Salle extends beyond what he produces on the court as he has also become a mentor to 18-year-old rookie Joaquin Tovera , who held the fort for the Green Archers while the former NCAA and UAAP champion struggled to find his rhythm. Tovera led La Salle with 15 points on 4-of-8 shooting from the field, along with 4 rebounds and 4 assists in 21 minutes as Cortez’s backup. “It’s nice for [Tovera] to be with Jacob in his young career. He gets to learn a lot from his kuya (big brother),” Robinson said. Robinson said Tovera did not fully understand the magnitude of an Ateneo-La Salle game, but that may have helped relieve some of the pressure on the rookie entering what could be their biggest game of the first round. “This is an 18-year-old kid who doesn’t even know the Ateneo-La Salle rivalry,” he said. “He was just chilling in the dugout. He doesn’t know the gravity of what he’s doing.” Aside from Tovera, JC Macalalag also scored 15 points and played a crucial role in limiting Ateneo’s prized rookie Kieffer Alas, who finished with just 5 points. Cortez and Macalalag, who are both playing in their final UAAP seasons, are expected to pass on La Salle’s championship culture into the next generation led by Tovera. “These two guys are going to be on their final year. We are really making sure that they will have somebody that’s going to follow their lead,” Robinson said. For now, Robinson is reminding Tovera that he is playing for a special squad led by a championship-caliber veteran in Cortez. “I just remind [Tovera] all the time that you’re going to look back at this and tell yourself how blessed and fortunate you are to be a part of this team.” – Rappler.com

title: What we know about the U.S. suspect connected to the Tumbler Ridge school shooting
body:
More details have emerged about the U.S. suspect accused of encouraging and advising the B.C. teenager who shot and killed multiple people in Tumbler Ridge earlier this year.
Court documents reveal the 30-year-old from Bellingham, Wash., was closely connected to the shooter online for months.
Global News knocked on the door of the unit where James Cody Bryant lived, but the person living there responded from behind the door, saying they did not want to comment.
Bryant, who according to authorities is trans and identifies as female, was arrested at the complex in Bellingham by the Federal Bureau of Investigation on Tuesday.
“I guess I’m kind of stunned,” neighbour Preston Coffelt said.
“It’s not something I’d expect to happen two buildings down.”
Bryant appeared in a Seattle courtroom on Tuesday on a federal felony charge of conspiracy to commit murder in a foreign country.
U.S. authorities have released months of alleged online correspondence between Bryant and B.C. teenager Jesse Van Rootselaar before and during the massacre on Feb. 10 in which eight people were killed.
The claims have not yet been tested in court.
The two had met online about three years earlier, investigators said. Van Rootselaar was about 15 at the time, while Bryant was about 27.
They met on the now-defunct Omegle messaging app, which enabled conversations with strangers but was closed down not long afterwards over lawsuits about child safety.
The two fell out of contact when Van Rootselaar was institutionalized after setting their room on fire. After that, they spoke daily in the six months before the murders, the FBI said.
“One thing that surfaced pretty soon after the shooting occurred was the company Discord identified some connections between the shooter and an individual in the United States, and notified the Canadian authorities — the RCMP,” said W. Mike Herrington, the special agent in charge of the FBI in Seattle.
“RCMP reached out to U.S. authorities, and we immediately began looking into this individual in the United States to see, you know, what was going on there.”
Discord is an online messaging and chat platform in which users can create different communities, like a hybrid between Slack and Reddit. It was initially built for gamers but is now used for many different purposes, such as social group communications.
Discord’s website says it collects certain information from users, including content users created.
“What Discord identified was a series of conversations that were dating back months or even years, where the shooter and the individual in the United States had ongoing discussions — a rather voluminous amount of discussions,” he added.
“This was their primary means of communicating, and they communicated quite regularly.”
Herrington said the FBI interviewed Bryant two days after the shooting in Tumbler Ridge.
The U.S. complaint against Bryant alleges the two spent months discussing tactics, locations and weaponry for the attack on Discord before they attempted to livestream the murders on Twitch.
The FBI said Van Rootselaar communicated online with Bryant, even sending photos on Discord showing what they were wearing for the attack.
Neighbours and coworkers say Bryant, who has asked to be identified as female in court proceedings, presented as one in everyday life.
“When you’re dressing like a girl, you’ve got your long hair and your fingernails done, you just assume,” neighbour Rodney Green said.
Bryant’s boss at a local McDonald’s said they were a reliable employee who worked at the fast food location for several years.
The manager told Global News their staff are shaken by the FBI allegations that Bryant entertained Van Rootselaar’s musings on achieving mass shooter notoriety and causing maximum damage.
Bryant was allegedly more concerned about not being caught, telling Rootselaar, “I think we should find a way to delete all our messages.”
“What we did see was, at some points, a bit of mixed feelings about this,” Herrington said. “But ultimately, Bryant was fully supportive to the point of providing, not just emotional support, but advice, financial support, material support to purchase items.”
“As well as ultimately, when it came down to it, made a very strong and repeated commitment to Van Rootselaar to conceal this plan and the impending attack from law enforcement before it occurred.”
Eight people, including six children, were killed in Tumbler Ridge before Van Rootselaar died by a self-inflicted gunshot wound.
They were Abel Mwansa, Ezekiel Schofield, Kylie Smith, Zoey Benoit, Ticaria Lampert, Shannda Aviugana-Durand, Emmett Jacobs and Jennifer Jacobs.

title: Government plans emergency capacity expansion at Korle Bu, KATH, Tamale, 37 Military
body: Government is planning to expand emergency capacity at four major hospitals as part of efforts to address Ghana’s persistent emergency care challenges. The Health Minister, Kwabena Mintah Akandoh, said the expansion will target Korle Bu Teaching Hospital, Komfo Anokye Teaching Hospital (KATH), Tamale Teaching Hospital and the 37 Military Hospital. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Wednesday, he said the expansion is part of measures being implemented following recommendations from a committee set up to examine challenges in emergency care. “We are looking at the expansion of the emergencies at Komfo Anokye, Tamale, Korlebu, 37 Military Hospital,” he said. Mr Akandoh said Korle Bu’s current emergency capacity is inadequate compared with the hospital’s overall capacity. “So Korle-bu, for example, the bed capacity at the emergency is around 67, and the total bed capacity in the hospital is over 1,000. So we say we think it’s not adequate,” he said. He said the expansion is being considered as part of a wider redevelopment of Korle Bu. “We are looking at the expansion as part of the remodelling of Korle-bu,” he said. The project will include a 400-bed facility alongside other infrastructure. “We are also doing what we call mother and child center, fertility center, and theaters, ICUs, car parks, a comprehensive one, we are doing a 400-bed capacity. The contractor is on site as I speak to you now. So we call it a hospital within a hospital,” he said. The minister said the government is also piloting a national electronic emergency bed management system to improve the use of existing beds. He said a command centre at Ridge Hospital is already providing visibility on emergency bed occupancy. “I have a screen in my office, that if Kolebu says there’s no bed, I’m able to see how many beds are, how many patients are in the emergency,” he said. The system is currently being piloted in some regional and teaching hospitals. Mr Akandoh said beds have been barcoded, and commanders have been assigned at facilities to continuously update the system. The ambulance service has also been integrated into the system to help determine where patients should be taken. He said the system is intended to improve the management of scarce emergency resources, rather than simply create additional beds. “So this system will not necessarily add more beds, but it will help us to manage the scarce resources, so that one patient will not be on one bed at emergency for more hours or another,” he said. The minister also disclosed that more than 200 ambulances are currently functioning, with government planning to add 100 new vehicles in 2027. “We are going to add 100 brand-new vehicles,” he said. He said the government has not yet decided how the new ambulances will be distributed, but it will consider replacing vehicles that are no longer functional. On disciplinary action against health workers implicated in the emergency care review, Mr Akandoh said the various institutions are still implementing the committee’s recommendations. Asked whether those recommended for sanctions would eventually face disciplinary action, he said: “Why not? They are all under the laws of Ghana, and so that’s how far I can go.” “Maybe I may have to tell you that in some instances it’s not a straightforward issue, as you said. There are some legal nuances, and that’s all I can add. So we are implementing the recommendations of the committee,” he said.

title: Newly aired recordings of paramedic Amit Mann renew push to let families access Oct. 7 records
body: Three years after Magen David Adom paramedic Amit Mann, 22, was killed by Hamas while treating the wounded in Kibbutz Be'eri on Oct. 7, newly aired recordings of her final calls revealed fresh and harrowing details about her last hours.The recordings, aired by Channel 12 on Tuesday, prompted her sister, Haviva Mann Izikson, to renew an appeal for a centralized system to ensure other families are not left searching for similar records years later. The calls capture Amit repeatedly calling emergency services as Hamas terrorists overran Be'eri, seeking assistance while continuing to treat wounded residents. The previously unknown calls came to light by chance, when, earlier this year, Mann Izikson contacted the Magen David Adom emergency service seeking the precise times of calls Amit had made on Oct. 7 as she updated a presentation she planned to give about her sister. MDA provided information on seven calls. Until then, the family had known of only four. Mann Izikson said hearing them revealed both that what Amit endured was “even worse than we had thought” and the extent to which Amit continued caring for others even as the situation around her deteriorated.“It showed me even more both the hell that she went through and, on the other hand, who she was. What she was dealing with, what she went through there, which was even worse than we had thought, and how despite all of that she keeps treating the wounded in every way she can,” Mann Izikson told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency Wednesday as she prepared to return to Be'eri for a memorial event at the dental clinic where Amit was killed. The recordings trace Amit's increasingly desperate attempts to summon help as terrorists closed in around the dental clinic. Hours later, she sent her sisters a chilling last message: “They're here, in the clinic. I don't think I'll make it out of here. I love you.”In one call, Amit is heard struggling to convey the scale of what was happening to a police dispatcher. “I don't understand what's going on,” she told the dispatcher, describing wounded and dead people around her and continued gunfire. She asked whether the army or police had reached the kibbutz. When the dispatcher told her help was coming and urged her to stay inside, Amit began to cry. “Just tell me you're here.” Hours later, at 10:41 a.m., after seven calls to Magen David Adom, Israel's national emergency medical service, Amit made her final recorded call to police. “Listen, terrorists have infiltrated Be'eri! We urgently need an ambulance or police here. Come urgently to the dental clinic.” Hearing the latest recordings was heartbreaking, Mann Izikson said. She was struck by Amit's ability to pull herself together after desperate calls for help and return to caring for the wounded, comforting them, asking about their families, bringing them water and improvising with what little there was. Amit placed helmets beneath their heads and covered those who were cold from blood loss.“She keeps them alive until her final moments, and she stays true to herself until her last breaths,” Mann Izikson said. “It just amazed us.”An urge to collect all October 7 documentationMann Izikson is urging the state to establish a central body that would collect all existing documentation from Oct. 7, including recordings held by emergency services and police as well as security-camera footage and other material, catalogue it by victim, and contact each family. Such a body, she said, should tell relatives: “We have documentation of your loved one. Would you like to receive it?” “If the family wants it, then all of it should be provided to them proactively,” she added. She pointed to the family of Gil Buyum, 55, a member of Be'eri's security squad whom Amit treated after he was shot. In one call, Amit reported him wounded; in a later call, she reported that he had died. The two recordings allowed Buyum's widow, Ayelet, to narrow down the time of her husband's death, Mann Izikson said. Buyum's 22-year-old son, Inbar “Buri” Buyum, was also killed while trying to defend the kibbutz that morning.“Only because of Amit's recordings was she able to identify the 20-minute window in which he died,” Mann Izikson said. “That's just one example of how someone can get some kind of closure from something like this.”She said families should be able to decide for themselves whether they want such material. “It belongs to the families. It is the families' material, and the families should decide what, if anything, to do with it.”A law passed in July established an Oct. 7 Memory Authority slated to include an archive and centralize documentation of the attack. The law is due to take effect in January, but it is unclear whether the authority will match material to individual victims and notify their families. JTA was unable to reach the Prime Minister's Office and the Israel State Archives, the government body responsible for preserving state records, in time for publication.Merav Israeli-Amarant, CEO and co-founder of the Civil Commission on Oct. 7 Crimes by Hamas, which released a major report in May documenting sexual violence during the attack and its aftermath, said Mann Izikson's proposal was “profoundly important.”“Families should not have to discover, years later and by chance, that recordings, footage, or other documentation connected to their loved ones exist,” Israeli-Amarant told JTA. She said there should be a mechanism that “approaches families with sensitivity,” while giving them the choice of whether to “receive it, view it, preserve it, or not engage with it at all.”But Israeli-Amarant also said there was “unique importance” in preserving such material through civilian institutions, noting that many Oct. 7 families feel abandoned by the state and that some prefer documentation to be handled independently and “outside political considerations.”Maya Gan-Zvi, manager of the National Library of Israel's Bearing Witness: October 7 Archive, which has collected hundreds of thousands of files from the attack, cautioned that proactively approaching families, as Mann Izikson proposes, also raised ethical questions because families differ widely in how, and whether, they want to encounter such material.“Some want to receive everything, and some do not want to know, or not yet,” Gan-Zvi told JTA, adding that even members of the same family may disagree. Contacting a family without first knowing its wishes could “reopen wounds,” she said, particularly in cases involving graphic material or footage filmed by the terrorists themselves.Gan-Zvi said she favored a system in which bereaved families themselves would take the initiative, registering that they wanted to be contacted, specifying the types of material they wanted and receiving a description of what had been found before deciding whether to obtain it.According to Israeli-Amarant, any system would face “significant” practical and legal hurdles because Oct. 7 material is scattered among government bodies, emergency services, police, the military, media outlets and private individuals, raising questions of ownership, privacy, consent and the rights of victims' families. Some recordings or footage may also be evidence in ongoing investigations or criminal proceedings against Hamas terrorists, she said, making chain of custody, publication restrictions and the integrity of those proceedings additional considerations.Mann Izikson said providing documentation would help answer fundamental questions that remained unresolved. “Three years later, we still don't know the full truth and don't understand how this happened,” she said. “Every piece of material like this can shed another bit of light and help us understand a little bit more.”She has listened to the newly aired recordings repeatedly, echoing a pattern she described to JTA on the first anniversary of the attack, when she said she reread Amit's messages from Oct. 7 every day, in part to piece together what happened during her sister's final hours and try to come to terms with it.It took two and a half days for Amit's body to be identified. Mann Izikson told JTA at the time that when her sister was lowered into the grave, “I felt like they were burying half of my own child. I wanted to go in instead of her.”Even amid the war, the hostage crisis and the wider grief in Israel on the first anniversary of Oct. 7, Mann Izikson said Amit's loss eclipsed everything else. “There is all the rest — and the rest is painful and scary,” she said. “And then there is Amit and nothing else at all.”

title: NIOA and AeroVironment sign deal for Australian loitering munitions
body: NIOA and AeroVironment announced a strategic partnership to support the introduction into service, sustainment and future growth of advanced loitering munitions capabilities across Australia and New Zealand. The partnership establishes a framework for cooperation across the AeroVironment portfolio, including the combat-proven Switchblade family of precision loitering munitions, and positions NIOA as AeroVironment’s local partner for distribution, customer engagement, support and long-term capability development. The agreement reflects a shared commitment to supporting Australian Defence Force requirements and exploring opportunities for local support, sustainment and future industrial capability development. Ben James, Executive Vice President of NIOA Australia and New Zealand, said the partnership combined Australian strategic munitions leadership with world-leading technology. “The Australian GWEO Plan identified the acquisition and introduction into service of Switchblade as a key objective,” he said. “Combining NIOA’s deep expertise in strategic munitions supply, manufacturing and support with AeroVironment’s global leadership in loitering munitions and autonomous systems technology represents a significant win for both the ADF and in the integration of Australian and US industrial bases.” Justin McFarlin, Vice President International Business Development, AeroVironment, said: “The operational success of loitering munitions is driving demand for these capabilities around the world, including Australia. “Through our partnership with NIOA, we are combining AeroVironment’s combat-proven technologies with a trusted Australian defence industry partner to support customers, strengthen sovereign capability outcomes and establish the foundations for long-term growth across the region.” The companies will also explore opportunities to expand support and industrial capability in Australia as demand for autonomous systems and loitering munitions continues to grow. title: How AI is supercharging fraud and making scams impossible to detect
body:
Cybersecurity experts warn artificial intelligence is making fraud nearly impossible to detect.
“With AI powering these scams, it’s just like rocket fuel, making them faster and more sophisticated,” said Chester Wisniewski, a cybersecurity specialist at Sophos.
“We don’t see hardly any of these poorly crafted scams anymore.”
Wisniewski has 30 years of experience in the cybersecurity industry and says scammers are targeting their victims at every angle via social media platforms, text messages, emails, voice cloning, and phone calls.
However, it’s the ease with which criminals are stealing personal information that experts say is alarming.
“They are just breaking in and stealing databases. Hundreds of millions of records are stolen every week from hacked websites where many of us have shopped or done business with,” Wisniewski told Consumer Matters .
When it comes to protecting your personal information, Wisniewski says a healthy paranoia goes a long way. He recommends avoiding anyone who reaches out to you unsolicited, asking for personal credentials.
“If you got a phone call from your bank, be suspicious. Hang up and call the bank back, verify it’s your bank. That needs to be the case with everything right now,” said Wisniewski. “Anytime something involves a financial transaction or a password, you need to have initiated the transaction; never allow someone else to initiate it.”
Guarding your email password is also a critical line of defence. Wisniewski says it’s the digital skeleton key to your accounts. He recommends using password managers to generate complex and unique passwords or passkeys to protect your identity.
Passkeys confirm your identity using facial recognition or a fingerprint to gain access to your accounts.
“I think you do have to give up on the idea your information is not going to be stolen. Unfortunately, we have to share our information with many organizations and a large percentage of them get broken into,” said Wisniewski.

title: Trump promises to prevent destruction of San Diego, Los Angeles
body:
WASHINGTON, October 8. /TASS/. The White House will not allow the American cities of San Diego and Los Angeles to be destroyed as a result of the conflict between Washington and Tehran, US President Donald Trump stated.
"I said it the other day: let them (Iran - TASS) hit a missile into San Diego or Los Angeles on the way. Let them hit. You want to see a horror show? You want to see problems? Let them hit San Diego, let them hit Los Angeles, and you want to see some bad things happen. <…> We're not going to let that happen. We protect our cities. We protect our country. We're not letting that happen," he said while addressing supporters in Texas.
The president had already spoken on Monday about the possibility of destroying these two cities. However, he did not elaborate on his remarks. White House Communications Director Steven Cheung later stated that Trump was referring to a potential threat to American cities if the US did not take military action against Iran over Tehran’s nuclear program.
The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on February 28. In June, Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding providing for an immediate cessation of hostilities on all fronts, including in Lebanon. However, in the early morning hours of July 8, the US resumed large-scale strikes against Iran, accusing it of violating the terms of the agreements reached on the Strait of Hormuz. Nearly 25% of the global oil trade and about 20% of the liquefied natural gas trade pass through the strait. The US administration then effectively signaled that it would cease the use of large-scale military force against Iran and shift to attempting to economically strangle the country through sanctions.

title: Municipal election candidates turn to humour, stunts and social media to stand out
body:
With 37 candidates competing for eight seats on Kelowna City Council, some candidates are taking unconventional approaches to getting noticed.
Brady Rogers is one of them, using humour to stand out.
“Do I enjoy politics? No. Do I know what I’m doing? No. But am I qualified? Also no,” is what his introduction states on his campaign website.
The 33-year old business owner has also been taking to social media with self-deprecating comments, such as, “I barely want to do this.”
But he says the messaging is intentional and not an indication that he doesn’t take the job seriously.
“I’m being a little bit tongue-in-cheek when I say I’m unqualified,” Rogers said. “I’ve never been a politician, but I certainly have experience that I think is very relevant and helpful.”
The campaign has been getting a lot of attention
Rogers said one of his posts was picked up by a U.S. social media account, with a significant following.
“It’s been crazy,” he said. “It resonated locally quite a bit, but then somebody in the U.S. picked it up on Instagram, and now it’s all over.”
Teresa May is also taking a different approach to the campaign.
The longtime Kelowna resident posted a video of herself wake-surfing on Okanagan Lake while wearing a suit jacket and high heels.
“I want to look still professional enough to look like a city councillor and at the same time, it was to be sort of outside the box,” May said. Thinking a little differently to attract the youth, especially through social media.”
She hopes her campaign encourages more people to come out and vote.
“With only 30 per cent of the population out voting the last time, that’s not good enough,” May said.
Across the bridge in West Kelowna, Garrett Millsap is taking a more furry approach.
His campaign signs feature his 10-year-old Beagle, Cooper, alongside the message “re-elect my human.”
Millsap jokes that Cooper may actually be getting more attention than he is.
“I’m hoping they’re not confusing me with Cooper,” Millsap said. “He’s a little bit better looking, a little more handsome than me.”
For Millsap, the humour is meant to make political campaigning more approachable.
“I want to engage people, let them see something different, give them a chuckle, and hopefully it engages them to vote,” he said.
Christopher Schneider, a sociology professor at Brandon University and former UBC Okanagan sociology professor, says these types of campaigns fit into a broader shift in how people present themselves online.
He describes it as the “mediated self,” a concept associated with influencer culture and the performance of identity through media.
Schneider said social media has created an increasingly crowded environment where people compete for attention.
Candidates, he said, are effectively creating personal brands—and unconventional behaviour can help them stand out, but he warns there is also a downside.
“There’s always a danger in a democratic society like Canada, where you have people who might be casting ballots for just names on a ballot sheet and not having a full idea or understanding of what that person is campaigning on,” Schneider said.
Municipal elections in B.C. are scheduled for Oct. 17.

title: Thales Australia and Deakin University partner on autonomous ground vehicles
body: Thales Australia announced a partnership with Deakin University that will help shape the future of autonomous land systems in Australia. The collaboration combines Deakin’s world-class autonomy, robotics and intelligent systems capability with Thales Australia’s industry-leading experience in defence technology. Together, the organisations will accelerate the development of advanced automation to meet the evolving requirements of the Australian Defence Force. Deakin will work alongside Thales Australia and 3ME Technology to develop, test and validate autonomy solutions for BladeHAUL, Thales and 3ME Technology’s new heavy-duty hybrid-electric uncrewed ground vehicle that builds on proven capabilities from the Bushmaster Protected Mobility Vehicle. It is designed to deliver superior payload capacity across a range of missions including logistics transport, mobile energy supply and surveillance. The partnership will focus on proving the platform’s effectiveness, reliability and mission readiness in complex operational environments. Jeff Connolly, CEO, Thales Australia and New Zealand, said: “BladeHAUL provides an ideal platform to apply and test next-generation autonomy technologies in demanding environments. The work undertaken through this partnership will help build the expertise, skills and knowledge needed to support Australia’s long-term defence and industrial objectives. This strategic partnership demonstrates the value of Australian industry and academia working side by side to solve complex challenges. By connecting cutting-edge education and research, engineering and practical application, we are creating an innovation ecosystem for new ideas to be developed, tested and delivered where they can have the greatest impact.” Dr James Mullins AM, Director Defence and Security, Deakin University, said: “Deakin supports those who protect, safeguard and serve Australia, and the systems and capability on which they rely. Our expertise in autonomy, robotics and intelligent systems allows the development of technologies that can improve safety, reliability and operational effectiveness. Working alongside Thales and 3ME Technology, in collaboration with government and end-users, will ensure we build a leading collaborative innovation ecosystem that can develop, test and validate autonomous systems to reduce risk to personnel and strengthen Australia’s sovereign capability.” Thales Australia named prospective anchor tenant for Western Defence Forge Thales Australia is pleased to be named as one of five prospective anchor tenants for the Western Defence Forge, leveraging our expertise in enduring advanced manufacturing, guided weapons and explosive ordnance to work with the WA Government to deliver a new facility to forge 155mm artillery munitions and assemble missiles in Western Australia. The new facility will be specifically-designed to support exports to global markets while drawing on the existing Commonwealth-owned, Thales-operated guided weapons and explosive ordnance footprint in Benalla. Thales seeks to build on its position as a trusted partner of Defence and the Commonwealth to join the Western Australian Government’s mission to drive investment, create skilled jobs, and strengthen Australia’s sovereign industrial capability. Western Australia’s strategic location as Australia’s gateway to the Indian Ocean and South-East Asia makes it an ideal hub for defence production. With Defence’s increasing focus on northern and western force posture, a resilient industrial presence in WA is becoming increasingly important. The State is also well positioned to export munitions to support global rearmament initiatives, serving as a key logistics point between hemispheres and contributing to allied supply chains across the Indo-Pacific and into Europe. The proposal includes development of a 155mm forging capability to help meet growing global demand for this critical munition, drawing on Thales’ role as a Strategic GWEO Partner to the Commonwealth and decades of expertise in energetics. It would also introduce missile integration, test and acceptance functions based on proven Thales UK technology, including significant transfer of technology, knowledge and production capability for advanced air defence and counter-UAS solutions. Thales to deploy advanced air traffic control radar in the Faroe Islands Thales has been selected by DALO, the Danish Ministry of Defence Acquisition and Logistics Organisation, to supply and deploy an RSM NG secondary surveillance radar at the Sornfelli site in the Faroe Islands. This project highlights Thales’ dual expertise in civil and military air traffic management, demonstrating its ability to address complex, shared airspace requirements. Although procured by a military authority, the radar will also support civil air traffic operations through integration with Air Navigation Services Providers Naviair and AVIANS systems, ensuring safe and continuous service across both domains. The RSM NG will replace an existing Thales RSM 970 radar. Building on decades of operational experience in ATC radars, the RSM NG represents the latest evolution in Thales’ proven portfolio of secondary surveillance radars, combining high performance, compact design, and ease of deployment. Thales will complete delivery and installation within six months, one of the shortest timelines achieved for a program of this scale, while ensuring full operational continuity, with no disruption to air traffic control services. Fully compliant with ICAO and EUROCONTROL standards, this system meets the stringent requirements of both civil and military aviation. The “all-in-one” RSM NG radar integrates Mode S interrogation and ADS-B detection capabilities, delivering enhanced accuracy, reliability, and situational awareness. The radar will be connected to the AVIANS control centre, with system integration managed by Naviair and AVIANS. title: Haverford professor accused of threatening, stalking Jewish person online
body: A Haverford College professor was arrested on Tuesday and charged with cyberstalking a Jewish person over several months, allegedly sending messages that included “Jew, get the f*** out of my country.”  Guangtian Ha, a religion professor at the Pennsylvania liberal arts college, was accused of sending the victim approximately 50 messages between October 2025 and May 2026, according to a federal indictment. He also posted information about the victim's home address and family.Haverford President Wendy Raymond said in a message to the college community that Ha was placed on administrative leave and barred from campus during the criminal case. Ha, who taught courses on Islam and religion in Asia, was on sabbatical and not teaching this semester.Raymond said she was “heartbroken and furious” about the allegations, adding that “any form of harassment or discrimination based on identity is unacceptable, antithetical to our values, and has no place at Haverford.” She said a Haverford representative had contacted people who were targeted by “these heinous online attacks, which were antisemitic in nature.” Ha contacted a victim through at least four different X accounts, according to the indictment. In various messages, he called the person a “Jew pig,” urged them to leave the country and the township, and said, “If jews are so special then they should also be placed in special camps and receive special treatments.” Ha is also accused of posting an image of the victim's home mailbox, which identified their address. After the victim took security measures, Ha allegedly wrote, “The goyim have woken up, jew. Run. Flee. Leave. Blurring your home on google map and installing a security camera next to your mailbox won't help.” He also threatened the victim's family and their son by name, according to the indictment. JTA could not reach Ha for comment.Ha named in previously settled suitHa was previously named in a 2024 antisemitism lawsuit against the school, which Haverford settled in August. The group Jews at Haverford said in the lawsuit that students and faculty showed “severe and pervasive hostility toward Jewish students” in the aftermath of the Hamas attacks on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023. That lawsuit accused Ha of writing posts that attacked Jews “committed to Israel.” In one post, Ha said he “will never forgive” Haverford community members who were “silent on this genocide or even tacitly support it,” referring to Gaza, adding, “I know their names, and I know their faces.”As part of the settlement, Raymond said that discrimination or harassment against students who were Jewish, Israeli, or identified with Zionism violated the school's policy. Haverford declined to clarify whether Ha was penalized as a result of the 2024 lawsuit or any other allegations of antisemitism on campus prior to his arrest.In 2025, Republican New York Rep. Elise Stefanik questioned Raymond during a hearing on campus antisemitism. Stefanik, whose grilling of university leaders in 2023 prompted two to step down, appeared to warn Raymond that her job was on the line after Raymond refused to discuss individual cases of alleged antisemitism. “Respectfully, president of Haverford, many people have sat in this position who are no longer in the positions as president of universities for their failure to answer straightforward questions,” said Stefanik.

title: Iowa’s Ashley Hinson slams the savings habits of millennials
body: Iowa Rep. Ashley Hinson took a swipe at the savings habits of millennials as she fielded a question Wednesday about Social Security during a Senate campaign debate. Hinson, the Republican candidate facing off against Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek, was asked about ensuring the solvency of Social Security when she raised the broader prospect of savings by millennials, the demographic consisting of people born from 1981-1996. She said the country needed to have a “serious conversation” about “how young people are saving money,” as part of the discussion about the future of Social Security. “We also need to be talking about millennials saving money,” she later added. “Millennials are the worst group of savers in the country right now and have the least amount of savings. So those are ways where I think we can help have a bigger conversation around saving in general, planning for retirement and making sure we're all able to experience a robust retirement.” Hinson faces a tough race in Iowa against Turek amid a difficult political environment for Republicans. Voters are overwhelmingly pessimistic about the state of the economy and their own personal finances, and they support Social Security while being concerned about the program’s future . Hinson said she would not support cutting benefits and suggested creating a bipartisan commission to present suggestions to Congress to save the program. When pushed on her statement that “all options should be on the table,” she turned her attention to young people. “I think my dad and I had this discussion when I was in sixth grade, looking at a ledger book and trying to figure out, 'Hey, how are we going to make sure you're set up for your life?'” she said. “So we need to be having a conversation simultaneously to all solutions on the table, to make sure that it can stay solvent, while we're also talking about, 'How do we get more young people to save?'” "She has never and will never cut Social Security," Hinson campaign spokesperson Billy Fuerst said in a statement. Turek, when asked about Social Security, said he supports removing the payroll tax cap. “The best way we can keep this solvent is by taking off the cap,” Turek said. “Let's make sure that billionaires and large corporations are paying their fair share. That will move the needle in a very serious way to keep Social Security solvent.” Hinson disagreed. “The only thing I'm hearing from him is that the only solution to everything is to raise taxes,” she said.

title: ‘Means more than just a trophy’ – Djokovic claims 102nd title of career
body: Novak Djokovic claimed the 102nd title of his astonishing career as Alex de Minaur retired injured from the China Open final. The 39-year-old led De Minaur – a player 12 years his junior – 7-6 (7-3) 0-1 when the Australian was forced to quit with an apparent left thigh problem. Both players took a medical timeout after a 68-minute first set, but De Minaur managed just one game on their return before shaking hands. It is the 21st year in a row that Djokovic has won at least one singles title. Only Jimmy Connors (109) and Roger Federer (103) have won more singles titles in their careers than the Serb. Djokovic is on a 34-match winning streak at the China Open, having claimed the trophy seven times. “I always have high expectations and want to visualise myself with the trophy, but particularly here in Beijing, the place where I’ve never lost,” Djokovic said. “This trophy means much more than one trophy, one tournament.” The 24-time Grand Slam champion was competing in only his second final of the year after losing January’s Australian Open showpiece to Carlos Alcaraz. Djokovic beat world number two Alexander Zverev on his way to the Beijing final and was a set and a break up on third seed Daniil Medvedev when the Russian was defaulted from their semi-final. Djokovic’s ability to compete at the highest level is rarely in question – he beat world number one Sinner to reach the Australian Open final and took a set off Alcaraz in the showpiece – but his body has let him down in recent years. He was left in tears following a gruelling first-round loss at the US Open and spoke about struggling with a “serious health condition” that particularly bothered him in oppressive conditions. He reached the semi-finals of Wimbledon, losing to eventual champion Jannik Sinner, but suffered a surprise third-round exit at the French Open at the hands of rising star Joao Fonseca. This is Djokovic’s first title in just over a year, having limited his schedule to protect his body. Victory will also see him return to inside the world’s top 10. “This year has been quite challenging for me, lots of ups and downs and physical and health issues, so I was just trying to find a good feeling on the court,” Djokovic said. “I know that when I’m feeling well and striking the ball well, I can still compete at the highest level. “This week has been evidence of that. I’m very proud.” Earlier, Alcaraz won the Japan Open, claiming a trophy in just his third tournament since injuring his wrist in April. The Spaniard came back from an early breakdown to beat Czech Jiri Lehecka 7-6 (7-4), 6-4 and successfully defend his title in Tokyo. Alcaraz returned to competitive tennis at the US Open in August, where he reached the quarter-finals before losing in five tight sets to Ben Shelton. It is Alcaraz’s third title of the season, having won the Australian Open in January to complete the career Grand Slam, and the Qatar Open in February. “It’s extra special after my injury,” the 25-year-old said. “It was a tough week; I didn’t find my best tennis, my best level, but I did find good solutions. “I think that’s what matters in the end.”

title: [Good Business] The AI nutrition label: Why we need to know what’s inside before we trust it
body: Whenever a new artificial intelligence (AI) application is introduced, the first questions are usually practical: What can it do? Will it make work faster? Can it improve productivity, reduce costs, or help us make better decisions? These questions matter as AI becomes increasingly integrated into our workplaces, schools, businesses, and everyday lives. But before we ask what AI can do for us, perhaps we should first ask a more fundamental question: Can we trust it? This question lies at the heart of Transparency and Explainability , one of the eight guiding principles in the Association of Analytics and AI of the Philippines (AAP) Code of Ethics for AI Professionals. It belongs to the pillar of Trustworthy AI, which challenges us to ask a simple but powerful Filipino question: “ Mapagkakatiwalaan ba ito? ” (Can this be trusted?) The question is familiar because we ask it in many areas of life. When we buy food, we read the label to understand its ingredients, nutritional value, and expiration date. When a doctor prescribes medicine, we ask what it is for, how much to take, and what side effects it may have. (READ: Warning labels on food? How a new bill could change Filipino diets ) We do not consume something simply because it is available or because someone says it works. We seek clarity because trust is built on understanding . We should apply the same principle to AI. Today, AI helps determine what appears in our social media feeds, what products are recommended to us, and what content we consume. Organizations use it to screen job applicants, assess employees, forecast outcomes, detect fraud, and support decisions. In healthcare, finance, education, and government, AI is increasingly becoming an adviser. Yet unlike a food label or medicine leaflet, many AI systems remain difficult for ordinary people to understand. Transparency means being open about when AI is being used, what data it relies on, and its capabilities and limitations. Explainability means that when an AI system makes a recommendation or influences a decision, people can understand the reasoning behind it in language that makes sense. Simply put: If AI affects people, people deserve an explanation. This becomes especially important when AI influences decisions about jobs, promotions, loans, insurance, healthcare, education, or access to opportunities. Imagine applying for a job and receiving an automated rejection without knowing why. Imagine being denied a loan because of a risk score no one can explain. Or imagine an employee being classified as a low performer by an algorithm, yet neither the employee nor the manager understands how the assessment was made. The issue is not simply whether AI was used. The issue is whether people can understand and trust the process behind the decision . As someone who has spent much of my professional life in human resources, talent analytics, and digital transformation, I find this especially important in the workplace. Organizations are rapidly adopting AI in recruitment, workforce planning, performance management, and talent development. These technologies can improve efficiency and help leaders process information at a scale that would otherwise be impossible. But efficiency alone should never define success. People are not data points. Careers are not algorithms. Human potential cannot be fully captured by a score generated by a machine. When technology begins influencing livelihoods and futures, transparency becomes more than a technical feature. It becomes an ethical responsibility . Must Read Limit AI now or humanity will lose its agency, says Nobel laureate Maria Ressa Trust is not created by sophisticated algorithms alone. It grows when people understand how decisions are made, when organizations are willing to explain their systems, and when individuals can question outcomes that affect them. Transparency also benefits organizations. Employees are more likely to accept AI-assisted processes when they understand them. Customers are more willing to engage with AI-powered services when they know how their information is being used. Regulators, investors, and stakeholders gain confidence when organizations can explain and justify the technologies they deploy. In this sense, transparency is not merely an ethical requirement. It is also a business advantage . This is why responsibility belongs to everyone in the AI ecosystem. For users , it means asking questions instead of accepting every AI-generated recommendation at face value. We need to understand when AI is being used, recognize its limitations, and verify important outputs. For developers and designers , it means building understandable systems, documenting how they work, testing for unintended consequences, and communicating limitations honestly. Innovation should never come at the expense of clarity. For leaders , it means establishing governance, ensuring meaningful human oversight, and creating environments where AI recommendations can be challenged. Most importantly, leaders must remember: Accountability cannot be delegated to a machine. When an AI-assisted decision causes harm, responsibility ultimately rests with the humans who designed, approved, deployed, and relied on the technology. Ultimately, the future of AI will not be determined only by how powerful the technology becomes. It will also be determined by how responsibly we choose to use it . The question before us, therefore, is not simply whether AI is intelligent enough. The more important question is: Is it trustworthy enough? Whenever AI influences our decisions, organizations, or communities, we would do well to return to the challenge posed by the AAP Code of Ethics: “Mapagkakatiwalaan ba ito?” (Can this be trusted?) If we cannot understand it, explain it, or question it, perhaps we should not trust it just yet. Because trustworthy AI is ultimately not about machines. It is about people—and our commitment to ensuring that technology remains transparent, accountable, and worthy of the trust we place in it. – Rappler.com Liza Manalo-Mapagu is the CEO of ASEAMETRICS, Program Chair of the Psychology Department at Asia Pacific College, and a member of the Responsible AI and Analytics Council (RAAIC) of the Association of Analytics and AI of the Philippines (AAP). She advocates for Trustworthy and Human-Centric AI that advances both organizational performance and human dignity. title: Hanwha and Milrem Robotics expand cooperation on unmanned ground systems
body: Milrem Robotics and Hanwha are expanding their cooperation in unmanned ground systems with the THeMIS Unmanned Ground Vehicle (UGV) at the centre of new initiatives in South Korea, Australia and New Zealand. Hanwha has acquired two THeMIS platforms for separate initiatives in South Korea and Australia, while the companies’ cooperation also establishes a framework for broader THeMIS activities in Australia and New Zealand. In South Korea, a THeMIS UGV will be used in multiple R&D projects in which Hanwha is participating. The platform will contribute to the development and evaluation of advanced unmanned and autonomous ground capabilities. In Australia and New Zealand, the cooperation will establish a framework for Hanwha to market, pursue local production, sell and sustain THeMIS locally. This includes developing an Australian supply chain, building local maintenance and upgrade capabilities, and integrating payloads and subsystems to meet the specific requirements of regional customers. Milrem Robotics will contribute localisation planning, technology transfer, technical know-how and engineering expertise to enable these activities. “Together with Hanwha, we are creating a strong foundation for expanding unmanned and autonomous capabilities across the Asia-Pacific region,” said Kuldar Väärsi, CEO of Milrem Robotics. “THeMIS provides a proven and highly adaptable unmanned platform, while Hanwha brings significant local industrial capabilities, market knowledge and expertise in the development and support of advanced defence systems. By combining these strengths, we can address regional requirements locally and build the capabilities needed to integrate, produce and sustain these systems in the region.” The cooperation also includes an option to integrate Milrem Robotics’ Intelligent Function Integration Kit (MIFIK) with Hanwha’s unmanned and manned platforms. MIFIK enables the addition of capabilities such as autonomous navigation and mission execution to different types of vehicles. The new initiatives build on existing cooperation between Hanwha and Milrem Robotics. title: UAE drive to cut sugar, salt and fat in food to make healthy choices easier, experts say
body: The UAE’s new limits on salt, sugar and fat in packaged foods are an important shift towards changing the food environment itself, rather than placing the responsibility for healthier eating entirely on consumers, health experts have said. The new rules , approved on Tuesday, place caps on levels of sodium, sugar and fat in packaged foods, whether locally manufactured or imported. The rules are to be implemented in phases, with the final limits taking effect by December 31, 2030. They form part of a much wider effort across the UAE to tackle obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular disease and other lifestyle-related conditions by changing the types of food people encounter every day. Dr Ahmed Al Khazraji, Executive Director of Healthy Living at the Department of Health – Abu Dhabi, said the Cabinet resolution represented a major milestone for public health. “By focusing on commonly consumed products and introducing these changes progressively through 2030, we can improve their nutritional profile while giving manufacturers time to reformulate responsibly and maintain the taste and quality consumers expect,” he said. Dr Al Khazraji said the Department of Health – Abu Dhabi, Abu Dhabi Public Health Centre and the Ministry of Health and Prevention worked together to advance the food reformulation agenda. “The logic is simple: improve the nutritional profile of products that people already buy and enjoy, rather than placing the responsibility entirely on individuals to make a different choice every time,” he said. “This is part of our work across the food ecosystem, collaborating with government, producers, retailers and food service providers to improve what is available, how it is promoted and placed, and the information people have when making choices.” The move builds on years of measures aimed at improving public health. The UAE introduced excise taxes on tobacco, energy drinks and fizzy drinks in 2017, before expanding the system to e-cigarettes, vaping products and drinks containing added sugar or sweeteners. The country also introduced a sugar-based tax system for drinks, under which products with higher sugar content per 100ml face a higher tax rate. Abu Dhabi has introduced a parallel series of measures under its Healthy Living Strategy, including restrictions on where foods high in fat, salt and sugar can be displayed in large supermarkets, tighter controls on fast food advertising, stronger nutrition standards in schools and healthier menu requirements in hotels and restaurants. The medical view Doctors and dietitians say the changes could have an important cumulative effect because many people consume more salt, sugar and fat than they realise. Dr Safa Hegazin, staff physician at the Digestive Disease Institute at Cleveland Clinic Abu Dhabi, said reducing excessive levels of those ingredients in commonly consumed foods could help support healthier dietary patterns over time. “Making healthier choices should not be difficult, and policies like these help ensure that the healthier option becomes the easier option,” she said. “As these changes are introduced over time, even modest reductions can contribute to meaningful long-term health benefits.” “Sustained improvements in diet can help reduce the risk of conditions associated with obesity and poor nutrition, including type 2 diabetes, hypertension, fatty liver disease, and cardiovascular disease,” she added. However, clinicians stressed that products meeting the new limits should not automatically be considered healthy. Heenana Mustaheena, clinical dietitian at LLH Hospital, Mussaffah, said much of the salt and sugar consumed by people is already present in packaged foods and can easily go unnoticed. “Most people consume far more salt, sugar, and unhealthy fat than they realise because much of it is already present in everyday packaged foods,” she said. “In the UAE, this is especially important given the high prevalence of excess salt intake.” She said consumers should continue to check nutrition labels and compare products, particularly by looking at nutritional values per 100g. “The limits represent maximum levels, and the actual amount consumed still depends on portion size,” she said. “Excess salt can raise blood pressure and increase the workload on the heart and kidneys, while excess sugar and fat can make blood glucose and weight more difficult to manage.” Dr Leila Kay Karimpoor, Consultant in Internal Medicine at Burjeel Medical City, also said the significance of the policy lay in addressing population-wide exposure rather than relying solely on individual behaviour. High sodium intake is associated with hypertension, cardiovascular disease, kidney problems and fluid retention, while excess added sugar can contribute to weight gain, insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes, she said. “Consumers should read labels and consider their overall diet, as meeting a regulatory limit does not necessarily make a processed food healthy,” she said. Industry is prepared Food manufacturers have already begun responding to the wider health drive. Al Ain Farms Group previously announced reductions of 10 to 20 per cent in added sugar across some juices, flavoured milk, flavoured yoghurt and laban products, saying the reformulations were aligned with Abu Dhabi’s Healthy Living Strategy. United Foods Company, which produces edible oils and assorted food products, and distributes name brands like Oreo and Cadbury, said the new standards are something they feel prepared for. “We are following the international standards even while supplying to 62 countries worldwide,” said Mohamad Ziad Al Najjar, United Foods senior manager B2B. “When it comes to the healthy standards that Abu Dhabi and the UAE are implementing, it is not something that we have ever faced any challenges with. There is no risk to quality. We are caring for the customer by having all the options.” The Danish company Arla is a major international dairy co-operative that has had a presence in the UAE for decades. Berta Zammar, head of corporate affairs, communications and sustainability for UAE, Oman and Qatar, told The National at Global Food Week that the regulations are welcome and will succeed with private and public collaboration. “This circular is totally aligned with our position,” she said. “As our health strategy, it's aligned with our ambition. We are working a lot to move all our products to make them healthier and to be a part of national strategies. It's always a good thing to provide the consumer with healthy food.” The global picture Restrictions on the salt, sugar and fat content of food have been brought in around the world. Several European nations, including Denmark, Finland, Belgium, Croatia, the Netherlands, Hungary, Greece and Portugal, already have limits on how much salt can be used in bread production, ranging from 1.3g to 2g per 100g. Some countries in Europe extend those limits to cereals, cheese and processed meats. Elsewhere, countries require producers to add warning marks to labelling for foods that exceed strict thresholds for sugar, salt and saturated fat. Chile pioneered black octagon labels warning consumers about high content, as well as school marketing bans which have been replicated in Mexico, Argentina, Peru, Colombia, Venezuela and Uruguay. Similar warning flags or contrast colours on labels are used in Canada, Singapore and India to help guide consumers.

title: Hero flydubai captain was always ‘two steps’ ahead when on duty
body: The experience and instinct of flydubai's Capt Smit Machchhar to prepare for any eventuality helped to prevent an “unimaginable” suspected terrorist attack, a friend has said. The flydubai captain saved the lives of 174 passengers when he opened the cockpit door of Flight FZ1073 despite life-threatening injuries from an emergency crash axe attack by a co-pilot. The mid-air attack began a few hours into a Dubai-Tel Aviv flight on September 30. Passengers overpowered the attacker, and reserve pilots diverted the Dubai-Tel Aviv flight to land safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. Dharav Gosalia, a former colleague of Capt Machchhar, shed light on the fortitude of his friend of 14 years. “When you’re in the cruise phase all you have to do is ensure that the flight is being monitored, but Smit always had the habit of staying at least two steps ahead of the aircraft,” Capt Gosalia, 33, told The National . “He would prepare for what could happen to the aircraft, or what could happen to the weather, or what is the situation at the runway. This is instilled within you when you have been flying for so many years – to think a little ahead of the aircraft because it's a fast-flying machine and whatever can go wrong goes wrong in a fraction of a second. He had this habit of staying ahead, ready with a prompt reaction.” Capt Machchhar has been praised as a hero for his quick thinking and bravery, and is recovering from deep wounds to his head and hands in an Abu Dhabi hospital. UAE authorities are investigating the motives of the attempted terrorist attack in which the co-pilot tried to take control of the aircraft. 'Land safely with all souls on board' The two men lived in the Ghatkopar suburb of northern Mumbai, completed flight training at the same academy in New Zealand and later flew Boeing 737s at India’s SpiceJet. Capt Machchhar was a commander with SpiceJet for 11 years and moved to Dubai with flydubai four years ago. Capt Gosalia then shifted to Air India. “It was a miracle that he came out of this,” Capt Gosalia said. “It was because of his presence of mind. It all boils down to all the experience and intuition built over the last 15 years of flying. Health Update: Capt Smit continues to make steady progress and is regaining his health. The Embassy remains in close touch with his family, doctors & local authorities, extending all possible assistance. We thank everyone for their prayers & wish him a speedy recovery. pic.twitter.com/Uh9h1F3rbW — India in UAE (@IndembAbuDhabi) October 6, 2026 “One thing is very clear for Smit or any captain – no matter what happens, the aircraft has to land safely with all the souls present on board. That would have been the only thing in his mind, that's what we have been taught.” Both captains had undergone training with retired senior Air Force commanders in India. But Capt Gosalia said no amount of training could prepare a captain for an attack from a co-pilot. "We have been trained for hijack protocols, incapacitation, security threats or abnormal scenarios, but an attack from a first officer sitting next to you who is your trusted wingman, it's impossible," he said. "I don't think in all years of flying anybody would have thought of this.” Emergency protocol Rehearsing emergency procedures, visualisation or "chair flying" and the right attitude as a commander were key. “It all boils down to those small ‘chair flying’ or visualisation techniques, your nature before the flight that makes you the best in the cockpit,” Capt Gosalia said. “Chair flying is about going through a sequence of actions during maybe an engine failure or depressurisation. This is useful for an abnormal situation in the cockpit. "When your motor skills and muscle memory are good, it helps rehearse procedures and your hands automatically move to the right direction, like automatically putting in the right squawk [emergency] code.” Working as a team Capt Machchhar’s approach was to treat the crew as his team, his friend said. “People want to fly with him,” Capt Gosalia said. “Whether it’s a crew member, loader or engineer he never treated anyone differently, he is that kind of person. He would carry the whole crew as a unit, as a team. Nobody felt left out. Smit is humble, warm and jovial.” When working for the Indian carrier, the men played cricket in a Mumbai suburb during their breaks and sometimes co-ordinated off-duty time overseas during layovers. “We used to fly a lot together. Apart from flying, we would check the roster to see where we could do our layovers and we would also meet for sports at home,” Capt Gosalia said. Time to heal He said his long-time friend needed time to heal . “For other people, this is a story but not for him,” Capt Gosalia said. “For him, it’s a real thing that happened. His family needs space. What he went through inside the cockpit is just unimaginable. "The aircraft plunging with a heavy rate of descent, it's almost vertical, he is trying to reach the door while completely wounded. Hats off to what he pulled off. He will definitely come out strong. And every one of us is proud to know him.”

title: Culture as a building block: How the Middle East can inspire future cities
body: This episode was produced by The National in partnership with LIVEX. This week on Culture Bites , host Enas Refaei sits down with speakers at LIVEX in Abu Dhabi to discuss how arts and culture can shape the cities in which people live. She speaks to Adrian Lahoud, professor of architecture and urban design, about why successful cities need more than buildings. He explains why communities should have a role in shaping projects from the beginning, and how culture needs the freedom and resources to grow organically. They also discuss what the Middle East can teach other parts of the world about designing cities for rising temperatures and the role architecture can play in social change. Enas also sits down with Bill Bragin, founding executive artistic director of The Arts Centre at NYU Abu Dhabi. He explains why he considers culture a form of infrastructure that can bring different communities together and make a city a place where people want to build their lives. They also look at how The Arts Centre has helped artists in the UAE connect, collaborate and develop professionally, and why introducing audiences to unfamiliar work is an important part of building a thriving cultural scene.

title: Hegseth praises sailors' resilience after record-breaking carrier deployment
body: US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth flew to the flight deck of the aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln on Wednesday and praised the resilience of sailors who endured an extended, wartime deployment that drew scrutiny over suicide attempts on board.The Lincoln, which is due to dock on Thursday in San Diego, is the flagship of a carrier strike group that had eight suicide attempts among US sailors during its time at sea, according to the Navy. Its deployment included more than 260 continuous days without a port call, a record, according to the Pentagon.Hegseth, whose speeches regularly target the media, accused reporters of trying to turn the crew of the Lincoln strike group into symbols of dysfunction or of a failed mission instead of heroes of the conflict, and presented a citation from President Donald Trump for their achievements during the Iran war.The Lincoln's accomplishments included sinking 64 Iranian warships, destroying 21 anti-ship cruise missiles, executing 3,693 combat sorties, launching 450 Tomahawk land attack cruise missiles and firing 1.37 million pounds of ordnance against Iran, Hegseth said.Despite the fast pace of combat operations, it suffered no casualties and had no aircraft mishaps, Hegseth said."What makes the US military and the US Navy and all these sailors different is that you adapt and that you're resilient and you overcome - you finish the mission nonetheless," Hegseth told the crew. "Yes, it's hard. That's why you're here. You do difficult and hard things."Typically naval deployments ​are for between six and nine months but can be extended during times of conflict. Mental health issues on long deployments have long challenged the US Navy.In August, amid reports of low morale and supply shortages on board, Trump was asked whether he thought the Lincoln had been deployed too long. Trump responded: "No, ​no, no. Not nearly long enough."Hegseth acknowledged some challenges on board, saying "there wasn't an easy resupply."Ahead of the carrier's return to port, Hegseth joked that he was "the only thing standing between you and home" and that he was also the one who signed the orders repeatedly extending the deployment."You deserve to see your families and see them as soon as possible," Hegseth said, adding he just wanted to see them for "a moment on the route, on the way in, just to say thank you."Crossroads in US-Iran warThe carrier's return comes at a crossroads in the US-Iran war, which has jolted global energy markets and become a political liability for Trump and fellow Republicans ahead of November midterm elections.The war — and its $3 billion monthly price tag — has become a key issue on the campaign trail. Higher energy prices have put Trump and Republicans on the defensive in competitive states that will decide control of Congress.Trump is weighing next steps against Iran, including whether to escalate strikes before or after the elections, as he presses a naval blockade meant to pile economic pressure on Tehran to reach a deal to end the conflict.Vice President JD Vance told Reuters on Monday that Iran must make a "meaningful" reduction in its uranium enrichment capacity to satisfy US demands and end the countries' seven-month war.Hegseth said the crew of the Lincoln had helped ensure the US objective of preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon."You have changed the arc of history," he told them on Wednesday.

title: African Union launches continent’s first credit rating agency
body: The African Union launched the continent’s first credit rating agency ​on Wednesday, seeking to provide an alternative to the “big three” global ratings agencies as debt burdens weigh on many ‌African economies. The Africa Credit Rating Agency (AfCRA) — the creation of which African leaders endorsed in 2018 — was launched at a ceremony in Port Louis, the capital of Mauritius, where it will be based, attended by African officials. The new agency will help investors better assess Africa’s investment risk by providing more information and context, said Denys Denya, executive vice president of Afreximbank, one of the agency’s backers. “When lenders don’t see clearly, they charge for ​the fog. Africa continues to pay for the fog that is generated by western centric examinations,” he told ⁠the launch ceremony. African leaders have long accused Western ratings agencies, including S&P, Moody’s and Fitch, of failing to fairly assess the risk of lending to ​African countries and of moving too quickly to downgrade them during crises such as conflicts and pandemics. The agencies reject that criticism, saying they apply the ​same methodologies globally. A 2024 Reuters investigation into Africa’s debt crisis found no evidence of systemic bias in the sovereign ratings assigned to the region by the three major global credit rating agencies. CREDIBILITY TEST IN TIMES OF CRISIS Rating experts said the success of the initiative will hinge on the perceived credibility of the new agency, especially in ​times of crisis. “A new rating agency begins with a promise while investors ultimately require a track record,” said Dennis Shen, a lecturer in finance ​at the International School of Management in Berlin and former sovereign analyst at Scope Ratings. “The hardest test, however, will come when markets are under stress, because ‌a rating ⁠agency’s credibility is tested most severely when its conclusions are uncomfortable rather than when it is highly convenient.” AfCRA may provide a counterweight to established rating agencies, but it must meet global standards, former Nigerian Vice President Yemi Osinbajo said. “It can’t just be a chauvinistic or nationalistic agency,” he said. BORROWING COSTS IN FOCUS AfCRA, which will rate sovereign borrowers, financial institutions and private companies, will operate independently and be funded through shareholder capital and ​its operations, the AU said. It ​did not provide details about ⁠the shareholders. The AU says the agency should help improve African countries’ access to capital markets and provide investors with more balanced and context-specific assessments of economies across the continent. It noted that African economies are currently rated B ​to B-minus on average, compared with BB for other emerging regions, a gap the AU says can ​limit some investors’ participation ⁠and raise borrowing costs. The drive to improve borrowing terms for the continent has become more urgent following years of increased government borrowing, which has pushed some countries into debt distress. “The stakes are significant,” the AU said, adding that the continent’s annual external debt service surged to $163 billion in 2024, ⁠up from $61 billion in 2010. In many countries, interest payments have exceeded the annual budgets for key social ​sectors such as health and education. AfCRA is also expected to boost coverage, with 23 economies on the continent lacking a rating from the three big agencies, the AU said.

title: Codan unit upgrades radios for contested environments
body: DTC has launched multiple updates to its MeshUltra Spectrum Overmatch capabilities, designed to give soldiers an information advantage in emerging battlefield electronic warfare environments. The update adds two beamforming capabilities to DTC’s high-performance MeshUltra waveforms, which create self-forming, self-healing networks that adapt as radios move and network conditions change. Available on compatible multi-antenna radios, including the Sentry Mesh 6161 and BluSDR family, the updates give the radios new ways to improve connections. For a dismounted soldier, dependable communications mean staying connected to the wider force: other soldiers, vehicles, sensors and increasingly, unmanned systems. DTC’s MeshUltra beamforming uses independently controlled antenna paths within its MIMO (Multiple Input, Multiple Output) architecture to direct radio energy towards connected receivers. This allows the radio to shape its transmission in ways a radio with a single antenna and transmit path cannot. The Adaptive Beamforming capability uses reports from connected radios to select a transmission pattern suited to the conditions. A second mode, Quasi-Beamforming, provides another performance option without requiring those reports. The release supports Codan’s development of its proposed Australian tactical edge radio solution for LAND 4140 Work Package 16.
