President Donald Trump on Wednesday hailed what he called the "historic" enrollment of 70 million American children into his Trump Accounts , calling them “a step to ensure every American child has a fair shot at the American Dream.”
The administration announced that beginning on Oct. 1, the Treasury Department automatically enrolled 60 million children under age 18 in the president’s signature investment accounts in addition to the 10 million whose parents opted into the accounts following their official release on July 4.
“With automatic enrollment now complete, every American child under the age of 18 has a Trump Account in their name, making it easier than ever for families to participate , ” White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said in a statement.
According to the administration, $2.2 billion has been deposited into the accounts since their release on July 4. The Treasury Department pledged to pour a one-time $1,000 seed contribution for each child born between Jan. 1, 2025 and Dec. 31, 2028. Children born outside of that range will not receive the seed contribution from the Treasury — but their family members and acquaintances are able to deposit money into the accounts. Several corporations — including Uber and Nvidia — and philanthropists — such as Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell and his wife, Susan, who seeded the program with a $6.25 billion contribution, also donated to the accounts.
Trump, encircled by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett, and the Dells, predicted, "So if all goes well, which I think it will, they'll end up being quite rich by the time they're 18 and then 21."
Trump said in January when he announced the initiative that a number of major U.S. companies pledged to match the federal government's initial contribution for eligible employees' children, including Charles Schwab, Robinhood, SoFi, Uber, Charter Communication and BNY, and that several others had agreed to make contributions.
In a notice published in the Federal Register, the Treasury Department said that auto-enrollment was geared to maximize children’s participation in the accounts, estimating that an additional 2 million children would benefit from the accounts every year as a result.
“An eligible individual should not lose the opportunity to receive contributions or investment growth merely because no adult completed an election,” the Treasury wrote in the notice .
Starting Oct. 1, parents no longer have to opt-in to the accounts, but can claim their children’s accounts on the Trump Accounts app.
According to the administration, the accounts are designed to boost future financial security for the most recent generation of Americans, with each child gaining access to the account in their name once they reach the age of 18. They can then allocate the funds in the account solely for purposes designated by the Treasury Department — including paying for university tuition or purchasing a house.
Some Democrats have praise the program. Maryland Gov. Wes Moore called it a "smart policy," and California Gov. Gavin Newsom, who called it "one of the best things [Trump] has done."
Democratic Sen. Cory Booker of New Jersey and Democratic Rep. Ayanna Pressley of Massachusetts introduced a similar proposal in 2023, which would have provided each American child with $1,000 at birth in an account that they could access at age 18, but it didn't make it out of committee. Booker also supported Trump's proposal.

title: Trump interrupted 12 times in 45 minutes during speech in staunchly Republican Texas
body:
WASHINGTON, October 8. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump was interrupted by 12 people during the first 45 minutes of his speech to supporters in Texas, which is considered one of the key Republican-leaning states, the White House press pool reported, noting that the American leader continued his speech nevertheless.
Police escorted one of the protesters out of the venue in handcuffs. Others were escorted out without handcuffs, or left on their own. A Trump supporter attacked one of the protesters as he was leaving the hall. "These are paid protesters. They're paid by enemies of our nation. Now, I'm telling you, they pay them for this," the US leader emphasized.
The US president is traveling across the country and speaking to his supporters ahead of the US midterm congressional elections, which will take place on November 3. In these elections, 33 of the 100 members of the Senate (the upper house of the US Congress) and all 435 members of the House of Representatives (the lower house of Congress) will be up for re-election. Republicans currently control both houses of Congress.

title: 2027 Hajj: Sokoto PWA seeks state passport offices
body: By Musa Ubandawaki, Sokoto The Sokoto State Pilgrims Welfare Agency, PWA, has called for the decentralisation of passport offices from Abuja and Lagos to states across the country, saying the current arrangement is creating administrative bottlenecks in the processing of travel documents for intending pilgrims ahead of the 2027 Hajj. Chairman of the agency, Alhaji Aliyu Musa, made the call in an interview in Sokoto, identifying passport processing as one of the major logistical challenges confronting Pilgrims Welfare Agencies during Hajj preparations. Musa said restricting passport services largely to Abuja and Lagos had placed pressure on state pilgrims’ welfare agencies, particularly those coordinating large numbers of intending pilgrims within tight timelines for documentation and visa processing. According to him, decentralising passport services to the states would reduce delays, ease pressure on pilgrims and enable welfare agencies to complete documentation more efficiently before the commencement of the annual pilgrimage. “The centralisation of passport offices in Abuja and Lagos is creating administrative bottlenecks for Pilgrims Welfare Agencies across the states. “There is an urgent need to decentralise passport services so that intending pilgrims can obtain and process their travel documents closer to their places of residence,” he said. The PWA chairman stressed that Hajj preparations operated within strict timelines, making timely access to passports and other travel documents critical to the success of the exercise. He noted that requiring intending pilgrims and state agencies to depend on only two major centres for passport-related services could result in unnecessary movement, additional expenses, congestion and delays, particularly during peak periods of Hajj preparations. Musa therefore appealed to the Federal Government and relevant authorities responsible for passport administration to consider establishing functional passport offices in all states or strengthening existing state-level facilities. He said such decentralisation would benefit intending pilgrims and strengthen coordination between state Pilgrims Welfare Agencies and federal authorities responsible for documentation and visa processing. PWA clarifies 2027 registration Meanwhile, Musa clarified that the Sokoto State PWA had not commenced fresh registration for the 2027 Hajj following the allocation of additional slots to the state by the National Hajj Commission of Nigeria, NAHCON. He explained that the additional slots were specifically allocated to intending pilgrims who had already paid their Hajj fares but could not be registered because the state’s initial quota had been exhausted. “The additional allocation is not for new applicants. It is meant for intending pilgrims who had already paid but could not secure seats because the available slots were limited at the time of registration,” Musa said. He urged members of the public to disregard rumours and unverified reports that the agency had commenced another round of registration. Musa advised intending pilgrims to rely exclusively on official information from the Sokoto PWA and NAHCON. He also commended the support of Sokoto State Governor, Ahmed Aliyu, for the annual Hajj operation, saying the governor had continued to provide backing to facilitate the welfare and smooth coordination of pilgrims from the state. Musa assured intending pilgrims that the agency would continue to pursue a transparent and orderly Hajj process while working with NAHCON and other relevant authorities to address administrative challenges and ensure that pilgrims were adequately prepared for the 2027 pilgrimage. title: Eurobond repayment: Ghana faces US$6.4bn repayment burden between 2027 and 2030 – World Bank
body: Ghana faces Eurobond repayment of US$6.4 billion with interest between 2027 and 2030, the World Bank has revealed. In Africa, South Africa faces the largest repayment burden of US$11.8 billion, with maturities in every year of the period. It is followed by Ghana (US$6.4 billion), Nigeria (US$6.4 billion), and Angola (US$3.9 billion), whose maturity profiles reflect a combination of pre-restructuring borrowing and post-restructuring exchange instruments. Kenya (US$3.2 billion), Côte d’Ivoire (US$2.8 billion), and Zambia (US$2.2 billion) complete the next tier of maturities. According to the October 2026 Africa Economic Update, redemption pressures were particularly acute in 2024, when Côte d’Ivoire, Ethiopia, Kenya, Senegal, and Zambia collectively faced approximately US$6.4 billion in maturing obligations, making it the most concentrated repayment year in the current cycle. Additionally, liability management operations by Angola, Kenya, and Côte d’Ivoire have reduced the 2028 concentration to approximately US$5.5 billion, but refinancing pressures remain significant across the remainder of the window — with 2029 ($7.5billion) and 2027 ($6.6 billion) carrying the largest forthcoming concentrations. Maturing Eurobonds has Been Refinancing For most sovereigns, the World Bank said primary response to maturing Eurobonds has been refinancing rather than repaying from fiscal resources or restructuring. Kenya rolled over its US$2 billion Eurobond maturing in 2024 through a US$1.5 billion issuance at a yield of 10.4%, supplemented by budget resources, thereby extending maturities while increasing future debt service costs relative to the original 6.9% coupon. Ghana also addressed its Eurobond obligations through the debt exchange completed in October 2024, converting defaulted bonds into restructured instruments. Zambia successfully completed a historic liability management operation to buy back and permanently cancel its outstanding US$ 1.36 billion Fixed-Rate Step-Up Amortizing Notes due 2053. Ethiopia’s US$1 billion debut Eurobond, which matured in December 2024 after the country entered default in late 2023, was restructured following an Agreement in Principle reached with private bondholders on June 29, 2026, resolving a prolonged impasse in negotiations. Meanwhile, the total Sub-Saharan African sovereign Eurobond principal maturing between 2024 and 2030 amounts to approximately US$43.6 billion across 13 countries, after adjusting for buybacks and liability management operations completed through August 2026.

title: EU tasks Sokoto Assembly on budget oversight, digital parliament
body: By Musa Ubandawaki, Sokoto The European Union, EU, has urged the Sokoto State House of Assembly to strengthen its oversight of public spending, improve legislative capacity and ensure that approved budgets translate into measurable improvements in the lives of citizens, particularly vulnerable groups. The call was made during a policy dialogue involving the EU, development partners and lawmakers on budget implementation, legislative effectiveness, social protection and institutional accountability. The EU, through its representatives, stressed that effective legislative oversight was essential to ensuring that public funds were released and utilised for the purposes for which they were appropriated. Head of UNICEF Field Office in Sokoto, Michael Juma, said continuous capacity development was necessary for the Assembly to effectively discharge its constitutional responsibilities. Juma said lawmakers needed stronger expertise in legislation, policy formulation, budget scrutiny, standard operating procedures and monitoring of government programmes to ensure that public spending achieved the desired results. He also commended the Assembly for embracing programme-based budgeting, describing it as a system capable of linking government expenditure to specific targets, expected results and measurable development outcomes. Juma urged lawmakers to pay particular attention to the timely release and effective utilisation of funds allocated to social programmes, warning that delays could undermine interventions targeted at children, women, persons with disabilities and other vulnerable groups. He also commended the state for allocating more than 16 per cent of its budget to education and other social sectors, stressing that sustained investment in human development remained important to addressing poverty and vulnerability. EU seeks stronger social protection EU Programme Manager for Social Protection in Nigeria, Chioma Osuji, acknowledged the Sokoto State Government’s commitment to social protection, particularly the establishment of a dedicated committee in the Assembly and the inclusion of social protection in the state budget. Osuji said institutionalising social protection through legislative and budgetary processes would provide a stronger foundation for sustainable interventions. She urged the state to strengthen its Social Registry to ensure that assistance reached the poorest and most vulnerable residents. She added that the EU was supporting Sokoto in areas including health, education and durable solutions, expressing confidence that the state would gradually assume greater ownership of the programmes. Assembly seeks support for Tsangaya reform, digitalisation Responding, the Majority Leader of the Assembly and Chairman of the House Committee on Social Protection, Hon. Muhammad Bello Idris, said the legislature valued its partnership with the EU, UNICEF and other development partners. Idris said lawmakers had benefited from several capacity-building initiatives supported by the development partners. He disclosed that the Assembly was considering the integration of English Language and Mathematics into the Almajiri and Tsangaya education system, describing the proposal as timely for equipping children with basic literacy and numeracy skills. He said budgetary provision had already been made for the initiative, adding that the Assembly would examine the proposal to ensure the necessary appropriation and legislative backing for its implementation. The Majority Leader also appealed to the EU and other development partners to support the Assembly’s transition from largely manual parliamentary operations to a fully digital legislative system. According to him, digitalisation would improve efficiency, transparency, documentation and access to legislative records. Representing the Speaker, Rt. Hon. Tukur Bala Bodinga, the Deputy Speaker, Hon. Kabiru Ibrahim Kware, assured the EU and other partners that the Assembly would continue to strengthen its constitutional oversight role. Kware said the legislature would also collaborate with development partners on initiatives aimed at improving democratic governance, accountability and service delivery. The Clerk of the House, Almustapha Sidi Attahiru, similarly called for additional support to strengthen the capacity of lawmakers and legislative staff in social protection, legislative research, policy development and parliamentary administration. The EU delegation reaffirmed its readiness to deepen collaboration with the Assembly in budget oversight, digitalisation, social protection and institutional development. title: Greek State Fined Another €20,000 Over Coco-Mat Hotel Demolition Near Acropolis
body: Greece’s Council of State has imposed another €20,000 fine on the Ministry of Finance for failing to demolish the top floors of the controversial Coco-Mat hotel near the Acropolis. The latest penalty concerns the hotel’s final two floors and rooftop structure , which exceed the legally permitted height in Makrygianni’s designated archaeological zone. The building stands approximately 33 metres high, compared with the permitted 24 metres . The Council of State has now issued three financial penalties over the authorities’ failure to fully comply with its landmark 2019 ruling. The latest decision, issued by the court’s three-member Compliance Council, found that the administration had not yet fully implemented the ruling, despite progress towards the demolition. The original 2019 ruling cancelled the building permit for the 10-storey hotel, which also includes three underground levels, a planted rooftop and an uncovered swimming pool. The court noted that approximately seven years have passed since the ruling , while about five years have passed since compliance proceedings began. Two previous penalties had already been imposed, including a €10,000 fine issued in April 2026 . Neither has yet been paid to the citizens who brought the proceedings. Citing the need to protect the monuments of the Acropolis, the Acropolis Museum and the surrounding environment , the court ordered the administration to pay the additional €20,000. If the Ministry of Finance fails to pay, responsibility will pass to the Decentralised Administration of Attica . The case continues to highlight the long-running dispute over the hotel’s height and its impact on the protected landscape surrounding the Acropolis, one of Greece’s most important archaeological and cultural sites. title: Canada Introduces Bill C-40 to Establish Defence Investment Agency
body: The world is more dangerous and divided. The international rules-based order is fading, and global conflict rages on. Canada’s Government is focused on what we can control: rebuilding, rearming, and reinvesting in the Canadian Armed Forces (CAF). In October 2025, Canada’s new government established the Defence Investment Agency (DIA) to overhaul and streamline our defence procurement. Since then, the DIA has facilitated key purchases that strengthen Canada’s strategic autonomy. In a rapidly changing world, Canada must move quicker to keep Canadians safe. That is why the Government of Canada introduced Bill C-40: Strengthening Canada’s Defence Sector , to establish the DIA as a Crown corporation. This reform will provide the DIA with the authorities, operational flexibility, specialized expertise and organizational structure needed to deliver critical capabilities quicker. The DIA will have greater commercial flexibility and more autonomous approvals, allowing it to work better with industry and deliver better value for money. It will maximise Canada’s generational defence investments to strengthen our industrial base, supply chains, and sovereign capabilities. This legislation: Creates the Canadian Corporation for Defence Investment, which will continue to operate under its existing name, the Defence Investment Agency. It will have more independence, its own Board of Directors, and greater authority to negotiate and manage contracts; Empowers the DIA to engage in defence production, procurement, and investment activities in support of national defence and the operational priorities, capability requirements and acceptance criteria established by the National Defence (DND) and the Canadian Armed Forces (CAF); Maintains the Government of Canada’s oversight of the new Crown Corporation; Amends the National Defence Act to create an Associate Minister of National Defence for Procurement, who will be responsible to Parliament for the DIA, consolidate procurement and commercial authorities and strengthen accountability for procurement delivery within the National Defence portfolio, and Integrates the DIA with the National Defence portfolio to further reduce red tape that slows procurement down and ensures that defence procurement in Canada is focused on equipping the National Defence and CAF with the tools they need to defend Canada. Bill C-40: Strengthening Canada’s Defence Sector represents the next step in the Government of Canada’s modernization and transformation of Canadian defence procurement. The DIA was launched to accelerate procurement and use defence spending to strengthen Canadian industry, build sovereign capabilities, and catalysing investment in the Canadian defence sector. As a Crown corporation it will have the commercial tools to deliver on its mandate. It will support Canada’s security and long-term economic growth, while remaining accountable to Parliament, and the Government of Canada. The DIA will continue to strengthen Canada’s ability to work with allies and security partners. The Corporation would support joint defence procurement programs, including initiatives aligned with Canada’s participation in Security Action for Europe (SAFE) and Readiness 2030. Greater international collaboration will improve interoperability, provide Canadian suppliers with greater access to allied markets and supply chains, capitalize on economies of scale, and support Canada’s broader security and diplomatic objectives. Canada is making generation investments to transform our defence sector. Empowered as a Crown corporation, the DIA will harness defence investment to catalyse industry, secure critical supply chains, and drive innovation and investment. In a rapidly changing world Canada’s government is building a stronger, more self-reliant country. One that is fully ready for the future. One that guarantees Canadians have tools needed to protect our country. “Canada is making a generational investment in our defence and security, and we need institutions built to match the scale and urgency of that ambition. Establishing the Defence Investment Agency as a Crown corporation would give it the flexibility and specialized expertise to move faster, make strategic investments and deliver the capabilities our Armed Forces need. Just as importantly, it would allow us to use our defence investments to strengthen our sovereignty while building a robust Canadian defence industry, attracting investment and creating lasting economic opportunities and good jobs here at home.” The Honourable Stephen Fuhr Secretary of State (Defence Procurement) “We look forward to continued collaboration with the Defence Investment Agency to further strengthen defence procurement. As a Crown corporation within the National Defence portfolio, the DIA will have the direct authorities and added flexibility to streamline procurement so that the Canadian Armed Forces and Canadian Coast Guard have more secure, reliable and quicker access to the capabilities they need to protect our sovereignty and keep Canadians safe.” The Honourable David J. McGuinty Minister of National Defence “In a more dangerous and divided world, Canada is taking action and establishing a clear and compelling path forward. With the introduction of this legislation, we are making clear that large-scale, agile defence production and procurement is here to stay. Procurement and investment must live together, by connecting the capabilities our armed forces need with the investments that will deliver them and the industrial capacity that will sustain them. As a Crown corporation, the Defence Investment Agency will integrate these priorities, delivering critical capabilities to our armed forces more efficiently while strengthening Canadian industry, driving innovation and creating economic opportunity for years to come.” The Honourable Joël Lightbound Minister of Government Transformation, Public Works and Procurement and Quebec Lieutenant “Establishing the Defence Investment Agency as a Crown corporation is an important step in building the organization Canada needs to meet today’s defence and security challenges. It will give the DIA the tools, flexibility, and expertise to move faster and make strategic investments that deliver capabilities for the Canadian Armed Forces and the Canadian Coast Guard. Our responsibility will be to turn Canada’s defence investments into results, strengthening our industrial base, building sovereign capacity, deepening partnerships with industry, and creating economic opportunities at home. I am proud of what the DIA team has accomplished since our launch, and I look forward to leading this transition and the organization’s next chapter.” Doug Guzman Chief Executive Officer, Defence Investment Agency ADDITIONAL INFO The DIA was initially established as a Special Operating Agency within Public Services and Procurement Canada, allowing the organization to begin operations while the Government of Canada developed its longer-term organizational model. Establishing the DIA as a Crown corporation within the National Defence portfolio is intended reduce handoffs, consolidate procurement and commercial authorities and strengthen accountability for procurement delivery. By consolidating responsibility and expertise within one organization, the DIA will reduce duplication, streamline decision-making, and accelerate procurement from validated requirement definition to contract award, while DND, the CAF and the CCG retain responsibility for defining capability requirements, operational priorities and acceptance criteria. The DIA is a central delivery partner for Canada’s Defence Industrial Strategy and its Build–Partner–Buy approach to defence procurement. The proposed Corporation will be accountable to the Government of Canada through a responsible Minister and subject to legislated governance, financial, audit, reporting and parliamentary oversight requirements. The post Canada Introduces Bill C-40 to Establish Defence Investment Agency appeared first on Canadian Defence Review .

title: Ability to fix errors in referendum ballot packages show system works: Alberta premier
body:
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith says the fact the provincial election authority is helping voters correct errors in about 3,000 mail-in ballot packages shows the system is working.
It comes after Elections Alberta announced those referendum ballot packages were returned with either declaration forms missing or with other errors, like missing the required copies of identification.
At an unrelated news conference Wednesday, Smith said the ability for electors to correct the necessary documents in time for their vote to be counted shows Elections Alberta is managing the situation as expected.
“I think that’s a sign the system works,” she said.
Smith and Elections Alberta also noted the problematic ballot packages represent a small number of those that have been sent back by voters — only 1.2 per cent of around 250,000.
Maia Hanrahan at Elections Alberta said in an email Wednesday they’ve contacted those whose packages had problems and are helping voters make the necessary fixes.
“Similar to an in-person voting experience where an election officer would assist the elector in making sure their information was correct and complete, that is what is happening with these special ballots – we are assisting electors in correcting their errors,” Hanrahan wrote.
She said voters are able to provide the required information via email, but if they do not, their special ballots will be rejected.
“Already we have had many people respond and provide the required information.”
Albertans are to vote on a series of questions on Oct. 19, including whether to stay in Canada or begin the process to hold a second, binding referendum on leaving Confederation. The other nine questions pertain to immigration and the Constitution.

title: CrowdStrike says China-based suspect used AI tools in South Korean bank hacks
body: SEOUL, South Korea – The suspect behind recent cyberattacks targeting South Korea’s financial sector may be a 26-year-old based in China’s Guangdong province who used a Chinese-developed AI agent toolcalled ARTEX and Anthropic’s ClaudeCode, US cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike said. In a report published on Wednesday, October 7, CrowdStrike said it uncovered personal details linked to the suspected attacker while analyzing AI coding-tool sessions and infrastructure associated with a campaign targeting South Korean financial institutions from late September to early October. The case is likely to intensify concerns over the rise of AI agents and whether organizations are prepared to defend their systems against them. Australia said last month that an OpenAI autonomous agent breached a government health statistics portal in June, marking one of the first known instances of an AI agent hacking a government system. CrowdStrike said the attacker used ARTEX, a recently released Chinese-developed open-source penetration testing tool, alongside large language models such as Claude. “While this activity has not been attributed to a named adversary, the threat actor is likely a Chinese speaker and financially motivated,” it said. “This assessment is made with moderate confidence based on the use of the Chinese-developed tool ARTEX and observed Chinese-language prompts.” Bank hacks CrowdStrike said the individual also asked Claude where threat actors typically sell Korean data breach information and sought assistance in finding Korean Telegram data sales groups. In another session, the person also requested Claude to create a security researcher resume, which included details such as a Telegram account, age, educational background and a location in Maoming, a city in the southern Chinese province of Guangdong, which CrowdStrike said likely belonged to the attacker. A man who answered a phone number provided by CrowdStrike in its report said he had no knowledge of the matter. Anthropic, South Korean police and China’s foreign ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment. ARTEX is an open-source AI agent for automated penetration testing that was published on GitHub this year by a Chinese security engineer with the handle Autumn. It is not a standalone large language model but connects to external LLMs such as ChatGPT, Claude and DeepSeek to help organisations test for vulnerabilities in the networks. The tool’s GitHub page says it is intended for personal learning, code research and local technical verification and should not be used to conduct real-world testing against online systems or websites. At least nine South Korean banks have disclosed or have been reported by local media as having been targeted by cyberattacks since late September, prompting South Korean police to launch a probe this week and President Lee Jae Myung to call for robust response measures. Shinhan Bank said last week that personal information of about 25,000 of its customers was compromised, while KB Kookmin Bank said that the personal information of 119 of its customers was leaked. – Rappler.com

title: Ukraine to have dry weather on Thursday, temperatures up to 24°C
body:
According to Ukrinform, the Ukrainian Hydrometeorological Center reported this on Facebook .
"On October 8, the weather pattern in Ukraine will result in comfortable, very warm and dry weather. As an atmospheric front approaches from Western Europe, pressure will begin to fall, more noticeably in the Right-Bank part of Ukraine and, during the day, in the north of the Left Bank. Air currents over Ukraine will shift from warm westerly winds to even warmer southerly winds," the statement said.
According to forecasters, no precipitation is expected.
In the southern part of the country, as well as in Kharkiv and Luhansk regions, fog is possible locally at night and in the morning.
Winds will be predominantly southerly at 5–10 m/s, with gusts of 15–20 m/s possible in parts of the Carpathians during the day.

title: Government to add 100 new ambulances to national fleet in 2027
body: The government will add 100 new ambulances to Ghana’s national fleet in 2027 as part of efforts to strengthen emergency medical services. Health Minister Kwabena Mintah Akandoh announced the plan during an interview on Joy News’ PM Express on Wednesday. He said the government inherited a situation in which several ambulances were grounded, and none of the existing ambulances was insured. According to him, the government has since insured the ambulance fleet and restored many of the vehicles to service. “As I speak to you now, we have more than 200 ambulances functioning,” Mr Akandoh said. He added that the government would replenish the fleet in 2027. “We are going to replenish the fleet in 2027. We are going to add brand new 100 vehicles,” he said. The Minister was also asked how the new ambulances would be distributed, particularly whether the government would continue the previous “one constituency, one ambulance” approach. He said no final decision had been taken on the distribution model. Mr Akandoh, however, suggested that areas with faulty or non-functional ambulances could be prioritised. “We have not taken the decision yet, but I believe that if you have an ambulance within a particular area, and that ambulance is faulty, or is no longer functional, it’s only fair to replace that ambulance,” he said. He said the government was also considering the strengths and weaknesses of the previous distribution system. “But then we think about what they did, the pros and cons of the system we’ve tried: can we continue, or do we have to review it as a country?” he said. The ambulance expansion forms part of wider measures being pursued by the Health Ministry to improve emergency care. Mr Akandoh said more than 200 ambulances are currently functioning, while an electronic emergency bed management system is being piloted. The system, he said, will give health authorities visibility over available emergency beds and help manage the limited capacity more effectively. “We have started the piloting. We have the command centre at Ridge Hospital,” he said. He said the system would also help authorities identify patients who remain in emergency units for more than 24 hours and prompt questions about why they have not been moved. The Minister said the government is also expanding emergency capacity at major facilities, including Komfo Anokye Teaching Hospital, Tamale Teaching Hospital, Korle Bu Teaching Hospital and the 37 Military Hospital. He said the measures are part of efforts to implement recommendations to improve Ghana’s emergency care system.

title: Russian Opposition Condemns EU Decision to Lift Usmanov Sanctions Without Freeing Political Prisoners
body:
Russian opposition figures accused Europe of showing weakness by lifting sanctions on Kremlin-linked billionaire Alisher Usmanov without securing the release of any Russian political prisoners, warning that the decision demonstrated how easily European governments could be pressured.
Speaking at an event in the French National Assembly on Wednesday, Oct. 7, exiled Russian opposition politician Ilya Yashin called the decision a “mistake” that had demoralized supporters of democracy in Russia.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“We believe it demonstrated Europe’s weakness. It sent a signal that Europe can be pressured into easing sanctions,” Yashin said, according to AFP.
The criticism follows France’s successful push last month to remove Russian-Uzbek billionaire Usmanov, 73, from the EU sanctions list as part of negotiations linked to the release of French citizen Martin Ryan, who was imprisoned in Azerbaijan on espionage charges.
Another Russian billionaire, Mikhail Fridman, 62, was also removed from the EU blacklist in a separate concession sought by other EU members. Both businessmen had been sanctioned following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 over their economic ties to the Kremlin.
Yashin acknowledged that France had acted in what it considered its national interests but said the decision had “nevertheless caused great disappointment and demoralization among supporters of democracy in Russia.”
“There are times when difficult decisions have to be made,” he said. “But in such situations, it is necessary to at least raise the cost.”
“What is profoundly disappointing is that Usmanov’s removal from the sanctions list did not lead to the release of a single Russian political prisoner,” Yashin said, adding that the issue had apparently not even been raised during the negotiations.
“That is deeply disappointing, despite all due respect for France.”
Another Kremlin critic, former Russian deputy energy minister Vladimir Milov, warned that allowing Usmanov to escape sanctions could have broader security consequences.
Milov said Usmanov was “capable of causing enormous harm to the national security of France if he remains exempt from sanctions.”
“I do not think everyone in France fully realizes this fact,” he added.
The controversy centers on Azerbaijan, whose involvement in negotiations over Usmanov’s sanctions helped secure the release of French citizen Martin Ryan.
Ryan had been sentenced to 10 years in prison on espionage charges that France rejected as unfounded. On Sept. 23, a day after the EU removed Usmanov from its sanctions list, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev pardoned Ryan alongside 19 other prisoners.
In Azerbaijan itself, reports of Baku’s role in securing sanctions relief for Usmanov prompted criticism from civil society activists, who questioned why their government had intervened on behalf of a Kremlin-linked billionaire.
The case also raised questions about Azerbaijan’s motives and what the country stood to gain from helping Usmanov.
Baku denied interfering in European sanctions decisions, although Azerbaijani officials acknowledged that their government had repeatedly supported efforts to remove Usmanov from Western blacklists.
An Azerbaijani diplomat told Reuters that Baku had joined other members of the Organization of Turkic States in sending letters to Western leaders advocating sanctions relief for Usmanov, describing him as an influential philanthropist who promoted relations between Central Asia and the West.
Azerbaijani human rights campaigners have repeatedly called for the release of imprisoned journalists, opposition figures and civil society activists.
The agreement also caused controversy within the European Union, with Ukraine strongly opposing sanctions relief for businessmen linked to the Kremlin while Russia continues its war.
Despite the removal of Usmanov and Fridman, the EU agreed to extend its broader sanctions regime against Russia for three years.
At the French parliamentary event, Russian human rights campaigner Oleg Orlov urged European lawmakers to prioritize the release of prisoners jailed for opposing the Kremlin.
Orlov, co-chair of Memorial, the Nobel Peace Prize-winning Russian human rights organization, warned that some prisoners might not survive their sentences.
“While there is still a chance, we must save at least some of those who will not survive imprisonment,” Orlov said, according to AFP.
He urged French lawmakers to take responsibility for individual prisoners and publicly follow their cases.
“It would be very important for members of parliament to take symbolic responsibility for specific political prisoners, to monitor their fate, and to speak about them publicly.”
According to Memorial, more than 1,800 people are recognized as political prisoners in Russia, while approximately 5,700 are imprisoned or facing prosecution for politically motivated reasons.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Museveni’s Confession on Dangote’s Day
body: Olusegun Adeniyi Last week Wednesday in Lamu county on the Kenyan coast, a Nigerian businessman stood before East African leaders to break ground on a $16 billion refinery complex that did not exist even as an idea six months ago. And he promised to be back in 40 months to commission an industrial complex that will process about 700,000 barrels of crude a day, generate 1,000 megawatts of power and produce a million tonnes of polypropylene a year, with some 60,000 people employed during construction. I was there to witness history and I took notes. But the most arresting line of the day did not come from Alhaji Aliko Dangote or the host President William Ruto of Kenya. It came from President Yoweri Museveni of Uganda. Evidently a popular figure in East Africa, Museveni was hailed by every speaker, including President Ruto, as their ‘father’ and quite naturally, he spoke at the occasion where he was also warmly received by the crowd. He started with all the Marxist jargon (bourgeoisie, comprador, proletariat etc.) that many of us used to entertain ourselves back in the days on campus at Ife. He then expressed delight at seeing Dangote helping to rewrite the story of Africa beyond “this 70-year betrayal of exporting raw materials and importing finished products.” To underscore his point, Museveni did the arithmetic with coffee. A kilogramme of Ugandan beans, once husked, earns about two dollars. Roasted and packaged in another country, according to Museveni, the same kilogramme sells for forty dollars. He made the same comparative deductions with cotton and gold. Done with the first of his four-point intervention, Museveni moved to the second. Uganda will still build its own ‘small’ refinery at Hoima and that, while he supports the Lamu project, he will not put Ugandan money in it until he has found out from President Samia Suluhu Hassan of Tanzania what became of an earlier plan for a refinery at Tanga. His third point was a renewed call for the political federation of East Africa, on the premise that while shares in a refinery sited in Kenya may bring Uganda profit, it will not answer the question of jobs for his people. The fourth and final point by Museveni, offered almost in passing, was a confession: Dangote, he disclosed, had come to Uganda before but made no investment. “I didn’t know that some people were disturbing him with bribes,” Museveni said. Before I deal with the substantive issue, what struck me most in Lamu was the gathering itself. The Presidents of Kenya, Uganda, Benin and Togo were in attendance. So was the Prime Minister of Ethiopia, Dr Abiy Ahmed. The bereaved President of Tanzania (she recently lost her husband) sent a representative and so did the Presidents of Rwanda, South Sudan, Somalia and Burundi. Former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo was also there with the Minister of State for Petroleum Resources (Oil), Senator Heineken Lokpobiri. I can think of regional summits that have not drawn that kind of attendance. And this was a private citizen, who holds no office and commands no army, getting leaders from West and East Africa to gather on a stretch of the Kenyan coast to watch him dig. That convening power is what private capital looks like when it has a track record. President Ruto was quite candid about this. The Lamu project, he said, is enabled by government but driven by the private sector, because no government can borrow or tax its way to every factory, port and power plant. Now, let me come back to Museveni. If the ‘African betrayal’ is 70 years old, questions must also be asked of the man lamenting it. Museveni took power in Kampala in January 1986 (40 years ago) and most Ugandans alive today have known no other president. That ‘betrayal’ is also part of his legacy in so many ways. Commercially viable crude oil deposits were confirmed in Uganda’s Albertine Graben in 2006. By Museveni’s own account in Lamu, that oil has still not come out of the ground, and he told the audience why: “Because I refused to export petroleum without a refinery.” As a principle, that is admirable. If you cannot process, you should not export. But a principle is not a refinery. In February 2015, Uganda selected a consortium led by Russia’s RT Global Resources to build one, and the Russians walked away the following year. In April 2018, an agreement was signed with the Albertine Graben Refinery Consortium for a plant of 60,000 barrels per day. It lapsed in June 2023 without a final investment decision. In March last year, a fresh agreement was signed with Alpha MBM Investments of the United Arab Emirates. Nothing has come out of it. Twenty years of planning. Three sets of partners. Not one barrel! Meanwhile, the refinery Dangote conceived in April this year will have nearly twelve times the capacity of the one Uganda has spent two decades trying to build! Finally, let’s come to the fourth of Museveni’s points. The biggest industrial investor on the continent went to Uganda looking for where to put his money. Some people, presumably with the power to say yes or no, asked him for theirs first. He left. And the president did not tell us that he held anybody accountable. That, right there, is the betrayal. It was not committed by a coffee roaster in Europe or a commodity trader in Geneva. It was committed at home, under a leader who has had 40 years to find out what goes on in his own government. It says a lot that President Ruto felt the need to reassure Dangote that nobody in Kenya would be allowed to extort anything from him. No president should have to say that to an investor at a public ceremony. But everybody in the audience understood why he did. It would be unfair to make Museveni carry the failure of a whole continent. The natural resources have always been here. So is the market. The challenge is about what we do with them. From the Lagos Plan of Action in 1980 to Agenda 2063, African leaders have never been short on declarations on industrialisation. What they have been short of is delivery. According to Afreximbank figures cited by Ruto, Africa produced about 6.8 million barrels of crude oil a day in 2024 and consumed about 4.5 million barrels a day of refined products, much of it bought back from abroad. Kenya alone spent KSh530 billion (about 4.1 billion dollars) importing petroleum products last year. However, before Nigerians laugh at Uganda, we should remember that the lamentation of Museveni is ours too. I once recalled Obasanjo’s admission that none of the 18 refinery licences he approved while in office was ever actualised just as many have written on the billions of dollars sunk into the endless turn-around maintenance of government-owned refineries. Dangote told the audience that the Lamu project “started like a joke” in April, when President Ruto sent emissaries to him to discuss buying fertiliser. Ruto’s version is that he wrote Dangote a letter that same month, inviting him to an infrastructure summit convened in Kenya with the Africa Finance Corporation, and asked him to imagine a refining platform for East Africa. Either way, the idea is barely six months old. By 30 September, the land had been set aside, the first equipment was on site, heads of government had been assembled and a completion date had been fixed. None of this should surprise anyone who followed the Lekki story. When Dangote decided to build a refinery in Nigeria, he recalled in Lamu, many said it was impossible. The project was too big, the financing too difficult, the engineering too complex. “Some doubted us. Some dismissed us. Some even mocked the scale of our ambition.” The Lekki refinery took far longer and cost far more than its promoter first imagined, as Dangote has often admitted. But Lekki now stands, and it is on the strength of that record that he could say in Kenya: “Lekki proved that it can be done. Lamu must prove that it can be repeated.” Addressing African leaders directly, Dangote said his group has $50 billion to roll out under a plan that ends in 2030, across infrastructure, minerals, ports, power and petrochemicals. “All you have to do is tell us what you want and our team is ready to work with you.” African businessmen used to visit presidential villas to ask for things. In Lamu, a Nigerian businessman stood before presidents and asked what they needed. There is one more thing we should give to Dangote. What he builds is never just a plant. The Lekki complex sits on 2,635 hectares, about seven times the size of Victoria Island. Lamu is Kenya’s least populous county with about 175,705 people (the 2019 Census Baseline recorded 143,920 residents). Dangote told the people that where they were standing, “an industrial city will begin to emerge,” and promised a school to train 1,000 local engineers and technicians. Meanwhile, shortly before the ceremony in Lamu, the Environment and Land Court in Malindi ordered the parties to maintain the status quo in a suit filed by 133 residents of Chandavai who say the site is their ancestral land. The case comes up next Wednesday (14 October). It is not a frivolous matter. Lamu Old Town is a UNESCO World Heritage site and its fishermen want to know what happens to their waters. Ruto, to his credit, told the people of Lamu that such questions are not obstacles to development but what responsible development must answer. Dangote himself said industrialisation must have a human face. Both men should be held to their words. With the African leaders in Lamu taking turns to eulogise Dangote, it was little surprise that they would call for more entrepreneurs like him. But in the separate conversations I had with some people on our punishing journey—which was almost like military troop deployment—including auntie Fatima Wali-Abdurrahman, Mr Asue Ighodalo, Mr Stanley Jegede and Mr Robert Ade-Odiachi (uncle Robbie), I said what we need is not necessarily more Dangotes but more entrepreneurs with his can-do spirit, especially among the young generation. We need to reverse this idea of chasing bubble government appointments and redirect their minds to entrepreneurship. Readers of this page already know where I stand on Dangote. As I wrote in May this year, Dangote and the Power Sector – THISDAYLIVE , Dangote has demonstrated the possibility of “a productive Nigerian capitalism and its extension to the rest of Africa.” Lamu is the latest in that extension. As a firm believer in local entrepreneurship as an engine for job creation and national development, the illustration I often use to defend the few big players we have in Dangote and Dr Mike Adenuga Jnr is the Biblical parable of talents that is set within the context of investment and productivity. In Lamu, Museveni brought the point home for me in a way he couldn’t have imagined. While both the first and second servants in the Biblical account made a hundred percent profit from what each was given, nobody knew about their business practices. Yet, as I once wrote, many Nigerian businesspeople have also been offered opportunities through the patronage system we run but they spend their winnings on vanities without adding any value to our society. These are billionaires who employ no more than drivers, cooks, gardeners, stewards and the likes—personal staff who merely minister to their indulgences and those of their families. From what the unproductive servant who buried his one talent in the Biblical parable tells us, which we can also see from the Museveni story in Lamu, not even a ‘monopolist’ can profit from a refinery that was never built! In his speech at Lamu, President Ruto said that the African leaders before them secured the flag for their countries and the task of his own generation is to build the industries that will make independence real. I completely agree with him. But between those two generations stands another, which has held the flag for 40 years and is still drawing up plans. Dangote has now shown them twice, first in Lekki and now in Lamu, what it looks like when somebody ‘gets on with the job’. Kenyans, Ruto warned Dangote, “are very good in keeping data” and they will count the 40 months he promised to deliver on the refinery. Just as well. But it is also a pity that nobody was counting the 40 years for Museveni and other African leaders for whom national development and the well-being of their people is forever ‘in the pipelines’ of unbuilt refineries! • You can follow me on my X handle, @Olusegunverdict and on www.olusegunadeniyi.com

title: Trump asks Pentagon for Iran strike options before midterms - report
body: The White House has asked the Pentagon to prepare options for strikes on Iran that could take place before the November 3 midterm elections, The Atlantic reported Wednesday, citing two administration officials.US Central Command is developing the options, a US official told the magazine. The potential targets, scope of an operation, and whether US President Donald Trump will authorize military action remain under discussion.According to the report, administration officials linked the planning to Trump's desire to show progress in the conflict and address high gasoline prices ahead of the vote.Supporters of limited strikes believe an operation could help the president present a military success before the elections, the magazine reported.However, even advocates acknowledged that such attacks alone would not secure an agreement with Tehran, restore safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz, or reduce gasoline prices before election day.White House weighs timing of renewed strikesThe Pentagon has also presented options for operations after the elections, ranging from limited attacks to a broader campaign that could include additional strikes on Iran's energy industry, according to The Atlantic.Some presidential advisers favor waiting until after the vote, the report said, amid concerns that renewed fighting, particularly if American troops are killed, could hurt Republican candidates.A White House official told the magazine that Trump “has all options available at any time,” but did not answer questions about the timing of potential strikes.The deliberations follow earlier reporting on preparations for possible escalation. The Jerusalem Post reported on October 2, citing The Washington Post, that the Pentagon was considering increasing its naval presence in the Middle East as Trump weighed renewed attacks after the elections. That report put the existing US deployment in the region at approximately 50,000 troops.Negotiations continue amid military planningWashington and Tehran are continuing to communicate through intermediaries, The Atlantic reported, although disagreements remain over a ceasefire, the US blockade, and reopening the Strait of Hormuz.The magazine also reported that Iranian attacks on shipping earlier this week had prompted some shipowners to reconsider transiting the waterway.The military planning comes alongside continuing disputes over Iran's nuclear program. In a Reuters interview published by The Jerusalem Post on Wednesday, Vice President JD Vance said an agreement would require concrete reductions in Iran's enrichment capacity.Vance also said Washington was uncertain how decisions were being made within Iran's leadership and how much authority its negotiating counterparts held.A senior Iranian official told Reuters on Wednesday that Washington's nuclear demands conflicted with Tehran's position, adding that recognition of Iran's right to enrichment remained a red line.

title: Ex-Spurs player Vega set to run for FIFA president
body: Former Tottenham Hotspur defender Ramon Vega says he intends to stand as a candidate in next year’s FIFA presidential election. The 55-year-old is the first person to confirm that they want to challenge Gianni Infantino, who has defied calls to step down in the wake of his failed plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors, a move that has sparked a major backlash across football. A former Switzerland centre-back, Vega also played for Celtic and Watford and has worked in finance since retiring from football in 2004. “I am standing to reunite the global football family, deliver genuine and lasting reform, modernise Fifa for the 21st Century, restore stability and credibility, and rebuild the trust that our game urgently needs,” he said. Meanwhile, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, president of the Asian Football Confederation, has written to Infantino, distancing himself from an external review of FIFA’s governance system. In his letter, seen by BBC Sport, Sheikh Salman proposes that FIFA’s council set up a working group to examine potential reforms, “rather than being outsourced to an external party”. Last month, Infantino said he was “fully committed to leading Fifa” despite Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation calling for him to quit. Vega considered running for Fifa’s top job in 2015 following the suspension of former president Sepp Blatter. Four years later, he said he would stand against Infantino, but failed to garner enough support to be included in the ballot, having required the backing of five of FIFA’s 211 member federations. Candidates must also be proposed by a member association, have played an active role in the game for two of the past five years, and pass an eligibility check by a review committee. “I am standing because my life has prepared me to serve the game,” Vega said in a statement announcing his candidacy. “Football does not belong to presidents, confederations or administrators. Football is greater than any position, any individual or any institution. “It is the people’s game and belongs to everyone: the players, coaches, referees, supporters, volunteers, clubs, leagues, associations and communities that give football its life. “It belongs to every child discovering the game, every professional carrying the hopes of a nation, and the billions of supporters whose passion makes football the world’s game. “Football must always come first. Yet for too long, division has fractured our football family. “The current leadership has demoralised the game. Weak governance has damaged FIFA’s credibility and eroded trust across the global football family. We must stop this conflict from escalating. “Ego-driven battles within football administration must never be allowed to damage those who matter most: the players, coaches, referees and supporters around the world. They are not responsible for these conflicts. They deserve better.” Vega concluded: “Football is in the emergency room, on life support. We cannot wait any longer. FIFA needs a new direction and fundamental reform. “We must reunite the football family, restore trust, bring stability and modernise FIFA’s governance. This requires decisive change – not cosmetic adjustments.” It comes with Sheikh Salman appearing to soften his stance towards Infantino just two months after the AFC president signed a joint letter with the heads of UEFA and CONCACAF accusing the FIFA president of breaking trust “through deception” over his FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) plan. At the time, the three confederations said any review of Fifa’s governance must be “conducted by a fully independent third party”. Now, however, Salman says he believes the process should be “driven by the football institutions themselves, rather than being outsourced to an external party”. He added: “I believe there is value in taking this opportunity to consider constructively whether Fifa’s existing governance arrangements can be strengthened. “The issue is not necessarily whether this requires a wholesale redesign of Fifa’s governance system.” FIFA’s council meets in Zurich next week for the first time since the FFE plan emerged in July.

title: 'Not yet out of danger': Israeli envoy to US shares update on son following terror attack
body: Israeli Ambassador to the US Yechiel Leiter, whose son Neria was seriously wounded during a car-ramming terrorist attack in September, said Wednesday that his son “has severe head injuries, but in recent days he has begun breathing on his own.”“He remains unconscious,” Leiter added in a video recorded for the Evangelical Christian community's memorial ceremony honoring the victims of October 7, held in Jerusalem.In an additional statement shared by the ambassador, the family clarified that despite several encouraging signs, Neria remains in very serious condition and is not yet out of danger.The Leiter family said Neria is receiving the best possible medical care in the intensive care unit at Shaare Zedek Medical Center in Jerusalem. The family thanked the medical staff and the public for their prayers and immense support and asked people to continue praying for the recovery of Neria Dov ben Chana.Seriously wounded in terror attack Neria Leiter, an IDF reservist and American citizen, was seriously wounded in a terrorist attack at the Bell checkpoint on Route 443.He underwent several hours of brain surgery at Shaare Zedek Medical Center, where his family later received a visit from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, The Jerusalem Post previously reported.The family also received numerous messages of support on X from Israeli leaders, including President Isaac Herzog, Defense Minister Israel Katz, and US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee.Pray for @yechielleiter & entire family. They lost a son in Gaza killed by Hamas. Now a Palestinian terrorist attempts to murder IDF soldiers at a checkpoint. Standing w/ @yechielleiter— Ambassador Mike Huckabee (@GovMikeHuckabee) September 23, 2026“Pray for Yechiel Leiter & entire family,” Huckabee wrote on X. “They lost a son in Gaza killed by Hamas. Now a Palestinian terrorist attempts to murder IDF soldiers at a checkpoint.”

title: Nnaji advocates increased funding for education
body: By Alumona Ukwueze NSUKKA — Former Minister of Power, Prof. Bart Nnaji, has called for increased funding of education at all levels, saying adequate investment in the sector is critical to building a globally competitive economy in the 21st century. Nnaji made the call on Wednesday in Nsukka while delivering the University of Nigeria, UNN, 66th Founders’ Day Lecture, titled, “Grappling with 21st Century Development Challenges through Higher Education in Nigeria.” He said Nigeria could not achieve sustainable economic development without substantial investment in education to strengthen institutions, promote research and drive technological innovation. The former minister urged governments at all levels to increase funding for education and promote strategic partnerships between universities and industries. According to him, such partnerships would strengthen collaboration between the academic and business sectors while bridging the gap between classroom knowledge and the skills required in the workplace. “I urge government at all levels to increase investments in education because records have shown that leading nations in economy and technology invest adequately in education. “With adequate investments in education, universities will not only produce graduates but also become centres of innovation, research and technological advancement capable of providing solutions to the country’s economic and developmental challenges,” he said. Nnaji, who is also Chairman of Geometric Power Group, stressed the need to prioritise Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics, STEM, education, noting that the future of the global economy increasingly depended on technological competence, innovation and the ability to develop home-grown solutions. He urged Nigerians to believe in themselves and have confidence in the younger generation, saying Nigerian youths possessed the talent and intellectual capacity to compete favourably with their counterparts globally if given the necessary opportunities and support. Nnaji also stressed the importance of competence and capacity in leadership, saying those entrusted with public responsibilities must possess the knowledge, ability and character required to deliver positive results. “Nigeria needs leaders who will think strategically, take difficult decisions and deploy available resources effectively for the benefit of the people,” he said. He, however, said Nigeria’s development challenges could not be addressed by government alone, urging universities, industries, professional bodies and other stakeholders to collaborate in developing the human capital required for national transformation. Nnaji commended UNN for sustaining the Founders’ Day Lecture, noting that its founder, Dr Nnamdi Azikiwe, envisioned the institution as a world-class university with global standards and a mandate to provide comprehensive education for Nigerians. He expressed appreciation to the university for finding him worthy to deliver the 66th Founders’ Day Lecture. The Chairman of the occasion and 13th Vice-Chancellor of UNN, Emeritus Prof. Bartholomew Okolo, said the university’s founding was anchored on a vision to establish an institution capable of attaining the highest standards of academic excellence. Okolo said the founding fathers of the university conceived a bold vision and mission that remained relevant to Nigeria’s development aspirations. The former vice-chancellor commended the current administration of the university, led by Prof. Simon Ortuanya, for its infrastructure transformation and efforts to improve the physical and academic environment. In his remarks, the Vice-Chancellor of UNN, Prof. Simon Ortuanya, said the Founders’ Day Lecture was instituted to commemorate the establishment of the university and honour the vision of its founder, Dr Nnamdi Azikiwe. Ortuanya said the annual lecture provided a platform for intellectual discourse on national and global issues, while promoting the ideals of the university’s founding fathers, encouraging scholarship and critical thinking, and reflecting on the role of the university in Nigeria’s socio-economic development. He said the best way to honour the founding fathers was not merely to celebrate their achievements but to sustain and advance the vision upon which the university was established. “Let us honour the founding fathers by finishing what they began,” Ortuanya said. title: Alberta, Saskatchewan premiers shut down Elon Musk’s call for separation
body:
The premiers of Alberta and Saskatchewan are shutting down a suggestion from U.S. tech titan Elon Musk that the two provinces should split from Canada.
The trillionaire tech businessman and former adviser to U.S. President Donald Trump said on his social media platform X that Quebec would benefit from independence, as would the two Prairie provinces.
Alberta and Saskatchewan should separate too.
Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe had a concise response to Musk on social media: “No.”
Moe has said he’s a true Canadian but wouldn’t halt a public vote on separation in Saskatchewan if residents petitioned for a plebiscite.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, who states she’s voting to stay in Canada in an upcoming provincial referendum, says she also strongly disagrees with Musk’s opinion.
On Oct. 19, Albertans go to the polls to decide if the province should stay in Canada or whether there should be a second binding referendum on separation.
While born in South Africa, Musk holds Canadian citizenship and has lived in several parts of the country.
His mother was born and raised in Saskatchewan, where the tech titan spent time working on a family farm as a teenager.
He moved on to Vancouver before attending Queen’s University in Ontario, where he met his first wife .
With files from Karen Bartko, Global News

title: AEDC expands digital channels for customer services
body: By Obas Esiedesa, Abuja ABUJA — The Abuja Electricity Distribution Plc, AEDC, has expanded its digital service channels with the launch of its MyPower Mobile and Web Apps to enable customers access and manage electricity services remotely. The platforms bring key customer services into a single digital ecosystem, allowing customers to purchase electricity tokens, pay bills, report power outages and other service issues, as well as lodge and track complaints without visiting AEDC offices. Customers can also use the platforms to monitor their energy consumption, access bills and payment receipts, manage multiple accounts and meters, and update their personal information digitally. A statement by the company on Wednesday said the launch, which formed part of its Customer Service Week activities, was part of AEDC’s broader digital transformation programme aimed at improving customer experience. Speaking at the launch, the Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer of AEDC, Engr. Chijioke Okwuokenye, said the initiative was designed to give customers greater control and convenience in their interactions with the company. He said: “Our customers are at the heart of everything we do. As their needs and expectations evolve, we must evolve with them. “The MyPower Mobile and Web Apps are significant steps in that direction, using technology to give our customers greater control over how they interact with AEDC and access the services they need.” Okwuokenye said AEDC remained committed to improving its customer service and building an organisation that was more responsive, accessible and aligned with customers’ expectations. The Chief Operating Officer of AEDC, Engr. Blessing Ogbe, said the digital platforms reflected the company’s commitment to continuously improving the customer journey. “For us, this launch is another step in how we are redefining the way we serve our customers. We are building a culture where customer feedback informs how we design our processes, improve our channels and deliver our services,” she said. Ogbe said the company would continue to listen, learn and innovate to ensure that its services kept pace with customers’ expectations. As part of the digital rollout, AEDC also introduced a staff verification feature that enables customers to confirm the identity of company personnel before granting them access to their premises. The company said customers who preferred mobile access could use the MyPower Mobile App, while those using computers or mobile browsers could access the Web App and enjoy similar services. title: Arteta signs new contract with champions Arsenal
body: Manager Mikel Arteta says this is “only the beginning” of Arsenal ‘s success after signing a new contract with the Premier League champions until 2030. BBC Sport reported earlier this month that an agreement had been made on an improved new contract. The Spaniard’s deal was set to expire at the end of this season, with his time in charge of the Gunners now possibly stretching to a decade following his arrival in December 2019. Atletico Madrid boss Diego Simeone is reportedly paid over £20m per year, as was former Manchester City manager Pep Guardiola – both of whom Arteta benchmarked his worth against. The new contract includes an increase from his current salary of £10m per year plus an additional £5m in bonuses. “This club is unique, its character and the way it makes you feel, and I have a great sense of privilege that our journey together will continue,” Arteta said. “We have already built a special bond and created memories that will last a lifetime, and what is so exciting is that this is only the beginning of what we can achieve together.” The 44-year-old has won a Premier League and FA Cup in charge of Arsenal , losing the Champions League final against Paris St-Germain in May. Arteta stay provides ‘competitive’ edge Guardiola’s departure from City at the end of last term made Arteta the longest-serving manager in the English top flight. And the Gunners’ chief executive, Richard Garlick, believes that factor will provide them with a “competitive advantage over the other teams” in the league. “Mikel is the only manager that’s won the Premier League that’s currently managing [in it],” he said. “You look at all the other teams in the sort of traditional top six, and they’ve all gone through managerial changes. “We’ve now got a manager who’s been with us for a significant period of time and has been allowed to build and develop a team over a period of time. “The excitement now is we see [the] platform that we’ve got and we build from there.” With Arsenal targeting a period of sustained success, Garlick added: “We can’t stand still. We can’t sit there, pat ourselves on the back, and say job done. “This is the beginning, not the end of our journey. This is where we want to go on and show the confidence that that win is going to bring to us. “We want to dominate football for the next number of years. We’re in a really strong position to do that, but we need to keep finding that edge that gives us that advantage.” Arteta wants to build a dynasty – analysis News of Arteta’s new deal at Arsenal won’t come as a shock. The fact his previous deal expired at the end of the season did put a slightly greater emphasis on the speed of discussions than normal. But Arteta has been transparent about his desire to stay at the club beyond the end of this campaign. Dynasty building is what has driven Arteta’s decision. Winning Arsenal ‘s first Premier League title in 20 years last season is viewed as just the start. Coming within a penalty kick of winning their first Champions League trophy came as a gut-wrenching blow – but also a huge motivation. “We share a special bond with Mikel. We are so proud of everything we have achieved since he returned to the club in 2019,” co-chairmen Stan and Josh Kroenke said. “He has a deep understanding of Arsenal ‘s values and carries them in his heart. He knows what this club means to everyone connected to it and is committed to building on everything we have achieved together.” With that in mind, there was never a sense Arteta was preparing to walk away from the team he has built to become one of the best in European football. So with a deal for their manager to stay now agreed, the foundation of Arsenal ‘s recent revitalisation into a footballing force remains in place. Does more history beckon? Arteta is committed to finding out.
